The design jointly shapes the beams and the compression to sharpen sensing of a possible spy while guaranteeing a worst-case secrecy rate for honest users, under power limits. A two-step algorithm based on successive approximation and relaxed matrix methods solves the design. Simulations show it beating simpler schemes such as random beamforming. The work fits future networks that must sense their surroundings and guard privacy at once.
arxiv-2412-09120:
Raphaël Belliard, Vincent Bouchard, Reinier Kramer, and Tanner Nelson widen a recursive machine from mathematical physics, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The machine is topological recursion. It builds all correlation functions of a theory from one starting curve. The widening lets it handle a broader class of quantum curves.

Their extension starts with Airy structures whose partition functions are highest weight vectors of W-algebra representations. Such vectors qualify only under specific conditions on the representation. In the curve picture, the generalization adds extra terms to the basic one-point functions, yielding a shifted version of the recursion. The authors prove the resulting wave functions solve families of quantized spectral curves, complete with correction terms. They also prove the converse: a connection is of topological type exactly when those same conditions hold. The work tightens the bridge between recursion, algebra, and quantization.
arxiv-2412-09220:
Wanjiang Weng and co-authors learn skeleton action features without the negative examples that contrastive methods usually demand, in a 2024 paper. Their framework, USDRL, decorrelates features across time, space, and instances at several grains, squeezing redundancy out so each dimension carries fresh information. A dense spatio-temporal encoder captures fine detail for prediction-heavy tasks.

Older contrastive systems need momentum encoders and memory banks to store negatives, which complicates training. Across four benchmarks, NTU-60, NTU-120, and two PKU-MMD sets, the new approach beat the state of the art on action recognition, retrieval, and detection alike. The authors release code and models for the dense prediction tasks that global features underserve.
arxiv-2412-09320:
Baptiste Claudon, writing alone, presents a simple quantum algorithm in this 2024 paper. Many quantum methods rely on reflections, operations that flip part of a quantum state. A common need is to reflect through the set of states tied to one value of a given operation.

Standard ways to build such reflections use phase estimation or mixes of operations. They scale well with precision and with the gap between values, but they need many extra qubits, and that count grows with both demands. Claudon's method matches that size and depth scaling while needing only a single extra qubit for every case. He expects it to become the standard route for this reflection task.
arxiv-2412-09420:
Axel Levy and co-authors present Hydra, a method for rebuilding three-dimensional protein structures from electron microscope images when the sample is a mixture. The technique freezes proteins and images huge numbers of them, then computes their shapes. Samples often mix several proteins, each bending in its own ways, and older methods assume one kind of molecule.

Hydra models the sample as a blend of several learned fields, one per protein kind. For each image it works out the structure, the pose, the kind, and the shape state together, from scratch. A new loss based on likelihood guides the fitting. The method aims to handle real, messy samples rather than purified ones. That could widen the range of biology open to this kind of imaging.
arxiv-2412-10020:
Federico Girotti and Damiano Poletti study Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups in two thousand twenty-four. These maps model how open quantum systems change over time. They are the quantum kin of a classic process for noisy drift. Each one is set by a drift matrix, a spread matrix, and a shift vector.

The pair pin down which of these maps keep a normal steady state. They describe the full set of such states as well. They also study long time acts, like loss of quantum links to the surroundings. Over time the motion tends toward closed dynamics, and they find the speed. Tests of mean returns and return or drift close the work.
arxiv-2412-10120:
Netzer Moriya solves a geometry problem in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The smallest enclosing sphere is the tiniest ball that contains a set of points. Fast algorithms exist, but they often fail when points form degenerate sets. In three dimensions, such special cases can cause wrong answers, stalled runs, or high costs.

Moriya proposes a hybrid algorithm that keeps linear time overall. It pairs robust preprocessing steps with an efficient core computation. That mix avoids the traps degeneracy sets without losing scalability. Theory and experiments back the claim that degenerate configurations are handled well. Readers in computational geometry get a sphere finder that does not break on awkward inputs.
arxiv-2412-10320:
Robots and game agents often move by stitching together short, physically valid motion pieces called motion primitives. Marat Agranovskiy and Konstantin Yakovlev note that searching over the lattice those pieces create is slow, because each step branches into many options. Their algorithm, MeshA*, instead searches over plain grid cells, as the classic A* does, while fitting valid sequences of primitives into the cells along the way.

The change keeps the guarantees that matter: the search still finds a complete, optimal path when one exists. In tests it ran one and a half to two times faster than conventional lattice-based planning. The authors present MeshA* as a way to keep the physical realism of motion primitives without paying the usual search cost.
arxiv-2412-10420:
Quoc Chuong Nguyen, writing alone in 2024, adds obstacles to the classic Boids flocking model and reads the result with a physicist's tools. Boids, from 1986, flock by three local rules: keep distance, align headings, stay cohesive. Empty space, though, is a fiction; real flocks dodge barriers.

Nguyen proposes two simple extra rules for obstacle handling, then runs Monte Carlo analysis on the physics of the flock: its order, spread, and energy-like measures. The metrics show flocking is not mere habit but a favorable physical arrangement, which helps explain why birds and fish choose company over solo travel. The project reframes a computer graphics classic as statistical physics. Simple rules, honestly measured, still yield insight about collective motion.
arxiv-2412-11220:
Zhenhuan Liu, Yunlong Xiao, and Zhenyu Cai tame a sticky kind of quantum noise in a 2024 paper. Some noise keeps a memory of past states, which breaks the plain tools built for memory-free noise. Such memory noise haunts real quantum chips and dulls both error fixes and error softeners.

Their trick recasts the whole memory-bound dance as one plain noise channel, a view they call the Choi channel. In that view, old channel tools can be used as-is, then mapped back to the chip. The gains and costs of the old tools often carry over whole. Design of memory-noise care turns far simpler.
arxiv-2412-11320:
Anton Pozharskiy, Armin Nurkanović, and Moritz Diehl connect, in a 2024 paper, two mathematical frameworks for systems whose states must stay inside a moving boundary. Such constrained dynamics model contact, friction, and switching. One framework sweeps the state along with the set; the other projects motion onto it.

The authors prove the two agree under stated conditions. Each can be rewritten in a common complementarity form. They then build an accurate step-by-step solver using finite elements with switch detection. The machinery serves optimal control of the systems. Engineers steering robots or power converters through contact events need exactly such reliable simulation.
arxiv-2412-12220:
Xiao Teng, Long Lan, Dingyao Chen, Kele Xu, and Nan Yin match people across normal and infrared cameras without labels. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, works on person re-identification. Night and thermal views make the task hard. With no labels, systems cluster images and treat clusters as truth, but bad clusters inject noise.

Their fix borrows labels from neighboring samples instead of hard cluster tags. Soft labels from near matches cut noise within and across camera types. A weighting module then mutes samples that look unreliable during training. Tests on two standard data sets beat past label-free methods. The approach stays simple, which the authors count as a plus.
arxiv-2412-12420:
Li-Tao Zhu and co-authors hunt shape-shifting galaxies by their color habits. Their 2024 paper develops a simple screen for changing-look active galaxies, whose spectra switch type as their brightness swings, a clue to how black holes feed.

The screen watches color during flares: galaxies that turn bluer as they brighten are suspects. Among over ten thousand quiet-type galaxies in a major sky survey, seventy-three showed the strongest version of the pattern, and thirteen were already known changers. The team observed nine candidates and caught five switching to the bright type. A reverse screen for reddening bright galaxies found no switchers among three observed. The authors plan more follow-ups to sharpen the criteria and chart what sets true changers apart.
arxiv-2412-12520:
Reza Hadadi wrote a 2024 paper on steering large groups of similar systems at once. The catalog title is cut short and the creator field is empty, but the head gives the full title and his name. Such groups, called ensembles, share the same rules but start from different states, like a fleet of drones or a batch of reactors.

Hadadi views the tracking problem through optimal transport, a math field about moving mass at the least cost. That view turns the task of guiding the group into a simpler linear program that computers solve fast. He also sets out what it means for such a group to be watchable and steerable when readings come only at set times. Tests on sample problems back the method.
arxiv-2412-13020:
Nico Föge and co-authors prove a limit theorem for a popular measure of variable importance. Their 2024 paper deals with random forests, a machine learning method in wide use since 2001. Forests can rank how much each input variable matters by permuting it and watching accuracy drop. That ranking is used a lot, but its statistical behavior was little understood. Consistency was known; the shape of its distribution was not.

The team proves a central limit theorem for the measure using theory for a class of averaged statistics. Their setup differs from the standard forest model. The number of trees is random, and conditions are placed on the regression functions and error terms. A small simulation study supports the result. The authors frame the proof as groundwork for future practical testing methods.
arxiv-2412-13120:
Saheed Popoola studies what interns actually do in Google Summer of Code by mining their pull requests. The paper from twenty twenty-four frames open-source work as a bridge between school and industry. Placements are scarce; mentored open-source stints give public, checkable proof of skill. The program pairs new contributors with seasoned mentors on live projects.

The sample spans thousands of interns and projects, with pull requests in the tens of thousands. Most tasks mix code work, like features and bug fixes, with chores like docs and restructuring. Reviewer notes cover function, logic, test coverage, error handling, readability, and best practice. Popoola draws lessons for software education from the mix. Programs like this, the study argues, keep a fresh pool of contributors flowing into open source.
arxiv-2412-13220:
Sudhanshu Shekhar, Bhabani Prasad Mandal, and Anirban Dutta studied in 2024 how relativistic particles cross repeating barrier patterns with a fractal twist. Their tool tracks waves through layered barriers of any chosen repetition order. For spinless particles, they compute how much bounces back and how much passes. The same math then treats electrons in graphene, a one-atom-thick carbon sheet.

Spinless relativistic particles tunneled through barriers in the Klein manner yet reflected more than slow particles would. In graphene, transmission formed resonance series set by barrier count and pattern order, with conductance and noise measures traced as well. Two fractal barrier families showed sharp peaks and near-perfect tunneling in set ranges. The work links abstract potentials to lab-ready graphene devices.
arxiv-2412-13520:
Yi Huang, Fangyin Cheng, and eight peers set out ROMAS for work on stored data sets. The work came out in 2024. ROMAS is a team of language model agents, each with a set role. The agents watch data stores and plan work on them. Such teams are strong at data tasks, but hard jobs with mixed needs can beat them.

Plain agent teams lack habits that men and women use each day. They plan less well, track their own steps less well, and split work less well. ROMAS gives its agents clear roles for watch tasks and plan tasks. That lets the team bend to fit new scenes. It is built for low-code work and one-click setup. It has been placed in DB-GPT, a known open tool that puts language models to work on data stores. The team says role shape cuts waste in free-form teams.
arxiv-2412-14020:
Ronald Schnitzer and four co-authors offered a method for building safety cases for AI-based autonomous systems in a 2024 paper. Such systems lack firm specifications, and their settings are complex, so proving safety is hard. Their landscape method catalogs AI-specific failure concerns in a structured map.

The assurance case then shows, concern by concern, that each is absent or handled. The method builds on earlier calls to analyze and defuse AI insufficiencies as safety evidence. A driverless regional train serves as the test case, showing the map in real use. The authors say the landscape turns scattered worries into an auditable structure. Regulators and builders can both work from the same picture of what could go wrong.
arxiv-2412-14120:
Jérémie Bettinelli, Éric Fusy, and Baptiste Louf build new counting tools for drawn maps in a 2024 math paper. Their objects are flat maps with arrows that fix a sense of flow, plus the tree-like codes called Schnyder woods that encode such maps. Counting these objects by hand is hard, so mathematicians use pairings that grow one object into another step by step.

The team craft such pairings, called growth bijections, for two classes of these maps. Their method cuts a map along a chosen path, slides the parts, and sews them back, then tracks how repeated re-rooting cycles through the set. The pairings give direct proofs of several known counting formulas. The work gives combinatorics a clean, hands-on way to see why the counts come out as they do.
arxiv-2412-14520:
Chihara studies double fibration transforms that have conjugate points in twenty twenty-four. Such transforms include Radon transforms, plane transforms, and geodesic X-ray transforms. They map a function to its integrals over families of curves or surfaces. The normal operator, built by applying the transform and its adjoint, is the object of study.

Under stable conditions on how conjugate points are distributed, Chihara splits the normal operator into parts. One part is an elliptic pseudodifferential operator. The other parts are Fourier integral operators, counted by the degree of the conjugate points. Earlier work by Stefanov and Uhlmann treated geodesic X-ray transforms. Holman and Uhlmann later refined those results by degree. The present work extends the picture to the wider class.
arxiv-2412-14820:
Rodrigo González Escudero, Sougandh Kannoth Mavila, and Jeroen Koelemeij show a way to send a rock-steady light frequency through a branched, passive fiber network to many users. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Each user hops the light's frequency in a code known just to them, in quick steps. On receipt, each user matches the code they get to the one they sent. That match lets them pick out their own signal and shut out the rest. The plan grows how many users the network can serve. It also cuts noise from stray bounce in the fibers, and eases how the system is run. Tests show a steadiness finer than one part in a vast count.
arxiv-2412-15020:
Matteo Quinzi, Tommaso Chiarotti, Marco Gibertini, and Andrea Ferretti hunt for broken-symmetry states in one-dimensional lattice models using many-body perturbation theory. Their 2024 paper solves the Dyson equation fully self-consistently, through an algorithmic inversion method built on sums of poles. The testbed is the one-dimensional Hubbard model, and the approximation is the GW method, a standard way to dress electrons with screening.

With local interactions the method behaves as expected. Adding long-range Coulomb forces sets two ordered states against each other: antiferromagnetism, where neighboring spins alternate, and a charge density wave, where charge bunches in a pattern. The authors also solve a companion equation. It recovers the non-interacting system with the same charge density, and lets them size up a jump in the effective potential that feeds the fundamental gap. In some cases that jump dominates the gap entirely.
arxiv-2412-15420:
Lu Hao and Yuhua Sun study diffusion and equilibrium on weighted graphs, the discrete cousins of surfaces, in this 2024 mathematics paper. Three properties that sound unrelated turn out to be one. They are a graph's resistance to spreading, a uniqueness property for a class of calm functions, and the stiffness of solutions to a paired system of nonlinear equations.

The bridge between them is the graph's Green kernel, whose total size decides all three at once. In a middle range of exponents, the authors add a simple volume-growth test that needs only a floor on how much weight each vertex carries. Under standard regularity conditions, a tweaked graph with an aperiodic random walk gives sharp two-sided estimates of the kernel. Examples on grid-like graphs of polynomial growth show the resulting threshold cannot be improved.
arxiv-2412-15520:
Linh Nghiem, Aidong Ding, and Samuel Wu published this statistics paper in 2024. It concerns data collected under a privacy scheme where noise is added at the source and values are masked by matrix mixing. Under that scheme, no one, not even the data manager, sees the true records. Simple models can still be fit to such data, but logistic regression, a standard tool for yes-or-no outcomes, had no valid method.

The authors build the missing method by leaning on a known link between logistic regression and linear regression estimates. They prove the approach works when samples are large, even as the added noise grows to meet strict privacy demands. Tests on simulated and real data showed their estimates beat the plain approach of running logistic regression on the protected data as if it were clean.
arxiv-2412-15620:
Henrique Oyama and Jun Tani modeled a familiar mental rhythm in 2024: the mind's drift between focus and wandering. They built the model on predictive coding and the free energy rule, using a variational recurrent neural network that perceives steady sensory sequences. The extension adds a meta-level setting that regulates how strongly the model penalizes hardness in its own beliefs. That dial turns out to govern focus itself.

In model tests, shifting the meta-prior between low and high values made autonomous shifts between focused perception and mind-wandering. The switches tracked changes in average rebuild and forecast actions. A single self-adjusting setting generating both states is an economical theory of attentional motion. It suggests mind-wandering is not a failure mode bolted onto perception, but one of perception's own regimes. Such models may inform research on focus disorders.
arxiv-2412-15920:
Gianmario Voria and co-authors propose a study in 2024 on fair data preparation for machine learning. Bias often enters through the data itself, long before a model trains. Fixes applied before training can work but may hurt performance and resist integration.

As a registered report, the paper lays out a planned test rather than final results. Their tool, FATE, will select preparation pipelines that jointly lift fairness and performance. The plan compares those pipelines against standard pre-training bias fixes. The authors argue everyday preparation steps are familiar to practitioners and easier to adopt. The study aims to show whether that friendly route can beat heavier methods.
arxiv-2412-16020:
Daniel Gillies, Andrea Banfi, Adam Martin, and Matthew Lim probe a subtle corner of particle physics in a 2024 paper. They study pairs of W bosons made when two gluons collide at the Large Hadron Collider. New physics, if it exists, may show up through extra terms in the standard equations, sorted by size into dimension-six and dimension-eight groups.

The team cataloged every dimension-eight term that can touch this process and worked out the math for decays into light particles. Their code also applies a jet veto that cuts a huge background. They find the new terms barely stir the results unless the usual ordering of sizes breaks down. They then set fresh bounds on both groups of terms.
arxiv-2412-16220:
Jiaqi Xiong and co-authors infer gene regulatory networks from expression data with a graph neural network built for skewed networks. Their 2024 paper targets a wrinkle most methods ignore: a few genes regulate many targets, and a few targets answer to many regulators. That lopsided degree pattern breaks standard directed graph embedding tools.

Their model, XATGRN, reads interactions through a cross-attention mechanism that weighs gene pairs by context. A dual complex graph embedding then handles the skew, keeping predictions of regulatory links and their direction sharp. Across several datasets the model beat the best existing methods. The authors release their code openly, aiming at wider use in systems biology.
arxiv-2412-16420:
Junyi Ye, Ankan Dash, Wenpeng Yin, and Guiling Wang proposed TextFlow in twenty twenty-four, a two-stage method for answering questions about flowcharts. Flowcharts come as images, and image-aware AI models read them end to end. That leaves users little control and hides where errors arise, in seeing or in reasoning.

TextFlow first turns the chart image into text, in formats like Graphviz or Mermaid that the user can pick. A second stage, a text reasoner, answers questions from that text alone, and the text can even be run as a graph object with tools. Errors can now be traced to the seeing stage or the reasoning stage. Strong language models can be swapped into the second stage. Tests on two flowchart benchmarks gave top scores and steady results.
arxiv-2412-16520:
Hernández, Mateu, and Prat pin down which sets a solution of the fractional heat equation can safely ignore. A set counts as removable when a solution defined away from it extends smoothly across it, as long as the solution stays tame in a set sense. Here the tameness tests are heat-adapted versions of two classic controls on roughness and slope.

To size up such sets, the team builds matching capacity measures: numbers that gauge a set as the heat process itself sees it. They prove these measures match, up to fixed factors, a purely geometric yardstick built from set size and time span. That match turns a hard question about equations into one about shapes, carrying classic capacity theory into a world with memory in time.
arxiv-2412-16720: OpenAI presents its system card for the o1 family of reasoning models in this 2024 report. A system card is the maker's own account of a model release. It records what the system is, how it was tested, and what risks the maker found and sought to curb before and after release. The byline runs to a very long list of staff, which fits the card genre, since safety work spans many teams inside the firm.
arxiv-2412-16820:
A classic formula counts how often each weight appears inside a symmetry representation, term by signed term. Anderson and co-authors study which group moves actually feed that count in a 2024 paper. The answer turns out to have a clean order shape.

The feeding set forms a lower ideal in the weak Bruhat order. Drops within the order never leave the set, in other words. For one key algebra family, the team lists the sets fully. That closes a question posed the same year. Counts for the highest root case come along the way. A finer q-version conjecture waits as next work.
arxiv-2412-17020:
Zhang and co-authors probe a magnetic material's electronic shift with light in a 2024 paper. The kagome magnet FeGe hosts linked charge order, magnetism, and electron interaction. How its bands rebuild at the charge-density wave transition was open. Samples annealed at different temperatures gave unlike cases.

Optical spectra were paired with first-principles calculations. One such sample showed a dramatic spectral shift at the transition. Weight moved from low energy to a higher band, signaling band reconstruction. A sample heated more showed no transition but gradual shifts on cooling. After that shift, the first sample mimicked that gradual pattern. High-energy behavior in both tracked magnetic traits. The team credits distortion of one germanium site for the shifts. It alters iron orbital energies and boosts magnetic moments via coupling rules. The work clarifies charge, lattice, and spin interplay in FeGe, and how each acts on the rest.
arxiv-2412-17620:
Daniel Iľkovič, Jared León, and Xichao Shu study a 2024 random graph game in which a builder buys edges under a tight budget. Edges of a full graph appear in random order, and each must be bought or passed on the spot. Past work set the best budget for building a tree or a single cycle, but graphs with two cycles stayed open.

The team gives a buy plan for the smallest two-cycle case, a near-complete graph of four points with one edge missing, and proves the budget bound is tight. They do the same for fan graphs, where many triangles share one point.
arxiv-2412-17720:
Hernández and co-authors probe the spin waves of a honeycomb magnet with beams of neutrons, in a 2024 paper. The material, YbBr3, is a clean example of a basic quantum magnet model on a honeycomb lattice. Magnets like it can show odd behavior in their excitation spectra even without frustration. The team measured the spectra with plain and polarized neutrons at fields up to full alignment.

At higher fields, broad continua washed out the single magnons, which decayed into other states. Sharp features survived: shadow copies of the magnons appeared beside them, plus a striking dip shaped like a roton. Computer calculations on cylinder geometries matched the data well. The authors offer the match as a benchmark for the marks that strong quantum fluctuations leave on a spectrum.
arxiv-2412-17820:
Martin Guillemaud and co-authors read the geometry of brain networks to forecast whether epilepsy surgery will free a patient from seizures. Their 2024 paper deals with temporal lobe epilepsy that drugs cannot tame. Surgery helps many, yet picking who gains remains guesswork.

Structural and diffusion scans from 51 patients supplied the networks. The team embedded each network, before and after surgery, in hyperbolic space, a curved geometry that fits brain wiring. The embeddings split good outcomes from poor ones. Tellingly, the giveaway regions sat in the hemisphere opposite the seizure source. The forecast scored 0.87 on the standard grading curve. The authors offer the map as a biomarker for surgical planning.
arxiv-2412-18120:
Xiaoyang Hu and Richard Lewis ask whether a language model that fails a memory test misunderstood the test in a 2024 cognitive science study. The n-back task, a staple of working memory research, asks whether the current item matches the one seen a fixed number of steps back. A prominent earlier claim read one model's worsening scores at higher back-steps as a human-like memory limit.

Hu and Lewis probe that interpretation directly, separating task comprehension from memory capacity. The distinction matters wherever human tests are borrowed to grade machines: a low score alone cannot say which ability failed. Their investigation is a caution for cognitive benchmarking of AI.
arxiv-2412-18720:
Gyeongmin Gu, Minseo Jeon, Hyun-Je Song, and Jinhong Jung learn node codes for signed bipartite graphs with a light method called ELISE. Their paper from twenty twenty-four targets link sign prediction: will a tie be positive or negative? Past graph networks wedge in extra same-type edges from balance theory. That bloat invites over-smoothing, noise, and slow runs.

ELISE extends personalized propagation to carry signs through message passing directly. Balance theory is honored with no added edges at all. Embeddings are also learned on a low-rank sketch of the graph, which trims noise and lifts global structure. Real-world tests show better sign calls than rivals. Training and inference both run faster. The design suits e-commerce-style data, where two node kinds meet with praise or blame.
arxiv-2412-19020:
Jorge Zubelli, Kuldeep Singh, Vinicius Albani, and Ioannis Kourakis wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It finds travelling wave solutions of a Harry Dym type equation that grows out of the Black-Scholes frame for option pricing.

The start point is a second-order operator with a shifting volatility term, in the spirit of the Dupire local volatility model. The authors ask what nonlinear evolution law a zero-curvature rule gives for a time-shaped form of that operator. The answer is a variant of the Harry Dym equation. Soliton tools then yield a family of waves that hold their shape as they move. The by-product opens finance volatility study to coherent structures.
arxiv-2412-19120:
Peter Bantay, in a solo paper from 2024, studies the internal structure of two-dimensional conformal models, theories used to describe critical physical systems and string worldsheets. He works within the deconstruction lattice, a framework that breaks a model into simpler pieces.

His focus is the centers of the different elements in that lattice, which encode how symmetries act. Bantay shows that the relationships between these centers can be captured by exact sequences of abelian groups, chains of groups where each map's image matches the next map's kernel. In particular, he exhibits one long exact sequence connecting the centers of higher central quotients. Exact sequences are a standard algebraic bookkeeping device. Here they organize a web of relations that would otherwise be hard to track across the lattice.
arxiv-2412-19220:
Qiankang Wang, DaYun Qiu, and Yi-Lei Tang build a tool for simulating sterile neutrino events at colliders, in a 2024 paper. Sterile neutrinos are heavy cousins of the known neutrinos, and at certain masses they can swing back and forth between forms as they fly. When several such fields sit close in mass, their crossing widths tangle the math. Standard event generators cannot handle that case directly.

The authors give an algorithm that works with ready-made generation tools and prove that it is valid. They also sharpen the theory of the oscillation process inside quantum field theory. The setup can track how far each particle flies before it decays, treating it as an inner line in the diagrams. They add practical tricks that keep the calculations manageable.
arxiv-2412-19720:
Chao Chen, Yu-Shen Liu, and Zhizhong Han wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about making computer models of surfaces sharper. A signed distance function describes a surface by giving the distance to it at each point. Neural networks can learn such functions, but they tend to smooth away sharp edges and fine detail.

The authors teach a method to recover the missing fine detail from a smooth version of a shape. They store parts of the shape as codes that separate smooth form from full detail. That split lets the learned knowledge transfer to new shapes at test time. On standard tests and real scenes, the method gave surfaces that matched the true shapes more closely than recent rivals.
arxiv-2412-19920:
A photograph taken from an odd angle can fool even strong vision models, and Mateusz Michalkiewicz and co-authors measure how unstable today's foundation models are to viewpoint. They define instability as large feature swings from tiny camera moves, and they hunt especially for accidental viewpoints, angles where an object's true shape hides. Nine leading models were probed using their internal features alone.

All models consistently registered accidental viewpoints, but they differed wildly on out-of-distribution angles, sometimes misclassifying by geometric resemblance. The team could sort viewpoints into stable, accidental, and alien classes from features without seeing the images. Tests on classification, question answering, and three-dimensional reconstruction showed the instability's cost. Robustness to viewpoint, they argue, deserves benchmark status.
arxiv-2412-20020:
Federated learning trains one shared model across many devices without pooling their private data, and each device then tailors the model to itself. Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su, and Baochun Li study a flaw in this setup in their 2024 paper. When the shared model is trained by self-supervised learning, its internal picture of the data has fuzzy class borders, so tailored models end up weak.

Their fix, called Calibre, adds a client-specific prototype loss during training and a matching way to merge updates across clients. The goal is to keep the shared picture general enough to be fair, yet sharp enough to be accurate. Across many uneven data settings, Calibre reached top scores on both average accuracy and fairness among clients.
arxiv-2501-00020:
Beibei Li, Yutian Chi, and Yuming Wang set space craft pull field data right with a change form model bound by physics. Gauges from craft are spoilt by craft moves, tool clash, and noise in the zone. Old ways to set data right need long data runs. They need weeks or months of work by hand.

Their model builds bounds from the laws of Maxwell into the net. That lifts both truth and sameness with physics in the data set right. Work that once took weeks ends in a span of hours or less. Calls come in mere ticks of the clock. The show case uses pull gauge data from China's Tianwen-1 Mars trip. The team sets the way out as a frame that scales for trips to worlds to come. It also fits work on space sky states.
arxiv-2501-00220:
Zixuan Yin, Han Sun, Ningzhong Liu, Huiyu Zhou, and Jiaquan Shen present DecoratingFusion in 2024, a network that joins LiDAR and camera data for 3D spotting in self-driving cars. Most fusion tools lean on learned soft links between point clouds and images, which are hard to read and skip firm links.

Firm links from sensor setup guide the hunt for objects here. Image traits paint the point cloud early on, and twin sparse filters pull out the mixed traits. Search seeds start from a center heat map with class tags mixed in. Tests on KITTI and Waymo beat prior tools.
arxiv-2501-00320:
Haibo Tong and co-authors teach artificial agents to act with altruism by imagining others' minds, in work published in 2024. Today's systems chase narrow wins and ignore those around them. That indifference creates safety risks as AI spreads. Human kindness grows from empathy plus imagining an act's effect before doing it.

The team gives agents two linked abilities. One models what others think and feel, in the spirit of theory of mind. The other rehearses actions in imagination and weighs their human cost. Together they let an agent choose considerate moves on its own. The work points toward AI that aligns itself with human values instead of merely obeying rules.
arxiv-2501-00420:
Fangchen Yu and co-authors introduce in 2024 an autoencoder built from a new kind of network layer, aimed at learning better data representations. The layer type puts learnable curve functions on the links between units, which can raise accuracy and clarity against classic designs. Their model folds that layer into the standard squeeze and rebuild design of an autoencoder.

Flexible curve shapes let the model catch tangled patterns and curved links in data. On standard data sets, it beat plain autoencoders and sibling variants on search, sorting into classes, and cleaning noisy inputs, with lower rebuild error. Code is shared. The authors offer the model as a general tool for representation learning.
arxiv-2501-00820:
Robert Vrabel tunes a common control method for curved systems in a 2025 paper. PID control steers many machines, but its best settings are hard to set when a system bends. Vrabel, writing as R. Vrabel in the catalog, works from the head byline.

His plan cuts the curved rule into short straight parts over a set range. Straight parts allow the usual frequency tools that curved systems bar. A swarm search then tunes the control gains by two error scores. More parts bring the copy closer to the true system. Tests show gains found on the copy keep the real system stable and on target.
arxiv-2501-01020: Nobuaki Obata computes a geometric invariant for a well-studied family of networks called strongly regular graphs, in a 2025 paper. The quadratic embedding constant measures how a graph's distance structure bends when placed into Euclidean space. Obata derives an explicit formula for this constant for every strongly regular graph whose second parameter is at least one. From the formula he obtains a clean test: a necessary and sufficient condition for such a graph to admit a quadratic embedding at all.
arxiv-2501-01320:
Jianyi Wang and seven co-authors restore damaged videos of any length with a diffusion transformer. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Real-world video damage is unknown and mixed. Restorers must keep detail faithful across frames. Flicker and drift betray weak methods. Diffusion models are strong but often slow and size-bound.

SeedVR's shifted window attention handles long sequences efficiently. Windows resize near spatial and temporal edges, lifting format limits. A causal video autoencoder compresses the footage first. Images and videos train together, and training grows progressively harder. The result targets generic restoration in the wild. Old broadcasts, phone clips, and archives all fit the brief.
arxiv-2501-02120:
Adam Siegel and co-authors propose moving logical qubits shaped like snakes in a 2025 paper. Silicon spin devices can shuttle physical qubits fast and cleanly. The authors extend that motion to the logical level.

A logical qubit becomes a one-dimensional string on a flat lattice. Defects in the device might scratch a passing string and cause linked errors. Monitor qubits and a gap measure can flag risky moves. When risk appears, the shuttle can be reversed to cancel harm. Snake qubits can also interact with each other. Readers see an architecture that turns motion from a threat into a routing tool.
arxiv-2501-02320:
Sivakumar Namasivayam and Elizabeth Winstanley study a quantum field on anti-de Sitter space in work from 2025. That space is a curved model of space-time used in physics. They look at a scalar field that is linked to the curve of the space.

The pair compute the mean stress-energy of the field for vacuum and warm states. They test three kinds of edge rules at the boundary of the space. Then they check whether two basic energy rules hold. The answer shifts a lot with the mass of the field, its link to the curve, and the edge rule used.
arxiv-2501-02420:
Pranav Nathan and Suhas Jain fix a counting flaw in two-phase flow simulations, in a 2025 methods paper. Such simulations track bubbles or droplets inside another fluid, and users need true volumes and counts. The standard flood-fill count cuts off the fuzzy edge zone of each bubble. That trims real volume and can merge close bubbles into one. The loss also swings with an edge cutoff that users pick by rule of thumb.

The pair add a simple volume correction based on a math estimate of the trimmed part. With the fix, recovered volumes stay near exact across a wide range of cutoff picks. Counts of bubbles and droplets come out right as well. The authors offer the fix as a tool for size studies and for hand-off to particle-based models.
arxiv-2501-02720:
Jiayin He and co-authors ask how much of the Milky Way's gamma-ray glow comes from unseen sources in a 2025 paper. Between ten trillion and a quadrillion electron volts, a Chinese observatory measured more glow from the galactic plane than cosmic ray models predict. One suspect is a crowd of sources too faint to catalog one by one.

From the observatory's first source catalog, the team derived how source counts fall with brightness, without assuming a shape. Extrapolating that trend downward gave the hidden crowd's total glow. In the outer galaxy, hidden sources plus the standard model matched the measured glow within uncertainty. In the inner galaxy they fell short, so extra components are needed there. The authors say unresolved sources are a real part of the story, but not the whole of it.
arxiv-2501-03020:
Mazen Elsaadany, Muhammad Hamza Ali, Amritanshu Pandey, and Mads Almassalkhi re-plan grid load cuts for the new grid in a 2025 paper. When a great fault drops the grid's beat, set cuts shed load by a stock plan to save the whole.

New small power posts and thin spin make that stock plan frail. Past smart plans used a bare beat tale that skips the grid's own wire play. The team's tale is cut down from the full one yet keeps the wire play, caps and all. A fore-see plan then re-sets the cut marks as the grid's state shifts, to shed the least load that saves the beat. On a vast test grid it met the rules where stock plans failed.
arxiv-2501-03120:
Junhong Shen and co-authors cut images into word-like bits by content weight in a 2025 paper. Most image coders use a fixed count of bits per image, no matter how rich or plain it is. Their coder spends more bits on rich images and fewer on plain ones, which saves room with no loss of truth.

A grade rig uses chat models to call each image's load and set its squeeze rate. Trained on mixed squeeze rates, the coder rebuilds images with true form and fine grain. Its stretch bits also train image maker models, which gain from the flex in length.
arxiv-2501-03220:
Following a single point through a long video is hard when the point hides behind objects or the scene cuts. Tingyang Zhang and co-authors propose ProTracker, which mixes two older strategies. Global methods search the whole frame and survive big changes but land imprecisely; local methods refine step by step and stay accurate until they drift. ProTracker uses local optical flow to predict where a point goes and global heat maps, sharpened by probability reasoning, to correct the guess.

The mix brings global scene knowledge together with fine, time-aware detail. In tests the system matched the best optimisation-based trackers and beat supervised feed-forward rivals on several benchmarks. The authors plan to release code and models after publication, aiming at long, dense tracking of any chosen point.
arxiv-2501-03320:
Arghyadeep Paul, Antoine Strugarek, and Victor Réville weigh in 2025 how much of a star world pull's wave power can land as heat in the star's low sky. Such pulls were said to light spots on stars with vast power. Waves ride in from the world toward the star.

A sharp jump zone splits the low sky from the hot crown, and wave speed leaps there. Low tone waves bounce back most there, so less heat lands low. Fluid sims track the pass rate by wave tone. The team then scores the full yield for known spot hosts.
arxiv-2501-03720:
Hegel Pedroza and co-authors built Guitar-TECHS in 2025, a broad data set for machine listening research on electric guitar. Tasks like transcribing guitar audio or copying its tone need training data with wide variety. Small collections limit how robust models become, since guitars, amps, and playing styles differ hugely.

Their data set spans techniques, musical excerpts, chords, and scales, recorded across a diverse array of hardware. That spread teaches models to hear the music rather than one rig's quirks. The authors document the recording plan and contents so others can build on it. Guitar AI has lagged piano and voice work for lack of such data; this release aims to close the gap.
arxiv-2501-03920:
Bacciotti and eight co-authors dissect the wind blowing from a young star's disk in 2025. HL Tau's ringed disk is the emblem of planet birth, yet the rings' origin is debated. The system also fires a two-sided outflow, and its outer layer, traced by carbon monoxide light, was mapped with the ALMA telescope array.

The maps show nested bubbles and arcs that grow and speed up with distance, stacking into a cone-like shape. Rebuilding the flow's geometry reveals shells spinning the disk's way, faster and steeper near the axis. Their launch points line up with three dust rings, suggesting disk winds that carry off spin from the outer disk.
arxiv-2501-04320:
Takuya Morozumi and Tomoharu Tahara work out the odds of a neutrino flipping its handedness when the neutrino is its own antiparticle, in a 2025 paper. Majorana neutrinos, if that is what neutrinos are, break lepton number conservation because their mass term mixes states. That means the lepton number of such a state keeps drifting over time, an effect called chiral oscillation.

The authors derive the flip probability inside quantum field theory. The transition amplitude is the overlap between the lepton-number state when made and that state when seen. A Bogoliubov transformation connects those states at different times, making the math work. The paper also draws out the picture it gives. The result puts chiral oscillation of Majorana neutrinos on firmer ground.
arxiv-2501-04620:
Nikhil Manoj and Sudarshan Kumar build and test a numeric scheme for conservation laws with a jump in flux. Such laws track flows like traffic or fluids, and the flux rule can switch at a point. Solutions may fail to sit in the usual bounded class, which breaks standard proofs. Their scheme is a second-order central method of a known type.

A correction term tied to mesh size tunes the slope limiter in the scheme. The proof leans on compensated compactness, a tool for weak limits of flows. Key steps bound the peak of solutions and show a built sequence packs tight in a weak sense. With those steps, computed solutions settle on the entropy solution. Numeric cases back the theory.
arxiv-2501-04820:
Allison Lahnala and four co-authors build a shared model of extremist traits in a 2025 paper. Online groups can slide into extreme camps through social media, and past work mostly chased one creed at a time. A shared frame that fits many creeds would help spot risk early across the web.

The team mined talk from a range of online forums and pulled out speech marks tied to extreme traits. Their model rests on eleven traits that mark users and whole groups alike. Tests show the traits can flag and forecast drift toward extreme camps, giving a common yardstick for a wide set of groups.
arxiv-2501-05220:
Ziqing Li, Mutlu Cukurova, and Sahan Bulathwela published a 2025 paper on software that writes quiz questions on the topic a teacher actually wants. Automatic question generation could cut teachers' preparation load, but generic generators wander off-syllabus. The authors' method steers generation by topic, so a request about fractions yields fraction questions, at scale.

They fine-tuned a compact pre-trained language model on datasets built for education. Topic control is the added discipline: the model's output must match a specified subject, not just sound like a question. The paper was presented at a learning analytics conference, where the audience tests tools against classroom reality. Automatic generation will not replace teacher judgment, but it can draft the raw material teachers then select and polish. The authors frame the contribution as workload relief with relevance guaranteed. For large courses and question banks, that combination is the practical bottleneck this work attacks.
arxiv-2501-05420:
Xiaomeng Xu, Dominik Bauer, and Shuran Song present a robot that uses its whole body both to see and to handle objects, in a 2025 paper. Most robots manipulate with a gripper while watching from a few fixed cameras. RoboPanoptes spreads cameras across its body surface, giving multi-angle views of itself and its surroundings. Its entire surface becomes a tool: it can lean on objects, use several contact points, and squeeze into tight spaces.

A single learned policy reads all the cameras and directs the whole body, trained from human demonstrations. The system stays robust when individual cameras fail. In tests it unboxed items in narrow gaps, swept several oversized objects, and stowed goods through multi-step routines in clutter. It beat baseline systems on adaptability and efficiency. The authors share video results on a project page.
arxiv-2501-05520:
Haoran Zhao and co-authors propose renting particle tracking as a remote service for collider experiments, in a 2025 paper. Rebuilding the paths of charged particles eats much of the computing at the Large Hadron Collider. Graphics chips speed the work, yet keeping them busy from many machines at once is awkward.

The team wrapped two trackers, one rule-based and one machine-learned, as network services. Many processors could then share the same chips with no added delay per request, and shipping data over cost little. The model points toward the leaner computing the high-luminosity collider era demands.
arxiv-2501-05720:
Akihiro Higashitani, Koji Matsushita, and Koichiro Tani study algebra bases from lattices in a 2025 paper. Khovanskii bases extend a known basis idea for polynomial subalgebras. Hibi ideals, tied to distributive lattices, have a rich theory beside Gröbner bases. The team ask when the polynomials from a lattice form a Khovanskii basis of the subalgebra they generate.

They characterize exactly which lattices qualify, in terms of the underlying posets. Snake like posets, in a generalized sense, and posets avoiding two small patterns get special attention. The answer builds the subalgebra side of the Hibi story. Such bridges let results proved for ideals travel into subalgebra problems.
arxiv-2501-05920:
David Bate, a solo author, studies a class of spaces with measure in a 2025 mathematics paper. A space is called 1-regular if small balls around almost every point grow in measure at a steady linear rate as their radius shrinks. Bate gives a full geometric description of the orderly and disorderly parts of such a measure, based on its tangent spaces.

A stricter class, called 1-uniform, requires the measure of every ball to equal its radius exactly. Bate proves there are exactly three such spaces. The result is a sharp classification: despite the freedom in building abstract spaces, only three examples meet the exact rule.
arxiv-2501-06120: Martin Ehler, Karlheinz Grochenig, and Clemens Karner study geodesic cycles on the sphere in this 2025 mathematics paper. A geodesic cycle is a closed curve that joins finitely many points by shortest paths on the sphere. The authors examine how such cycles serve in equal weight quadrature rules and in approximation, where sums over points stand in for integrals over the sphere.
arxiv-2501-06220:
Wu explores how to design small vision transformers that beat expectations on the tiny CIFAR-10 dataset. Transformers shine on huge datasets but often trail convolutional networks on small ones. The study varies four design levers in a systematic sweep.

Those levers were data augmentation, patch token starts, low-rank compression, and multi-class tokens. Compressing queries in latent attention cost almost no accuracy, hinting at spare capacity. Adding several class tokens strengthened global features and lifted scores. The results form a practical recipe for compact, efficient vision models. Code is posted on GitHub under the PoorViTs name.
arxiv-2501-06520:
A research team defines a new class of matrices by blending two classic generalized inverses, in a 2025 paper. The core EP inverse and the Drazin inverse each extend the idea of flipping a matrix that has no ordinary inverse. Their hybrid, the core EP Drazin matrix, contains all EP matrices and all normal matrices as special cases.

The authors work out the class's basic algebraic properties. They then turn to partial isometries, operators that preserve lengths on part of their space, and derive results about both inverses for them. From those, they extract conditions under which a partial isometry belongs to the new class. Numerical examples illustrate the main theorems. The paper is pure matrix theory, aimed at the community that uses generalized inverses in equations, control, and statistics. A tidy definition, they show, can organize scattered facts.
arxiv-2501-07520:
Eric Van Clepper, Ellen Price, and Fred Ciesla present a 2025 astronomy paper on how dust moves in a disk where a giant planet is growing. Young stars are ringed by gas and dust disks, and a growing planet carves a gap in its orbit. Whether solids can cross that gap shapes what the planet and its neighbors are made of.

The team ran fluid simulations with planet embryos up to three hundred Earth masses, in calm and in turbulent disks. Particle tracking then followed single grains through the flow. Gas falling onto the planet can carry small, well-coupled grains across the gap once the planet passes a threshold mass. Mixing runs both ways. In calm disks, extra pile-ups may preserve distinct chemical reservoirs.
arxiv-2501-07920:
Arthur Correnson and Bernd Finkbeiner give a proof method for traits of systems that span many runs at once. Such hyper-traits can state, for one, that for each run there is a mate run with a set link. Logic for these traits has grown fast, yet proof tools for them lag far behind check tools. Their work takes the hard class where a for-all then a there-is chain wraps a safety link.

Each trait of that class can be matched by a coinductive link, they prove. That match turns proofs into a form many logicians find natural to build. Their tool, HyCo, runs that method inside a known proof aid and is proved sound in full. Case runs on toy reactive code show the flow. The frame fills a clear gap in proof kits.
arxiv-2501-08220:
Tobias Rohe and co-authors test learning based control for satellite links in a 2025 paper. A satellite transponder shares limited power and bandwidth among many links, and setting that mix well is a hard puzzle with many knobs.

No earlier study had tried reinforcement learning on this exact task. The team built a simulated transponder for the agent to practice in. They then compared a leading learning algorithm against simulated annealing, a classic search method that cools random changes over time. The classic method won on this fixed problem. Still, the learning agent came close enough to show promise, and the authors frame the work as a first map of where learning helps in satellite operations.
arxiv-2501-08520:
Ihab Mohamed, Mahmoud Ali, and Lantao Liu present a control method that steers robots around moving obstacles, in a 2025 paper. Their method plans motion by sampling many possible paths and scoring them, a family known as model predictive control. The twist is a chance constraint: paths must keep the risk of collision below a set level, even when sensing and motion are uncertain. The method builds on an unscented sampling strategy that captures that uncertainty well.

Unlike methods that simplify the math by straightening curves, theirs applies the risk limits directly in their curved form. A layered picture of obstacles lets it handle several movers at once in real time. Tests in simulation and in real spaces shared with people showed the method producing safe, feasible paths. The authors offer it as a robust option for robots working near humans.
arxiv-2501-08720:
The black hole at our galaxy's center flickers, and that flicker may test whether Einstein's gravity is the full story. Kotaro Moriyama and co-authors simulated gas falling into black holes that bend the rules a little, in a 2025 paper. Their spacetime model lets gravity deepen or soften against set measures. Limits came from weak-field tests and from the size of the black hole's shadow.

Flows behaved more weakly in the deeper-gravity versions, with slower gas and wave speeds. Light output at the radio band used by the Event Horizon Telescope also shifted in a set pattern. Flicker strength fell as the gravity deepened. The team says future timing data could turn those patterns into a test of gravity itself.
arxiv-2501-08820:
Evgueni Dinvay presents new numerical methods for quantum mechanics in a 2025 paper. The methods rest on a fresh way to express the Laplace operator, a tool that models kinetic energy in quantum systems, through the heat semigroup. Solving the heat equation can be fast in a multiresolution framework, and Dinvay uses that speed as the core advantage.

His wavelet-based approach approximates the operator in a way that stays efficient as systems grow. He tests it on two basic tasks from quantum chemistry: self-consistent field calculations and the time evolution of Schrödinger-type equations. The paper offers a scalable route for computing kinetic energy, a step that often limits larger quantum simulations.
arxiv-2501-08920:
Daniele Notarmuzi, Silvano Ferrari, Emanuele Locatelli, and Emanuela Bianchi build a simulation toolkit for particles with patchy electric charge. Real tiny particles often carry mixed positive and negative regions on their surfaces, so they attract in some orientations and repel in others. Most existing models handle the attraction side well but stumble on directional repulsion, or are built for one material only. The team's model is simple and flexible: each particle holds interaction sites of several types inside its volume, and a pair's energy sums the site-to-site terms.

They coded several versions of the model twice, once in their own Monte Carlo program and once in the popular LAMMPS dynamics package. Comparing the two versions on physical results and on speed shows where each method and algorithm shines. The paper shares optimization tricks for others who simulate such particles.
arxiv-2501-09020:
A team of computer scientists redesigns shared memory pools for server groups in a paper from 2025. A new link standard, CXL, lets servers share memory devices to cut cost. Sharing conflicts with fast server-to-server messaging, and old designs stay small or need costly switches. Their design, Octopus, connects each memory device to only a chosen subset of servers.

Servers are grouped into islands with fast internal links, while islands connect in ways that favor pooling. A three-server hardware prototype ran messages far faster than network or switch rivals. Simulations of ninety-six-server pods showed net cost savings where switch designs raised costs. The authors say sparse wiring, not full wiring, is the way to scale.
arxiv-2501-09520:
Yuxuan Shi and co-authors build a coding system for sending images when the decoder, not the sender, holds a related picture. Their 2025 paper works in the Wyner-Ziv setting, where the shared information between two images can save bandwidth. The catch is that the overlap shifts from pair to pair, and many learned systems break when it does.

Their method first models the simple geometric link between the paired images, a shift and warp, and lets that model drive both masking and rate control. A second network undoes warping damage and channel noise at the far end. Tests on real images show clear gains in sharpness scores over leading methods, which the authors credit to trusting geometry over complex statistics.
arxiv-2501-09820:
Lawrence Scafuri, Dmytro Bozhko, and Ezio Iacocca study waves in a large-scale artificial spin ice in two thousand twenty-five. Their system is a square lattice of bar magnets, each on hinges so it can rotate. Such macro systems mimic the behavior of their tiny, nanoscale counterparts.

Using numerical simulations, they ask what a defect called a Dirac string does to driven waves. Waves lost coherence fast, as they scattered between modes in the system. They also found a distinct mode tied to the lone vibration of the string itself. That mode sits below the band of traveling waves, as expected for a localized one. The results echo edge modes seen in nanoscale spin ices with defects.
arxiv-2501-10020:
Chao He and co-authors present Textoon, a system that turns a written description into an animated 2D cartoon character. Cartoon figures are popular with young audiences, and the Live2D format lets flat drawings move as if they had depth without the cost of full 3D models. Research had focused on realistic digital humans instead. The catalog creator field carries lab affiliations and emails, so the clean head byline governs here.

Textoon pairs large language and vision models to read the user's intent and draw a matching character. The output is a working Live2D figure that can move and react, not just a still image. The team reports that a character takes about a minute to build. Their 2025 report offers the method as a fast route for creators who need varied, lively cartoon characters.
arxiv-2501-10520:
Angelo Bianchi, Adriana Freitas, and Marcelo Veloso coin the tame still group of a drift rule on a polynomial ring, in a 2025 math paper. A drift rule picks how each base part slides under a flow. Its still group holds all tame maps that keep that slide in place, a new lens on such rules.

The team works out that group for set bent drifts in up to three parts. Plain drifts in two parts get the same care in turn. Plain Shamsuddin drifts in any ring size close the set. Forms for the groups fall out in each case.
arxiv-2501-11020:
Congcong Li and co-authors tackle three-dimensional car reconstruction in a 2025 paper. Cars are hard to rebuild digitally because paint reflects light sharply and glass is both see-through and shiny. Standard scene methods blur these surfaces, so the team designs a method tuned to cars, named Car-GS in the paper.

Three fixes do the work. View-dependent primitives model reflections, each primitive gains its own geometry-only opacity for transparent parts, and a quality-aware module leans on a pretrained normal estimator where camera angles face glass head-on. Tests show cleaner surfaces and clear wins over prior methods. The authors target uses in self-driving, virtual reality, and games.
arxiv-2501-11420:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports on the triggers that pick out jets from b-quarks at the Large Hadron Collider. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The collider makes a huge rate of proton hits, far more than can be stored. A staged trigger cuts that rate in steps, down to a level that can be kept.

Jets and event shape cut the rate first. To reach the last low rate, the system must spot jets with b-hadrons in real time, at low jet push. The paper sets out how these tools were built and tuned for the first years of Run three. Gains are large for key cases, such as pairs of Higgs bosons.
arxiv-2501-11720:
Jeff Kim and co-authors build machine learning models that predict whether liver cancer will spread to the lungs, in a 2025 paper. Lung spread is the most common distant site for this cancer and darkens the outlook sharply.

The team trained four model types on a large United States cancer registry. Random forest and a neural network scored best overall, catching most true cases. Yet all models flagged many patients wrongly, so precision stayed low. A custom training goal pushed the network to miss fewer cases, and a combined model caught still more. Surgery status, tumor stage, and follow-up length mattered most among the inputs.
arxiv-2501-11820:
Raihan Khan Akash compares five control plans for holding a DC servo motor at a set position, and ranks them by how cleanly they settle. His 2025 study starts from the motor's role: a closed-loop drive that reads its own position and corrects toward the target. Such motors serve tasks that need both power and precision.

All five plans were built and run in simulation. The set runs from a plain proportional loop up to state feedback with integral action added. Each was graded on overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, rise time, and peak time. The state-feedback plan with integral action won across the board, with zero steady error, the least overshoot, and the fastest settle. The study backs it for work that needs stability and precision.
arxiv-2501-11920:
Albert Mathew and co-authors demo in a 2025 paper a flat surface that passes light unevenly by direction, at ultrafast speed. One way light flow, like a diode for optics, today needs bulky kit. Nonlinear surfaces promised thin versions, but past demos leaned on slow heat or phase change effects.

Their surface uses indium tin oxide near its epsilon near zero point for speed. It works across 1200 to 1300 nm at high incident power levels in the tests. The one way effect spans both brightness and phase of the passed light. That dual reach opens a path to one way wavefront shaping at tiny scales. Response time is ultrafast, a sharp break from the slow routes before it.
arxiv-2501-12220:
Alexandre Nieto, Rubén Capeáns, and Miguel Sanjuán offered in 2025 a simple trick for keeping chaotic systems on their desired attractor: swap a fixed parameter for a memristive function. A memristor's behavior depends on its history, and here a smooth sigmoid-shaped version does the work inside the classic Hénon map.

The idea leans on neighboring attractors with wider basins. The memristive term lures wandering orbits toward the wide basin and hands them over to the target attractor. Simulations showed a substantial widening of the target's basin and sturdier stability. No explicit parameter steering was needed during the run. The authors pitch the method as a lightweight control for discrete chaotic systems. One component, swapped in, does the herding.
arxiv-2501-12320:
Isaac Smith, Elie Wolfe, and Robert Spekkens built a fully quantum version of a causal inference tool in 2025. Causal find asks which network of causes could have made a seen multipartite state. The classic inflation method answers such questions by imagining enlarged copies of the network. The authors lift it into quantum theory, powering it with the quantum marginal problem, the question of which local states can arise from one global state.

Their showcase is the triangle case, the smallest network where the method bites, three parties pairwise sharing sources with no common cause. Using fully quantum inflation they completely classify pure three-qubit states into those compatible with the triangle and those that no triangle network can produce. Further examples treat mixed states, higher-dimensional systems, and when incompatibility of a normal chance spread already certifies the quantum state's incompatibility.
arxiv-2501-12820:
Štefko Miklavič sorts a special family of highly regular graphs whose shortest loop has length six, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The graphs are distance-regular and carry a Q-polynomial structure, terms the author uses in their strict math sense. An older result capped the shortest loop at six for this family.

Miklavič shows the cap is reached in just two cases. One is the Odd graph built on a set sized by the graph span, and the other is a generalized hexagon of a stated order. No other graph in the family attains the bound. Readers in algebraic graph theory get a clean end to a classification question.
arxiv-2501-12920:
Raquel Flügel and four colleagues wrote a 2025 climate paper on the future of Atlantic ocean upwelling systems. Along certain coasts, winds drive deep, nutrient-rich water to the surface. These eastern boundary upwelling systems are hotspots of marine productivity with high economic and ecological value.

Past studies estimated upwelling from surface data, but the IPCC has suggested measuring vertical velocities directly. The authors apply that method to two upwelling cells of the Atlantic in two CMIP6 climate models, HadGEM3 and CNRM. They compare the historical period with a high-emissions future scenario at several resolutions. The spatial pattern of change, not just the average, decides which fisheries and ecosystems face the greatest disruption.
arxiv-2501-13520:
Bakhtin and co-authors test in 2025 whether network centrality measures give fresh insight into microservice software design. Such systems split an app into small services that call each other. Bad shapes, like hub services, are often hunted with graph tools.

They rebuilt the design of 24 open source projects and studied 53 services. Size, complexity, and quality metrics were set against centrality scores for each service. Of 902 metric pairings, about a third showed weak to mid correlation. Ratio based centrality looks promising for spotting named bad shapes. The authors say centrality adds a view that standard metrics miss.
arxiv-2501-13820:
Ian Valimaa and Lasse Leskela set out a block model for sparse multiway data and a grouping method that provably works when data are thin. Multiway data show up in gene work, product advice, and social network study, but they are sparse and large. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The model fits whole number tensors with few entries. The grouping method adds a trimming step to cut noise swings, and the authors find a density line above which it stays correct. Noise is framed in a way that allows heavier tails than the usual case. The model class stays closed when modes are merged, which lets them weigh signal loss against noise cuts.
arxiv-2501-14120:
Esther Villar-Rodriguez and co-authors wrote a reference paper in 2025 on the transfer of knowledge in quantum algorithms. Transfer means reusing what one task taught to speed another, a proven habit in classical computing. Quantum computing, still young, can borrow that habit if the ideas are stated in one frame.

The paper unifies transfer learning and transfer optimization under a single formal notation, bridging two lines that grew apart. It sorts existing strategies into a taxonomy so researchers can place their methods on one map. It then extends transfer protocols to quantum settings, with two new use cases built on reverse annealing and multitasking versions of a standard approximate algorithm. The catalog creator field appends affiliation numbers; the head byline governs. Readers get a shared language for knowledge reuse as quantum methods grow.
arxiv-2501-14420:
Francesco Belli, Eva Zurek, and Ion Errea propose a bonding-based score that predicts whether quantum jiggling of hydrogen nuclei will help or hurt a hydrogen-rich superconductor. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Hydrogen nuclei are so light that quantum motion reshapes the crystal itself. That reshaping can raise or lower the superconducting temperature, or wreck the structure entirely.

Their score comes from a chemical bonding index summed over the crystal. Structures whose atoms sit in symmetric bonding surroundings shrug off the quantum perturbations. Asymmetric surroundings, by contrast, bend under them, and the bending often boosts superconductivity. The catch was that such effects were unpredictable in advance. A cheap descriptor changes screening strategy for new hydrides. Candidates can be triaged before costly quantum simulations. The work targets the hunt for room-temperature superconductors.
arxiv-2501-15320: Sukanta Dutta, Purnath Unnikrishnan, and Yashasvi gauge how sharply a planned muon collider could probe couplings that let leptons change flavor, a process barred in the standard model. They work with an effective frame of six dimension operators. The team computes signal strength at two collider energies, with set data volumes for plain and polarized beams. An optimal observable method reads the shape data to bound errors on the couplings at the one sigma level.
arxiv-2501-15520:
Bhattacharyya, Das, and Mitra build TSOR, a self-supervised system that grades prostate cancer from whole slide images using only slide-level labels. Grading under the ISUP system guides treatment but is subjective and expert-hungry. Gigapixel slides, stain differences between centers, and scarce patch labels all block automation. The core puzzle is learning patch features of Gleason patterns from slide tags alone. Their model pre-trains with a task-specific self-supervised method. Sample diversity is treated as key to that training.

A patch-level dataset was built to feed the pre-training. Ordinal regression then fine-tunes the model for the ordered grade scale. The design aims at efficient grading without hand-marked patches.
arxiv-2501-15620:
Tyushev and co-authors simulate, in a 2025 physics paper, pattern shifts inside a Penning discharge, a plasma held between electric and magnetic fields. An electron beam along the magnetic field keeps the low-pressure plasma alight. The discharge forms rotating structures whose shape depends on the field strength.

Running two-dimensional particle simulations, the team watched the patterns change step by step. At weak fields, multi-armed spirals appeared as confinement improved and the density profile sharpened. Stronger fields replaced the spirals with a single spoke mode. The transitions follow a clear sequence the simulations map out. Understanding these modes matters for plasma devices, where such structures can help or hinder performance.
arxiv-2501-15720:
Eight authors present ESGSenticNet in 2025, a public knowledge base for judging how firms act on environment, social, and governance goals. Firm reports on these goals are long, hard to scan, and often vague or slanted. The base was built with a mix of concept parsing, GPT-4o inference, and label spreading in a ranked topic tree.

The base holds 44,000 knowledge triplets that link acts to the goals they support or harm. Used as a word tool, it beat strong rivals with no training at all. Topic terms scored higher on goal relevance and on action focus by about a quarter to a third.
arxiv-2501-16220:
Mandal, Patwardhan, Patidar, and Vig define in twenty twenty-five a new task: sending a user's plain-language question to the right company database. Large firms store data across many sources, and finding the source that can answer a question is a basic hurdle. Their task assumes each source is a structured database with its own topic and tables.

They built test datasets by extending sets made for turning language into database queries. They tried both large language models and vector-based methods, with and without task training. Language models scored higher but struggled with long inputs. Trained vector methods gained most when sample questions per database were plentiful. More sources, close topics, and vague questions all made the task harder.
arxiv-2501-16320: Alessio Cela and Alberto Landi compute algebraic invariants of moduli stacks in twenty twenty-five. Their series concerns Prym pairs, objects in the geometry of curves. This first paper works with hyperelliptic Prym pairs. It computes the integral Chow ring for pairs arising from a single pair of Weierstrass points. It also handles up to a stated number of pairs when the genus of the curve is odd. The Chow ring encodes intersection data for the stack.
arxiv-2501-16920:
Can and co-authors derive flow equations for a workhorse setup in lattice studies of quantum chromodynamics. The field simulates quarks and gluons on a space-time grid. Many grid spacings are now available, so how results scale between them matters.

Their equations suit a 2+1 flavor setup with clover-improved fermions. Combined with pion mass and gradient flow data at five spacings, the equations let the team study scaling directly. The work was presented at a lattice conference. Scaling checks separate real physics from grid artifacts. The catalog record names only the last author; the paper itself lists seven. Technical talks like this keep big simulations honest.
arxiv-2501-17220:
Oren Ironi and co-authors test the rule that links a star's birth mass to its white dwarf remnant mass, inside pairs of stars about one orbit apart. Their 2025 study uses cluster binaries spotted by a space survey. Companion pull lets them weigh the dead star directly.

Thirty-three main-sequence stars held likely white dwarf partners, and twenty-six yielded birth masses. Two odd groups emerged. Some dwarfs are too light, shaped by a giant-phase swap with the partner. Others lost more mass than the rule allows. The rest stay murky, and some may hide triple systems. The authors say pair life bends the single-star rule strongly. Far-ultraviolet follow-up is the next step.
arxiv-2501-17720:
Yuwei Zhu and Paolo Barucca model networks where links fire over time and excite each other. Their 2025 paper uses Hawkes processes, which let one event raise the odds of the next. Snapshot views of such networks throw away the order of links and their pull on each other. Their model adds community structure plus wide gaps in node activity.

That mix captures clusters with lone loud influencer nodes beside quiet ones. Fit scores beat earlier continuous-time models by a steady margin. The model also spells out how influencers and communities trigger each other directly. The authors say that detail maps activation chains in real systems, from social feeds to finance.
arxiv-2501-17820:
Buldağ, Jacelon, and Kwietniak prove that a weak form of predictability in a dynamical system forces its well-behaved behaviors to fill the whole space of possible ones, in a 2025 paper. The system is a space with a transformation applied over and over. Its invariant measures describe long-run statistics, and the ergodic ones are the pure, unmixable cases. The vague specification property, a loosened version of a classic gluing property, says orbits can be approximately shadowed and combined.

The team proves density of the ergodic measures by embedding the system into a shift space of two-way infinite sequences and approximating it with simpler subsystems built from near-orbits. Each approximating system has the strong classical specification property, so its ergodic measures are dense. Careful distance arguments then carry that density through the limit to the original system. The approximation method, the authors note, should be useful elsewhere.
arxiv-2501-18120:
Giacomo Marocco and John Wheater explore in 2025 whether flat magnetic materials could serve as detectors for spin linked dark matter. If dark matter couples to the spin of electrons, it could scatter in a magnet and excite magnons, which are waves of the aligned spins. A material whose spins link only within a plane would react in a direction sensitive way.

Such layered magnets have response patterns that vary with direction. As Earth turns, the rate of excitations would rise and fall with the sidereal day. The team computes the expected signal for several candidate magnets, both of the aligned and the opposed kind. They target light dark matter, from thousands to millions of electron volts in mass. A daily rhythm would be a strong sign against background noise.
arxiv-2501-18520:
