Seamus Albion proves, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a family of character factorization formulas that unifies several known results in the theory of symmetric functions. Symmetric functions encode the characters of many symmetry groups. Certain operators on them, one for each integer, act on basis elements in a way that splits neatly by a partition's core and quotient parts.

The classic result says the action vanishes when the core part is nonempty, and otherwise factors into a product indexed by the quotient. Newer work extended the pattern to the symplectic and orthogonal groups. Albion embeds all of these in one infinite family, using a general symmetric function and an asymmetry parameter for partitions. The proof rests on a fresh characterization of cores and quotients for those asymmetric partitions. Unifying separate formulas into one frame usually exposes the structure that made each of them work.
arxiv-2501-18620:
Ping-Rui Tsai and four peers find that shots obey the same count laws as speech and text. The work came out in 2025. The shots are first turned into sign-like bits by a trained net. Shots hold much of what men and women sense each day. Like speech, they turn raw sense flow into shaped form.

Led by sign-ground thought, the team treats shots as goods built from sense flow. They run trained nets on shots and note which core bits fire. From that they pull bits that act like words in a text. Those bits heed Zipf's law of word rates. They heed Heaps' law of word-list growth. They heed Benford's law of first digits. The laws show up on their own, with no signs built into the rig. The find hints that such count laws may mirror sense flow itself, not just speech.
arxiv-2501-18720:
Vertex algebras are math structures that grew out of physics, packing endless lists of operators into one tidy frame tied to a curve. Colton Griffin stretches that frame in a 2025 paper. Instead of one coordinate, his version allows many at once, as if the stage were a higher-dimensional shape rather than a line.

The new objects are built from the shape of spaces that track curves, swapped in for the old punctured disk. Griffin proves core facts about how they behave and sets out the stronger form that adds a vacuum and grading. Standard examples carry over, from a basic field pair to the algebras named after Heisenberg and Kac-Moody. The frame then supports a reduction step that mirrors a known route to a famous family of algebras.
arxiv-2501-18820:
Ying Li and co-authors wrote a 2025 survey that maps the field of automated vulnerability repair. Software flaws are common, and fixing them by hand is slow. Auto repair tools promise to patch code on their own, across both lab made and real world flaws.

The survey sorts past methods into four families: template guided, search based, constraint based, and learning driven. Bench tests across data sets weigh the strengths and limits of each family. Learning methods shine in narrow cases but lack deep grasp of program logic. Hard flaws strain all families. The authors close with trends and open paths for the field.
arxiv-2501-18920:
Yacine Chitour and six co-authors settle a long-open question in a branch of geometry where motion is allowed only along set paths. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In sub-Riemannian geometry, curves must follow a restricted set of directions. The open question asked whether the shortest such curves are always smooth.

The team shows the answer is no. They build a concrete case where the shortest curve is only twice smooth, not three times. The underlying setup is as clean as can be: its rules are given by plain polynomial formulas. That makes the counterexample hard to dismiss as a quirk of rough data. The result tells geometers that shortest paths in this world can hide corners of a subtle kind. It closes a question that had stood for years.
arxiv-2501-19020:
Red light chips lag their blue and green kin, and the gap is a physics puzzle. The authors, a five-name team writing in 2025, simulate how charge moves through the red chip's stacked wells. Three quirks share the blame in their model: pits in the crystal face, uneven alloy mix, and leak paths along flaw lines. In blue and green chips the pits help by giving charge a side door in.

In red chips that door barely cuts the start voltage, and the math still calls for more volts than labs see. Leak paths fill the gap: stray charge slips in early, pools in the wells, and screens the inner walls that block flow. The same leaks waste some charge as heat near the flaws. The team map the trade and point to build tweaks that keep the gain.
arxiv-2501-19320:
Xavier Crean, Jeffrey Giansiracusa, and Biagio Lucini wrote a work in two thousand twenty-five on data shape in gauge theories. Their field is quantum chromodynamics, rules of the strong force. A claim ties the lock-in of quarks to how magnetic monopoles act. Some work hints at a second shift of state at higher heat.

The three use topological data analysis, maths tools for the shape of data. One such tool is persistent homology. With it, they count how loops of these poles change across the shift out of lock-in. They first try the tools on a test case, compact U(1) lattice gauge theory. Checks at distinct sizes gave the known key value for that shift. They then use the same tools on SU(3) gauge theory. There the key value came out more true than with usual heat ways, with the same data.
arxiv-2502-00620:
Yihao Xue, Jiping Li, and Baharan Mirzasoleiman studied weak-to-strong generalization in two thousand twenty-five. In that setup, a weak model teaches a stronger one, and the strong model can still beat its teacher. The setup mirrors how people might one day guide systems smarter than they are.

The authors explain the effect with the inner features that weak and strong models build. Those features define a space of what the weak model cannot learn but the strong one can. Projecting labels onto that space shows how far weak teaching holds the strong model back. Their measure also predicted real results on molecule tasks and five language tasks.
arxiv-2502-00820:
Behrooz Montazeran and Ullrich Kothe show that partly trained generative models can spot out of distribution inputs as well as fully trained ones. Likelihood based models often assign higher scores to foreign inputs than to their own training data, a flaw that hurts trust. A recent fix scores inputs by the pattern of gradient sizes across model layers.

Training a model to full convergence is slow and costly, so the authors test models stopped early in training. Across model types and image dataset pairs, these immature models match or beat mature ones on the detection task. The finding reshapes views of how such models learn their data distribution. It also offers a cheaper path to a useful safety check.
arxiv-2502-01220:
Hichem Ammar Khodja and co-authors stress-test language models on facts that hold only for a set span of time. A model may know a fact yet fail to match it with the right years. Their 2025 study built a data set called TimeStress, which asks models to tell right time frames from wrong ones. Errors were sorted by how far the wrong frame sits from the true one and by frame size.

Eighteen models were tested. The best model separated right from wrong frames perfectly for only eleven percent of facts. Rare but serious errors appeared that a person would not make. The authors say time sense stays a weak point in current models.
arxiv-2502-01420:
Essl and co-authors probe in 2025 why some physics solvers settle on a false answer for systems of many electrons. Such self checking methods are a main tool for strongly linked materials. In those hard cases, the solver often converges, but to a state that cannot be real.

The team derives the math rule for when the true state stays stable in the solver. That rule links false settling to a split valued core function, though false settling can occur without the linked warning signs. They end with a step by step way to hold the solver on the true state. The work has clear use for groups that model strong electron systems.
arxiv-2502-01820:
Hesameddin Safari and Henning Wessels present fast models for heat in laser based metal printing, in a paper from 2025. In this printing method, a laser melts powder track by track to build a part. Knowing the heat pattern helps makers tune the process and cut cost.

Their models blend physics rules with neural networks that learn from data. One design handles single tracks, and a step by step version handles many tracks, where training gets harder. Checks against a standard math method showed good match. With the fast model, the team could study how scan paths and laser settings shape the heat history of a part, without running slow full simulations each time.
arxiv-2502-02020:
Yijia Zhao and Qing Zhou tackle trial-and-error learning in systems where causes form a hidden web, in a paper from 2025. The head title frames the work as causal bandits over unknown graphs. A bandit problem asks a learner to pick the act with the best payoff while still probing options. Here the graph of causes is not known at the start.

Their method mixes watched data with results from live trials. From both, it picks sets of factors that can cleanly reveal the effect of each act. Those sets feed bounds that guide the next pick. Proofs bound how much payoff the method loses over time, with weaker growth than plain bandit methods. The frame also stretches to cases with hidden common causes. Test runs show far lower regret than rival methods.
arxiv-2502-02420:
Clemente Smarra uses the steady ticking of pulsars to hunt for ultralight dark matter in this two thousand twenty-five conference paper. Millisecond pulsars are superb natural clocks, and tiny shifts in their pulses can betray unseen fields sweeping through the galaxy.

Working with data from the European Pulsar Timing Array, Smarra first treats particles that interact only through gravity. In that case the array can rule out their making up more than a few tenths of the dark matter in the studied range. He then considers particles that also couple to ordinary matter. There the pulsar bounds improve on existing limits by several orders of magnitude. The work shows how astronomy's best clocks double as particle detectors.
arxiv-2502-02720:
Muhamad Felemban, Abdulrahman Almutairi, and Arif Ghafoor design, in a 2025 paper, a risk-aware way to place virtual machines in cloud data centers. Tenants share the same hardware, and careless neighbors can leak data across the walls. The authors treat the leak risk as a cost to be managed when each new virtual resource is assigned a home.

They measure how sensitive each data set is with two information scores, then weigh those profiles against the known weak points of the cloud stack. The placement task becomes an optimization problem, which they prove NP-complete. Two shortcut heuristics follow, tested in simulation on centers holding data of mixed sensitivity. The paper aims at operators who must serve many tenants without letting sharing turn into exposure.
arxiv-2502-02820:
Lucia Quirke and Nora Belrose study how neural networks learn in a 2025 paper. Networks tend to pick up simple patterns in data first, then move to subtler ones. The pair ask what happens when those simple patterns are surgically removed from the model's internal signals.

They derive a new erasure method, QLEACE, that strips out all information about a concept that can be read from squared features. A simpler linear method reliably slowed learning. The quadratic method's effect varied: it slowed feedforward networks, but cleverer designs found ways to use extra injected information. Some near versions of the method even sped learning, acting like extra training data. The results show how strongly simple features steer early learning.
arxiv-2502-02920:
Briti Gangopadhyay and co-authors split ad budgets across channels with a learning method, in work from 2025. Good splits drive campaign gains, yet public data and test worlds for this task are scarce. Classic bandit methods also stall when markets shift fast, since they adapt too slowly.

The team built a simulator that replays logged real campaign data over long spans. Their method pairs a saturating reward curve with targeted search and a change-point alarm. It filters regions by domain sense and adapts as markets move. Math checks and tests on real campaigns showed higher rewards and lower regret than rival plans.
arxiv-2502-03020:
Nortier, Dobson, and Battiston put forth a size mark in twenty twenty-five for short paths in nets where links can join more than two nodes. Such nets, called hyper-graphs, fit group acts that plain nets miss. How their links shape reach was not well known.

They read a range of real hyper-graphs, with and without time change, next to shuffled fakes. Group links oft sit at the core of the shortest paths and keep the net whole. Pair links still tie the fringe nodes in, most in nets that shift in time. The split gives a more fine view of net build.
arxiv-2502-03220:
Four authors tackle language bias in cross-language job search in 2025 from a hiring platform view. Resume and post text must be read as a whole, yet past tools split the parts and lose reach across a full file. Their joint encoder learns many text parts at once in a dual frame.

The small model beat top rivals on match scores in the tests run by the team. A new bias score based on curve distance shows marked bias cuts and stronger cross-language work. The gains matter for fair hiring search across tongues and for shops that serve mixed markets, the team argues.
arxiv-2502-03620:
Mikael Møller Høgsgaard wrote this 2025 theory paper on PAC learning, a frame for asking how well a program can learn a rule from examples. Recent work by Hanneke and by Larsen produced learners with the best known sample use. Both, though, lean on a step that picks the rule with the least error on the training data, and their cost tracks the cost of that step.

Høgsgaard asks whether that link to the error-picking step can be loosened. He shows that an optimal learner exists which trades the cost off in a different way. Readers in machine learning theory get a fresh angle on what makes such learners costly to run, and on where gains in speed might come from.
arxiv-2502-04320:
Alec Helbling and co-authors show that image diffusion transformers already hold sharp maps of where named ideas sit in a picture, in a 2025 paper. Their method, ConceptAttention, rebuilds the model's own attention parts to point at text concepts, with no extra training. A key trick is projecting in the attention output space, which yields far crisper maps than the usual cross attention route.

On a standard segmentation test, the method beat fifteen rival zero shot tools and took the top score. It works across popular image models and carries over to video generation. The authors offer it as first proof that such models transfer well to vision tasks.
arxiv-2502-04820:
Ruben Strässle and co-authors present a solver that computes compressible gas flow from kinetic theory while conserving mass, momentum, and energy. Their method splits the Boltzmann equation's velocity space into steps, uses two particle groups near balance, and refines its mesh where the flow demands detail, in parallel.

Careful refluxing at coarse-fine mesh borders keeps the conservation laws exact. Validation was extensive in scope and detail. The solver recovered the behavior of the Euler and Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with correct, frame-independent wave speeds across a thousandfold temperature range and speeds up to Mach one point eight. It matched reference solutions on shock-tube and Riemann benchmarks up to Mach three point two. Adaptive refinement cut computing cost and memory four- to ninefold on two-dimensional problems, with overhead capped near thirty percent. The authors offer the solver for supersonic flows with sharp discontinuities.
arxiv-2502-05120:
Paweł Weichbroth interviews experts on what makes mobile apps hard to use. His paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from a gap in the evidence. Apps bring big gains to people and firms, yet real-world usability flaws are poorly mapped. Twelve practitioners took part in structured interviews for the study.

Five top trouble spots stand out from their answers. They span how content is organized, screen design, speed, touch patterns, and looks. The paper then names five paths for future work. They include AI-driven apps, layered-reality apps, and mixed input modes. Personal app ecosystems and access for all users complete the list.
arxiv-2502-05220:
Balakrishnan Dharmalingam and co-authors spread language models across a drone fleet for safer missions in a 2025 paper. Drones on critical work need tight, secure links to ground stations, and a single model is a bottleneck and a target.

Specialized models split the jobs, guessing, anomaly spotting, and forecasting, and live aboard the drone, at the edge, and in the cloud. Tests show strong task scores and stiff defense against cyber attacks. The split design lifts both smarts and resilience over one model setups, the team report, setting a bar for guarded drone work.
arxiv-2502-05720:
Benomar and co-authors (2025) close a gap in the theory of a classic trading problem. In one-max search, a trader watches prices arrive one by one and must accept exactly one, for good, trying to land the highest. Modern versions give the trader a prediction of what is coming. Good algorithms should do well when the prediction is right, stay safe when it is wrong, and shift smoothly between the two. Earlier methods could not manage all three at their best.

The authors present the first algorithm that hits the optimal trade-off between consistency and robustness while varying smoothly as prediction error grows. They then extend the analysis to settings where both the prices and the prediction carry randomness. The work rounds out the learning-augmented theory of the problem.
arxiv-2502-05920:
Frederic Koessler, Marco Scarsini, and Tristan Tomala study how a designer can steer outcomes in games with a vast crowd of small players. Their 2025 paper uses direct information structures, where players get advice and follow it. The setting covers shared-resource games such as congestion and Cournot markets.

Main results give full implementation for games with a strictly curved potential in each state. Any target outcome with finite support and rational play shares can be forced as the sole stable result. With a weakly curved potential, all stable outcomes share the same total payoff. Even outcomes with endless support or irrational shares can be matched closely. The work widens what information design can guarantee.
arxiv-2502-06520:
Mondal, Mukherjee, and Pramanik work out how a key simplification step changes the algebra of discrete Morse theory, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. That theory shrinks a geometric complex to its essential cells, making homology, the count of holes, far cheaper to compute.

Cancelling a pair of critical cells reduces the work further, but it scrambles the paths the computation follows, forcing a costly recount. The authors derive an explicit formula for the new boundary operators directly from the old ones, and show it matches a sequence of elementary row operations. They obtain the matching result for coboundary operators as well. The shortcut removes the recounting step from a routine operation in computational topology.
arxiv-2502-06720:
Lykiardopoulou and co-authors weigh, in a 2025 paper, sodium and magnesium atoms at the edge of a shell map. The N=20 shell was long thought closed and firm; near it, odd forms bloom, the island of inversion. Fine mass reads from TRIUMF's TITAN rig set the weights of sodium 31 to 33 and magnesium 31 to 35. The mass of sodium-33 grew sharp by over a hundred fold in truth. A flash-lived twin form of sodium-32 showed in the runs as well, a fresh find.

Bind force for the shell dips at magnesium-32, then leaps for sodium-31. That leap hints the shell gains strength toward oxygen-28, past the drip line. Fresh first-rule math reads clash with the weights in ways that raise new asks.
arxiv-2502-06820:
Zhekai Du and co-authors present a fine-tuning method for large models in a 2025 paper. Low-rank adapters are the standard cheap way to adapt a model, but their simple form can cramp what the adapter can express. The new method, LoCA, works in the frequency domain instead, placing learnable parts at chosen spots of a cosine spectrum.

Theory shows picked frequency parts can out-express low-rank forms. A finite-difference trick finds the best spots during training. Tests on language and vision tasks gave stronger results per parameter while keeping compute near the standard method. Readers get a sharper adapter for model tuning on a budget.
arxiv-2502-07020:
Maximiliano Castillo and co-authors apply network science to mixed martial arts in a 2025 study. They treat each UFC fighter as a point and each bout as a link between points. That view lets them track how matchmaking changed over time and how it shapes fame and crowd interest.

Early UFC cards reused tight clusters of fighters again and again. Later cards spread links more widely and picked fights with more care. Fighters who won often stayed near the centre of the network. Fresh, spread-out cards also linked to stronger pay-per-view sales and search interest. The authors note that official ranks match network fame only in part.
arxiv-2502-07120:
Outlining a colon tumor in 3D scans guides radiation and prognosis, and the fashionable tools for it borrow long-range sequence machinery, transformers and Mamba blocks, to see the whole volume at once. Abhishek Srivastava and co-authors question in 2025 whether that global reach is needed. On their new 204-case dataset they pit such models against MambaOutUNet, a network built for strong local interaction.

The local model won. For small, anatomically tangled targets like colorectal tumors, rich neighborhood detail beat long-range context. The authors suggest segmentation research rebalance toward the local, at least where the quarry is compact.
arxiv-2502-07320:
Tai Huy Ha and Takayuki Hibi prove a bound in graph theory in a 2025 paper. A graph is a web of points joined by lines, and its connectivity counts how many points must be removed to break it apart. They study chordal graphs, a family where every long loop has a shortcut line across it.

The pair focus on chordal graphs where no single point touches all the others. Using tools from algebra that track how equations depend on each other, they prove such a graph can only be so strongly connected. The cap depends on the number of points in a precise formula. They then build, for every allowed value, a graph that hits exactly that level of connection. The result closes the question for this family of graphs. Both the proof and the building method are part of the contribution.
arxiv-2502-07720:
Martin Ehler builds hybrid designs on spheres in a 2025 math paper. A spherical design is a set of points on a sphere chosen so that averaging a polynomial over the points gives the exact average over the whole sphere. The idea was later extended from points to curves traced on the sphere. Clear examples of design curves, though, are rare.

Ehler constructs design curves for small degrees from the edges of special convex solids. He then defines hybrid designs that mix points and curves, reaching exact averaging for higher-degree polynomials. The constructions rest on corners and edges of paired dual solids and on the symmetry of those solids. One hybrid design reaches degree nineteen, a notably high mark for an explicit example.
arxiv-2502-07820:
Jeon, Rhe, and Ko squeeze brain tools for store-math chips in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such chips do the math in store, which cuts the haul cost of big tools. Clip cuts shrink tools too, yet force spare parts and tangled flows.

Inside, a rank cut keeps flows smooth with no spare parts in the plan. Two snags dog rank cuts: idle chip ranks and grade loss in the split. A shift-and-twin map fills idle ranks with twin work in their build. Group cuts on bent tools then mend the grade loss from the split. Tests show big pace gains or grade lifts gainst clip cuts.
arxiv-2502-08220:
Gerrit Behner, Abdur Rehman Jalil, Detlev Grützmacher, and Thomas Schäpers measure a one-way supercurrent in a topological junction in a 2025 paper. A Josephson diode passes current more easily one way when time and mirror symmetries both break. Topological insulators supply strong spin-orbit coupling, one ingredient, for free.

Their junctions sandwich a bismuth antimony telluride layer between niobium contacts. With a sideways magnetic field, the critical current differed by direction with efficiency up to seven percent. The current-phase curve was not a clean sine and carried an anomalous phase shift. The team credits a ballistic surface current, a signature of the topological surface states.
arxiv-2502-08520:
Daria Grigorash and co-authors sharpen an open-source model that predicts how chemicals mix, by handling a force it had slighted. Their 2025 paper improves openCOSMO-RS, a thermodynamic model used across chemical engineering. Dispersion, the weak attraction between all molecules, is added through atomic polarizabilities, the ease with which each atom's electron cloud deforms.

The team compares ways to scale and combine the data into segment-to-segment energies, testing on halocarbon systems. The new term beats the group's earlier attempt while needing fewer adjustable parameters. Better mixing predictions ripple into solvent choice, separations, and process design wherever this free model is used.
arxiv-2502-08620:
Michael Douglas and Kyu-Hwan Lee ask whether machine learning can help find new math structures in this 2025 article. Their approach, which they call mathematical data science, studies math objects in bulk rather than one by one. It builds data sets of objects and runs learning experiments on them.

After an overview of the method, the authors give two case studies. One concerns murmurations in number theory. The other concerns loadings of partitions, tied to numbers used in representation theory and combinatorics. In both cases, learning tools surfaced patterns that reward a second look. The authors present the approach as a new way to explore mathematics with data.
arxiv-2502-08920:
Antonin Brun and co-authors test whether chat agents that sense user mood change how folks judge service. The work dates to 2025. Chat agents now fill much of help-desk work. They oft lack both the warmth and the skill of real staff.

Thirty users met a mood-aware agent and a flat one in set runs. Mood checks on user text helped read how each talk felt. Users rated the mood-aware agent as more apt to trust and more skilled than the flat one. Fix rates for the help task did not split by kind. The team weighs what warmer agents could mean for aid services.
arxiv-2502-09220:
Van-Giang Trinh and co-authors present 2025 results on when a logic program has regular models, and how many it can have. Regular models are a kind of three-valued model that keeps the unknown share as small as it can be. The team reads the program's dependency graph, the map of which rules lean on which, for signs that settle the question.

Three main results come out of the graph checks. One gives a needed trait for a program to hold a model that is truly three-valued, not just two-valued. One gives a trait that is enough to force a single regular model. Two bounds cap the count of regular models based on sets that break all positive loops in the graph. The proofs lean on a bridge to Boolean network theory.
arxiv-2502-09320:
LEDs beat most light sources, but shaping their glow for a room or a street usually takes bulky extra lenses. Poulsen and co-authors shape the light with a flat metasurface instead, one designed by the rules of non-imaging optics rather than by forming a picture. They lay out the theory, build a numerical tool that computes the surface's phase pattern, and fabricate a test piece.

Measurements of the sample showed the promised beam shaping works outside the computer. Numerical experiments then probed how good the design method is and where it strains. The authors frame the work as a bridge between two fields that rarely meet: non-imaging optics, which herds light rays, and metaoptics, which sculpts waves with nanostructures. Flat shapers like this could slim down lighting products for both steady and flickering sources.
arxiv-2502-09520:
Francesco Pezone, Sergio Barbarossa, and Giuseppe Caire present a smarter image compression method in a 2025 paper. Their system is built for communication where what matters is meaning: a machine at the other end needs the scene's content, not every pixel. It first maps the image's semantic regions with ready made software, then encodes mainly the parts that matter for the task.

A new masking module, trained with class importance weights, selects the relevant features before quantization and reconstruction by a generative network. The method works at the source only, so it stays compatible with existing systems. At extremely low bit rates it beat standard and learned codecs on picture quality and on how accurately the rebuilt image could be segmented again.
arxiv-2502-09720:
Semyon Savkin and co-authors present NestQuant, a compression scheme for large models in a 2025 paper. Shrinking models after training is key to cheap deployment. Their method rests on nested lattice codes with a self-similar shape.

Theory shows such quantizers are optimal for low-precision matrix products. A practical version uses the Gosset lattice for low complexity. Weights, cached keys, and activations can all be compressed. A large Llama model was squeezed to four bits per value. Quality loss stayed small on a standard text benchmark. Readers learn a math-first route to smaller, faster models.
arxiv-2502-10120:
Xinfeng Zhao and Yaoru Sun redesign how a vision transformer, in a 2025 preprint, cuts an image into patches. Vision transformers split pictures into tiles and reason over the tile sequence. Deeper models and bigger images make that cost explode. The tiling step is blind too: it ignores what the image shows. Their module, CI2P, compresses the image first and builds the tile sequence from the compressed form.

The new module drops into models in place of the old patch step. It cuts the number of tiles fed to the attention layers to a quarter. On a dataset of animal images, a model trained from scratch with CI2P beat the standard baseline by over three percent in accuracy. It also used about sixty-three percent fewer operations, and training ran twice as fast on the same hardware. The authors credit the compression stage's sense of local structure.
arxiv-2502-10420:
Elija Perrier and Michael Timothy Bennett argue, in a position paper published in two thousand twenty-five, that language model agents should not be treated as ordinary agents. These systems are increasingly deployed to act on their own, dealing with people and tools across industry, society, and government.

That deployment rests on shaky assumptions: that the agents hold steady goals, adapt across settings, and act with something like intent. The authors say the underlying models carry built-in flaws, including hallucination, jailbreaks, misalignment, and plain unpredictability. Scaffolding such as external memory and tool access does not cure the core issues. The agents remain stateless underneath, random in their outputs, and touchy about exact wording. The paper lists these pathologies of agency one by one. Treating such systems as normal agents, the authors warn, undercuts their usefulness and the trust placed in them.
arxiv-2502-11020:
Jafar Isbarov and co-authors build a test set in a 2025 paper for language understanding in Turkic languages. Big test sets exist for major languages, but Turkic languages have been left out or tested through rough machine translation. Translation can warp grammar and culture, so the team wrote questions in the native languages from the start.

Their benchmark spans eight Turkic languages and eleven school subjects at middle and high school level. A smaller, hand checked subset is released with scoring scripts for public use. The team ran many leading models on the set and compared scores by language, subject, and alphabet. The results show where models still lag on these languages and give builders a fair yardstick.
arxiv-2502-11120:
Zi-Fan Wang, Jie Jiang, and Jing-Xiu Wang revisit a puzzling pattern in the sunspot cycle using a map built from observations. Their 2025 paper studies the Gnevyshev-Ohl rule, the old claim that an even-numbered solar cycle is followed by a stronger odd one. Later work found the rule in varied and conflicting forms, with rival physical stories behind it.

Their iterative map suggests a broader truth: any cycle is statistically more likely to be followed by a stronger one, whatever its number. That tilt comes from the map's own lean away from the diagonal. Over spans like the historical record, the classic rule and its reversal can each appear by chance.
arxiv-2502-11220:
Justin Yeakel simplifies food web dynamics to two states for each species, high or low. Counts of wild species are often unknowable, above all for tiny, hidden, or dead species. Classic models track exact counts, which can hide the role of web shape. His model sets each count by the balance of food from below and hunting from above.

Across model webs, hunting pressure from above drove most cycling in counts. Species high in the web faced the most risk of staying low. Short-cut links, where top hunters eat low prey direct, buffered shocks and changed loss patterns. Yeakel argues the stripped model can sit beside classic ones to expose how web shape drives stability.
arxiv-2502-11420:
Yingqing Guo and co-authors steer image and molecule makers without retraining them, in a 2025 paper. Diffusion and flow models build outputs step by step, and users often want to push the result toward a goal. Common steering tools need smooth, math-friendly goals, which rules out many real aims, such as rules that pass or fail. The team's method, TreeG, grows a tree of candidate paths at each step and keeps the best.

TreeG proposes options, scores them, and prunes the weak, all in parallel. Three flavors of the method cover smooth and rough goals alike, for both smooth data and symbol-like data. Tests on music, small molecules, and DNA stretches beat the best older steering tools by wide margins. Gains grew as more compute went in, a scaling pattern the authors chart for future work.
arxiv-2502-11820:
Katharina Ring and Michael Schomaker build a diagnostic for a silent flaw in causal studies in a 2025 paper. Causal estimates need positivity: every treatment level must plausibly occur for every kind of person studied. With continuous treatments, violations are common and rarely checked. When one is found, the usual advice is to change the question, the estimand, with little guidance on how.

Their diagnostic shows, person by person, how well the data can support a given estimand, before any model is fitted. Simulations map how treatment policies behave as violations deepen, and where bias should be expected. A drug study in children with HIV illustrates the tool in practice. The authors aim it at applied researchers who must defend their estimand. It answers both whether trouble exists and how to retreat to safer ground.
arxiv-2502-12120:
Prasanna Mayilvahanan and co-authors ask what drives the links between training loss and task loss in language models, in this 2025 paper. Such links help builders guess how a model will do on real tasks from its training scores. The team varied many parts of the training setup.

One factor stood out above the rest: the training data itself set the trend. Model size, tuning choices, the text splitter, and even the basic design, whether transformer or state-space, had little effect. The authors advise builders to spend care on choosing and cleaning training data first. Other choices can then be tuned freely for speed and cost.
arxiv-2502-12220: Darryl Holm and Oliver Street wrote a 2025 paper that extends a model of ocean surface waves. The Green-Naghdi model tracks long waves in shallow water. The authors derive a thermal form of the model from a symmetry based variational principle. Their version adds a sea floor that shifts over time, the full Coriolis force from Earth spin, and uneven thermal buoyancy in the mixed layer. The form suits future study of waves kicked up by changes to the sea floor shape.
arxiv-2502-12320:
Atalay Donat and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on robot learning that joins two kinds of sight. One kind gives a 3D cloud of points, which captures shape well. The other gives flat color images, which carry texture and meaning that point clouds miss.

Past fusions pasted image traits onto points and lost the wide scene context. The new method, FPV-Net, feeds both wide and local image tokens into the point cloud coder by way of adaptive scaling. Tests on the RoboCasa bench, a hard set of home tasks, showed the limits of each sense alone. The fused method set the best scores across all tasks in the bench.
arxiv-2502-12420:
Fine-tuned copies of one big language model can be merged into a single model, but flat merging treats every parameter as equally worth keeping. Shuqi Liu and five co-authors present Sens-Merging in a 2025 paper, a method that weighs parameters by sensitivity before blending. It works as an add-on to existing task-vector merging methods.

The method scores how much each parameter matters inside its own task, and how well that importance carries across tasks. Those scores set the merging coefficients, parameter by parameter. On Mistral and LLaMA2 models, the merged results improved across general knowledge, math reasoning, and code writing. In code tasks the merged models even beat the single-task specialists they were built from. The authors also chart the trade-offs between the two kinds of scaling.
arxiv-2502-12720:
Francisco Brito and co-authors explore, in a 2025 cosmology paper, whether a modified theory of gravity can match what telescopes see of the early universe. Their model joins a scalar field to a gravity law that depends on both curvature and the trace of matter.

The team shows that the usual smooth potential in such models fails to fit the Planck satellite data from 2018, and a wider family of potentials fails too. The fix, they argue, lies in a middle-strength coupling between the scalar field and gravity. In that in-between regime, the model's predictions for the young universe's growth spurt line up fully with the data. The paper narrows where this theory can live.
arxiv-2502-12920:
Thomas Lee and four co-authors present ELF, a light mechanism that adapts time series foundation model forecasts while they are running. Their paper came out in 2025. Foundation models are large pre-trained models, but they are usually frozen after deployment because retraining them live is too costly.

That freezing wastes the feedback arriving as new data comes in. ELF adds a small forecaster that learns the current data pattern directly. A second component, a weighter, blends the foundation model's forecast with the small forecaster's output. Across a suite of standard datasets and several recent foundation models, adding ELF always improved performance. The work shows that even cheap use of online feedback can lift forecast quality.
arxiv-2502-13020:
When lead nuclei collide at the Large Hadron Collider, the spray of particles called a jet ploughs through a droplet of quark-gluon plasma and loses energy. The CMS Collaboration measures a subtle property of such jets: the angle between two definitions of the jet's axis, built by clustering its particles in two different ways. Data from 2018 lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV anchor the study.

Across collision geometries and jet momenta, the angle distributions narrow as collisions become more head-on. That narrowing may reflect the plasma reshaping the jet's insides, or the colour charge of the jet's source changing how it loses energy. Because the measurement reaches kinematic ground not probed before, the authors present it as a sharp new test for models of jet quenching and its dependence on colour charge.
arxiv-2502-13320:
Zixin Zhao and co-authors present a 2025 study on whether writing software truly fits what creative writers need. Digital tools for writers have multiplied, from draft apps to AI helpers. The authors asked writers directly about their process, then mapped the tool landscape against those needs.

They analyzed survey answers and Reddit discussions from a writing community. In parallel they reviewed 115 tools and 67 research papers. Research tools cluster on the drafting act itself and slight the planning stage before writing starts. Visualization support also proved thin. The authors distill ten takeaways for future tool builders. The paper gives a current, whole-picture account of how software shapes the act of writing.
arxiv-2502-13520:
Khalid Elmadani, Nizar Habash, and Hanada Taha-Thomure present a large new corpus for grading how hard Arabic texts are to read, in a 2025 paper. The corpus holds 69,441 sentences and more than a million words. Each sentence is labeled by hand on a fine scale of 19 levels, from kindergarten to graduate study.

The set was built to balance genre, topic, and audience, and a large team of annotators labeled every sentence. Agreement between annotators was high, which supports the labels' quality. The authors also test automatic grading methods at several levels of detail. They release the corpus, its labeling guide, and the test results openly for research and teaching use.
arxiv-2502-13620:
Bingnan Zhang upgrades a classic particle tracking method with a neural network, in a 2025 paper. The Woodcock method follows particles through absorbing material by sampling fake collisions, and its acceptance rate is usually held fixed. Zhang lets that rate vary from place to place as an unknown function, then trains a neural network to represent it.

The network's training target is the method's figure of merit, which it must maximize; the network in effect solves the equations that define the best rate function. On a one-dimensional test with a bell-shaped absorption profile, the tuned method scored far better than both the fixed-rate and original versions. Zhang notes that extending the idea to three-dimensional voxel models remains open work.
arxiv-2502-13820:
Aleksander Ficek, Somshubra Majumdar, Vahid Noroozi, and Boris Ginsburg evaluated synthetic verifiers for code and reasoning in 2025. Such verifiers, from generated test cases to reward models, are a common way to push coding skill in language models past fixed tests. They also sit at the heart of recent gains in reasoning from reinforcement learning.

The team turns existing coding benchmarks into scoring and ranking data sets that can grade the verifiers themselves. They propose several metrics for different sides of verifier quality. Four new benchmarks are released, and methods are analyzed across standard, reasoning-based, and reward-based models. Early results show reasoning can sharply improve test case generation. Readers get a way to check the checkers before trusting them to train the next model.
arxiv-2502-14120:
Damiano Paniccia and six co-authors model a helicopter shaft engine's behavior with machine learning trained on real flight data. Such engines are complex heat systems that work in shifting air and flight states. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Exact physics models of the engine are hard to build due to its tangled inner workings. Learned models can track non smooth behavior and give live gauges of output. The team trains varied neural networks to predict engine torque for a named prototype craft. Training data came from a broad set of real test flights with many moves and flight states, which gives a full picture of how the engine acts.
arxiv-2502-14220:
Qingcai Jiang, Buxin Tu, and Hong An present a 2025 chip design paper on memory access for near-data processors. Such chips compute beside the memory to dodge the traffic jam of big data work. They still need virtual memory to stay easy to program. The standard four-level address map, though, costs too much here: lookups flood in and the small top cache can not hold the map entries.

Two fixes form their design, NDPage. Map entries skip the top cache, which speeds their reads and keeps real data in place. The map's last two levels merge into one flat layer, cutting lookup steps while keeping small pages. Tests weigh the gains. Tailored maps could make near-data chips fit real systems.
arxiv-2502-14620:
Xinghan Pan asks if the RWKV language model can give useful sentence embeddings with no fine-tuning at all. RWKV is known for its linear attention method. That method scales in a way that differs from standard transformers. Pan asks what sense of likeness between sentences its hidden layers hold in a zero-shot setting.

The study looks at embeddings layer by layer from a trained RWKV model. Scores are gauged on the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus with Spearman correlation. The base for contrast is a GloVe-based model. RWKV embeddings catch some sense of likeness, but they do worse than the simpler GloVe base. Pan also times how fast the model runs and how much graphics memory it uses. The results say RWKV's linear scaling gains do not yield embedding quality on their own.
arxiv-2502-14720:
Florian Krause and seven co-authors thread optical fibers into battery cells to watch their temperature, in a 2025 paper. Heat inside a lithium-ion cell is hard to track, yet it drives both safety and aging.

Their method sends light along a glass fiber and reads how it scatters, giving temperature at every point along the fiber at once. Standard fiber sensors report only at fixed spots. The glass is barely affected by electric fields, so it can sit inside a cell. Between 0 and 80 degrees Celsius the reading was linear and sharp, with detail down to a few centimeters. Early tests show that building the fiber into a real cell does not spoil the readings.
arxiv-2502-14820:
Luis Antonio Gutiérrez Guanilo, Mir Tafseer Nayeem, Cristian López, and Davood Rafiei teach language models to write product reviews from spec sheets. E-commerce runs on structured product tables plus specific customer questions, yet lacks tailored data sets for training. Their new data set captures detailed attributes and user-specific queries from real online retail. The task built on it turns a table into an attribute-focused review.

Fine-tuned models were judged by standard table-to-text metrics and by correctness, faithfulness, and fluency checks. Results showed substantial gains in contextually accurate generation. The authors credit the pairing of a domain-specific corpus with deliberate fine-tuning. Generic models, however versatile, stumble on retail's particular blend of facts and persuasion. The work argues e-commerce language tasks deserve their own benchmarks, not borrowed ones.
arxiv-2502-15120:
Yen-Che Hsiao and Abhishek Dutta hunt for the size where language models start to reason in this 2025 paper. They tested a range of decoder-only models, from small to large, on common-sense and logic questions. A clear pattern emerged around a threshold size.

Models above roughly one and a half billion parameters did far better at step-by-step reasoning, above all on long chains like proof by contradiction. Smaller models caught up partly after fine-tuning on worked examples, at least for short chains. Maps of the models' internal attention showed that correct reasoners focus more on the right upcoming words. The study links size, training, and inner focus to reasoning skill.
arxiv-2502-15520:
Matteo Buzzegoli presents a 2025 physics paper working out how spin polarization behaves in a hot, swirling relativistic fluid. Such fluids, born in heavy-ion collisions, carry both flow and spin, and recent theory tries to fold the two together. Buzzegoli uses linear response theory to organize every effect that can appear at first order in the fluid's gradients.

The list covers ordinary flow gradients plus two newer players, an axial chemical potential and a spin potential. Each effect gets a Kubo formula tying it to microscopic correlations. Most dissipative contributions, it turns out, need a chiral imbalance or parity-breaking interactions. With that imbalance, a spin Hall style effect appears: heat and particle gradients push spin sideways.
arxiv-2502-15820:
Yusuke Hayashi and Koichi Takahashi argue that a universal AI would naturally chase power, in a 2025 theory paper. They connect AIXI, the classic model of optimal learning agents, with empowerment, an intrinsic drive to keep future options open. In the self-predicting version of the agent, one known term of its objective reads exactly as a variational empowerment goal.

Planning in such agents can also be recast as shrinking expected free energy, the principle behind active inference, blending goal pursuit with curiosity. Power-seeking then appears not just as a route to reward but as a direct pull toward states of high control. The authors offer the link as groundwork for debates on AGI safety.
arxiv-2502-16120:
Zhehao Li, Yanchen Wu, and co-authors reframe a classic estimation problem through a modern loss function, in a 2025 paper. Inverse optimization works backward: given the choices a decision maker made, infer the hidden costs or goals that explain them. Real observations are noisy and often less than perfect, which breaks older methods or slows them badly.

The team connect the problem to the Fenchel-Young loss, a tool built for predicting structured outputs. That link yields a method trainable by plain gradient steps, far faster than earlier solvers. Theory backs the estimates, and tests on simulated and real data show gains in accuracy of the recovered goals and in the quality of later decisions.
arxiv-2502-16320:
Ali Shirali and co-authors study in 2025 how to align AI systems with human tastes when tastes differ across kinds of users. Standard practice assumes one shared reward function, yet real preferences vary. The team splits users into types and probes what the single taste assumption costs.

They show that one policy for mixed tastes is best built from the average reward across types. That, though, needs extra facts about who gave which feedback. With even a little of that information, direct alignment methods gain a first order boost. With full feedback from each type, the optimal policy can be learned steadily. Yet no method learns it both steadily and with few samples, a surprising limit. The results guide how feedback should be gathered.
arxiv-2502-16820:
Tiejin Chen and five co-authors present a 2025 method for measuring how unsure a large language model is about its own answers. Knowing when a model may be wrong matters most in high-stakes fields such as health care and finance. Older methods judge doubt by how alike the model's answers are in wording, which misses what the answers claim as fact.

The new framework draws several answers to one question, then uses helper models to pull out the facts inside each. It builds two maps of likeness, one for wording and one for facts, and blends them with a tensor method into one doubt score. The split keeps word changes apart from fact changes. In tests, the method flagged shaky answers better than prior tools, which the authors offer as a firmer base for trusting model output.
arxiv-2502-17120:
Hamidreza Mazandarani, Masoud Shokrnezhad, and Tarik Taleb design a smarter way to share radio power among camera drones covering an area. Their 2025 paper looks ahead to 6G networks linking air and ground systems. Instead of pushing raw bits, the drones send meaning, and power should follow the value of what each drone sees.

Their learning method rewards agents for the quality of the areas they observe. Several drones decide power together in a distributed way, each learning from shared feedback. Simulations showed the approach beat both classic bit-focused learning and fixed rule-based schemes. The authors argue it also scales as drone counts grow, a key need for future networks.
arxiv-2502-17420:
Tom Wollschlager and co-authors mapped in 2025 how language models refuse harmful requests, looking inside the model geometry. Safety training can be bypassed by crafted inputs, and the inner reasons are poorly understood. Past work pointed to a single direction in the model inner space that drives refusal.

Using a new gradient method, the team found many independent refusal directions, and even multi-dimensional cones. Lying at right angles in space did not by itself mean two directions act independently. So they define a stronger notion that counts nonlinear effects too. Under that notion, several refusal paths are truly separate. Refusal, they conclude, is run by complex spatial structure, not one switch.
arxiv-2502-17620:
John Bodenschatz and Daniel Rowe presented a software package for simulating brain scan data in two thousand twenty-five. Functional MRI records blood-flow signals tied to brain activity. Researchers need tools that can generate realistic fake data to test methods and learn the physics behind the signal.

Their package, SHAKER, is written in MATLAB and centers on k-space, the raw frequency domain where MRI data are first collected. A graphical interface lets users enter scan parameters and receive simulated complex-valued time series with ease. The authors aim to deepen understanding of the MR signal equation and how simulated data are built and read, for neuroimaging researchers and students.
arxiv-2502-18020:
Joshua Sakthivel Raju and four co-authors shrink a multilingual AI model in a 2025 paper. Big language models are hard to run where computing power is scarce. Shrinking them often hurts languages with little training data. The team focused on five African languages.

Their student model learns from a larger teacher in two ways. It copies the teacher's answers and also matches its attention patterns. The result, AfroXLMR-Comet, is over eighty five percent smaller. Languages covered include Swahili, Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, and Kinyarwanda. The small model kept most of the teacher's accuracy in tests. The authors offer the method as a path to usable AI on modest hardware. That matters for schools and services across Africa.
arxiv-2502-18420:
Yiyuan Chen, Jonas Helsen, and Maris Ozols price out what it would cost a quantum computer to simulate a famous toy model of strongly interacting particles, in a 2025 paper. The model, called SYK, is a stand-in for black hole physics and quantum gravity in the lab of theory. Simulating its motion over time is done by slicing time into small steps, a method whose error and gate count the authors bound carefully.

Building on recent work, they bound the slicing error for first-order and higher-order versions of the recipe. The resulting gate counts sit close to the best possible, given how many terms the model has. Simulating one fixed starting state turns out cheaper still, by large factors. They also price the sparse version of the model, which drops most terms at random. The results tell builders of quantum simulators what SYK will demand of their machines.
arxiv-2502-18720:
Zhi-fu Chen and Luis Ho ask how often quasars show gas absorption tied to their own galaxy, sorted by radio age, in a 2025 paper. Jets from a quasar push gas outward, and that gas can block light at a magnesium fingerprint. The team merged four sky surveys into a sample of 3,141 radio loud quasars, of which 418 showed the absorption.

Older quasars, judged by their radio spectrum shape, showed the lines far more often than young ones. The oldest style beat the youngest by about seventy percent in rate. The authors explain it as jets spreading expelled gas over wider ground with time, so more sight lines cross it.
arxiv-2502-19020:
Marcin Hoffmann's paper from 2025, printed with a Polish title, tackles serving clusters in future 6G networks. The design in view is an open, user-centric cell-free web, where many access points jointly serve each user instead of one tower owning them. Picking which points form each user's cluster is a core hard problem. Hoffmann proposes an algorithm that splits the work between two layers of network apps, one near-real-time and one slower.

In simulations, the method lifted the median user throughput by sixteen percent over the standard network-centric design. The paper is short, so it states the setup and the gain more than it dwells on proof. It speaks to engineers shaping open radio networks, where cluster choices set both speed and cost.
arxiv-2502-19120:
Ricardo Reyes speeds up time-dependent simulations by detouring through the Laplace transform. Solving an evolving equation at full size, step after step, is costly. His method first transforms the problem into a steady one that depends on a complex parameter. A set of sample solves at chosen parameter values then forms the raw material.

A compression step distills those samples into a small basis of representative shapes. The time problem is then solved inside that tiny space with any standard stepping scheme. Hardy space theory, through a classic theorem, justifies the swap. It implies the compressed basis is accurate to an exponential degree. Tests on several evolution equations measure the speed and error in practice. The work offers model reduction a new, frequency-first route.
arxiv-2502-19220:
Silpa Babu, Sajan Lingala, and Namrata Vaswani rebuild dynamic MRI scans in twenty twenty-five. Dynamic MRI captures moving anatomy, but fast, accurate reconstruction is hard. Methods often need tuning for each application, sampling scheme, and rate. The team wants one algorithm that works across many settings without such tuning, and with low latency.

They call that property generalizability. It is possible, they argue, only with simple models and simple algorithms. Their models split the signal into a low-rank part plus a sparse part. Two approaches are developed, one based on alternating gradient descent and one on alternating minimization. Both rest on few parameters by design. Readers get reconstruction methods meant to be accurate, fast, and portable across dynamic MRI uses.
arxiv-2502-19420:
Alfred Carasso and Andras Vladar (2025) adapt a sharpening method from telescope images to electron microscope pictures. The method undoes blur without knowing the exact blur shape, a task called blind deconvolution. It works when the image's frequency pattern falls in a smooth, convex way, though it cannot fix blur from bad focus. The authors assume the blur follows a Linnik probability curve. They fit its settings to the prepared microscope image by least squares.

Sharpening then walks backward through a logarithmic diffusion equation in frequency space. The best result usually appears partway back, not at full reversal. Tests on scanning electron and helium ion microscope images showed real gains in crispness. The process needs a user who knows microscope images and can search the settings by hand. The authors present it as a practical tool for nanoscale imaging labs.
arxiv-2502-19520: Cristian Ciulica, writing alone in 2025, studies which complex sub-shapes can live inside Endo-Pajitnov manifolds. These spaces generalize a classic family of complex surfaces to higher dimensions. Whether they contain compact complex curves was open in general. He identifies a class of them that does contain compact complex submanifolds. He also gives an algebraic condition under which no compact complex curves exist. Both directions together map where such curves can and cannot sit.
arxiv-2502-19920:
Marco Pleines and five colleagues train a deep reinforcement learning agent to play Pokémon Red, the classic Game Boy role-playing game. The game is a demanding testbed for agents. It requires multitasking, long horizons of tens of thousands of steps, hard exploration, and choosing among a vast array of potential policies.

The team introduces a simplistic environment and a training methodology, producing a baseline agent that completes the opening segment of the game through Cerulean City. Ablation experiments reveal vulnerabilities in reward shaping, where agents learn to exploit specific reward signals instead of playing well. The authors also discuss limitations of the approach. They argue that games like Pokémon hold strong potential for future research on large language model agents, hierarchical training algorithms, and advanced exploration methods. Source code for the environment is publicly available.
arxiv-2502-20320:
Azuka Chiejina, Subhramoy Mohanti, and Vijay Shah present a network framework for machine-centric applications in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cameras and sensors now offload tasks like plate reading and vehicle tracking to remote servers. Legacy networks were built for human users and handle these shifting machine demands poorly.

Their framework, ACCORD, runs a feedback loop between the application and the network. It first builds context from device ability, user movement, and channel state. A learning controller then tunes settings across several network layers in real time to meet each task's quality needs. Tests with a standard 5G simulation toolbox showed the design works and uses spectrum better.
arxiv-2502-20420:
Shaharukh Khan and a ten-author team wrote a 2025 paper describing Chitranuvad, their system for translating English into Indic languages with images in the loop. Multimodal translation uses a picture to disambiguate text, a help for captions and low-resource languages. Their entry competed in a shared task at the Workshop on Asian Translation 2024.

The system pairs a multilingual language model with a vision transformer. Image features are extracted, then projected through an adapter into the language model's space as visual tokens. Translation is generated step by step from text and image together. The team entered all three tracks: captioning, text-only, and multimodal translation into Hindi, Bengali, and Malayalam. They took state-of-the-art results for Hindi on every track's challenge set. Performance stayed competitive for the other two languages.
arxiv-2502-20620:
Ayana Niwa, Masahiro Kaneko, and Kentaro Inui fix wrong answers from language models by editing what the models believe. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Models can reason well yet still land on false answers. The authors blame hidden false beliefs: claims the model treats as true inside, which quietly steer its reasoning off course.

Their method first asks the model to explain its answers, hunting for the beliefs behind right and wrong replies. A beam search works forward and backward to surface those beliefs. Then a forgetting technique dims the false beliefs while boosting the true ones. On several question sets, past mistakes were corrected without hurting overall scores. The fix also carried over to unseen data, which hints at a general cure.
arxiv-2502-20920:
Jigyasa Watwani and colleagues ask how the shape of a cell's boundary steers the patterns its inner scaffolding makes. The actomyosin cortex, a living layer of fibers and motors, generates mechanochemical patterns that drive cell behavior. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team studies a hydrodynamic model of that layer. They build a Galerkin analysis framework that works far from the calm linear regime, on domains of any shape. On a circular disk, the analysis predicts a switch. Weak active stress and turnover give uniform patterns; stronger values break them into directed ones.

Explicit numerics confirm those nonlinear bifurcations are real. Bending the disk with harmonic deformations then shows the patterns answer to boundary curvature too. The resulting layouts resemble cells grown on micropatterned substrates. Geometry, the authors conclude, is a genuine control knob for cellular patterning.
arxiv-2503-00120:
Ali Ahmad Khostovan and a large team of co-authors release a vast catalog of spectroscopic redshifts for the COSMOS field, a well-studied patch of sky. A redshift measures how far a galaxy's light has been stretched, and so how distant it is. The catalog gathers about twenty years of measurements from many telescopes and instruments.

The compilation holds 487,666 redshifts for 266,284 distinct objects, drawn from 138 observing programs. It reaches out to redshift 8, when the universe was very young. Color and star-formation patterns show the catalog is rich in low- and mid-mass star-forming galaxies, plus heavy quiet galaxies at lower redshift. The authors test the catalog by checking photo-based distance guesses against it. They also map which kinds of galaxies still lack spectra, to guide future observing. The catalog will grow with later releases.
arxiv-2503-00220:
John Duchi revisited in 2025 a basic promise of conformal prediction: that its confidence sets should hold not just on average but for the case at hand. The paper gives fresh arguments for how split conformal methods nearly hit their target coverage with high probability, judged on the validation data itself rather than in expectation.

It then turns to group-conditional coverage, where the set must cover for patients, places, or classes of interest. Running quantile regression on held-out data, Duchi shows, gives guarantees that are optimal in the minimax sense. Experiments round out the picture with a warning: efficient, valid conditional methods are still unfinished business. The note is short but sharp. It separates what is proven from what is merely hoped.
arxiv-2503-00520:
Shinji Mukohyama, with Kazufumi Takahashi, Keitaro Tomikawa, and Vicharit Yingcharoenrat, studies ripples around black holes in a modified theory of gravity. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In this theory, a scalar field fills space and changes with time. Some black hole solutions hide the field almost completely, which makes their ripples hard to compute.

A known fix adds a small extra term that keeps the math well behaved. The team focuses on the simplest ripple type, a uniform breathing of the hole. With a smart choice of coordinates, the scalar ripple splits off from the ripples of space itself at leading order. That split is a key step toward full equations for all ripple types. Those equations would let tests of gravity use real black hole signals.
arxiv-2503-00920:
Brandon Kaiheng Tay, Saumitra Kapoor, Wenwei Yu, and Shao Ying Huang present a radio sensor that reads blood sugar without breaking the skin. Their 2025 paper joins a transmission line with split ring resonators, shapes that focus electric fields. The finger itself acts as part of the sensor.

Blood sugar changes the electrical traits of blood, which shifts the sensor's reflected signal at set frequencies. The design was tuned in simulation, then built and tested on sugar solutions across the normal body range. It was also tested on a human subject. In both tests, the signal peak moved in a near straight line against sugar level, in reverse direction. A painless, needle-free reader could ease daily life for people with diabetes if accuracy holds up.
arxiv-2503-01520:
A team of detector researchers tested how silicon sensors heal after radiation damage, in work published in 2025. The sensors are being built for a new calorimeter in the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. That machine will shine far more brightly than before, so its parts must survive strong neutron doses. Small test diodes on the new eight-inch wafers served as the test pieces.

The team exposed diodes to neutrons at a reactor in Slovenia, at thirteen dose levels. They then measured how much charge each diode could still collect while it was held warm, a step called annealing. The tests used an electric pulse method to read charge flow. Results helped the group judge whether thicker sensors can work in the harshest zones, and how much healing to expect during planned shutdowns.
arxiv-2503-01820:
Yi-Lin Sung and co-authors shrink large language models by teaching the compression which tokens matter. Their 2025 paper improves layer-wise quantization, which rounds a model's numbers down to fewer bits without retraining. Earlier methods treated every output token equally when fitting each layer.

Their recipe, RSQ, first rotates the model to tame outlier values, then scales each token's features by its importance, measured by attention or dynamic cues, and only then quantizes. Important tokens thus dominate the fit. The finding is intuitive once stated: a compressed model should spend its limited precision where the meaning concentrates, not spread it evenly over filler.
arxiv-2503-02120:
One of the brightest X-ray sources in a nearby galaxy has gone quiet, and its star may have collapsed without a bang. André-Nicolas Chené and co-authors report fresh X-ray and optical views of NGC 300 ULX-1. The source flared in twenty ten as a fake supernova, then fed at extreme rates for years. New data show the feeding has dropped below that extreme level. The partner star's light has also faded by more than two and a half magnitudes since it was classed as a red supergiant.

The team blames the donor star's fast evolution and swings. One bold option is that the donor silently collapsed into a black hole. That would make the pair a newborn black hole and neutron star system. The case shows how fast such binaries can change face.
arxiv-2503-02320:
Takahisa Igata reframes the strong bending of light near a photon sphere in terms of local matter. In round, still spacetimes, photon deflection blows up in a logarithmic way near that sphere. Old formulas price the blow-up rate with coordinate-bound metric parts. Igata instead uses coordinate-free geometry plus the matter sitting at the sphere itself.

Einstein's equations turn that into one compact formula. Local energy density plus tangential pressure at the sphere set the rate. When the two cancel, the rate takes the universal value one. A scalar field puzzle about that value dissolves under the new light. Quasinormal ringing frequencies echo the same local facts.
arxiv-2503-02620:
Stijn Schepers and Jeroen van Oijen model unstable lean hydrogen flames in this 2025 paper. Burning very lean hydrogen air mixtures could decarbonize industry while keeping flame temperatures, and thus nitrogen oxide emissions, low. Such flames wobble because heat and species diffuse at different rates, a thermo-diffusive instability.

Fast flame models tabulate chemistry in advance, but they usually drop the uneven diffusion that drives the wobble. The new implementation keeps the diffusion terms only for the handful of species that matter most, including the hydrogen radical, whose drift strongly affects heat transport along the flame front. In test flames with full chemistry, the richer model predicted flame shape and motion well, above all when heat loss was included.
arxiv-2503-03620:
Mengzhen Liu and co-authors design beamforming across three timescales in 2025. The catalog lists three authors, but the head byline names four. Their antennas can reshape their own radiation pattern on the fly, adding a layer beyond classic analog and digital steering.

The three layers split the work: pattern shaping for alignment, analog steering for gain, and digital cleanup for interference. Optimizing all at once is costly in pilots and compute. Their scheme tunes each layer at its own pace, from slow pattern changes to fast digital updates. Simulations confirm gains for the combined design in multi-user settings.
arxiv-2503-03720:
Kuni Iwasa models how ear hair cells stiffen and push in a 2025 arXiv paper. Outer hair cells in the cochlea have two sense parts: a hair bundle with gates, and a body wall that acts like a piezo film. Iwasa drops the cells into the plainest local ear models to watch the parts interact. High tones and low tones split the tale by how charge flows.

At high tones, bundle charge drives the body, which fights drag and lifts the peak rate by stiffening. At low tones, body strain adds drag instead, and bundle sense stiffens the body. The peak is thus half-piezo in kind.
arxiv-2503-03820:
Evgeny Gorbunov, Daniel Groselj, and Fabio Bacchini simulated cosmic ray escape from turbulent plasma in a 2025 paper. Standard boxes keep fast particles trapped, which distorts how acceleration settles. Their three-dimensional runs inject particles from an outside heat bath and let them diffuse away.

A steady state formed, with nonthermal particles reaching the theoretical energy ceiling. Plasma and magnetic pressures balanced, and that balance capped the acceleration rate. As the cold plasma's magnetization rose, spectra hardened and more of the spent energy left as cosmic rays. Past a threshold, escaping rays carried over half the dissipated energy. The method opens steady-state kinetic studies for many cosmic settings, from jets to galaxy clusters.
arxiv-2503-04120:
Yuan and Sahay studied how a spy can name which radio sent a signal, even when senders try to hide, in twenty twenty-five. Radio frequency fingerprinting names a device by quirks in its signals, left by how it was built. Senders have begun to add adversarial perturbations. These crafted flaws aim to fool the deep learning that spots the marks, when outsiders listen in.

The pair built a spy tool that reads signals in time and frequency at once. Their theory shows the flaws pile up in time-frequency zones that count for little when naming a sender. So the hit rate on attacked signals rises. Tests on a real-world dataset backed the theory. The guarded tool named senders about as well as the receiver the signals were meant for. The pair warn that transferable adversarial attacks alone will not keep future radio systems safe.
arxiv-2503-04220:
Haba, writing alone in 2025, works on a special state in quantum theory of light. The state has zero energy and solves the core equations for the electric and magnetic field. Haba builds a new way to quantize the field around that state, using a random process in place of fixed paths.

The random process rests on an equation for the field that favours self-dual forms. It yields solutions that start from the special state times a smooth factor. Haba then extends the same idea to stronger force fields and to massless spin-two fields. The last step points toward a quantum view of gravity itself.
arxiv-2503-04520:
Jonas Faltinath and co-authors study tiny magnetic sensors that can report heat or pressure from hard-to-reach spots. Each sensor holds two magnets, one fixed and one that twists. The twist rate shifts with the gap between the magnets, which links it to the trait being measured. Their 2025 work pins down how that rate depends on the gap.

The team built three sensors with ball and cylinder magnets and tested them across a wide range of rates. Their way of reading the base rate proved steady, with tiny error bars. A tweaked dipole model fit the gap-rate link well once one factor absorbed flaws in materials and build. Median error fell below a fifth of a percent. The results should help design and tune new sensors of this kind.
arxiv-2503-05120:
Ring-shaped carbon molecules float in space dust, and their glow in infrared light tells astronomers what is out there. Xinghong Mai and co-authors compute that glow with a learning-based dynamics method in a 2025 paper. Their method follows how each molecule jiggles at heat, which bends its light pattern in ways simple math misses.

The method matched costly quantum chemistry in accuracy at a small share of the cost. It also grows in cost only in step with molecule size. The team ran it on 1,704 molecules from a NASA data set, some with up to 216 carbon atoms, at varied heat levels. The runs stock a library that space telescopes can match against the sky.
arxiv-2503-05320:
Zitao Fang and eight co-authors take on clashes that come when staff join more than one tuned model into one. Fine tuning lifts task scores but often hurts skill on new tasks, and plain joins can make scores worse. Their frame, NeuroMerging, works at the level of nerve cells. It does not treat the model as a black box.

The team splits task traits into two nerve cell spaces. One space rules how the model takes in new data. The other rules how it fits a task. Joining in those spaces cuts clashes with no more train time. In tests on speech tasks and sight tasks, NeuroMerging beat old ways. The team says match of nerve cell acts is a good path for joins of what models know.
arxiv-2503-05420:
Timo Zwettler and co-authors create a new ordered state in 2025 by shining cavity light on an ultracold gas. Light trapped between mirrors can push atoms to arrange themselves in waves, but past work coupled light to single atoms only. Here the gas is so strongly interacting that atom pairs act as units too, and light couples to both at once.

The team watches order appear as they vary the light-pair coupling in strength and sign. The single-atom wave and the pair wave boost or cancel each other, a clear interference of three orders at once. A standard theory model matches the pattern when pair links are tuned. The work shows cavities can stage exotic states of strongly linked matter.
arxiv-2503-05520:
Romain Hermary and co-authors tackle in 2025 hidden geometric bias in one-class anomaly detection. Such tools learn only the normal class and must flag all else as odd. Top tools fake odd samples by image tricks, but they lean on bias baked into test sets.

The new method works in a frozen rich feature space from a pretrained model. Fake odd features come from an adaptive line shift that fits each sample's own spread. Contrast training then guides the yes-no step that splits normal from odd. Tests on both standard and bias-free sets beat like baselines. The gain holds where past tricks lose their edge.
arxiv-2503-06220:
Talking with an AI about a live video feed demands answers at the speed of the stream itself. Xin Ding and seven co-authors built StreamMind in 2025, a video language model that watches at one hundred frames per second and speaks up on its own when something happens.

The bottleneck is that transformer costs grow much faster than the stream. Their answer is a gate: a small network watches the video and wakes the big language model only when a relevant event appears. A state-space feature extractor keeps the watching cost flat over time. On sports and first-person video tasks the system set new marks for both quality and speed, pointing toward always-on assistants for games and live media.
arxiv-2503-06420:
Debraj Chakraborty, Clemens Dubslaff, Sudeep Kanav, Jan Kretinsky, and Christoph Weinhuber explain control policies with a new diagram form in a 2025 paper. Synthesized and learned controllers work well but resist human reading. Decision trees are the usual readable stand in, yet they repeat shared choices down many branches.

Predicate decision diagrams merge tree clarity with the sharing trick of binary decision diagrams. Predicates label the edges, and common sub decisions are stored once. The team builds a pipeline that converts controller trees into these diagrams using reduction rules carried over from the binary case.
