Smaller diagrams should be easier to audit for safety critical systems, where an unreadable controller is a liability.
arxiv-2503-06620:
Xiangyu Zhang, Beena Ahmed, and Julien Epps present a computing paper from 2025 on spotting depression from speech and text. Pre-trained speech models do oddly poorly at this task without heavy data tricks. Big language models had not been tried on the joint speech-text version. The team built such a system and probed why the older models fail.

Their probe found a tangling problem: high-level facts about what was said and how it sounded blur together inside the models. That blur makes a clean decision line hard to draw. Their fix pulls the two fact streams apart before judging. With the streams apart, both speech models and language models scored far better. The authors say the split is a general lesson for joint media tasks.
arxiv-2503-06820:
Wei Dai and co-authors present a 2025 data set and model for fine-grained video question answering. Video tests often miss detail in time and space. Models then pass while still weak at pinning when things happen, where actors stand, and how objects relate. The new data set was built to close those gaps.

It holds questions tied to scene graphs and to marked time spans, with a stress on actors and objects. The paired model guesses the scene graph, pulls the right frames, and answers with a large language model. Tests on the new set and on public sets put the model ahead of prior work. The authors frame it as a new bar for video tests.
arxiv-2503-07020:
Yuting Hu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on self-driving cars that lose part of their view of the road. A blocked sensor can hide a key object and break the car's grasp of the scene. The usual response is to stop at once, which is safe but blunt, and a full stop is not always needed when the risk is minor.

Their system uses a large language model to add human-like road sense to the car's choices. Four parts work together: one infers hazards, one plans short moves, one checks each action, and one sets safety limits. A new data set of video clips with hidden key objects trains the model for such cases.
arxiv-2503-07120:
Zhen Zou and Feng Zhao speed up image generation models in a 2025 paper. Diffusion transformers make strong images but cost heavy computing time. A popular shortcut caches intermediate features for reuse, yet output quality drops, and the reason was unclear.

The pair show that caching greatly amplifies a known flaw called exposure bias, a drift between training and generation conditions. They trace the flaw to a mismatch in frequency response: the model's attention and feed-forward parts favour different signal frequencies. Their method, FEB-Cache, caches the two parts on separate schedules guided by frequency. Tests showed better quality at the same speed gain. The authors present frequency as the right lens for designing future caching schemes.
arxiv-2503-07420:
Syed Danial Ali Shah and co-authors propose in 2025 a framework for sharing compute between radio networks and AI workloads on a converged 6G platform. Future networks want accelerated hardware to serve both live signal processing and heavy generative AI jobs. The architecture and resource strategy for that sharing are still young, so practical designs are needed now.

Building on open radio network design, they extend the near-real-time controller with a monitoring app that feeds radio analytics to an orchestrator. A reinforcement learning agent then splits graphics processor capacity between urgent radio tasks and AI jobs. Simulations show the sharing benefits.
arxiv-2503-07720:
Julien Drapeau, Shreya Banerjee, and Stefanos Kourtis adapt a quantum algorithm for counting problems in a 2025 paper. Counting valid solutions to hard puzzles is a classic tough task in computing theory. Random sampling and counting turn out to be two faces of one problem.

Their method uses a quantum alternating ansatz as the sampler inside a counting scheme. Theory shows it needs exponentially fewer samples than earlier quantum counting routes. Shallow circuit simulations test two notoriously hard counting problems. A trade-off appears between hitting solutions often and sampling them evenly. Tuning that balance beats both naive sampling and a standard quantum counting method in their tests. The work maps where variational quantum counting helps and where it strains.
arxiv-2503-07920:
Samuel Cahyawijaya and a large team of co-authors build in 2025 SEA-VL, an open vision language data set for Southeast Asia. That region holds rich tongue and culture mix, yet image text research scarce covers it. Models then miss the culture cues of the region's daily life.

Three build paths are set side by side: crowd work by folk in the region, web crawl, and made images. Crawl shots hit near eighty five per cent culture fit at low cost and time. Made shots, by contrast, oft missed true culture marks. The set aims to pull more of the region's tongues into sight text work.
arxiv-2503-08020:
Daping Weng builds weighted cycles on woven diagrams in a 2025 paper. Weaves are braid like pictures tied to root systems of many shapes, and cycles drawn on them can carry numbers.

A pairing between weighted cycles is defined that tolerates skewed symmetry. The cycles turn out to span a Laurent polynomial algebra, and in the symmetric case the pairing yields a quantum version of it. Functions along the cycles live on a decorated flag space and match cluster variables, with matching change rules on both sides. The bridge links diagram combinatorics to a rich algebra family.
arxiv-2503-08320:
Lima and co-authors report the spin of a white dwarf in an unusual binary star system, in a 2025 paper. The text's title is shorter than the catalog's, which adds instrument details; the description follows the text. The system, V1082 Sgr, pairs a magnetic white dwarf with a companion star. The team watched its light for a repeating swing in circular polarization.

The swing repeats every 1.943 hours, which unmasks the white dwarf's rotation and confirms the system as an intermediate polar, a class where the dwarf's magnetism channels infalling gas. Its twenty-point-eight-hour orbit is extraordinarily long for such systems, putting the pair at an extreme of the spin-versus-orbit chart. Modeling the glowing impact region gives a magnetic field of eleven million gauss at the pole. The dwarf may still be spinning up rather than settled.
arxiv-2503-09220:
Fabio Llorella and Jose Cebrian wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on sorting stars, galaxies, and quasars with formulas a human can read. Black-box models sort well but cannot say why, so the team aimed for an explicit expression instead.

They used a public data set of one hundred thousand sky objects from a sky survey. Symbolic regression searched for a math expression that splits the three classes, trained on a tenth of the data. A genetic algorithm then tuned the expression's settings. The final formula reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.81, a strong match with the true labels. The authors say the pairing of symbolic regression with genetic tuning offers accurate, open models. Such models let astronomers argue with the rule, not just trust it.
arxiv-2503-09720:
Milton and co-authors build tools for a histogram-free way of correcting particle physics data, in this 2025 paper. Detectors distort measurements, and unfolding removes that distortion. New machine learning methods skip the classic binning step, but labs need shared standards before adopting them.

The team show that boosted decision trees can unfold data well with a few summary features, easing the load on heavy deep models. They extend a benchmark data set with acceptance effects that real detectors face. A head-to-head test isolates the effect of binning itself. Two software packages wrap the leading method for lab use, one inside a common framework and one standalone.
arxiv-2503-09820:
Robots that move among people must judge a crowd and pick paths that feel safe and polite. Mohamed Elnoor and five co-authors present a method, named ViLAM in the text, that borrows the judgement of large vision and language models. Their 2025 work turns that judgement into attention maps, charts that light up the parts of a scene a robot should watch or favour.

Rather than learn from human demos, the method aligns the focus of a trained vision model with focus maps drawn from a large model's social sense. A new training loss blends the two sources. The refined maps then act as cost charts for a local planner, which steers the robot through busy spaces. The aim is motion that fits social norms without hand-made rules for each scene.
arxiv-2503-09920:
Some gravity models describe black holes that bounce at their core instead of ending in a point. Pereira and co-authors study such black-bounce forms in a 2025 paper. They work inside a field theory called k-essence, joined with a model that breaks a basic symmetry of space and time.

The team checks one known bounce form and adds a new one with a fresh area rule. For each form, they work out the field, its stored energy, and the rules that energy must obey. They show the broken symmetry can come from the field itself, with no extra field added. The results back earlier work on wormhole forms in the same theory.
arxiv-2503-10920:
Pierre Nazé and Fabrício Potiguar study heat loss in gently driven systems in a 2025 paper. Their setting pairs a slow-driven particle with a viscoelastic bath, one with memory, like a thick fluid that remembers past motion. Textbook rules need care here, since memory can break thermodynamic consistency unless a sharp term is added.

Within linear response, the authors work out how fast the system relaxes for two drive styles: a moving trap and a stiffening trap. Surprisingly, memory sometimes sped relaxation and cut wasted work. They also derive drive shapes that waste the least energy. Readers get fresh control rules for tiny machines in thick media.
arxiv-2503-11120:
Gökhan Özbulak and four colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on evaluating machine learning systems for both usefulness and fairness at once. A model can be accurate overall yet unfair to particular groups. Judging that trade-off is difficult because metrics conflict and definitions of fairness vary.

The authors present a multi-objective evaluation framework borrowed from the field of multi-objective optimization. It collects comprehensive information about each system's utility and fairness together, rather than collapsing them into a single score. Systems are then summarized both quantitatively and qualitatively, so decision-makers can see which trade-offs each model offers. The framework aims to close gaps in how fairness evaluations are currently done in practice.
arxiv-2503-11220:
Mousavi studies how quantum links between two particles fade when each particle sits in its own heat bath, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The work uses a known model of open quantum systems, doubled so both particles have an environment. The particles start in a squeezed state, a state where one trait is held more tightly than usual. Mousavi tracks four kinds of quantum behavior over time.

The study finds that a shared bath protects local coherence better than two apart baths. Heat speeds the loss of these effects and blocks their brief returns. A shared bath also gives entanglement a dark pause before it dies, while apart baths kill it at once. Squeezing shapes the early motion but not the long-run end point.
arxiv-2503-11620:
Jamison Sloan, Sachin Vaidya, Nicholas Rivera, and Marin Soljačić show how a one-way flow effect can shield parts of a light system from noise. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Big optical systems can carry huge power and fast data streams. Noise, though, caps how well they work, and tangled systems tend to grow noisier on their own.

The team shows that when flow is forced to run one way, noise drains off in that same sense. The effect comes from a known quirk of open systems, where waves hug one edge. In quantum terms, the noise leaves the steady state rather than piling up inside it. That shield could guide designs for strong amplifiers and oscillators that stay clean. It also links two fields that rarely meet: open-system topology and many-body light.
arxiv-2503-11720:
Hanyang Zhao and seven co-authors fine-tune image generators with critiques from vision-language models instead of bare reward scores. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents Rich Preference Optimization, or RPO. Classic preference tuning leans on a reward model's labels. Those labels hide their reasons and invite hacking. Their pipeline asks a vision-language model to critique each generated image in words first.

A second pass turns the critique into concrete edit instructions. Applying the edits yields a refined image. The flawed and refined pair forms a preference example with a visible rationale. Such synthetic pairs then tune top diffusion models. The team shows the pipeline and its data lift fine-tuning results. The pitch is preference data that explains itself, not just ranks.
arxiv-2503-11820:
Antonio Lorenzin and Fabio Zanasi rebuild two classic transformations of probability models as algebra. Moralisation turns a Bayesian network with arrows into a Markov network without them. Triangulation travels the other way. Both let users switch factorizations of the same distribution. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair model the transformations as functors between classes of the two network kinds. Each network is itself a functor, from a syntax domain to a meaning domain. Moralisation and triangulation then become pre-composition, built up by induction on the syntax.

The framing is modular by design. Meaning and translation are kept apart, so each can be studied on its own. Category theory supplies the tracking. The paper offers the probabilistic modeling community a language of parts for transformations usually shown as graph surgery.
arxiv-2503-11920:
Khadija Hafeez and three co-authors examine local differential privacy for smart grids in a 2025 paper. Smart meters report power use almost in real time, which threatens household privacy. Local privacy methods let each user scramble their own data before sending it, removing the need for a trusted middleman. Putting that theory into practice on real grids brings its own problems, and the paper maps them.

They compare existing mechanisms for numeric grid data and review how privacy settings get chosen, noting no best method exists. Dataset size effects on privacy and accuracy, and attacks that manipulate the system, are also covered. Future research directions close the paper.
arxiv-2503-12220:
Yunbo Long, Liming Xu, Ge Zheng, and Alexandra Brintrup propose privacy adaptive clustered federated learning for retail sales forecasting. Retailers can train shared models without pooling raw data, yet shifts in how people shop, from place to place, make one global model weak. Their method groups them into separate bubbles, each with its own federated system.

The grouping uses levels of differential privacy and patterns of feature importance to split off data that differ. Transformer models inside each bubble predict local sales. Adaptive noise and client range per bubble, plus early removal of high risk clients, guard the system. Against standard federated averaging and local learning, the method beats both on forecast accuracy for all clients, with large error cuts over local learning alone.
arxiv-2503-12320:
Eight researchers recheck what a famous neutron star merger tells us in a 2025 paper. The 2017 event gave both gravity waves and a glow from hot debris, a pairing that can pin down the star's size and mass. The team used a fresh model that predicts the glow from simulations.

The glow data alone favor a narrow range for the debris traits, even when wide model error is allowed. Claims about the star itself, though, swing a lot with guesses about how much matter the merger throws out. The authors warn against using debris fits without that context. Better first principle models of the ejection are the key need, they argue.
arxiv-2503-12520:
Cenk Tüysüz and co-authors present a streaming method to learn how analog quantum computers respond to their settings. Their 2025 paper deals with machines that simulate time-changing quantum systems. The knobs a user sets rarely match the physics that comes out, and that mapping, the response function, shapes every result.

Their algorithm learns the mapping from ordinary user runs, so no special calibration runs are needed. They apply it to several generations of simulators built on two platforms: superconductor circuits and arrays of neutral atoms. Comparing the learned responses shows how each platform distorts inputs in its own way. Knowing the true response lets users program the machine they actually have, not the one they imagine.
arxiv-2503-12620:
Sajad Dabiri and Reza Asgari wrote a physics paper in 2025 on light in driven quantum systems. Some systems are pushed by a field that repeats in time, which creates new states. The team built a math frame to compute how such systems respond to light in a nonlinear way.

Their frame uses a gauge based on velocity rather than one based on position. They test it on a simple model of an atom driven by light. Results from the two gauges agree in full. The driven system shows effects absent in still systems: jumps aided by photons, mixing of frequencies, and steady currents made by the drive. Responses peak when the light pitch hits whole multiples of the drive pitch. The work links theory to lab tests on fast light control.
arxiv-2503-13320:
Fang, Pu, and Yang computed how radiation-like corrections change the spin polarization that swirling hot quark-gluon matter induces in fermions. When such matter rotates, particle spins tend to line up, an effect seen in heavy-ion collisions. The authors work out corrections that come from gradients in the fermion self-energy, using the Keldysh equation within quantum kinetic theory, and apply a hard-thermal-loop approximation suited to hot matter.

They obtain new terms for the spin-polarization spectrum of massive quarks, valid to leading order in the QCD coupling. The same framework gives corrections to the axial-charge current tied to the chiral vortical effect. They also analyze how these effects shift the spin alignment of vector mesons, a quantity experiments can measure. The work sharpens theory predictions for spin observables in hot, rotating nuclear matter.
arxiv-2503-13420:
Akbar, Brewer, and Modumudi revisit the spacetime of an accelerating black hole pair in two thousand twenty-five. Their metric is Ernst's one parameter twist on the classic C-metric. It solves the vacuum Einstein equations without a line source. Past claims on its key parameter clash in print.

They settle which value keeps the axis regular in the metric. The pair of holes thus accelerates with no strut or string. Work with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem maps knots and horizon shapes. Both horizons embed in flat three space in their study. Odd traits at infinity block a standard Bondi form.
arxiv-2503-13920: Roberta Di Gennaro and Rosa Miro-Roig classify a family of algebras tied to a two-term formula in a 2025 mathematics paper. The algebras are Artinian complete intersections, built from a power series called a Macaulay dual generator. The authors pin down which of these algebras arise when that generator is a binomial, a sum of two monomials. They prove every algebra in this family enjoys the Strong Lefschetz property, a form of symmetry in its multiplication maps. The result closes the classification for the binomial case.
arxiv-2503-14020:
LAMMPS is a widely used open program for simulating particles, from single atoms up to coarse models of materials, but its many options can overwhelm new users. Simon Gravelle and co-authors introduce a set of tutorials designed to make learning the package easier. The first four lessons cover the basics of running simulations on systems of growing complexity. The next four move to advanced methods.

The advanced lessons cover a reactive force field, grand canonical Monte Carlo, enhanced sampling, and the REACTER protocol for building reacting systems. The tutorials are built around LAMMPS-GUI, a cross-platform editor that can edit input files, run the program, pull out data, and show the system on screen. By walking through real examples step by step, the set helps beginners avoid common mistakes. It also helps experienced users reach the package's deeper features.
arxiv-2503-14220:
ChungHa Lee and Jin-Hyuk Hong present a web library that turns music into live visuals for creative work. Their 2025 study notes that past music visualization work stressed tech and theory over daily use. How listeners and makers use such visuals in real creative flow was little known.

The library, called musicolors, runs in real time in a browser. A qualitative study then watched composers, developers, and listeners use it. Users sketched musical ideas with it, wired it into other tools, and listened with a synesthetic bent. Gains spanned idea capture, system play, and richer listening. The authors draw design guides for future tools that aim at lively, creative use.
arxiv-2503-14420:
Marc Levine and Anna Viergever compute a set of counts for shapes built from three copies of the line of points at a set range. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, sits in deep math.

The counts, called quadratic Donaldson-Thomas invariants, track how curves sit in a three-fold shape. The team uses a place-based method in a refined form of the math of cycles. They show the counts' full series takes a clean form, set by a known product rule. That proves a changed form of a claim one author had put forth. They show a like result for shapes made by blowing up the base shape, and for kin smooth shapes of the same toric kind.
arxiv-2503-14720:
Vihaan Misra, Peter Schaldenbrand, and Jean Oh presented ShapeShift in 2025, a method that arranges rigid physical objects so the arrangement itself pictures an idea named in words. A mosaic of blocks or tiles, seen from above, should read as the requested concept. Pretrained diffusion models can judge how well a layout matches a concept, but the objects must also obey physics and not overlap.

The hard part is fixing overlaps without wrecking the picture, since pushing shapes apart in the geometrically obvious direction often destroys the recognizable arrangement. ShapeShift represents the boundary as a deformable phase field that grows unevenly, steered by features inside the diffusion model that encode direction and shape. Experiments show layouts that stay physically valid while keeping the intended meaning clear.
arxiv-2503-14920:
Hiroo Azuma designs a heralded single-photon source from patterned nonlinear crystals, in this 2025 paper. A heralded source announces each lone photon by spotting its twin, a trick quantum optics relies on. The plan shines pump and signal beams into a striped crystal that squeezes the light; two such beams then meet at a splitter and become entangled.

Detecting one photon heralds the other. Azuma computes the source's yield and purity, then tests how both degrade with an imperfect herald detector. A worked example uses lithium niobate, a standard nonlinear crystal, at optical frequencies.
arxiv-2503-15120:
Live captions let deaf and hard of hearing people follow talks, but trained caption writers are costly and scarce. Korbinian Kuhn, Verena Kersken, and Gottfried Zimmermann studied a cheaper mix in a 2025 conference paper: speech software writes the first draft, and untrained helpers fix its errors in real time. The approach is known as CART, short for communication access real-time translation.

The team ran a user study with 75 people to test how well the shared editing worked. They also held focus groups with 25 deaf and hard of hearing users to ask what level of accuracy they accept. Group editing raised caption quality enough that users rated the text well for clarity. The groups also said they value the human effort in the loop, which supports the mixed approach.
arxiv-2503-15220:
Rrubaa Panchendrarajan and Arkaitz Zubiaga build a claim spotter for fact-checkers that works across languages. Automated fact-checking starts with finding claims worth checking, and social media spreads them in many tongues at once. Fine-tuned multilingual models help, but how well they carry skill from one language to another was untested. Their 2025 paper presents a model called EX-Claim.

The model leans on entities: it marks named people, places, and groups in a post and links them to known records, then uses that signal alongside the text. Tests on three data sets from different platforms covered 27 languages. The entity-aware model gained steadily over rivals, in languages it trained on and in ones it had never seen. The authors offer it as a practical front end for fact-checking pipelines that face mixed-language feeds.
arxiv-2503-15320:
The Euclid Collaboration published a research paper in 2025 presenting the active galaxies found in the space telescope's first quick data release. Euclid surveys huge sky areas in sharp detail to map the dark universe, and its early release already catalogs feeding black holes. The paper describes the release and the active galactic nuclei identified in it.

Active galaxies matter because their brightness traces black hole growth across cosmic time. A large author team spanning the consortium lays out the selection and properties of these objects in the new data. Quick releases let the community test pipelines and chase follow-ups years before the final survey. The catalog seeds studies of how black holes and galaxies grew together.
arxiv-2503-15420:
Amirhossein Kazerouni, Soroush Mehraban, Michael Brudno, and Babak Taati wrote this 2025 paper on one encoding scheme for every kind of signal. Implicit neural representations store data as functions inside small networks, saving memory and ignoring resolution, but most frameworks lean on a single global code or run slowly. Their framework, LIFT, splits the job among many local implicit functions working in parallel.

A hierarchical generator produces codes at local, regional, and global scales, and the local functions blend smoothly across their borders. An enhanced variant, ReLIFT, adds residual connections and richer frequency encodings, closing the gap between how fast such models converge and how much they can express. Benchmarks put the approach at the state of the art across tasks and data types. The authors frame it as a step toward truly task-agnostic encoding.
arxiv-2503-15520:
Mandar Kulkarni proposes in 2025 an AI agent that carries out standard operating procedures on its own. In customer care, such a procedure spells out the steps a human agent takes to solve a case. Each step is either a talk with the user or a call to a software tool, and the chart of steps sets the path.

His design, Agent-S, uses three task-tuned language models backed by a shared action store, a memory of past steps, and links to tools and knowledge sources. When stuck, the agent can retry a step or look up help. Tests on three seller support procedures from online retail showed the agent held up in messy, real-style cases.
arxiv-2503-15820:
Katherine Goldman and Amy Herron prove a key curvature property of the Deligne complex for the B3 Artin group, in this 2025 paper. These groups encode braid-like symmetries, and their complexes carry a piecewise flat metric. Non-positive curvature would unlock strong group-theoretic tools.

The authors set a test for complexes built from B3 pieces to have the needed sphere-level curvature. The test speaks in terms of embedded edge paths and applies to the spherical version of the complex. Passing it shows the full complex carries the CAT(0) property. The result advances a program aimed at all three-dimensional Artin groups.
arxiv-2503-15920:
Sahil Gehlawat wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on foliations, which slice a space into stacked surfaces like pages in a book. Here the pages are Riemann surfaces inside a complex space, and the slice has singular points where pages meet oddly. Usually those bad points sit apart from each other. Gehlawat studies the harder case where they crowd together into a non-discrete set.

The focus falls on singular points that have an invariant sheet passing through them. Points are sorted by the size of that sheet. For a class called hyperbolic foliations, the author shows that having such points keeps a natural leaf-wise distance measure continuous away from the bad set. The result orders a wild corner of foliation theory.
arxiv-2503-16220:
Stefana-Lucia Anita writes a solo 2025 arXiv paper on games played by very large crowds. In mean field game theory, each player reacts to the mass of others rather than to any one rival, and the whole system settles, if at all, at a balance point. Such systems are written as linked equations for the crowd's spread and each player's best reply.

Anita shows the game system can be read as the first-order rule of a control problem tied to a crowd flow equation. From that reading she proves a weak solution to the system exists. Under tighter terms, she also proves the solution is the only one. The paper is pure theory, aimed at readers who work on crowd games and control.
arxiv-2503-16420:
Paul Engstler, Aleksandar Shtedritski, Iro Laina, Christian Rupprecht, and Andrea Vedaldi present SynCity in a 2025 paper on building 3D worlds from text. Most 3D generators make single objects, not full places. SynCity makes large scenes with no training and no tuning runs at all.

It blends the shape skill of trained 3D models with the style range of 2D image makers. The world grows tile by tile, each new tile made with its place in the scene in mind. Each tile is then fused into the growing scene before the next one starts. Users get fine control over layout and look as the world expands. The results are rich, varied scenes that feel deep and full.
arxiv-2503-16520:
Ji-Eun Han and Yoonseok Heo present KoPersona, a 2025 data set of 200,000 personas written to reflect Korean culture. Chatbots with personas feel more real, but most persona data mirror Western norms, which limits how well systems serve other cultures. The authors built a two-step pipeline that generates personas carrying Korean values, behaviors, and social nuances.

A battery of metrics checked the set's quality and cultural fit. The authors say the pipeline is a template: the same steps can build persona sets for other languages and cultures. The work targets AI that interacts in a culturally aware way rather than with one-size-fits-all characters. It also gives persona research a large non-English resource to build on.
arxiv-2503-17020:
Joachim Tomasi, Sandrine Anthoine, and Hachem Kadri design a new kind of quantum kernel for machine learning, in a research paper from 2025. Kernels judge how alike two inputs are. Quantum versions encode data into quantum states, which may capture patterns that classical tools miss.

Many quantum kernels blur out, so the model memorizes training data and fails on new data. The team borrows an idea from classical learning where some overfitting can be harmless. Their design mixes a local part, from small pieces of the system, with a global part, from the whole system. Theory and tests show this mix learns well without the usual collapse.
arxiv-2503-17220:
Nuno Saavedra, João F. Ferreira, and Alexandra Mendes present InfraFix, a framework for automatically repairing infrastructure-as-code scripts, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Infrastructure as code automates IT infrastructure at scale. Errors in these scripts can cause security vulnerabilities, outages, and data loss. Detection of such issues is well studied, but automatic repair is not, largely for lack of specifications.

InfraFix is technology-agnostic and lets repair techniques draw on diverse information sources. The authors also introduce a method for generating repair scenarios at scale. Their implementation pairs an SMT-based repair module with a state inference module using system calls. Across more than a quarter million generated scenarios, the success rate reached ninety-five point seven percent. The work lays a foundation for program repair research on infrastructure code.
arxiv-2503-17720:
Robin Quade and Michael Potthoff study how to braid exotic particles without moving them in tiny wire networks. Their 2025 paper works with Majorana zero modes, prized states for future quantum hardware. The wires are short Kitaev chains joined by weak links, a setup close to real devices.

For two joined chains, a full turn of the phase in one chain braid swaps the modes in effect. Exact many-body sums confirm the swap through a phase measure on the low-energy states. Maps over chain length, link strength, and site energy show two outcome zones. One zone acts like one logic gate and the other like a second gate. A simple four-mode model pins down where the zones cross.
arxiv-2503-18020:
Anjali and three co-authors take a fresh look at scale values for operators on a two-fold number space in this twenty twenty-five paper. The space stacks two layers of the kind of numbers used for waves and spins. Scale values sort how such operators stretch space, a core tool in the field.

Inside, the team sets terms for when a value counts as a true scale value here. They prove a run of claims that pin those terms down in clean form. The spaces of matched scale paths are then mapped for their shape and traits. Kin claims on those spaces close the work and round out the frame.
arxiv-2503-18120:
Hoang Nhan Luu, Yu-Cheng Qiu and S.-H. Henry Tye wrote a 2025 paper on dark energy that changes over time. New survey data hint that dark energy does not act like a fixed constant. Its strength seems to shift, or at least to sit off the constant value. The authors test one cause: a very light particle called an axion.

They give the particle a tiny mass and show how it could match the new data. In their model, the key value stays at or above a set floor. A negative constant also fits better here. They offer a simple formula so others can fit the model to data.
arxiv-2503-18320:
Models that see and read are trained on image instructions written by other models or by humans, in styles unlike the base model's own voice. Dong Jing, Nanyi Fei, and Zhiwu Lu argue that this style mismatch quietly damages the model. Forced to speak in a foreign manner, the base language model drifts from the strengths it was trained into.

Their fix lets the base model rewrite the instructions in its own manner, keeping the meaning intact. Human raters confirmed the rewritten instructions closed the style gap. Two well-known multimodal models trained on the aligned data resisted hallucination better. They also improved across fifteen vision and language benchmarks. The work was completed in late 2023.
arxiv-2503-18620:
The BESIII Collaboration published this particle physics paper in 2025. The catalog title is garbled with raw typesetting, but the paper itself reports the observation of a rare decay. In the process, a particle called psi(3686) breaks apart into a sigma particle, its antimatter twin, and an omega particle.

Large teams run the BESIII detector to record huge numbers of particle collisions and decays. Most decay routes of psi(3686) were mapped long ago, so each new confirmed route sharpens the picture of how this particle behaves. Seeing this channel at all shows how much data the team has gathered and how finely they can sift it. Results like this one test the rules that govern quarks inside particles, and they guide the search for decay routes that theory says should be even rarer.
arxiv-2503-18720:
Jurgen Rossmann works in 2025 on a mixed edge task for the non steady Stokes flow system set in an angle. Two edge rules are set, one on each side of the angle wedge. Such flows model slow, thick fluid moves with a fixed wall state on one side and a free push state on the next.

Most of the work treats the form that comes from a Laplace shift of the time task. In a class of weighed spaces, Rossmann proves a lone strong solve exists and grades its smoothness. Shift traits then lift those claims back to the time form of the task in full.
arxiv-2503-19020:
Abby Mintz and co-authors present new spectra of massive hot stars in the dwarf galaxy NGC 3109, in work from 2025. Such metal-poor stars likely drove the reionisation of the early universe, yet spectra of single stars at these low metal levels are rare. NGC 3109, a nearby dwarf galaxy, holds just twelve percent of the Sun's metal content.

Using a major telescope in Hawaii and Hubble imaging, the team measured seventeen O and B stars and derived their temperatures, gravities, sizes, and masses. Two O stars showed strong winds despite the low metals. One is the hottest, youngest, and most massive star confirmed in the galaxy, with an ambiguous evolutionary state. The sample nearly doubles the known measured stars there, giving modellers a firmer testbed.
arxiv-2503-19120:
Armineh Nourbakhsh and co-authors argue that tests for document question-answering systems miss a key trait: whether answers are grounded in the document, in a 2025 paper. Top systems now rival humans on standard scores, yet those scores treat lucky guesses and true reading alike.

The authors propose a scoring method that checks both meaning and placement. It asks whether the answer says the right thing and points to the right spot in the document. Users can tune the score to their own priorities. Human judges backed the method's verdicts. Applied to popular leaderboards, it reshuffled rankings and favored models whose answers were better calibrated, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-19720:
Steel grains that harden fusion reactor steel melt under heavy radiation, and Stroud and co-authors probed flaws in those grains with atom tools and models, in work from twenty twenty-five. The grains are vanadium nitride flecks inside a heat-tough steel. Atom probes, learning-based force models, and fine math all fed the study.

Before any radiation, the flecks held missing nitrogen spots and swapped-in chromium atoms. Ordered gaps at working heats help blunt radiation harm in the models. Added stray atoms break that order and speed the harm, which may speed the melt. Bench checks with a fine scope backed the model tale. The work guides steel mixes for fusion walls.
arxiv-2503-19920:
Neutrinos may weigh almost nothing, and pinning that weight down tests the core rules of physics. The HOLMES team reports the tightest calorimetric bound yet in a 2025 paper, with Alpert and co-authors. Their array of cold sensors counts decays of a holmium isotope atom by atom.

Seventy million decays were logged over two months. The sensors split energy with a fineness of six electron volts. A Bayesian read of the decay curve set the neutrino mass below 27 units at ninety percent belief. The array can be scaled up with shared wiring. The run proves the path for a next, sharper mass hunt.
arxiv-2503-20020:
The Gemini Robotics Team at Google DeepMind presents a family of AI models built to control real robots, in a 2025 report. Large models that mix text, images, and sound have shown broad skill in digital tasks. Moving that skill into physical agents has proved far harder. The new models rest on the Gemini 2.0 base and are shaped from the start for robotics work.

The main model reads vision and language and turns them straight into robot actions. It moves smoothly and reacts fast, handling hard handling tasks across varied objects and places. It also copes with rooms it has never seen and follows open-ended spoken or written commands. With extra tuning, the model learns long, deft task chains, picks up new short tasks from as few as one hundred demos, and adapts to wholly new robot bodies.
arxiv-2503-20120:
Real data misbehave: outliers and wild noise break regression methods tuned for tidy errors. Hongwei Wen, Annika Betken, and Wouter Koolen study a kernel method armoured with the Cauchy loss, a penalty that refuses to chase extreme points. Earlier theory demanded noise with a finite average size, an assumption Cauchy and Pareto noise themselves violate. So the authors built a broader framework covering noise with any finite moment, even an infinite mean.

Inside it, they prove the method's error bounds approach the best possible rate, and that shrinking one tuning knob, the loss's scale, tightens performance in a controlled trade-off. Experiments on synthetic and real data under varied corruption confirmed the theory: the Cauchy armour holds where gentler losses dent.
arxiv-2503-20220:
Weijie Guo, Guofeng Zhang, Wufei Ma, and Alan Yuille present DINeMo, a 2025 neural mesh model that learns 3D pose with no 3D annotations at all. Estimating an object's category-level pose is a key step toward scene understanding for robots. Earlier neural mesh models leaned hard on 3D labels for part learning, which confined them to few categories. DINeMo instead mines fake correspondences from large visual foundation models, checking them in both directions.

On car data sets, it beat prior zero- and few-shot pose methods by a wide margin, closing about two-thirds of the gap to fully supervised systems. It also scaled well as more unlabeled images were added. The authors argue annotation-free training is the path to broad 3D understanding. A project page accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2503-20420:
Zanelli and co-authors ran computer models of space plasma to explain a common shape in electron speeds, in a 2025 paper. In the near-Earth plasma, electrons often show a flat-top spread of speeds rather than a bell curve. The team solved the plasma equations for ions and electrons in one space and one speed dimension.

An outside electric push fed energy into waves, and much of that energy passed to electrons caught inside the wave's wells. Early swirls in the speed maps merged over time into one lasting hole. The caught electrons also spread along the speed axis, which built the flat-top shape. Fake spacecraft passes through the model checked that real craft could spot the pattern.
arxiv-2503-20720:
Federico Mariani, Michele Zhu, and Maurizio Magarini set out a new approach to semantic communication, in a paper from 2025. In this field, senders aim to pass meaning, not exact bits. The rise of sixth-generation wireless work has drawn fresh interest to the idea. Yet the field still lacks a clear, workable frame for how to do it.

Their method names a message by its key features rather than resending it whole. The slack and blur inside meaning can help pin down which message was meant. They test the approach with machine learning tools in simulations. Results show clear gains over classic bit-by-bit sending. The team frames the work as a bridge between two schools of post-Shannon thought. It gives engineers a concrete element to build semantic systems around.
arxiv-2503-21020:
Sharat Paul, Nahid Hasan, and Pai Wang show in 2025 how to design special wave patterns in phononic crystals. These are materials built in a repeating pattern that steer sound or vibration waves. At certain wave numbers, two wave bands can cross at a point, a feature called a degeneracy that shapes how waves travel.

Most known crossings sit only at the center or edge of the allowed range. By using links that reach beyond nearest neighbors, the team placed crossings at any chosen wave number. Odd-numbered far links set how many crossings appear and where, while even ones mainly shift the pitch. They also found fading wave modes with their own crossings, and mapped how the modes play together in time.
arxiv-2503-21220:
Hidetsugu Sakaguchi works out exact formulas in a 2025 paper for systems jostled by random noise while out of balance. The systems are pairs and trios of linked quantities, each pulled by spring-like forces and kicked by noise, described by Langevin equations. When the kicks and pulls do not balance, the system's spread settles into a Gaussian shape that is not the textbook one.

The author derives that shape in explicit form for the two- and three-variable cases, together with the heat flows that run through the system. Such closed forms give physicists a firm test case for the wider theory of noisy, driven systems.
arxiv-2503-21520:
Sergio Rey and co-authors study ultrafast sound waves in a layered alloy crystal in a 2025 paper. The waves, called coherent acoustic phonons, travel as strain and can reshape a crystal as they pass. Such control could serve future nano devices. The alloy blends tungsten, sulfur, and selenium in a lopsided Janus-like form.

Bright light pulses at high fluence launched the waves in the crystal. Fast reflection measures tracked carriers and lattice motion step by step. A strong wave mode emerged after early exciton and heat steps. Its size far beat waves in the plain parent crystals. The team credits a built-in electric field from the alloy's lopsided build. A paired-pulse method then let them steer the wave by light alone. The authors present the alloy as a versatile block for light-driven sound devices.
arxiv-2503-21620:
Zhengxi Lu and a large team of co-authors train screen agents with reinforcement learning in this 2025 paper. Phone and computer agents must predict the right tap or swipe from a screenshot. A recent wave showed that rule-based rewards can teach language models to reason, and this team extends the idea to vision.

Their system, UI-R1, rewards correct actions by clear rules and trains with a policy method that compares groups of tries. Training used only one hundred thirty-six hard tasks across five common phone actions. The small model gained strongly on phone control tests, both familiar and new. It rivaled larger models trained on tens of thousands of examples. A refined version improved further still.
arxiv-2503-21820:
Yide Di and co-authors present UFM, a pre-trained model for matching features across image types. Their 2025 paper addresses a core vision task: finding the same points in two images. Matching across unlike images, such as scans versus photos, usually needs special training per dataset. UFM aims to handle many modes with one model.

Special transformer assistants, called MIA blocks, adapt the model to varied matching jobs. The model works within one image mode and across modes alike. A data-boosting method and staged training fight sparse and lopsided data. Tests show strong accuracy and wide generalization across matching tasks. The team plans to release the code for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-21920:
Marco Ardu and Nicola Valori published a research paper in 2025 on what electron dipole experiments truly measure when new physics hides at high energies. Labs hunt the electron's electric dipole moment with molecules, a signal that would prove new sources of matter-antimatter imbalance. In truth, the experiments sense a blend of several effects, not the dipole alone.

Working in the standard effective theory that packages heavy new physics, the pair compute the full blend at leading order. They add selected finer corrections and show the net catches more operator types than earlier work assumed. That widens the discovery reach of tabletop experiments and sharpens how collider and molecule results combine.
arxiv-2503-22020:
Qingqing Zhao and co-authors add visual foresight to robot control models in a 2025 paper. Vision-language-action models learn control from large robot and non-robot data. Most map inputs straight to outputs with no planning step. Complex manipulation suffers from that missing foresight.

Their model, CoT-VLA, first predicts future image frames as visual goals. It then generates a short action sequence to reach those goals. The seven-billion-parameter model handles visual and action tokens together. Real-world manipulation tests beat the prior best model by a wide margin. Simulation benchmarks also improved over the leader. Autoregressive frame prediction supplies the chain of thought. Temporal planning thus enters the control loop explicitly. The authors release a project site with examples. Generalizable robot skills are the long-term aim of the line.
arxiv-2503-22320:
Jannes Kordilla, Marco Dentz, and Juan Hidalgo release a karst flow simulator in twenty twenty-five. Karst systems channel water through networks of underground conduits. Their flow is hard to model because conditions vary wildly inside one network. Flow can switch from free-surface to pressurized, and from laminar to turbulent.

Those transitions can happen at the same time in different branches. The code, openKARST, is open-source and written in Python. It solves the transient dynamic wave equation with an iterative, vectorized scheme. A Preissmann slot handles the shift between free-surface and pressurized flow. Standard friction formulas cover smooth and rough round conduits. Readers in hydrogeology get a public tool for a notoriously unruly flow problem.
arxiv-2503-22420:
Jiangyong Huang and seven co-authors argue in a 2025 paper that current tests for AI models that link 3D scenes and language are flawed. Weak test data, such as vague referring phrases, can give wrong scores. Simple average scores also hide how models cope with varied wording, and tests treat finding objects and answering questions as if they were unrelated.

The team proposes a new benchmark that tests each object many times with clear, natural language. A chain of analysis method checks whether answers rest on solid object finding. Testing current models showed weak generalization on questions and fragile links between finding and answering. Adding large language models, a common practice, actually hurt object finding in their tests.
arxiv-2503-23020:
Tatsuya Yoshida and Eric Gaidos showed that water vapor can save a small planet's atmosphere in a 2025 paper. Sub-Neptunes near low-mass stars are thought to shed their light envelopes under stellar radiation and dwindle into bare super-Earths. Running a coupled flow, radiation, and lab science model of the escaping wind. The authors found water changes the ending: as a fast infrared coolant. More water at the wind's base can cut the escape rate by an order of magnitude.

Waterlogged envelopes then survive billions of years. A ceiling on how much water reaches the upper air could explain why temperate sub-Neptunes vanish faster than closer-in ones. A seeming paradox, and dry birth disks may explain their scarcity around the smallest stars. Telescope tests are put forth.
arxiv-2503-23420:
Massimo Pappalardo, Nguyen Nang Thieu, and Nguyen Dong Yen attack a stubborn optimization puzzle with flowing dynamics in a 2025 paper. Indefinite quadratic programs, where the squared terms can pull both ways, resist the standard tricks and underlie hard decisions in engineering and finance.

Instead of jumping to an answer, the authors let a point flow downhill through a landscape shaped by two classic algorithms. They prove the flow exists, is unique, and settles at points meeting the optimality conditions. One special case gets a full convergence proof. The paper is frankly preliminary, closing with open problems meant to draw other solvers into the flow.
arxiv-2503-23520:
Christian Grussler studies discrete-time systems that keep the shape of repeating signals intact, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. He looks at linear systems that map signals step by step and asks which ones leave certain wave shapes unchanged.

Two nested classes are at stake. One keeps period-wise single-peaked signals single-peaked. The other preserves signals with at most two sign changes per period and keeps constant-sign signals in kind. Grussler finds workable tests for membership in each class, built on total positivity and the shapes of certain curves. The tests also cover feedback loops with common fixed nonlinear parts, such as relays, saturation, and quantizers. The work lays ground for future fixed-point results based on signals.
arxiv-2503-23620:
Maicol Ochoa, writing alone, offers a 2025 theory paper on how electric current flows in very small devices. In such devices, electrons interact with vibrations in the material, and those vibrations can move as fast as the current itself. Older theory often treats the vibrations as fixed, which can miss real effects.

Ochoa builds a simpler form of a standard theory that lets the vibrations change over time with random noise. He then tests the ideas on a tiny dot that charges and drains, and on a model pump that moves single electrons. The results show how the moving vibrations change current and device output.
arxiv-2504-00220:
Liming Wang and co-authors ask whether diffusion models can separate the factors that make up data in two thousand twenty-five. A disentangled code splits apart traits such as shape and color, which aids control and trust. Whether the popular diffusion family learns such splits was open.

Their theory sets terms under which the true factors can be picked out, traces how training moves, and bounds how much data the learning needs. Tests span toy mixtures, image coloring, image cleanup, and voice conversion for speech sorting. Training tweaks drawn from the theory, such as style guidance, steadily improved the split in practice. The work gives a base for building more legible generators.
arxiv-2504-00720:
Jordan Gué, Peter Wolf, and Aurélien Hees present a 2025 physics paper hunting axion dark matter with a space mission. Axions tied to the strong force would pull differently on different materials. That breaks the equivalence principle by a tiny amount. The MICROSCOPE satellite tested that principle in orbit with paired test masses. The authors search its final data release for the axion signal pattern. No positive signal consistent with the model appears.

The null result still bites: upper limits on the axion-gluon coupling improve lab bounds by up to a hundred-fold. The gain covers axion masses from 10^-17 to 10^-13 electron volts. Dark matter hunters get tightened fences in a mass range where few tools reach. Reusing a finished mission's data is also a lesson in thrift. Equivalence tests and dark matter searches turn out to be the same experiment read two ways.
arxiv-2504-00820:
Kevin Wang, Hongqian Niu, Yixin Wang, and Didong Li study deep generative models in a 2025 theory paper. Note that the catalog creator field also lists department names, so the byline in the text governs here. Such models learn complex data patterns and build new high-dimensional samples.

A common belief says the hidden input must be at least as large as the data's true shape dimension. The authors show that belief is wrong, drawing on space-filling curves. Inputs of any size can work, they prove. The cost is a sharp rise in network size, which reveals a trade-off among error, dimension, and model complexity.
arxiv-2504-01020:
Junyu Xie and seven co-authors generated audio descriptions for films by thinking in shots in a 2025 paper. Audio description narrates the visual track for blind viewers, and edited video is built from shots, so the team made shots the unit of work. Context from neighboring shots and film grammar cues like shot scale guide the writing.

The framework wraps around any vision-language model, open or commercial, with add-on expert modules and no retraining. It beat all past training-free methods and even some fine-tuned ones on several benchmarks. A new action score grades how well motion is conveyed. A second protocol asks systems to draft several candidate descriptions for a human to pick, treating them as assistants.
arxiv-2504-01220:
Banafsheh Adami and Nima Karimian wrote a 2025 paper on recovering the heartbeat's shape from face video using a generative adversarial network. Remote photoplethysmography reads tiny color changes in skin to track vital signs without contact. Existing methods often recover only heart rate, blurring the systolic and diastolic features that carry extra health information.

Their network judges candidate signals with three discriminators at once: one in the time domain, one in frequency, and one on the signal's second derivative. Four loss functions shape training, penalizing noise-driven wobbles, misalignment, and wrong spacing between the systolic and diastolic phases. Sparsity and variance terms tune heart rate and spread energy correctly. The goal is a faithful waveform, not just a number. Such detail could widen camera-based health monitoring.
arxiv-2504-01420:
Athena Wen and five co-authors build a bench to test bias in AI resume grading in a 2025 paper. Firms now let language models score job seekers, which raises a sharp fairness worry. Their bench, FAIRE, swaps identity cues in resumes and watches the scores move.

Each model was tested two ways: scoring resumes one by one, and ranking them head to head. Every model showed some bias, but the size and the direction swung widely by model and by trade. The data and code are public. The authors say such benches must gate any hiring use of these models.
arxiv-2504-01520:
Dayasri Ravi and Andreas Groll predict survival times while forcing the model to pick from every data family in a 2025 paper. Cancer data arrive in blocks, gene methylation here, clinical measures there, and blocks repeat themselves internally. Standard penalized regression may drop a whole block, losing its distinct information.

Exclusive Lasso regularization instead selects a subset from each group, respecting the block structure. Plugged into a Cox survival model, it competes variables within groups rather than across the whole pool. On a real cancer data set the approach improved survival prediction over the conventional model. The authors offer it for the common case where data types are individually weak but jointly informative.
arxiv-2504-01620:
Haidong Wu, Snehal Bhayani, and Janne Heikkilä speed up a camera geometry task in this 2025 paper. The perspective-three-point problem finds a camera's position from three known landmarks. Robots and augmented reality systems solve it many times per second. Standard solvers intersect two curves and work through heavy algebra.

Their trick reshapes the coordinate system so one curve becomes a standard parabola. That change lets one unknown be written directly in terms of the other. The needed arithmetic drops, and only real answers need checking. Wide tests showed faster solving with stability matching the best current methods. Small speed gains matter when the solver runs inside a live tracking loop.
arxiv-2504-01820:
Zhihao Tao and Athina Petropulu protect privacy in radar health monitoring in a 2025 paper. Radar can read breathing and heartbeat without touch, a boon for home care. The same echoes could let an eavesdropper steal those vital signs.

Their fix changes the transmitter itself: it switches which antennas are live in a set pattern. That switching adds phase noise that plants false frequencies in an eavesdropper's reading, hiding the true heartbeat and breathing rates. The intended receiver knows the pattern and removes the noise, recovering clean vital signs. Simulations confirm the privacy gain while monitoring stays accurate.
arxiv-2504-02120:
Romain Dagnas, Michel Barbeau, Joaquin Garcia-Alfaro, and Reda Yaich quantify cyber-physical resilience with graph analytics in two thousand twenty-five. Smart infrastructure links tight to the cyber world and draws attacks. Their method models a system as a knowledge graph in layers. Graph metrics then score its resilience potential.

Critical points are parts whose loss can cascade through the system. A water treatment testbed in Singapore serves as the test case. Three resilient designs of it are modeled and compared. Metrics differ in how well they spot the critical points. Attacker knowledge levels shape the final resilience read.
arxiv-2504-02420:
Grzegorz Czechmanowski and three co-authors teach in 2025 a self-driving race policy with reinforcement learning, then run it on a real F1TENTH car. Racing pushes a vehicle to its physical limits, exactly where safety-critical control is hardest. Trial-and-error learning in simulation, hardened by varied conditions, is their route to the track.

The design leans on randomized training conditions, faithful actuator modeling, and a tuned policy network. On the real car, the learned driver beat a state-of-the-art predictive controller outright. It also outran expert human drivers, a first for this class of RC racing. The team dissects which design choices carried the win, offering a recipe for robust learned control in full-size vehicles.
arxiv-2504-02820:
Ibragim Alikhanov, a solo author, proposes a new way to excite a rare particle resonance in a 2025 physics paper. The Glashow resonance is a sharp boost in interactions when an antineutrino hits an electron at just the right energy. Huge ice and water detectors have recorded only a few candidate events after more than a decade of watching.

Alikhanov shows the same resonance could be produced in electron positron colliders, with no neutrino beam at all. One particle emitted at the start converts the incoming positron into the needed antineutrino, in disguise. Twin reactions with muons and other particles are also possible. Future high output lepton colliders could test the resonance in the lab.
arxiv-2504-03020:
Shaoyuan Xu and four co-authors built a sorter that tells a printer what kind of page it is about to print. Printers and copiers tune their ink work by page kind, since text and photos need unlike care. An older sorter from the team split pages three ways: text, photo, or mixed. Some jobs call for a finer split than that.

The new sorter adds four fresh marks read off the page. With them it sorts pages five ways, adding bills and marked-up pages to the old three. The core tool is a support vector machine, a known sorter that learns from set cases. Finer sorting lets the print chain pick the right tune for each page, which guards print grade on mixed stacks of office work.
arxiv-2504-03120:
Haejoon Lee and Dimitra Panagou design control rules for robot teams with bad actors in two thousand twenty-five. A team must agree on a shared state even when some robots lie or fail. Past rules often need a fixed network or full knowledge of all states. Those needs fail in tight spaces where safety also matters.

The pair give a condition for sound agreement in networks that change over time. It rests on how many honest robots each robot can reach. They then build a controller that keeps agreement and avoids crashes. Each robot uses only local facts, with no need for global state. Tests in simulation back the design.
arxiv-2504-03220:
Lifan Hu, a solo author, tackles the reverse task of finding the hidden driver behind a path of poses in a matrix Lie group. Such a path comes from one fixed driver in the group's algebra, stretched over time like a steady twist.

Hu turns the task into a learning problem. Steps between poses are mapped into the algebra, scaled, and fed to a plain neural network that must give back the one driver. The network is trained across four well known groups, for flat and space moves and turns. It stayed true under clean and noisy data, which backs the use of shallow networks here.
arxiv-2504-03520:
Chen Wei Kuo and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on using AI to strip bias out of news articles. Slanted crime and politics coverage bends public opinion, while human moderation is subjective and cannot scale. The team assembled over 30,000 crime articles from five politically diverse outlets across a decade, 2013 to 2023.

Six large language models first scored and justified bias paragraph by paragraph, with human checks anchoring the truth. Then one model rewrote the flagged text in loops, verified by both machines and people. GPT-4o Mini proved best at both spotting and fixing bias. The analysis also mapped how slant shifts across years and regions with real events. The authors offer the pipeline as scalable infrastructure for fairer news.
arxiv-2504-03820:
Chiara Marmo and Stéphane Érard report on new tools for mapping other worlds, in a 2025 conference paper. Map makers need a shared way to mark spots on a planet's surface, just as latitude and longitude do on Earth. Earth map groups, space data groups, and image file standards each grew their own rules, and the rules do not always agree.

The work adds the planet version of these map rules to Astropy, a free code library used by many space scientists. The new parts arrived with Astropy 6.0 and focus on frames fixed to a planet's surface. Such frames help studies of land and air on other worlds. The effort links with wider work on Sun and space weather frames.
arxiv-2504-04320:
Carlos Fernández-Loría argues in a 2025 essay that causal inference is not a special science. Estimating what a treatment causes is usually framed as its own field with its own language. He recasts it as plain prediction under a shift: learn from a source domain, then generalize to a target where outcomes are hidden.

The twist is that the labels, the possible outcomes under each choice, are only partly seen, filtered by who got which treatment. Standard prediction tools like reweighting and domain adaptation then apply directly. Causal assumptions, he says, are not uniquely strong, just more openly stated. The view aims to demystify the field for practitioners and teachers.
arxiv-2504-05020:
Charco Hui and Yalu Wen improve text sorting when training data are scarce in this 2025 paper. Fields like clinical trials often have few labeled texts. A common fix grows the data by rewriting texts while keeping their labels.

Standard sorting treats each rewritten text as if it stood alone, which can add errors. Their method, called Batch Aggregation, models the link between texts grown from the same source. An extra layer pools the results from each linked set before the final call. Tests on several benchmark sets check the gain. The work targets tasks where linked copies are the norm.
arxiv-2504-05120: Vasilis Metaftsis and Dimitra Tsipa compute two deep intersections inside a family of groups built on trees, in a 2025 paper. The groups, generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups with a tree as their underlying graph, are a test bed for group-theoretic structure questions. One intersection runs down the lower central series, a standard chain of subgroups. The other runs through all subgroups whose index is a power of a chosen prime. The paper determines both intersections exactly for this family.
arxiv-2504-05520:
Taiwei Shi, Yiyang Wu, Linxin Song, Tianyi Zhou, and Jieyu Zhao make the final training stage of language models cheaper. In that stage the model practices math problems and learns from rewards, but grinding through problems that are far too easy or hopelessly hard wastes enormous computing time.

Their method watches the model's recent rewards and adjusts the difficulty of the practice set on the fly, keeping problems in the sweet spot: hard, but within reach. The change is a light add-on that needs no new reward design and no change to the model itself. On contest-level math sets it cut training time by as much as half while also lifting the model's final reasoning skill.
arxiv-2504-05820:
Giacomo Magni presents a doctoral thesis, from 2025, on the inner parts of the proton as seen in collider physics. Sharp maps of those parts, called parton distribution functions, set the error bars on every collider forecast. The thesis gathers studies that sharpen those maps with a shared fitting method.

The fits cover both plain and spin-linked maps of the proton's parts. They add higher-order corrections from the strong force theory and count the doubt from the theory itself. One study weighs whether the proton holds charm quarks of its own. The work feeds the hunt for new physics at high-energy colliders, where a soft map can hide or fake a signal.
arxiv-2504-07920:
Julia Meusel, Matthias Müller-Hannemann, and Klaus Reinhardt mapped the hardness of designing train and bus timetables in 2025. A periodic timetable repeats through the day, and its quality is caught by a grid of promised fastest travel times between major stops. Realization asks whether departure times exist achieving at least those promises. Requiring exact equality is too rigid, so the authors add a slack setting bounding the waiting time any fastest path may include. And they allow each direction of a link its own departure time, as real networks do.

Restricting to tree-shaped networks, they give a complete characterization of when the realization problem is easy and when it is hard. As a function of just two amounts: the period length and the minimum slack. Such a full hardness landscape tells timetable builders exactly which relaxations buy them a lean method.
arxiv-2504-08020:
Bi and co-authors present a 2025 method that teaches image models to tell apart fine classes, like bird species, in new places they have never seen. Fine classes differ by tiny marks that fade when light or color shifts between places. Their method first invents fresh styles for training images to widen the mix.

Style shifted copies are then mapped into a curved math space that tracks higher order patterns. Pulling the pre and post shift codes close in that space strips style's grip on the fine marks. On three test sets for the task, the method set new best scores. The authors frame style invention as cheap practice for the unseen.
arxiv-2504-08120:
Daniil Larionov and co-authors test in a 2025 paper how well reasoning language models judge translations and summaries. Reasoning models shine at logic tasks, yet judging generated text is a different skill. No prior study had scored them on this evaluation work.

Eight models entered, from flagship reasoning systems to distilled small ones and plain rivals. Tests ran on a 2023 translation benchmark and a standard summary rating set. One maker's mini models improved as reasoning deepened on translation judging. The other flagship generally trailed its plain twin, bar one summary consistency task. Distilled models held up to 32 billion parameters, then fell off hard at 8 billion.
arxiv-2504-08220:
Elizabeth Bersson, Kate Hoffman, Heather Stapleton, and David Dunson improve estimates of how chemical exposures vary together in two thousand twenty-five. Their test case is a study of toddlers' contact with flame-retardant-like chemicals indoors. Small samples make raw co-variation estimates shaky, and common Bayesian tools shrink them too far toward zero.

Their method is a factor model that also reads each chemical's traits, such as its class and structure. Those traits guide the shrinkage toward richer patterns rather than a flat diagonal. Grouping chemicals by class, the older fix, can hide fine links. The feature-aware route keeps detail while still steadying the estimate, as the toddler data show.
arxiv-2504-08620:
Emmanuel Azuh Mensah and four co-authors build a leaner species spotter for field cameras in a 2025 paper. Conservation teams want smart cameras that name animals on the spot, without sending images away, but modern vision models are heavy for small devices. The team asks whether a model can run only the parts it needs, chosen by where on Earth it sits.

Their single detector uses conditional computation: sub-networks act like local experts, and the model leans on the experts that fit the camera's geography. A pruning step trims the expert set for each location ahead of time. Tested on two globe-spanning wildlife data sets, the approach kept detection quality while cutting the computing bill. The authors aim the work at near-sensor insight for ecology, where power and bandwidth are scarce.
arxiv-2504-08920:
Nicolas Garrel, a solo author, describes all Witt invariants of quaternionic forms, in a 2025 math paper. These forms are anti-hermitian forms over a quaternion algebra with its standard involution. Witt invariants are special functions on such forms that stay unchanged under certain equivalences.

Garrel shows the invariants are built from defined lambda-power operations, much as in the classic theory of quadratic forms. Unlike that classic case, the module of invariants is not free over those operations, so relations among them matter. The proof extends scalars to a field where the algebra splits and tracks residues at special points. The result also covers orthogonal groups of related algebras.
arxiv-2504-09020:
Debshikha Banerjee and four co-authors study electron pairing traces in a one dimensional model in this 2025 physics paper. The model joins electron interaction with a coupling to lattice vibration, and carries a long name: the extended Hubbard–Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. The team computed the spectrum for adding one electron, in the dilute limit, with a numerical method called density matrix renormalization group. They compared singlet and triplet channels.

A strange spectral feature showed up only in the singlet channel. A check against perturbation theory, in the limit where the lattice responds fast, tied the feature to a known attraction. That attraction comes from strong electron interaction carried by the lattice coupling. The team tracked the feature as doping rose. Their results give predictions for what future spectrum searches should look for. They frame it as a leftover fingerprint of pairing.
arxiv-2504-09320:
Yingxiang Hu, Mohammad N. Ivaki, and Julian Scheuer settle a shape question in pure math in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The question is a form of the Christoffel-Minkowski problem, now set for curved shapes that meet a flat wall at a fixed angle. Such shapes are called capillary shapes in the work.

An older result by Guan and Ma showed when a given bend rule comes from a smooth closed shape. The team proves the same kind of result for the wall case, for angles below a right angle. If the rule meets two plain tests, it does come from a strict curved shape. Readers who work on curved shapes get a clean existence result.
arxiv-2504-10220:
Pavlyuchenkov and Akimkin refine a model of heat in young planet-forming disks, in a 2025 paper. Such disks are flat rings of gas and dust around new stars. Their heat map sets where ice and rock form. The base model spreads radiation by a diffusion trick and treats starlight apart. Averaging light traits over all wavelengths, though, blurs the heat map.

The new model splits star and disk light into bands, each with its own traits. Its heat profile across the disk then bends in slope like top-grade Monte Carlo runs show. It also catches vertical heat shifts near the midplane that the old model missed. Settling times shrink, a fact modelers of young disks must heed.
arxiv-2504-10420:
Lithium projectiles breaking up on a heavy thorium target are modeled by Patel, Rangel, and Lubian in a 2025 paper. Both electric and nuclear forces tear the light lithium nuclei apart, and their interplay matters near the energy barrier. The team runs coupled-channel calculations with short-range absorption for the fragments.

Their setup matches measured elastic scattering patterns better than the standard choice. Turning on the target's own excitation changes scattering strongly below the barrier, less above it. Breakup rates for the lighter lithium isotope exceed those for the heavier one across energies. Interference between the two breakup routes proves destructive in the studied range. Nuclear theorists gain a cleaner read on breakup near barriers.
arxiv-2504-10620:
Srivathsan Amruth presents a 2025 method to cut the size of a data set while keeping its patterns in view. The hard case in view has three traits at once: few items per class, many traits per item, and few items in all. Standard cuts can lose the very patterns that make such sets worth study.

The method maps a high-dim ball of data onto a flat, many-sided shape that can be drawn and read. Its build leans on geometry rules adapted to the grid world of computers. The aim is not just to shrink the data but to show hidden trends in a form a user can grasp. The author frames it as a core tool for modern data work on small, rich sets.
arxiv-2504-11020:
Siddharth Mehrotra and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on trust in AI used for predictive policing. Such tools guess where crime may occur. Users can trust them too much or too little, and both skew acts. Past work said that giving reasons for a call can tune trust to the right level. The team tests text, visual, and mixed forms of reasons.

Retired police staff and lay users took part. Mixed reasons raised how much expert users said they trusted the tool. Yet no form led to better choices, and none built apt trust. The authors urge a rethink of reason giving in high risk tools. They close with policy hints for such systems.
arxiv-2504-11720:
Pritchard and three co-authors spot sky noise with spike nets that read wave spin in this twenty twenty-five paper. Man-made noise plagues sky ears and grows as their reach and sky traffic grow. Spike nets run on time flow, which fits the pulse of such noise well.

Inside, spin facts from the wave join the time facts the net reads per blip. Fake data from a known sky rig drills the net for its first tests. First scores hit the top band for noise catch truth in those runs. Power draws for brain-chip runs of the net are gauged as well. The team sees big fuel saves if the net ships on such chips.
arxiv-2504-12020:
Six authors present MixSignGraph in 2025, a graph network for sign language tasks. Standard image backbones read edges and texture well but miss how hand and face zones work as a team. Their model turns sign clips into mixed graphs read by three graph parts.

One part links zones inside each frame, one tracks zones across frames, and one stacks zones across detail grades. A text-driven pre-training step makes fake gloss tags from text tags for gloss-free sets. Tests on five public sets beat top rivals on many sign tasks with no extra cues.
arxiv-2504-12120:
Gernot Akemann, Francesco Mezzadri, Patricia Passler, and Henry Taylor study random matrices in a 2025 paper. Their ensemble mixes normal and chi-distributed entries in a three-band complex matrix. The spread of its eigenvalues, or spectral density, is the core target. Past work covered a related ensemble from two of the authors.

The team finds the limiting density when both a power and the matrix size grow large. In the cold, large-power limit the ensemble reduces to a centered matrix with zero diagonal. A theorem from free probability then yields the density from polynomial coefficients. The result is radially symmetric on a disc and follows a log law in radius. A symmetric twin ensemble gives the same density. Computer runs confirm the formulas. Local spacing checks also match two-dimensional Poisson behavior for this ensemble.
arxiv-2504-12620:
Xiaolan Hu and co-authors colored signed graphs in a 2025 math paper. In a signed graph, each link carries a plus or minus sign, and a good coloring must keep each color class free of unbalanced cycles.

The graphs here are subcubic, meaning each point has at most three links. The authors show that every such signed graph takes a balanced coloring with a certain fractional palette. There is one exception: a four point complete graph with all signs negative, and graphs that can be flipped into it. For that lone exception, they pin down the best possible colorings.
