Fractional coloring lets a point hold several colors at once, in fixed shares.
arxiv-2504-12720:
Huanhuan Zou, Zongwei Li, and Xiaoqi Li study in 2025 how machine learning can spot malicious code hidden in smart contracts. These self-running programs now handle finance, supply chains, and connected devices, so hidden bad code can cost users money or crash systems. Their paper focuses on the first step of detection: turning contract code into numbers a model can learn from.

The team worked at the level of the contracts' operation codes. They grouped and simplified the codes by their structure, then turned them into vectors in two ways, one that counts short code pairs and one that weighs rare codes more heavily. They compared that route with applying the same two methods to raw codes directly. A chain of classifiers then handled the final detection task. The training results judge which feature route works better.
arxiv-2504-12820:
Drozda, Hellwing, and Bilicki present a paper from twenty twenty-five on using skewness of galaxy counts to test gravity. Simulations compare Einstein gravity with two modified rivals. Counts in cells measure how lumpy matter, halos, and galaxies are. Distance errors from galaxy motion suppress the lumpiness signal. One modified model still deviates clearly in galaxy samples. Its gap reaches about two-sigma significance in their runs. The ratio between distorted and true skewness barely depends on gravity type.

True-space predictions can thus forecast observed skewness reliably. Coming galaxy surveys gain a new gravity test. Screening mechanisms in the rival models frame the comparison.
arxiv-2504-13120:
Yongqian Peng and co-authors probe whether sight-word models can blend known thoughts in fresh ways, and steer them to do so. The work dates to 2025. Blend flair counts as a core mark of mind. New models spark fights on whether their outs show true blend or mere match of past prints.

Their frame splits blend in three acts: spot the source thoughts, pull their shared traits, and draw fresh sense. A set of near seven hundred art-made mash prints, tagged by the frame, grounds the tests. Top models beat mean folks at read tasks yet trailed pros. The frame in the make pipe lifted outs' flair grade.
arxiv-2504-13720:
Michel Berthier and co-authors model color perception in a 2025 paper as a relativistic phenomenon. Light entering the eye becomes perceived color through receptors and opponent channels in the brain, so perception depends on both scene and observer, much like measurement in physics. A physicist argued this analogy from experiment in 1962, but a rigorous theory was missing.

Their model rests on a quantum-style reading of color vision plus one axiom that sums up three-receptor vision in an algebraic frame. From that base they reconcile three-color theory with the opponent theory of Hering. They also derive the relativistic traits of perceived colors with no extra assumptions, giving the old claim a full mathematical footing.
arxiv-2504-14120:
Ricardo Fitas reviews how AI can make early schooling fairer for all children. The chapter from twenty twenty-five notes that young classes now mix many home tongues and many skill levels. AI tools can help teachers close those gaps. The review covers two broad tool classes.

One class aids language, with live translation for mixed-tongue rooms. The other class adapts lessons for children with special needs. Fitas weighs what these tools mean for teachers' roles and daily load. He notes gains seen so far, such as stronger student engagement. He also flags risks: uneven access to the tools, and the need for fair, safe use. The chapter ends with hands-on advice for teachers, policy makers, and tool builders.
arxiv-2504-14220:
Jukka Ruohonen, Kalle Rindell, and Simone Busetti wrote a 2025 paper on how European Union law now treats cyber security crises, not just incidents. Incident management is a classic security topic. Lately the EU has asked when an incident becomes a crisis, and its new laws encode an answer.

Reading the laws and policy documents, the authors find crises defined as large-scale incidents that overwhelm one member state or hit at least two. The new laws sharply expand mandatory incident reporting, including for such large events. New governance bodies were created as well. Even so, how crisis management would actually work at the EU level stays unclear. The paper maps this legal shift and opens research questions with practical stakes for governments and operators.
arxiv-2504-14320:
Nimisha Karnatak and co-authors build a design tool that helps small business owners create ads with generative AI beyond plain text prompts, in work from twenty twenty-five. Novice users often struggle to put brand feel into words. Output then comes out generic and hard to fine tune.

A study with six United Kingdom business owners named three pain points: stating brand intuition, making fine edits, and getting brand true results. The tool answers with three input panels for branding, audience and goals, and an inspiration board. Users feed context and visual taste in a structured way. The work shows how guided interfaces can lift co creative control for novice designers.
arxiv-2504-14720:
Berger and three colleagues gauge video call quality from scrambled network traffic in twenty twenty-five. Network firms need to know if calls look and sound good, but scrambling hides the app's own quality scores. Past tools learned from scores that not all apps will share. Their method reads quality straight from traffic traits, with no need for the app's help.

They built a data set from WhatsApp calls run under varied network states. It holds about seven hours of traffic plus matched quality scores. Their method called frame rates within a small margin most of the time. It also sorted image quality grades with high success. The approach should port to other call apps.
arxiv-2504-15320:
Qinghao Li and four colleagues design a driving planner for highway ramps, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Merging on a ramp forces an automated vehicle to balance safety against efficiency. Change lanes too late and traffic suffers; change carelessly and collisions loom.

Their integrated planner attacks both sides of the trade-off. An unsatisfaction level metric scores efficiency, with the vehicle's velocity as a key factor. Arrow-cluster-based sampling then evaluates candidate lane-changing curves for collision risk. The planner picks both the right moment and a safe curve. Extensive simulations in a ramp scenario verified the design. The vehicle completed its maneuvers efficiently and without collisions in the reported tests.
arxiv-2504-15820:
Friedman and Gal test, in twenty twenty-five, whether a recent signal of a bound state between a Xi particle and a nucleus fits other such signals. Xi particles are heavy, short-lived particles with two strange quarks. A Japanese experiment recently hinted at a Xi bound to a boron nucleus, held by a stated binding energy. The authors use a density-dependent optical potential, a model for how the Xi feels the nucleus, to check which assignments of past capture events fit that signal.

They find only the new boron assignment works as a ground-state case, unless the potential has an oddly strong repulsive part. That supports reassigning older nitrogen capture events to a different Xi charge and orbit. They then fix the potential depth at normal nuclear density.
arxiv-2504-16020:
Soham Sane introduces AlphaGrad, a lean optimizer that normalizes gradients through a smooth squashing curve. Adaptive methods like Adam carry heavy memory and many knobs to tune. AlphaGrad rescales each tensor's gradient to unit length, then passes it through a tanh curve. One steepness parameter steers the whole method.

A formal proof guarantees stationarity on non-convex problems. Trials span three reinforcement learning styles against Adam. Off-policy DQN training wobbled and sometimes failed. TD3 stayed competitive with careful steepness tuning. On-policy PPO shone, beating Adam by a clear margin. The lesson is fit between optimizer and algorithm, not a universal crown.
arxiv-2504-16120:
Chaima Njeh, Haïfa Nakouri, and Fehmi Jaafar cleaned up toxic model output after making in a 2025 paper. Rather than retrain a text model or craft defensive prompts, their data-centric method passes finished text through a corrective model based on BART. Rewrites threatening or toxic content into safer form while keeping the answer usable. The filter sits downstream, so it can guard models the team does not control.

Across several toxic data sets and four well-known models, toxicity and jailbreak success scores fell by double-digit percentages in most pairings. Gains varied by model, with some jailbreak scores dropping only slightly. A post-making corrector offers deployers a useful safety layer that works today.
arxiv-2504-16220:
The Steenrod algebra is a central tool in algebraic topology, and its motivic versions track deep patterns in the field's computations. Daniel Isaksen and co-authors study one sparse family of elements in the complex-motivic version in this 2025 paper.

The family stands out for unusual repeating patterns, spaced far apart compared with typical families. It ties to two other landmarks: a localization process that isolates certain elements, and the algebraic shadow of a spectrum built from modular forms. Short as the paper is, it maps a curious corner of a major computational chart and links it to questions other researchers are chasing.
arxiv-2504-16620:
Haoran Liu and co-authors probe a charge pattern in a kagome superconductor in a 2025 paper. The material, KV3Sb5, hosts many odd states at once, and the force behind its charge density wave is still debated. Tangled effects have made the cause hard to isolate.

Using fast laser pulses and angle-resolved photo tools, the team split the electron response from the lattice response. A folded band from lattice shift stayed present up to 150 degrees, well above the ordering point near 78 degrees. Pulse-driven shifts matched heat-driven shifts at that lower point. The findings favor a lattice-driven wave that flickers far above the final ordered state.
arxiv-2504-16820:
Anuj Dawar, Erich Grädel, Leon Kullmann, and Benedikt Pago published this paper in 2025. It studies symmetry inside mathematical proofs. Their arena is the Ideal Proof System, where proofs are algebraic circuits, and they ask which statements admit proofs that respect the symmetries of the problem.

The question links to a famous open problem: telling whether two graphs are the same up to relabeling. The authors connect symmetric proofs to the power of logics that can count and recurse, and to a model of computing that makes no arbitrary choices. They weigh trade-offs between symmetry and proof size, degree, and linearity. Test cases include the pigeonhole principle, subset sum, and a hard family of graphs built to fool algorithms. For several of these, symmetric proofs turn out surprisingly small.
arxiv-2504-16920:
Jacob Zavatone-Veth, Blake Bordelon, and Cengiz Pehlevan review a theory of learning in two thousand twenty-five. Making sense of huge neural recordings during learning is hard. Theories from statistical physics suggest a fix: for a given task, a small set of summary statistics often suffices to predict performance as a network learns.

The authors survey recent progress on such statistics in artificial networks. They then argue the same lens can sharpen analysis of brain data. Tracking a few well-chosen numbers may reveal how representations change while skill grows. The perspective aims to connect artificial and biological learning under one framework. It offers experimentalists a principled way to compress complex activity into interpretable signals.
arxiv-2504-17020:
Kasper Engelen, Guillermo Pérez, and Shrisha Rao wrote this 2025 computer science paper on parametric Markov chains. These chains model systems whose chance of each step is not fully known, since some probabilities are left as parameters. Checking reachability claims for such systems is known to be very hard in theory.

One easier angle is monotonicity, asking whether raising a parameter never lowers a reachability chance. The authors first show that this question can be turned into a comparison of two states and their reachability chances. Recent results on that comparison then give a fast way to merge states that share the same value. They built the method and tested it on known and custom benchmarks. Merging shrank some known cases and cut custom cases by large amounts.
arxiv-2504-17220:
Feng and co-authors ask whether knowledge distillation helps large language models build product bundles. Language models can reason well enough to suggest bundles, but their size makes training and use costly. Distillation moves skill from a big teacher model to a small student. The team studies the process in a systematic way. Three questions lead: how format, amount, and use of distilled knowledge each affect results.

Their framework extracts knowledge in stages from the teacher. It then tests how the student best absorbs it. The goal is bundle quality near the teacher's at far lower cost. Findings speak to any task where small models must inherit big ones' judgment.
arxiv-2504-17820:
Dorje Brody and Tomooki Yuasa prove in 2025 a boomerang effect in information theory: fake news can end up pushing a careful reader the opposite way from what its spreader intended. Their setting combines two sources on one topic, one genuine and one carrying disinformation, read by someone unaware of the plant.

Two conditions flip the poison into antidote. The genuine source must be sharp relative to its noise, and the noise in the two sources must rise and fall together. Then the disinformation's effect reverses sign, moving the receiver against the lie. The result offers a mathematical defense worth understanding.
arxiv-2504-18020:
Guyue Hu and co-authors teach hospitals to train one shared model for cutting organs out of X-ray scans, without pooling their private data. Each site trains locally and shares only model updates, but sites differ a lot, which can make joint training wobble.

Their frame adds a small adapter tuned to each client site. The adapter draws on a big pretrained medical model to steady the training. It splits into a shared part and a site part, updated in step at world and local level. Tests on three large data sets show steadier, site fit results than a single global model can give.
arxiv-2504-18620:
Natalia Lahén, Thorsten Naab, Antti Rantala, and Christian Partmann simulate the birth of a massive star cluster in a 2025 astronomy paper. The setting is a crash between two gas-rich dwarf galaxies, rendered star by star. Ancient globular clusters were born in crowds this dense, but telescopes cannot see inside their birth sites. The simulation includes gas phases, starlight, winds, and exploding stars, plus collisions between stars.

Bound clusters up to two hundred thousand solar masses form with tight cores. The biggest one nears the extreme densities telescopes report in the young universe. Stars collide and merge inside it, stacking the deck toward giant stars. The run shows how present-day cluster shapes may be fossils of such violent births.
arxiv-2504-18920:
Pattern matching lets a program pick a branch by the shape of its data, a feature shared by many language families. David Binder and Lean Ermantraut argue in 2025 that the usual rule, try each clause in order until one fits, makes programs depend on clause order. Their fix gives patterns a logic of their own, in which the opposite of a pattern can also be written.

With that algebra, a match no longer needs its clauses in a set order. A new default clause covers the leftover cases without breaking that freedom. The authors show the design in a formal way, as an extended version of their work. They aim it at language designers who want matching that reads as facts, not as a queue.
arxiv-2504-19220: Eita Haibara wrote a 2025 set of research memos, the second in a series on stable symplectic structured spaces, an abstract setting the author is developing in algebraic geometry. The memos build a scheme theory adapted to that setting. Within it, Haibara defines symplectic motives and a matching motivic cohomology theory. The text is a research announcement: it lays out definitions and claims a new research direction rather than reporting completed proofs or experiments.
arxiv-2504-19620:
Stefano Trivini led a large team studying superconductivity in graphene in a 2025 paper. When a superconductor touches a normal metal, pairing effects can spread into the metal. In graphene, a single-atom-thick carbon sheet, that spread can be tuned by changing its charge. The team wanted to see how far the effect reaches.

Using a fine scanning probe, they moved lead islands on graphene to build junctions with gaps they could adjust. At some charge levels the paired state stayed local, and at others it spread as one shared state. Theory showed that how well the contact passes current decides the strength and reach of the pairing.
arxiv-2504-19720:
Ranran Zhen and nine co-authors survey efficient inference serving for large language models. These models carry vast parameter counts and heavy attention costs, which makes low latency and high throughput serving hard. Rapid research progress calls for a comprehensive map of the solution space.

At the instance level the survey reviews model placement, request scheduling, decoding length prediction, storage management, and the disaggregation paradigm. At the cluster level it covers graphics processor deployment, multi instance load balancing, and cloud service solutions. Emerging scenarios are organized by tasks, modules, and auxiliary methods. Niche but critical areas receive attention too, and the survey closes with open research directions for the field.
arxiv-2504-20320:
People are turning to chatbots for mental health support, and a 2025 paper by Kyuha Jung and co-authors studies that trend through Reddit posts. Users wrote about late-night talks with ChatGPT on hard personal issues. The team read those posts and comments to learn what people value and fear in such talks.

Many users prize the bot as a safe space with no judgment, open at any hour. They report advice, comfort, and help planning hard talks or therapy steps. Risks also appear: wrong health advice, praise that feels too easy, and privacy worries. The authors weigh what these tools should and should not do in daily care and in clinics.
arxiv-2504-20720:
Folding clothes is easy for people and hard for robots, since garments crumple into countless shapes. Yiming Liu and co-authors propose a general model for the task in this 2025 paper, built on the folding structure that stays visible as cloth moves. They turn that structure into a compact graph that stands for the garment's state.

Image segmentation sorts out which parts hide which, and keypoint detection anchors the graph. A graph neural network then learns how the graph evolves, and its predictions feed a control law through a deformation matrix. Tests with jackets show the system can read and fold complex clothing even when parts cover each other. The authors aim at one model that folds many garments, not one trick per item.
arxiv-2504-20920:
Golubeva, writing alone, models how antideuterons collide with atomic nuclei in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Antideuterons are rare antimatter nuclei of interest in cosmic ray searches near Earth. Predicting how they shatter inside nuclei sets the background for those searches.

Golubeva applies an intranuclear cascade model across a wide energy range and many target nuclei. The computed inelastic cross sections match the ALICE experiment's data on tantalum well. A Monte Carlo generator built from the model can simulate these collisions for experiment planning. The work supports efforts to spot a few antideuterons against a large ordinary background. Agreement with the one measured case lends the predictions weight.
arxiv-2504-21320:
Tanaka, Prabhu, Kapadia, and Suyama proposed a way to spot lensed gravitational waves in twenty twenty-five without assuming a lens model. Gravitational lensing bends waves from merging black holes or neutron stars, and finding such events would map matter, including dark matter halos. None has been confidently found yet.

Two hurdles block the search: the source and lens shapes are unknown beforehand, and some unlensed events can mimic lensing. The authors invoke the Kramers-Kronig relation, a causality rule from physics. Lensing systems, as linear response systems, must obey it whatever their structure. Unlensed events generally need not. Checking the relation could therefore certify lensing while rejecting mimics. The paper lays first steps and tests the idea under idealized conditions.
arxiv-2504-21520:
Springer and co-authors release a test set for finding where functions begin inside Windows program files, a basic step in studying compiled code. Prior work leaned on Linux files, leaving Windows formats thinly covered. Their 2025 dataset, FuncPEval, covers a browser and a known ransomware sample, with hand-checked truth for more than a million function starts.

They grade five rule-based and three learning-based tools on the set. One rule-based tool tops the accuracy chart on the 64-bit browser, while a learning tool nearly matches it and runs far faster. Random filler bytes between functions hurt nearly all tools, some badly. The team improves two learning tools, lifting their scores by about ten percent. Padding behavior, they argue, deserves more study.
arxiv-2504-21620:
Benjamin Jauregui, Pedro Montealegre, and Ivan Rapaport give a deterministic distributed algorithm that finds cycle separators in planar graphs, and with them a depth-first search tree, in a paper from 2025. In distributed computing, many machines each hold one graph vertex and must cooperate by passing short messages. Random methods were the best known for this task.

A cycle separator is a ring of vertices whose removal splits the graph into balanced parts, enabling divide and conquer. Their algorithm computes one recursively in near-diameter time, with no coin flips. A depth-first tree then follows in the same time, matching the best randomized result and the known lower limit up to small factors. Other planar problems fall to the same machinery.
arxiv-2505-00020:
Sruly Rosenblat, Tim O'Reilly, and Ilan Strauss probe in 2025 whether a top AI model was trained on paywalled books. Their test set was thirty-four copyrighted books from one publisher, lawfully obtained. A membership test checks if a model treats a text as one it has seen before, rather than as new writing.

The newer, larger model showed patterns that fit recognition of the non-public books, they report, with a strong but uncertain score. The wide doubt range reflects the small book count. A smaller sibling model showed little recognition of any of the publisher's content. The authors call for more openness from AI firms on training sources, and for clear licensing paths. Their method offers one way to audit claims with data, not trust.
arxiv-2505-00420:
Shock waves in fluids obey conservation laws whose rough solutions may not be unique, a scandal the theory has lived with for decades. Alberto Bressan and co-authors carve out a uniqueness island in a 2025 paper for two-by-two systems. Their solutions start small and, crucially, calm down fast: their total variation fades faster than the classic rate.

Within that fast-calming class, solutions depend on the starting data in a Hölder-continuous way, with the exponent pushed close to one by shrinking the data. They also exhibit starting profiles that achieve the fast calming. The result sharpens what Glimm and Lax began in 1970.
arxiv-2505-00520:
Tuva Bardal, Markus Brill, David McCune, and Jannik Peters measure how proportional ranked elections truly are in a 2025 paper. Voters rank candidates, and the single transferable vote is the most used proportional rule for such ballots. Its claim rests on an axiom about large solid coalitions backing a shared ranking.

Real data from Scottish local elections show such coalitions almost never reach the needed size. That gap prompts the team to build numeric measures of proportionality instead of axiom checks alone. They score several rules on real ballots with those measures. They also test how cut off ballots skew the outcomes by filling them in artificially.
arxiv-2505-00620:
Erdenebayar Bayarmagnai and co-authors tackle a hard task in program checking, in work from 2025. Rather than test a loop against a fixed trait, they build loops that are sure to hold the trait. Past tools could only build plain loops with no guard terms and with traits of a fixed shape.

Their method uses tools from algebraic geometry to turn the task into a set of equations. The answers to those equations match exactly the loops that keep the stated traits. A solver then finds those answers in set regions of the number plane. The team built the method into working software.
arxiv-2505-00820:
Zhaoxing Li and co-authors published this study in 2025. It frames HMCF, a system where language models coordinate teams of robots with a human on standby. Multi-robot teams struggle with varied machines, new settings, and safety. Each robot here carries its own model agent that knows its skills. The agent turns broad tasks into steps the robot can run. Checks on each plan, plus human supervision, cut the risk of confident nonsense.

In simulations, the framework beat leading task planners, lifting success rates by about five percent. Real-world trials showed it could take on fresh tasks and mixed settings with little human input. People step in only when the system flags a need. The authors pitch the design for jobs like disaster response, where teams must scale fast and stay safe.
arxiv-2505-01120:
Kutay Tire, Berk Cakar, and Eray Tuzun test whether cleaning training data improves machine-written pull request summaries in a 2025 paper. Pull requests are how coders propose changes, and their written summaries guide reviewers. Many are empty, vague, or off-topic, which poisons the data used to train summary-writing models.

The team gathered over 169,000 pull requests from 513 GitHub projects and built four rules to filter the noise. They then trained four known models on the raw data and on the cleaned data. Cleaned training lifted standard quality scores by roughly nine percent across the board. Human readers also rated the cleaned-data summaries as clearer and more on point. The best model was BART. The authors offer the cleaning rules as a base for better coding assistants.
arxiv-2505-01220:
Zhazira Zhumabay and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, how to shape a messy wave guide so waves pass it in full at all tones. The trick is to design from the back: start with one tone that passes clean, with set in and out shapes. The guide is kept mirror-even, which cuts the search cost and leaves room for more rules. Steps then widen the pass band: first a flat-top form at a still point, then thin filters, then a wide band where each tone slips through, a rainbow act. Dice-like stacks of parts stand in for the mess.

Runs by a pair-dip math were proved in a microwave guide with clay and metal bits. Wide pass through walls is the prize they name.
arxiv-2505-01320:
Barisi Kogam, Yevgeniya Kovalchuk, and Mohamed Gaber build a search method that copies how gut bacteria hunt food. Bacteria swarm, feed, and breed in cycles that balance wide search with close focus. Their method, called ABCO, runs those three stages in a loop and can bend its rules per task. Such nature-led methods vie to solve hard tuning tasks where exact math is too slow.

The team raced ABCO against two known swarm methods on a set of test tasks with known best scores. ABCO ran far faster than both rivals in their runs. Its scores matched the rivals where time was tight, and beat both where time was free to spend. The speed edge held across the test set in full. Code traits that let users bend the stages are laid out for reuse.
arxiv-2505-01420:
Mary Phuong and co-authors build tripwires for a feared AI behavior: scheming, where a model secretly pursues goals against its makers' intent. Before a model could scheme successfully, it would need two skills: stealth, reasoning about how to slip past oversight, and situational awareness, reasoning about itself, its training, and its deployment. The team wrote five stealth tests and eleven awareness tests.

Run on today's frontier models, none showed worrying levels of either skill. That null result is the point: the suite anchors a safety case arguing a model that fails these tests cannot scheme in deployment. The authors offer the evaluations as pre-release evidence, a way to rule out harm before it can happen.
arxiv-2505-01520:
Feeding is a daily struggle for many autistic children, with most experiencing significant difficulties around food. Christopher Cofie Kuzagbe and co-authors review the phone apps meant to help their parents, in a 2025 analysis. They searched the Apple and Google stores in late 2024 using fifteen terms.

Of 326 apps found, only two met all their tests: English language, free, recently updated, aimed at autism feeding, reachable in Africa, and downloaded more than a hundred times. No Android app qualified. Both chosen apps taught, trained, and rewarded in several ways, but neither covered the full range of behavior strategies. Ratings showed decent usability, with sensory-friendly routines among the strengths. Neither app had clinical testing behind it. The authors call the gap striking.
arxiv-2505-01620:
Bruno Celiz, Julio Navarro, Mario Abadi, and Volker Springel use the TNG50 simulation to ask why heavier galaxies spin in discs while dwarfs stay puffy. In the simulation, rotational support rises steadily with stellar mass, from pressure-supported dwarf spheroids to big disc galaxies. The team traces it to where stars are born inside each galaxy.

Star formation concentrates in two zones: a compact, non-rotating central clump and an outer rotating disc, with a quiet gap between. Dwarfs are dominated by the clump, which is why they all end up about the same size and barely rotate; big galaxies grow their discs outward over time. The authors are candid that the clump is likely an artifact of the simulation's recipe for gas physics and wind feedback, which preserves clumps and disrupts nearby disc growth. Their moral: read TNG50's dwarf morphologies and size evolution with caution.
arxiv-2505-01720:
Saeed Ahmed and Javed Hussain prove that a noisy pattern-forming equation always has a global weak solution, in this 2025 paper. The equation models how patterns arise in nature, here boxed in by a constraint and driven by a special kind of noise. Their solutions are of the martingale kind, built on a rich probability space.

Energy-style bounds tame the wild terms first. A tightness test then keeps the approximating solutions from scattering. A general form of a classic limit theorem lets the team pass to the true solution. The work extends the safety net for a family of stochastic equations used in physics.
arxiv-2505-02220:
Pooling health studies boosts power, but each lab's biomarker reads carry its own slant. Yujie Wu and co-authors give a pooling method that corrects that slant in a 2025 paper. Their setting is matched case-control studies with grouped biomarker levels.

A likelihood method folds each study's calibration step into the pooled fit. A sandwich estimator then gives honest error bars for the pooled effects. Simulations across sample sizes show the method behaves well. The team applies it to a vitamin D and colon cancer pooling project. The recipe lets groups merge data without pretending the labs agreed.
arxiv-2505-02520:
Callum Jones and Shruti Paranjape trace the hidden zeros and smooth splitting of scattering amplitudes to a simple recursion trick. Their 2025 paper spans four theories, from scalar models to the special Galileon. Recent work found amplitudes vanishing or splitting at odd kinematic points, with no clear origin.

A new linear shift in kinematic space sets up a contour argument in the style of on-shell recursion. Standard factorization plus better high-energy behavior does the rest. For two theories the shift proves the good behavior; for a third it stays a conjecture. Looser near-zero settings yield wider splitting formulas, including a triple-product limit. Four-dimensional zeros get a full compatibility study. The Galileon case also splits, the authors show.
arxiv-2505-02820:
Judging an AI agent by task success alone is coarse. Hao Zhu and co-authors propose AutoLibra, which turns open-ended human comments into fine-grained metrics. A remark like 'the button was disabled, stop clicking it' becomes a scored behavior. The framework grounds each comment in the agent's recorded actions. Similar praise and complaints are clustered. Each cluster becomes a metric with a definition and examples, scored by a model judge.

Two meta-metrics rate the metric set itself: coverage of the feedback and redundancy among metrics. Tuning for both produced sharper metrics than older benchmarks offered. The authors also use the metrics to coach prompt writers and to let agents self-improve.
arxiv-2505-02920:
Giant black holes grow with their home galaxies, and Francesco Shankar and co-authors probe that link in a 2025 paper. The team uses a fresh sample of nearby quiet galaxies with direct black hole mass measures and uniform photo data. Instead of raw trends, they study leftovers from paired trends to find which galaxy trait tracks black hole mass most tightly.

Star speed spread in the galaxy core tracks best, with the dark matter halo mass close behind. Bulge mass shows a weaker secondary link. Learning model tests back the ranking. The result narrows the hunt for the true driver of the black hole and galaxy partnership, a long open question in astronomy.
arxiv-2505-03020:
AI systems that read images, text, and tables together beat single-source systems, but their fairness is less often checked. Kishore Sampath and co-authors ask what happens to bias when sources are added or go missing, in a 2025 study.

Working with health data sets that mix scans, time series, and records, the team ran two tests. First, they added data sources one by one during training. Accuracy rose steadily, but fairness measures moved unevenly across data sets. Second, they dropped sources at test time, mimicking real gaps. Both accuracy and fairness fell. The authors warn that a model tuned in a rich lab setting may act unfairly in the messier real world.
arxiv-2505-03620:
Lois Smith, Jessica Steele, Hossein Karimi-Varzaneh, and Paola Carbone use active learning to map how plastic additives mix into a polymer melt. Their paper, under a broader title in the catalog, is from two thousand twenty-five. Additives called plasticizers soften plastics, but only if they blend in well. Testing each blend in a lab or a full simulation is slow and costly.

Their cycle starts with a coarse simulation model of the melt and small hydrocarbon additives. A random forest model guesses which untested blends are worth simulating. It picks cases that are uncertain or random, to learn the most per run. Over cycles, the guesses sharpen across the whole design space. The team distills new design rules for non-polar additives from the map. Those rules can guide formulators before any lab work begins.
arxiv-2505-03720:
Sungkyung Kang, JungHwan Park, and Masaki Taniguchi prove a result about cables of the figure-eight knot. A cable wraps one knot around another in a set twist pattern. The 2025 paper asks whether such cables can ever cancel out in the smooth concordance group, a system that sorts knots by whether one can be reshaped into the other. The team gives one proof that covers all the cables in one family.

They show every nontrivial cable of the figure-eight knot has infinite order, so no number of copies cancels it out. To do this they built a family of new invariants from branched covers and Floer theory. The tools extend an earlier invariant and may serve for other knot questions.
arxiv-2505-03820:
Keidai Iiyama, Daniel Neamati, and Grace Gao propose a way for satellites to catch their own clock faults without ground help in a 2025 paper. Lunar navigation and timing services will need robust timing from mixed fleets of satellites run by different operators. Their method uses range measurements between satellites gathered over dual one-way inter-satellite links.

The approach builds on Euclidean distance matrices and on graphs with redundant rigidity. It can detect a sudden jump in a clock's phase without prior knowledge of satellite positions or clock biases. That independence suits future lunar networks with diverse satellite types, sizes, and operators.
arxiv-2505-04220:
Zhenyu Xiu and Xu Zheng build new averaging operations in 2025 for fuzzy logic on bounded lattices. A uninorm blends the behavior of two classic operations, acting like one below a neutral point and like the other above it. Fresh ways to build them widen the designer's toolkit.

The pair construct uninorms from two comparable closure operators, or from two matching interior operators, under exact conditions they state. The outcome depends on both the lattice's shape and the chosen operators, so the products can fall outside the known families. Simpler versions using a single operator recover several classic results from the literature as special cases.
arxiv-2505-04420:
Balkis Youssef, Yassine Karoui, and Remco Leine studied how friction changes a bouncing vibration damper in a 2025 paper. The device, a symmetric vibro-impact energy sink, drains shaking by rattling inside a host structure. Dry friction at its contacts was long left out of the math.

The team extended a multi-scale method to include friction and paired it with a generalized impact map. Periodic responses, their stability, and their sudden shifts could then be charted. Thresholds emerged where impact behavior gives way to sliding, with stick-slip motion between. The results sharpen forecasts of how these dampers behave on real hardware. Designers gain a firmer base for tuning energy drain and robustness.
arxiv-2505-04720:
Christodoulou and a large team of colleagues check if claims of beating prior work in scan-based AI hold up, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Most new methods claim a win based on mean scores alone, with no check that the gap is real. A false win can steer later work in the wrong way.

Inside, the team studies a set of scan AI papers and rates the chance that each claimed win came from luck. Most papers in the set did claim a win over prior work. Yet the chance of a false win was high in most class papers and in about half the outline papers. The authors call for stricter tests before wins are claimed.
arxiv-2505-04920:
Manju Nair, Aparna Lakshmanan, and S. Arumugam study a puzzle idea that mixes Sudoku with graph coloring. In graph theory, coloring means assigning labels to points so that linked points differ. A partial coloring is called a Sudoku coloring if it can be completed to a full coloring in exactly one way. The smallest partial coloring with that trait is the graph's Sudoku number, and the paper works out this number for several families of graphs.

The authors focus on bipartite graphs, whose points split into two sets with links only between sets. They find the number for paths, even cycles, complete two-part graphs, and some related forms. They also give exact conditions for when a bipartite graph's number equals its full point count or falls just one or two below it. A final section links a graph's number to that of a larger graph containing it.
arxiv-2505-05120:
Simon Cha simulates baseball seasons with Bayesian inference and random walks in a 2025 paper. After a twenty-game burn-in, the framework forecasts each team's final win total and playoff odds across a 162-game season. Team strength is never directly observed, so it must be inferred and projected.

A posterior over win probability blends win percentage, batting average, and pitching earned run average for each matchup. Games are sampled as coin flips from that posterior. Future batting lines drift by random walks, while pitching runs through Kalman filters. Many simulated seasons yield a full distribution of win totals for all thirty teams, plus postseason chances for each.
arxiv-2505-05220:
Federico Viola presents a 2025 mathematics paper proving a fixed point theorem. The stage is a symmetric space: infinite in dimension, finite in rank, with curved geometry. The actors are higher-rank algebraic groups over local fields. Such groups act on the space by distance-preserving motions. The theorem says every continuous such action must fix some point. Conditions on the field are mild: characteristic zero, and a residue field with at least three elements.

If the group contains the three-by-three special linear group, even those conditions drop. The result extends to the group's grid-like subgroups when the residue field is large enough. Geometers get a rigidity statement: these groups cannot move such spaces without anchoring somewhere. Fixed point theorems power classification results across group theory. Infinite-dimensional spaces with finite rank are a newer frontier where classical tools strain.
arxiv-2505-05420:
A swarm of active particles can act as a computing reservoir, reading a chaotic signal and guessing its next move. Mario U Gaimann and Miriam Klopotek hunt for the swarm settings that compute best, in a 2025 paper. One regime of particle motion had been missed in past work. It sits just below a damping edge and relaxes in stages. Single particles already show the pattern.

In that regime, the swarm stayed best at the task across many settings and tasks alike. Its motion varied richly under wild driving forces. Links between particle motion and the driving force ran tight. The authors say the regime's power comes from how the system relaxes. The model stays in plain physical terms, which aids design.
arxiv-2505-05720:
Minyong Jung and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 comparison of galaxy simulations from the AGORA project. Eight leading computer codes each grew galaxies like the young Milky Way. The team tracked how disks formed between early cosmic epochs. They asked why the codes build disks that look so different. Star feedback, the push from young stars and blasts, was the prime suspect.

In some codes, a tight spinning core formed fast, helped by a big merger of galaxies. Other codes showed a weaker form of the same squeeze of gas into a dense burst. Galaxies in the two groups differed in size and in the age pattern of their stars. Dust made the groups look more alike in mock views, and closer to real galaxies. The authors pin most of the spread on how each code handles star feedback.
arxiv-2505-05920:
Faneela and four co-authors present a privacy-preserving credit check in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Banks using cloud machine learning risk exposing client data. Fully homomorphic encryption lets computers compute on encrypted data, but it is slow and costly.

Their scheme, PP-FinTech, runs an encrypted support vector machine under a modern encryption method. A hybrid kernel captures nonlinear patterns, and an adaptive threshold steadies the encrypted decisions. On a credit card approval data set, the encrypted model matched plain-text models in performance. The authors argue the design balances privacy and efficiency for secure finance. It points toward approval systems that never see raw applicant data.
arxiv-2505-06120:
Philippe Laban and co-authors show that chat models lose the thread over long conversations. Their 2025 paper notes that real users rarely state the whole task at once, yet most tests use single, complete prompts. The team simulated talks where the task arrives in pieces.

Every top model tested scored far worse across multiple turns, dropping about 39 percent on average over six task types. Breaking down 200,000 simulated talks showed skill fell only slightly. The big change was reliability: models guessed early, locked onto their first full answer, and rarely recovered. The authors warn that multi-turn skill needs its own tests and fixes before deployment in schools, workplaces, and support chats.
arxiv-2505-06320:
Jan Kościałkowski and Paweł Marcinkowski improve sentiment classification for mixed tone texts in this 2025 paper. A long review may praise the acting and pan the plot; one label must somehow cover both. Standard models fade as passages grow and conflicts multiply. The authors split the text into constituents, judge the parts, then resolve the conflicts with an aggregation step. One aggregator, a small perceptron network, beat the baselines on Amazon, Twitter, and a standard movie review set.

The cost argument is sharp: the method ran at about a hundredth of the cost of fine tuning the baseline. Divide and conquer works here because local tone is easier to read than global tone. The aggregator learns how parts usually combine, including which kind of segment carries the verdict. The authors offer the approach for any setting awash in long, ambivalent text.
arxiv-2505-06420:
The youth of all space may be a warm sea with a set heat, and one patch of it, the part we can in time touch, holds a deep sum tale. Chakravarty, Maloney, Namjou, and Ross work that tale in a 2025 study for the flat three span case of the sea. A path sum over all shapes is their route to the patch's tone stock.

A bent path ties the sum to the sea's far rim. Count less rest points feed the sum, and their tale is plain at the end: a bounded, runged tone stock with whole counts of states per tone. The heat count lands on the famed rim law. Dense tones hide dark shares that no smooth read can see. Some veils stay shut, the team grant.
arxiv-2505-06620:
Dima Alattal and co-workers boiled down an expert working group's advice on plain AI in medical devices in a 2025 paper. The group, called by the United Kingdom's medicines regulator, mixed health staff, regulators, and data scientists. It drew on a pilot study of how health staff behave with AI help during diagnosis. Black-box decision support worries regulators because a forecast nobody can inspect is hard to trust at the bedside, however exact it tests.

Picks span technical design, health workflow, and regulatory expectations, arguing account must enter from the start rather than as an extra. Stakeholder training receives weight equal to model quality. The paper gives makers a useful map for building devices that health staff can question and regulators can approve.
arxiv-2505-06720: Semenov, Latyshev, and Zaikin wrote a 2025 paper on paired tunneling in two tiny Josephson junctions linked by shared capacitance. A fluxon, a quantum of flux, can tunnel through such a junction. When two junctions couple, a fluxon in one can drag a response in the other. The team sorts behavior into strong, middle, and weak regimes by coupling size. For the middle and weak regimes they derive the paired tunneling rates stepwise. Drag survives at any nonzero coupling, and the nonlocal voltage reflects a trade-off between two processes.
arxiv-2505-07020:
Suyeon Choi presents a 2025 model for designing how AI systems show emotion in long term contact with a user. Past work on affective computing chased expression, immersion, and quick response. It paid less mind to what repeated emotional contact does to a person's thinking over time. Choi's model treats emotional output as a design structure that needs control, not as a simple reaction.

The model grew from observed signs in long sessions, such as head tension, fixed readings of the system, and emotional lag. It has four control blocks that set rhythm, shape sensory input, guard how claims are framed, and align replies with the user's sense of self. The stance puts recovery, freedom of interpretation, and identity continuity first. The goal is to shield users from overload while keeping long term contact sustainable.
arxiv-2505-07320:
Yuhao Li, Ling Luo, and Uwe Aickelin clean noisy labels in health records in a 2025 paper. Outcome prediction leans on time series pulled from electronic health records. Label errors creep in despite careful checks and can wreck those predictions. Their framework uses attention and a two-part Beta mixture model to sort records by label trust.

Sure records can be boosted with extra copies, and unsure records get their labels recalibrated over time, they show. Tests run on two large intensive care data sets and on standard time series benchmarks. Performance reaches top levels, in special under heavy label noise, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-07520:
Tiny bright flashes in the Sun's outer air may be small loops of plasma heated in a sudden burst, test A. Dolliou and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. The flashes, only hundreds to thousands of kilometers wide, were caught by a high resolution space telescope all over the quiet Sun.

The team simulated short loops with a one dimensional hydrodynamics code, in cool and hot versions, then built fake telescope views to compare with the real ones. Cool loops under sudden heating matched the timing pattern between color channels. Hot loops matched only under extreme heating. The result backs sudden heating of cool, short loops as the flash source.
arxiv-2505-07720:
Trapped atoms excited to huge Rydberg states make a laboratory for quantum magnetism, and Maksym Prodius, Adith Sai Aramthottil, and Jakub Zakrzewski scramble that laboratory on purpose in a 2025 paper. Their atoms sit in a dimerized chain, paired up in a pattern linked to symmetry-protected topological order, while random jitters in position add disorder.

Simulating the excited states, the authors find both pairing and disorder push the system into a localized phase, but not the standard many-body localized kind. Instead, states shatter into fragments, an effect of atoms that happen to sit very close together. Across the spectrum, a large share of states keep the topological character despite a whiff of spin-glass order. The work maps where topology survives inside a disordered, fragmented quantum system.
arxiv-2505-08020:
Stijn Cambie and co-authors prove, in a 2025 math paper, how far apart two fair paints of one graph can be. Each node holds a private list of paints. A step swaps one node's paint to a free one in its list, with no clash at its links. Lists run one past each node's link count. The team proves that, for a linked graph with top link count at least three, any two fair paints can be morphed one to the other. The path takes at most the square of the node count in steps, if one node can move at all.

Cut one node's list by one and the space can shatter: no path may join two paints. The edge is sharp, a phase shift in the walk's math.
arxiv-2505-08120:
Mingjian Jiang and co-authors present a 2025 study that asks whether agent scaffolds are needed at all when a model can hold a whole task in view. Agent stacks pile on tools, sub-agents, and harnesses tuned per model. On a bench of real code fixes, the team instead fed one long-context model the entire work space and a clean prompt. A past model, with no tools at all, matched tuned scaffolds at near two fifths solved.

A newer model on the same bare setup passed half the bench. A two-stage pairing of two models also scored near the top pack. Scaffolds may be scaffolding around weak memory, the authors hint. As context grows, plain setups gain ground. Builders should test the bare floor before stacking machinery.
arxiv-2505-08320:
Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiho Choi, and Chong-Kwon Kim present SpecSphere, a graph neural network designed for certified robustness, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Modern graph networks often combine spectral and spatial branches, but their guaranteed resistance to attack is rarely studied.

SpecSphere trains each branch against a different threat: the spectral branch resists edge flips and captures homophilic structure, while the spatial branch resists feature perturbations and heterophilic patterns. A context-aware gating network routes each node's prediction to the more reliable branch. The authors prove expressivity and robustness guarantees, and experiments report top node classification accuracy with tighter certificates on real benchmarks.
arxiv-2505-08620: Tollef Emil Jørgensen reviews post-training quantization, a set of tricks for shrinking large language models after they are trained. The 2025 review explains how lowering the precision of model weights speeds up use and cuts hardware needs. Heavy resource demands otherwise lock many users out of running these models. The paper surveys the main schemes, levels of granularity, and trade-offs, aiming to balance theory with practice for end users who run models themselves.
arxiv-2505-09520:
Artem Kalmykov revisits a link between algebra and a quantum system in twenty twenty-five. The system is the quantum Toda lattice for a general linear group. It had been tied to a truncated shifted Yangian, an algebra tied to a smaller group. Earlier work reached that link through topology and the homology of a space called the affine Grassmannian.

Kalmykov gives a purely algebraic route to the same link. A key step reads a known map into difference operators through a finite form of the Miura transform. He builds that step by relating certain Hecke algebras to a simple shuffle product. As a bonus, he presents that shuffle product in a new way. Readers get the result without the topological middle layer.
arxiv-2505-09820:
Sajib Biswas, Mao Nishino, Samuel Jacob Chacko, and Xiuwen Liu present a new jailbreak method for large language models in a 2025 paper. Even models trained to refuse harmful requests can be tricked by crafted prompts. Older attacks search word by word, which is slow, or tune smooth number vectors that lose force when turned back into words.

Their method tunes within the true shape of the word-choice space, using exponentiated gradient descent with a projection that keeps each choice a valid spread over words. The authors prove the method settles and test it on five open models across four data sets. It beat three leading attacks on success rate while running faster.
arxiv-2505-10420:
Andrei Arhire and Radu Timofte train a light image processor for phone cameras without paired training data, in work from 2025. The processor turns raw sensor data into finished photos. Deep learning versions can rival pro camera quality, but they need aligned pairs of raw and polished images, which are costly to make.

Their method learns from unpaired sets instead. A multi part loss, guided by several adversarial judges, keeps the scene's structure while learning color and texture from reference photos. The judges work on feature maps from pretrained networks. Removing the pairing step could make learned processors far cheaper to build for new phones.
arxiv-2505-10520: Ovidiu Munteanu and Jiaping Wang prove a sharp bound on the total scalar curvature inside large balls in three dimensional spaces with non negative Ricci curvature. Scalar curvature is a local measure of how a space bends. The result holds when scalar curvature stays between two fixed positive bounds. For large balls, the total curvature grows at most in line with the radius, with a sharp constant given in closed form. The bound is sharp, so its constant cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2505-10620:
Kazuho Kayama and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on the jets of the microquasar SS 433. This binary system sits inside the W 50 nebula and fires twin jets that sweep like a lawn sprinkler. Bright knots along the jets glow in X-rays and gamma rays, proof that particles reach extreme energies there.

Earlier work mapped the western lobe; this study adds the eastern side with the XMM-Newton observatory. No synchrotron glow appeared between the star and the innermost eastern knot. The eastern jet's X-ray spectrum steepened steadily with distance from the source. The western jet behaved much the same, with small differences the authors note. Together the lobes trace how jet particles cool as they travel.
arxiv-2505-10720:
Watching a material react while it reacts takes a chamber that can heat a sample fast, hold vacuum or exotic gases, and let X-rays through. Lauren Moghimi and co-authors built one for a synchrotron beamline and describe it in a 2025 paper. The chamber serves the powder diffraction station at the NSLS-II light source.

Laser heating drives rapid, dynamic temperature changes under conditions from ambient air down to vacuum. Two demonstrations show the range: laser-driven heating in polycrystalline iron oxide and in a single crystal of WTe2. Reaction progress resolved over minutes with one-second time steps. The authors offer the setup as a general tool for live diffraction studies of bulk and single-crystal materials.
arxiv-2505-10820:
Takumi Kaneda, Keisuke Fujii, and Hiroshi Ueda propose in 2025 a benchmarking method for large quantum devices that classical simulation can still check. Standard cross-entropy benchmarking needs exact simulation of circuit outputs, which fails beyond about fifty qubits. Modern devices already exceed one hundred qubits, leaving a verification gap.

They restrict random circuits to conserve particle number, which shrinks the state space sharply. Circuits past one hundred qubits then become simulable when particle number stays small. A modified benchmark estimates fidelity under that restriction. Simulations map when the estimates stay accurate, guiding use on real hardware.
arxiv-2505-10920:
Ioannis Emmanouil and Olympia Talelli published this algebra paper in 2025. It studies group algebras, systems that blend group symmetry with algebra, and asks when their modules behave well under the tools of Gorenstein homological algebra. That field extends classic ideas about well-behaved modules to rougher settings. The authors list four target properties, including that certain chain-like structures called complexes are totally acyclic.

They consider a class of groups whose algebras enjoy all four properties at once. The main work shows this class stays closed under two known group-building operations, one due to Kropholler and one due to the second author. In plain terms, bigger groups assembled by those operations keep the good behavior of their parts. The result gathers earlier scattered findings into one framework and extends them.
arxiv-2505-11120:
Popova and Karachentsev search a thousand square degrees toward the Local Void for faint dwarf galaxies. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Voids are the emptiest regions of the nearby universe, and their rare residents test theories of galaxy birth.

Deep survey images yielded twelve strong dwarf candidates. Four likely belong to the nearby galaxy M 83 as companions. The rest sit in isolation. Twenty weaker candidates join the list. Nearly all look like late-type dwarfs, small and still forming stars. The team also found a tight cluster of blue stars at high galactic latitude. At its likely distance it may be a globular cluster tied to the Sagittarius stream, or a new faint Milky Way satellite.
arxiv-2505-11520:
Himaja Papala, Daniel Polani, and Stas Tiomkin use intrinsic motivation to ease traffic flow in two thousand twenty-five. Traffic jams can form on their own from single car acts. Their setting is a classic cell based traffic model. Control must stay local, with no central plan or direct talks.

A share of cars swap default acts for empowerment driven acts. Empowerment is a drive to keep future options open. The swap lifts flow through the whole system in their tests. Jams shrink and mean jam time falls. The proof of concept shows local motives can yield global gains. It holds up under doubt about the world state.
arxiv-2505-11720:
Shijun Liang, Ismail R Alkhouri, and their co-authors present UGoDIT, a 2025 method for rebuilding images from very little data. Deep generative models work well but need large sets of clean training images, which medicine and science often lack. Training free methods need no clean images, yet they overfit noise and must be retrained for each new scan.

UGoDIT learns a set of weights that transfer across a small group of degraded scans, using a shared encoder and separate decoders for each scan. Only a handful of under sampled measurements are needed during training. The shared structure captures the common image prior while each decoder handles its own scan. The method suits dynamic imaging, where clean reference scans are rarely available.
arxiv-2505-11920:
Guangrun Li, Yaoxu Lyu, and their co-authors convert human hand videos into robot training footage. Their 2025 paper, H2R, addresses a mismatch in robot pre training. Models learn from first person human videos, but human hands look nothing like robot grippers. That visual gap dulls the transfer.

The pipeline estimates hand pose from video and retargets the motion onto simulated robot arms. It then erases the human limbs by segmentation and inpainting. Last, it pastes the rendered robot into the original frames with matched camera geometry. Two large video collections were augmented this way. A similarity metric based on image text matching checks that the rendered frames keep the original actions' meaning. Broad tests weigh whether robots trained on the converted footage learn better.
arxiv-2505-12020:
Xi Han and co-authors present GeoMaNO in a 2025 paper on solving partial differential equations with neural operators. These learned models map one function to another, letting them predict how a physical system evolves without a classic solver. Transformer-based versions capture long-range links well, but their cost grows steeply with size and they treat geometry loosely, which hurts them on regular grids.

GeoMaNO swaps the transformer core for a Mamba block, a design with cost that grows only in step with problem size. It also builds in stricter geometric handling. On standard test problems, from slow seepage flow to full fluid motion, the model beat earlier baselines clearly. The largest reported gain cut the approximation error by well over half. The authors pitch the design as a faster, more faithful operator learner.
arxiv-2505-12120:
Dmitry Nechaev, Alexey Pchelnikov, and Ekaterina Ivanova present HISTAI, a large open dataset for computer-aided pathology. Their 2025 paper notes that public whole slide image sets often lack scale, tissue variety, and rich clinical records. Weak data of that kind limits how robust and general pathology AI models can become.

HISTAI holds over 60,000 slides spanning many tissue types. Each case comes with detailed records: diagnosis, basic patient details, careful pathology notes, and standard diagnostic codes. The team built the set to close the gaps they saw in older resources. They hope open access will spur new work, make results easier to repeat, and push computational pathology toward tools that clinics can actually use.
arxiv-2505-12220:
Yuhan Zhang and co-authors review machine learning work on suicide risk in soldiers and veterans, in a 2025 paper. Suicide is a leading preventable cause of death in these groups, and early warning signs are hard to catch by hand. Learning models can sift records for risk patterns at scale.

The team screen four databases and keep 32 studies that meet their bar. The models lean on a shared set of risk factors: depression, trauma stress, past suicidal thoughts and attempts, body illness, and background traits. Accuracy was fair across studies, but the review flags gaps. Few papers report how often alerts are wrong in each direction, few handle follow-up data over time well, and few tie model output to clinical reasoning. The authors call for work that closes those gaps before tools reach clinics.
arxiv-2505-12520:
Himanshu Murari and co-authors model heat and thermoelectric flow in a two-dimensional material in a 2025 arXiv paper. The material is a monolayer of h-NbN, which lacks mirror symmetry and has a wide phonon gap. First-principles calculations drive their transport analysis.

They find that flexural phonons and four-phonon scattering shape heat flow, though acoustic phonons carry most of it. The four-phonon effects stay mostly within the acoustic branch. Stretching the sheet eased scattering and raised heat conduction. Strain also tuned the thermoelectric response, pushing the figure of merit near one at high temperature. The work stresses microscopic modeling for honest predictions.
arxiv-2505-12620:
Haiquan Wen and co-authors build a system to detect AI-made videos and explain its verdicts in words. Their 2025 work notes that fakes now look highly real, so both accuracy and clear reasons matter. Past tools lean on opaque yes-or-no labels and stale test sets.

The team first built a fair set of more than two hundred thousand clips from top generators. A three-track benchmark then tests models in-domain, out-of-domain, and in the wild. Their model treats detection as a reasoning task, where the chain of thought is itself the detector. Trained with reinforcement learning, it beats several leading multimodal models on both accuracy and reason quality.
arxiv-2505-12920:
Paul Van Eecke and Katrien Beuls (2025) present PyFCG, a Python library that brings Fluid Construction Grammar into the Python ecosystem. Construction grammar treats language as learned pairings of form and meaning. The fluid variant is built for experiments on how such systems emerge and change. Until now the framework lived outside Python, cutting it off from that language's rich library ecosystem. PyFCG lets users call the grammar machinery inside ordinary Python programs and combine it freely with other tools.

Three walkthrough tutorials show the intended uses. The first formalizes and tests construction grammar analyses. The second learns usage-based grammars from text corpora. The third runs agent-based experiments on emerging communication, the framework's home territory. The library is open source. The authors pitch the port as an integration play. Grammar research gains Python's data tooling, and Python users gain a mature grammar formalism.
arxiv-2505-13020: Donato Bini and Giorgio Di Russo study how paths bend near a compact object called a topological star in a 2025 paper. They track the small departures from free-fall paths, called geodesic deviations, for objects that are massive, charged, and spinning. They set the results against the classic black hole case of Schwarzschild spacetime, where the behavior differs. The study also covers charged string-like probes in five dimensions, and it frames all the cases in one unified picture.
arxiv-2505-13120:
Alessio Cela and Aleksander Doan prove a counting result in 2025 for curves inside symplectic spaces. A conjecture in algebraic geometry claimed that certain abstract counts, called Gromov-Witten invariants, simply tally actual curves with signs. That claim was recently disproved in its original setting.

The pair show the statement survives in the symplectic world when the near-complex structure is chosen generically. Their proof builds the relevant counting cycle without the usual tricks of perturbing the equations or letting them vary over the domain. The result also settles a question posed by Ruan and Tian about whether such a clean construction exists.
arxiv-2505-13420:
Ripples in the early universe can ring spacetime twice: once directly, and again when they reenter the horizon and stir up gravitational waves at second order. Samuel Sánchez López and José Jaime Terente Díaz compute that second ringing in a 2025 paper. Their stage is Palatini f(R) gravity, a variant theory already proven able to drive inflation and late-time acceleration.

The authors build a general framework for these scalar-induced waves under a radiation era with a pinch of matter. The kernel and density spectrum come out numerically, with accurate formulas fitted to them. In the Starobinsky-like example, the spectrum departs from the prediction of standard gravity under certain conditions. Upcoming detectors sweep the right frequencies, so the differences could one day tell the two formalisms of the theory apart.
arxiv-2505-13720:
Guangle Du and co-authors cut a hard set of balance laws for driven three-stuff salt baths down to a lean set. The work dates to 2025. Such baths model charge flows out of rest. Their wave ties rest on laws whose count grows fast with stuff kinds.

For three stuffs the law set is far more than for two, and few clean forms were known. The team shows the set folds to one law per stuff kind. They then work the far pull between two slabs that hold such a bath in a side field. The pull leans on each stuff's spread pace, a true out-of-rest mark.
arxiv-2505-13820:
Jun Liu and co-authors present in 2025 a way to shrink large language model agents into small student models without losing skill. Agent models mix reasoning with actions, but their size and cost block wide use. Plain copy training treats all tokens alike, which blurs that mix.

The new frame splits each teacher run into reason spans and act spans. Each span gets its own loss, so the student matches both thought and deed. Tests on home tasks, question tasks, and web shopping beat plain copy and mimic baselines. Strong compression came with small drops in scores, and span-level matching proved to be the key part.
arxiv-2505-13920:
Five authors compare finite and infinite quantum wells in this 2025 physics paper. A quantum well traps charge carriers in a thin layer of semiconductor, and its shape strongly affects how fast carriers move, a key trait for devices like lasers.

The team modeled a gallium arsenide based structure and weighed six scattering sources, from impurities and alloy disorder to surface roughness and lattice vibrations. Finite wells won at low temperature, narrow width, and low density, helped by higher indium content. Infinite wells won at room temperature, where one scattering type dominates. The trends give device makers clear rules for picking well shape by working conditions.
arxiv-2505-14120:
Kathleen Barsse and co-authors separate signalling from causal influence in quantum channels in a 2025 paper. Two parties can use a shared interaction to send messages, which is signalling. A broader effect lets one party reshape the other's correlations by local action, which is causal influence.

The authors define measures for both effects and prove they grow smoothly and stack well in parallel use. Sequential use breaks that tidy growth, a result they disprove rather than assume. Values are computed for the SWAP and CNOT gates in single, parallel, and long-run use. The split refines how scholars talk about cause in quantum networks.
arxiv-2505-14220:
Agile software teams organise themselves, so how each developer takes responsibility — and feels ownership of the work — really matters. Tomi Suomi and co-authors survey what is known about ownership in software engineering and, in parallel, in psychology, where the concept has a longer history. Architecture and working methods shape how ownership forms, and the two literatures do not yet speak to each other much.

The authors argue that a fuller view of ownership could improve how software teams work, and they offer initial positions to open discussion and lay groundwork for further research. The paper is a position and survey piece rather than an experiment: its contribution is the map of perspectives in its title, joining technical and human angles on one question. It invites researchers to test and refine the positions it sets out.
arxiv-2505-14320:
Cuellar, To, and Mehrotra test how image quality affects facial recognition systems of the kind police use. Most accuracy studies feed these systems clean portraits, but real investigative photos are often blurred, dark, or low in resolution. The authors ask whether errors and racial or gender gaps grow as images degrade.

They generated synthetic faces, applied five kinds of damage, and ran identification tests. False negatives rose as quality fell, especially with blur and low resolution, while error rates stayed higher for women and for Black individuals, with Black women most affected. Even so, the system beat many traditional forensic methods, so the authors argue for validation and oversight rather than abandonment.
arxiv-2505-14420:
Five researchers wrote a finance paper in two thousand twenty-five on predicting when a firm's earnings will beat or miss forecasts. The clues sit in long texts: earnings calls, filings, and news. Such documents often run past five thousand words, full of repeats and trade terms that strain language models.

Their framework, SAE-FiRE, first splits the dense output of a language model into sparse, readable parts. A tool called a sparse autoencoder does that split. Statistical tests then pick the parts that best separate surprise from no surprise. By cutting noise, the method aims to stop the model from memorizing quirks of its training data.
arxiv-2505-14520:
Sayantan Ghosh and co-authors study in this 2025 paper how solids made of breathing particles soften and flow. Their particles swell and shrink in cycles, an inner activity found in some living and synthetic matter. Simulations at two scales, atom-level and a patchwork plastic model, track how this pulsing changes stiffness and yielding.

Gentle breathing leaves the pack jammed, with small, reversible local shuffles. Past a threshold size of pulse, the mass fluidizes: plastic events surge and the yield stress falls away, until flow turns smooth and Newtonian. The patch model blames stress reshuffling around each swelling particle. Tuning inner activity, the authors suggest, can set a material's state without outside force.
arxiv-2505-14620:
Morgan Lindsay Heisler leads a team helping small adapters speak up against their base models. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. LoRA adapters fine-tune large models cheaply for special tasks. At decoding time, the base model's habits can drown the adapter's lessons. Outputs turn generic instead of task-specific. Standard greedy or beam search decoding worsens the pull.

Their CoLD framework scores tokens by contrast. It compares probabilities from the adapted model against the base. Tokens the adapter favors get boosted. The method runs efficiently on Ascend neural processors. Huawei Cloud users are the intended beneficiaries. Downstream task scores improve in their tests. Fine-tuned knowledge finally survives the decoding step.
arxiv-2505-14720:
Antonios Athanassiadis and co-authors propose a detector for electrons thrown off in extreme laser collisions, in this 2025 paper. New lasers are strong enough to probe quantum effects that weak-field theory cannot handle. One effect bends how electrons scatter off light itself. Two planned experiments, in Germany and the United States, will smash laser pulses into fast electron beams to catch these effects.

The flood of scattered electrons will be huge, and counting it cleanly is a design problem in itself. The team lays out a detector system built for that high flux. It must sort true signal electrons from a storm of background hits. Such tools are the unglamorous base that lets the headline physics happen at all.
arxiv-2505-14820:
Rushit Shah, Nikolaos Agadakos, Synthia Sasulski, and three co-authors rethink how machines learn by copying in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The standard view holds that demos are near best under some hidden cost rule. Satisficing theory says people pick acts that clear their own goal bar. That bar can shift. A moon landing that works, but is slow and jerky, may be fine for a new hand.

Their focused satisficing method uses a margin-based goal to guide deep reinforcement learning. The learned plan aims to beat the goal bar of the person who gave the demos. It does so on new demos, and never spells out that bar in a model. Tests showed it copies the best parts of demos better than past methods. It also won higher rates of acts sure to be fine for the demonstrator. Its true returns held up across test worlds.
arxiv-2505-15320:
Barahona and co-authors analyze the ABC team audio front ends for a 2025 speaker recognition contest. A front end turns a voice clip into a compact vector that captures who is speaking. The contest, run by NIST, set two training rules: a fixed track using only given phone recordings, and an open track that allows public data.

The team explored network designs with varied pooling, a newer network shape, and a large pre trained speech model. In the open track they trained on a data set with 110 thousand speakers in many languages. Those models proved strong and robust. The paper distills workable recipes for building top speaker front ends.
arxiv-2505-15720: Gaborit, Garnier, and Ruatta introduced a new family of error-correcting codes in twenty twenty-five. The codes are built for rank and sum-rank measures, which judge errors by a different yardstick than the usual count of wrong symbols and matter for some network and storage systems. Their construction rests on a working version of the Chinese remainder theorem for linearized polynomials over finite fields. The authors also propose a decoding algorithm that can recover the original message for some versions of these codes.
arxiv-2505-16220:
Liang-Yeh Shen and four co-authors present a speech emotion system that adapts to each listener in this 2025 paper. People hear emotion in voices differently, so pooled labels blur those differences. Standard systems trained on averaged labels often miss how a given listener judges a voice.

Their system, Meta-PerSER, learns how to adjust quickly from just a few examples labeled by the listener. It builds on strong speech features from pretrained models, then tunes itself to the listener's style. Added training tricks steady the fast adjustment. Tests on a standard speech corpus beat earlier methods on both seen and unseen data. The authors present the work as a step toward emotion tools fitted to the person listening.
arxiv-2505-16320:
Huijse and co-authors built a machine learning method in 2025 to sort stars that change in brightness, using data from the Gaia space mission. Gaia's third release gave light curves, faint spectra, and class labels for millions of such sources. The team trained three autoencoder networks, one for each data type. Each source was squeezed into fifteen numbers that sum up its behavior.

The squeezed form kept the main classes of variable stars apart. Light curves and spectra worked better together than alone. Maps of the numbers showed clumps that matched known star traits. The method can help sort, group, and flag odd sources in the far larger release to come.
arxiv-2505-16520:
Giovanni Servedio and co-workers test whether the inner states of language models encode whether a statement is true, in a 2025 paper. False output is a major problem for these models, and past work suggested truth signals hide inside them. Those studies often used artificial data, which may not reflect real model output.

The team built more realistic test sets, drawn from tables and from question-answering collections, tied to each model. They studied two open models.
