Past findings held in part, but the truth signals did not transfer well to text the models themselves produced. The paper offers guidance for better tests of factuality.
arxiv-2505-16620:
Herdeanu and co-authors present CausalDynamics, a large benchmark for testing methods that reconstruct causal structure from time series. In many fields experiments are impossible, so cause must be read from observations, but existing tests use small, clean, mostly deterministic systems. Their benchmark builds thousands of true causal graphs from systems of equations, linear and nonlinear, some with random noise built in, plus two simplified climate models.

They ran leading causal discovery algorithms on the data, which includes noise, hidden confounders, and time lags, and report where each method stands. The framework is plug-and-play: users can assemble new systems in a hierarchy and generate fresh test data. The authors aim to push the field toward algorithms that survive realistic, messy dynamics.
arxiv-2505-16720:
Magnús Halldórsson, Nicolaos Matsakis, and Pavel Veselý improve streaming estimates of spread in a 2025 paper. A stream of points in high-dimensional space arrives one by one, and memory is too scarce to keep them all. Yet users still want the diameter, the widest gap between any two points, plus answers about farthest neighbors and the smallest enclosing ball.

Their deterministic methods store only a small set of points, cutting the previous space bound by a full factor tied to the error tolerance. The argument is also simpler and more complete than the earlier one from 2010. They prove a matching floor: below a certain count, no method can promise the stated accuracy for farthest pair questions. The limits matter for sensors and data pipelines that must summarize huge point clouds on the fly.
arxiv-2505-16920:
Parity violation in the early universe would leave a fingerprint in the four-point correlation of scalar fluctuations, the trispectrum. The three authors compute that signal in dynamical Chern-Simons gravity. Earlier work used a graviton-mediated diagram with both vertices from general relativity and a modified graviton dispersion. This paper instead pairs one Chern-Simons vertex with a relativity vertex, adds a contact diagram, and keeps standard propagators.

After working out the cubic and quartic interactions the Chern-Simons term creates, they find the parity-odd trispectrum vanishes under Bunch-Davies initial conditions. That agrees with a no-go theorem for such signals. The paper then discusses how non-Bunch-Davies initial states could yield a non-zero result, pointing to where a real signal might hide.
arxiv-2505-17120:
Dillon Plunkett, Adam Morris, Keerthi Reddy, and Jorge Morales ask whether language models can describe their own inner work. Their 2025 paper notes that neural networks are hard to read from the outside. The team takes a second path: test how well a model can report the rules it uses to choose.

The authors fine-tuned two GPT-4o models to choose between homes, loans, trips, and the like. Each choice used set weights for traits such as light or quiet. The models could report those weights with care. More training made the reports still better, and the gain spread to new tasks. The work suggests that self-reports, when trained and tested, can be one real tool for grasping how these systems decide.
arxiv-2505-17720:
Hampus Linander and co-authors present a weather forecasting model that works on an equal-area grid of the globe, in work from 2025. Top AI forecasters now rival classic physics models, but most use a grid that crowds points near the poles. That crowding bends the data in ways that have no physical basis.

Their grid gives every cell the same area, pole to equator. The model, a transformer adapted from a landmark design, runs natively on that grid. It beat the same design on the standard grid, and other baselines, at no extra compute cost. The authors argue the equal-area base is the fairer stage for global forecasting, and interest in it is growing in climate work.
arxiv-2505-18020:
Hearing where a sound comes from is easy in a bare room and harder in a echoing hall, and listeners quietly change tactics to cope. Fulvio Missoni and co-authors study that adaptation in a 2025 experiment where people located sounds while free to move. Some worked in a dead-sounding space, others amid reverberation.

Head turns grew more frequent in the echoing condition, as if listeners were sampling the sound field to steady their judgment. Distance did not change the tactics but did change accuracy. The findings suggest the brain treats listening strategy as a tool it retunes to the room, which matters for hearing aids and virtual sound design.
arxiv-2505-18320:
Joining two shapes into one, a move called connected sum, is a basic way to build new spaces in geometry. Gioacchino Antonelli and Kai Xu ask in this 2025 paper whether a curvature condition survives that join. The condition is a spectral form of a lower bound on Ricci curvature, mixing the shape's bending with a smoothing operator.

They prove that if each of two smooth shapes carries a complete metric meeting the bound, then their connected sum carries one too. The construction resembles a tunnel built to merge geometries, a classic trick in this field. The range of the key parameter for which the proof works is shown to be sharp, so the result cannot be widened by the same means.
arxiv-2505-18420:
Harsh Vardhan and co-authors prove when the classic clustering algorithm still works after being split across machines, in a 2025 paper. K-means, run by Lloyd's algorithm, groups data by alternating assignments and center updates. In their setting the data sit on many machines; each runs local rounds and syncs only every so often, saving chatter.

The question is the price of those local steps. The team show convergence survives, but the data's signal must stand out more strongly against noise. Latent cluster identities make the proof harder than for supervised learning. Their method adapts a virtual-iterate trick to a jagged, non-convex objective. Distributed clustering gains firm ground rules.
arxiv-2505-18820:
Kong and Wang compute momentum space entanglement in a four fermion field theory in twenty twenty-five. Entanglement usually concerns regions of space, but modes of momentum can also share it. They use the Wilsonian effective action, which describes physics scale by scale. A replica trick turns the action into an entanglement calculation.

Perturbative checks show local terms in the low energy action do not create this entanglement. Only nonlocal terms link different momentum modes. The final result is expressed through a set of basketball shaped Feynman diagrams. New Feynman rules are proposed to interpret those diagrams. The work clarifies how interactions generate entanglement across momentum scales.
arxiv-2505-19020:
Jiawei Xue and seven colleagues propose HGCL, a recommendation method that uses the hierarchical structure of items. Graph contrastive learning already helps user-item recommendation, but most methods ignore that items resemble each other at multiple resolutions. Products and local businesses naturally form such hierarchies, and those groupings carry useful signals.

HGCL first pre-trains with cross-layer contrastive learning to obtain user and item representations. It then compresses and clusters representations to build a two-level user-item graph. Fine-tuning on that hierarchical graph produces the final recommendation scores. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, ranging from seventy thousand to 382 thousand nodes, show HGCL beating existing baselines.
arxiv-2505-19120:
Xiaoyang Liu and co-authors clean the rainbow smears that ruin photos taken of screens, in a 2025 paper. Those wavy patterns, called moiré, appear when a camera's grid clashes with a display's grid. They corrupt both texture and color at once, which makes them hard to remove without blurring real detail.

Their transformer model, Freqformer, attacks the problem in the frequency domain, where moiré separates more cleanly from true image content. Earlier frequency methods used rigid transforms that leaked errors at block edges. The new split is smoother and learned for the task. Cleaner screen photos matter for everyone who photographs monitors, documents, or stage displays.
arxiv-2505-19320:
Michail Spitieris, Massimiliano Ruocco, and co-authors build a data maker that learns from small data sets by adding physics rules, in a 2025 paper. Fake data tools often need huge data piles to train well. Physics rules can fill gaps when real records are short.

Their model pairs a known physics core with a learned fix term for what the core misses. Checks keep made data close to real data while still varied. Tests on indoor heat records beat past top tools. The maker also gave sound samples past the range it was shown, which hints at strength when conditions shift.
arxiv-2505-19820:
Feifei Li, Mi Zhang, Wang, and Min Yang explain three-dimensional perception models by finding the small point clusters that drive their decisions. Point cloud models steer cars and robots, so their failures demand human-readable diagnoses. A good explanation subset must be faithful, keeping the points that truly move the prediction. It must also be coherent, forming shapes a person recognizes.

Their framework, InfoCons, uses information theory to split the cloud into three-dimensional concepts. Learnable priors guide which groupings count as meaningful. Each concept's causal effect on the output can then be tested directly. On synthetic classification data, the method faced four baselines in qualitative and quantitative comparisons. Two real-world data sets and two applications of the critical scores show range. The goal is diagnostics an engineer can act on, not a heat map to shrug at.
arxiv-2505-19920:
Sebastian Groß, Stefan Heindorf, and Philipp Terhörst propose in 2025 a face recognition method that stores a small personal network for each identity. Standard systems store fixed face vectors, which can be hard to explain and raise fairness and privacy fears. Small systems feel those costs most.

At sign-up, the method trains one small yes-no network per person from a single photo. Fake balanced samples let staff tune fairness for each person at that stage. Tests across data sets and base systems show large gains in fairness and strong gains in privacy. The trade-off is slower checks and more storage, a fair price for small setups.
arxiv-2505-20020:
Natallia Kokash and co-authors presented a two-step method in 2025 for aligning health records across hospitals so federated learning can run on them. Federated learning trains a shared model without moving raw patient data, which suits strict privacy rules. The blocker is that each site records care in its own terms, so the data do not line up.

Their strategy joins ontologies, the formal vocabularies of medicine, with large language models to map local terms into a shared meaning. A real-world project on semantic mapping of record data shows the method at work. Readers get a bridge between privacy and scale: hospitals keep their data home, while their records still learn to speak the same language.
arxiv-2505-20120:
Simpson Zhang, Tennison Liu, and Mihaela van der Schaar argue AI agents need metacognition and strategy for labor markets in this 2025 paper. Markets run on incomplete information, which breeds adverse selection, moral hazard, and reputation effects. Agents entering work will face the same forces as humans. Skills for handling them split into two kinds.

Metacognition covers self assessment, task understanding, and judging ones own strategies. Strategic reasoning covers beliefs about rivals and partners and learning about them over time. The paper surveys current research on both abilities. Gaps for agent training are named plainly. Booking work, keeping clients, and pricing fairly all test these skills. Technical competence alone will not carry an agent career.
arxiv-2505-20320:
Satya Narayana Cheetirala and co-authors show that a language model needs only the best bits of a long clinical note. Their 2025 paper tackles a cost problem: full notes are long, and feeding them whole is slow and dear. The team asks whether retrieval can match whole-text scores.

Notes were split into chunks, indexed, and the top 4,000 words for each query were passed to the model. Three models were tested on spotting surgical complications. Scores for the retrieval route matched whole-text runs, with no real gaps on any metric. The authors pitch the method as a cheaper, scalable way to read long records without reading every page by hand.
arxiv-2505-20420:
Mu-En Liu and co-authors show, in 2025, that large chunks of a typical many-part quantum state are entangled from every angle. For two-part systems, high entanglement in random states is well known. For many-part systems, what happens to a large piece after the rest is ignored was much less clear.

The team proves that pieces covering about half or more of the parts are entangled across every split. Such pieces resist losses and suit protocols where different subsets of users may cooperate. They also show entanglement in one piece can force it in others, making that transfer a generic feature. Computer checks suggest the pattern holds even more widely.
arxiv-2505-20520:
Néstor Espinoza and Marshall Perrin review, in a 2025 chapter, the first wave of exoplanet results from the James Webb Space Telescope. The telescope has changed the field's reach in a few short years. For giant planets, it reads chemical inventories and physical processes in fine detail. The murky sub-Neptune class, planets between Earth and Neptune in size, is yielding its structure and variety. Even rocky planets now give up hints about their air. The authors pick the highlights they judge most telling across these fronts.

A theme runs through the chapter: the new data are bending intuition itself. Methods for taking and reading observations are being rethought under the telescope's precision. So are mental pictures of our own solar system's planets, now seen as one sample among many. The review is written as a field guide to a revolution still under way.
arxiv-2505-20820:
Hyomin Kim, Yunhui Jang, and Sungsoo Ahn use a team of language model agents to improve molecules. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Drug and materials work often needs a molecule tuned toward a target trait. Language models can call chemistry tools and refine candidates step by step. That promise has been little tested with clear, structured reasoning. The authors aim to close that gap.

Their system, MT-Mol, splits the work among expert agents. Each agent owns one family of RDKit tools, such as structure measures or fragment groups. Five families cover the main angles of chemical analysis. The agents give feedback that chemists can read and check. Candidates are then revised in rounds. The design favors clarity about why each change was made.
arxiv-2505-21020:
Yuan Gao and co-authors present NeuralOM, a neural model that simulates the ocean weeks to months ahead. Forecasting slow systems such as oceans and climate is hard for learning models, because small errors pile up until the forecast drifts. Their 2025 framework attacks that drift with two ideas built into one neural operator design.

First, a staged correction scheme breaks each forecast step into fine refinement passes, which keeps errors from compounding over long runs. Second, a graph network carries built-in message rules that mirror physics, such as flows down a gradient, which keeps the model honest and cheap to run. On global ocean tests at seasonal range, the model beat leading rivals in accuracy and steadiness. At a sixty-day lead it cut the main error score by about thirteen percent against the best rival.
arxiv-2505-21320:
Five physicists propose a better single-magnon source for quantum devices in a paper from 2025. A magnon is a quantum of spin wave in a magnetic material. Magnon blockade stops a second magnon from entering once one is present, making a clean single source. The team couples a magnon mode to a spin qubit in diamond. They add a frequency detuning between the two parts.

Detuning lets both conventional and unconventional blockade appear, even under weak coupling. Driving both parts at once makes the two effects combine. A standard correlation measure then drops far below earlier results, showing near-perfect single-magnon behavior. The delayed correlation also stays smooth. The authors say detuning relaxes hardware demands.
arxiv-2505-21520:
Spiros Baxavanakis, Manos Schinas, and Symeon Papadopoulos ask whether models that name the deepfake method behind a clip still work on fresh data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Most fake hunts just say real or fake. Naming the forge tool adds trust and a trail, yet few teams test it.

The team ran five top image nets across six fake sets. They set plain yes no models against multi class namers for cross set skill. They also asked how well namers spot known tricks in sets they had never seen, where the spread of the data shifts. A contrast trick was tried as a fix. Plain models spread best. Big nets, contrast help, and clean data could lift the namers. The work maps a gap in fake defense.
arxiv-2505-21820:
A team of ten authors watches a swarm of tiny magnetic robot spinners build nets with a rare hidden order. Each spinner has three magnetic grip points and can link with mates as it spins. From near a thousand robots, the swarm forms a wide range of spinning three-link nets. Some of those nets show a trait called hyperuniformity, where large-scale density wobble is hushed like in a crystal, though the net looks wild.

Those ordered nets grow from a honeycomb net by steady small swaps in its links. Two forces fight to set the swap rate: magnetic grip strength, which can be tuned, and local twist from each robot spin. Past active systems had not reached this swarm size in tests. The route hints at new matter that can be built to order with set traits.
arxiv-2505-22120:
Runyu Wang and co-authors present a gentle way to teach language models new tasks without wiping old skills. Fine-tuning often causes this loss, known as catastrophic forgetting. Their 2025 method, called LoKI, grows out of new findings on where models store facts inside their networks. It tunes only a small set of parts, chosen with that storage map in mind.

The team tested LoKI against leading tune-light methods in two real-world settings. LoKI kept far more of the models' broad skill than its rivals did. At the same time, its scores on the target tasks matched or beat full fine-tuning. The results held across several model designs. The authors say the method bridges lab insight and daily practice.
arxiv-2505-22220:
Denis Petrov and co-authors present a tool that detects and names malware hiding inside DNS traffic, in a 2025 paper. Some malware smuggles data through the internet's address system. Defenders have ways to spot tunneling, but telling one culprit from another is young work. Simple marks inside the traffic are easy for attackers to change.

Their system, Domainator, reads patterns in traffic metadata instead. Sequences of request traits form a fingerprint for each tool. Tests covered seven malware samples and tunneling tools. The system named the culprit from its DNS traffic alone. It could even infer roughly what the malware was doing. Behavior clues of this kind help responders prioritize infections.
arxiv-2505-22420:
Alexander Sattler and Maria Daghofer test topological edge states in spin chains against their setting in two thousand twenty-five. Both Haldane and dimerized chains host edge states with topological cover. Such chains can now be built atom by atom on surfaces. No real system sits alone, so surface links may erode that cover.

They solve a Lindblad master equation that couples the chain to a surface. Gauges span degeneracy, correlations, entropy, and edge magnetization over time. Chains are varied in coupling type, anisotropy, and range. Su-Schrieffer-Heeger like chains kept their marks best. Haldane like chains faded faster under the same links.
arxiv-2505-22520:
Anthuparambil and colleagues used an advanced X-ray method in twenty twenty-five to watch fat-carrying particles move inside egg yolk. These particles, called low-density lipoproteins, feed the growing embryo and are also promising drug carriers, but their motion in crowded fluids was hard to measure.

Yolk plasma packs the particles tightly, and the team found they creep far slower there than in thin solutions, about one hundred times slower at the highest density. The particles seem to rattle inside temporary cages formed by their neighbors. Water flow effects, direct crowding, and the particles' own softness all add to the drag. Even so, the yolk stays liquid rather than setting solid. That balance lets the embryo draw on its food store steadily. The work clarifies how soft particles travel in dense living fluids.
arxiv-2505-22820:
Sawarni, Sarmasarkar, and Syrgkanis show how the time people take to answer can sharpen preference learning, in this 2025 paper. Reward models for AI systems are usually trained on simple either-or choices. Those choices throw away a signal: a fast answer often means a strong preference, a slow one a weak preference.

The team builds loss functions that fold response time into training, grounded in a classic model of decision making. Their method learns as fast as an ideal learner that already knew average response times. Plain choice-only learning, they prove, degrades steeply as rewards grow, while their approach degrades gently. The guarantees extend to flexible, non-linear reward models. Image experiments backed the theory.
arxiv-2505-23220:
Li, Shi, Chen, and Sun collide pairs of charmonium particles inside a simulated quantum world. Using lattice QCD at two unphysical pion masses, they compute how eta-c pairs and J/psi pairs scatter. The energies reach up to 6.6 gigaelectronvolts. The interactions are extracted from energy levels in two box sizes. The two channels barely influence each other, so each is analyzed on its own.

Quark rearrangement drives the interaction. In one channel the J/psi pair attracts near threshold, leaving room for a structure that may match the reported X(6200). In the spin-2 channel they find a resonance near 6.54 gigaelectronvolts whose properties fit the X(6600) seen by the big collider experiments. The authors back its spin-parity assignment while noting caveats about precise pole positions.
arxiv-2505-23420:
Marco Gaido, Sara Papi, Luisa Bentivogli, and co-authors study how the early pace of training affects speech-to-text models, in a 2025 paper. When these models grow large, trainers often raise the learning rate slowly at first, a step called warmup. One well-known system even used a two-stage warmup, but no one had compared that fix with other choices.

The team tested warmup schedules across large training runs. Large speech models, they found, need a warmup that grows more slowly than a straight line. A higher rate early on sped the first learning but did not improve the final scores. The results give trainers of speech systems a firmer guide for a knob they once set by feel.
arxiv-2505-23520:
Zhang and colleagues present AnchorAttention in twenty twenty-five, a faster way for large language models to weigh long texts. When a model reads a very long prompt, the weighing step grows costly in a steep curve. Past speed ups skipped blocks of text judged by local clues alone. That misses the broad sense and leaves waste inside each block.

The new method first sets a high bar score shared across inputs. It then marks thin stripes of text that clear that bar by a wide gap. Work runs only on those marked parts, loaded piece by piece. At a set text length, it ran faster than the best past method and missed less of note.
arxiv-2505-23820:
Bhaktipriya Radharapu and co-authors examine how language models behave on questions where people themselves do not agree. Such models are increasingly used in place of humans to judge and align other models. The team built a benchmark of deliberately ambivalent cases, each with two defensible stances, and tested the models in three roles: answering questions, judging answers, and debating.

When writing open-ended answers, the models handled the ambiguity with some nuance. As judges or debaters, though, they tended to pick one stance and push it, even where the human population is split. The authors argue this shows a real limit: the models do not faithfully mirror human disagreement. They call for better alignment methods that do not assume a single correct view exists.
arxiv-2505-24520:
Mithuss Tharmalingam, Feodor Svetlanov Konomaev, and Kjetil Hals show how squeezing or stretching a kagome antiferromagnet can flip its spin order, a control knob spintronics needs. Their 2025 paper works with non-collinear antiferromagnets, whose spins point in a pinwheel rather than a line. Reliable, tunable control of that order is the gate to real devices.

Starting from a microscopic spin model, the team derives an effective action that couples the spin order to the strain field. The coupling enters through two known interactions the strain reshapes. Two effects follow. Strain helps thermal flips between spin states of opposite handedness, setting both the average flip time and its direction. Strain also induces a net magnetization, with a testable prediction attached.
arxiv-2505-24720:
Severi-Brauer varieties are geometric objects tied to algebras, and a long-standing question asks when two of them that are linked in an algebraic sense can be reshaped into each other. János Kollár takes up Amitsur's conjecture on this question in this 2025 paper. Amitsur showed one direction long ago and guessed the converse, given equal dimensions.

Kollár proves the conjecture for varieties whose index is not a prime power. His route runs through a clean description of the product of two such varieties: under a coprime condition, the product matches a simple reshaping of the pair. That description yields the main theorem, covering cases where the dimension plus one has at least two distinct prime factors. The proof settles ground that earlier inductive methods had left open.
arxiv-2505-24820:
Yu Xi and co-authors improve keyword spotting, the task of catching a wake word in speech, with a training trick that curbs overfitting. Their base system reads speech in a streaming way and writes its guess step by step. A weak prediction part in that design can be leaned on too hard, hurting scores on hard audio. The 2025 paper reworks both training and decoding.

During training, parts of the input are masked so the model cannot lean on its predictor. That allows a decoding mode that ignores the predictor fully. A mixed mode then blends stepwise and masked decoding, keeping the best of each. Tests on several keyword sets show the training trick lifts scores, and the mixed decoding keeps accuracy high.
arxiv-2506-00220:
Xingru Zhou and five co-authors present a 2025 system for curating and sharing human-robot interaction data sets under FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Robotics data is growing fast, but uneven curation makes much of it hard to find or reuse. The system pairs a structured method for preparing and publishing data sets with a chat interface, powered by a large language model, that answers questions from the data sets' own documentation.

The team built the system while curating data from labs at the University of Texas at Austin. Testers found the data easier to reach and understand than before. Users can explore, compare, and pull data sets through plain language questions. The authors present the work as a step toward human-centered data access for embodied AI research.
arxiv-2506-00320:
Xiao Yu and co-authors teach AI agents to daydream before acting in this 2025 paper. Long computer tasks need planning, yet the reasoning tricks that shine in math do not transfer cleanly. Their framework, Dyna-Think, weaves an inner world model into the agent's thinking loop, so each planned action gets simulated first.

Two training stages build the skill. One rewrites an expert reasoner's traces to stress simulation of the chosen action, and the agent imitates those traces. The next stage first sharpens world modeling through prediction and critique tasks, then polishes action choice. On two computer-use benchmarks, the agent matched a top reasoner's best-of-many scores while using half the words.
arxiv-2506-00620:
Ming-Yu Chung and co-authors explain why model reprogramming works, using neural tangent kernel theory, in a 2025 paper. Reprogramming adapts a big pretrained model to a new task by changing only its inputs and a small output layer. It succeeds surprisingly often, but theory lagged behind practice.

The authors show that success is governed by the eigenvalue pattern of the kernel matrix on the target data. The quality of the source model matters just as much. Their framework ties source and target together in one account. Experiments back the predictions. Clear rules for when reprogramming will work help practitioners choose source models instead of guessing.
arxiv-2506-00720:
Siddharth Prabhu, Srinivas Rangarajan, and Mayuresh Kothare cut the cost of fitting differential equation models to data. To estimate parameters for ordinary differential equations means to cut the gap between model and experiment again and again. The famed single-shooting method integrates the equations at each step. To compute gradients calls for sensitivity derivatives through the integrator, which is costly.

The team uses interpolation to cut the cost of those sensitivity calculations. On that base, they propose a bi-level optimization frame. It uses the structure of the differential equations and solves a convex inner problem. They use the frame for standard parameter gauges and for data-driven dynamic model discovery. The path gauges correct parameters on benchmark problems. It also extends with ease to delay, stiff, and partly seen equations with no large changes.
arxiv-2506-00920:
Philip Heejun Lee wrote this 2025 paper on helping transformers handle sequences far longer than those they trained on. Deep sequence models usually lose accuracy when test inputs run much past training length. Yet tasks such as multi-step arithmetic and step-by-step reasoning demand exactly that skill.

Lee's method, called PRISM, treats position as a probability rather than a fixed mark. It learns relative positions through a filter that updates a histogram step by step. Position doubt is kept as a blend of options instead of one hard choice. In tests, the method reached top scores on length generalization. It held up at ten times the training length on tasks that were out of reach before. The test set spans addition, multiplication, and the SCAN composition tasks.
arxiv-2506-01120:
Iiyama presents faster ways to build the full symmetry set of a few matrices, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The task matters for quantum computing and quantum control. For most real cases, the set cannot be found by formula alone. It must be built step by step on a computer.

The slow step checks if a new matrix adds anything new to the set so far. The old check grows costly fast as sets get large. Iiyama gives new checks that cut both time and memory by a wide margin. One new method was tested and matched known results. The gains let researchers study larger quantum systems than before.
arxiv-2506-01220:
Naoyuki Shimizu and Masaki Hashimoto presented a framework in 2025 for ranking which software flaws to fix first. The count of known flaws grows fast, and single scoring systems either flag too many as urgent or miss flaws that attackers are already using.

Their method chains three public systems in a decision tree. A first filter keeps flaws known to be exploited, or likely to be, and a second step grades severity, which lets teams safely downgrade the rest. Tested on more than 28,000 real flaws, it was eighteen times more efficient and kept most coverage. Urgent work fell by about ninety-five percent. All data used are free, so any team can adopt it.
arxiv-2506-01320:
Taehoon Yoon and co-authors improve how reward-guided image generation picks its starting samples, in this 2025 paper. Score-based generators can be steered at run time by rewards, using sequential Monte Carlo over the denoising steps. Standard setups seed particles from a plain Gaussian cloud, which misses the regions rewards care about. Sampling then wastes effort and aligns poorly.

Their framework, Psi-Sampler, instead seeds from a reward-aware posterior. A special sampler, mixing robust proposals with gradient guidance, makes that feasible in high-dimensional latent space. Tests cover layout-to-image work, count-aware generation, and aesthetic preference tasks. Starting from the posterior beat prior seeding across the board. The authors present the seeding step as the missing lever in inference-time alignment.
arxiv-2506-01420:
Kyuyoung Kim, Hyunjun Jeon, and Jinwoo Shin train small language models to scrub personal details from text, in a 2025 paper. Big models can guess private facts from innocent-looking writing, a growing privacy hazard. Existing scrubbing tools lean on costly closed models, which means sending the sensitive text itself to an outside service.

Their framework, called SEAL, pits a large anonymizer against a model trying to re-infer the hidden facts. The rounds of attack and defense yield training traces, which are distilled into a small model that anonymizes on its own at use time. Nothing private then leaves the user’s machine. The approach offers hospitals, law firms, and journalists a local redaction tool that learns from an adversary rather than from fixed rules.
arxiv-2506-01720:
Ellyn Baines and a team of co-authors report star size measures taken with all six arms of a Navy light array at once. That full mode had not been used since the early years of this century. They measured six stars and got sizes for four in a mid range and two much smaller ones.

The two small sizes are the smallest yet seen with this tool. Spread in the results was wider than with fewer arms. The team links that to uneven light flow and cross talk in the gear. They plan to fix it with a new beam mixer.
arxiv-2506-01920:
Serry Sibaee and co-authors set out new guidelines for testing Arabic language models, and a harder test to go with them. Their 2025 paper reviews existing Arabic test sets and finds gaps in language accuracy, cultural fit, and method. Models can score well on such tests while still missing deep cultural knowledge.

Their new mini data set holds hundreds of hard questions across ten broad domains and many sub-domains. They ran five leading models on it, and scores varied widely by domain. The best model reached only a modest top score, with strength in math, language, and Islamic topics. The authors argue that cultural skill should be graded beside raw technical skill in Arabic AI.
arxiv-2506-02120:
Mariana Londe, Luciana Pessoa, Carlos Andrade, José Gonçalves, and Mauricio Resende reviewed random-key genetic methods in a 2025 chapter. The method encodes every option answer as a list of random numbers between zero and one. Then lets a problem-set decoder translate each list into an actual answer and its cost. Because all the evolutionary tool set operates inside that unit cube, one core setup serves many unrelated tuning problems, easing maintenance and reuse.

Each making keeps an elite set of the best vectors unchanged, injects a few fresh random mutants. Fills the rest by crossing pairs of parents with a parameterized uniform crossover. The chapter lays out the rules, the historical development through biased variants. Applications across discrete and global tuning, serving as the source summary of a widely used metaheuristic family.
arxiv-2506-02220:
Xun Tang, Yuehaw Khoo, and Lexing Ying studied in 2025 a lifted spin model at warm temperatures. The classic Ising model gives each site a spin of plus or minus one. Their lift lets spins roam a whole sphere in many dimensions, with pair pulls of any shape and a fixed length rule. As the dimension grows, the spin spread settles to a limit at a known rate.

That limit is set by a best-fit task over well-formed matrices. Its top value gives the system's free energy, and its winner gives the spin links. At warm settings the task is a softened form of the famous Goemans-Williamson cut method, and cold settings land on that method itself. The team calls the bridge between the two fields a first of its kind.
arxiv-2506-02720:
Xiaochong Lan and four co-authors test, in a 2025 study, how well large language models handle local life services. Such services cover food delivery, bookings, and errands near a user, a field tied to the Meituan platform. The team built a comprehensive benchmark for the field and ran many models through tasks drawn from it.

Two improvement paths were then tried: fine-tuning on field data, and agent-based workflows that break tasks into steps. A compact model with seven billion parameters, once tuned, matched a much larger model with seventy-two billion. That balance of cost and capability matters for live services, where each call must be fast and cheap. The authors say tuned small models make such AI help practical for daily local applications. The work also sets a shared yardstick for the field.
arxiv-2506-02820:
Marine Aulnette and seven co-authors watch plastic microspheres ride a single whirlpool, in this 2025 fluid dynamics study. Particles in flows matter everywhere, from blood to rivers to drug factories. Their behavior is well mapped in creeping flow and in full turbulence, but the middle regime between them was murky.

A microfluidic cross-slot device generated one steady, three-dimensional vortex at a Reynolds number near 50. Neutrally buoyant spheres of increasing size were tracked, with simulations alongside. Small particles spiraled in a self-similar pattern like a Burgers vortex. As diameter grew, particles were pushed out of the vortex core, and their paths departed from the simple pattern, bent by fluid inertia and their own finite size. The findings feed directly into designs for sorting and separating particles in microfluidic chips.
arxiv-2506-02920:
Angela Sara Cacciapuoti and co-workers argued that entanglement rewires how quantum data centers should be built in a 2025 paper. Linking many small quantum processors into one virtual machine is the useful path past today's noisy, qubit-poor devices. A data center that networks processors inside one site is the most viable near-term design. Entanglement shared between processors is the resource that makes the linking work at all.

Entanglement orchestrators, the authors stress, must reconfigure the network topology on the fly using local operations. The hardest hardware gap is transduction, converting quantum signals between unlike real platforms. Linking several such centers into wide quantum networks raises further topology questions, and open challenges are cataloged for the field.
arxiv-2506-03320:
Foundation models know a great deal, but their knowledge freezes at training time. Jack Bell and co-authors argue that continual learning, the discipline of updating models over time without full retraining, is not obsolete in this era but newly central. They make the case along three directions, two familiar and one they expect to define the field's future.

First, models need continual pre-training to stay current as facts and distributions shift. Second, continual fine-tuning lets models specialize for domains and individual users cheaply. Third, and most important in their view, continual compositionality: building intelligence by composing, recombining, and adapting many models and agents as a living ecosystem. The authors predict the future belongs not to one static model but to systems that keep evolving together.
arxiv-2506-03420:
Muhammad Zubair Hasan and Fahmida Yasmin Rifat built a mixed AI system to spot skin cancer. Their 2025 paper uses a large set of lesion photos from full-body imaging taken under phone-like conditions. Early spotting of skin cancer saves lives, yet photo-based calls are hard. The dataset holds over four hundred thousand cropped lesion images.

Their pipeline first outlines each lesion, then classifies it with vision models. A boosted tree model joins the image scores with patient data and engineered features. Fake lesions made by a diffusion model balance the rare cancer cases. Extra relabeling aligns outside datasets into three classes. On the chosen partial accuracy metric, the mixed system scored best among all their setups.
arxiv-2506-03820:
Ahmad Mustapha Wali and Sergiu Nisioi built a tool to fix writing flaws in Hausa texts. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with wrong letters and bad spacing in Hausa. Such flaws slow down language tech for this tongue. They built a large set of paired lines, flawed and clean, from public sources. The set held more than four hundred thousand pairs. Fake flaws were added to mimic real errors.

They then tuned a range of language models on the fix task. One model, though small, gave the best scores. Readers who work on African language tech get a path to clean text for a tongue with few tools. Clean input can lift all later steps, from search to translation.
arxiv-2506-03920:
Melody Lee personalizes the cleanup of readout errors on quantum computers, in a 2025 paper. Standard mitigation inverts a measured error model, but the model drifts after calibration and ignores how the whole gate set behaves. Her method refines it with probability patterns from a batch of shallow circuits, fitted by machine learning.

Tested in simulation on IBM's Perth device layout with seven qubits, the tuned approach improved fidelity by a median of about seven percent over the standard method. Error measures improved more, with mean squared error down about thirty percent. The author frames incremental gains like these as steps toward dependable quantum machines, where every layer of mitigation counts.
arxiv-2506-04120:
Ben Moran and co-authors build digital twins of real robot scenes that are fit for physics simulation, using messy robot data. Real logs suffer from blocked views, shaky camera poses, and moving parts, which breaks most twin building tools. Their 2025 framework takes on all three flaws at once.

The key is a mixed scene model: photo real rendering from 3D Gaussian splatting joined with hard meshes for physics. One tuning loop refines shape, look, robot poses, and physical traits straight from raw motion logs. It needs no hand labels for pose fixes. Tests in simulation and on a two arm ALOHA 2 robot show sharp meshes and photo real new views.
arxiv-2506-04320:
Midhuna Duraisamy Suganthi and co-authors report precision measurements on a hard-to-reach state of ytterbium ions in this 2025 paper. Trapped ytterbium ions are a leading platform for quantum computing, but parts of their energy structure are still poorly known. The team reached a high-lying state that theory describes only roughly.

The state turned out to live far longer than expected, about thirty-eight microseconds, long enough for clean control and fine spectroscopy. Using careful state preparation and high-quality detection, the team measured how the state decays into three lower states. The shares came out near 0.36, 0.64, and a trace for the third path. They also measured the state's magnetic factor and improved one decay rate's precision tenfold. The results should sharpen models of this ion and support schemes that use high states to read out and steer qubits.
arxiv-2506-04620:
Alan Robertson, Haowen Gao, and Yuval Sanders describe a compiler that turns a quantum circuit into steps for a method called lattice surgery, in a 2025 paper. Fault-tolerant quantum work will need millions of qubits, far too many to plan by hand. Cost estimates for such work depend on good placement and routing tools.

Their compiler manages memory as patches of a surface code and counts the space and time a circuit will need. Compiled blocks can then be reused as gates inside larger compilations, which keeps big jobs tractable. The code is shared on GitHub under a permissive license, and the authors invite others to build on it. The paper serves readers who estimate what real quantum hardware must deliver.
arxiv-2506-04920:
Junior Cedric Tonga and co-authors test whether language models can tutor math in many languages, in work published in 2025. Under the head's title, the study simulates student-tutor interactions with language models for multilingual math feedback. A strong model plays the tutor and gives hints, while a weaker model plays the student and tries to learn from them.

The team ran 352 settings across 11 languages, four leading models, and several ways of prompting. They varied the language of the student's work and of the tutor's hints. English hints usually worked best, even for students working in other languages, with a few exceptions. The findings give builders of school tools a guide to where same-language feedback helps and where it does not.
arxiv-2506-05020:
Haokun Liu and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a two-brain control scheme for a drone-and-rover team that tidies objects over long tasks. Mixed robot teams promise much, but fixed task models break when scenes change. Their design splits thought by level.

A large language model breaks the job down and builds a global semantic map. A vision-language model, sharpened by a grid masking trick, spots and locates objects precisely for the rover's gripper. The drone scouts from above, drawing semantic paths that steer the rover's local moves, even when the target is missing or the scene is ambiguous. Trials in simulation and the real world showed the pair arranging objects over long horizons without retraining. The authors claim the first such system marrying vision-language perception to language-model planning.
arxiv-2506-05320:
Avery Hee-Woon Ryoo and co-authors present POSSM, a hybrid model for decoding neural activity in real time, in a 2025 paper. Real-time decoding is central to neuroscience and brain-computer interfaces, where latency limits are strict. Simple recurrent models are fast but generalize poorly to new data.

Transformer models generalize well after large pretraining, but they are heavy and not always fit for low-resource, real-time use. POSSM joins spike tokenization through cross-attention with a recurrent state-space backbone. That pairing aims at fast, causal online prediction and efficient generalization to new sessions and individuals. The design bridges two families.
arxiv-2506-05620:
Paula Mellado, writing alone, reviews magnetic moiré systems, a fast-growing corner of materials physics. Her 2025 review covers what happens when two thin magnetic layers are stacked with a slight twist or mismatch. The overlap pattern, called a moiré pattern, can reshape the magnetism of the stack.

The review gathers recent lab and theory work on both small and large pattern periods. Topics include new magnetic phases, low-energy excitations, transport, light response, and phase changes. A theme is that the mismatch at the interface itself acts as a control knob for magnetism. Mellado frames the field as a frontier for steering complex quantum states. Its advances may feed into materials science and quantum information work.
arxiv-2506-05720:
Changshuo Hu and co-authors survey earable technology, wearables worn in or around the ear, in a 2025 review. Once simple audio accessories, earbuds and their kin now pack sensors that track health, read context, and support new ways to interact with devices. The team reviewed more than one hundred studies published since 2022.

The survey maps how the field has shifted in three years: new sensing principles, fresh applications, sharper accuracy on older tasks, and a stock of shared tools and datasets. It asks how the research has evolved, what resources now exist, and what chances remain open. The authors close with the field's main challenges and a proposed path for the next phase of earable work.
arxiv-2506-06020:
Zhou and co-authors stage a debate inside the model to decide whether a supplied passage deserves trust. Language models often clash with provided context and then hallucinate or fold. Their 2025 framework first gauges the model's own confidence token by token. Then a critic, blind to the passage, attacks a defender who argues from it, and a judge scores the clash.

The verdict mixes with the confidence score to pick the final answer. On a benchmark built for such clashes, the method beat both plain debate and confidence-only rules. It hardened answers against misleading passages while keeping accuracy on honest ones, at small computing cost. Code is public. The authors pitch it as lightweight reliability gear.
arxiv-2506-06220:
Diji Yang and co-authors study image search where the target lives only in the user's mind, in a 2025 paper. Real searches unfold over rounds, guided by a mental picture that may be vague or vivid. Text feedback from the machine is often too abstract to steer by, though.

Their system, GenIR, answers each round with a generated image that shows what the machine thinks the user wants. Seeing that picture, users can correct the search in plain, visual terms. The team also built an automated way to make multi-round test data for this task. Trials show the visual feedback loop finds target images better than word-based loops. The work reframes search as a shared sketching session between user and model.
arxiv-2506-06320:
Beatrice Citterio and Andrea Tangherloni merge two styles of optimization into one framework. Their 2025 paper starts from a split: gradient training powers deep learning, while evolution and swarm methods search hard spaces without gradients. The second group leaves useful slope data on the table.

Their framework, EvoGrad, rewrites the classic moves of those methods, like selection, mutation, and crossover, as smooth steps. Gradients then flow through the whole search, end to end. On standard test functions and small neural nets, the smooth versions beat the classic ones in most runs. The authors pitch the blend as a new bar for hybrid optimization across science and engineering problems.
arxiv-2506-07120:
Zhao Zhang, Jiajun Ren, and Wei-Hai Fang cut the cost of copying messy molecular systems in 2025. In molecular aggregates, every molecule sits in a slightly varied static setting, and honest forecasts of spectra need averaging the quantum motion over thousands of those settings, one costly model each. Tensor network methods had already squeezed single models, and an auxiliary-factor trick had folded mess into the state, but not for the correlated thermal starting states real tests begin from.

The authors extend that grid product state method to system-bath correlated balance initial states. Testing it on the Holstein model by computing the dipole link function behind molecular aggregate release spectra. They show the messy physics comes out accurately from a single one-shot model, at only a moderate growth in the tensor network's bond size. While in effect representing far more mess samples than direct sampling could afford.
arxiv-2506-07320:
A twisted microwave ring stores waves with a geometric twist of their own, in a 2025 paper by Paterson and co-authors. The resonator is a triangular prism, bent into a Möbius loop, whose mirror-broken shape lets electric and magnetic fields intertwine.

Waves running the loop pick up a Berry phase, a shift owed to the path's geometry rather than its length. The team measured two such phases, equal in size and opposite in sign, on modes without rotational symmetry. Modes with threefold symmetry picked up none. Comparing against an untwisted twin resonator exposed the shifts. The result shows geometry alone can sort microwave modes by a topological signature.
arxiv-2506-07420:
Kiran Luecke and Eric Peterson prove match rules for repeat derivatives of a classic curve function with tools from abstract shape math. The curve is the Weierstrass elliptic function, a core brick of number theory. Its repeat derivatives at prime-based scales should fall in neat match sets, a Kummer-style claim. Old roads to such claims run through hard hands-on algebra.

Their road runs a known machine in reverse, which is the fresh twist of the work. The machine once took match rules as feed and gave deep ring maps as output. Fed with fresh ring map results on fixed-point sets, it now yields the match rules as the prize. Number facts thus drop out of shape theory in a few clean steps.
arxiv-2506-07520:
Shun Lei and co-authors present a song generation system in a 2025 paper. Turning lyrics into full songs is hard: voice and backing must blend, quality data are scarce, and taste is personal. Their framework pairs a language model for song structure with a codec that renders the audio.

The model writes two token streams at once, one mixed track for harmony and one split track that keeps voice and backing apart for clarity. Training runs in modular stages so the streams do not fight. A preference tuning step, fed by semi automatic ranking data, sharpens musicality and instruction following. Tests beat open rivals on measured and human scores and rival industry systems.
arxiv-2506-07620:
Aavishkar Madhunlall and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 showing that a modified gravity theory can keep collapsing matter from ever crushing into a singularity. The theory adds higher-order curvature terms to Einstein's while staying free of ghost instabilities. The team solved its equations for a uniform, expanding-or-collapsing fluid in higher dimensions.

The scale factor, which measures the size of space, turns out to have a hard floor: it can shrink only to a finite minimum set by the dimension and the fluid's stiffness. Since singular collapse needs that factor to hit zero, singularities are ruled out entirely. The authors note this loophole in the classic singularity theorems could let regular black holes form naturally.
arxiv-2506-07720:
Yufei Guo and co-authors flip in 2025 the usual design of spiking neural networks to win back accuracy. Spiking nets send binary pulses, swapping multiplications for additions and saving energy, but the coarse pulses lose information. Their design, ReverB-SNN, keeps real-valued spike activations and makes the weights binary instead.

The event-driven, multiplication-free charm survives, while activations carry more detail. A trainable factor lets binary weights learn their scale during training, then folds away at inference through re-parameterization. Across static and event-based data sets and several architectures, the flipped nets beat prior spiking state of the art.
arxiv-2506-07920:
Hossein Babaei, Mel White, and Richard Baraniuk present a 2025 design for sequence models that must remember far back. State space models handle long sequences through a repeating linear step. Their power depends heavily on one internal matrix and how it is set at the start. The team's new variant builds that matrix from wavelet frames, which are overlapping sets of wave shaped functions. The design builds on an earlier frame based line of work.

The wavelet design can be split into a stable diagonal form and supports fast computation without rough shortcuts. In tests, it held information over long spans far better than the standard design it rivals. Gains appeared in memory reconstruction tasks, in classification, and in long range modeling, both alone and inside a deep model. The authors offer it as a base for the next wave of sequence models.
arxiv-2506-08020:
Zi-Ying Chen, Chuan-Xian Ren, and Hong Yan move knowledge between domains when the target holds only some classes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Partial domain adaptation must align shared classes and shun outlier ones. Standard weighting schemes down-weight likely outliers by sample. Those schemes miss cluster structure. Wrong predictions can also poison the weights. Confusion on outliers follows.

Their model, BUOT, uses optimal transport at two levels at once. Sample-level transport carries structure between domains. Class-level transport guards the label alignment. The two levels cooperate inside one framework. Unbalanced transport lets mass differ where classes do not match. The design explores clusters that plain weighting overlooks. Transfer learning gains a steadier tool for messy label shifts.
arxiv-2506-08220:
Octave Mariotti and four co-authors study semantic correspondence in a twenty twenty-five paper. The task is to match points that mean the same thing across different images of the same kind of object. Recent methods learn from a small set of marked points. The authors show these methods fail to spread what they learn to new points.

In effect, the methods act as detectors for the marked points alone. The team offers a new way to learn dense matches instead. They lift flat keypoints into a shared three-dimensional space using depth guesses from a single image. They also extend a known test set with new marked points. Their model beat the older methods by a clear margin on unseen points.
arxiv-2506-08320:
Vivek Vaidya, Aditya Patwardhan, and Ashish Kundu published this paper in 2025. It asks a sharp question for cybersecurity: can language models be trusted to write password policies? System administrators increasingly ask AI for configuration files, and a subtly wrong password rule can quietly weaken an entire network.

The team had pre-trained models translate plain-language requests into working configuration files for the standard Linux password-quality tool. One group of runs gave the models no help; another supplied the official documentation as a baseline. They graded every output for soundness, accuracy, and consistency across repeated tries. The verdict was sobering: outputs varied and erred often enough to matter in a security-critical setting, even with documentation in hand. The authors draw lessons for deploying language models in access control: verify configurations independently, and treat consistency as a security property in itself, not a nicety.
arxiv-2506-08720:
Frédéric Zheng, Yassir Jedra, and Alexandre Proutière identify a linear system's true size from noisy in-out traces, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their method ranks a Hankel-style matrix with a threshold rule that adapts as it goes. Big singular values are read keenly while the rest stay cheap to fit.

Error bounds for the matrix come in closed finite-sample form. The method also gives back the system order and its pulse response marks. Sample needs match the best known methods that cheat by knowing the order first. Readers in control get order finding without the usual guess tax.
arxiv-2506-08820:
Cecilia Mac Cormack and co-authors unraveled in 2025 why one solar eruption looked simple low down but complex higher up. A coronal mass ejection is a vast cloud of magnetized gas thrown from the Sun. All such clouds should hold a magnetic flux rope, yet most lack the classic white-light shape of a front edge plus cavity, due to distortion, merging, or viewing angle.

The event of 28 March 2022 began as a single eruption and looked textbook in the low corona, then appeared as a two-rope structure in white light. Views from several spacecraft, plus a thermodynamic model of the corona, were combined to trace its change. Readers get a worked example of how a single rope can masquerade as two, a lesson for reading space weather events.
arxiv-2506-08920:
Zeyu Leo Liu, Greg Durrett, and Eunsol Choi address a weakness in how language models absorb new facts. Editing methods can plant a fact so the model repeats it word for word, yet the model often fails on questions that require reasoning with that fact. Their system, PropMEND, uses a hypernetwork that reshapes the training updates themselves, so planted knowledge spreads to related questions. The design extends an earlier editing method with a training goal aimed at multi-step reasoning.

On the RippleEdit benchmark, the system nearly doubled accuracy on hard multi-hop questions whose answers never appear in the planted fact. The authors also built a tougher test set using relations and entities the system had never seen. PropMEND still led there, though the gap narrowed, which they take as a sign that spreading knowledge across many relation types remains open work.
arxiv-2506-09020:
Zichao Dong, Jun Gao, Ruonan Li, and Hong Liu study a transfer effect in extremal graph theory. Many classic results about bipartite graphs give the largest graph that avoids a forbidden pattern. The authors show such results often carry over to the stricter induced setting. In that setting, the pattern must not appear even as part of a larger structure. The transfer holds as long as the host graph contains no large complete bipartite piece.

As a showcase, they prove every rational number between 1 and 2 can serve as the Turán exponent of a small family of forbidden induced bipartite graphs. That extends a result of Bukh and Conlon with a much smaller family. Supporting results cover induced trees and cycles, and the team also settles best bounds for graphs avoiding induced theta and prism shapes. The pattern suggests a broad principle rather than isolated tricks.
arxiv-2506-09120:
Supernova remnants glow in X-rays, but beyond our local group of galaxies they are hard to spot, and each one needs an optical match to be believed. Maria Kopsacheili and co-authors re-survey the galaxy NGC 7793 in a 2025 paper. Only one X-ray remnant was known there, against nearly 240 optical candidates from a recent census.

The team mined nineteen years of Chandra archive, about 230,000 seconds of exposure, and catalogued fifty-eight X-ray sources. Matching those against the optical list confirmed new remnant counterparts. The spectra from a second telescope characterized the confirmed and candidate remnants. Such detections matter beyond bookkeeping: remnants are how massive stars return energy to their neighborhoods, and each new population sharpens the picture of that feedback.
arxiv-2506-09220:
Karen Joy, Tawfiq Ammari, and Alyssa Sheehan present a 2025 paper on how early adopters make sense of AI assistants. A wave of devices and services in 2023 and 2024 promised an autonomous second self that learns routines and acts across apps. The authors interviewed nine early users of products such as wearable pins and subscription helpers.

Users faced three kinds of uncertainty: what the device can do, how to get it to do things, and what it should be to them, including what it may remember. Hype, the authors argue, pre-shapes these encounters just as it did for voice assistants. The happiest users built their own bundles of narrow tools rather than trusting one grand assistant.
arxiv-2506-10920:
Or Shafran, Atticus Geiger, and Mor Geva build a way to read the inner features of large language models in plain terms. Single neurons often mix several ideas, so researchers hunt for directions in the model's activity space instead. The usual tool learns those directions from scratch and can be hard to read. Their 2025 method breaks down one layer's activity with a kind of matrix split.

The split yields features that are sparse mixes of neurons firing together, each tied to the inputs that wake it. That tie makes the features readable at once. On three well known models, the features beat the usual tool and a strong guided rival at steering model behavior. Shared neuron mixes also revealed a layered order in how ideas are stored.
arxiv-2506-11320:
Yuxi Chen, Hongyang Zhou, and Gabor Toth curb fake waves and grain noise in plasma sims that track bits in cells, in a 2025 paper. Such sims are key for plasma work but oft buzz with noise, most of all in fast flows. A stock gap scheme also spawns fake waves near sharp jumps.

The team adds a spread term with a flow cap to the field solver in one code. A new trick finds flow in the drift frame of the plasma, which cuts bit noise in fast streams. Shock and field join tests show both fixes work in play.
arxiv-2506-11620:
Stefan Bleeck, writing alone in 2025, designs a hearing test entirely inside a computer before any human hears a sound. Standard audiometry misses the above-threshold speech problems common in age-related hearing loss. His SimPhon method uses a speech recognition system as a stand-in listener, degrading audio in controlled ways to map which phonemes get confused.

Those confusion patterns guide the picking of minimal word pairs from a large corpus. Simulated testing, expert curation, and sensitivity analysis then prune the candidates to a final 25 pairs. The striking result: the test's diagnostic power does not track the standard Speech Intelligibility Index, suggesting it catches deficits beyond mere audibility. The optimized set is ready for first human trials. Bleeck pitches simulation-first design as a faster road to sharper hearing tests.
arxiv-2506-11720:
City air is usually measured at a few fixed stations, which miss how pollution changes street by street. Anastasios Noulas and co-authors turn taxi fleets into moving sensors. Their dataset holds over one hundred million readings of fine particle pollution, PM2.5, from more than three thousand vehicles across six large American cities over one year.

Taxis gave fine-grained, street-level detail while still covering each city well, and their readings ran near real time. The team then modeled pollution from traffic congestion, the built environment, and human movement. Seasonal patterns differed from city to city, tied to local geography. Strikingly, models using only traffic and wind speed captured each city's pollution swings well. The authors present taxi fleets as a scalable monitoring tool that could feed cleaner-air research and policy.
arxiv-2506-11820:
Xintong Wang and ten co-authors wrote a 2025 paper rethinking how machines translate text seen in images across languages. Vision-language translation has to read multilingual text inside a picture and render it in another language, using the visual scene as a clue. Big vision-language models look capable, but nobody had systematically tested them on this task.

The team attacks from three sides. They expose flaws in existing datasets and release AibTrans, a human-verified parallel dataset with corrected text recognition. They benchmark 17 commercial and open models in end-to-end and cascaded designs, revealing heavy dependence on the reading step. Finally, they propose a density-aware score that stays reliable as scenes grow complex. The findings set a new baseline for the field.
arxiv-2506-11920:
Piotr Put and co-authors steer crowds of electron spins in diamond with magnetic gradients, in this 2025 paper. Dense spin ensembles interact strongly, which could serve quantum computing and sensing, but disorder usually scrambles their joint motion. The team combined shifting field gradients with global control pulses to tame that problem.

They wound the spins into nanometer-scale spirals and watched the patterns evolve. By reshaping the interaction itself, they made the joint motion shrug off disorder. The result points toward sharper quantum sensors and nanoscale imaging of materials and living samples under normal conditions, the authors argue.
arxiv-2506-12120:
Azaz Ahmad's 2025 thesis studies how electrons move through Weyl semimetals, odd materials where particles act like the Weyl fermions of theory. The work centres on the chiral anomaly, a quantum effect usually read through two signals: how conductance answers a magnetic field set along the flow, and the planar Hall effect.

Using a lattice model and the Boltzmann transport method, Ahmad maps how those signals shift across settings. A smooth cutoff in the particle spectrum can flip the sign of the first signal on its own, with no scattering between valleys needed. Strain in the material acts like a built-in magnetic field and can flip it too. The thesis also builds a theory of the nonlinear Hall effect and checks a second fermion family, giving experimentalists fresh signs to hunt for in real materials.
arxiv-2506-12220:
Hantao Yu and Josh Alman ask whether small transformers can stand in for a large transformer on long inputs. Self attention grows with the square of input length, so long texts are costly to process. Modern chips, by contrast, handle short inputs in small models very fast and well.

The authors prove that any transformer on inputs of length N can be simulated by a set of small transformers that take inputs of length M. In the worst case the count grows as the square of N over M, and they show that bound cannot be improved in general. In common cases such as average inputs or windowed attention, the count drops to a linear bound, which is far cheaper.
arxiv-2506-12320:
Weipeng Jiang and co-authors open the hood of the code bases that run big word models in a 2025 study. Those bases are the roads and pipes of the age of smart text, yet bugs in them can shake all that is built on top.

The team mined more than three hundred bug-fix notes from two famed bases. They sorted bug signs five ways and roots in more than a dozen kinds. The top root was a wrong use of the code's own doors and knobs, a shift from the math faults of old deep tools. Most bugs slip past the tests for want of cases, of drivers, or of firm checks. Test sets ran to near eight thousand checks in all. The authors give tips to lift the grade of such bases.
arxiv-2506-12420:
Guangxu Yang and Jiapeng Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proves a lifting theorem that moves one-way communication bounds from two players to the many-player number-on-forehead game.

In that game each player sees all inputs but their own. Lifting theorems are a main tool for lower bounds in talks, with uses in proofs, circuits, and data structures, but past ones stuck to two players. The new deterministic lift turns one-way two-party bounds into one-way forehead bounds. It yields a sharp split between random and fixed play, even with many players, and a sharp split between one and two rounds. A fresh proof for the disjointness bound shows the reach.
arxiv-2506-12620:
Mattia Paciarini and co-authors extend in 2025 a model-free frame for describing black holes to test which space-times stay smooth everywhere. Many smoothed models of dense objects have been built over past decades. A new frame describes hole warps from observed traits without picking a model first.

The authors derive rules for when curve measures stay finite at every point and paths can run without end. Those rules sort the cores of smooth space-times by how they behave near the center. Known black hole cases serve as checks of the rules. The work gives builders of smooth hole models a shared test for sound form.
arxiv-2506-12720:
Dongzhe Zheng proposed a new angle in 2025 on the Hodge conjecture, one of geometry's deepest open problems, built on constraint geometry. The conjecture asks when certain shapes inside a complex space can be described by algebraic cycles. Zheng's framework starts from Spencer theory, where extra structure ties pairs of objects together under constraints.

A key step shows that under special algebraic conditions, the theory's own differential collapses to the classical exterior derivative, bridging the new machinery to standard cohomology. Onto that bridge he adds hyper-constraint conditions drawn from Lie algebra symmetry. The filters pick out special classes, which he defines constructively inside the theory. Solo-authored and openly programmatic, the paper offers a route, not a proof. Readers get a constraint-based lens for an old question.
arxiv-2506-12820:
Neeraj Deshmukh and Felix Sefzig extend a key construction in algebraic geometry in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Morel-Voevodsky construction builds the motivic homotopy category, a framework that blends algebra and topology. It was first made for schemes. These authors rebuild it for algebraic stacks, which are broader spaces that carry symmetry data. They work in both the stable and unstable settings.

They prove their version agrees with a recent one by other authors. As a payoff, they extend a spectral rigidity theorem to stacks. They also build the framed version of the theory for stacks and prove a reconstruction theorem there. The paper closes with notes on coefficient systems. Specialists in motivic homotopy theory are the main audience.
arxiv-2506-13020:
Ikeoluwa Abioye and Jiani Ge test word translation from English to Yoruba with aligned word vectors in a 2025 paper. Aligning vectors from two languages can give word translations without paired texts, but most work uses rich languages with strong single language vectors. Yoruba is a low resource language, so whether the method holds there was unclear.

They applied a known supervised alignment method. Higher quality vectors and a step that normalizes vector length both raised translation precision, and the two gains interacted. The results show limits of the top method for low resource languages. Care in building the single language vectors matters more in that setting.
arxiv-2506-13320:
Wenlong Wan and co-authors define a new task for video analysis: finding exactly where and when audible actions happen. Their paper appeared in 2025. Usual action spotting scans the whole clip. Audible actions, such as knocks and claps, hinge on sudden changes in motion. The team argues collisions announce themselves through sharp bends in movement, which can be timed without listening to the sound at all.

Their network measures the second derivative of motion, the jerk-like change, to time the hits. During training it also learns where in the frame the sound source sits, teaching itself with contrast checks. They built a benchmark of 623-item scale from two public video sets, scrubbed of pure voice clips. Tests showed strong timing accuracy and good transfer to counting repeated actions.
arxiv-2506-13420:
Jiang Wang and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on letting a ground robot calibrate its own senses. The cameras, laser scanner, microphone array, and wheel sensors of a robot must agree on where each one sits, or its picture of the world warps. Hand calibration is slow, and hearing sensors are usually left out entirely.

Their method has the robot plan its own driving path to make the sensor offsets easiest to pin down. A Fisher information score grades each candidate path, and the robot follows smooth spline routes, replanning online as data arrive. Simulations and real robot runs show the approach working. The team released their code so other groups can build on it.
arxiv-2506-13620:
Superconducting cuprate films usually grow on a matched crystal base. That base chains them in place and mixes its behavior into every measurement. Sandik and co-authors freed the film itself: they made a membrane of an electron-doped cuprate that stands alone after lift-off. Tests showed the freed sheet kept a coherent crystal structure.

A scanning magnetic microscope then compared the membrane's superconductivity with the film before release, and the two closely matched. That means the delicate quantum state survives the peeling process. The authors say such membranes let engineers place complex superconductors into devices whose materials would never allow the films to grow directly. They also let physicists study the cuprate's own behavior without the base talking over it.
arxiv-2506-13720:
Pengyu Liu and co-authors give a parallel way to tune quantum circuits for local best form. The work dates to 2025. Tuning such circuits is a core task and a hard one. Past top tools lean on gut rules and can take huge time.

Local best form asks each short chunk of the circuit to be best by an outside gauge. Past local tuning ran in line and paid steep costs. The new plan keeps marker fingers in the circuit and tunes just the chunks that hold a finger. Rounds pick fingers, tune their chunks in parallel, then reset the set. Proofs bound its work and span, and the end circuit is locally best.
arxiv-2506-14620:
Daniel Bernard Bonnéry and Julien Jamme link two fields that rarely meet: survey sampling and data privacy. Their paper from twenty twenty-five looks at a classic survey tool, the Horvitz-Thompson estimate of a total. They show this estimate can be read as a privacy-keeping device in its own right. The privacy frame they use is differential privacy.

The authors give formulas for the privacy scores of this estimate. They treat it both alone and with added Laplace or Gaussian noise. From these formulas a user can set the noise size to hit a chosen privacy level. They give simple forms for the plain case of random sampling on yes-no data. The work helps survey teams state clear privacy bounds for their totals.
arxiv-2506-15320:
Sebastian Zeilinger and eleven co-authors demonstrate a three-axis magnetic field sensor, in this 2025 paper. The device uses spin-orbit torque, where a current through a layered stack twists magnetization, in a tantalum, cobalt-iron-boron, and magnesium oxide sandwich. Good sensors must be sensitive and must cancel their own offset drift in every direction.

Measurements showed small residual offsets in all three axes, around 36 to 50 microtesla. Sensitivity was high and similar across axes. The team also showed the sensor holds up under bias fields, and they used single-spin simulations to sweep cross-axis effects up to one millitesla. By fitting those simulations to data they extracted the two torque parameters that describe the physics. The authors present the design for uses needing compact, precise field sensing.
arxiv-2506-15620:
Modar Sulaiman and Kallol Roy present GFLC, a method that cleans biased training labels while guarding fairness, in a 2025 paper. Labels in real datasets are often noisy and skewed, which distorts both accuracy and fairness scores. Their method corrects labels before training rather than adjusting the classifier afterward.

The approach joins three parts: a confidence score for each label, graph-based smoothing that uses a Ricci-flow-tuned network of similar examples, and a built-in reward for demographic parity. In experiments, the corrected data improved the trade-off between performance and fairness over baseline methods. The authors frame clean labels as a root fix for unfair models.
arxiv-2506-15720:
A learner that adds new classes from a handful of photos tends to forget the old or overfit the new. Juntae Lee, Munawar Hayat, and Sungrack Yun blend three model selves to dodge both traps in a 2025 paper. Base, last, and current weights merge in weight space.

The merge leans hardest on the shared classifier heads. Mixed-up copies of the few photos enrich teaching signals. A distillation loss pulls old knowledge across the blend. Scores topped three standard few-shot sets. Updating the whole model beat freezing its eye, the trend they buck. Small data, they show, can still teach broadly.
arxiv-2506-15920:
