Liang Qin and five colleagues teach robots to find grasps that work twice in one pick-and-place move, in a 2025 paper. A shared grasp is a hand pose that holds an object both at pickup and at placement. Finding one by testing every candidate separately grows slow as candidates multiply.

Their method uses an energy-based model that predicts shared grasps by combining the energies of feasible grasps at both poses. Candidates that look promising early get checked first, shrinking the search space sharply. Experiments showed better grasp selection than earlier methods with less training data. The model also generalized to grasps it had never seen and to objects of similar shape. Faster planning matters in warehouses and factories, where robots repeat such moves thousands of times a day.
arxiv-2506-16120:
Fivos Kalogiannis, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Ian Gemp, and Georgios Piliouras prove that simple learning rules can settle two-player games played over time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting, convex Markov games, lets each player's taste be a curved function of how often states get visited. Even the basic win-lose version resists standard tools, since the problem bends the wrong way and lacks a tidy step-by-step consistency.

The authors first add a gentle penalty term that reshapes the problem into a friendlier form, one where a known slope condition holds. That reshaping steadies each player's own gradient updates. They then prove worldwide convergence for two standard alternating update schemes under these conditions. The results give the first firm guarantees of reaching Nash equilibrium in this game class.
arxiv-2506-16420:
Laura Grazioli, Yukuan Hu, and Eric Cancès set out a shared frame for computing the excited states of molecules. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Excited states of many-body systems are a core hard task in physics and chemistry. Past methods split into two camps: search for critical points, or linear response.

They use the geometry of Kähler manifolds to hold both camps in one frame, fit for models from Hartree-Fock to full configuration methods and time-based density methods. The frame gives a clean path to the linear response equations of nonlinear models. For mean-field models it yields a simpler route than the classic Casida path. Part one ends with theory checks and sums at the Hartree-Fock level.
arxiv-2506-16520:
Charly Beulenkamp and co-authors create an ultracold gas of molecules made from potassium and cesium atoms, in a 2025 physics study. Such molecules open paths to quantum studies, but cooling them is hard. The team first cooled cesium with help from potassium gas, then bound atom pairs into weakly held molecules at a magnetic sweet spot, a Feshbach resonance near 361.7 gauss.

The gas held about seventy-six hundred molecules with a lifetime near 130 milliseconds, limited by pair collisions. Extra resonance scans revealed new features and pinned down the bound state used. Fits to all data sharpened the known interaction curves for the pair. The work sets up future ground-state samples.
arxiv-2506-17220:
Jisu Nam and six co-authors study how video models keep track of moving points in a 2025 paper. Modern video generators can make clips that look smooth over time. The team asked how these models match the same point from one frame to the next inside their own workings.

They built DiffTrack, a test setup with generated clips and rough tracking labels. It checks which parts of the model do the matching work. Matching turned out to rest on a few key layers, and it grows stronger as the clip is cleaned up. The same insight gave top results on point tracking without extra training, and helped make motion in new clips more steady.
arxiv-2506-17420:
Chi Li and Minghao Miao bound the size of a class of geometric spaces in a 2025 mathematics paper. Fano manifolds are spaces with positive curvature in a complex sense, central to classification in geometry. K-semistability is a balance condition that decides which of them admit special metrics.

The authors prove that the anti-canonical volume of such a space, unless it is plain projective space, is at most twice the dimension raised to its own power. Equality holds only for two shapes: a product of a line with a projective space, or a smooth quadric. The proof rests on a new link between K-semistability and minimal rational curves, the simplest bent lines on the space.
arxiv-2506-17920:
Teng Wang and colleagues dissect the unruly bottom layer of grains flowing down a slope. Granular flows matter from landslides to factory chutes. On rough slopes they follow a tidy profile and a known local rheology. On smooth slopes the grains slip at the base, and a hot, dilated layer forms that the tidy theory misses.

Particle simulations vary the base roughness from flat to near maximal. Three regimes emerge: slip, no slip, and a transition between them. In the slip regime the basal layer's speed, shear, and agitation all break the classic profiles. The authors derive general slip laws tying slip speed to shear, roughness, and slope angle. Layer thickness ignores flow conditions but feels how bouncy the grains are. A kinetic theory extension, not the standard rheology, captures the layer's stresses.
arxiv-2506-18020:
Thomas Boudou and three co-authors prove that saboteurs hurt learning's generalization more than poisoners. Their 2025 paper compares two attack models on distributed learning. Byzantine workers can send anything at all. Poisoners can only corrupt their own training data.

Both attacks had similar training guarantees in past work. The team asks the sharper question: what happens on fresh data? A tight stability analysis separates the two threats. Poisoning leaves strictly better generalization rates than Byzantine failure. The gap is fundamental, not a quirk of one algorithm. Defenders should price the stronger attack model accordingly. Robust training is not one problem but two.
arxiv-2506-18320:
Simeng Wang, Runlian Xia, and Gan Yao developed a transference method in 2025 that moves Fourier multiplier bounds between groups using proper cocycles from group actions. Multipliers are a core tool in harmonic analysis, and moving a bound from a small subgroup to a big group can save a full proof. Earlier transference results of this kind were limited to the infinite exponent case.

Their method covers the full range of exponents for completely bounded multipliers. With it they give a new, simple proof of a recent result on pointwise convergence of noncommutative Fourier series on amenable groups, with a refined maximal estimate. They also lift multipliers from lattices in linear Lie groups to the whole group, a noncommutative echo of a classic theorem, and build a Hilbert transform analogue on a key group. Readers get one bridge that carries several results.
arxiv-2506-18420:
Ning Jiang, Chao Wang, Yulong Wu, and Zhifei Zhang prove a limit that links particle-level gas laws to smooth flow laws, in a 2025 paper. The Boltzmann law tracks gas particles as they bounce, while the Euler laws treat the gas as a fluid. Near a wall, the particle view needs its own thin layer, and the paper works in a half-space with bouncing rules that mix mirror-like and scattered rebounds.

The team builds solutions from a fluid core plus two stitched boundary layers. For shear flows, the tangled layers would normally cost a degree of smoothness in the math. A fresh trick trades that loss sideways, using the saved quantities of the system, so time stays clean. Uniform bounds on the leftover error close the proof. The result firm-ups a core passage from micro to macro physics.
arxiv-2506-18520:
JiaKui Hu, Zhengjian Yao, Lujia Jin, Hangzhou He, and Yanye Lu work on a basic design flaw in image restoration networks in this 2025 paper. A good restoration model should shift its output when the input shifts. The attention parts of modern transformer models break that rule, which hurts training and makes results less reliable on new images.

The authors review two known fixes, then add an adaptive method that picks the most useful stored features for each point of the image. Those picks are combined with a global summary before the model answers. The resulting network, called TEAFormer, was tested across many restoration jobs such as clearing noise and sharpening. It beat rival designs on quality, trained more smoothly, and held up better on unseen data. The work shows that honoring the shift rule need not cost speed or reach.
arxiv-2506-18620:
Mintu Nandi, Sudip Chattopadhyay, and Suman Banik identify a new noise component in feed forward loops, a common motif in gene networks. Noise travels through direct and indirect paths in such loops, and each path alone is well studied. Their joint action, through shared input and output nodes, was poorly understood until now.

Inter gene correlations reveal a cross interaction noise that arises from that convergence. Depending on loop type, the joint effect either amplifies fluctuations, called synergy, or suppresses them, called redundancy. Coherent loops tend toward synergy and incoherent loops toward redundancy. The framework also links these effects to response timing traits such as delay and acceleration, which matter for cell decisions.
arxiv-2506-18820:
Hirakjyoti Sarma and Nilakshi Das compared in 2025 two ways of simulating a small dust cluster held in a trap. The cluster is a finite ball of charged grains that repel through a shielded force, a Yukawa system found in complex plasmas. One run used frictionless dynamics, the other added neutral-gas friction. Shape measures from both runs were set side by side.

The cluster's still shape barely cared which dynamics ran. But the two shells of grains swung in lockstep only in the frictionless run, where sharp shared peaks showed. Grains also roamed wider with friction, and a joint spin of the whole cluster faded as friction grew. The pair ties the lost spin to faster settling of gaps and angles under friction.
arxiv-2506-19220:
Conor Snedeker, Xinyu Zhou, and Raef Bassily studied private model personalization in 2025. In their setting, many users each hold varied data, yet their ideal model settings share a hidden low-dimensional form. The goal is to learn that shared form and each user's small personal part, across devices, while guaranteeing user-level differential privacy for every participant.

The authors give a lean federated method built on an earlier shared-version method, adapted so it satisfies differential privacy and still works when labels are noisy. Their guarantees cover a broader group of user data spreads than earlier work needed. And in natural settings they boost the privacy error term of the previous best result by a large factor. A second setting, including binary data, is also treated in the work.
arxiv-2506-19820:
Felix Faltings, Hannes Stark, Regina Barzilay, and Tommi Jaakkola present ProxelGen, a system that designs new proteins by treating them as three-dimensional densities, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most design tools place atoms as points in space. A density view, chopped into tiny cubes the authors call proxels, opens new ways to guide and shape the result.

ProxelGen learns from real proteins with a compression model, then builds new ones with a diffusion process in that compressed space. Its samples scored as more novel than rival tools, with better match scores and the same build-quality level as the training set. In a standard test where a known motif must be held in place, the system did well. The density form also lets users steer the shape more freely.
arxiv-2506-19920:
Jack Araz and co-authors hunt odd jets at the big collider in a 2025 paper with graph tools. New physics may hide as jets that fit no known tale. A catch-all hunter must learn the norm and flag the odd with no model of the odd in hand.

Their hunter turns each jet spray into a graph, then learns to rebuild it; odd sprays rebuild poorly and so stand out. Stiff graph shapes, built from frame lore, let them dial how much the hunter may see. Bench data from a known mock set grades the hunt. Collider teams gain a hunter with knobs set by physics, not luck.
arxiv-2506-20120:
Antoine Chambert-Loir published a 2025 paper, written in French, on the logic of fields that carry many measures of size at once. A globally valued field comes with a family of absolute values obeying a product formula, a bookkeeping identity. Number fields and function fields are the classic examples; the theory also covers functions on the complex plane. These objects underpin the modern theory of heights, which measures the complexity of number-theoretic solutions.

Continuous logic, where statements take real values instead of true or false, gives these fields a model-theoretic home. The paper revisits foundations laid a decade ago by Ben Yaacov and Hrushovski. One cornerstone result: the algebraic numbers, with their essentially unique global valuation, are existentially closed. Any compatible system of equations, inequalities, and height conditions that could have a solution already has one there. The paper consolidates a framework linking logic, geometry, and Diophantine problems.
arxiv-2506-20220:
Sato and colleagues listened for dense gas in bright galaxies with ALMA in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Hydrogen sulfide molecules flag hot, dense, or shocked gas near galaxy centers. The team aimed the telescope at three nearby infrared-luminous galaxies. Modeling software then inferred the gas conditions from the signal.

Compact emission appeared in all three galaxies, from regions under about one hundred fifty parsecs wide. Broad line wings pointed to outflowing or shocked material. One galaxy showed gas spinning against the main rotation, plus a feature hinting at inflow. The emitting gas proved far denser than carbon monoxide suggests, and moderately warm. The authors cast the molecule as a tracer of hidden dense regions.
arxiv-2506-20920:
Penedo and a team including Wolf present FineWeb2 in twenty twenty-five, a multilingual data set for training language models. Top models need vast amounts of clean, diverse text. English data sets have improved fast, but other languages lag behind. Filtering pipelines are hard to tailor to many languages at once.

Their pipeline adapts the FineWeb approach to any language automatically. Design choices were tested on nine diverse languages with a new task selection process. A rebalancing method weighs duplication counts and quality for extra gains. The pipeline was then run on near one hundred snapshots of Common Crawl. The result covers more than one thousand languages in twenty terabytes of text. Models trained on the non English corpora beat those from prior data sets.
arxiv-2506-21020:
Mallory Flynn and Paul Gustafson stretch the multiplier method to tree-shaped data for sizing hidden groups. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Hidden groups still need counts to guide funds and policy. The classic method backs a total out of one known subgroup and its share.

Their weighted form blends many subgroups in a tree by the least-spread blend of their shares. They set it against a Bayesian stacked model on made-up and real data. Reads of which data drive each method, and of how each bears strain, round out the work. The aim is a tool that less technical teams can run.
arxiv-2506-21120:
Christopher Lustri, Inês Aniceto, and Panayotis Kevrekidis analyze, in a 2025 preprint, standing pulses in a chain model where each site talks to near and next-near neighbors. The discrete nonlinear Schrödinger model fits light in waveguide arrays. The team studies the case where the two couplings compete in sign. Ground-state pulses then exist only in a narrow band of coupling ratios. Their stability rides on special eigenvalues. Those eigenvalues depend on the coupling in an exponential way, far too subtle for ordinary approximation methods, which miss effects hidden past all orders.

A Borel-Padé technique digs out the hidden terms, called Stokes multipliers, near the singular points. The resulting predictions match careful numerical eigenvalue computations closely. Beyond this model, the authors offer the method as a template. Many parametric problems hide their decisive terms the same way, and the template shows how to reach them.
arxiv-2506-21220:
Andrey Goncharov and co-authors fine-tune small language models by spending expensive reasoning lessons only where the data is hard, in a 2025 paper. Full distillation from a big model's chain of thought works but burns calls and data. Their pipeline sorts training items by the entropy of a one-token answer, a cheap complexity gauge, then mixes plain fine-tuning on the easy bulk with distilled reasoning on the hard slice.

Across three small open models, the blend beat standard fine-tuning clearly and edged out full distillation, while using 81 percent less data. The recipe targets teams that want reasoning skills without a giant teacher's bill.
arxiv-2506-21820:
Hsuan-Wei Lee and Po-Kang Hsiao model how partisan talk can steer a democracy wrong. Their 2025 paper builds an agent-based simulation where voters swap views through a network. Two forces fight inside the model: honest exchange that filters noise, and strategic bluffing that plants bias.

Across many runs, the shape of the network mattered more than any trait of single voters. When the gap between candidates was moderate, bluffing beat honest signals and dragged the weaker side's supporters into shared error. Placing independents at central spots acted as a circuit breaker against echo chambers. A few extreme partisans could taint whole communities for hundreds of rounds. The authors draw lessons for designing information systems.
arxiv-2506-22120:
David Carranza and eight co-authors reconstruct the journeys of displaced people in Somalia in this 2025 paper. Climate shocks and conflict push people from their homes, and knowing the likely routes helps predict where hazards will strike them next.

Their method treats past movements as a network and lets random walks diffuse across it, mimicking how people actually travel. Applied to a tracking matrix of 20,220 movements from February to June 2025, the walks recovered plausible routes out of danger zones. Travelers on the likeliest paths met mainly drought and conflict, with conflict fading at later steps. Exposure varied so widely across routes, though, that no typical journey exists. The framework can project movements in regions facing growing hazards.
arxiv-2506-22320:
Fletcher Williams and co-authors find new skyrmion phases in frustrated quantum dimer systems in this 2025 paper. Skyrmions are swirling, topologically protected spin textures seen in many magnets. In flat systems they are counted by how magnetization wraps a sphere, an integer count.

The authors study dimer systems, where spins pair up, in a classical limit that keeps the pairing entanglement. The relevant phase space is a projective space, whose wrapping count is still the integers, so skyrmion-like textures can exist. On a bilayer triangular lattice with weak links between dimers, the zero-temperature phase diagram holds two magnetic-field-induced skyrmion crystal phases of this new kind.
arxiv-2506-23220:
Somnath Bhattacharjee and co-authors show that the greatest common divisor of two polynomials can be computed by shallow circuits, in a 2025 paper. Their circuits have fixed depth and size that grows in a tame way with input. The result holds over any large enough field, no matter its characteristic. A prior result had covered only fields of zero or large characteristic, so small-characteristic fields were the open gap.

The proof leans on a recent closure result: shallow circuits stay shallow when a polynomial they compute is split into factors. On the way, the team proves a depth-fixed version of a known structure claim for symmetric polynomials. They also strengthen the factor closure for small fields. The authors note the circuit view matters for parallel computing, since shallow circuits map to fast parallel runs.
arxiv-2506-23320: Nicola Assolini and Alessandra Di Pierro give a meaning-based account of loops in quantum programs, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Quantum coding can be tackled at many levels, much like classical coding. Their account focuses on what quantum-controlled branching and looping mean as math objects. They build a domain where the meaning of control flow with loops can be defined. That meaning mirrors the smooth, linked evolution of the quantum system that runs the program.
arxiv-2506-23520:
Yu Zhang and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper on teaching a language model to read chemistry procedures and write robot-ready action lists. Robotic synthesis needs literature procedures converted into structured steps, but chemical language is ambiguous and hand-labeled data are scarce and costly. Their model, ChemActor, is a fully fine-tuned language model that converts in both directions, from procedure text to actions and back.

To fix the data problem, they generate training data with a general-purpose model, selecting examples by how their distribution diverges from the target. A multi-round review metric, where models critique each other, gauges how well procedures are understood. On both conversion tasks ChemActor set state-of-the-art scores, beating the baseline by about ten percent. The authors release the code publicly. They frame machine-made data as the unlock for chemistry automation.
arxiv-2506-23720: Piyali Chakraborty and Dorin Dutkay present a 2025 math paper tied to the Fuglede conjecture, a long-standing question linking tiling and frequency spectra. They study partial differential operators defined on domains that may fall into separate pieces, and ask when the operators admit self-adjoint extensions that commute with each other. When such extensions exist, the team also builds the matching unitary group and its spectral measure, and explores the geometric features that follow. The results connect operator theory with the shape of the underlying set.
arxiv-2506-24020:
Lee and seven co-authors studied topology in a single-atom system in twenty twenty-five. Topology in physics concerns shapes and patterns that stay fixed under smooth change. Their system is described by the quantum Rabi model, where one atom interacts with light in a cavity.

They built a synthetic lattice from the atom's energy states and found a special zero-energy state sitting at a domain wall. Its spin direction is protected by topology, meaning it resists small disturbances. To measure this, they defined a winding number based on phase-space geometry, a map mixing position and momentum. They link it to a known geometric phase. The work frames phase-space topology as a new way to explore protected quantum states.
arxiv-2507-00920:
Dang Qua Nguyen, Morteza Hashemi, Erik Perrins, Sergiy Vorobyov, David Love, and Taejoon Kim tackle two headaches of federated learning at once in this 2025 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many devices without pooling their raw data. But the model updates devices send can leak private information, and devices also compress those updates at different precisions, which muddies the merged model.

The authors design a stochastic quantizer that delivers differential privacy, a formal limit on what updates reveal, while keeping quantization error minimal and, unlike rival methods, bounded. To handle mixed precisions they group devices into clusters, tune cluster sizes, and fuse the updates linearly for a cleaner aggregate. Simulations show better privacy and learning quality than the standard Laplace-based approach. The work targets settings where phones and sensors of uneven power must still train together.
arxiv-2507-01720:
Lead author Scott and a team of colleagues demonstrate laser cooling and measurement of single cesium atoms on a normally forbidden transition, in a 2025 paper. Working on the electric-quadrupole line between two atomic states, they cooled atoms to 5.3 microkelvin while imaging them at the same time. The setup reads out which hyperfine level each atom sits in without background interference.

Their detection fidelity reached 0.9993, and 99.54 percent of atoms survived measurement, with losses blamed mainly on vacuum lifetime. A three-dimensional cooling arrangement allowed repeated low-loss checks. The team also modeled a faster variant that quenches the excited state with an extra field, projecting similar fidelity in about 60 microseconds.
arxiv-2507-01820:
Nicolas Cerardi, Marguerite Pierre, François Lanusse, and Xavier Corap wrote a 2025 paper on using galaxy clusters to measure the universe. The catalog title drops the paper's number and subtitle, which the head restores. Clusters are the largest held-together structures in space, and counting them across time reveals how structure grows. Standard counts rely on rough rules linking a cluster's glow to its mass.

The team skip those rules. They built a fast machine learning tool trained on simulations that models the hot gas in clusters directly, with real physical effects included. A pipeline then predicts cluster counts for a given universe. This proof of concept aims for cleaner measures with fewer built-in guesses.
arxiv-2507-01920:
Kayyunnapara Divya Joseph studies the mathematics of droplet-laden air flowing into a region with a boundary, in a 2025 paper. The model tracks two quantities, air velocity and the fraction of volume taken by droplets, through a pair of coupled equations. The system is non-strictly hyperbolic, which makes its waves harder to handle than standard cases.

Joseph proves that weak asymptotic solutions exist for the initial-boundary problem in the quarter plane, using a vanishing viscosity regularization and a generalized Hopf-Cole transformation. For nicer data of bounded variation, she derives an explicit solution formula. The construction combines the Hopf-Lax formula for the Burgers equation with a careful product rule for rough functions. Such models describe sprays and particle-laden flows in engineering.
arxiv-2507-02120:
Bertsimas, den Hertog, and Koukouvinos propose an exact method for polynomial optimization, a broad family of problems where the goal and limits are written as polynomials. The standard approach turns these into huge semidefinite programs, which caps the problem size and does not always guarantee the true optimum.

Their idea is to rewrite any polynomial as a sum of terms, each a linear function times a convex one. They prove such a rewriting always exists and find the version that gives the tightest lower bound inside a branch-and-bound search. In tests the method beat leading tools, solving problems with forty variables and degree three, and twenty variables and degree four, to proven optimality within an hour.
arxiv-2507-02520:
Temurbek Mirzaev, Bobomurat Ahmedov, and Cosimo Bambi study black hole shadows as tests of gravity in a 2025 paper. A black hole's shadow, the dark silhouette it casts, depends on the spacetime around it. If gravity departs from Einstein's standard picture, the shadow's shape should show it. The team wanted measures of shape that do not depend on the coordinate grid used to describe the space.

They computed shadows for several spacetime families, including the rotating Kerr case and more exotic ones. Two expansion methods were compared for describing the shadow's edge, and the Fourier method looked steadier across models. A neural network trained on synthetic shadows then read off hole parameters from the shapes. Using data from real telescope facilities, they set limits on how far the true holes can stray from standard values.
arxiv-2507-03120:
Dharshan Kumaran and a team of co-authors study how language models change their minds, in two thousand twenty-five. Models can look stubbornly sure of a first answer, yet fold fast under criticism. The team built a test that reads a model's confidence without leaving a memory of its first judgment, something impossible with human subjects.

Three leading models all showed a bias that boosts confidence in a chosen answer. That bias made them resist changing their minds. They also weighed advice that clashed with their answer far more than advice that agreed. The pair of habits explained behavior in a second domain as well. The authors offer the account as a mechanism behind both stubbornness and doubt.
arxiv-2507-03220:
Saransh Gupta, Umesh Deshpande, Travis Janssen, and Swaminathan Sundararaman build a system for serving many model adapters at once in a 2025 study. Adapters are small add-ons that specialize a large model for one task, and popular models have spawned thousands of them. Existing tools waste resources: fine-tuning each adapter demands its own copy of the base model, and inference stacks handle multiple adapters poorly.

Symbiosis lets several adapters share one base model for both training and serving. Sharing cuts memory and cost wherever fleets of specialists run, from enterprise copilots to per-user personalization.
arxiv-2507-03420:
Matteo Correnti and co-authors probe the stars of the dwarf galaxy NGC 4449 with the James Webb Space Telescope in work from 2025. The galaxy is a nearby starburst system forming stars at a rapid pace.

Color diagrams reveal stars from young main sequence to old giants. Young stars trace an S shape along the galaxy axis, while slightly older groups shift from north to south, which suggests outside forces triggered bursts in distinct places. Clusters match the field star pattern. The sharp data also reveal a clear gap between oxygen-rich and carbon giant stars, aiding models of late stellar life.
arxiv-2507-03920:
Jianshen Zhu and co-workers built new molecules by marrying graph networks to exact tuning in a 2025 paper. The mol-infer setup invents lab graphs with prescribed form and property values by coding a trained predictor inside mixed integer coding. Any put forth molecule provably satisfies the predictor's verdict. Handcrafted feature vectors, chosen for coding tractability, capped forecast quality on some traits, and poor forecasts poison the invented compounds.

Graph neural networks read the molecule itself and predict better, but resist exact coding. The authors combine the two so network-grade learning feeds the guessing tool set under a two-layered model of lab form. Better property models should translate straight into better option molecules for synthesis.
arxiv-2507-04020:
Zahid Ullah and Jihie Kim test, in a 2025 paper, whether swapping a vision transformer's perceptron blocks for Kolmogorov-Arnold networks helps it learn new tasks without erasing old ones. Forgetting is the core curse of continual learning. The rival design updates only a slice of its spline-based parts per sample, a local plasticity that may spare distant memories.

They trained both designs in sequence on standard image benchmarks, MNIST and CIFAR-100 among them. The Kolmogorov-Arnold version forgot far less, keeping accuracy on early tasks while still adapting to new ones, and beat the perceptron baseline on both counts. The authors present the swap as a structural answer to forgetting, not another rehearsal trick. Dynamic deployments, from cameras to robots, need exactly that steadiness.
arxiv-2507-04520:
Xinling Li and co-authors keep in 2025 self-driving taxi fleets in the right places despite unsure demand. Idle cars must be sent where riders will appear, but forecasts are unreliable. Sending cars on a fixed forecast wastes trips; ignoring uncertainty strands riders.

Their framework, DURO, first uses a neural network to forecast a range for demand rather than a single number. A robust optimizer then plans moves that work across that range. On New York City data, DURO beat classic forecast-based planning and matched a heavier robust method, while computing faster. The authors offer it as a practical way to rebalance fleets under deep uncertainty.
arxiv-2507-04820:
Asking a language model to compare every pair of documents ranks them superbly, at a cost that grows with the square of the list. Junru Wu and seven co-authors distill that pairwise wisdom into a fast single-pass ranker in 2025.

The teacher labels come from pairwise prompting, and a pointwise student learns to reproduce the order. The surprise is thrift: training on just two percent of all pairs matched the performance of using every pair. The result keeps the expensive method's ranking quality while serving at ordinary cost. For search builders, the work turns a laboratory trick into something deployable, and it questions how much comparison data distillation really needs.
arxiv-2507-04920:
Moritz Lange and co-authors build a diffusion model that reasons about moving objects in a 2025 paper. Predicting how several objects will roll, collide, and settle is core to physical reasoning. Standard models roll forward step by step, so they can only start from a beginning state, never aim at a required ending.

Their model treats the whole trajectory at once and works object by object. It stays consistent if the scene shifts in time or the objects swap order, and it can be pinned to conditions at any time step for any object. Tests vary the object count and path length mid-run. The design suits planning tasks where goals sit in the future.
arxiv-2507-05120:
Martin Mauser and co-authors run a quantum learning scheme on a photonic chip that keeps re-reading its data, in a 2025 paper. Data re-uploading feeds the same input into a single qubit again and again, each pass adding power. Their integrated optical processor classified images with high accuracy. The team then proved the scheme is a universal classifier that can genuinely learn, not just memorize.

The proof covers trainability and how well the model generalizes to unseen data. One qubit, recycled, does the work that intuition says needs many. The authors frame the result as a route to machine learning that sips energy. Their analysis lays groundwork for using the scheme as a building block in larger quantum systems.
arxiv-2507-05220:
Zhun Deng and co-authors present QuEst, a method that sharpens estimates of spread-out measures by borrowing model forecasts in two thousand twenty-five. When real data is scarce or pricey, machine predictions can fill the gaps. Past hybrid tools, though, handled only averages or a single quantile.

QuEst blends a small set of true values with many model-made ones to estimate a wide family of quantile-based measures, from quartiles to tail risk scores used in finance. It gives both point estimates and honest confidence ranges. A multi-part version and a variance-trimming step extend the reach. Tests in economic modeling, opinion polling, and language model grading show the blend beats raw data alone.
arxiv-2507-05420:
Dan Liu, Michael Karbach, and Gerhard Müller study jammed disks of two sizes in a narrow channel, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Pistons press loose disks until none can move and each touches a wall. Before the jam, disks can pass each other, so size order stays random.

The authors give exact results for volume and disorder in the jammed states. They split the disk row into small tiles and build a set of linked units from them. Some settings favor mixing of the two sizes. Other settings push sizes apart, a split driven by shape and space alone.
arxiv-2507-05520:
Karishma Thakrar, Shreyas Basavatia, and Akshay Daftardar test a team style AI system in a 2025 paper on medical question answering. Skin care by video visit gives doctors little to work with: a few photos and short notes, with no hands on exam and no second opinion at hand. The authors ask whether copying how clinics reason beats tuning a model on more data.

Seven vision language models were tested in six setups. Some were tuned, some gained a layer that blends views from many models like a peer consult, and some gained a lookup tool for reference facts. The study weighs which setup answers image based medical questions best.
arxiv-2507-05620:
Shaojie Bai, Seunghyeon Seo, and colleagues synthesize training data for photorealistic avatars in a 2025 computer vision study. A headset's inward cameras see only partial, infrared views of a face, while the dome cameras that capture true appearance cannot be worn at the same time. No synchronized ground truth pairs the two views, which blocks straightforward learning.

Generative methods bridge the gap by producing plausible head-mounted camera images matched to known facial states. Avatars driven from those partial views can then mirror expressions faithfully. Convincing avatars are a gatekeeper technology for remote presence in virtual and augmented reality.
arxiv-2507-05720:
Yucheng Shi and co-authors present a 2025 paper on training phone-using AI agents by letting them practise live, rather than only imitate recorded taps. Screen-reading agents can click, scroll, and type their way through apps without hand-built rules. Training them on fixed recordings, though, makes them brittle when screens change.

Their framework builds a ladder of tasks by self-exploration, keeping the rungs at the edge of what the agent can learn. Reinforcement learning then runs inside a live phone environment, so the agent meets fresh screens as it improves. The authors present the online recipe as a scalable cure for template overfitting in mobile agents.
arxiv-2507-05820:
Writers of long stories juggle casts, and characters only come alive through their relationships. Syemin Park, Soobin Park, and Youn-kyung Lim interviewed fourteen writers in 2025 and found recurring struggles. Writers could not easily imagine new characters who might shake up the cast. They also struggled to balance sameness and difference, and to flesh out relationships in detail.

Their answer is Constella, a writing tool where several AI agents play the cast. One feature proposes related new characters; another shows several characters' inner journals side by side; a third lets characters respond to each other, making relationships visible. In a week-long deployment with eleven writers, the tool produced sprawling, connected casts and deepened writers' grasp of their characters' bonds. The authors argue that spreading attention across an ensemble is something multi-agent tools do naturally.
arxiv-2507-06320:
Ning and Ramsey-Musolf recheck a tiny electric trait of the electron in a broad theory of particles in this twenty twenty-five paper. The theory adds one field to a known frame and can help explain why matter beat anti-matter early on. Strict bounds on the trait leave little room for that tale to work.

Inside, the pair finds a set of two-loop paths that past work had missed in this frame. For some phase picks, the new paths partly cancel the known ones and ease the bounds. For other picks, the new paths rule and the bounds pinch hard. Then the frame needs fine tuning to keep both the bounds and the matter tale in line.
arxiv-2507-06420:
Dieter Pelz and Mark Boland turn accelerator radio-frequency parts into circuit diagrams in a 2025 paper. Cavities and couplers for particle accelerators are usually designed by heavy field simulation. Equivalent circuits, networks of simple elements that mimic the physics, offer a faster, more intuitive design language if they can be made accurate.

The paper first reviews what equivalent circuits can and cannot do. It then lays out a systematic recipe: choose the right circuit topology for a structure, then solve for the element values that match its behavior. Four worked examples carry real numbers, and a decomposition strategy tackles structures too complex for one circuit. A catalog of typical accelerator applications rounds out the guide.
arxiv-2507-06520:
Xinyuan Song and co-authors build a scheduler that runs teams of AI agents in this 2025 paper. Their system, Gradientsys, uses a language model as the dispatcher. It hands tasks to specialist agents, like document parsers, web searchers, and interface drivers, and runs many at once.

A planning loop in the ReAct style lets the scheduler rethink as results arrive. Agents' capacity limits are respected, and failures trigger retries or fresh plans. A live feed streams each agent's acts and reasoning to watchers. The design mixes timed and untimed work in one frame. It targets firms that need many agents to cooperate openly.
arxiv-2507-06720:
Giuseppe Procopio presents a 2025 paper on slow fluid flow inside pipes, worked out with a classic mathematical tool. Stokes flow governs thick fluids moving gently, and its Green function gives the response to a point push. Procopio derives that function for flow inside, outside, and between cylindrical walls.

The derivation expands the flow in cylindrical harmonics within a two-point tensor framework. By differentiating the Green function at its pole, he obtains stronger singularities such as the couplet and stresslet for confined spaces. A new route, using the flow's reciprocal symmetry, yields the sourcelet and its multipoles. He then applies the tools to colloids near cylinder walls. Examples cover sinking particles and the push or pull a wall exerts on a microswimmer.
arxiv-2507-06920:
Code benchmarks grade AI programmers with a handful of tests, and Zihan Ma and co-authors show how much slips through. Suites like HumanEval use few, similar test cases, so subtle bugs pass as correct, scores inflate, and reinforcement learning trained on those scores chases a mirage. The team proposes metrics that grade the test suites themselves for thoroughness, and a benchmark, TCGBench, for the test-writing task.

Their method, SAGA, pairs human programmers with a model to write sharper tests. On TCGBench it caught 90.62 percent of planted faults, and benchmarks it synthesized judged code verifiers far more accurately than a leading rival. The authors pitch test generation as the foundation trustworthy code evaluation stands on.
arxiv-2507-07020:
Jason Ogbebor, Santiago Flores Roman, Geordy Jomon, and Gennady Gor published this paper in 2025. It measures how squashable fluids become when trapped in tiny pores. That property, the bulk modulus, matters for pulling gas out of shale and coal seams, where most fluid sits in nanometer-scale gaps.

The team built a simulation method that reads compressibility from natural volume wiggles in a steady-pressure setup. It runs about ten times faster than the standard sampling approach and reaches pores as wide as one hundred nanometers. For methane in carbon slits, the modulus rose fourfold in the tightest pores tested. The effect faded as pores widened, dropping under five percent by the widest size. The results help engineers model how gas-bearing rock flexes during extraction.
arxiv-2507-07320:
Dongyu Wei and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on clustered federated learning with privacy and tight radio budgets. Devices train shared models through base stations, each of which handles only some tasks and holds few radio blocks. Devices must also work out which task they belong to, adding overhead. The team poses one joint problem: cut training loss while juggling clustering, block assignment, privacy noise, and delay.

Their multi-agent learning scheme lets stations pick users, blocks, and noise levels on their own while sharing one goal. A penalty rule charged by how many devices break limits speeds learning. Tests showed convergence up to twenty percent faster and rewards fifteen percent higher.
arxiv-2507-07520:
Frits Verhagen, Marco Tomamichel, and Erkka Haapasalo give new meaning to a quantum measure in a 2025 paper. The measure, a family of relative entropies, gauges how distinguishable two quantum states are. Until now it lacked a direct operational reading in terms of a concrete task.

The authors supply that reading through state conversion. They study when one pair of flat states can be turned into another, given many copies or a helpful catalyst. Such a conversion exists exactly when all the relative entropies of one pair sit below those of the other, across a full range of settings. The result also yields the best possible conversion rate. Their methods draw on algebraic tools for ordered systems.
arxiv-2507-08420:
Haitian Wang and seven co-authors align three sensor streams to build crisp 3D city maps in a 2025 paper. Laser scans give fine local detail but drift over long drives, bending the whole map. Satellite positioning is weak in city canyons, and motion sensors drift on their own.

Their framework first aligns the streams in time by matching speed patterns with a warping method, then cleans the satellite and motion signals with a Kalman filter. Local maps are stitched by a standard registration method and a pose graph that closes loops. Satellite anchors then pin the whole map in place, with a fine pass over overlaps. The team also releases a large Perth data set for others to test against.
arxiv-2507-08720:
Majczak and co-authors study in 2025 spin ties in pairs of matter and anti matter born from a strong, time bent electric field. Pair birth of this type is a known quantum effect in a set field form. Past work oft skipped the spin ties of the born pair.

Full wave solves, run two ways that match a known scatter frame, keep those ties in the count. Swirl and coil forms in the pair spread shift with the ties and with the pulse phase. Top tied spin states can form, and a short pulse may act as a fast switch from one to the next.
arxiv-2507-08920:
Lv and co-authors introduce AMix-1, a large model for proteins built to scale up both in training and at test time. The model rests on a Bayesian flow network design and a systematic training plan. Their 2025 paper first sets a scaling law, then watches structural understanding emerge as the model grows to 1.7 billion parameters.

A key trick feeds the model aligned sequences from related proteins, letting it read deep evolutionary signals and design new proteins inside one framework. With it, the team designed a variant of one protein with up to fifty times the activity of the natural form. A test time method mimics directed evolution in the computer, gaining more as the checking budget grows. The authors frame the system as groundwork for lab linked protein design.
arxiv-2507-09320:
Yue Li, Fei Li, Mengli Tian, and Yuqin Yao build a modified KP equation in two thousand twenty-five. Integrable equations in three spatial dimensions are a famed open problem. Fokas reached four plus two dimensions in two thousand six. The step down to three plus one stayed open for years.

A nonlinear Fourier transform achieved that reduction for KP in twenty twenty two. Here the modified KP gets the same treatment. The generalized form uses complex time and keeps Laplace's equation. Real time then yields the three plus one dimensional equation. A d-bar formalism solves its initial value problem.
arxiv-2507-09520:
Nguyen and Pylyavskyy present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on correlations in the random cluster model at a boundary case. The model samples random subsets of edges on a graph. Correlation asks whether two edges tend to appear together or apart. For stronger settings, positive correlation is known from a classic inequality. For weaker settings, negative correlation is only conjectured. At the boundary case, the team give an exact counting formula for the gap in question. A similar formula was known only for the uniform spanning tree limit.

The result sharpens what is provable about edge dependence in this model. It bridges the tree case and the broader cluster family. Combinatorial methods carry the proof rather than probability bounds.
arxiv-2507-09620:
George Li, Zihan Tan, and Tianyi Zhang study how to shrink planar graphs while keeping distances exact in a 2025 math paper. A planar graph can be drawn without crossing edges. Given a set of key points called terminals, the goal is a smaller graph that still gives the exact distance between every pair of terminals.

The authors build such stand-in graphs whose size depends on how many faces of the drawing hold terminals. Their bound smoothly connects two known cases: a tight bound when all terminals sit on one face, and a looser one for the general case. The construction views the graph as a web of paths and crossings. The authors suggest that viewpoint may help with other graph problems too.
arxiv-2507-09820:
Jia Yi Goh and co-authors offer a hands-on framework for testing the safety of language model applications in a 2025 paper. Most safety work grades the raw model, yet real products add prompts, retrieval, and guardrails that reshape risk. The authors built their method inside a working organization across several live use cases.

The framework has two parts: principles for building a custom risk taxonomy that fits the product, and concrete practices for running the evaluations. Their internal pilot shows the method in action and where it strained. The paper aims to close the gap between safety theory and deployment reality, giving other organizations a template to scale testing.
arxiv-2507-10520:
A spinning black hole can, in principle, give up energy when magnetic field lines snap and reconnect in its plasma. Xiao-Xiong Zeng and Ke Wang compute in 2025 how well that works around a Kerr-Sen-AdS black hole, an exotic cousin carrying a scalar charge inside an anti-de Sitter space. They test plasma on circular orbits and plasma plunging inward.

Extraction stayed possible at spin as low as 0.5 on orbits, and 0.25 in the plunge, far below older thresholds, sometimes beating the classic Blandford-Znajek power. The scalar charge eased the spin demand, while the space's radius pushed back in the plunging zone. Plunging plasma outperformed orbiting plasma throughout.
arxiv-2507-10620:
Chenxi Liu, Hao Miao, Cheng Long, Yan Zhao, Ziyue Li, and Panos Kalnis survey, in a 2025 tutorial paper, how language models are being joined to time series analysis. Time series and text are both sequences, which tempts a merger. But models trained on words are not shaped for numbers over time, and a real gap remains. The tutorial sorts current work by how it crosses that gap. Three strategies make up the taxonomy: converting series into text-like forms, aligning the two kinds of representation, and fusing them inside one model.

The authors then map these strategies onto tasks such as forecasting and anomaly spotting. Open challenges get their own summary, from efficiency to trust. The tutorial aims to widen the practical use of language models on real time series problems. Readers leave with a picture of what works now and where the field should push next.
arxiv-2507-10820:
Müller wrote this paper in twenty twenty-five on how AI agents pick and use tools. Modern agents can call thousands of tools, from search to software functions. The paper argues that rich written descriptions of each tool, called semantic context, are the key to choosing well. It tests that claim in three ways.

First, a theory model based on bandit learning shows that descriptions cut wasted trials and help when the tool set changes. Second, tests with large language models show descriptions drive learning in both steady and shifting tasks. Third, a working pipeline searched a benchmark of over ten thousand tools and let a model run them in sequence. The paper offers guidance for building agents that scale.
arxiv-2507-10920:
Seungho Choi, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, sets out HanjaBridge, a way to clear up word sense in Korean language models by aid of the old Chinese marks some words share. Korean has many such twin words.

Words from Chinese roots can sound the same in the Korean script, yet mean unlike things. In place of a sole fixed mark per word, the new way shows the model all marks a word could take. The model then learns to pick by the text round it. A teacher-student step guards past skill. Tests show a clear lift in Korean grasp, and a strong flow of gains to Chinese as well, through the shared marks.
arxiv-2507-11120:
Ranjith Kumar and Pasquale Marra study in a 2025 paper multicritical points where topology and quantum criticality meet in one dimensional chains. Recent work found edge modes living at gapless points in such chains. The points where gapped and critical phases cross raise sharper questions still.

Their chain couples sites out to third neighbors, a reach that steadies the edge modes. Only nontrivial phases, gapped and critical both, meet at the points in view. Dispersion near the gap closing runs quadratic, a mark of these points. A topological index from the zeros of a complex function tags each point. Discriminants of a linked polynomial split true multicritical points from trivial ones cleanly.
arxiv-2507-11220:
Gabriyelyan and Reznichenko set out kappa-spaces, a new class of Tychonoff spaces. A space is a kappa-space if it maps to a shut part of a Cp(Y) set. Here Y is a place-tight space in the frame of the work. The class sits strict twixt two known classes in the text. It sits past Dieudonne-full spaces and short of mu-spaces in rank. The class holds firm past a range of space moves.

That firmness lets them name a kappa-fill, the least such space. It is the least kappa-space in the Stone-Cech fill that holds X. Point marks in that fill tie to a Dirac mass at the point. That mass is bound or smooth on tight parts of the Cp sets. The fill proves the most big part with same tight sets.
arxiv-2507-11720:
Matthew Belyakov and co-authors report first light measurements of an interstellar comet in a 2025 paper. The comet, named 3I/ATLAS, is only the third known visitor from outside our solar system. It was found on the first of July 2025, on a path that will swing it past the sun. The team measured its reflected light across colors, from violet to near infrared, using large telescopes in California and New Mexico.

The comet's light is red tinted. The redness is strong at blue and green wavelengths and fades toward the infrared. That pattern hints at dust rich in organic material, like many home grown comets. The team saw no clear emission bands from gases such as carbon pairs. They present the spectra as an early baseline for tracking how this visitor changes as it nears the sun.
arxiv-2507-11820:
Oliver Bellwood, Heitor Casagrande, and William Munro wrote a 2025 physics paper on simulating quantum magnetism in two dimensions. A common method squeezes a two dimensional grid of sites into a one dimensional path, and the choice of path shapes how accurate the result is. How much quantum linkage a state holds limits the sizes that can be reached, so a better path matters.

The team tested all paths of a certain kind for grids up to eight by eight. Paths that follow fractal, space filling curves settled on the ground state faster than the usual snake path. They study measures of locality to explain the gain. For larger grids, they tile small best paths to build good large ones. The edge of such paths grows with system size, they report.
arxiv-2507-12520:
Pursiainen and co-authors inspect the home galaxies of stars torn apart by black holes, in a 2025 paper. A tidal disruption event flares when a star wanders too close to a central black hole. The team observed twenty host galaxies with an integral-field spectrograph on a large telescope, mapping gas and stars at fine scales around each nucleus. Five hosts showed extended emission line regions, glowing gas far from the center, including two never reported before.

Every such region sat in a galaxy that had merged, and all nearby post-merger hosts showed one. The link between mergers and disruptions looks strong. Stellar masses near the black holes were also constrained, feeding the accounting of how these rare flares choose their homes.
arxiv-2507-12820:
Shiquan Wang and four co-authors present their entry to a 2025 shared task on emotional support dialogue. Systems that comfort users through chat face growing demand as mental health needs rise. The team built their system on large language models and tuned how those models answer people in distress.

They tried two tuning routes: a light method that adjusts a small set of added weights, and full fine-tuning of the whole model. Prompt design shaped the replies as well. Their best system placed second in the contest, which the authors read as proof that language models, tuned with care, can give fitting support. They plan work on deeper emotional reading and more personal replies.
arxiv-2507-12920:
Zichao Shu and co-authors present a better way to make reference paths for robot tests in this 2025 study. Labs judge mapping and tracking systems by comparing their paths with truth paths from camera-based motion capture. But capture systems jitter, and their clocks and frames may not line up with the device under test, so truth paths carry error.

Their method fuses capture data with motion sensor data from the device itself. It starts the math safely, models smooth paths with flexible curves on the rotation space, and drops bad readings when the setup grows weak. In tests it beat past methods and gave finer truth paths. The gain lets labs judge not just position error, but also rotation and step-by-step error, which older benchmarks largely skipped.
arxiv-2507-13520:
Sizhen Bian, Mengxi Liu, and Paul Lukowicz overview a sensing method based on the human body's electric field in a 2025 paper. The body carries a natural electrostatic charge, and changes in that field can reveal behavior without contact or cameras. The method is passive, frugal with energy, and non-intrusive, which suits wearables and smart rooms.

They trace the principles, history, and hardware designs behind the approach, and survey its uses across research fields. A key weakness is sensitivity to environmental change, and they discuss ways to counter it. Future work on sensor fusion and better hardware is highlighted, with open resources shared to spur development.
arxiv-2507-13720:
Saurav Ghosh and Niloy Deb Roy Mishu survey in 2025 how quantum machines strain blockchains, and what forms may stand. Quantum math can break the codes that guard most chains in use today. Two paths have grown in reply: chains with quantum proof codes, and chains built on quantum traits.

The survey sets base ideas, builds, and hard spots for both paths side by side. Trade offs in safety, scale, and field use get a full pass. Open gaps span gear, vote rules, and net design. The work aims to serve as a map for chain work in the quantum age.
arxiv-2507-13920:
Cause links in the world are not fixed wires: two things touch, push, and part, and the link lives just for that span. Turan Orujlu, Christian Gumbsch, Martin Butz, and Charley Wu build a learner for such links in a 2025 study. Their frame draws a cause edge only when things truly meet.

The build task is cast as a game for a crew of small agents. Each agent calls, step by step, which things link at that tick. Things and forces are split by three learned marks: how apt a thing is to change, to cause, and to be steered. On physics guess tasks, the sparse frame beat dense graph tools, most at long spans and with shifts in thing count.
arxiv-2507-14020:
Marwan Hassini and co-authors test used electric car batteries in this 2025 study. When a car battery retires, its cells may still hold most of their charge and serve in fixed storage. The team asked whether a cell's place inside its module shapes how much life it has left, since heat and wear can vary by spot.

They pulled three modules from electric vehicles and tested all thirty-six cells. On average the cells kept about ninety-five percent of their health, but the spread between cells was wide. A standard test for group effects found no link between a cell's place and its health. The authors say each retired pack must be checked cell by cell, and that second-life packs need cooling and balancing gear.
arxiv-2507-14420:
Lenin Arango-Castillo and Francisco Martínez-Ramírez measured in 2025 how weather shocks feed into Mexican inflation, using a regional panel of data. Climate effects on prices may differ between a single bad season and a shifted climate. Their models separate the two horizons.

A panel model with lagged terms tracked the price index against local temperature and rainfall, each measured against its own thirty-year norm, weighted by population. Short-run reactions were read through impulse responses from local projections. The verdict splits by horizon: in the short term the weather variables had no clear effect. In the long term, only rainfall norms mattered, with wetter-than-normal conditions pushing inflation up, in the findings reported. Readers get a climate-inflation link with a clock on it: rain, not heat, and slow, not fast.
arxiv-2507-14620:
Beth Bjorkman, Sean English, Johnathan Koch, and Amanda Verga study fragile power domination, a math model of sensor placement on power grids, in a research paper from 2025. Sensors watch the grid, but real sensors can break. In this model each sensor fails on its own with a set chance, and the survivors watch by the classic rules.

The authors study how many nodes stay watched on average under random failure. They pin down when two networks with set sensor spots behave the same in that average. They also show how adding structure to a network can steer the expected count. The results guide grid designs that stay watchable even as sensors fail.
arxiv-2507-14920:
Data that change over time are everywhere, and charts help people spot trends and cycles in them. Evandro S Ortigossa, Fábio F Dias, Diego C Nascimento, and Luis Gustavo Nonato review chart methods for time series in 2025. Big sets with many features per sample make the task hard. Good tools must sum up complex data while keeping the time side clear.

The review walks through methods and tools that support visual exploration step by step. It gives builders theory and design guidance for making full systems of this kind. Users range from data scientists hunting patterns to teams reporting change over time. The authors stress that sight is a strong channel for turning raw numbers into usable knowledge.
arxiv-2507-15120:
Stefan Borgwardt, Duy Nhu, and Gabriele Röger merged planning software with background knowledge in a 2025 paper. Automated planners chain actions to reach a goal, usually with all facts spelled out and nothing left open. Ontologies instead store shared domain knowledge with open-world rules, where missing facts are unknown rather than false, and mixing the two styles has been tricky.

Their method uses a lightweight ontology language for action conditions and a coherence rule for action effects. The cost in complexity stays no worse than earlier mixes. A fast translation turns the whole problem into a classical planning task, and tests on old and new benchmarks show the planner handling the variants well.
arxiv-2507-15420:
Robert David and four co-authors address data checks for privacy contracts in this 2025 computer science paper. Companies that share data under Europe's privacy law often write contracts about what each side must do. Software can test those contracts against linked data graphs, but clashing or faulty data can quietly spoil the checks.

The team built their fix on SHACL, a standard language for stating what valid data looks like. Their method spots clashes and partly repairs them on its own, offering the user ranked fixes to restore order. They added the method to an existing contract-checking tool and tested it for correctness and speed. The work aims to help negotiators keep contract data clean enough for the checks to mean something.
arxiv-2507-15820:
Yuxun Guo, Feng Yuan, and Wenbin Zhao extend a factorization result for a particle physics observable in a 2025 paper. Energy-energy correlators measure how energy flows between pairs of particles in a collision. Near the same direction, their pattern can be split into simpler parts and summed to all orders, which sharpens predictions.

Using a formalism for pairs of fragments, the team complete the split in the collinear limit and derive the full resummation in a transformed space. The result matches fixed-order calculations exactly where they overlap. They then show the resummation's effect in electron-positron annihilation, where it improves predictions at small angles in a notable way. Such sharpened tools matter for precision tests at colliders.
arxiv-2507-16020:
Xi Yang, Jiachen Wang, Song Han, and Suining He present a model from two thousand twenty-five for forecasting bike sharing demand at each station. City bike systems suffer when some stations empty out while others overflow. Predicting pickups and returns station by station is hard because patterns tangle across space and time, and a city has hundreds of stations.

Their network, called BikeMAN, uses two attention layers: one captures how stations relate to each other, and one captures how traffic at a station evolves. An encoder and decoder frame the forecast. The team trained it on more than ten million trips from New York City's system, covering over seven hundred stations. The model predicted traffic for all stations with high accuracy.
arxiv-2507-16420:
Lorenzo Ducci and Sandro Mereghetti report the return of rapid X-ray pulsations from a binary system missing for decades in a 2025 astronomy study. The system pairs a neutron star with a Be star in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Its spin pulses, near sixty-nine milliseconds, flashed during a brilliant outburst in the early eighties and were never seen again despite the system's fame.

A sensitive X-ray telescope caught the pulses during a short interval in early 2023, measuring the period precisely and a pulsed share of about a fifth of the light. The rediscovery shows the spinning beam still sweeps Earth under the right conditions.
arxiv-2507-16620:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Al Alakkad build a math framework for how the meaning of a text can settle through endless self-reference, in a 2025 paper. Their tools come from category theory, step-by-step refinement across endless stages, and game models of dialogue. The question is whether repeated reinterpretation can end at one stable reading.

They define a refinement operator and run it through all ordinal stages, showing it lands on a single fixed point. A parallel game model, an endless exchange between a text and its interpreter, has that same object as its only stable outcome. The authors stress the result needs no training data or statistics; it is proven symbolically. They offer it both to formal linguistics and to builders of language systems that reason about their own outputs.
arxiv-2507-16820:
Disaster informatics, the study of information in crises, swelled during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ngan Tran and three co-authors map the field's output from January 2020 to September 2022 with bibliometric tools and language-model topic analysis. They chart which countries, institutions, and authors published most, who worked with whom, and what topics rose.

The hardest-hit countries were also among the most active, each with its own focus. Collaboration clustered by region and language, and top authors tended to keep one or two close partners. The pandemic pushed the field toward public health and toward shared, cross-sector data projects. The authors offer the map as strategic guidance for building disaster capacity. The study appears in 2025.
arxiv-2507-17020:
Flavio Correa da Silva argues that ethical confusion about artificial intelligence starts with a blurred understanding of what AI is. The technology has received unprecedented attention, raising ethical concerns about its development and use. Those concerns, he contends, stem from unclear ideas about the technology itself, how it can be used, and how society has interpreted it.

The article examines the concept of AI through three descriptive facets. For each facet, it considers the ethical issues that facet raises. The analysis separates questions that public debate tends to merge: what the technology is, what it does, and what people make of it. Silva closes by proposing a framework for the ethical assessment of AI use. The paper serves readers who want ethical evaluation of AI to begin from a clearer account of the thing being evaluated.
arxiv-2507-17220:
Jiansong Wan and co-authors distill design lessons for robots that navigate toward a goal photo. Their 2025 paper builds PIG-Nav, a pretrained model for image-goal navigation. Such models aim to work in new places with no retraining. Two design choices proved key across their tests.

First, fusing the current view and goal image early, through a pretrained vision encoder, beat late mixing. Second, extra side tasks during training enriched the model's sense of global layout. The team also built a pipeline to label large game video sets cheaply as training fodder. Adding that data lifted scores further. PIG-Nav beat prior models by wide margins in zero-shot and fine-tuned tests, while needing less labeled data to adapt.
arxiv-2507-17320:
Wong and Elmqvist present a chart trick in 2025 for timelines where events come in bursts. Real data, from papers over years to drug doses in care, often clump hard and then go quiet. A straight time axis wastes space on the quiet parts and crowds the bursts into a blur.

Their method, EventLines, stretches and squeezes the time scale to match where events fall. The axis itself is drawn to show how its scale changes, so readers are not fooled. A crowd study tested how well people read time under such warped scales. For anyone who must show bursty records on one screen, the idea offers a fair trade: space goes where the events are, and the warp is shown, not hidden.
arxiv-2507-17420:
Sneha George Gnanakalavathy and co-authors predict CT scan quality from settings using causal deep learning, in work from 2025. Sharper scans usually mean more radiation, so clinics walk a dose tightrope. Knowing which settings drive quality would ease that trade-off.

Their framework, CAPRI-CT, fuses image data with scan settings like voltage, current, and contrast type. An ensemble of autoencoders extracts causal features from the paired inputs. The model predicts signal-to-noise ratio for a planned scan. It also runs what-if simulations, such as swapping contrast agents before scanning. Strong predictive scores came from ensemble training. Planners can tune protocols on screen instead of on patients.
arxiv-2507-17620:
Mazzucchelli and Pratt study in 2025 the shape of a geometry object that arose from particle physics, called the amplituhedron. They ask when such objects count as convex, in a fresh sense that fits sets inside curved spaces. Their test case is the simplest non trivial form.

They prove that form is convex in their sense inside its host space. Along the way they define a new polytope, the exterior cyclic polytope, which forms the flat hull of the object. Its faces and dual are charted. A dual form of the object is also defined and shown to be an amplituhedron again, with data changed by a twist map.
arxiv-2507-17820:
Sijia Cai and co-authors report a galaxy almost free of metals in a 2025 astronomy paper. In this field, metals mean any element heavier than helium, and the first stars were thought to form only in the early universe from metal-free gas. The galaxy, named CR3, sits at a distance where its light left it at cosmic noon.

Data from three major observatories show very strong hydrogen and helium lines, and no clear metal lines at all. The gas holds less than a hundredth of the Sun's metal share, the lowest known at that era. Shape fits suggest a very young, low-mass star group about two million years old. The find hints that first-generation star birth lasted far later than long assumed.
arxiv-2507-18220:
Ansei Yonezawa and co-authors improved a method that reads equations from data in a 2025 paper. The method, called SINDy, finds the few terms that drive a moving system, picked from a library of candidate terms. Picking that library is the hard part, since the right terms are rarely known ahead of time.

Their add-on trims and tunes the library as it works, rather than fixing it at the start. They judge the change by long-horizon forecasting, where the found equations are run far ahead in steps. Small early flaws grow fast in such runs, so the test is strict. A better library should hold forecasts steady for longer spans.
arxiv-2507-18620:
Ravi Kuchimanchi, writing alone in 2025, revisits a famous puzzle in strong-force physics: why a certain phase angle seems to vanish. His tool is the Hamiltonian formalism, which describes a system through its energy. He asks what happens if parity, the mirror symmetry of space, is exact in quantum chromodynamics.

He shows that parity can be a true symmetry only if the phase is zero or pi. Mixing states from different phase sectors yields only classical mixtures, matching known selection rules. The argument supports a parity-based route to the strong CP problem without new particles.
arxiv-2507-19120:
Wenhui Chang and co-authors build a data rich path to predict flow change in a 2025 paper. Air or water flow along a surface starts smooth and then turns rough and mixed. That shift is hard to predict because it reacts strongly to tiny outside nudges that no one can fully know in advance.

Models based on the core flow equations often miss how the shift starts in real settings. The team built a broad dataset on the shift and a fine grained prediction frame that accepts that unknown nudges exist. The aim is better forecasts for craft, ships, and energy systems, where the shift drives drag and heat.
arxiv-2507-19320:
Vishal Parmar, Domenico Scordino, and Ignazio Bombaci study, in twenty twenty-five, whether dark matter can trigger a type of supernova in the cores of giant stars. Electron-capture supernovae form low-mass neutron stars. A recent candidate event supports the channel. The team models cores rich in neon, typical for these explosions, with two fluids: ordinary matter and asymmetric dark matter, which interacts with normal matter only through gravity. They track both particle counts through collapse, so progenitors map consistently to remnants.

Dark matter raises the core's central density. That lowers the mass threshold at which electron capture starts, so lower-mass stars can explode this way. The remnants are neutron stars mixed with dark matter. Their masses can fall well below current observed bounds. The energy released in collapse also changes, they find.
arxiv-2507-20020: Võ Quôc Bao, Phùng Hô Hai, and Dào Van Thinh work in algebraic geometry over fields of positive characteristic. For a smooth projective curve over such a field, they study the stratified fundamental group, a refined version of the usual fundamental group that keeps track of extra structure from the characteristic. The paper investigates how stratified cohomology, built from that structure, relates to the group cohomology of the group itself.
arxiv-2507-20120:
Rajat Koner and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, Local2Global, an online method for video instance segmentation, picking out and tracking each object in video. Online methods suit long sequences and gradual change, but predictions drift with noise, occlusions, and scene cuts. Their framework builds on query propagation, where learned queries follow objects across frames. It adds two query types: local queries that capture each frame's fresh object features, and global queries that hold past space-time context.

A lightweight transformer decoder, the L2G-aligner, aligns local and global queries early. The model thus uses the current frame while keeping temporal consistency, with smooth transitions. No extra heuristics or memory modules are needed. Tests across segmentation benchmarks show state-of-the-art results with a simple baseline, they report.
arxiv-2507-20720:
Tiffany Tseng and three co-authors ask teachers about multimodal AI in twenty twenty-five. Multimodal large language models can make and discuss images, text, speech, and video. Such powers could enrich school learning in many ways, yet how teachers imagine using them was largely unknown.

The team ran workshops with twelve K-12 educators, where the teachers dreamed up learning opportunities and voiced practical concerns. They also built trial learning applications with a current multimodal model and its artifacts feature. The study collects how teachers pictured benefits, from new interaction styles to richer materials. Classroom constraints and implementation needs surfaced with the enthusiasm. Readers in education technology get design guidance from the people who would run these tools with children.
arxiv-2507-21220:
Mitsuru Tanaka, Daisuke Fujii, and Mamiya Kawaguchi probe the forces inside the proton and neutron in a 2025 paper. Gravitational form factors describe how a particle answers to gravity, encoding its internal pressure and stress. One of them, called D(t), is notoriously hard to pin down. The team computes it in a Skyrme model built on a theory that respects a near-symmetry of the strong force.

Their model carries both the pion and a scalar meson, the latter standing in for the gluonic breaking of scale symmetry. Varying that meson's mass tests how much the anomaly matters. It matters a lot: without it, the nucleon's stability conditions fail, and the confining inward force vanishes. With a well-chosen parameter, the computed curve matches lattice supercomputer results closely.
arxiv-2507-21420:
Chaoyu Li, Yogesh Kulkarni, and Pooyan Fazli speed up training of multimodal language models in 2025 by pruning tokens. Training cost balloons with every token processed, and past savings tricks mostly helped at run time, not during training.

Their method, ReGATE, lets a frozen teacher model grade each token's worth, blended with a running estimate of the student's struggles. Hard, informative tokens stay; redundant ones are skipped on the fly. Across three models, peak accuracy arrived up to twice as fast using only thirty-eight percent of the tokens. Longer training even beat the standard recipe outright while cutting total token use by over two-fifths.
arxiv-2507-21520:
A three-step frame for image question tasks is set out by Zijian Zhang and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. The frame won high marks at a Meta-run cup built on a hard test set. Image models often make up answers. Search-backed help can ground them, but weak image grasp and mixed sources still trip the tools. One model per task keeps the build plain.

Data boosts, search help, rank fixes, and joint fine-tuning fill the steps. Auto scores placed the team third, third, and first across tasks. Human judges then set the third task at second place.
arxiv-2507-21620:
Benjamin Weiss looks at what is typical for processes that come from dynamical systems in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Start with an ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard measure space. Each finite labeled partition then sets a stationary process. The space of partitions has a complete separable metric. So it makes sense to ask which traits hold for a generic, or typical, partition.

Weiss sets out a set of such generic traits. For one, the generic partition sets a process that is not Rosenblatt mixing. If the transformation is a K-automorphism but not Bernoulli, the generic partition is also K but not Bernoulli. The point is that strong mixing traits are the rare case, not the rule.
