Existing methods were mostly adapted from text-only unlearning, and they treat every answer token as equally important.

That uniformity is the flaw this 2026 preprint attacks. Some tokens carry the private content, while others are harmless filler. The authors propose visual-guided key-token regularization, which uses the image to identify the tokens that matter and focuses the unlearning there. Precise unlearning matters for privacy law and safety: erase too little and secrets leak, erase too much and the model loses useful skills.
arxiv-2601-22120:
Qian Zhang and co-authors compare two tools grid operators use to stay flexible. High shares of renewable power make net demand ramp steeply up and down. Operators respond either with look-ahead economic dispatch, which plans generation over a coming window, or with ramp products, which pay for standby ramping ability.

Both remedies are widely deployed, but whether they are equivalent under the industry-standard rolling-window dispatch was not well understood. The team's 2026 preprint assesses the two side by side. The comparison matters for market design. If one tool quietly buys less flexibility per dollar, operators across whole regions are overpaying for insurance against the same ramps.
arxiv-2601-22420:
Roelien Timmer, Necva Bölücü, and Stephen Wan built MetaLead, a hand-checked data set for making leaderboards from papers. Leaderboards rank models and track progress in machine learning. Their 2026 preprint notes that past auto-built sets keep only each paper's best score and cover few fields.

Human curators built MetaLead to be broader and more exact. It can train and test tools that read papers and post their scores. Clear, full boards help the field trust its own progress claims. They also save hours of manual checking. The data set is the product here.
arxiv-2601-22620:
Hyunseo Shin and Wonseok Hwang swap layers between models to spread safety to low-resource languages. Their 2026 preprint notes that safety data are mostly English, so models tuned in other languages tend to be less safe. Those expert models still hold the language skill their users need.

Layer-wise swapping grafts safety traits into them, layer by layer. The aim is safe models that keep their local tongue. That goal matters for fair, global access to AI. The work offers a surgical fix, not a full retrain. It respects both safety and language.
arxiv-2601-22820:
Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam and four co-authors tackle drug advice for patients a system has never seen. Large hospital record systems can suggest treatments, but new patients have little history to learn from. That cold-start gap makes early advice shaky and sometimes unsafe.

Their method adapts fast to each new patient, a style called meta-learning, and filters out cases where it is too unsure. Filtering low-trust cases keeps weak advice from reaching doctors as fact. Safer early advice matters most in busy clinics, where new patients arrive daily.
arxiv-2601-22920:
Wulin Xie and six co-authors improve how machines judge image quality the way humans do. Image quality assessment predicts scores that match human opinion of a photo or video. Recent methods use large multimodal models trained with rewards, but they treat all training samples the same.

Some samples give stable predictions and others are noisy, so equal weighting boosts the noisy ones. Their method, Q-Hawkeye, weights training by reliability for steadier learning. Trustworthy quality scores matter for photo apps, streaming, and medical imaging. Reliability weighting addresses the first flaw, while a second flaw concerns models that produce confident scores without stable grounds.
arxiv-2601-23020:
Stefan Schott and four co-authors hunt for risky code hiding inside Java projects. Modern software leans heavily on open-source parts, which saves time and raises quality. The same habit can pull known security flaws into a codebase, sometimes in ways that stay hidden.

Their study uncovers inclusions of vulnerable dependencies in real-world projects. Hidden flaws are dangerous because scanners and audits may report a project as clean. Knowing how flaws sneak in helps teams design checks that actually catch them. Heavy reliance on open-source parts is the root exposure: each included component can carry its known flaws into the product.
arxiv-2601-23220:
Anglin Liu and four co-authors cure a perceptual flaw in medical multimodal models. These models speak fluently about diagnoses, yet the authors find even top systems suffer spatial blindness. They fail to ground answers in objective spatial constraints, producing plausible but wrong claims.

Their Med-Scout post-training uses geometry-aware reinforcement learning to fix the grounding. Training rewarded on spatial fidelity, not just fluent text, should cut visual hallucinations. In medicine, a confident wrong measurement can misdirect real treatment. Geometric fidelity, not linguistic fluency, is the training target, reversing the priorities that produced the blindness.
arxiv-2602-00220: Tomasz Les and colleagues present a hybrid two stage framework that builds 3D kidney anatomy from macroscopic slices, with CT models as a shape standard. Their pipeline first runs Optimal Cross-section Matching for global alignment in translation, rotation, and uniform scaling. A light deep refinement network then predicts residual local deformations between neighboring slices. The staged design aims to fix the limits of learned registration on scarce, distorted slice data, where fully learned methods often fail.
arxiv-2602-00420: Yihang Chen and team introduce Text-DJ, a jailbreak attack on vision language models using text alone. Defenses often focus on explicit textual inputs or relevant visual scenes. Text-DJ bypasses safeguards by exploiting optical character recognition capability, in three stages. First, a harmful query is decomposed into benign sub queries. Second, distraction queries maximally irrelevant to the harmful query are picked. Third, all queries are presented simultaneously as a grid of images, with sub queries in the middle.
arxiv-2602-00520: Minghui Sun and colleagues keep the layers of event streams intact instead of flattening multisets into one sequence. Flattening wastes compute on dense attention, learns false links within sets, and yields weak set-level vectors from pooling. Their Nested Event Stream Transformer, or NEST, keeps that hierarchy as a built-in bias, lifting both speed and representation quality. The team adds Masked Set Modeling, a way to strengthen set-level learning. Tests on real multiset sequence data show NEST tracking dynamics while lifting pretraining speed and downstream results.
arxiv-2602-00720: Guo-He Yang investigates inclusive weak decay of beauty-charmed baryons in the non-relativistic potential quark model. Treating heavy diquarks as colour anti-triplet bound states, the author calculates transition form factors from Cornell-potential wave functions. Decay rates are computed for four channels. Background from Bc decays to doubly charmed baryons is roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the signal. The inclusive decay offers a discovery channel that could reveal the doubly heavy baryon at the LHC, following doubly charmed decay chains.
arxiv-2602-00820: Supakorn Katewongveerachart and colleagues find several axion fields can oscillate while keeping w0 below minus one third, with some models flipping wa sign. They test whether dark energy comes from several slowly rolling axion fields rather than the cosmological constant. The work is motivated by DESI results and the string axiverse. They model universes with two to four axions and compute prior probabilities for the equation-of-state parameters w0 and wa. Adding fields and interactions pushes prior support away from thawing quintessence and DESI distance measures.
arxiv-2602-00920: Stefano Bellucci and colleagues set out a basic test separating operator standing, dynamical spectral realization, and particlehood, using gravitino mass pairs as model. A quantum field theory containing a field does not alone mean a matching asymptotic particle exists. Particlehood ranks shape and state, effective algebra, dynamics, and spectral study, with placing set by a real spectral atom of non-zero weight. They obtain four results, including blocked global supercharges on de Sitter space under sign flip, and loss of the Minkowski two-particle threshold.
arxiv-2602-01120: Youkang Wang and co-authors give sequential scaling at run time a firm math base, where past gains were small and murky. Old plans lean on rules of thumb that hide clear best bounds. By casting step-by-step scaling as a two-state Markov chain, they draw out its core traits and solve in closed form when scores rise plus the top, flat, and floor bounds. Their MarkovScale plan then uses those rules to trade score against cost on firm ground, beating top parallel and serial plans.
arxiv-2602-01320: Andreu Rocamora Martorell builds a variable-slope smooth-k filter for halo counts under damped and wavy power spectra. The plain smooth-k filter catches small-scale drops but glues them to mid-scale waves. Letting the window's log slope drift between two end regimes unglues small-scale drops from mid-scale dark-acoustic waves. One parameter set then matches N-body sims for warm dark matter and ETHOS wave models in both regimes at once. It gives a single bendy analytic frame for non-cold dark matter halo counts.
arxiv-2602-01620: Caitlyn Hardiman and colleagues confirm nonthermal line broadening in the DM Tau disk, a turbulence probe. The team fits high resolution carbon monoxide observations from exoALMA with a radiative transfer code, searching five million disk models in a Bayesian framework. The fit finds a nonthermal share near four tenths of the sound speed, too large for thermal motion alone. The same structure reproduces sulfur monosulfide emission well, and a constrained background model exposes leftover moment map structures that may trace forming planets.
arxiv-2602-01720: Peisen Yao and colleagues present Phoenix, a modular framework for C/C++ pointer analysis that unifies alias analysis algorithms behind one stable interface. It separates solver backends, IR building, constraint making and client queries, making analyses simple to compare, swap and compose while showing precision cost tradeoffs. Tests on 28 GNU coreutils programs compare Phoenix against SVF across sensitivity variants. Phoenix flow insensitive analysis beats SVF on all benchmarks, with speedups near threefold, while the flow sensitive matchup splits thirteen faster, fourteen slower and one tied.
arxiv-2602-02020: Jens Egholm Pedersen and colleagues connect wavelet transforms with spiking neural networks through scale-space theory, using scale-covariant guarantees in leaky integrate-and-fire neurons to build mother waves close to plain wavelets. A rebuild test shows the approach is feasible, while further analysis should cut current errors. Their work points to a new spiking signal picture for more energy-saving signal handling methods.
arxiv-2602-02220: Bo Miao and colleagues present LangMap, a hierarchical benchmark for open-vocabulary goal navigation by embodied agents. Existing benchmarks focus on category-level goals or use vision-language descriptions containing ambiguities and semantic errors. LangMap enriches real indoor scans with human-verified annotations across four goal levels: scene, room, region, and instance. It covers hundreds of categories with thousands of tasks, improves text-to-view matching over a prior benchmark, and passes an independent audit with most matches unique and correct.
arxiv-2602-02320: Feiyang Cai and others propose an auto method for molecular descriptions at scale, building the MolLangData dataset. Human annotation costs make large high-quality data out of reach. The team extends a chemical nomenclature parser based on rules to interpret IUPAC names and build XML metadata encoding structure. Validation mixing human and model reconstruction on a subset shows sharpness. The dataset trains a model via reinforcement learning for conditional molecule output.
arxiv-2602-02420:
Martha Valentina Guarin Escudero and 1 co-author compare two ways of organizing graded manifolds, a geometry where coordinates carry integer weights, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They treat these manifolds as semiformal homogeneity structures and contrast two polynomial filtrations coming from local models. In finite dimensions the filtrations agree component by component, though one generally induces a finer topology.

A classical theorem says every such manifold matches, noncanonically, a bundle built from its own data. The authors extend a graded Borel lemma into a Borel-Whitney theorem: maps defined on formal neighborhoods lift to smooth maps between those bundles. From this they study a functor, a structure-preserving map between categories, sending bundles to formal neighborhoods of their zero sections. The functor turns out to be full and surjective on objects, tying the two categories tightly together.
arxiv-2602-02620:
Weining Fu and 3 co-authors build a foundation model for cryo-electron microscopy density maps, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cryo-EM reveals biomolecular assemblies at near-atomic resolution, and data volume and complexity are growing fast. Deep learning models built for one task scale poorly across the many analyses researchers need.

CryoLVM learns structural representations directly from measured density maps paired with solved structures. A joint-embedding predictive design, the same family used in self-supervised vision, pairs with a specialized backbone network. A novel histogram-based distribution alignment loss speeds convergence and sharpens fine-tuning. The team tests three downstream tasks: density map sharpening, super-resolution, and missing wedge restoration, an artifact of limited tilt angles in the microscope. CryoLVM beat state-of-the-art rivals across multiple quality metrics on all three. The authors present it as a flexible base for the wider cryo-EM workflow.
arxiv-2602-02720:
In a 2026 paper, Manimala Mitra and 3 co-authors ask whether the next layer of effective field theory, dimension-eight operators, can be told apart from the standard dimension-six ones. The testbed is the High-Luminosity LHC. Their setting extends the Standard Model effective theory with right-handed neutrinos. Using Hilbert series methods, they derive the complete dimension-eight basis and confirm it matches the known basis lists.

One sample operator gets a full collider study. It predicts right-handed neutrino pairs produced with jets, decaying into electron-jet final states with vertices that may sit displaced. Dimension-six terms can fake similar signatures, which is the crux. A boosted choice tree trained on kinematic observables separates the dimension-eight signal cleanly from each dimension-six hypothesis. The upshot reshapes analysis practice: dimension-eight effects are resolvable in practice and belong in collider interpretations, not in the truncation error.
arxiv-2602-03020:
Generating realistic power flow answers much faster is the goal of Shashank Shekhar and 4 co-authors in a 2026 paper. AC optimal power flow datasets support data-driven power system tools. Producing them requires balancing score against computation. Diffusion models make high-quality samples, but their slow sampling limits how large a dataset can practically grow for training.

The authors argue the generator only needs good starting points, since solvers enforce exact real feasibility afterward. Their fast diffusion uses implicit deterministic steps plus physics-guided corrections during sampling. Tests on standard six, twenty-four, and one-hundred-eighteen bus systems followed. Sampling ran up to twenty times faster than standard diffusion. Statistical accuracy and physical consistency stayed comparable. Code is publicly released.
arxiv-2602-03620:
Could enthusiasm for a technology feed on itself until the whole network crashes into a winter? Sabin Roman and Francesco Bertolotti build mathematical models of that cycle in a 2026 paper. In their first model, technologies grow by drawing development potential from related technologies, so no technology advances in isolation.

A second model couples supply, demand, and investment in three dimensions, and oscillations appear when investment runs too high. Merging the two through a shared variable produces chaotic boom-bust cycles when investment or diffusion gets excessive. The combined model reproduces long computing trends and the boom-bust pattern in NFT transaction data. The authors draw out the implication for AI itself: a new winter is a modeled outcome, not just a metaphor.
arxiv-2602-03920:
A robot's success rate means little if users misread it. Isaac Sheidlower and 6 co-authors studied how non-experts interpret evaluations of robot foundation models, the general-purpose systems behind home robots. Their 2026 paper gave users real evaluation data, including success rates, failure descriptions, and videos.

Non-experts used success rates much as experts would expect. They also prized failure case reports, which research projects rarely publish. Users wanted the underlying real data rather than summaries alone. The findings argue for richer public reporting, so people can judge what a home robot can safely attempt.
arxiv-2602-04220:
Simple videos should not cost as many tokens as complex ones. Yao Teng and 5 co-authors built a video autoencoder that adapts in a 2026 paper. Standard video autoencoders compress at a fixed rate, waste room on easy footage, and use rigid convolutional designs with fixed decoders.

Their One-Dimensional Diffusion Video Autoencoder uses query-based transformers to extract features and produce variable-length latents. A dropout trick adjusts latent length to how hard the content is. A diffusion transformer decoder then rebuilds pixels, recovering detail that fixed decoders smear. Two-stage training reached reconstruction quality on par with three-dimensional convolutional autoencoders, the backbone of modern video generation.
arxiv-2602-04320:
The gut-brain axis needs a benchmark as careful as its science. Marco Martinelli and colleagues present GutBrainIE in a 2026 paper, a curated dataset for pulling facts from biomedical literature. It covers named entities, their links to concepts, and relations between them.

Over sixteen hundred PubMed abstracts were labeled by hand by biomedical and language experts. Fine-grained entities and relations target links between gut microbes and brain disorders. Older benchmarks lean on distant supervision and narrow scopes, which caps their value. GutBrainIE mixes highly curated data with weakly supervised material, making it useful for training as well as honest scoring.
arxiv-2602-04520:
Wei-Han Tan and Hua-Xing Chen calculate how hypothetical glueballs might decay, in a 2026 paper on particles made only of gluons. Gluons normally bind quarks together, so a particle built purely from them would test our picture of strong-force matter.

The authors use Fierz rearrangement, a method based on the internal symmetries of hadrons, to estimate relative decay rates without a detailed model. They cover two-gluon and three-gluon glueballs with several spin and parity settings. Nearly one hundred ratios result. Their findings suggest two known particles likely contain much glue, while another contains little. They also name promising channels where experiments could hunt for three-gluon glueballs.
arxiv-2602-04620:
Doyeon Lee and 5 co-authors propose QUATRO in a 2026 paper, a fine-tuning method for language models based on reinforcement learning. Popular group-based methods approximate trust regions, limits on how far a policy may move per update, with clipping heuristics that can behave brittlely.

QUATRO enforces the trust-region constraint directly through a principled optimization. The resulting objective is clearer and gives explicit control over updates, with stabilizer terms arising naturally from the exact formulation. Entropy, a measure of output randomness, stays controlled. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, training remained stable under stale policies and aggressive learning rates. The method aims at dependable fine-tuning where heuristic clipping fails.
arxiv-2602-05020:
In large networked control systems, a disturbance at one node should matter less at faraway nodes. Lars Grüne and Mario Sperl prove a version of that intuition in this 2026 control theory paper. Their setting is a nonlinear optimal control problem whose parts interact along a graph, with decoupled dynamics and a quadratic cost.

Starting from the zero state, they perturb a single node's starting condition and track the optimal response. The response at each node shrinks exponentially with its graph distance from the perturbed node. The proof leans on a nonlinear null-controllability condition, which measures whether the system can be steered back to rest. The result is a first step toward carrying known spatial decay results from linear-quadratic problems to nonlinear ones, and a numerical example illustrates the effect.
arxiv-2602-05120:
Neural networks that exist on paper can reason through any Boolean task, but trained networks often cannot. Wenhao Li and 3 co-authors close that gap in this 2026 theoretical computer science paper, submitted to COLT 2026. They show an architecture whose samples are guaranteed to be valid Boolean circuits, so each prediction carries a circuit-level certificate.

The model sets out a distribution over circuits built from simple gates. For any Boolean function at all, some parameter setting makes the sampled circuit compute it with probability as high as desired, which is the universality claim. Simple functions that depend on few inputs, called juntas, need only a count of parameters growing linearly with input size. On a truth-table completion benchmark, the architecture trained reliably and stayed exactly Boolean inside. Ordinary multilayer perceptrons matched its accuracy but left only about a tenth of their units interpretable as Boolean.
arxiv-2602-05220:
People hear audio as a whole: speech, a door slamming, and music blend into one scene with meaning. Jinchuan Tian and 16 co-authors built Bagpiper in this 2026 paper, an eight-billion-parameter audio foundation model that takes the holistic route. Where earlier audio models trained on rigid, task-specific labels, Bagpiper routes everything through rich captions, detailed natural language descriptions of what is heard.

Pretraining on a corpus of 600 billion tokens taught the model a two-way mapping between raw audio and that conceptual caption space. At fine-tuning time it first captions, then reasons over the caption to solve the task, a caption-then-process workflow that needs no task-specific practice. The system generates speech, sound effects, music, and arbitrary mixes of them, and understands audio about as well as a leading seven-billion-parameter rival. The authors promise public release of model, data, and code.
arxiv-2602-05420:
Sorting single cells in microscope images is hard when cells crowd and overlap each other. Rui Sun, Yiwen Yang, and 9 co-authors tackle this task for digital pathology, where clear cell outlines guide later study of tissue samples. Their work starts from graph coloring, a way of labeling linked items so that neighbors get different labels, and asks how well that idea holds up in dense, real tissue.

The authors release a large new data set of packed cell nuclei and study the link patterns in four data sets. They find that most real cell graphs cannot be colored with just two labels, since short odd loops are common. Their system, called Disco, splits the cell graph, marks the hard conflict zones, and trains the model to keep features of nearby cells apart. The goal is cleaner outlines even where cells press tightly together.
arxiv-2602-05820:
Wolf Rayet stars are massive, wind blown suns, and the nitrogen rich kind in the Magellanic Clouds vary in brightness in ways that are still being catalogued. Jana Marković and 5 co-authors analyze long term photometry for forty seven such stars from the OGLE survey, choosing stars with no nearby Gaia counterparts. They characterize overall and short term variability and hunt for periodic patterns.

Variability turned out to be everywhere: about a third of the stars vary strongly, and four fifths vary at least moderately. Eleven cases are periodic, on timescales from two days to nearly two months, pointing to rotating wind structures, binary effects, or pulsations. Nine targets show quasi periodic outbursts, a newly recognized type of variability for these stars. Signals are often transient, fading or vanishing over time.
arxiv-2602-06120:
How fluids resist shearing shows up in the physics of black holes through a deep link between gravity and quantum matter. Paolo Arnaudo studies shear transport values for gravitational ripples around black branes in anti-de Sitter space, a curved space with a boundary. At long wavelengths, the wave answers take a neat form.

Arnaudo shows those answers are fully described by multiple polylogarithms, a family of special math functions. He computes the shear values for a leading theory of quantum matter to a high order, going past earlier results. He then extends the method to other dimensions and maps the shape of the resulting formulas.
arxiv-2602-06220:
Given a set of finite groups, a cover is a single group that contains a copy of every group in the set. Mihai-Silviu Lazorec studies minimum covers, the smallest such groups, and a question about when the minimum cover can be chosen inside a nice class. The classes must be closed under subgroups and direct products.

A recent paper asked for which classes the answer is always yes. Lazorec gives a negative answer for two classes: supersolvable groups and metabelian groups. In both cases, he shows the hoped-for minimum cover inside the class need not exist. The result sharpens the boundary of a question left open by earlier work on minimal cover groups.
arxiv-2602-06920:
Samir Abdaljalil and three co-authors built a test set for a stubborn flaw in language models: making up facts. Most tests are English-only, yet factual slip-ups shift across tongues and output styles. Their set, Halluverse-M3, spans English, Arabic, Hindi, and Turkish, and covers two jobs: answering questions and summing up dialogues.

It splits errors into three kinds: wrong entities, wrong links, and wrong whole sentences. Fake outputs were made by controlled edits to true text and checked by human readers, so each fake lines up cleanly with its source. Tests on a wide mix of current models show answering beats summing up, and sentence-level slips stay hard even for the strongest models. Scores run highest in English and lowest in Hindi.
arxiv-2602-07020:
Amin Haeri and four co-authors improve bond similarity search for fixed-income work. Finding similar bonds is hard. Number-based financial traits tend to swamp categorical traits, such as issuer sector and domicile. Yet the authors show those categories drive how well spread curves can be predicted. Their embedding models capture semantic similarities among categorical traits.

Tests used sparse-issuer augmentation. The embeddings beat one-hot encodings and many other baselines. They improve risk modeling and yield curve construction. The lesson is clear: treat categorical bond traits as meaningful similarities, not as isolated labels. That yields more useful similarity search for portfolio analysis and pricing.
arxiv-2602-07120:
Language models often repeat long stretches of their training data word for word, which creates legal trouble when that data is copyrighted.  Jacqueline He and five co-authors answer with Anchored Decoding, an inference-time technique that keeps output within a set distance of a second model trained only on permissively licensed text.

The method hands out a user-chosen information budget across the generation and enforces a limit at each step, so users can trade risk against quality.  The paper also releases TinyComma 1. 8B, a permissively trained safe model, plus a byte-level version of the technique.  Readers get a useful, model-agnostic way to lower verbatim copying without retraining the risky model.
arxiv-2602-07220:
Symplectic capacity measures the size of a shape in a way that respects Hamiltonian mechanics, and mean width measures it in usual geometric terms.  Jonghyeon Ahn and Ely Kerman explore the relationship between the two for convex bodies, in a short note with two parts.

First they give a new route from the symplectic Brunn-Minkowski inequality to a capacity-width inequality, connecting both to quermassintegrals and to a local version of Viterbo's claim near the ball.  Then they claim which bodies already have minimal mean width among all their symplectic images, and test it on a simple class of quadrics.  Symplectic geometers get fresh links and a precise claim to attack.
arxiv-2602-07320:
Neural networks that survive corruption of their own weights matter for low-power hardware, where noise is a fact of life.  Philip Jacobson and five co-authors study training methods that find minima robust to internal weight perturbations, from both generalization and tuning angles.

They show theoretically and empirically that an over-regularized random-weight perturbation objective is optimal for noise-robust generalization. They map where sharpness-aware minimization helps or hurts, especially under small noise.  The paper connects flat minima to a concrete engineering need: models that keep working when their weights wobble.  Hardware-aware machine learning teams get guidance on which training objective to trust.
arxiv-2602-07720:
Putting a team together means planning for the worst pairing, not just the best one. Sharareh Alipour studies the weighted max-min T-join problem, which picks a set of agents so that even the weakest pairing within it is as strong as possible. Uses range from reviewer assignment to fair resource sharing.

The paper gives an upper bound for a fixed-size version of the problem. It then builds a general algorithm with a proven approximation guarantee that runs in polynomial time, plus exact solutions when weights are only 1 or 2. Tests on real collaboration data show the bounds hold up in practice. It is a solid work in robust combinatorial optimization for multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2602-08020:
Virtual garments should drape like real cloth, but neural draping methods usually trade shape fidelity against collision-free results: soft penalties either distort the mesh or let cloth pass through the body. Minghai Chen and four co-authors present PhysDrape, a hybrid solver that enforces physics explicitly instead.

A physics-informed graph network predicts residual displacements from material parameters and body proximity, then a differentiable two-stage solver applies explicit forces and collision constraints. The combination resolves the usual trade-off by construction rather than by tuning penalty weights. Graphics researchers and virtual-try-on developers gain a draping method that looks right because it respects the physics, not just the training data.
arxiv-2602-08120:
Estimating expectations nested inside expectations arises in optimal stopping and risk analysis, and quantum tech promises speedups there. Yihang Sun and two co-authors study repeatedly nested expectations with a constant number of nestings and propose a quantum recipe costing roughly inverse error, up to logarithmic factors.

Standard lower bounds show that scaling is essentially optimal, giving an almost quadratic speedup over the best old method. Extending prior single-nesting results required a derandomized variant of randomized multilevel Monte Carlo, since careful derandomization overcomes a variable-time issue that otherwise inflates quantized algorithms. Quantum-recipe teams gain a near-optimal method for a broader class of nested estimation problems.
arxiv-2602-08620:
Image diffusion models lean on vision foundation models for meaning features, but those features drop low-level detail like color and texture. Siyu Liu and eight co-authors propose LV-RAE, an autoencoder that restores the missing detail while staying aligned with the meaning distribution. Their arXiv paper targets rebuild quality, a bottleneck for scaling diffusion models.

Rich, high-dimensional latents bring a second problem: decoders grow touchy about small latent shifts, producing artifacts in made images. The authors trace that touchiness to excess decoder response off the data surface. Tuning the decoder for toughness plus controlled noise smoothing of made latents improves output quality. Readers get a two-part fix for sharper rebuilds and cleaner samples.
arxiv-2602-08820:
Making a video from a written request, or editing one with a plain-language order, is the job of Omni-Video 2. Hao Yang and nine co-authors link a large multimodal model, which reads and reasons about the request, to a video diffusion model that draws the frames. The reader model first writes a clear caption of the target scene, which then guides generation.

A light adapter feeds those guiding signals into a ready-made text-to-video model, reusing its skills at low cost. Scaled to 14 billion parameters, the system handles object removal, additions, background swaps, and tricky motion edits. On the FiVE editing test and the VBench generation test, it follows complex orders better than rivals while matching them on quality.
arxiv-2602-08920:
Pretrained transformers rarely say how sure they are, a flaw that matters in high-stakes use. Manh Cuong Dao and five co-authors rework each transformer block as a probabilistic mapping, so uncertainty can flow through the whole stack. Chaining those mappings traces a probability path that mirrors a diffusion process, carrying data mass from input to learned features.

That path is then recompiled onto a single diffusion model with a shared transition rule, giving principled uncertainty propagation without changing what the model predicts. Across vision and language benchmarks, the method beats existing uncertainty-aware transformers on both calibration and accuracy. It offers reliability upgrades for models already in service.
arxiv-2602-09020:
Simulating quantum chemistry on classical machines is key to knowing when quantum computers will truly win. Carla Rieger and seven co-authors present a hybrid simulator that blends full-state simulation with Clifford simulation, aimed at the time evolution of chemistry Hamiltonians. Its core trick is efficient emulation of multi-qubit rotations, the costly step in Trotterized evolution.

By tuning how multi-qubit moves are stored and run through the Pauli frame, the method cuts simulation cost sharply. On tested 24-qubit chemistry Hamiltonians it runs about 18 times faster, or 22 times with MPI parallelism. The same trick should speed any workload heavy in multi-qubit rotations.
arxiv-2602-09220:
Big transformer models forecast loads well but risk overfitting and instability, especially as old data ages out of relevance. Julien Guité-Vinet and two co-authors propose a lightweight multi-view forecaster for short-term loads, using single-value embeddings plus a scaled time-span input to catch time-fitting traits fast. An embedding-dropout mechanism stops the model leaning too hard on any single feature and aids interpretability.

The method matches larger rivals with far fewer parameters and proves robust across data sets, including noisy and sparse cases, while revealing each feature's contribution to the forecast. For energy, finance, and weather forecasting, it offers competitive accuracy without the bulk and brittleness of heavy models.
arxiv-2602-09320:
Cindy Tsang's single-author 2026 paper works on a corner of algebra where a set carries two linked operations, a structure known as a skew brace. It asks when such a structure has no smaller left ideals apart from the trivial one and the whole thing, a property called left-simple. The paper offers a partial classification of the finite left-simple cases, sorting out which forms they can take.

The result matters beyond pure algebra. Finite left-simple skew braces match up exactly, through earlier work by Stefanello and Trappeniers, with minimal Hopf-Galois structures on finite Galois extensions of fields. In plain terms, the classification speaks to two fields at once. It covers the internal shape of these two-operation structures, and the ways a field extension can carry a Hopf-Galois structure with nothing smaller inside it. The paper advances the first side of that bridge.
arxiv-2602-09420:
Meir Shimon's single-author 2026 paper proposes that our observable universe may be only a minute patch of a far larger, older spacetime. On that view, the classic flatness and horizon problems of the hot Big Bang become tricks of selection. We occupy a small causal domain of a much larger connected spacetime that need not be flat. A large positive cosmological constant sets the future horizon scale, capping the accessible region regardless of when it is observed.

The bound is purely about shape, free of inflation, anthropic reasoning, or claims about the hosting spacetime. Inflation then becomes one viable realization of the small-patch picture, not a necessity. A non-inflationary alternative with a slowly growing early spectrum can mimic an inflation-like spectrum over our narrow observable window. Large-scale smoothness, isotropy, and even the arrow of time may follow from restricted access to a larger universe in equilibrium.
arxiv-2602-09520:
Models that score almost alike can still draw very different decision edges, a pattern caught by the Rashomon set. Seeing that variety matters for clarity, fairness, and toughness, since standard metrics hide edge wobble. Xenia Heilmann and two co-authors provide the first formal take on Rashomon sets for shared learning in their 2026 paper, where clients train together without sharing raw data.

Three views organize the idea: a global set over pooled stats, a t-accord set sharing local sets across a fraction of clients, and single sets per client's local spread. The paper shows how standard variety metrics can be estimated under shared-learning privacy constraints, then introduces a variety-aware chain tested on standard benchmarks. All three takes prove useful, letting clients deploy models better matched to local data, fairness needs, and practical demands.
arxiv-2602-09620:
Constraint Answer Set Coding adds number constraint work to answer set coding, but most solvers express constraints in the number back-end's terms rather than the logic field's. Jorge Fandinno and three co-authors note what gets lost in that switch: number fields as claims allow default values, blank fields, chance sets via choice rules, and summed values. Their 2026 paper presents flingo, a language and tool bringing back that power inside linear integer constraints.

Cases show flingo's use, and a mapping converts the new syntax to regular constraint answer set programs in clingcon input format, building on prior work setting meaning base. The paper thus lets coders keep claim-style fields, defaults, choices, and sums while still solving number constraints. Power and constraint solving, long traded against each other, are joined in one language.
arxiv-2602-09820:
Behdad Jamadi and three co-authors present a low-jitter hybrid voltage level shifter architecture for high-speed mixed-signal and digital power-amplifier applications in their 2026 paper. The design uses a regenerative cross-coupled feedback network to generate two synchronized voltage-domain outputs at once: the nominal supply voltage and one at twice its value. Direct drive of cascoded class-D power amplifiers follows without additional delay-calibration circuitry, among other mixed-signal uses.

Fabrication in a twenty-two-nanometer process produced a prototype circuit alongside a pre-driver used for off-chip characterization at high speed and an impedance-matching network. Measured at about twelve gigahertz, the circuit dissipates under half a milliwatt and achieves measured root-mean-square jitter below about forty femtoseconds, limited by the noise floor of the measurement setup. Two synchronized levels from one compact shifter thus serve high-speed amplifier drive.
arxiv-2602-09920:
In fluids with a twist, currents can hug the edges and resist fading, a behavior continuum theory describes well but does not explain from below. A 2026 paper by Jan Wójcik and Erik Kalz builds a microscopic model for it: a lattice walk with an internal state and a tunable twist. The model spans the gap between ordinary random diffusion and a fully quantum walk.

Dialing the twist parameter moves the walker from plain diffusion to a deterministic walk with topological character. Strikingly, the protection found at the pure quantum end survives when dissipation enters, grounding the toughness of edge flows in classical chiral systems. The result offers a discrete toolkit for predicting transport in confined or disordered chiral media.
arxiv-2602-10320:
Global protocols describe far-flung message-passing systems from a bird's-eye view, and implementability asks whether a far-flung build exists. A 2026 paper by Elaine Li and Thomas Wies presents the first broad study of global protocol implementability modulo network architectures. Network-tuned Coherence Conditions are proposed, with enough assumptions under which they exactly pin down implementability.

Those assumptions shrink to a small set of working axioms covering insert and remove behavior of single message buffers. The reduction at once covers five widely studied async architectures: peer-to-peer FIFO plus mailbox, senderbox, monobox, and bag. The account yields optimal complexity results, links among classes of implementable global protocols, plus symbolic decision algorithms. Built into the first network-tuned tool Sprout, it achieves network breadth without giving up speed or modularity.
arxiv-2602-10420:
Jiadong Hong and four co-authors examine a popular training recipe for creative models in a 2026 paper. The recipe predicts a clean signal, converts that prediction into a velocity, and then trains through a loss measured in velocity space. Applied to binary data, the conversion step can amplify errors near the endpoints and threaten stable training.

The paper traces that instability to the conduct of slope noise before tuning. Under uniform timestep sampling, a key second moment can diverge, while sampling that suppresses the edges can restore control under extra settings. Matching the prediction space to the loss space removes this source of trouble outright, the authors argue, keeping training stable across samplers. Controlled tests on steady and binary settings support the analysis.
arxiv-2602-10820:
Max Cairney-Leeming and two co-authors enforce fairness and privacy jointly in machine learning in a 2026 paper. Human-centric methods should work comparably well across societal groups and respect data privacy. But worst-case group tuning and differentially private training often pull against each other. No useful method before enforced both at once.

Their recipe, ASC, adaptively controls both sampling rate and clipping in worst-case group tuning under differential privacy. By tuning how often each group is sampled and how strongly updates are clipped, the method weighs group results against privacy loss. The paper overcomes a tension builders usually resolve by sacrificing one requirement, offering a route to models that are both fair and private.
arxiv-2602-11220:
Fine-tuning on downstream data can clash with a model's own habits, causing forgetting. Jiacheng Wang and six co-authors treat data rewriting as a policy problem to close that gap. A lightweight rewriting policy, trained by reinforcement learning, aligns supervision with the backbone's natural question-answering spread.

The policy optimizes distributional matching and semantic diversity under a strict task-consistency gate, producing verified supervision for fine-tuning. Across three instruction-tuned backbones, downstream gains match standard fine-tuning while damage to other benchmarks falls in every setting. Extra tests on logic and medical questions suggest one rewriting policy can transfer across domains for the same backbone.
arxiv-2602-11320:
Neural tangent kernel methods drown in Jacobian computations. Jamie Mahowald and three co-authors show the data dimension itself can be compressed, not just the Jacobian. Data set distillation tuned to the tangent kernel can induce the same tangent space from far fewer points.

That yields a twenty- to one-hundred-fold cut in required Jacobian calculations. Per-class kernel matrices keep their low effective rank through the reduction. Combining distillation with leading projection methods, the distilled kernel cuts overall hardness by up to five orders of magnitude while preserving kernel structure and predictive results. The work makes tangent-kernel analysis feasible at scales where it was previously out of reach.
arxiv-2602-11620:
China's first cosmic microwave background telescope, AliCPT-1, sits high on the Tibetan plateau, hunting faint polarization patterns left by inflationary gravitational waves. Before and after every observing season its optics must be calibrated with care, from beam shape and far sidelobes to spectral response, polarization angle, and cross-beam behavior. Xu-Fang Li and thirteen co-authors built the two sources needed for that job.

The paper presents the design and measured performance of a W-band source and a D-band source, developed specifically to characterize the telescope beams. Calibration sources of this kind are the unglamorous backbone of precision cosmology: without them, a claimed primordial signal could be an instrument artifact. The work documents the tools that let AliCPT-1 trust its own maps.
arxiv-2602-12320:
Frictionless flow is the hallmark of superfluids, yet Landau theory says it should fail in one-dimensional Bose gases. Milena Horvath led this work with eight co-authors, testing that claim with ultracold atoms. A microscopic impurity is injected into a strongly interacting one-dimensional Bose gas at speeds from subsonic to supersonic, and its motion is tracked.

At supersonic speeds, a shock wave forms, then relaxes remarkably fast to a steady regime, with relaxation time growing as starting speed falls. Once steady, the impurity keeps moving at finite speed with no friction. Quantum effects thus conspire to erase dissipation for a tiny object in a quantum fluid, reshaping ideas about how matter and information move at that scale.
arxiv-2602-13020:
Unsupervised segmentation must balance global meaning against crisp boundaries, a tension existing methods handle poorly. Boujemaa Guermazi and two co-authors introduce DynaGuide, an adaptive framework with dual guidance and dynamic loss optimisation. Global pseudo-labels from zero-shot models like DiffSeg or SegFormer set the semantics, while a lightweight convolutional network trained from scratch refines local boundaries, correcting coarse or noisy global predictions.

A multi-part loss balances feature similarity, smoothed spatial continuity including diagonal links, and semantic alignment with global pseudo-labels. Training uses no labelled data from the target domain, and guidance sources can be swapped plug-and-play style. On BSD500, PASCAL VOC2012, and COCO, DynaGuide reaches state-of-the-art results, improving mean IoU by 17.5%, 3.1%, and 11.66% respectively, with a small compute footprint.
arxiv-2602-13120:
Register machines read data words over endless letter sets, guessing values as they go, and their logical profiles have lagged behind standard machines theory. Radosław Piórkowski presents Scoped MSO, a logic with a novel segment mode and grammar limits on data matches. He proves it equal to non-fixed register machines with guessing, over domains where strong guessing can be cut.

He also defines Data-Regular Expressions, a minimal math of regular phrases built from counter-free pieces with k-shrinking joining. It is shown equal to register machines over any linked shapes. Jointly, the two systems bridge machines, logic, and phrases for data words. They give the class a robust telling theory like the standard link between finite machines, monadic second-order logic, and regular phrases.
arxiv-2602-13520:
Fourier's 1822 treatise on heat gave the world two ideas that now underpin fields from physics and engineering to computing and music. The first, a method for finding coefficients of a trigonometric series for an arbitrary function, was seized on by Ohm and Helmholtz. It became the basis for a theory of musical tones. The second, Fourier's double integral, became a way to handle certain infinities in discontinuous functions, as De Morgan showed in 1842.

Together they form the Fourier theorem. With Dirac's insights into those infinities, they yield a compact account of a time function's frequency spectrum, or conversely of the waveform for a given frequency function. Working only from primary sources, the paper traces the path from heat physics to modern musical signal theory. Victor Lazzarini is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-14120:
Juan Carlos Carbajal and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv problem in auction design with budget limits. A seller holds one object, while a buyer privately knows both value and budget. Private budgets make the classic monopoly problem hard to solve exactly, so the paper tests simple approximation mechanisms against optimal ones.

Three measures judge performance: the guaranteed share of optimal revenue, the gain from relaxation, and a revenue non-monotonicity gap. For bounded distributions, simple menus of polylogarithmic size can approach optimal revenue closely, even with correlated values and budgets. For unbounded support, and even some bounded cases, no finite or sublinear menu guarantees any positive revenue share, even under independence.
arxiv-2602-14320:
Alexandra Henzinger and two co-authors give a 2026 arXiv catalyst method for tree tests. Two prior routes traded space against time: one used super-log space with super-poly time, while a drop to circuit tests used log free space and poly time but poly catalyst space. The paper betters the second route.

The new catalyst method runs in log free space and poly time, with sub-poly catalyst space, 2 to the power log-to-the-epsilon n, for any epsilon above zero. That opens a fresh attack on placing tree tests in logspace. By a drop of Williams, it also at once betters the run of time by catalyst space, a notable complexity-theory payoff.
arxiv-2602-14420:
Lucas Ferreira R. de Moura and three co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv dispersive interferometry protocol for joint sensing. It gauges both the unit-free inverse heat of a warm two-level helper and a spreading phase at once. Photon counts yield odds ruled by fringe clarity, whose size steers phase response and whose slope sets heat response.

A single binary outcome gives only a rank-one Fisher matrix, so local naming needs several set guide phases. A multi-setting odds form is built, and a max-odds guesser is shown by numbers to hit the Cramér-Rao bound in the limit. For one photon, the twin qubit circuit ran on IBM Quantum hardware as a careful odds emulation, with contrast shrink matching a noise skew toward endless heat. NOON, cat, and squeezed probes are weighed under damping.
arxiv-2602-14620:
The 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole is a classic lump of field in particle theory. Michal Malinský studies the equations for its spatial shape through resurgence theory, which links small expansions to hidden non-perturbative terms. The gauge part shows a simple pattern in its Borel transform.

That simplicity lets the author control singularities to all orders and track log jumps in full. A partial resummation reveals simple universal background shapes. Around them, a uniformly convergent expansion of the exact solutions can be built for any coupling ratio. The work also pins down numbers that govern the shapes near the origin and far away.
arxiv-2602-15520:
Agudelo and colleagues widen the idea of quantum correlation beyond the usual tensor-product split. Standard quantum correlations arise when a state cannot be written as a product across given parties, and that fact powers much of quantum science. Here the authors frame correlations through arbitrary products, then show a universal link back to tensor products, so generic non-product states can be tied to ordinary entangled states.

They build the free operations for such general products by extending the local-operations-plus-classical-communication frame, giving a resource theory of correlations for general products and for more than two factors. Uses include factoring fermionic states, splitting multi-photon states into single-photon parts, and even reading prime numbers as a form of single-party entanglement. The paper offers a broad lens for what counts as correlated.
arxiv-2602-15720:
Moon and colleagues make vision transformers cheaper to run without giving up accuracy. Structured weight pruning and token compression help, but they suffer from long retraining and tangled inter-layer dependencies respectively. Their ToaSt frame decouples the problem, applying distinct strategies to distinct components: coupled head-wise structured pruning for multi-head self-attention modules, chosen for robustness, and token channel selection for feed-forward networks.

Token channel selection is training-free and filters redundant noise channels at inference time, which matters since feed-forward networks account for over 60 percent of FLOPs. Tests across nine models, including DeiT, ViT-MAE, and Swin Transformer, show better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than baselines. On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt reaches 88.52 percent accuracy with a 39.4 percent FLOPs cut, and it transfers well to detection, segmentation, and classification tasks.
arxiv-2602-15820:
Zimmel and colleagues stabilise test-time tuning for high-dim simulation stand-ins. Machine learning stand-ins accelerate costly engineering runs. Yet when training conditions differ from deployment conditions, performance often drops sharply, as with shapes or setups never seen before. Test-time adaptation can mitigate such shifts. But most current methods target lower-dimensional classification, with set outputs and inputs that visibly line up with them. That makes them unstable for high-dim, messy fitting problems.

The team proposes a test-time tuning framework based on storing D-optimal statistics. That enables stable tuning and sound setting selection. Applied to pretrained stand-ins, the method yields up to 7 percent out-of-distribution improvements at negligible compute cost. To their knowledge, this is the first full demo of working test-time tuning for high-dim simulation fitting and making design tuning, validated on SIMSHIFT and EngiBench.
arxiv-2602-16020:
Zeng and colleagues attack crystal structure prediction with a flow based generative model. Predicting how large molecules pack into periodic crystals is hard. Molecule shape and packing interact, and earlier generative successes with molecules, solids, and frameworks had not carried over to fully periodic crystals.

MolCrystalFlow separates the two problems. It treats molecules as rigid bodies and jointly learns the lattice, orientations, and centroid positions on their native curved manifolds. Benchmarks against a leading rival model and a rule based generator show it beating the former and matching the latter on open data sets. Coupling the model to a universal machine learning potential then speeds prediction further, opening a data driven route to finding new crystals.
arxiv-2602-16420:
Dmitry Zharikov, Maxim Piskunov, and Dmitry Kolomenskiy argue droplet-wall impact models need more than one validation metric. Many studies validate droplet impact using only maximum spreading, yet that alone cannot guarantee dynamics. The authors present a combined dynamic contact angle model merging geometric accuracy of the generalized Hoffman-Voinov-Tanner law with a Hoffman approach.

They simulate water-glycerol impact on sapphire at Weber numbers twenty to two-fifty. Simulated radial velocities are compared with Particle Image Velocimetry measurements. The Hoffman function-based model captures main trends and gives more consistent receding dynamics. The generalized law matches maximum spreading within seven percent but errs up to three times more in radial velocity. Using the maximum spreading factor and a capillary number from mean internal velocity above the substrate, the authors introduce a diagram relating spreading to flow. They hypothesize contact-line geometry may estimate kinematics given enough data.
arxiv-2602-16620:
L. R. Ecker and co-authors model the binary lens galaxies behind Supernova Winny, a strongly lensed supernova with five images. Lensed supernovae are powerful probes of cosmology, supernovae, and galaxies, but only if the lens system is modeled well. Adaptive-optics images from the Large Binocular Telescope confirm a fifth point source whose color matches the other images, supporting its identity as another image of the same supernova.

The team measures all five image positions precisely and builds the first mass models with lenstronomy and GLEE. The best model class pairs a singular isothermal ellipsoid for one galaxy with a singular isothermal sphere for the other, plus external shear. Fits to image positions are extremely tight, and ruling out configurations with extra images further constrains the lenses. Cosmologists get a refined lens model for a rare five-image system.
arxiv-2602-16820:
Xinyi Lu and co-authors run a randomized trial of AI-mediated feedback on student rewrites in a large undergraduate economics course. Little was known about how students respond to AI-mediated versus human feedback on writing. The team deploys FeedbackWriter, which drafts AI tips for teaching assistants as they give feedback on knowledge-heavy essays. Assistants may take, edit, or drop each tip.

Students were randomly assigned to handwritten assistant feedback or AI-mediated feedback, then rewrote drafts that were graded. Over thirteen hundred essays were graded through the system. Students with AI-mediated feedback wrote much better rewrites, with gains rising as assistants took more AI tips. Assistants found the tips useful for spotting gaps and clarifying rubrics, giving teachers proof that mediated feedback can lift rewrite quality.
arxiv-2602-16920:
Zhi-Guo He, Bernd Kniehl, and Peng Zhang compute relativistic corrections to gluon fragmentation into triplet P-wave states of heavy quarkonium. They work within non-relativistic QCD factorization. At sub-leading order, S-D mixing must be included to absorb the infrared divergence of spin-triplet P-wave output in full QCD into long-distance matrix elements. Unlike the S-wave case, short-distance coefficients at leading and sub-leading order are no longer in proportion.

Upon convolution with the gluon output cross section, their ratios stay almost constant across the whole transverse momentum region. Relativistic corrections prove negative and large, making them a key ingredient in studying J/psi output at the LHC. Heavy quarkonium physicists get a corrected fragmentation account needed for accurate output predictions.
arxiv-2602-17120:
Liming Liu led a six-author team chasing real-time, high-quality video streaming on phones. Traditional codecs decode fast but degrade badly at low bandwidth, while generative neural codecs look far better yet demand heavy frame-by-frame generation that phones cannot sustain. The paper asks whether both strengths can combine. Its answer is HybridPrompt, the first generative video system to decode full high-definition video in real time on a commercial smartphone.

Keyframes go through a generative model while traditional codecs handle the rest. A key insight makes the pairing work: the traditional decoding process is differentiable. Later frames can thus supervise keyframe generation end to end. The generative model thus crafts keyframes that are both good-looking and ideal references for the codec. A two-stage generation strategy rounds out a system far faster than pure neural baselines and visibly better than traditional codecs at low bitrates.
arxiv-2602-17220:
Chi Sun led a five-author team modeling how orbital angular momentum crosses a metal interface. Interfacial orbital transport lags far behind bulk understanding despite its central role in orbitronics experiments. Using a model Hamiltonian with crystal-field effects, the authors track transmission and conversion of orbital angular momentum across the boundary.

An injected orbital dipole wobbles strongly under the crystal field and spawns quadrupole moments set by the orbital's orientation to the interface. Unlike spin precession, the dipole settles to a finite value away from the interface rather than fading out. The team also quantifies interfacial orbital memory loss and shows that orbital absorption yields a sizable mechanical torque, derived from the orbital continuity equation. The work sharpens the theory of orbitronic interfaces.
arxiv-2602-17320:
Stefano Lambiase led a five-author team surveying the social health of quantum software communities. Quantum computing draws heavy investment from corporations and academic institutions, and open-source quantum projects multiply, yet these communities face socio-technical anti-patterns known as community smells. Such patterns can harm product quality and community health by breeding technical debt and amplifying architectural and code smells.

Despite their importance, research on these factors inside quantum open-source communities remains scarce. The paper takes a first step with a cross-sectional study of the socio-technical well-being of quantum communities. By mapping the dynamics at play, it aims to build foundational knowledge for mitigating community smell risks and sustaining open-source quantum initiatives over the long term.
arxiv-2602-17520:
Yogeswar Reddy Thota led a four-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on a quiet failure mode in large language models. The paper asks what happens when a prompt redefines a familiar operator or gate, as circuit specs and hardware documents often do. A model strong under standard rules may still fall back on its usual reading instead of the local definition just given.

The authors call that failure semantic override. A second fault, assumption injection, is when a model fills in missing hardware detail alone rather than asking for it. To test both, they built a compact set of logic and circuit tasks laid out as verifier traps, then ran three leading models through them. The models kept breaking local rules, making confident guesses that clashed with the spec, and dropping stated limits. Standard test success, the paper argues, is not faithful reasoning to a given spec.
arxiv-2602-17620:
Marco Graziani wrote a thesis on a possible light dark-sector particle, the particle known as X17. Hints from the ATOMKI and PADME teams point to a new resonance of about seventeen mega-electron-volts. ATOMKI has seen it in nuclear transitions since 2020, and PADME hinted a similar excess in 2025.

The thesis asks if such a particle, coupled to electrons as PADME suggests, could link the Standard Model to hidden sectors not yet probed. That link could offer a fresh route toward the nature and origin of dark matter, a chief open puzzle. The wider picture stays unsettled, with recent MEG II limits in play and no firm confirmation or exclusion yet.
arxiv-2602-18320:
Fengwei Xu and fourteen co-authors trace how a fourteen-parsec gas filament assembles massive stars. Their 2026 paper, first in the LANCET project, maps the nearly straight filament G316.8 with the Atacama Compact Array at fine resolution, plus Herschel and APEX data. The filament holds three side-by-side zones at different life stages, each with a similar gas reservoir.

From the youngest infrared-dark zone through a massive young stellar object to an evolved ionized zone. Peak fragment mass climbs from eight to nearly five hundred solar masses, and the dense-gas share rises from under half a percent to nearly ten percent. The column-density distribution grows a second power-law tail, and the variance slope flattens, signs of dense sub-parsec structures still assembling. Future ALMA data will push the view down to eight hundred astronomical units.
arxiv-2602-18420:
Jiamin Yao and one co-author built SPQ, an ensemble recipe for shrinking large language models. Their 2026 paper combines three complementary tricks: activation-based pruning, variance-retained singular value decomposition, and post-training linear quantization. Pruning removes redundant neurons in MLP layers, SVD compresses attention projections into compact low-rank factors, and 8-bit quantization compresses all linear layers uniformly.

At matched compression ratios, SPQ beats each ingredient alone on perplexity, showing the combination pays. On LLaMA-2-7B it cuts memory by up to seventy-five percent while holding or improving perplexity and preserving accuracy on C4, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K. Against GPTQ and SparseGPT it offers competitive perplexity and accuracy with less memory, plus up to one point nine times faster inference. The method suits deploying language models where memory is tight, and code is public.
arxiv-2602-18520:
Aayam Bansal builds a feedback tool for student STEM diagrams. His 2026 paper notes timely, rubric-aligned feedback on student diagrams is a persistent challenge. Large multimodal models parse images and generate explanations jointly, but hallucination undermines classroom trust.

Bansal presents Sketch2Feedback, a grammar-guided framework in four stages: perception, graph construction, constraint checking, and constrained feedback. The language model states only violations confirmed by an upstream rule engine. Evaluation uses FBD-10 for free-body diagrams and Circuit-10 for circuits, each with five hundred images spanning standard and hard noise, against end-to-end models and an ensemble oracle. Results are mixed: Qwen2-VL-7B scores highest on both benchmarks but hallucinates heavily, while an ensemble oracle reaches strong F1 with lower hallucination. An LLM judge finds the grammar pipeline gives more actionable circuit feedback. All code, datasets, and scripts are released.
arxiv-2602-18820:
Stablecoins are meant to hold their peg, but when one breaks, does trouble spread? Does the design of the coin matter? Wenbin Wu, with one co-author, investigates systemic risk transmission across stablecoin markets in 2026. He uses quantile vector autoregression on eight major coins from 2021 to 2025. Minute-level studies of three coins that suffered major depegs supplement that analysis.

Fiat-backed coins act as anchors, sending almost no net risk outward across quantiles. Algorithmic and crypto-collateralised designs become risk amplifiers under extreme conditions. Stress also opens direct volatility channels between the dollar index and Bitcoin that bypass stablecoins altogether. Contagion tests across four depeg events are heterogeneous. The authors argue that uniform regulation is inappropriate, with capital buffers for extreme losses needing to be far higher for non-fiat-backed coins.
arxiv-2602-18920:
Research agents that can generate truly new ideas need more than clever prompts. Tianyu Fan, with seven co-authors, proposes DeepInnovator in 2026, a training framework designed to trigger innovative capability in language models. It has two core parts.

First, standing on the shoulders of giants, an automated pipeline extracts and organises structured research knowledge from a huge corpus of unlabelled papers. Second, conjectures and refutations, a Next Idea Prediction paradigm treats idea generation as iterative prediction, evaluation, and refinement of plausible, novel next ideas. Automatic and expert tests show the resulting model beats untrained baselines by wide margins. It reaches performance comparable to current leading models. The dataset will be open-sourced. Ideas can be trained, not just prompted. That is the claim here.
arxiv-2602-19020:
Detecting whether a text was in a language model's training data is usually framed as membership inference, using likelihoods or generations from fixed weights. Junjie Oscar Yin, with four co-authors, introduces Active Data Reconstruction Attack in 2026, a family of attacks that actively pushes a model to rebuild a given text through training.

The hypothesis is that training data are more reconstructible than non-members, and that difference can be exploited. Motivated by findings that reinforcement learning sharpens behaviours already encoded in weights, the authors use on-policy reinforcement learning to elicit reconstruction by fine-tuning a policy initialised from the target model. Reconstruction metrics and contrastive rewards make reinforcement learning effective for this attack. The resulting methods, ADRA and its adaptive variant ADRA+, consistently beat existing membership inference attacks across pretraining, post-training, and distillation data, with notable gains on standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-19120:
Does the order of hidden updates and emissions change a quantum process? Abdessatar Souissi, with one co-author, answers yes in 2026. Causal hidden quantum Markov models reverse the usual order. Conventional models emit then step. Causal models step then emit.

A simple qubit model with a rotating hidden state and sharp measurements proves the difference. The two architectures yield truly different processes. Readings at arbitrarily late times still distinguish them. No initialisation choice erases the gap. Yet equivalence returns in one special case. Entangled liftings of classical hidden Markov models share classical statistics, so both orders coincide there. That line separates standard from truly quantum hidden memory.
arxiv-2602-19520:
Prices on prediction markets are often read as probabilities, but that reading needs calibration. Nam Anh Le measures calibration using trades on Kalshi and Polymarket, tracking how it varies by event domain, time left to resolution, and trade size. Trade counts run to 353 million, across 429,000 binary contracts. A descriptive decomposition of recalibration slopes at cell level explains 87.3 percent of in-sample variance on Kalshi.

The sturdiest pattern is lasting underconfidence in political markets, where prices squeeze toward 50 percent, a pattern that replicates on Polymarket. Big political trades on Kalshi show further compression, with a calibration-slope gap near one-half. That gap survives market- and event-clustered bootstraps, but fails to hold on Polymarket. A Bayesian measurement-error model agrees, with caveats under conservative standard errors.
arxiv-2602-19620:
Rules and weights are both popular ways to explain AI decisions, yet no shared cognitive yardstick says which to pick when. Louth Bin Rawshan and two co-authors run a user elicitation study covering forward and counterfactual decision tasks. It finds seven reasoning strategies across three XAI schemas: weights, rules, and a mix of both. To compare them, they propose CoXAM, a Cognitive XAI-Adaptive Model built on a shared memory store for instance traits, linear weights, and decision rules.

CoXAM uses computational rationality to pick among reasoning paths by trading utility against reasoning time, separately for forward and counterfactual tasks. In a validation study it lines up with human choices better than baseline machine-learning proxy models. It also reproduces key findings. Counterfactual tasks run harder than forward ones, tree rules are harder to recall and use than linear weights, and XAI help hinges on the data context.
arxiv-2602-20020:
Adaptive testing usually picks the next question from the predicted chance a student answers correctly, ignoring the rich information in open-ended responses. A 2026 arXiv paper by Wanyong Feng and three co-authors proposes CodeGENCAT, a testing framework that adjusts and generates code for open-ended coding problems.

Code structures and bugs reveal much about student knowledge, above all in coding classes. The framework's item response theory model writes code answers based on estimated knowledge. It trains with supervised fine-tuning, then direct preference optimization for knowledge-response alignment. Three question-selection algorithms then weigh uncertainty, coding style diversity, and signals in forecast responses. Tests on two real coding class data sets show CodeGENCAT beating all testing baselines, with its largest margin in the early stages of testing.
arxiv-2602-20220:
What actually makes online reinforcement learning work on physical robots? Many design choices are left implicit in prior work, and practitioners lack large-sample evidence about which ones matter. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yarden As and six co-authors investigates that question directly, running one hundred real-world training runs across three distinct robotic platforms.

Algorithmic, systems, and experimental decisions are systematically ablated. Some widely used defaults turn out to be harmful. A set of robust, readily adopted choices within standard reinforcement learning practice yields stable learning across tasks and hardware. The study is the first large-sample empirical examination of such design choices, giving practitioners a route to deploy online reinforcement learning with lower engineering effort.
arxiv-2602-20420:
The lowest allowed quantum state of a trapped ultracold Fermi gas at unitarity is a superfluid state, studied widely in experiment and theory. D. K. Watson investigates its zero-point energy through the combined effects of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the Pauli principle. The method comes from a recent series of papers that explain superfluidity with microscopic dynamics based on normal modes, rather than real-space Cooper pairs.

That approach already matched experimental data well for several properties and exposed the microscopic behavior behind them, including the basis of universal behavior, using the group-theoretic basis of a general many-body approach. Watson now uses it to clarify the roles of uncertainty and Pauli exclusion in setting the energy and character of the lowest state. That includes its squeezed character and the suppression of the Pauli principle.
arxiv-2602-20520:
Diffusion-based fill-in rebuilds masked image parts, but how do its flaws affect text output? Pratham Yashwante and three co-authors study the question in vision-language models with a two-step test setup. Masked parts are rebuilt, then fed to caption models. This allows set checks between captions from first inputs and rebuilt inputs. Across many sets, they link rebuild match to later caption quality.

Pixel-level and seen rebuild scores track both word-level and sense-level caption scores each time. Study of middle visual codes and focus patterns shows fill-in flaws cause steady, layer-tied shifts in model acts. Together, the results give a handy test method for how visual rebuild quality shapes text output in mixed-media systems.
arxiv-2602-20620:
Some memory systems recall patterns under different conditions. Munetaka Sasaki builds a neural net model that recalls two patterns depending on temperature. The trick is to embed each pattern in a different graph: the first into a fully connected graph, and the second into a sparse graph. Because a fully connected graph resists thermal fluctuations better than a sparse graph, tuning the relative pattern weights properly flips which pattern the system recalls as temperature changes.

Equilibrium Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the temperature-driven recall switch does occur in the model. Results strongly indicate a first-order phase transition at the switch point. Annealing simulations add a caution: at low temperatures, the system fails to recall the sparse-graph pattern when the free-energy barrier is too high to cross within the simulation time. The paper thus links recall switching to both graph structure and thermal barriers.
arxiv-2602-21020:
Multi-agent imitation learning copies expert behavior, but closeness to experts does not guarantee closeness to equilibrium. Antoine Bergerault, Volkan Cevher, and Negar Mehr expose that gap in this 2026 arXiv paper. They prove impossibility and hardness results for learning low-exploitability policies in general multi-player Markov games, showing even exact measure matching can fail and the Nash gap can resist characterization.

The picture improves under strategic dominance assumptions on the expert equilibrium. For dominant-strategy expert equilibria, bounded behavioral-cloning error yields a bounded Nash imitation gap. A new notion of best-response continuity generalizes the result, and the authors argue standard regularization already encourages it. Readers learn when imitation is safe and when it fundamentally is not.
arxiv-2602-21220:
Agent memory usually means discrete database entries, but Subhadip Mitra treats memory as continuous fields in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stored information diffuses through semantic space, decays thermodynamically by importance, and interacts through field coupling between agents, following partial differential equations drawn from classical field theory.

Tests on two long-context benchmarks show large gains: multi-session reasoning more than doubles, temporal reasoning rises about forty-four percent, and retrieval recall on knowledge updates rises about twenty-eight percent. Multi-agent experiments reach above ninety-nine point eight percent collective intelligence through field coupling. The approach offers agents a memory that behaves like a physical field, not a filing cabinet.
arxiv-2602-21720:
Human counting systems like English base-10 numerals are strikingly regular, and earlier work ties cross-language patterns to learning biases. Andrea Silvi and five co-authors ask whether regular systems are common because regularity makes them easier to learn. Using reinforcement learning methods, they confirm that highly regular human-like systems are easier to learn than possible but unattested irregular systems.

The edge rests on a natural assumption: numeral systems must generalize from limited data to represent every integer exactly. For deeply unnatural, highly irregular systems, regularity stops mattering, and learnability instead tracks signal length. The findings link learnability to cross-linguistic prevalence, with different pressures dominating different parts of the system space.
arxiv-2602-22020:
Code editors shape a developer's whole workday, yet hard evidence about their usability gaps is scarce. Andrés Rodriguez and two co-authors mine user-reported issues from the Visual Studio Code repository and sort them with a validated taxonomy plus expert review. Their goal is to spot recurring UX smells, the small design flaws that nag users again and again.

Most of the smells cluster around four qualities developers prize: informativeness, clarity, intuitiveness, and efficiency. The paper thus gives editor teams a ranked map of what actually frustrates users, drawn from real complaints rather than guesswork.
