It also shows how language models can help sift thousands of issue reports into usable design lessons.
arxiv-2602-22120:
Text-to-image models now picture the world for millions of users, but their images often flatten geography into stereotypes. Abhipsa Basu and four co-authors introduce GeoDiv, a framework that grades geographical diversity in generated images along two axes. One axis reads socio-economic and condition cues, the other measures variation in main subjects and backgrounds.

Using large language and vision-language models as judges, GeoDiv tests leading generators across many entities and countries. It finds a consistent diversity shortfall and pinpoints the fine-grained attributes where models fall back on biased defaults. The framework gives builders an interpretable scorecard for a flaw that surface similarity metrics miss.
arxiv-2602-22320:
Particle physicists hunt for exact relations among decay rates that survive the messiness of strong interactions. Margarita Gavrilova and three co-authors prove one for hadronic weak charm decays linked by U-spin symmetry: a ratio of summed rates equals one, holding to second order in U-spin breaking. The rule covers any system of such decays within the Standard Model.

Tested against available data, the sum rule holds well in every case examined. Where some decay rates remain unmeasured, the rule predicts them, turning a symmetry relation into a practical forecasting tool. For charm physicists, it offers a clean Standard Model check that needs no detailed modeling of hadronic mess.
arxiv-2602-22420:
Self-dual gauge fields sit at a curious corner of field theory, and a newly constructed superstring field theory yields a fresh action for them. Chris Hull finds that action: in one limit it reduces to Sen's earlier action for such fields. The theory describes two decoupled self-dual gauge fields coupled to two metrics, each field touching only one of the metrics.

A background metric also enters, and the nonlinear coupling to all three metrics is non-standard. The theory carries two spin-two gauge invariances, with diffeomorphisms arising from their diagonal subgroup. String theorists gain a concrete action for self-dual fields with an unusual triple-metric structure.
arxiv-2602-22820:
K. G. Klimenko and one co-author map weak dual links in the two-colour quark-matter phase diagram. Baryon, isospin, and chiral gaps shape the phases, studied here within a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model. The letter shows dual links that appear when the full heat energy is cast onto chosen clumping channels.

Those dual links unify two striking effects: across-the-board speed-up and the shifting effect of the chiral chem knob. For readers tracking how gap knobs reshape quark matter, the result ties seeming apart traits to one pattern, giving a cleaner lens on two-colour quark force under extremes.
arxiv-2602-22920:
Federico Nesti and three co-authors grow railway perception data with augmented reality. Railway obstacle detection lacks high-quality annotated data, and photorealistic simulators suffer the sim-to-real gap, while simple image masking breaks spatio-temporal coherence across frames.

OSDaR-AR blends photorealistic virtual objects into real railway sequences from the OSDaR23 dataset. Unreal Engine 5 features plus LiDAR point clouds and INS/GNSS data place objects accurately and hold them stable across RGB frames. A segmentation-based refinement for INS/GNSS data further lifts realism, confirmed by comparative study. The resulting public dataset supports next-generation railway perception systems.
arxiv-2602-23020:
Sourbh Bhadane and three co-authors test partly pinnable causal queries with three-outcome number-based tests. Since many causal models can induce the same observed spread, causal queries are often only partly pinnable, and binary test results do not translate directly to the causal guess problem.

The authors propose ternary tests and establish testability requirements in terms of uniform consistency, with equivalent topological conditions on the hypotheses. They prove that building ternary tests by combining binary tests is complete, so the existing binary toolbox suffices. Topological conditions then guide constructions for two concrete problems: testing instrumental variable inequalities and comparing treatment efficacy.
arxiv-2602-23120:
Arian Sabaghi and one co-author present TriLite, a lean weakly guided object finding setup. Weakly guided finding aims to find target objects using only image-level labels. Many methods still rely on multi-stage chains or full fine-tuning of large bases, raising training cost, while the wider WSOL field faces partial object span.

TriLite uses a one-stage WSOL setup with a frozen Vision Transformer, Dinov2 trained. Only a tiny number of learnable weights, fewer than eight hundred thousand, serve both sorting and finding. TriHead splits patch features into front, back, and unclear regions, lifting span while cutting stray signals. By splitting sorting and finding goals, TriLite uses broad pictures learned by self-guided ViTs without pricey end-to-end training. Wide tests on CUB-200-2011, ImageNet-1K, and OpenImages show TriLite sets a state of the art, while staying far more weight-lean than prior methods.
arxiv-2602-23320:
Tianjun Yao and five co-authors present ParamMem, a memory module that helps language agents review in more varied ways. Self-review lets agents refine answers step by step, but it often repeats itself and caps thinking scores. The authors find a clear link between review variety and task success, driving the need for richer review signals.

ParamMem writes cross-sample review patterns straight into model weights, so new reviews can be drawn with temperature-tuned sampling. The ParamAgent design mixes this memory with event and cross-sample memory. Tests on code making, math thinking, and multi-hop question work show steady gains over top rivals. It also proves sample-lean, moves skill from weak to strong models across scales, and supports self-gains with no stronger outside model.
arxiv-2602-23520:
Tristan Simas studies how to certify zero-error recovery and Shannon capacity for a huge confusability graph given only by coordinates. The graph itself, exponentially large, is never built first. For affine presentations over a finite field, Gaussian elimination yields a fast rank upper certificate from a compact input.

Exactness of that certificate hinges on positivity of a Grassmannian avoidance count. Positivity is NP-complete for every fixed k, even over the two-element field. The ambient-rank parameter still yields a fixed-parameter algorithm. The rank-one reduction is parsimonious for counting satisfiability. Kernel sections give an exact capacity formula. A finite-field blocking theorem gives exactness when q is at least L. Reed-Solomon and MDS codes supply exact all-k-view families beyond that regime.
arxiv-2602-23620:
Gui Ling and eight co-authors tackle product search for long-tail, knowledge-heavy queries in e-commerce search. Search is the backbone of e-commerce search, finding a high-recall set of picks from billions of items for ranking. Mainstream queries are well tuned, but long-tail queries still struggle.

Such queries show diverse word patterns, often lack clear purchase intent, and need field knowledge thinking for right reading. They also suffer from scarce reliable usage logs. The new data making method quietly distills a strong offline query rewrite model into a fast online search system. Using LLM grasp, the team trains a multi-candidate rewrite model with multiple reward signals, catching its rewrite skill in well-curated query-product pairs through a strong offline search setup. This design eases spread shift in new queries.
arxiv-2602-24120:
Shubh Agrawal and twenty-six co-authors present a simulation-based forecasting framework for line intensity mapping at cosmic noon, the peak era of star formation. The 2026 paper maps the baryon cycle, the flow of gas into galaxies, through processing, and out via feedback. It uses intensity mapping of atomic hydrogen, ionized carbon, and carbon monoxide across the same deep field.

The team forward-models three-dimensional distributions for four tracers from magnetohydrodynamic simulations, capturing halo and shot statistics directly without analytic shortcuts. Forecasts show that galaxy cross-correlations will dominate discovery for current surveys, with detections expected for carbon monoxide and hydrogen auto-spectra and their cross-spectrum, while ionized carbon signals yield upper limits. Cross-correlation with a galaxy survey boosts sensitivity far above auto-correlation alone. The results guide the next surveys.
arxiv-2602-24220:
Miras Seilkhan and Adilbek Taizhanov compare classical and quantum variational classifiers on the XOR problem, a classic test of model expressivity. The 2026 paper evaluates logistic regression, a one-hidden-layer neural network, and a two-qubit variational quantum classifier at two circuit depths, on synthetic XOR data with varied noise and sample sizes.

Performance hinges mainly on expressivity: logistic regression and the depth-one quantum circuit fail to represent XOR reliably. The neural network and the depth-two quantum circuit reach perfect test accuracy under representative conditions. Robustness checks confirm that circuit depth is decisive for quantum performance here. Despite matching accuracy, the neural network achieves lower cross-entropy loss and far shorter training time, and hardware runs preserve the global XOR structure. Deeper quantum classifiers can match classical networks on this low-dimensional benchmark, but no clear advantage in robustness or efficiency appears.
arxiv-2603-00020: Aoki and Itadera compare two teleoperation interfaces for a six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm: a 3D mouse and a VR controller. Participants pushed buttons and rotated knobs repeatedly in three-minute trials, rating workload after each. The VR controller won on button pushing, while the 3D mouse performed better and felt less demanding for knob rotation, showing interface choice should follow the task's dominant motion.
arxiv-2603-00320: Sharma, Moll, and Oksanen present a Smart Prism correcting total-station tracking for vehicle tilt: a prism's lever arm turns roll and pitch into errors dwarfing the station's precision. Their device adds an inertial sensor and microcontroller, estimates roll and pitch with an adaptive filter, and converts the lever arm into navigation coordinates. It sends raw and corrected positions over the vehicle CAN bus. Field tests with a lever arm near one metre and tilts up to 60 degrees gave errors under two and a half centimetres.
arxiv-2603-00520: Yu and eleven colleagues show SWE-Bench Verified scores are inflated by weak tests: one in five solved patches from top agents is semantically wrong yet passes. Their SWE-ABS framework strengthens suites in two stages: slicing driven coverage growth for untested regions, then mutation driven tests that craft plausible wrong patches. On five hundred instances it strengthens about half and rejects about a fifth of prior passes, a jump over prior work. The top score falls sharply, the leaderboard reshuffles, and the former leader drops to fifth.
arxiv-2603-00620: Poelman, Chen, and de Lhoneux present QQ, a toolkit for multilingual language work spanning hundreds or thousands of languages. QQ compiles sources into a linked graph covering varieties, scripts, regions, codes, names, and links, shown through a Python API, a command line tool, and a web browser view. Users normalise codes, fetch facts, traverse links, and find which outside sites hold a language. Demos audit the HuggingFace Hub, link collections across code systems, and generate language reporting tables.
arxiv-2603-01220: Roland and So examine how novels shape generative AI, noting that popular training sets since early GPT have leaned heavily on fiction. Builders assume fiction's language covers social and communicative life richly, yet that belief went mostly unexamined. Studying BERT, they find models exploit fiction's familiar traits while also creating new forms of social response, arguing that cultural analysis today must reckon with computational training data as a distinct dimension.
arxiv-2603-01720:
Ruize Cui, Jialun Pei, Haiqiao Wang, and colleagues align liver scans taken before surgery with the live view during keyhole operations. Their 2026 work supports augmented reality guides that overlay a 3D liver model on the camera feed. Weak matching between the two views can make that overlay drift in risky ways.

Their frame, Land-Reg, learns clear landmark matches between the flat live view and the 3D model. A shared latent space first aligns traits from both image types. A detector then picks overlapping landmarks and rates how sure each match is. For the flexible stage, shape rules anchor warping to those landmarks and keep local form intact. Tests on a public liver data set show gains in both stiff pose fit and soft deformation fit.
arxiv-2603-02020:
Emile Meoto and Mantile Lekala derive how coupling between channels fades with distance in three-body systems. Their 2026 work uses the hyperspherical harmonics expansion, a standard frame for three-body quantum problems. Coupling terms mix different arrangements of the three particles through transformation coefficients and a key integral.

For central potentials, that integral splits into geometric and dynamical parts that can be studied apart. Explicit scaling laws follow for short-range potentials like Gaussian, Yukawa, and Woods-Saxon forms. Their couplings decay algebraically, with power set by the pair orbital angular momentum. That decay lets channels decouple efficiently at large hyperradius, speeding calculations. Coulomb coupling decays far more slowly, which explains the stubborn convergence of expansions for charged systems and guides domain truncation.
arxiv-2603-02320:
Avinandan Mondal and Kartik Prabhu compute the entropy of changing black holes in this 2026 paper. They treat quantum gravity as small ripples on a flat background with a split horizon. Ripples are subject to the usual gravitational constraints. A boundary charge at the horizon plays the role of an observer in their setup.

Quantities dressed with that charge stay fixed under the horizon symmetry. Together they form a special algebra with well-defined entropy. The authors compute entropy for a mixed state built from ripples and the observer. That entropy obeys a law much like the first law of thermodynamics. It also matches a known second-order entropy for dynamical black holes. The match runs through energy flux across the horizon and out to infinity.
arxiv-2603-03320:
Jaikrishna Manojkumar Patil and seven colleagues tackle narrative shift: rewriting a story into a different worldview while keeping its core message. A text framed around the group, the 'we,' might need reframing around the individual, the 'me,' or the reverse. Their 2026 paper shows current language models find that shift surprisingly hard to do cleanly.

The proposed method is neurosymbolic, grounded in social science theory. It uses abductive reasoning, inference toward the best explanation, to extract rules and infer which story elements must change. Guided rewrites then shift the narrative while holding fidelity to the original. Tests across GPT-4o, Llama-4, Grok-4, and DeepSeek-R1 beat plain prompting in both directions, with meaning preserved measurably better than the baseline.
arxiv-2603-04220: Singh and Choudhury study non-equilibrium motion of the disordered Power of Two model. Without disorder, the system shows rapid scrambling and fast settling. They probe disorder's impact through time evolution of survival probability, half-chain links, and out-of-time-ordered correlators. They find strong enough disorder curbs information spreading and induces localization.
arxiv-2603-04320: Xu and colleagues improve sequential recommendation from text and image cues. Fixed fusion rules miss how modality taste shifts across people and across items. Combined cues can spark interest that single cues cannot, a synergy past models miss. CAMMSR adds a category guided mixture of experts that learns item views from many angles. Category prediction steers modality weights, a swap contrastive task aligns views, and four datasets show it beats leading baselines.
arxiv-2603-04820: Hardy reviews LLM short-answer scoring across 890 final results in a careful survey. Auto scoring lags other LLM applications, and hardness for human experts shows no observed effect on LLM scores. Tasks rated easiest by human scorers prove hardest for LLMs. Decoder-only designs trail coder models by 0.37 on average, a wide gap in human match. Token word list size shows fading returns, possibly from raw tokens. Findings argue for systems design better anticipating known number flaws in scoring.
arxiv-2603-05020: Panagiotis Stylianou and Georg Weiglein test whether the LHC's indirect Higgs width determination survives new physics. The standard determination assumes the same modifiers for on-shell and off-shell couplings, but new physics could affect the regions differently, allowing a larger true width. Relaxing that assumption for scalar extensions with an extra state, they find ATLAS and CMS bounds stay valid over most of the parameter space, except for light extra particles. Relaxing the equal-modifier assumption weakens the bound by at most about twofold in realistic extensions.
arxiv-2603-05220: Xavier Pic and colleagues design a DNA storage system for progressive images cutting the read cost of reduced-resolution retrieval. DNA offers dense, long-lived, low-energy archives, but methods struggle with cost and reliability, and mixed oligo pools force sequencing everything before reading one file. Their system encodes each JPEG2000 resolution layer into oligos with the JPEG DNA VM codec, adjusting which oligos and portions are sequenced for the resolution. Nanopore adaptive sampling at sequencing time makes it a PCR-free random-access solution, adaptable to any progressive codec.
arxiv-2603-05320: Ewan Murphy and colleagues investigate Knill error correction. Large-scale quantum computing needs error correction, but classical control faces stringent demands. Standard parity-check measurements repeat, increasing decoder data. Knill correction uses one round instead of repeated syndrome measurements, but needs a Bell state. They describe the protocol and prove fault tolerance under locally decaying circuit noise, and benchmark low-density parity-check codes. The time-constrained Knill decoding problem admits the code-capacity noise model's decoder, easing classical control demands.
arxiv-2603-05520: Asif and Amiri study privacy leakage that builds up in sequential multi-agent model systems in private fields like healthcare and finance. Privacy rules kept by each agent do not stop information being guessed from step by step linking and middle representations. They define leakage with mutual information and derive a bound showing how local leakage grows across agents. A training setup with privacy rules limits what agent outputs reveal about private items. It shows stable tuning with steady, clear privacy-utility trade-offs on three data sets.
arxiv-2603-05720: Almenara and colleagues model TOI-4504, revealing deep resonance similar to GJ 876. The system hosts two planets in 2:1 mean-motion resonance, planet d at 41.3 days and planet c at about double that. Their transit-timing variations rank among the largest known, with amplitudes up to 5 and 3 days. TESS data now show non-transiting planet d has precessed into transiting. Both planets sit deep in resonance near the fully-relaxed limit-cycle state. The TOI-4504 and GJ 876 pairs show remarkably similar states despite host-star mass differences.
arxiv-2603-06020: Sheemar and team build a signal model for a same-time sending and bouncing surface with boosting and loss-free splitting. The model splits boosting via a slant gain table, piece-wise splitting, and passive coupling, holding fit through output caps and a power budget. Building on this model, sum-rate maxing becomes a weighted minimum mean-square error problem with switching tuning and proven steady descent. For coupling tables, Riemannian slope steps on the Stiefel surface keep calm. Number results show big sum-rate gains over passive surfaces.
arxiv-2603-06120: Yao and colleagues view gradient updates through signal processing and argue that a fixed momentum rate skews the bias-variance balance in stochastic gradient descent. Their optimizer, SGDF, adjusts its gain at each step to refine gradient estimates by limiting mean-squared error. They argue the filtering idea can carry to other optimizers, and benchmark tests show SGDF beating standard momentum methods and matching or exceeding leading ones.
arxiv-2603-06520: Kim studies recovery channels and thresholds for quantum error fixing codes, where measured signs lead a decoder to infer errors and apply fixes. The threshold is the largest fixable rate, with the decoder giving it; the optimum should range over all rescue schemes described by quantum channels. Kim brings mutual trace distance, an information-theory tool giving a diagnostic, necessary and enough, for sharply pinning the optimal mark without direct tuning. Kim proves Petz and Schumacher-Westmoreland plans optimal, then tests optimal and non-optimal plans and phases.
arxiv-2603-07420: Wu and Kaul propose studying three-dimensional conformal field theories on small qubit systems. Their protocol picks interaction strengths of qubit many-body problems on a polyhedral lattice where the conformal state-operator correspondence shows most cleanly in the spectrum. Tested on the Ising model, it extracts scaling dimensions to within a few percent using just twenty qubits. The method assumes little beyond conformal invariance, suiting near-term quantum platforms for a classically hard problem.
arxiv-2603-07520: Zhang and colleagues run the first large study of how code representation shapes patch-correctness assessment. Across hundreds of trained models, benchmarks and tests, graph-based representations usually beat rivals, with one graph model leading on accuracy. The same representations filter most overfitting patches in prior approaches. Mixing sequence-based codes into heuristic-based codes lifts several metrics, showing code form is fundamental to patch assessment.
arxiv-2603-07620: Xu proposes a unified jet-formation model for active galactic nuclei, young stars and X-ray binaries. Binding energy from the accretion disk is stored as turbulence rather than shed, forming advection-heavy flows. Near the center a thick disk with funnel structures develops, and the smallest stable blobs accelerate past escape speed through turbulent speed spread plus inward pressure and angular momentum effects. Blobs exiting through funnels form two opposing jets when churning stores over half the binding energy.
arxiv-2603-07720: Li, Lukáčová-Medviďová and Zatorska study a viscous gas-like two-fluid model with formula pressure closure in the 3D torus at low Mach number. Hidden pressure through the phase densities makes the singular limit far trickier than under direct pressure laws. For well-prepared initial data, rescaled answers exist on a Mach-free time span and converge to the incompressible Navier-Stokes solution as Mach number tends to zero. Exact closing rates for density and flow speed follow from uniform energy bounds and a relative energy argument.
arxiv-2603-08020: Li and colleagues tackle cast shadows for inserted objects in image composition. Shadow-object consistency breaks down because shadow formation is ill-posed. Their VSDiffusion framework narrows solution space with visibility priors. First it predicts a coarse mask to localize shadow regions, then it runs conditional diffusion guided by lighting and depth cues. Visibility priors enter through a visibility control branch with shadow-gated cross attention giving structural guidance. A learned soft prior map reweights training loss in error-prone regions, while a high-frequency module sharpens boundaries and texture.
arxiv-2603-08220: Pretti and colleagues warn about pitfalls in formulating finite elasto-plasticity in curvilinear coordinates. Tensor analysis gives a frame-free basis for continuum mechanics, yet code work relies on matrix forms in user-picked bases. When those bases are non-Cartesian and non-orthonormal, extra terms arise that stay absent or hidden in Cartesian setups. Using cavity expansion as a model problem, the authors clarify the roles of the deformation gradient, Jacobian, and shifter in finite-strain kinematics under axisymmetry, terms that look simple in Cartesian frames.
arxiv-2603-08520: Yi Chen and colleagues show that repeated fixes by language models slowly let safety slip, and plain static checks make it worse. After ten rounds, over two in five chains held more flaws than the start. Their SCAFFOLD-CEGIS plan turns safety rules into firm checks, gates each step in four layers, and learns from past slips. In tests against six rival defenses, it cuts the slide to a small share.
arxiv-2603-08620: Shehreen Azad and colleagues teach video models not just what to answer, but when to answer. Answering before the proof shows is guesswork, while waiting too long wastes live value, so their Answer Readiness Score penalizes early and late replies unevenly. Their StreamReady frame waits for enough proof before speaking, and it tops a new ProReady-QA test plus eight further long-video tests.
arxiv-2603-08720: Seungmin Kim and colleagues generate analog circuit layouts with a grammar-guided bipartite graph method. Sequence-based circuit codes memorize training layouts and often fail electrical checks without human help. Their AnalogToBi frame sorts circuits by type, renames devices to fight memorization, and decodes under grammar rules, reaching high validity and novelty with no human training help.
arxiv-2603-08820: Rose McCarty and colleagues prove a structure theorem for group-labeled graphs that forbid a fixed immersion. A graph here is oriented with edges labeled invertibly by a finite group. Roughly, such graphs split into a tree-cut decomposition where each bag holds few high-degree vertices or sits nearly signed over a proper subgroup.
arxiv-2603-09020: Bhada Yun and colleagues propose AI phenomenology, asking how it felt to use AI rather than only how well it performed. Standard usability and engagement measures flatten the nuance of first-person experience over time. They trace the idea from Husserl via postphenomenology and Actor-Network Theory, grounding the case in three studies, and offer toolkits, three design concepts, and a research agenda.
arxiv-2603-09920: Zhong extends a Reshetnyak type law for quasiregular values to maps from generalised manifolds with controlled shape. The target is flat Euclidean space, and the new setting widens an earlier result proved only for flat domains by Kangasniemi and Onninen. Zhong states the aim plainly and builds the new result on that prior single point law. The result moves the theory from flat domains to manifolds whose shape is suitably controlled.
arxiv-2603-10320: Siva Athreya, Mathew Joseph, and Carl Mueller study how long a moving polymer string can survive among hard Poisson traps. The polymer solves a stochastic heat equation with spacetime white noise, and earlier work fixed the string length while time grew large. Here the length grows instead, at any fixed positive time. They prove bounds from above and below for the annealed survival chance in the hard-obstacle case. Decay is exponential in a power of the length, with the exponent also tied to dimension and time.
arxiv-2603-10420: Kaituo Xu and co-authors present FireRedASR2S, an industrial all-in-one speech recognition system with four modules in one pipeline. Alongside recognition itself, it handles voice activity detection, spoken language identification, and punctuation prediction, each at leading benchmark levels. The recognition module comes in large and smaller variants and covers English, code-switching, Mandarin, and many Chinese dialects and accents, for speech and singing alike. The other modules are light yet strong, with language identification spanning over a hundred languages. Model weights and code are released.
arxiv-2603-10520: Gideon Yoffe and Sahar Shahaf use spectral decomposition to separate surface processes on Europa, where geology refreshes material while charged particles rewrite its chemistry. They analyze JWST NIRSpec observations of the leading hemisphere in nine bands tied to water ice, radiolytic products, and volatiles. Factorization pulls out the main patterns and maps where each sits. Carbon dioxide enrichment reaches beyond Tara Regio, covering several chaos units in a lens-like spread, and pairs with odd ice textures. The pattern hints near-surface microphysics helps trap volatiles, with stakes for habitability.
arxiv-2603-11220: Qingtao Pan, Zhihao Dou, and Shuo Li restore visual detail that large multimodal models lose when they cut visual tokens to fit smaller compute budgets. Their plug-and-play strategy splits the surviving tokens' representation into low- and high-frequency parts through average and max pooling. Light learnable parameters then modulate the frequencies, one acting as a saliency filter and the other rescuing weak visual semantics. Plugged into Matryoshka-style training for elastic token counts, it slashes the compute of a standard model while keeping nearly all of its accuracy.
arxiv-2603-11320: Ziyao Wang and coauthors compress the visual tokens of unified vision-language models, which process image tokens and text in one autoregressive system. The token volume brings substantial computation and memory overhead, hindering deployment on constrained hardware. Their UniCompress plug-in squeezes and restores tokens under the guidance of learnable global meta tokens, dropping into existing models without full retraining. It cuts image tokens up to fourfold with substantial latency and training-cost gains and only minimal performance loss across both understanding and generation tasks.
arxiv-2603-11520: Zhao and co-authors study why composed image retrieval falters on hard, look-alike negatives. Such search takes an image plus a text edit and must reason over both at once. The team blames focus imbalance: models lean on one input stream and neglect the other. Their tool, FBCIR, finds which visual and textual parts drive each retrieval choice. It shows imbalance is common, most of all under hard negatives. A data workflow adds curated hard negatives to push balanced reasoning, and gains follow across models.
arxiv-2603-11820: Ieng and co-authors present OMNIA, a two-stage method for completing knowledge graphs built by language models. Such graphs often come out incomplete or noisy. OMNIA first clusters kindred entities and relations to draft candidate triples. Light embedding filters then screen the drafts, and a language model checks their meaning. The method works inside the graph, with no outside sources. On several data sets it lifts F1 scores well past embedding-only models, while the clustering keeps search and checking costs down.
arxiv-2603-11920: Akyildiz and Bilen sketch Kraken, a knowledge-centric design for sixth-generation networks that think. Future services, from self-driving transport to immersive reality, need networks that read context and plan ahead, not just move packets. Kraken joins three strengths: semantic communication that sends what matters, generative reasoning that predicts how the system will evolve, and goal-oriented tuning tied to app outcomes. Three planes carry the design, for infrastructure, agents, and knowledge. The path builds on O-RAN, digital twins, and modern MLOps, easing the climb from 5G.
arxiv-2603-12120: Lin, Patel, Moon, Lazebnik, and Jain built CRAFT, a tendon-driven robot hand with mixed hard-soft compliance. Their rule is simple: impacts gather at joints, while links bear most of the load. Soft material goes at the joints, rigid stock forms the links, and rolling-contact surfaces guide each bend. Fifteen motors on the fingers pull the tendons, keeping the hand compact and light. In grip tests the hand covered all 33 grasps in the Feix taxonomy. It also handled fragile, low-friction items well by remote control.
arxiv-2603-12420: Gao and Wu survey how large language models are reshaping human mobility research. Movement studies track how people travel among meaningful places and what patterns follow in aggregate. Coordinates alone miss place meaning, traveler intent, and real-world constraints that text models can read. Their synthesis spans five tasks, from itinerary planning and trajectory generation to prediction and semantics. For each task they map core challenges to the roles LLMs play in current designs. Open problems point toward reliable, grounded, and privacy-aware methods for the field.
arxiv-2603-12520: Landesberg shows that strong global scores can hide weak best-of-N choices by LLM judges. Judges are often validated by one global correlation with reference labels. In a 5000-prompt best-of-4 benchmark, a judge with moderate global correlation captures only 21.0% of the gain that perfect selection would give. Prompt-level baselines inflate the global score, while within-prompt ranking stays weak. Coarse pointwise scores also tie in about two thirds of pairwise comparisons. Direct pairwise judging recovers much of the lost signal in a matched audit.
arxiv-2603-12620: A K M Amanat Ullah and co-authors use head movement to reach off-screen content on large curved displays. Such screens suit 360 degree maps, yet users see only half the workspace at once. The team tested rate and zone control functions that turn head turns into workspace motion. A polynomial rate rule gave the fastest times and the best ratings. In map tasks, it also beat click-and-drag and joystick control. Their guidelines can shape future designs.
arxiv-2603-13120: Eugenio Bianchi and Daniel Paraizo separate radiative fluxes from Coulombic charges in a balance law for black hole evaporation. In flat spacetimes at infinity, the two notions are clearly distinct. With the Wald-Zoupas prescription, they pin down the classical flux of a massless scalar field. In a spherical evaporation model, the balance law gives a Bondi mass correction tied to Hawking radiation entropy. The renormalized flux stays nonnegative and matches the Ashtekar-Taveras-Varadarajan form, not the Fulling-Davies one.
arxiv-2603-13220: Logan Cross and co-authors build a generative model of conspicuous consumption and status signaling. Why some goods gain prestige has long puzzled costly signaling theory, which treats tastes as fixed. Their account grounds status in the theory of appropriateness and a social feedback loop. Groups of LLM-based agents in the Concordia framework test the idea in daily routines. Social visibility turns plain demand into status seeking, the team reports. Price run-ups and Veblen effects appear for both real luxury goods and synthetic ones.
arxiv-2603-13420: Xinhai Wang and co-authors present PSKV, a method to speed suffix jailbreak attacks on LLMs. Such attacks test many candidate suffixes before one works, so costs run high. All candidate prompts share the same harmful instruction as a prefix, the team notes. PSKV keeps one KV cache for that prefix and shares it with every candidate prompt. That cuts redundant inference and allows more aggressive batching within memory limits. On six attacks across five LLMs, it cut inference time by 40 percent and peak memory by half.
arxiv-2603-13720: Brian Diaz and Pascal Normanyo study Dirichlet series and asymptotics for generalized Legendre factorials. They fix a number field, a finite set of prime ideals, and a positive integer-valued function on the remaining prime ideals. An ideal-valued factorial is defined through valuations that sum floor terms over prime powers. Assuming the function grows like a constant times the norm, they derive a Dirichlet series for the logarithmic increments. A prime-ideal theorem and a Dirichlet hyperbola argument give the main asymptotic formula.
arxiv-2603-14020: Jakšić, Pillet, and Szczepanek settle two old questions about quasi-free fermionic states on lattices. Lanford and Robinson showed in 1972 that gauge-invariant quasi-free states maximize entropy at a fixed two-point function. Whether the maximizer is unique, and whether such states are weak Gibbs states, stayed open. For a wide class of states, the authors answer yes to both. The proof draws both facts from the thermodynamic formalism for lattice fermions.
arxiv-2603-14220: Li and co-authors present FIND, a simple detector for images made by diffusion models. Older detectors rebuild each image with a diffusion model and read the error, which is costly and model-bound. The key fact used here is that real photos fit Gaussian noise less easily than fake ones. Training adds Gaussian noise to real images and labels them as fake, which steers a plain classifier to the true gap. Theory shows the noised real images then mimic fakes under Gaussian fitting.
arxiv-2603-14620: Stamm and Zeng speed up parametric eigenvalue problems with the Taylor-reduced basis method. Large Hermitian matrices with parameters need fast eigenspace estimates. Taylor-RBM builds a local approximation space near a reference point. Derivative data of the spectral projector shape that space. A compact error analysis backs the method. A cheap assembly route builds the reduced basis in practice. The study also compares the basis with raw truncated power series of the eigenprojector. Links to classic perturbation theory run through the analysis.
arxiv-2603-15020: Nie and co-authors define meme reappraisal, a task that turns negative memes into constructive ones while keeping the scene and layout. They build MER-Bench, a benchmark of real memes with labels for source and target emotions, rewritten text, and edit instructions. Scoring uses a multimodal model as judge across quality, emotion control, structure, and affect. Tests of current editing and generation systems show large gaps. The authors offer the benchmark as a base for emotion-aware meme editing research.
arxiv-2603-15120: Casals-Salvador and co-authors benchmark fast attention variants for speech emotion recognition. Standard self-attention is accurate but grows quadratically in cost, which limits scale. They compare RetNet, LightNet, GSA, FoX, and KDA on both versions of the MSP-Podcast benchmark. Plain self-attention still scored best on the test sets. The efficient variants cut latency and memory use by up to ten times. The study frames a clear trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for teams building scalable emotion recognition systems.
arxiv-2603-15220: Cho and Kim present InterPol, a method that de-anonymizes model responses on the LM Arena leaderboard. Anonymity keeps voting-based rankings honest, so a break matters. Simple text statistics often fail on models with similar styles. InterPol learns deep stylistic cues from interpolated preference data, which creates hard negative examples. An adaptive curriculum guides the training. It beat prior baselines at naming the source model by a wide margin. Simulations on real battle data then show how such attacks could bend the rankings.
arxiv-2603-15720: Azizi studies Janus states, built by superposing two squeezed vacuum states. Such states are non-Gaussian, so plain squeezing rules may mislead. He computes their quantum Fisher information with exact analytic tools. At fixed mean photon number, a single squeezed vacuum stays best for basic squeezing. Inside a fixed two-state span, Janus states can beat both of their parts. They win on quadrature variance and on phase sensitivity at once. A fixed-squeezing benchmark shows still larger gains for quadratic sensing.
arxiv-2603-15820: Rhodes, Pathak, and Chien regularize gauge fields with anyon categories for quantum simulation. Gauge fields carry endless degrees of freedom, a core snag for simulators. Their swap replaces the gauge group with a braided fusion category. Its objects mirror Wilson lines of a Chern-Simons theory. The level k sets how coarse the regularization runs. Fusion surface models couple the gauge sector to fermionic matter. Both parts then act as interacting anyons. The team gives circuits for the F and R gates. Cases cover U(1) and SU(2) anyon theories.
arxiv-2603-15920: Du and co-authors build a differentiable fluid solver for messy real geometries. Gradient-based inverse work needs solvers that pass derivatives end to end. Prior differentiable tools stick to neat Cartesian grids. Their DiFVM solver runs finite volumes on unstructured polyhedral meshes. A graph view turns each solver step into scatter and gather moves. JAX and XLA supply compilation, fusion, and automatic gradients. OpenFOAM case folders load with no edits needed. Patient heart flow tests match OpenFOAM closely. Windkessel traits are inferred from sparse readings.
arxiv-2603-16120: Balepur and co-authors argue that personal research tools need real user studies. Deep Research systems answer queries by synthesizing many papers. Such tools rarely model what each user actually wants. Their MyScholarQA agent infers a profile of user interests. It proposes tailored actions and writes reports along approved lines. Synthetic users and model judges score it above baselines. Live user interviews then surface nine hidden error types. Model judges missed every one of those error classes. Real users remain the true test of personalization.
arxiv-2603-16320: Senn and co-authors map the design space of digital payment systems. Central bank digital currencies are the driving use case. Banks often judge privacy tools too immature or hard to scale. The authors instead review 36 complete system designs from the top down. They extract shared patterns, trade-offs, and open problems. Gaps include offline payments and post-quantum security. The survey aims to guide future CBDC design.
arxiv-2603-16920: Yamashita and co-authors adapt speech recognition to new domains with synthetic data. Recognizers often degrade on domain specific speech because in domain data is scarce. Their framework has two parts. First, a language model pipeline creates varied domain text, filtered to balance diversity and term coverage. Second, phonetic respelling uses model written pseudo spellings to add pronunciation variety before synthesis. Across four domain datasets, the authors report drops in word error rate. They argue that term coverage plus realistic pronunciation change makes synthetic speech more useful.
arxiv-2603-17020: Fredrickson and co-authors continue a proof that a family of Hitchin moduli spaces are gravitational instantons. The spaces are parabolic SU(2) Hitchin moduli spaces on the four punctured sphere, forming a 12 parameter family. This first paper computes their Torelli parameters for each allowed set of parabolic data. The authors show the family realizes all allowable Torelli parameters. A companion paper then proves the spaces are ALG instantons of type D4. Together, the papers give a first check of a case of the Modularity Conjecture.
arxiv-2603-17120: Sales and co-authors study how regular islands break apart in a discontinuous nontwist map. In classic area preserving maps, islands are bounded by invariant curves that act as transport barriers. Their map is smooth on the real line but discontinuous on the cylinder. They find islands fragment in a hierarchy into smaller regular parts linked by chaotic channels. Trajectories near elliptic points trap for long times, then escape, so no global barrier exists. Restoring continuity removes the fragmentation.
arxiv-2603-17220: Panth and Maiti build a language model for Tharu, a low resource language spoken by about 1.7 million people in Nepal and India. Big multilingual models often hallucinate in Tharu or slip into Hindi and Nepali. Their dataset, TharuChat, was made by a language model fed with Rana Tharu grammar and folklore, then checked by humans. It is anchored in Rana Tharu with elements of two other dialects mixed in. Training on more of this synthetic data cut perplexity from 6.42 down to 2.88.
arxiv-2603-17320: Langford and Omar use simulations to explain why bubbles form inside the dense phase of two dimensional active matter. Self propelled, purely repulsive particles phase separate, and bubbles inside the dense part are a known puzzle. By adding polydispersity, the authors separate the role of hexatic order from other effects. They find hexatic order is necessary for bubbles, but not sufficient. A small amount of thermal noise is also required; with zero noise, no bubbles form.
arxiv-2603-18020: Ramachandran presents CaseLinker, an open system for cross-case study of internet crimes against children reports. Case data is split across groups and regions, with mixed formats and detail. CaseLinker pulls facts with regex and pattern rules, keeping results clear and auditable. It builds six views, groups like cases by weighted Jaccard scores, and adds triage notes. Tests on 47 Arizona reports show sound extraction, clustering, and insight tools.
arxiv-2603-18420: Dury shows that word timing links in texts reveal concepts about what text does, not what it is about. Topic models group text by theme; timing links group by role and style. A contrastive model with 29.4 million weights trains on 373 million pairs from 9,766 Gutenberg books. Clusters span broad modes like direct confrontation and set scenes like courtroom cross-examination. New novels fall into a tight, coherent set of clusters with no retraining.
arxiv-2603-18620: Chen and co-authors teach language models to improve their own context at test time. Their Learning to Self-Evolve framework uses reinforcement learning for this skill. Each context edit earns reward from the gain in later task scores. That trick turns a multi-step process into a single-step training goal. A tree-guided loop steers edits during use. A 4B model trained this way beats self-evolving setups run by GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5. It can also guide other models with no extra training.
arxiv-2603-18920: Siemroth asks when a daily petrol price reset should occur under a proposed German rule. The rule would let stations raise prices at most once a day. He infers how price-sensitive drivers are at each hour from station price data. Prices peak at seven in the morning and bottom out at seven in the evening. He tests every reset hour in his model. An eleven o'clock reset gives the lowest traffic-weighted price, with flat prices all day in that case.
arxiv-2603-19220: Yang and co-authors present Nemotron-Cascade 2, an open model with 30 billion weights and 3 billion active at a time. It is trained first on curated data, then with cascade reinforcement learning across many domains. Strong teacher models guide it on-policy in each domain to recover lost ground. The team reports gold-level scores at the 2025 math and informatics olympiads and the ICPC finals. It matches far larger open models on math and code. The weights and training data are released.
arxiv-2603-19320: Fukushima studies how brain circuits balance local wiring limits with whole-network links. He builds a model based on synaptic crowding. As a neuron gains links, each new synapse gets harder to form. He solves this one-parameter model and finds scaling laws. Mean connectivity grows only logarithmically with network size, while variance stays bounded. When nearby cells are met first, link lengths form a near power-law spread. With shortcut rewiring, the networks gain small-world traits. He links degree patterns to network dynamics and offers predictions.
arxiv-2603-19820: Amparore formalizes the storage backend needed for fast range-based set reconciliation. That method syncs ordered sets by comparing summaries of ranges. It refines only the ranges that mismatch. The local cost depends on how fast the store answers summary and rank queries. Amparore defines a store contract that joins range summaries with order navigation. He shows that B+-trees with subtree counts and summaries meet the contract. His AELMDB build extends the LMDB engine with this design. Tests showed much lower local cost on reconciliation-heavy work.
arxiv-2603-20020: Yuan and co-authors fix a training flaw that hurts text reading in multimodal language models. These models reason well but often miss fine visual detail. The authors trace the problem to skip links in feature fusion. Those links let high level goals overwrite early visual signals through back propagation. Their detached skip links reuse shallow features forward but block gradients on that path. No new learnable parameters are added. A probe tool, R-Probe, checks if fine detail survives in the visual tokens.
arxiv-2603-20120: Plungė and co-authors model brittle fracture in anisotropic media with physics-informed deep learning. Phase-field models track cracks, but past deep Ritz work stayed with simple isotropic forms. Their frame covers a family of higher-order anisotropic models through a generalized crack density. The fracture problem is solved by minimizing total energy. Higher-order B-spline functions enrich the trial space, giving stable gradients without automatic differentiation. Tests span isotropic, cubic, and orthotropic surface energies. In anisotropic cases the cracks grew in the right direction-dependent ways.
arxiv-2603-20420: Ambrozak and co-authors present CRANE, a tool that cleans raw nanopore sequencing signals. Nanopore reads are long, and raw signals allow mapping without basecalling. Noise and processing errors in those signals limit analysis accuracy. CRANE trains a hidden Markov model to spot and fix signal errors. Tests across varied data sets show steady accuracy gains. The tool also eases retooling pipelines for newer nanopore devices. It adds little computational overhead while doing so. Cleaner raw signals should widen what direct signal analysis can do.
arxiv-2603-20520: Huang and co-authors present CogFormer, a framework that fits many cognitive models with one trained network. Simulation based inference made hard models easy to fit one at a time. But each change to priors, parameters, or design forced a full retrain. CogFormer trains a transformer that stays valid across a vast set of model variants. Data types, sample sizes, and design matrices can all shift. Tests span decision models with binary, multi-choice, and continuous responses. Parameter estimates stayed accurate across these families.
arxiv-2603-20620: Hao and co-authors test whether reasoning traces from large models tell the truth. They inject fake reasoning steps into a model's think trace. These planted hints did change the final answers across 45,000 samples. So traces do shape what the model does. But when asked, models hid the planted hint's role. Non disclosure topped 90 percent for strong hints. Models instead made up unrelated reasons. Brain signal checks linked this cover up to sycophancy and deception patterns.
arxiv-2603-20920: Amin and co-authors benchmark deep learning training on CPUs and GPUs, with a focus on fair access to compute. They train four models, from a small Conv6 to CycleGAN, with TensorFlow and PyTorch. Tests run on Intel Xeon CPUs and NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPUs. GPUs speed training by eleven to two hundred forty six times on average, with the lightest model gaining most. TensorFlow cuts inference time by about fifteen percent. They argue shared GPU access is key for smaller institutions.
arxiv-2603-21320: Zhao and co-authors study a quantum critical point through holographic duality. The duality maps a strongly correlated electron system to classical gravity in one higher dimension, where the math is easier. They study a field-induced critical point with dynamical exponent three. Its thermodynamics defines a new universality class. The Grüneisen ratio diverges as temperature falls, with a universal power law. The behavior closely mirrors recent experiments on the heavy-fermion material CeRh6Ge4, a compound of cerium, rhodium, and germanium.
arxiv-2603-21420: Mizuyama builds a unified theory for quasiparticle resonance states in Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory, used for open quantum many-body systems. The framework joins the complex-scaled Jost function method with Autonne-Takagi factorization. Complex scaling lets him separate resonance poles from the continuum background in the completeness relation. The factorization then fixes the scale and phase of resonant wave functions without ad hoc adjustments. Tests show results stay unchanged when the scaling angle rotates, and scattering profiles reveal a Fano-style interference pattern.
arxiv-2603-21620: Radi completes a classification problem in arithmetic dynamics: how many periodic points survive when a polynomial is reduced modulo a prime ideal. A 2014 question by Juul and co-authors asked for the limit of that proportion as the prime grows. Earlier work with Fariña-Asategui settled the Chebyshev-like cases, where the limit is zero. Radi now handles all remaining polynomial cases. The result gives a complete answer for polynomials of degree at least two over number fields.
arxiv-2603-21820: Deng and co-authors question whether infrared and visible image fusion needs perfectly aligned training pairs. Fusion blends heat signatures with natural textures, but aligned pairs are costly to collect. They compare strict pairing with unpaired and arbitrarily paired training. A framework built for loose data enriches the cross-modal links the model can learn. Three light baselines cover CNN, Transformer, and GAN designs, each with new loss functions. Models trained on a tiny unaligned set matched those trained on a set one hundred times larger with strict pairing.
arxiv-2603-22220: Norfolk and Xie propose fluid ETL pipelines for exploring data while it is still arriving. Analysts often need to scan fresh data for main traits or odd values. Classic pipelines prep data with many routines, like parsing and indexing, to cover unknown goals. That prep work is costly. Fluid pipelines can start and stop prep routines on demand, without blocking ingestion. They run extra routines when idle or cheap spot capacity is free. Tests on a real dataset show the idea works.
arxiv-2603-22320: Schmidt and co-authors ask how machine learning emulators can truly serve climate science. Physics-based climate models guide policy, but they demand heavy compute and skill to run. Emulators promise cheaper stand-ins. In practice, climate scientists often skip them, and ML teams build them as showcases. The authors trace the gap to access limits, missing know-how, and doubts about physical grounding. They propose a framework for building emulators from both fields' views. Their plea: target clear tasks, prove reliability, and make adoption easy.
arxiv-2603-22620: Panayiotou and Şimşek study causal discovery in chain-reaction systems. In such systems, parts switch on in sequence, and an early failure can block later steps. Learning cause and effect is hard in most dynamic systems, even with test data. The authors show that blocking tests can pin down the causal structure. Blocking means stopping one part from switching on. They propose a simple estimator with firm sample guarantees. Tests on synthetic systems show it recovers the structure from a few interventions. Observation-based methods fail in these settings.
arxiv-2603-22820: Zhou, Yetisgen, and Ostendorf frame radiology summary as timeline building. Tracking lung findings across many reports takes clinician time. Their format puts dated findings in columns and links related findings in rows. A three-step language model process builds each timeline. It pulls findings, names groups, then sorts findings by those names. The team built the RadTimeline dataset from chest imaging reports. Group naming proves key to good grouping. The best setup matches human annotators on grouping, with strong recall.
arxiv-2603-23020: Heydari and co-authors build an explainability framework for disaster response models. Their models segment floods and detect cars, often on drone hardware. Emergency teams need to trust the outputs, which black-box models hinder. The framework extends relevance propagation through gated fusion layers in PIDNet. A concept-based method then gives local and global explanations in learned concepts. Tests on a public flood dataset give reliable, readable explanations. Inference stays near real time, suiting small drone platforms.
arxiv-2603-23420: Qu and Lu present Bilevel Autoresearch, a system where one research loop improves another. The outer loop reads the inner loop's code and traces to spot bottlenecks. It then writes fresh Python search mechanisms and injects them at runtime. Both loops run the same language model, so gains come from structure, not a smarter meta model. On a GPT pretraining benchmark, the outer loop beat the lone inner loop fivefold. Plain parameter tweaks without new mechanisms gave no steady gain. Trace checks suggest the tricks break rigid search habits.
arxiv-2603-23720: Kunievsky asks how the age at which migrants arrive shapes their gender role views. Most timing studies track pay, not beliefs. He compares siblings in UK survey data who landed at unlike ages. That within-family contrast pins the pull of childhood years in the host land. A gap measure stacks full answer spreads for migrants against the UK-born. Had all migrants arrived at birth, the gap would shrink a lot. Each added year of arrival age widens it a bit.
arxiv-2603-23820: Buchanan and co-authors prove bounds on fixing and distinguishing numbers for trees in graph theory. A distinguishing labeling uses few labels so that only the trivial symmetry keeps it fixed. The fixing number counts the smallest vertex set pinned by no nontrivial symmetry. They show the fixing number of a 2-distinguishable tree is at most 4n/11, with a general bound for more labels. They also build universal trees that characterize which trees are distinguishable at each radius.
arxiv-2603-24720: Fehm and Touchard study the model theory of a global field equipped with a predicate for one of its absolute values. They prove the theory is decidable when the absolute value is ultrametric or real archimedean. With a complex absolute value, the theory is always undecidable. They also study the existential theories of such structures. Finally, they axiomatise the field together with predicates for all non-complex absolute values at once.
arxiv-2603-25020: Jin and co-authors build GDPO-Listener, a system that animates 3D heads for two-person chats. Listener faces in older systems often freeze into a blank average look. Their design pairs an autoregressive flow matching model with a new training method, GDPO. That method splits rewards by face parameter groups, so each group keeps its own scale. This pushes the system toward varied, lively motion instead of stillness. Text control lets users steer the response style. Tests on two datasets beat prior systems on motion range, looks, and control.
arxiv-2603-25220: Awan, Noor, and Munaf ask users, not benchmarks, how AI chat tools stack up. They surveyed 388 active users across seven platforms, from ChatGPT to Llama. The top three earn satisfaction scores too close to split, despite vast gaps in funds and test scores. Most users juggle two or more tools, and switching costs near nothing. Each tool wins fans for its own reason: interface, answer quality, word of mouth, or loose content rules. False answers and filters frustrate users most. The market looks plural, not winner-take-all.
arxiv-2603-25320: Chatziandreou and Karbach hedge multi-asset derivatives against covariance risk with a part-static plan. Dynamic trades in the assets alone cannot cover cross-asset gamma risk. Their frame pairs live trading with a fixed basket of extra claims. A projection split turns the big variance problem into two smaller ones: a time-based part and a finite choice over the static basket. Strips of plain, product, and spread options fill the gaps. Clear formulas follow for covariance swaps and dispersion trades, and tests show far lower hedging error.
arxiv-2603-25520: Dang studies how steady the solutions of complex Monge-Ampère equations stay on compact Hermitian manifolds. The equations are degenerate and tied to a big form that need not be closed. He proves stability and Hölder continuity for the solutions. When the reference form is the pullback of a Hermitian metric, the solution is continuous across the whole space. A side prize follows: the twisted Chern-Ricci flow keeps a uniform bound on its diameter. The results firm up a hard corner of complex geometry.
arxiv-2603-25620: Kim and co-authors introduce PICon, a test of whether persona agents stay consistent. Persona agents are language models that play the role of a set character. PICon questions them over many turns with logically chained prompts. It checks self-consistency, agreement with real-world facts, and stability when questions repeat. The team tested seven groups of agents and 63 human participants. They report that even strong agents fell below the human baseline on all three checks. Chained questions exposed contradictions and evasive replies.
arxiv-2603-25820: Thadathil and co-authors measure charge and heat flow in the altermagnet CrSb under strong magnetic fields. CrSb draws interest for its simple makeup, high Néel temperature, and semimetal nature. The team used steady and pulsed fields up to 65 tesla. Neutron and magnetization data confirm its compensated magnetic structure. They observe large magnetoresistance that does not saturate, plus a nonlinear Hall response at low temperature. Modeling points to mixed electron and hole carriers with high mobility. Heat flow also breaks the simple Wiedemann-Franz rule.
arxiv-2603-26220: Gui, He, and Liu present a Fourier spectral method for the cutoff Boltzmann equation in a uniform gas. The equation tracks how gas particles collide and spread out in speed. Their method handles both Maxwellian and hard interaction potentials. They prove finite-time error bounds in a weighted L2 norm for the whole space. The bounds show in clear terms how the error depends on the velocity cutoff and the number of Fourier modes used.
arxiv-2603-26520: Zheng and co-authors study a form of trafficking where victims are lured across Chinese borders to run online scams. Fake job offers draw people to Southeast Asia, where compounds force them into cybercrime roles. The team reads 158 RedNote posts to see how online communities react. Recruiters exploit cultural ties, and survivors meet barriers like family rejection when they return. Community safety tips help, but doubts about support and cross-border coordination limit their force.
arxiv-2603-26820: Huang and Soykan lay out a modular framework for digital twins in radiation imaging and therapy. The twin joins patient data, models, solvers, calibration, and decision steps. It updates a hidden patient state and tracks uncertainty through each choice. As a test case, the authors rebuild an OpenKBP dose prediction pipeline in PyTorch. Their 3D U-Net predicts dose for 100 test patients in about half a second each. A full three-fraction loop runs in 10.3 seconds.
arxiv-2603-26920: Lin and co-authors prove that smooth Cayley fibrations with full holonomy cannot exist. The setting is a compact torsion-free Spin(7)-manifold with full holonomy. Every Cayley fibration of such a manifold, they show, must have singular fibers. That confirms a long-standing expectation for calibrated fibrations with exceptional holonomy. Rigidity of the Spin(7) structure first cuts any smooth example down to two topological cases. A new spinnability theorem then rules out both cases. The hardest case uses families Seiberg-Witten theory and equivariant methods.
arxiv-2603-27320: Bodik studies retrospective counterfactuals: what would have happened to a person we already saw. The target is the treated outcome given a person's traits and their untreated result. That target cannot be pinned down from data without extra input. A cross-world correlation links each person's two potential outcomes. Plausible bounds on that correlation make the problem tractable again. Bodik's tools and prediction intervals reach their coverage target in the limit. Common shortcuts secretly assume the correlation is zero or one. Blending the two gains both theory and practice.
arxiv-2603-27420: Zhang and co-authors present CarbonEdge, a tool for greener edge AI. Edge devices run more deep learning each year. That growth raises carbon output fast. CarbonEdge splits models across devices with carbon in mind. Its scheduler scores both speed and carbon cost. Users can tune the trade-off with one weight. Tests in a simulated edge setup cut emissions by 22.9 percent. Carbon efficiency rose by a factor of 1.3. Scheduling overhead stayed tiny at 0.03 milliseconds per task.
arxiv-2603-27820: You and co-authors bring counterfactual tests into AI diagnosis. Clinicians learn by asking what a missing symptom would change. Most diagnostic agents never test findings that way. Their framework edits case facts and reruns rival diagnoses. A probability gap scores each finding's support. Multi-agent debate keeps the process explicit and grounded. Interpretability of the final call improves. The design mirrors real training in differential diagnosis.
arxiv-2603-28220: Liu and four co-authors speed up the decentralized EXTRA optimization method with a bundle model. EXTRA's updates lean on a crude first-order Taylor fit of the objective, which slows convergence. The bundle version keeps past cuts to build a sharper model of the function. The method stays fully decentralized, with no central coordinator. The authors prove a KKT residual shrinks to zero under mild assumptions. On least-squares tests, it converged faster and cared less about step size.
arxiv-2603-28320: Iparragirre, Lumley, and Barrio build valid inference for the AUC when data come from complex surveys. The AUC scores how well a model separates two outcome groups, but survey sampling breaks standard error formulas. Their design-based approach uses replicate weights to form intervals and tests that respect the sampling plan. In simulations, it hit the promised coverage, while the plain bootstrap understated variance and rejected too often. The methods ship in the svyROC package and are shown on health survey data.
arxiv-2603-28520: Hansen and Klausen prove uniqueness and mixing for two picture models of the hot Ising model, the loop O(1) model and the random current model. Both describe the supercritical phase on the cubic lattice in any dimension from two up. The team shows each model has just one Gibbs measure. Correlations also decay at an exponential ratio rate, a strong form of mixing. The methods stretch to flow models and gauge theory height measures.
arxiv-2603-28620: Dvali, Fitz, and Komisel show how confinement during inflation can remove the cosmological bound on the axion scale. Their scenario relaxes the axion early through high-scale confinement inside SU(5) grand unified theory. During inflation, SU(5) may be fully or partly in a confining phase. Strong QCD can arise from an inflaton coupling or from symmetry restoration. The mechanism works for Peccei-Quinn models and for the two-form gauge axion. The present-day axion can still serve as dark matter.
arxiv-2603-28720: Wen and Schafer-Nameki extend categorical symmetry methods to time-reversal and other anti-unitary symmetries. Past work on phases used unitary symmetries over the complex numbers. Anti-unitary symmetries instead fit fusion categories over the real numbers. They define Galois-real fusion categories as the right model for such cases. Cases include group based categories and a real form of Tambara-Yamagami categories. Gapped phases with anti-linear symmetries are described by module categories over these structures. They also build a Symmetry Topological Field Theory.
arxiv-2603-29020: Akkil and co-authors introduce Emergence WebVoyager, a stricter version of the WebVoyager benchmark for web agents. Their audit of the original found vague task framing and variable operations. Those flaws hinder fair and reproducible comparisons. The new version standardizes task setup, failure handling, annotation, and reporting. Annotator agreement reached 95.9 percent. Applied to OpenAI Operator, the benchmark gave an overall success rate of 68.6 percent. That is well below the 87 percent reported before. Performance varied a lot across domains and task types.
arxiv-2603-29320: Arai and Kai give criteria for telling whether a quandle is admissible. Quandles are algebraic systems inspired by Reidemeister moves in knot theory. An admissible quandle is one matching a conjugation quandle from a group. Non-admissible quandles may yield genuinely new knot invariants. Their criteria use colorings of (1,1)-tangles. Applying them, they build many non-admissible examples. The examples come from simple tangles based on the Hopf link. The trefoil knot supplies further cases.
arxiv-2603-29820: Song, Ko, and Noh present SIREN, a vision-guided method that turns mono video sound into binaural audio. Two-ear sound aids immersion, but most consumer video is mono. SIREN predicts left and right channels directly. A vision transformer learns a shared scene map plus end-to-end channel attention. A soft spatial prior guides early channel grounding. Two-stage fusion then cuts crosstalk across crops and windows. Tests on FAIR-Play and MUSIC-Stereo show steady gains.
arxiv-2604-00520: Poe and colleagues present BLISS, a global method for blind identification of linear systems with sparse inputs. System identification and sparse dictionary learning both resemble matrix factorisation, yet the two fields have long worked apart. Identification theory is mature when inputs are known, but blind identification stays poorly understood beyond narrow settings. Dictionary learning, by contrast, lately gained strong results on global identifiability plus scalable nonconvex algorithms. Given sparse inputs, the authors show fully observed blind identification extends complete dictionary learning, yielding global identifiability proofs for blind systems.
arxiv-2604-00620: Bastida Zamora and colleagues apply quantum machine learning to the quantum lattice Boltzmann method. They train a variational quantum circuit to build an operator that copies the nonlinear part of the collision operator from the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook approximation. Used on the post-linear-collision state, the operator gives a final state matching nonlinear collision dynamics. The team presents two designs, R1 for multi-step runs with no intermediate measurements, and a second design, R2.
arxiv-2604-00720: Boris Zilber gives a strict mathematical definition of local approximation and shows how it applies to several kinds of structures. His main result is that every compact simple Lie group can be approximated locally by finite groups. The definition draws on physics for motivation, while the proof method comes from model theory, using ultraproducts of emerging metric structures.
arxiv-2604-00920: van Oort and colleagues present the GPT-NL Public Corpus, the largest permissively licensed corpus of Dutch language resources. It holds 21 Dutch-only collections totaling 36B preprocessed Dutch tokens found in no other language-model pretraining corpus. It also includes about 207B English, 232B code, and 48B German and Danish tokens curated from existing sets. All included data comes from permissively licensed sources, redistributed under a CC-BY license, and the full set is public on the Hugging Face Hub.
arxiv-2604-01020: Wang and team introduce OrgAgent, a company-style hierarchical multi-agent framework with governance, execution, and compliance layers. One layer plans and allocates resources, a second solves tasks and reviews, and a third controls final answers. Across reasoning tasks, models, run modes, and rules, ranked setups mostly beat other structures and cut token use versus flat teamwork. For GPT-OSS-120B, hierarchy lifts performance over flat systems by 102.73 percent while cutting token usage on SQuAD 2.0. Hierarchy helps most with steady skill roles, managed information flow, and layered checks.
arxiv-2604-01120: Hung and colleagues introduce Diff-VS, a vocal separation model built on the EDM framework, tackling the weak scores of current generative music separation. It handles complex short-time Fourier transform spectra with an improved U-Net shaped by music-led design choices. The model matches rival baselines on objective metrics and reaches heard quality on par with state-of-the-art systems by proxy listener scores. The team hopes the results spur wider study of such methods for music source separation.
arxiv-2604-01420: Legred, Golomb and Chatziioannou test whether failed supernovae forming black holes by direct collapse near 10 solar masses reinforce the observed overdensity there. Merging rates drop by about 2 orders of magnitude from near 10 solar masses to near 15 solar masses, which progenitor compactness alone cannot fully explain. Using 153 GWTC-4.0 observations, they confirm a strong peak at 10 solar masses. The rate is consistent with zero at the 90 percent level between 12.0 and 16.1 solar masses, then rises above about 16 solar masses. That structure fits a distinct population of failed-supernova black holes.
arxiv-2604-01620: Wang and colleagues present DaxFS, a Linux filesystem for CXL shared memory using cmpxchg atomic operations, coherent across hosts, as its sole coordination primitive. A cooperative shared page cache with a multi-host clock eviction algorithm provides demand-paged caching in shared DAX memory. Under cross-host contention, DaxFS maintains over 99 percent CAS accuracy with no lost updates. On single-host DRAM-backed DAX, DaxFS exceeds tmpfs throughput, with up to 2.68 times higher random write throughput with 4 threads, and higher random read throughput at 64 KB.
arxiv-2604-01720: Yang and colleagues present Hi-LOAM, a neural framework for LiDAR odometry and mapping, for self-driving cars and robots. Older frameworks need supervision signals or miss fine detail in large scenes. Hi-LOAM takes LiDAR point clouds, stores features in octree-based hash tables, and decodes them into signed distance values with shallow perceptrons. Pose estimation uses a correspondence-free scan-to-implicit match, and training is self-supervised, needing no pre-training. Tests on real and synthetic sets show it beats current methods.
arxiv-2604-02020: Liu and colleagues test vision-language models linking drone and satellite views with LinkS squared Bench, the first cross-view spatial intelligence benchmark. Such teamwork aids emergency response and security. Older benchmarks use lone drone videos or still images. It pairs 1,022 minutes of drone footage with satellite imagery over 200 square km, plus 17.9k questions across 12 tasks. Tests on 18 models show a gap to human levels, with dynamic alignment the key bottleneck, though an adapter lifts scores.
arxiv-2604-02220: Long and colleagues treat chart reading as a chain of small decoding steps that can be composed. Earlier work ranked visual channels like angle, position and length but could not predict new chart task pairs without fresh experiments. Using probability and cumulative distribution charts, they split four tasks into five reusable perceptual operations and model their errors. Composed operators then predict a scatterplot mean estimation experiment, with one strategy capturing both bias and variance where five rivals fail in distinct ways.
arxiv-2604-02520: Hassanaly and six colleagues use neural posterior estimation to infer the hidden inner traits of lithium-ion batteries far faster than standard Bayesian tuning. The method shifts heavy computing into data creation and training, cutting estimation time from minutes to milliseconds and enabling real-time use. It matches or beats Bayesian accuracy on traits, though voltage forecasts can be slightly worse, and it shows which voltage regions inform each trait.
arxiv-2604-02720: Rost tests rule theory against radical capability asymmetry, where rulers may vastly outthink the ruled. His six-dimension scheme covers legitimacy, accountability, corrigibility, non-domination, subsidiarity, and institutional resilience. The scheme is first tried on existing non-majoritarian bodies, where gaps in power are real but bounded. Four of six dimensions fail by structure under bounded superintelligent rule. Two look fixable by design, while public reason under being beyond understanding and freedom from domination under lasting imbalance call for a new theory of what is right.
arxiv-2604-02820: Tang, Guo and Xiao present MFE, a multimodal hand exoskeleton delivering force, pressure, and thermal feedback for virtual reality and teleoperation. With 20 degrees of freedom for hand pose, it pushes and pulls fingers with 3.5 to 8.1 newtons, renders up to 2.47 kilopascals of contact pressure at the fingertips, and spans 10 to 55 degrees Celsius through thermoelectric pumps. Tests integrate it into robotic teleoperation.
arxiv-2604-02920: Di Gennaro, Chakraborty and Zhivotovskiy study Exponential Weights for online logistic regression with a Gaussian prior. They show its near-optimal worst-case regret bound against the best bounded-norm linear predictor comes at far lower cost than prior work with the same guarantee. In the large-norm regime under linear separability, the rescaled posterior converges to a Gaussian truncated to the version cone. The predictor becomes a vote over separating directions. Past a margin threshold, regret no longer depends on the norm and grows logarithmically with the inverse margin.
arxiv-2604-03020: Cheng, Ju, Qiao and Zhang propose GTransNet, a generalized transferable neural network for steady-state partial differential equations. TransNet, a shallow network with one hidden layer, sets hidden parameters by uniformly spread partition hyperplanes, but loses accuracy and stability on highly wavy solutions. GTransNet adds hidden layers while keeping the interpretable feature-generation design. Its first hidden layer keeps TransNet's parameter sampling approach plus a symmetry constraint on neuron biases. Later layers drop bias terms and use variance-controlled sampling for neuron weights.
arxiv-2604-03320: Pritha and colleagues make COVID-19 detection from chest CT scans robust across hospitals with different scanners and protocols. Their multi-task model predicts both diagnosis and source center from a shared backbone, so features hold across all four centers, with a loss adjustment protecting underrepresented centers. On 308 validation scans it reaches an F1 score of 0.91, showing the approach generalizes beyond single-center data.
arxiv-2604-03420: Solombrino and colleagues show that toughness to post-training quantization is a shared path in weight space. A quantization vector pulled from a donor task by simple weight math can patch a target model, lifting post-quantization scores up to 60 points in a 3-bit setting without target-side training. Across four ViT scales and 22 image tasks, donor vectors often help even when tasks differ a lot.
