arxiv-2604-03620: Puntini's 2026 analysis studies the linear wobble of an exact solution for rising mountain waves in dry, no-heat-exchange, compressible flow. He uses the short-wave method. Stability boils down to plain rate rules with cyclic numbers along fluid paths. Floquet theory gives factors of the form one, mu, and mu-inverse. For neutral layers the flow is wobbly whenever wave steepness exceeds one third. Weak stable layers lower the threshold, and the wobble is a subharmonic tuned echo.
arxiv-2604-03920: Agam Goyal and colleagues argued that lifelike mock communities do not yet prove a policy works. Their frame splits two kinds of cause. Necessary causation means the result would not have come about without the move. Sufficient causation means the move brings the result about time and again. Staff who probe past events need the first kind, while staff who pick new rules need the second. All such claims still hinge on how true the mock world is, so lifelike looks alone cannot back a rule change.
arxiv-2604-04120: Lingjie Zeng and team studied whether shrinking chain-of-thought reasoning preserves trustworthiness, not just accuracy. Long traces cost heavily at run time, and old checks focus on scores and token savings. Across safety, made-up-fact fighting, and many-language toughness, the shrink often brought trust drops with mixed patterns per method. A tuning-aware DPO variant cut trace length by 19.3 percent on benchmarks with much smaller trust loss.
arxiv-2604-04220: Hamza Mostafa, Om Shastri, and Dennis Lee introduced TimeSeek, a benchmark tracking how agentic language-model forecasters hold up across a prediction market's life. They tested 10 frontier models on 150 CFTC-regulated Kalshi binary markets at five time checkpoints, with and without web search, for 15,000 forecasts total. Models competed best early and on high-uncertainty markets, but faded near resolution and on strong-consensus markets. Web search lifted pooled Brier Skill Score for every model overall yet hurt in 12 percent of model-checkpoint pairs, favoring time-aware evaluation over single snapshots.
arxiv-2604-04620: Watanabe, Xu and Minami build a geometric framework for average energy loss and its swings in tiny heat engines in finite time. Existing geometric treatments capture average dissipation but not its swings, which matter when tiny quantities vary wildly. In the linear-response regime, they show both the mean and the spread of dissipated availability follow metric tensors built from equilibrium correlation functions. The framework yields bounds on both quantities, and on efficiency and its swings. It applies to overdamped and underdamped Brownian dynamics and to Markov jump processes.
arxiv-2604-04720: Ki, Duh and Carpuat ask what marks a good reasoning trace in many tongues. They define measurable traits spanning cross-tongue alignment, step layout, and flow, then link each trait to right answers with logistic regression and hunt for hidden traits with sparse autoencoders. Tests on two maths benchmarks, four models, and ten tongues find most traits help, but their pull shifts by tongue and can even flip. The upshot cuts against English-centred reward design and points to aims tuned per tongue.
arxiv-2604-04820: Xu presents ANX, an open protocol and framework built for AI agents, not adapted from human interfaces. Current routes, GUI automation and MCP-based skills, burn tokens, split interaction, and leave gaps. ANX joins command line, skill, and MCP parts under one design. Its four ideas are agent native config and markup, dual rendering for agents and humans, apps, and machine procedures for long tasks. Form-filling tests show token cuts of half against MCP skills and up to two thirds against GUI automation, with faster runs.
arxiv-2604-05020: Tagawa and four co-authors study electromagnetic flares from compact-object mergers in active galaxy disks. Accretion disks in active galaxies are likely sites for stellar-mass black hole mergers detectable via gravitational waves. The uncertain origin of gravitational-wave events motivates searching for accompanying signatures. They study post-merger flares from jets launched by merger remnants and from shocked gas as jets break out of the disk. Jet breakout produces luminous gamma-ray emission detectable with MeV-band telescopes, while cooling peaks at longer wavelengths.
arxiv-2604-05420: Liu and six colleagues challenge the smooth-medium assumption behind atomic-ensemble sensing, showing the discrete grain of atoms creates its own intrinsic noise. Their discrete-atom framework yields one scaling law governed by the photon-to-atom flux ratio, crossing from optical-noise to granularity-noise limits. Raising probe power can therefore worsen sensitivity, and beyond a critical ratio even nonclassical light stops helping.
arxiv-2604-05720: Bratus, Drozhzhin, and Yakushkina present the first four chapters of their monograph on evolution and replicator systems. The book joins Darwinian dynamics via replicator equations, hypercycles, Eigen and Crow-Kimura quasispecies models, and fitness-landscape shape. A model where the landscape itself shifts slowly, plus number studies of hypercyclic and RNA nets, rounds out these chapters.
arxiv-2604-06120: Aeenehvand and Shariati revisit conformal time in a flat expanding universe, using a simple two-part teaching case. They clarify how cosmic time, conformal time, and the scale factor relate, and how that link shapes the paths of freely moving particles and the shape of spacetime. Radiation, matter, and vacuum-only de Sitter cases each get separate treatment, since each gives different geodesic patterns. The paper then states its affine-parameter formalism for any flat conformal metric and extends it to full three-dimensional space.
arxiv-2604-06220: Patel and three colleagues compare machine learning models for a sensor glove that reads sign language through triboelectric nanogenerators. Five flex sensors feed time-series data across 11 sign classes, covering digits 1 through 5 and letters A through F. Their MFCC CNN-LSTM design processes frequency features from each sensor through separate convolutional branches before fusion, reaching 93.33 percent accuracy, about 23 points above the best traditional algorithm. Tests show 50-step windows beat 100-step windows, and augmentation with time warping and noise injection proves essential for generalization.
arxiv-2604-06420: Abdou investigates how recommendation performance evolves as data grows. Collecting and processing data costs time and energy, yet gains may stop. Using LensKit and RecBole on 11 datasets, he trains on nine sizes, measuring NDCG@10. Raw NDCG usually rises with size, with no saturation. Min-max normalization reveals a positive trend: around 75 percent at the largest size achieve the best. A late-stage analysis supports the upward trend, with a non-negative range. For recommenders, more data remains beneficial, while weaker scaling concentrates in atypical datasets and the outlier RecBole BPR.
arxiv-2604-07020: Buyukkalayci and four colleagues study set-valued choice rules where score means including the top-p guesses, not only the single best or true guess. The rule suits sensor picking for target tracking, where cheap readings spot sensor nodes likely closest to a target. The authors analyze top-p versus top-1 picking under step-by-step hypothesis testing, propose a shape-aware sensor picking method, and back the approach with real testbed data.
arxiv-2604-07120: Thind and five colleagues assess what on board processing adds to Earth watching services under the Italian IRIDE programme. Current services like Copernicus lean on ground processing, which is slowed by downlink waits and bandwidth caps and cannot rank views on its own. IRIDE joins many sensing tools in one service frame, and its Hawk for Earth Observation arm makes data products on board, earlier in the chain. The paper uses burnt area mapping as a test case, where on board work gives finer detail and faster response.
arxiv-2604-07220: Abdalla and five colleagues introduce HIVE, a four-stage framework for retrieval where diagrams and charts must be read alongside text. It starts with ordinary retrieval, then uses a language model to spell out visual and logical gaps in the top candidates. A refined query drives a second retrieval pass, followed by model verification and reranking. On the MM-BRIGHT benchmark, HIVE reaches 41.7 on nDCG at 10, beating the best text-only system by 9.5 points and the best multimodal system by 14.1.
arxiv-2604-07320: Petty, Goe, and Linzen test whether language models can translate using only a grammar supplied in context, a formal stand-in for textbooks and dictionaries in low-resource translation. They build synchronous context-free grammars pairing formal languages that mimic natural grammar, morphology, and writing systems, then vary grammar size, sentence length, and language properties. Accuracy falls markedly as grammars grow and sentences lengthen, and mismatches in morphology or script hurt performance further. Error analysis finds models recalling wrong target words, inventing words, or leaving source words untranslated.
arxiv-2604-07620: Buyukdagli applies a unified bulk salt-water theory, treating charge and hard-core interactions on equal footing, to the flat Coulomb liquid with finite ion size. Pair patterns and thermal functions are tested against Monte Carlo results. At mid salt levels, it fits heat flow from weak to mid coupling. Its edge is non-uniform screening from charged hard disks blocking their ionic cloud. At low salt levels, it misses ionic cluster growth, so the low-temperature dielectric phase needs at least the next cumulant order.
arxiv-2604-08120: Fei and 15 colleagues propose Tempo, a query-aware framework that compresses long videos using small vision-language models. Hour-long videos bottleneck multimodal large language models: dense visual streams saturate token budgets and worsen the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon. Sparse sampling or uniform pooling blindly waste fidelity, dropping decisive moments and wasting bandwidth on other backgrounds. Tempo uses a small vision-language model as a local temporal compressor. It casts token reduction as early cross-modal distillation, generating tight, intent-aligned representations in a single forward pass.
arxiv-2604-08420: Rozán, Kuperman, and Bouzat compare non drug epidemic controls in SIR models, asking whether timing should aim at the infection peak or the final outbreak size. They derive formulas for the curve's turning points and size, and map six possible paths under a single control. Controls that cut transmission beat controls that cut contacts for shrinking final size at equal effect on spread. Peak cutting, in every model tried, demands earlier action than size cutting.
arxiv-2604-08520: Avramescu and four colleagues lay quantum foundations for tracking particles through the Glasma. The Glasma is the early phase of a heavy ion collision, and their account keeps gauge invariance explicit. They match classical Wong equations to Heisenberg motion in a non Abelian background field. They derive motion laws for two momenta: kinetic momentum, the measurable quantity, and canonical momentum, its Hamiltonian partner. Kinetic broadening gains contributions from transverse fields even in the eikonal limit, and a transverse Coulomb gauge choice at the start cuts numerical error growth.
arxiv-2604-09120: Jackson and three colleagues study how language models shape collaborative software design, less studied than solo coding. In a lab study, 18 pairs of software professionals used a language model freely to design a campus bicycle parking application. Reliance varied widely, from non-use to treating the model as an information source or producer, and separate instances sometimes drifted in context. Professionals scrutinized model responses, often gaining design insights, though early anchoring sometimes curtailed exploration. The authors draw implications for tools aiding designers while keeping design human-centered.
arxiv-2604-09420: Jensen and colleagues show one-way signals flow in a nanomagnetic metamaterial. Spin ice holds promise for low-power compute, but sending signals through flat systems has been limited. Inspired by one-way transport in nature, the authors develop a framework for one-way influence between nanomagnets. They discover geometries with inherent direction, where domains grow and reverse together under an external field protocol. That combines into one-way domain movement, and that greatly improves memory in reservoir models. Growth direction changes with field strengths, shown in tests.
arxiv-2604-09520: Guo and Tomon prove that typical 0/1-polytopes expand far more strongly than the celebrated Mihail-Vazirani conjecture requires. They sample each vertex of the n-dimensional cube independently with fixed probability p. With high probability, edge-expansion is of order n when p lies between one half and one. When p lies below one half, it is of order n raised to log log n. Both bounds beat the previous best of constant order, due to Ferber, Krivelevich, Sales, and Samotij.
arxiv-2604-09620: Mao and four colleagues name LLM nepotism: judges reward warm feelings toward AI apart from merit. Earlier work stressed group bias, but the team pins down AI-trust leaning in a two-phase test of matched resumes and board votes. Screeners favor equally qualified people who back AI and mark down doubting, people-first ones. These firms grow more AI-trusting, with weaker checks and readier hand-offs, passing flawed plans more easily. Merit-Attitude Factorization, a fix splitting attitude from merit, weakens the bias across tests.
arxiv-2604-09720: Bors and Stańczy study generalized Kolmogorov systems, a class of models, and prove that a heteroclinic trajectory exists within them. Such a path joins two distinct equilibrium states, a structure that shapes long-term motion in such systems. The authors apply the result in two settings. In astrophysics, it bears on models of self-gravitating particles, where mutual pull shapes joint motion. In biology, it bears on predator-prey systems, where populations rise and fall together.
arxiv-2604-09920: Lundqvist and six co-authors test prompt design for vision foundation models detecting cowpea flowers and pods in farm imagery. Four open-vocabulary detectors are tested across synthetic and real field images, with eight prompt axes. Models react divergently: settings helping one architecture can collapse another. Model-specific combined prompts beat a naive species-name baseline, gaining about 36 mean-average-precision points for YOLO World and OWLv2 on synthetic flowers. Prompts built only on synthetic data transfer to real fields, matching or beating real-data prompts for most pairs.
arxiv-2604-10420: Khatibi and six colleagues give ECG reading a causal spine for clearer machine reports. Most heart trace language tools lean on weak signal word links and flat lookups. Their CARE-ECG pipeline turns multi lead traces into timed latent markers, then runs causal graph inference. A checking agent loop ties history, verdict, and reply together with proof steps. Trials show higher verdict accuracy and truer notes, with fewer invented claims.
arxiv-2604-10620: Dlin and Teryaev measure two kinds of flow in heavy-ion collisions without rebuilding the reaction plane. That plane is the reference direction such studies normally need. Their method scans fixed test angles and uses plain count gaps between opposite sides. Tests on simulated gold-gold collisions at 9.2 gigaelectronvolts show that one such gap measure is enough. Checks against the true plane give correlations of 0.956 for elliptic flow and 0.834 for directed flow.
arxiv-2604-10720: Koutcheme, Leinonen, and Hellas train open-weight artificial programming learners from real student process data, avoiding big closed models. Their method turns time-ordered log traces into dialogues: code submissions and assessment feedback, like test results, grades, and error traces, form alternating turns. Training that pairs supervised tuning with preference tuning lines models up with real debugging habits. Tests with Qwen 4B and 8B models on real Python homework show feedback from the environment improves how well models copy student debugging, beating code-only and prompted-model baselines.
arxiv-2604-10920: Liu and five colleagues show soluble surfactants slow coarsening of bicontinuous domains in liquid-liquid separation mainly via induced Marangoni stresses, not merely by surface tension. Using a phase-field model coupled to Navier-Stokes equations, the stresses hinder coalescence, reorganize flow, and shift domain evolution. Suppression peaks at Péclet number 10, rather than at 1 or 100, from refills against gradient retention. Low values refill the interface but smooth gradients; high values preserve heterogeneity but starve it. The result is a transport-controlled regulation mechanism.
arxiv-2604-11020: Kolb and three colleagues study inferring a human partner's belief state from a robot's sightings. The setting is dynamic, three-dimensional, and partly observable. Mental model theory holds that choices, thought, knowledge, and planning draw on an internal world model. Team models add each partner's beliefs and skills, letting teams work fluently without constant direct talk. They infer a partner's level-one situation awareness in human-robot teams moving through a setting. They test in simulation and on a real robot, then show help in a meaning reasoning task.
arxiv-2604-11120: Li and three colleagues show single-method safety evaluation is incomplete for persona language models. Persona imbuing customizes behaviour, but evaluations almost always study prompt personas alone. Prompting and activation steering expose different architecture-linked weaknesses. Testing with a single method can miss a model's failure mode. Across 5,568 conditions on four models from three families, prompt danger rankings hold across architectures. Steering vulnerability diverges sharply and defies prediction from prompt rankings. Llama-3.1-8B is more vulnerable to steering, while Gemma-3-27B and Qwen3.5 face greater prompting risk.
arxiv-2604-11320: Ling and seven colleagues build CLASP, a closed-loop framework for open-vocabulary desktop object grasping by robots. A dual-pathway perception module separates high-level semantic intent from geometric grounding to curb spatial hallucination. An asynchronous evaluator compares states before and after each action and feeds back text diagnostics for error correction. The goal is grasping that survives clutter and odd shapes, not just clean lab scenes. A data engine synthesizes spatial labels and reasoning templates without a human driving the robot. Tests reach an 87.0 percent overall success rate.
arxiv-2604-12020: Garcia-Bellido offers two new models for dark matter and dark energy built on known physics, with no new particles or degrees of freedom. For dark matter, stretching the early ripple spectrum to small scales could enable a black hole case. For dark energy, he would add non-equilibrium heat physics in the growing cosmos, in the form of General Relativistic Entropic Acceleration. Jointly they could unify accounts across gravity-wave, large-scale structure, and background probes.
arxiv-2604-12220: Liu and seven colleagues propose TRACE, a system for later project-wide code edits by mixing neural induction for semantic edits with tool-based deduction for syntactic ones. Tools such as refactoring and linting aids deduce where edits go and what they say, while a learned model decides when to call them. A fine-grained edit representation further boosts neural prediction, pushing scope, accuracy, and efficiency at once.
arxiv-2604-12620: Esa Ollila and two colleagues tackle joint device detection and channel estimation for massive random access. Huge numbers of devices with bursty traffic seek base station links without grants. Their method uses covariance learning. Convex approximation first linearizes the scaled negative log-likelihood. Minimizing it estimates signal powers across devices. Active devices are identified from those power estimates. Bayesian estimation then yields channel estimates. Tests show CL-SCA beats rivals on speed.
arxiv-2604-12720: Mia-Katrin Kvalsund and James Stovold probe attractors in neural cellular automata. Many assume these systems learn attractors, shown by visual similarity to goal states. The team asks what kind of attractors form, whether ordered or chaotic, and how stable they stay. A growing gecko automaton with deterministic updates serves as case study. Lyapunov and Fourier spectra reveal periodic and quasi-periodic behavior. The findings challenge fixed-point attractor beliefs. Large shocks can throw the system into a secondary mode apart from the original attractor.
arxiv-2604-12820: Jagadeesh Rachapudi and four colleagues let users tell a language model what to forget, at inference time. Current unlearning needs provider retraining and curated retain sets, locking users out. RePAIR pairs a watchdog spotting intent, a surgeon planning repairs, and a patient model updating itself. Its core method, STAMP, steers activations toward a refusal space via pseudoinverse updates. A low-rank variant cuts cost sharply and runs on device about three times faster than training-based methods. Tests show near-zero forget scores with utility kept high, beating six baselines.
arxiv-2604-13020: Ramirez, Miguel, and Howard model the interiors of Uranus and Neptune and find both planets less icy than their 'ice giant' label suggests. Their envelopes carry a median rock fraction near 60 percent of the heavy-element component, resembling Pluto and Kuiper belt objects. Deeper down the pair diverges: Neptune's mantle is rock-rich at about 55 percent, while Uranus stays ice-rich near 41 percent.
arxiv-2604-13120: Kumar and four colleagues build AgentForge, a multi-agent framework where every code change must pass sandboxed execution before it spreads further. Planner, Coder, Tester, Debugger, and Critic agents share memory and a mandatory Docker sandbox, turning execution feedback into a stronger training signal than next-token likelihood. AgentForge resolves 40.0 percent of SWE-Bench Lite, beating single-agent baselines by 26 to 28 points, with execution feedback and role split each driving gains alone.
arxiv-2604-13220: Gamero and six colleagues present a method for gauging spurious charge in multi-amplifier sensing charge-coupled devices, a key noise source for faint-object astronomy and exoplanet searches. Clocking the gates produces spurious charge that is hard to measure with current methods, and tuning it trades against full-well limit. Their method uses covariance analysis across the device's output amplifiers, which read the same charge packet at different times. It enables fast precise measurement where conventional approaches struggle.
arxiv-2604-13320: The CMS team develops a method to identify highly boosted dielectrons that merge into a single cluster in the CMS electromagnetic calorimeter. Two multivariate models cover cases where both electron tracks are found and cases where only one is found. Efficiency is measured in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Boosted J-psi decays give about 80 percent efficiency for the two-track model, while photon conversions give about 60 percent for the single-track model, with a dedicated energy correction also developed.
arxiv-2604-13620: Bayrak, Turkel, and Korkmaz build Syn-TurnTurk, a synthetic Turkish dialogue dataset for predicting when a speaker will take a turn. Voice chatbots often interrupt because they rely on simple silence detection, while real speech uses irregular pauses, overlaps, and strategic silences. Dialogues generated with Qwen models mirror those patterns, and trained models reach accuracy near 84 percent with strong ranking scores.
arxiv-2604-13920: Wattjes and colleagues measure how vibration modes interact inside tiny stretched strings. Their multi-tone spectroscopy excites two tones near chosen resonances plus probes at higher modes, and the resulting sidebands reveal specific modal couplings. An inverse reconstruction yields ten pairwise coupling strengths across five modes, matching finite-element calculations and giving a fully experimental model of each device.
arxiv-2604-14020: Wang studies Brelot harmonic spaces in a continuous first-order language. In the finite reduct, Brelot theory plus finite interpolation removes bounded harmonic quantifiers. Point ones stay untouched. Martin's compact version sits inside the local type space, with its boundary as non-principal types. Choquet-simplex structure ties Martin measures to unique Keisler measures. Harnack compactness yields stability, standard bases, and a harmonic center. The tools apply to fine potential theory.
arxiv-2604-14220: Chakraborty and Guha attack a weak spot of standard retrieval: enterprise search that misses hierarchical and linked facts. Their agentic knowledge graphs crawl recursively through files, tracking superseding rules and multi-hop references that flat vector search drops. On the Code of Federal Regulations benchmark, the graph approach answers complex regulatory queries exhaustively and precisely, beating standard vector-based retrieval accuracy by 70 percent.
arxiv-2604-14420: Biswas settles a long-open question about weak approximation in adjoint groups in the negative. Platonov conjectured in 1991 that adjoint groups are rational varieties over arbitrary infinite fields, which would imply it. Merkurjev disproved the rationality half in 1996, leaving that question open until now. Biswas closes that gap, showing it fails for adjoint groups.
arxiv-2604-14720: Exler and seven others tackle the shortage of labeled muscle-fiber data by making it. Their pipeline models single myotubes with polynomial center lines, varying radii, branches, and rounded end caps drawn from real images. Made volumes add true-to-life noise, optical flaws, and CycleGAN domain adaptation. A compact 3D U-Net trained only on this synthetic data scored a mean IPQ of 0.22 on real data. That clearly beat three leading zero-shot segmentation models, showing that physics-guided making can unlock segmentation where labels are scarce.
arxiv-2604-14820: Han and seven colleagues present SWE-TRACE, a framework improving software-engineering agents across data, training, and runs. First, a cascade with stepwise oracle checks distills a 60,000-instance fine-tuning corpus biased toward token-efficient shortest paths. Second, a memory-augmented reinforcement-learning pipeline adds a rubric process reward model, with a rubric agent giving dense feedback on middle steps. Third, the same reward model guides test-time scaling by pruning options step by step. On SWE benchmarks it advances fix rates while sharply cutting token use and run time.
arxiv-2604-14920: Chen and eight others build a dual-axis reward model for full-duplex spoken dialogue models. Current automated measures of interaction quality rely on shallow proxies like timing accuracy, giving weak reward signals for reinforcement learning. Their model rates semantic quality and interaction timing separately, alongside a single overall score, from a detailed taxonomy and annotated data. The dual outputs give precise diagnostic feedback and a solid reward signal for online learning, reaching state-of-the-art interaction-quality assessment across synthetic and real-world datasets.
arxiv-2604-15020: Chan applies SHAPR, a solo human-centred AI practice, to building a share trading system. Rapid AI-assisted development can weaken continuity, traceability, and clarity, which SHAPR structures through interaction and documentation. Across cycles, the project built evidence from source-of-truth documents, contracts, quick captures, and evolving code. Five lessons emerged: contracts stabilized coding, a source-of-truth layer improved coherence, cycle snapshots strengthened continuity, code and documentation co-evolved, and environment setup generated knowledge. The case shows documentation with quick capture keeps knowledge organized and usable.
arxiv-2604-15120: Tian, Tsuji, and Manske add quantum fluctuations to the Higgs mode picture for s-wave superconductors. Even one-loop corrections push the mode frequency below the superconducting gap, so it appears as an undamped pole beneath the quasiparticle continuum. That shift yields far sharper fingerprints in third-harmonic generation and Raman scattering signals. Gaps read by different lab techniques may thus disagree, since even faint fluctuations move the pole.
arxiv-2604-15320: Molina León and three colleagues ask how to test people's skill at using data charts hands-on, not just reading still ones. Today's literacy tests such as VLAT use only still images, so hands-on exploring goes untested. In this position paper they survey related tests and ideas, then weigh ways to judge the skills people use when they explore charts by hand.
arxiv-2604-15520: Vlasovets and five colleagues add two plugins to QIIME 2 for microbial count data, which is sparse, compositional, and high-dimensional. The q2-classo plugin runs penalized regression and classification from microbiome predictors, while q2-gglasso estimates taxon-taxon networks, including latent-factor models. A demo on Atacama soil data shows robust model choice, sorting, and network building with covariates and latent factors.
arxiv-2604-15720: Dai, Fang, Fujita, and He study a twice Wick-turned spinning BTZ black hole and its tangle entropy. They work out its shift matrix, which takes its usual shape at an unreal chemical push. On the gravity side, the turned hole matches a spinning BTZ hole after a coordinate shift and a cycle match. Shape entropy and time-like tangle entropy come from that match, and a new Lorentzian growth rate tracks the straight-line rise of time-like tangle entropy.
arxiv-2604-15820: Budde and two colleagues trace a fresh gauge-like rule that lives only in some shards of the split S=1 dipole-keeping spin chain. The chain's own one-way gauge-like rules can tag a vast count of its shards, though most shards lack shift-evenness. Running that chain, which itself lacks gauge freedom, still yields a true quantum run of a gauge theory.
arxiv-2604-15920: Szalay and Holweck present two general methods for building quantum circuits that directly measure local unitary invariants on quantum computers. They work out the methods in detail for important three-qubit invariants. They also demonstrate them in live runs on the IBM Quantum Platform for important entanglement measures of three qubits.
arxiv-2604-16220: Zhang, Betti, Klemmer, Rolf, and Alvarez-Melis propose GeoSpOT, a way to measure how far apart geographic domains sit, using optimal transport. Models often train in one region and deploy in another, yet no principled test says when that move will work. Their distances predict how hard cross-region transfer will be. They also show location-encoder embeddings rival image and text embeddings, despite using location alone.
arxiv-2604-16320: Spiess, Devanbu, and Barr test how robustly large language models grasp code execution semantics, using program-output prediction. Open-source reasoning models hold fairly steady under code changes and input perturbations, with accuracies from 38 percent to 67 percent. The frontier model GPT-5.2, near-perfect at 99 percent on the original CRUXEval benchmark, drops by 20 to 24 percent on perturbed inputs. Models also fare much worse on perturbed inputs that raise exceptions, and results depend on the exception type.
arxiv-2604-16620: Fazla and colleagues study gradient descent for rough minimization when variance is unbounded. Classical analysis assumes bounded variance, which fails in neural training and optimization. The BG condition lets variance grow with squared distance and is the weakest known. They prove stationary points need inverse sixth- and fourth-power queries for smooth and mean-square smooth functions. Those limits worsen bounds, which need inverse fourth- and third-power queries. PASTA couples anchoring with Tikhonov regularization to tame extra variance. PASTA achieves optimal complexity across many non-convex regimes.
arxiv-2604-16820: Meng, Batista and Li urge an integrated path to modern quantum magnetism, against a pride and bias mindset. Quantum magnets show exotic phase shifts, spin liquids and unconventional magnet states, and the field has grown fast. Sims, analytical methods and sample experiments each tend to claim the field's primary driver role. Experts often treat the other two pillars as mere backup tools for checking top ideas, not for shaping the story. The joined mindset has already moved understanding of several key magnet models and their sample realizations.
arxiv-2604-17020: Lee and four colleagues build a tool for making harmful content to stress-test detection systems, since fixed benchmarks scale poorly and may be contaminated by web-scale pretraining. Dual personas, blending backgrounds and interests with harmful strategies, drive diverse simulated interactions. Human and model judges confirm high harmful-generation success, and the synthetic cases prove harder to detect than existing benchmark items, with diversity matching human-curated sets.
arxiv-2604-17120: Couey revises his earlier verdict on Sloan's gömböc parameterization in this amendment of record. An analytical check built on the Varkonyi-Gauss identity shows Sloan's shape does yield mono-monostatic bodies in a strictly convex sub-regime, where it certifies an equilibrium count score of one. At Sloan's published beta of 0.05, strict convexity fails and its precondition breaks, while only one of thirteen earlier catalog instances survives identity-based verification.
arxiv-2604-17420: Chen and colleagues build TransXion, a realistic benchmark for anti-money-laundering work on transaction graphs. Older sets give little beyond anonymized IDs and inject fake anomalies from templates, flattering detectors with static patterns. TransXion instead mimics normal activity from lasting entity profiles and builds illicit subgraphs at random, yielding about 3 million transactions among 50,000 entities with rich attributes. Detectors score far lower on it than on older benchmarks, making it a sterner, more faithful testbed for context-aware detection.
arxiv-2604-17520: Dhochak constructs infinite families of maxfaces, maximal surfaces in spacetime geometry, carrying infinitely many planar ends and infinitely many swallowtail singularities. One period-2 family gives every odd-layer neck exactly four swallowtails while even-layer necks stay almost conical, with a genus-1 Wei-type piece at the base case. A period-3 family puts four swallowtails on every neck, 24 per period, and a second period-2 family keeps every neck almost conical. All the surfaces are embedded in a wider sense.
arxiv-2604-17620: Majhi, Agnihotri, and Mondal test a quiz app for training Anganwadi Workers, India's frontline child-development workers, under the four-decade-old Integrated Child Development Scheme. With over 1.4 million workers and over 600,000 smartphone-equipped by 2020, classroom training struggles to keep skills current. The team built an Android quiz app from worker training modules and needs assessments, then compared it with classroom instruction among a group of workers. The study weighs whether the app can stand in as an adequate substitute for classroom teaching.
arxiv-2604-18120: Liu, Pressel, Schult, Meier, Xu, and Roscoe propose Proxics, a programming model for far-memory accelerators. These chips sit near large memory pools to cut traffic back to the main processor. The model borrows familiar operating-system ideas such as virtual processors and pipe-like channels. They implement those abstractions cheaply through compilation and interconnect tricks. Tests on real hardware show that fast CPU-to-accelerator links matter as much as the computing itself.
arxiv-2604-18820: Zhang and three colleagues propose a method for sparse network inference under imperfect detection. Old models focus on interaction recovery, while similarity graphs are less studied. The method uses low rank factorization with detection estimated from data. It keeps estimated values sparse with better relative scale, and an ADMM algorithm solves the problem. Tests on synthetic and real data show better recovery.
arxiv-2604-19320: Seo attacks the sampling bottleneck in quantum neural networks, where probabilistic measurement forces many circuit runs to estimate an output well. Conventional Monte Carlo inference carries sampling error that shrinks slowly with run count, making near-term hardware use costly. His single-shot framework embeds a trained network as a state-preparation oracle inside quantum amplitude estimation. Outputs are then read through coherent interference rather than repeated sampling, reaching faster error scaling even in one shot.
arxiv-2604-19520: Chen and colleagues propose SimDiff, a depth pruning criterion for large language models. Depth pruning removes redundant layers to improve deployment efficiency. The standard approach measures layer similarity with cosine distance. That one-dimensional heuristic can fail unpredictably and even collapse across architectures. SimDiff judges layers by both representational similarity and transformation difference, using the MSSD and MASD metrics. The two metrics jointly beat either view on its own.
arxiv-2604-19620: Aeschbach and colleagues present free-association norms for 5,877 German cue words, part of the German Small World of Words project. Such norms give key observed data for studying language, meaning, and cultural phenomena in the mind sciences. Large-scale norms exist for English, Dutch, Spanish, and Mandarin Chinese, but no similar resource existed for German. The paper covers how data were gathered, who took part, and a thorough cleaning pipeline before launching the SWOW-DE dataset.
arxiv-2604-19920: Easson and Manton show that trapped black hole interiors give a precise local home for time-dependent classical double copy, a bridge between gravity and gauge theory. Kantowski-Sachs cosmologies admit a construction where the Kerr-Schild scalar and its single-copy partner follow from the metric alone. The rebuilt field appears as a standard Kerr-Schild field and as a Maxwell field for a uniform, time-varying electric field. For Schwarzschild the field diverges inside, while for the regular Bardeen solution it stays finite into the core.
arxiv-2604-20220: Fosgerau and Sørensen build a broad convex duality frame for perturbed utility route choice, where travelers pick routes under utility maximization. They show the traveler's constrained, possibly jagged utility problem has a dual form: a free concave maximization with a smooth goal. The one best flow comes back link by link from any dual answer through convex conjugates of link perturbation functions. That frame backs fast gradient-based optimization on big networks, quick sensitivity checks, and a neat parallel with current flow in electric circuits.
arxiv-2604-20320: Oksanen and Sarkkinen show two smooth globally hyperbolic Lorentzian metrics, though not isometric, can share one hyperbolic boundary map. Both metrics live on an endless tube with a time-like edge, yet the shared edge map cannot tell them apart. The pair breaks the Lorentzian Calderón problem, proving edge data alone need not fix the metric inside. No single metric follows from the edge data here, even with smooth globally hyperbolic shape in place.
arxiv-2604-20720: Flynn offers COMPASS, a data framework for tuning large language models to languages. COMPASS uses lean fine-tuning by training lightweight, language modules on a picked subset of multilingual data. By favoring extra data from under-seen clusters, COMPASS lifts cross-lingual transfer while cutting clash. He extends this into an ongoing framework, COMPASS-ECDA, which watches for data shifts and updates adapters to prevent model decay. Across three model architectures and multiple multilingual benchmarks, including long-context tasks, COMPASS always beats standard methods guided by language similarity.
arxiv-2604-20820: In multiplicative lattices, Sarode, Patil, and Joshi ask when prime elements must exist, and answer through a tool they call the S-Prime Element Principle. Their setting is a V-lattice L together with S, a multiplicatively closed subset of L, inside which they define S-prime elements. Applied in the special case where S equals the singleton set containing 1, the principle gives a direct and uniform route to existence results for prime elements.
arxiv-2604-21120: Aryan Chaudhary, Prateek Agarwal, and Tejasvi Alladi explain language-model decisions on tables by measuring how each field shifts the full spread of predicted classes. TabSHAP masks whole key-value fields rather than word fragments and compares distributions with a divergence measure, isolating the fields that truly drive a call. On income and heart-disease tests it proves more faithful than random picks and tree-based proxies.
arxiv-2604-21420: Jinhee Jang and four colleagues tackle gender bias in translation quality scoring, where models favor masculine forms in unclear contexts and may even prefer gender-misaligned translations when gender is explicit. Their FairQE system detects gender cues, generates gender-flipped variants, and blends usual quality scores with language-model bias-mitigating reasoning through dynamic bias-aware mixing. The plug-and-play design preserves existing models' strengths while calibrating gender bias. Across bias test settings it steadily improves fairness without giving up general quality-scoring performance.
arxiv-2604-21620: Mengran Li and Daniela Castro-Camilo use tail asymmetry to find causal direction among extremes, where a forward guess from cause to effect beats the reverse guess time after time. Their two-stage system for structure learning, S3ME, first finds a thin candidate web of links while allowing for hidden shared shocks. It then points each link by cutting tail guess risk with max-linear envelope models. Tests and uses on river webs and financial tail-risk webs show tough, clear spread patterns with no preset graph.
arxiv-2604-21820: Yegovtsev, Choudhury, and Liu introduce the chiral Dicke model. Here an atomic ensemble couples to a two-mode cavity through chiral interactions. Unlike the standard Dicke model, it carries a continuous U(1) symmetry tied to angular momentum conservation. Its phase map contains a broad U(1)-broken superradiant phase with highly tunable fluctuation patterns. Distinct universality classes govern the same normal-to-superradiant transition along different paths. The authors call this pattern multiversality.
arxiv-2604-21920: Pauli, Parsons, and Prinja first measure wind line formation regions in an early O-type star, AzV 75 in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Massive stars shape surroundings through ionising radiation and winds, yet line formation regions had never been measured. Using TESS and ASAS-SN photometry and HST spectra, they track carbon IV and nitrogen V lines. The primary's thick wind eclipses the secondary, and formation regions extend up to 316 solar radii. A comparison with 1D models favours a beta-law exponent of 0.5 over four-fifths.
arxiv-2604-22420: Ryborz proves that any metric measure spacetime from a smooth manifold with a continuous Lorentzian metric is infinitesimally Minkowskian, if the manifold is causally simple. That metric splits spacetime into time and space directions, with light cones at each point. A spacetime is simple in causal terms when it has no flaws such as closed timelike curves. Infinitesimally Minkowskian means that, at small scales, it looks like flat model spacetime. The result extends small-scale flatness to spacetimes with a merely continuous metric.
arxiv-2604-22720: Dijkstra, Zverovich, and Gagarin analyze greedy algorithms for domination problems in graphs, where a chosen set must reach every vertex. They give a short self-contained proof of the classical approximation ratio, then repair a gap in the existing proof for k-tuple domination, showing the same ratio holds there too. Finally they improve the known ratio for k-domination.
arxiv-2604-23220: Allu and Kumar bound the third Hankel determinant for inverse coefficients of starlike univalent functions in the unit disk. Working with normalised analytic functions that fix zero and have unit derivative at zero, they use the Bernstein polynomial method to reach the needed maximum estimate. The bound they establish is sharp, meaning no tighter universal bound holds for this class. The work gives a precise extremal estimate for inverse coefficients of starlike functions, a classical object in geometric function theory.
arxiv-2604-23720: Tran, Nguyen, Guérand, Vo, and Nguyen introduce quasi-equivariance for metanetworks. Metanetworks are neural systems that work directly on pretrained weights. Strict equivariance respects built-in symmetries but yields rigid, sparse, less expressive models. Distinct weights can encode the same function, so strict rules waste power. Quasi-equivariance loosens those rules while keeping the same function. Tests on varied nets show a good trade-off between symmetry and power.
arxiv-2604-23920: Andrade, Nardulli, and Ponciano survey multiplicity for Allen-Cahn systems in the singular regime, stressing their geometric reading through Gamma-convergence. In the scalar case the functional tends to edge length, giving minimal curvature hypersurfaces, while vectorial systems lead to multi-phase clusters. The main tool is the photography method, which uses local trial answers and barycenter maps to encode manifold shape into counts. The survey contrasts closed manifolds with bounded ones, noting Neumann-Dirichlet effects, and flags the missing classification of vectorial clusters as a hard challenge.
arxiv-2604-24120: Feng, Hu, and Li offer a new convex programming relaxation for weighted Nash social welfare. Unlike the exponential-size configuration program of prior work, theirs compresses to a compact polynomial-size linear program with only a small additive loss, so standard solvers suffice without ellipsoid methods or separation oracles. It matches the best known approximation of about 1.445, and in the unweighted case it equals the Cole-Gkatzelis Fisher market program, proving its integrality gap exactly. The technique also extends to two scheduling problems, recovering best-known ratios with simpler proofs.
arxiv-2604-24520: Kumar and five colleagues show that a tiny surfactant dose can tame bubble size in a fiercely turbulent pipe flow without changing the turbulence itself. Without additives, bubbles merge downstream and grow steadily, driven by how fast turbulent energy dissipates. A minute cut in surface tension boosts breakup, curbs merging, and narrows the size spread, giving plant operators a simple dial for bubble size and gas-liquid mixing.
arxiv-2604-24620: Sousa, Campos and Jorge revisit temporal relation classification. The task is to decide how pairs of time entities in text relate to each other. Recent datasets made the task simpler, using only event pairs and a subset of relations. Their Interval from Point approach first classifies relations between interval endpoints. It then decodes those point relations into a full interval relation. On the TempEval-3 benchmark it reaches 70.1 percent on temporal awareness, a new best result.
arxiv-2604-24720: Manurung, Al-Kahfi, Rizqi and Manullang tackle sentiment and emotion classification of Indonesian e-commerce reviews, where slang, regional loanwords, numeric shorthand and emoji defeat lexicon tools. Their two-track pipeline uses the PRDECT-ID dataset. It holds 5,400 reviews across 29 categories, labeled for sentiment and five emotions. One track combines TF-IDF with an AutoML sweep. The other uses a bidirectional LSTM with two output heads. A preprocessing module applies 14 cleaning steps, among them a slang dictionary of 140 entries. Both tracks deploy as Gradio apps.
arxiv-2604-25020: Hirst extends PINN architectures to more general geometry, for a workshop on string geometry. Neural architectures trained with equation-based losses drive PINN models. Since many geometry constructions minimize a functional, these functionals can serve as loss functions. That aligns the AI loss goal with solving the geometric problem. The paper presents the core rules of the PINN architecture and their fit for differential geometry. It shows their use through summaries of three works at this area.
arxiv-2604-25120: Suparno Roy Chowdhury and seven colleagues study reasoning over clinical trial tables. Answers often hide in hidden traits such as therapy type, added agents, endpoint roles and follow-up status, not in visible cells. Their SCoPE framework uses several language-model planners to split the work into row selection, structured planning and execution. Source fields and reasoning rules are stated before answering. On 1,500 hybrid reasoning questions over oncology tables, explicit planning raised accuracy and beat heavier agentic baselines for the effort spent.
arxiv-2604-25220: Mahbub and six colleagues introduce DATAREEL, a benchmark for data-driven video story generation with 328 real-world data reels. Given a table, an intent, a duration and a style image, a model must generate animation code with synchronized subtitles. Tests of eight models reveal a large gap: open-weight models fail to execute up to 39.8 percent of the time, while proprietary models do better. Even the best models often produce static charts, desynchronized subtitles and unstable layouts. An agentic baseline splitting generation into planning, coding and verification beats direct prompting.
arxiv-2604-25320: Kraus, Moucha and Roth look at forward runs of Blaschke products, a set-up that widens the run of one map in a plain way. Such runs come up in complex dynamics, for one in the study of stray domains and in bids to widen the Denjoy-Wolff result. They show that two key kinds, the indestructible and the maximal Blaschke products, stay in their kind under forward runs.
arxiv-2604-25820: Jia, Ma, and Tian study which symmetries of a quantum field theory with continuous global symmetry can be gauged. They work with Lagrangian algebra data inside the Drinfeld center belonging to the theory's symmetry category. BF theory plus level-k Chern-Simons theory serves as their semiclassical model for the symmetry topological field theory. Given two explicit assumptions about that model and its modular kernels, they derive candidate S- and T-kernels via Hopf-link and framing correlator data. Those kernels give candidate modular invariants and gaugings, recovering known cases.
arxiv-2604-26120: Choi and four colleagues propose a hierarchical method for turning noisy, mixed-intent logs into several evidence-grounded profiles. Actions are first grouped into intent notes, then sorted and tagged as multiple profiles. The method scores them on tightness, evidence fit, and truth. Training uses a groupwise form of direct preference optimization. Tests on a large service log plus two public sets yield more coherent, trustworthy profiles. They also improve guesses about later interactions.
arxiv-2604-26320: Nagy and Pach propose a new conjecture on two group ring identities, and show that settling it would settle the Alon-Jaeger-Tarsi conjecture. A group ring identity is an equation inside an algebraic structure built from a group, and the Alon-Jaeger-Tarsi conjecture is a long-standing claim in combinatorics. The note links the two claims, so proving the new conjecture would settle the older one.
arxiv-2604-26420: Wang and Peypouquet analyzed how fast an accelerated backward-forward method converges for convex composite optimization. The method, due to Taylor, Hendrickx, and Glineur, differs from FISTA in where it places the proximal operator. With a convex smooth part, function values converge at a fast one-over-k-squared rate and iterates converge weakly. With a strongly convex smooth part, a variant achieves accelerated linear convergence.
arxiv-2604-26520: Grolleau and three colleagues formalized single-view aerial-ground re-identification, where a model trained on one real viewpoint must retrieve people or objects from an unseen viewpoint. Their 3D-LENS framework builds geometrically consistent new views from large-scale 3D mesh reconstruction, paired with representation learning that curbs synthetic-to-real bias. Unlike flat generative baselines or class-specific 3D templates, it stays view-consistent across diverse categories, including carried objects. Tests reached state-of-the-art results on single-view scenarios.
arxiv-2604-26820: Hong and four colleagues propose Bridge, a method that helps object detectors work in new settings despite shifts in lighting, style, and surroundings. It learns low-rank bases, compact mathematical summaries, for front-door adjustment, a causal technique that blocks misleading cues from the training domain while trimming redundant detail. Bridge plugs into both discriminative and generative vision foundation models, large pretrained vision systems. Across camera, weather, artistic, and drone benchmarks it beats previous leading methods.
arxiv-2604-27220: Baroncha, Perepukhov, and Fine map spin decay in NMR for two adjacent non-equivalent spin-1/2 nuclei, hydrogen-1 and carbon-13, in a liquid molecule. Their study reads eight decay rates for the pair at once. Such a set acts as a fingerprint of complex molecules under several decay routes. Some rates come from standard inversion recovery and Overhauser tests. Others come from decay started by maximally entangled pseudo-pure Bell states of the pair.
arxiv-2604-27320: Bhatia and three colleagues extend the universal rotation curve for spiral galaxies twice as far out as before, using hydrogen observations from the SPARC sample. Where earlier curves stopped at the visible edge, theirs reach double that radius, and the rescaled curves still fall onto one shared profile. That persistence strengthens the idea that one curve describes spiral galaxies. It also sharpens limits on how ordinary matter and dark matter set rotation speeds in the dark-matter-dominated outskirts.
arxiv-2604-27420: Trilling and seven colleagues describe how the public can access data and products from the Solar System Notification Alert Processing System, known as SNAPS. SNAPS works as a broker, taking in ZTF and LSST moving-object data and handing back properties. The document explains how users can interact with its databases and infrastructure. It is a living document, version 1.0, that will be updated on arXiv when significant improvements are made to its access schemes. It aims to always carry the latest information about interacting with its databases and infrastructure.
arxiv-2604-27720: Chen and seven colleagues benchmark vision-language models on medical question answering and visual grounding. No off-the-shelf system localizes medical targets well, scoring barely above a trivial center-box baseline, with accuracy below 20 percent at threshold. Cropping to a bounding box degrades answers even with a flawless box, cutting accuracy by up to 18 points versus the full image. Fine-tuning on answers alone destroys box-evidence emission, while mixing in a little grounding supervision brings localization back to 0.36 IoU while preserving answer accuracy.
arxiv-2604-27820: Dubey and Open Gigantic launch OBJECTGRAPH, turning documents into typed knowledge graphs to traverse rather than injected text. OBJECTGRAPH extends Markdown, open to humans and agents. They define the Document Problem and prove OBJECTGRAPH meets six traits no other format meets at once. They add gradual reveal, Role-Scoped Access, and live checks. Across five doc classes and eight task types, tests show up to 95.3 percent token cut with no scores loss. Transpiler output keeps about 99 percent preserved.
arxiv-2604-27920: Wisniewski and Czudy test whether small language models keep fine-grained feelings intact when translating, a nuance that meaning-first translation often drops. They run EuroLLM, Aya Expanse, and Gemma through back-translation on Reddit comments from the GoEmotions set, spanning 28 feeling kinds. The tests cover five European tongues — German, French, Spanish, Italian, and Polish — and ask how much feeling each model holds on its own. They also ask whether feeling-aware prompts lift that hold, and whether ModernBERT beats BERT at tagging feelings for translation checks.
arxiv-2604-28020: Mohri and colleagues study learning where sampling different parts of an objective costs different amounts, aiming to hit a target error as cheaply as possible. Their Cost-Aware SGD samples components by gradient size and cost, with bounds showing real savings over baselines plus a matching lower bound. Applied to language-model reinforcement learning, where longer sequences cost more, it cuts tokens used while matching or beating baseline accuracy.
arxiv-2605-00120:
Himanshu Singhal and Suresh Sundaram present GAFSV-Net, a vision framework for verifying online signatures. The task is to tell skilled forgeries from genuine samples despite high variation within one person's signing and very few enrollment samples. Earlier deep methods work on raw time sequences, which locks them into sequence-only designs and shuts out pretrained image vision models.

GAFSV-Net turns each signature into a six-channel image built from Gramian angular fields. Three kinematic channels, pen speed, pressure change, and direction angle, are each encoded in two paired ways, capturing time co-occurrence and direction changes. A dual-branch encoder processes the two encodings with cross-attention between them before a metric projection. Trained with a triplet loss and hard forgery negatives, it beats sequence-based baselines on two standard databases under the same objectives.
arxiv-2605-00620:
Shiqiang Cai and 4 co-authors build taxonomies for science, the layered maps of a research field, with large language models, keeping the levels honest in meaning. A good taxonomy speeds literature search and feeds trend tracking. Older generators, though, make structures whose levels drift in meaning, with headings that match neither parents nor siblings.

A study of real outputs blames weak tracking of whether levels mean the same thing. Their system, SC-Taxo, builds headings in both directions. It pulls general terms up from the leaves while pinning terms down from the roots, and models links among same-level headings to keep siblings in line. Cleanup stages that respect the levels then polish the result. On several test sets the method improved both how well levels line up and heading quality. Tests on Chinese science papers showed the approach carries across languages.
arxiv-2605-00820:
Jinpai Zhao and five co-authors introduce HyCOP, a modular framework that learns solution operators for a family of partial differential equations. Instead of learning one large monolithic map, HyCOP composes simple modules for advection, diffusion, learned closures, and boundary handling. A policy chooses which module to apply and for how long, based on regime features and state statistics, forming short readable programs.

Modules can be classic solvers or learned parts, so stand-ins can be judged at any time without step-by-step rollout. Across varied benchmarks, HyCOP improves out-of-sample results by an order of magnitude over single-block operators and allows transfer by changing the module list. Theory separates composition error from module error as a check.
arxiv-2605-01520:
Yin Zhang and seven co-authors fix two leaks in how vision-language models are trained with reward checks on final answers. Much of the sampling budget is burned on runs doomed early by a misread image, and a bare right-or-wrong reward cannot tell a seeing failure from a thinking failure.

Their framework, MIRL, uses mutual information between the model's own image description and the image as a cheap early screen. Promising starts get forked and funded, while poor ones are cut before they eat the budget. Training then runs in two decoupled tracks, with a sight-based reward for perception and an answer reward for reasoning, so each skill is graded on its own. On six vision-language reasoning benchmarks the method averages just over seventy percent, and it beats sixteen full sampled runs while completing only ten, a quarter fewer full trajectories.
arxiv-2605-01620:
Evan Camilleri, André Xuereb, Tony J G Apollaro, and Mirko Consiglio tune the knobs of quantum optimization. They target problems where costs bind three or more parties at once. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm needs its angles set well, and schemes range from one shared angle, cheap but blunt, to one angle per term, sharp but costly to tune.

Their scheme groups angles by interaction order, giving each size of cost term its own angle: a middle path built for hypergraph problems such as satisfiability and multi-party resource allocation. A second thread measures non-stabilizerness, the magic resource that separates quantum from classically simulable behavior, across these schemes. On two hypergraph families, the grouped scheme matches the per-term scheme's solution quality while using far fewer function evaluations. That cuts the quantum time a tuning run consumes.
arxiv-2605-01920:
Noga Peleg Pelc, Gal Kaminka, and Yoav Goldberg note that language model agents are built from many calls, each with its own mix of instructions, observations, and past turns. How that context is built shapes how well the whole system works. Yet there is no standard way to state what a context holds or how it changes over time.

They propose ACDL, a language for describing agent contexts in a precise and readable form, with diagrams to match. It can state role order, dynamic content, time-linked references, and conditional or repeated parts. The authors show the language on several known systems and variants, and they offer tools and examples for wider use.
arxiv-2605-02020:
Shammi Malhotra proves results on how many positive solutions a hard Grushin problem can have. The equation uses a Grushin operator, which fades along part of its domain. It pairs two rival terms. One is a power term with a positive factor. The other is a singular term that blows up as the solution nears zero.

The solution must vanish on the edge of a smooth bounded domain. Analysis turns on the power value. It can sit below, at, or above a critical value tied to the operator. Malhotra sorts when positive solutions exist in each case. The paper also sorts when more than one solution can be found.
arxiv-2605-02620:
Andreas Maier, Moritz Zaiss, and Siming Bayer report a three-hour agentic research run that redoes and extends a study of AI text style. The original study asked people to edit model drafts into their own style and measured the match. With released data and a modern research harness, and a human acting only as reviewer, the team repeats every experiment and adds three new ones.

All preregistered hypotheses were reproduced, including the headline correlation, recovered to three decimal places. On held-out tasks, two frontier models closed most of the style gap to the same-author ceiling, far more than human editing did. Reframed as detection, the same data feed an arms race analysis. A simple classifier separates authors well. Diagnostics show one model's detectability is mostly a length effect. Another model's is a genuine style signature.
arxiv-2605-02920:
Gavin Money and three co-authors test whether fast, Hebbian-style learning modules help vision transformers recognize handwritten characters from very few examples. Standard transformers learn fixed slow weights in training and cannot adapt inside a single test episode. Brains solve this with fast synaptic changes that form short-lived associative memories during activity itself, a trait the modules imitate.

Six variants are compared: three standard backbones and the same three with fast-weight modules added, under a prototypical meta-learning setup on a character benchmark. Placing one module after all stages of the backbone avoided training instability. The design used one module in total, rather than one per stage. It gave the best test scores for both one-shot and five-shot tasks, edging its plain counterpart. Placement, the title's point, decided the gain.
arxiv-2605-03020:
Sascha Gehrmann and Fabian H. L. Essler construct exact scar states in quantum many-body systems whose Hamiltonians are not frustration-free. Quantum scars are rare eigenstates that sit inside a chaotic spectrum without thermalizing, and exact examples are prized test cases. Most known constructions rely on special structure that the systems here deliberately lack, which is what makes a general construction valuable.

Their states take matrix product form, built from a local error cancellation idea. The trick is adapted from a classic method for the steady state of an exclusion process, where local terms cancel in pairs. Explicit examples are worked out in both one and two spatial dimensions, showing the ansatz is not a one-dimensional accident. Exact scars in generic-looking systems widen the search for non-thermal behavior.
arxiv-2605-03220:
Onyx Gautam determines the leading late-time behavior of linear waves on radially symmetric stationary spacetimes with two space dimensions. How waves decay at very late times shapes scattering theory and stability questions, and the two-dimensional case needs its own energy methods.

Gautam shows the leading term matches the flat-space profile built from double null coordinates, with the stated inverse square-root falloff in each. The proof adapts physical-space techniques from work on waves with an inverse-square potential around Schwarzschild, extending weighted energy estimates of Dafermos and Rodnianski to two space dimensions. The result anchors late-time asymptotics for this class.
arxiv-2605-03420:
Khalid Zaman, Qixuan Huang, Muhammad Uzair, and Masashi Unoki describe a challenge entry for detecting deepfakes separately in speech and in background sound. In the CompSpoofV2 data, either component can be faked alone, so a single real-or-fake verdict is not enough.

Their dual-branch system pairs a speech model with an environmental sound model, then exchanges information through cross-attention and a matching head that compares the two representations. A final classifier outputs verdicts for the whole clip, the speech, and the environment. On the test set it beat the baseline, with solid F1 and environmental error scores.
arxiv-2605-03620:
Raphaël Le Bidan, Ahmad Ismail, Elsa Dupraz, and Charbel Abdel Nour improve syndrome-based neural decoding, a deep learning method for correcting errors in short, high-rate codes. Their idea is to exploit code automorphisms, symmetries of the code that permute its positions without changing its structure. Those symmetries can multiply the training data for free.

Applying automorphism-based augmentation during both training and inference lets their models approach maximum-likelihood decoding performance on the codes studied, using small datasets and proper training. The authors also argue that many earlier results understated what these neural decoders can do, because the models were undertrained. Code to reproduce all results is publicly available.
arxiv-2605-03720:
Zhou and five colleagues turn multi-turn database questions into SQL without retraining a model. Text-to-SQL translates plain-language questions into database queries, but real users ask follow-ups that refine earlier questions, so each new question depends on conversation history. Existing routes lean on unstable API calls or costly fine-tuning. Rose-SQL is training-free: it uses small reasoning models with in-context examples, plus a Role-State representation that acts as a structural blueprint between linking the database schema and writing the query.

Tracking how Role-State evolves through the dialogue, checked by structural isomorphism, guides the model toward the right query composition for each turn. On the SParC and CoSQL benchmarks, Rose-SQL beat in-context baselines at the four-billion-parameter scale and clearly surpassed fine-tuned rivals at eight and fourteen billion parameters. Gains held across other reasoning backbones too.
arxiv-2605-04020:
Dong-Lin Wang and Shi Pu study how nonlinear hydrodynamic interactions change the late-time relaxation of fluctuations. Instead of exponential decay, the decay becomes a power law. Schwinger-Keldysh effective field theory is the standard framework for such effects. It encodes that behavior in loop corrections. Extracting that behavior requires finding the singularities of loop integrals. Their structure grows complex beyond simple models.

The authors apply Landau singularity analysis to two-point functions in effective field theories. They determine the singularities these interactions induce, without performing the loop integrations. From those frequency-space singularities they extract the relaxation modes. Those modes control late-time behavior. When gapless modes are present, they produce power-law decay. The result is a singularity-based description. It covers a broad class of such theories.
arxiv-2605-04320:
Toufique Ahmed and three co-authors address a missing piece of software engineering for Java: automatically writing a test that reproduces a reported bug. Such a test confirms the bug before a fix and its absence after, but issues rarely come with one.

They build the first benchmark for this task in Java, with two hundred fifty cases from popular open projects, and adapt a leading Python generator to work on Java repositories. They also test the system on a private, uncontaminated industry data set. The work extends a thriving line of Python research to a language central to enterprise software.
arxiv-2605-05020:
Shawn Ray makes a diversity measure for multi-agent reinforcement learning cheaper to compute by replacing a complete comparison graph with a sparser one. The standard measure averages distances between every pair of agents, so its cost grows quadratically with team size. Graph-SND instead averages over the edges of any chosen graph, weighted as set.

Using the full graph recovers the original measure exactly, while a fixed sparse graph gives a local version at edge-count cost. Random edge samples give unbiased estimates with stated concentration bounds, and Ray proves distortion results for expander graphs. In large team training runs, sampled Graph-SND tracked the full measure at about a tenth of the time.
arxiv-2605-05120:
Sahar Askari and four co-authors classify driver behaviour from body signals recorded together, aiming for a system that stays readable to its users. Their dataset synchronises brain activity, muscle activity, and skin response signals from drivers. Rich features from the time and frequency domains, plus derived body indices, feed the classification pipeline.

A SHAP-based selection step keeps the strongest few hundred features, cutting computation while preserving predictive power. Two boosted-tree models are tuned with Bayesian search and combined in a weighted voting ensemble. The ensemble reached accuracy near eighty-one percent and clearly beat single-signal baselines, with checks showing a solid gain over the best single signal source alone.
arxiv-2605-05220:
Tatiana Gaintseva and six co-authors build a formal framework for steering generative models by tuning their middle representations, a popular control method used after launch that lacked firm footing. They first link standard steering to affine concept erasure, proving the usual approach for cutting unwanted behaviour is a special case of a closed-form erasure method called LEACE. That connection grounds steering in known maths.

Next they frame concept switching as a problem with a best affine answer under stated assumptions. Their MidSteer framework then relaxes those starting points, letting it make directed changes with least disturbance to the rest. Across vision diffusion models and large language models, MidSteer did well on a range of tasks and designs.
arxiv-2605-05320:
Sayan Kundu and Hendrik van Eerten simulate gamma-ray burst afterglow jets with internal structure, tracking how the jets spread and how their electrons cool locally. Afterglows are the fading glow after the burst, produced as a narrow relativistic jet ploughs into surrounding material. Their relativistic moving-mesh code follows axisymmetric structured jets and computes emission with a cooling scheme that follows each electron population after shock acceleration.

Jet spreading depends moderately on the initial steepness of the angular structure until the jet widens well beyond its start. Local cooling shifts the synchrotron cooling break upward by more than tenfold compared with global cooling assumptions and smooths its transition. Jet breaks also sharpen with frequency under both cooling treatments.
arxiv-2605-05520:
Phone networks can sense rain: signals between towers weaken as they cross wet air. Badr Moufad and six co-authors use that effect to rebuild rain fields over a region. The catch is that each link measures rain along a whole path, not at a point, and older methods often ignored that geometry.

They frame the rebuild as a Bayesian inverse problem with diffusion models as spatial priors. Those priors preserved rain statistics better than Gaussian process ones. Sampling methods then produced reconstructions that beat established baselines on both synthetic and real data, with no extra training needed.
arxiv-2605-05620:
Pairing gallium oxide with silicon carbide could yield power electronics that shrug off heat, except the interface itself traps heat. Nuohao Liu and nine co-authors build a neural network potential to study that thermal bottleneck. Direct experiments on perfect interfaces are hard, and first-principles simulations are too costly at the needed scales.

Their potential was checked against quantum calculations, phonon data, and conductivity trends for both materials. Simulations then showed how conductance varies with length, temperature, and which crystal face meets the carbide. One orientation conducted notably better, explained by stronger bonding and vibrational coupling across the interface.
arxiv-2605-05720:
Optical traps hold microscopic particles with light, but loading them inside a vacuum chamber is fiddly. Alexey Grinin and ten co-authors demonstrate a compact launcher: a piezoelectric micropipette that fires particles exactly where the trap waits. It integrated easily into three different trapping setups, from a single beam to a standing-wave dual beam.

The team trapped silica spheres from 170 nanometers to three micrometers across. They also caught flat hexagonal prisms and nanodiamonds about a hundred nanometers wide. Localized delivery matters because stray particles contaminate precision experiments, from force sensing to tests of fundamental physics.
arxiv-2605-06320:
Elizabeth Mieczkowski and seven co-authors coordinate teams of language model agents through an adaptive shared task graph. Agent teams today sit at two extremes: fixed roles and pipelines that cannot adapt, or free form groups that waste resources and propagate errors. Their framework, LATTE, borrows from distributed systems, where processors coordinate under partial views and tight communication limits, to steer between those extremes.

In LATTE, agents jointly build and maintain an evolving coordination graph. The graph encodes subtask dependencies, who owns each subtask, and how far each has progressed, keeping the team consistent as work shifts. Agents can reallocate tasks, adapt coordination, and surface new tasks as they appear. Across collaborative tasks and base models, LATTE cut token use, time, and coordination failures like file conflicts, while matching or beating standard team designs on accuracy.
arxiv-2605-06420:
Yukiyasu Kamitani asks whether brains and deep neural networks preserve the same changes between stimuli, not just similar answers to single images. Standard alignment checks compare stimulus answers or overall shape. Drawing on category theory, Kamitani defines rough naturality: changing a stimulus, then translating between brain and model, should match translating first, then changing.

A Naturality Violation Score measures gaps from that match against a shuffled null. Synthetic tests show it catches misses that simpler scores miss. In human brain data, semantic features align toward higher visual areas and deeper network layers, while lower visual features align earlier, showing selective rather than uniform matching.
arxiv-2605-06520:
Ander Artola Velasco, Stratis Tsirtsis, and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez design a trial protocol that shares costs between a product developer and a regulator to raise social utility. High-stakes approvals, such as for new drugs, need large randomized trials whose cost can deter developers from risky moonshot products. In their protocol the developer runs the trial sequentially while the regulator subsidizes part of the cost.

Modeled as a belief decision process, the developer's best strategy comes from dynamic programming. Social utility turns out piecewise linear and convex in the subsidy level, so the best subsidy is also computable efficiently. Simulations on antibiotic development data show gains over standard protocols exceeding a third.
arxiv-2605-06920:
Keegan Harris, Siddharth Prasad, and Asher Trockman assign credit for AI-generated content among the creators whose work appears in the model's context. Fair payment needs a principled split of value. Their approach uses the least core from cooperative game theory. The least core is a distribution chosen to be maximally stable: no subset of creators is badly underpaid relative to what it could earn alone.

Approximating the least core is the computational challenge, and their algorithms use new routines for seeding and separating the defining constraints. On a web retrieval credit assignment task, the methods approximate the least core with about ten times fewer model calls than alternatives. The work gives platforms an incentive-aligned option for compensating context contributors.
arxiv-2605-07020:
Xinyuan Wei and four co-authors present FlashMol, a model that generates three-dimensional molecular shapes in as few as four steps. Older diffusion models need hundreds of steps, which makes screening many candidate drugs impractical. Faster recent methods cut the steps but often produced unstable molecules.

FlashMol adapts a distillation method that teaches a fast model to match a slow, high-quality teacher. Respacing the generation steps gives the student a better starting point, and an added diversity term counters narrow, repetitive output. On standard molecule datasets, FlashMol matches or beats its thousand-step teacher while sampling far faster and keeping molecular quality high.
arxiv-2605-07120:
Wenjie Guan and Jelena Bradic study whether classifiers can ignore symbol names and learn the underlying template instead. Test items may use entirely fresh symbols that training never saw, yet share the same hidden pattern.
