Math at the distribution level says the target can be built by combining the sources geometrically. The authors conjecture that no inference time technique can do this efficiently in certain well motivated settings.

Theory guided arguments and experiments on synthetic and realistic data support the conjecture. Correction methods cut one kind of error, yet score error hits far harder when the target lies outside the training combinations. Small score errors tolerable in distribution become ruinous out of it. The task needs a different approach, not better inference patches.
arxiv-2606-24220:
Nersisyan builds links inside four-dimensional spaces that are split one way yet stay joined smoothly. Mazur manifolds are contractible four-dimensional building blocks. They anchor the study of exotic smooth structures: shapes that look plain yet are smoothly strange. Writing alone in 2026, Nersisyan explores links, sets of surfaces, inside such manifolds and simple ambient spaces.

Non-split two-component links are constructed inside the four-sphere, their components cannot be pulled apart smoothly. Moved into connected sums of complex projective planes, the links become split topologically. Yet they remain non-split smoothly, a gap only dimension four makes possible. Results include exotic pairs of simply connected, definite four-manifolds with boundary, and exotic embeddings of various Mazur manifolds inside the four-sphere. Nersisyan's constructions add concrete, Kirby-calculus-friendly examples to a field where exotic effects are often proved to exist without ever being drawn.
arxiv-2606-24320:
Clark and colleagues at Zyphra present ZONOS2, a text-to-speech model built for naturalness, prosody, and voice cloning fidelity. The 2026 technical report scales its predecessor sharply. An eight-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone keeps only a fraction of parameters active per token. That improves latency and throughput. Training data expands from hundreds of thousands of hours to several million hours, through a new processing pipeline.

Simplified post-training and conditioning recipes are credited for gains in naturalness and cloning fidelity. Evaluation covers synthesis quality, speaker similarity, and word error rate. It also covers ZTTS1-Eval, a new benchmark released alongside the model. ZONOS2 holds its own against state-of-the-art systems, while keeping good streaming latency. Zyphra releases the weights and inference code under an Apache 2.0 licence.
arxiv-2606-24420: This paper builds a multi-signal confidence engine for LLM-based document field extraction, beyond logprobs. The building builds. Their engine is multi-signal confidence. The extraction is LLM-based document field. It is AI. The building is beyond logprobs.
arxiv-2606-24520:
Yan Gao, Luxian Yang, and Jinsong Zeng classify a family of fractals from complex dynamics. Their objects are the Julia sets of McMullen maps. A Julia set records which starting points stay bounded when a formula is applied again and again. In this family the sets take carpet, necklace, and cluster shapes. The authors ask when two such sets can be reshaped into each other by a quasisymmetric map, one with controlled distortion.

Gao and colleagues settle the question for the postcritically finite maps, those whose critical points end in repeating cycles. They give a complete quasisymmetric classification of these sets. They also prove each set has only the symmetries forced by the map itself. Its symmetry group is exactly the finite dihedral group those symmetries generate. The result proves rigidity for every topological class in the family. It also gives the first rigid examples known in each class.
arxiv-2606-24820:
Hovhannes Tamoyan and four colleagues present SHERLOC, a framework that helps code repair agents find faults before editing. Language model agents solving repository level tasks spend about half their interaction budget just locating the bug. Existing localisation tools are graded as file retrieval, returning locations without the diagnostic context that a repair agent needs. SHERLOC pairs a reasoning model with compact repository tools and a self recovery mechanism.

The name expands to Structured Hypothesis driven Exploration and Reasoning for Localization. On SWE-Bench Lite it reaches 84 percent top one localisation accuracy. On SWE-Bench Verified its top one recall is about 81 percent. At roughly thirty billion parameters it matches or beats rival agentic methods. Feeding its locations and findings into repair agents lifts the resolve rate by about six points on Verified. Localisation tokens fall by about 37 percent, and total tokens by about 23 percent.
arxiv-2606-24920:
K. N. Santhiya and P. S. Vinayagam build higher order nondegenerate soliton solutions of the Manakov system. The Manakov model is the integrable coupled nonlinear Schrödinger system, a model for multi component nonlinear waves. Their tool is the Darboux transformation in Gram determinant form. From the seed solution, they build explicit first and second order solitons by direct iteration. The algebra grows fast with each step, so higher orders need the compact form.

The Gram determinant version gives a unified construction for all orders. Explicit third and fourth order solutions follow, and the general Nth order case is stated. The wave structures show asymmetric profiles with several intensity peaks, fixed by distinct spectral parameters. When these solitons collide, the dynamics show asymmetric energy redistribution and complex interaction behaviour. Santhiya and Vinayagam offer the scheme as a systematic route to wave forms that step by step methods handle awkwardly.
arxiv-2606-25120:
Aviation software certification has enforced three demands on governed systems since 1992. Christo Zietsman sets them out. They are a traceable link between specifications and operating evidence, validity bounded by context with revalidation on change, and an objective account of what counts as sufficient proof. The demands live in the DO-178C and DO-330 standards, enforced by regulators. No comparable demand, he notes, is made of single AI governance documents.

A system prompt or policy file can be deployed while satisfying none of the three. Zietsman argues the aviation demands fail at the level of whole AI systems, which are non deterministic. They transfer at the level of the document, a static artifact whose properties can be checked alone. He maps the aviation machinery onto three findings for AI governance: epoch limits on document validity, proof surfaces as the feedback that triggers revalidation, and a structural gap in current practice.
arxiv-2606-25520:
Finding where heat or a pollutant enters a system, from measurements of how it spread, is an inverse problem prone to blow up under tiny noise. Asim Ilyas and Stefano Serra-Capizzano build fast solvers for one such problem in 2026, governed by a fractional diffusion equation in two space dimensions and time. Fractional derivatives give the spread a long memory. A quasi boundary value repair first tames the ill posedness, then finite differences produce a huge structured linear system.

Spectral analysis through generalised locally Toeplitz theory explains the system's eigenvalue behaviour and guides preconditioners that keep its multilevel block structure. With those preconditioners, the iterative GMRES solver clusters its eigenvalues near one and converges far faster. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and show practical source reconstructions where a naive solve would crawl.
arxiv-2606-25720:
Spacetime might twist as well as curve. Neutrinos carry spin and change flavour as they travel, so they would feel that twist. R Serao, G De Maria, S Monda, A Quaranta, and A Capolupo analyse the effect in 2026. Their setting is Einstein Cartan gravity, where torsion is allowed. They use the full quantum field theory of flavour mixing, not the simpler textbook picture. Curvature is switched off to isolate the twist's role. Both steady and slowly varying axial torsion backgrounds are studied.

A steady spatial torsion splits the two spin orientations. They gain different effective masses and energies. The mixing amplitudes also depend on spin, through Bogoliubov coefficients. So oscillation frequencies and strengths both shift. Slow neutrinos show the largest effects when the torsion scale rivals their masses. An overpowering torsion term instead flattens the mass differences. It can choke off flavour conversion altogether.
arxiv-2606-25820:
Groundwater and oil move through rock whose permeability jumps wildly from place to place, and every new guess at that hidden field demands another expensive simulation. Maria Vasilyeva and Raphael Pangilinan build a neural operator in 2026 that learns the whole mapping at once. A coarse multiscale space, constructed from local snapshots of fine scale solutions, captures how flow patterns actually look in such random, high contrast media. That basis forms the operator's trunk. A branch network reads a permeability field and predicts the coefficients on the basis.

Because the network learns the map directly, no nonlinear coarse solve is needed when a new field arrives. Tests on nonlinear flow in heterogeneous media show good accuracy at substantially lower cost than projection based multiscale methods. Flexibility is the deeper win: one trained operator answers for many random rock fields.
arxiv-2606-25920:
Shaowei Du and colleagues work in quantum metrology, the science of measuring physical quantities with quantum sensors. The famous quantum Cramér-Rao bound states the best precision possible, but only in the limit of endlessly many measurements. It says nothing about how many measurements a real estimator needs. Real work happens far from that ideal limit.

Method-of-moments estimation, which infers a parameter from the average of one measured quantity, is the setting Du's team analyzes for finite measurement counts. Curved calibration responses bias the simple estimator. The team builds a corrected version whose bias shrinks much faster. Their formulas give the corrections beyond the usual leading term. They also give a condition under which the first correction vanishes entirely. Concrete thresholds show when the textbook limiting sensitivity becomes visible in practice.
arxiv-2606-26020:
Cameron Pike and Animesh Yadav simplify the maths of distorted signals in nonlinear power amplifiers. Amplifiers bend signals in ways that spawn non-Gaussian distortion. The distortion warps beam patterns and eats array gain in millimetre-wave vehicle links. Rice's classic method handles such analysis through a characteristic function. Its original form demands heavy double and triple integrals.

Fourier series replace the Fourier transform in their version. Correlation calculations then become plain sums instead of hard integrals. The framework keeps the old method's reach. It accepts several sine signals at once. Noise need not be Gaussian. A worked example drives a gallium nitride transistor curve with a sine signal plus Gaussian noise. Results show the tool fits real device behaviour. Engineers gain a cheaper way to study radio front-end flaws in future wireless systems.
arxiv-2606-26520:
Johnny Peng and four colleagues tackle forecasting for mammalian cell cultures. Such cultures produce many modern medicines inside bioreactors. Key process measures drift over days, and trouble is often confirmed too late to fix. Forecasts several days ahead could guide feeding and sampling in time. The data, though, are sparse, unevenly timed, and quick to diverge between similar runs.

Their framework combines two parts. A latent differential equation model, which tracks hidden states that evolve smoothly, uses gating and a bottleneck to handle sparse inputs. A just-in-time step then finds similar past runs, groups them into regimes, and fine-tunes one model per regime. The output is several plausible futures, each with a confidence score, not one averaged guess. Raman spectroscopy, a light-based chemical measurement, is fused in as extra pseudo-observations to enrich the sparse record.
arxiv-2606-26720:
Peter B. Denton, Shao-Feng Ge, Chui-Fan Kong, and Pedro Pasquini study how new physics could distort neutrino measurements between production and detection. Neutrinos change flavour as they travel. If unknown physics operates near experiment energies, its parameters could run, meaning drift with energy, along the way. Different experiments would then measure seemingly inconsistent values.

The authors examine this running effect without assuming a specific new-physics model. They consider varied flavour patterns and three planned facilities spanning wide energy ranges. Combining the experiments gives strong sensitivity to running effects. Multiple experiments measuring the same parameters can separate several running values at once. Cases where rival accounts mimic each other can also be addressed. The study argues for treating inter-experiment comparisons as a new-physics probe in their own right.
arxiv-2606-27120:
Jakovac and colleagues define a chase game on networks that mixes two classic game families. In each round, Runner moves along a fresh edge from her current spot. Blocker then deletes one edge anywhere on the graph. Runner wants to visit as many vertices as possible before the network traps her. Blocker wants the opposite. In 2026, with both playing perfectly, the count Runner reaches is called the sabotage number of the graph.

For any tree, a formula gives that number exactly, and it can be computed in polynomial time. For graphs with exactly one loop, the value sits within one of a matching lower version. A sharp upper bound for bridgeless cubic graphs, where every vertex has three edges, uses the girth, the shortest loop length. Bounds also cover complete bipartite graphs and generalised Sierpiński graphs. Several special families get exact values, closing the picture.
arxiv-2606-27320:
Bralios, Smaragdis, and Kim give neural audio codecs a flexible sense of time. Audio autoencoders squeeze sound into compact latent codes for storage, features, and generation. Nearly all run at a fixed frame rate, spending equal time steps on dense and sparse sound alike. Their Elastic Time method adds a dynamic frame-rate bottleneck to existing fixed-rate models. A light latent predictor learns which frames can be skipped and rebuilt later. In their 2026 audio paper, greedy boundary choice at run time then sets the effective rate.

Deployment-time rate control comes with the design, letting one model serve many budgets. Efficiency against sound quality improves relative to baseline systems in the reported experiments. Temporal resolution becomes a dial rather than a fixed design choice. Existing autoencoders convert rather than being replaced, which eases adoption across compression and creative pipelines.
arxiv-2606-27720:
Rebuilding people and their surroundings from one moving camera is hard. Scale is unclear, people drift out of line with the scene, and other objects block the view. Boao Shi and three colleagues present SHOW in 2026 to treat the two tasks as one. Models of the human body give structure and scale cues. The scene in turn gives spatial context for placing each person.

SHOW lets a user pick which person to rebuild with a mask prompt. Body-based cues feed into point-map prediction, so the scene comes out at true metric scale even from a single camera. The recovered scene then constrains the body meshes, which improves placement and alignment. Joint training teaches features that know about both sides. Tests on the 3DPW, EMDB, and RICH benchmarks show gains in scale consistency, alignment, and accuracy. The gains hold under hard camera motion, blocked views, and cluttered scenes.
arxiv-2606-27820:
Aykut Özdönmez reports monitoring of the flat-spectrum radio quasar 4C 29.45. The observations ran for thirty-nine nights between February and July 2022 with the T60 telescope at the TÜBİTAK National Observatory in Turkey, covering four optical bands. The study targeted flux, colour, and spectral variability. The work was published in 2023.

The quasar sat in an active phase and varied in all bands. Its average R-band brightness was magnitude fourteen point seven. Amplitudes reached about two hundred twenty percent in V band, with similar values in R and I. Spectral energy distributions were derived for thirty-three nights. Their indices ranged from about one point zero to one point six. Modest correlations linked the light curves and the spectral index, with lags of several hours to days. Colour changes stayed achromatic in the bright phase. No short-timescale periodicity was found; a period exceeds one hundred days.
arxiv-2606-28120:
Software and scientific knowledge co-evolve, but they are catalogued separately. Audris Mockus links the two worlds in 2026. World of Code mirrors public version-control history. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex hold the literature. A typed cross-corpus graph joins them, with sixty-nine point eight million edges across eight relation types. A curated set of 18,247 science repositories anchors the analysis. Two reciprocal questions are asked, one per direction of impact.

The two directions illuminate different layers. Literature reaches software mainly through a reproducibility and packaging layer, tools like nf-core, Nextflow, Singularity, and Bioconda, plus sequence-analysis software. Software reaches back mainly through a hidden machine-learning and data-science infrastructure tier, including PyTorch, seaborn, and NLTK. That second signal is proxied by dependency counts, since direct paper-to-software naming is too sparse to rank. The study is a feasibility probe, not a definitive measurement.
arxiv-2606-28320:
Justin Yu and nine colleagues, including Ken Goldberg, clean up the messy demonstration data used to teach robots by imitation. People teleoperating robots hesitate, fumble, and recover, and standard training copies those flaws. Earlier progress-scoring models needed costly human labels or learned from noisy stand-ins for progress.

Yu's team trains WARP-RM, which learns a signed progress score for each video frame using only successful demonstrations. Time-warped copies, sped up, slowed, or reversed, supply the training targets without any annotation. A companion method then upweights the action chunks the scorer rates highly. On a two-armed robot folding crumpled T-shirts, their approach kept succeeding on nineteen of twenty trials even as training data grew sloppier, while plain training collapsed to two.
arxiv-2606-28420:
I. García-Marco, R. Tapia-Ramos, and A. Vigneron-Tenorio extend a notion from one-dimensional algebra into higher dimensions. Numerical semigroups are sets of whole numbers closed under addition; strong ones obey an extra mixing property. Affine semigroups generalize them to several coordinates, and the authors define and study the strong ones.

Non-numerical strong affine semigroups, they show, behave structurally unlike their one-dimensional cousins. For the important C-semigroup family with a fixed set of multiplicities, they prove a largest member exists and the family organizes into a tree. They characterize when the family is finite and give an algorithm listing all members up to a fixed genus. Special strong semigroups sharpen several earlier results. Finally, the toric ideals attached to these semigroups get a careful treatment, including their indispensable monomials.
arxiv-2606-28620:
Oscar Miró López-Feliu, Daimy van Loo, Xanthos Kekkos, Mikel Blom, and Clara Rus conducted this reproducibility study of FACTER. The framework promises fair, statistically covered recommendations from language models by setting conformal thresholds and repeatedly repairing its own prompts. Reproduction matters because the original report left its target-set scoring underspecified.

Under a strict reproduction, the team finds recommendation utility diverging from the original report, and traces the gap to that underspecification. In a constrained re-ranking variant, where the candidate set is fixed, FACTER does cut adaptive-threshold violations. But the cuts do not consistently show up under fixed thresholds or global fairness metrics. A static fairness instruction matched the dynamic repair loop's parity outcomes, suggesting the online loop adds little here, a useful deflation of an appealing device.
arxiv-2606-28820:
Bright and Zelek present CoGS, a method for rebuilding a moving scene of a person handling an object from a single ordinary video. One camera view makes the task hard, because the person, the object and the room follow different motion rules while sharing the same pixels. Earlier methods often let the object's motion leak into the person or the background, and parts rarely seen stay poorly constrained.

CoGS splits the scene into three coordinated parts: a jointed human body started from a complete template, a rigid object field following its estimated path, and a still background field. A six-stage schedule steadies the person and object separately before merging them with the room under checks on silhouettes, motion and visibility. On two public benchmarks the system improved both the interaction scenes and wild footage of people in real places.
arxiv-2606-29320:
Kim and three colleagues show that a memoryless physical system can still compute with memory, by trading time for space. Reservoir computing uses a physical system's dynamics as a computer, and memory capacity is usually thought to come from the system's own history-dependence. Their approach instead uses multidimensional input nodes as a spatial memory axis, so the reservoir need not remember anything itself.

They test the idea on a generalised quantum dot, whose discrete energy levels supply strong nonlinearity. In simulations, the memoryless quantum reservoir performed well on chaotic Mackey-Glass forecasting and on nonlinear transformation tasks. Looking at the geometry of the quantum state paths, they find the mechanism: the added spatial memory builds a hysteresis loop in the quantum state space. The loop becomes topologically stable when the system's evolution locks to the input signal's rhythm.
arxiv-2606-29420:
Asadi and four colleagues merge two game traditions into generalized bidding games. In turn-based games on graphs, players move a token and each vertex dictates whose turn it is. In pure bidding games, players bid at every step for the right to move, and under Richman bidding the winner pays the loser. The new model mixes all three vertex types together.

That simple change has deep consequences. Generalized bidding games prove more expressive than pure bidding games, with several applications given. More importantly, generalized Richman bidding games turn out to be structurally equivalent to simple stochastic games, a model studied for decades; each can be converted into the other by linear-size translations. The link lets the authors solve temporal parity and quantitative mean-payoff specifications with the best known complexity bounds. They also study a repair problem about assigning owners to bidding vertices, and prove it NP-complete.
arxiv-2606-29520:
Santilli, Daghero, and Moghaddam introduce SAKE, a benchmark that tests whether large language models understand software architecture. Models increasingly assist across the software development lifecycle, yet design knowledge stays largely unmeasured. Architectural judgement involves quality trade-offs, design patterns, and system-level limits. Benchmarks about syntax or algorithms exercise none of that.

SAKE holds more than two thousand multiple-choice questions written by experts, each with four options. Questions spread across eight categories and four context-length levels. The team evaluates eleven models, proprietary and open-weight, in zero-shot settings, with no examples, and five-shot settings, with a few examples given. Overall accuracy is high. Performance still varies markedly across categories, exposing gaps in areas at the heart of professional practice. SAKE, its scripts, and all results are made public as open source, giving the field a shared baseline for tracking design reasoning in language models over time.
arxiv-2606-29720:
Liu examines a hidden cost of resampling, the standard fix for class-imbalanced data where one class vastly outnumbers another. Methods such as SMOTE, which creates new minority examples, are usually judged by rare-class accuracy. Far less attention goes to probability calibration, whether stated chances match real rates. 

Across five public datasets and two tree ensemble models, random forest and gradient boosting, Liu finds that SMOTE's calibration cost, though real, is small. Its discrimination gains outweigh that penalty. Random undersampling, by contrast, is the genuine danger, and its damage grows sharply with imbalance, largely because shrunken training sets estimate probabilities poorly. One recalibration step, Platt or isotonic, removes the damage at tiny cost. The analytic prior-shift correction that repairs undersampling fails to transfer to SMOTE. Liu recommends reporting calibration alongside discrimination.
arxiv-2606-30020:
Pathology foundation models read whole-slide tissue images, but clinics cannot yet trust them. Their predictions carry no reliable confidence estimates. Also, no single model wins across all tasks. Gbègninougbo Tchokponhoue and four colleagues propose DICE to fix both problems. DICE is a plug-and-play framework built on frozen models. It treats disagreement between models as an uncertainty signal.

DICE ensembles several frozen pathology models and watches where they disagree. Deep mutual learning aligns the members so disagreement stays meaningful. The authors prove this objective upper-bounds the model's uncertainty. The ensemble's consensus also spots abnormal patches on each slide. It does so with no direct supervision for that task. On three hard whole-slide benchmarks, DICE flags failure-prone cases reliably. It works both on familiar data and on shifted, unfamiliar data. Its accuracy, calibration, and patch spotting match or beat leading baselines.
arxiv-2606-30120:
N. Filonov, writing alone, compares two classic eigenvalue problems for the Laplace operator in high dimensions. Dirichlet conditions force functions to vanish at the boundary. Neumann conditions instead force the boundary derivative to vanish. The matching eigenvalues form two increasing sequences. A basic inequality already orders them term by term.

Filonov studies the index shift that strengthens that inequality. The shift counts how many extra Neumann eigenvalues fit below a Dirichlet one. Classic results give shifts of one, or of the dimension itself. He asks how the shift behaves as dimension grows large. For the first eigenvalue, the shift grows at least exponentially in dimension. The lower bound holds for every bounded domain. For convex domains, the same exponential bound covers all indices. Constants in the bounds do not depend on the domain's shape.
arxiv-2606-30220:
Sena Korkut, María Bravo Sarmiento, Sanghwan Kim, and Zeynep Akata audit traffic video question answering for a quiet failure: models answering without looking. Correct answers ought to rest on scene-specific visual evidence. Models may instead exploit textual shortcuts and language priors. High benchmark accuracy can hide that collapse completely. The authors measure visual dependence directly across four benchmarks.

Several recent open-weight vision-language models do suspiciously well blind. On one benchmark, removing video actually improves accuracy consistently. Adding more frames makes performance worse still. Two diagnostics quantify the problem at dataset level. Blind Gap measures above-chance performance from text alone. Visual Gain measures what video actually adds when present. An instance-level Shortcut Score then flags shortcut-prone questions. Filtering by that score yields subsets with less bias. Grounded evaluation, they argue, matters as much as accuracy.
arxiv-2606-30620:
Wolfgang Enzi, Coleman Krawczyk, Tian Li and Thomas Collett tackle source reconstruction in strong gravitational lensing. To infer what a lensed background galaxy really looks like, modellers rebuild it on a mesh. Resolution needs vary sharply by position, but adaptive meshes usually rely on jagged operations that block smooth optimisation and restrict regularisation, the rules keeping reconstructions sensible.

Their answer places a Gaussian process, a flexible probability model for surfaces, on a uniform grid, then warps that grid using the paths of light rays traced back to the source plane. Each source pixel then holds a more even share of rays. The warp stays fully differentiable, the spectrum of the process can be chosen freely, and Fourier methods keep computation fast. On mock data the grid matched standard fit quality with about half as many pixels per dimension, and scored better at equal pixel counts.
arxiv-2606-30820:
Philip Smith, Ahmad Ahmad and Kevin Leahy synthesise robot controllers from timed task specifications. Time Window Temporal Logic is a language for tasks with timing windows, such as dwell in this region, then visit that one by a deadline. The team build on the logic's quantitative semantics, a robustness score saying how well a behaviour satisfies the formula.

They encode robust satisfaction as mixed-integer linear constraints, turning synthesis into an optimisation problem that maximises the robustness degree. Any feasible solution with positive score provably satisfies the task. Two settings are covered: open-loop, which plans the full control sequence at once, and a receding-horizon controller that re-solves at each step from the measured state. Their controller shortens its horizon adaptively, using the task automaton to plan only through the current window. That makes each solve much cheaper than the full open-loop one.
arxiv-2606-30920:
John Schreck, William Chapman, Charlie Becker and David John Gagne estimate how likely a tropical disturbance is to grow into a hurricane, a rare event that brute-force simulation can barely sample. They couple Forward Flux Sampling, a rare-event technique from statistical mechanics that splits a hard transition into a chain of easier crossings, to a neural weather emulator running at one-degree resolution. The emulator's stochastic layers supply the spread the method needs, and its speed supplies the tens of thousands of trajectories each estimate requires.

Applied to 98 Atlantic initial conditions from the 2022 season, the method resolved genesis rates that spanned nearly three orders of magnitude, with a seasonal cycle matching observations in shape. An independent direct-sampling check gave a mean rate ratio of 1.03, with a spread of 0.15 across conditions. Speed-ups over direct sampling ranged from 3 to 140 times.
arxiv-2606-31120:
Hao and six colleagues use a quantum battery to probe how motion changes the vacuum. The Unruh effect says an accelerated observer feels empty space as a warm thermal bath. The team models an accelerated Unruh-DeWitt battery and measures ergotropy, the maximum work that can be extracted from it. That work serves as a witness to vacuum fluctuations reshaped by the battery's path.

Two paths are compared: uniform linear acceleration and uniform circular motion, each with and without a reflecting boundary. At low Unruh temperature, linear motion gives more ergotropy. At high temperature, circular motion wins. Near a boundary, ergotropy oscillates with large peaks, because the boundary protects quantum coherence. Far from the boundary, the oscillation fades and the value settles. Circular motion stretches the oscillation out longer.
arxiv-2606-31220:
Benth and two colleagues develop fast ways to compute Delta sensitivities for derivatives in energy markets. A Delta measures how a contract price moves when the underlying price shifts, and traders need it to hedge risk. In energy markets both prices and traded volumes move randomly and together, which complicates the maths.

The team set up a stochastic framework and compare two routes. The density method works when the process density is known, shown on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and CARMA models. The Malliavin calculus route needs no density and covers jump and time-changed processes beside them. Worked examples for both routes agree closely in their Delta values. The pair of methods gives energy desks a choice matched to whichever model they already run.
arxiv-2606-31320:
Cao and five colleagues present AutoSafe, an architecture for reinforcement learning that must stay safe while it learns online. Hard action blocking keeps a system safe but jerks the interaction and the learning signal. Soft penalty terms keep learning smooth yet give weak safety promises, and neither extreme suits live control.

AutoSafe builds safety monitoring and intervention into the action generator itself. The policy then slides smoothly between performance-driven and safety-preserving behaviour as risk changes, instead of switching with a jolt. Learning and interaction stay continuous, which helps both training stability and real behaviour. Tests across continuous control suites back the design, and the authors frame structured composition, not after-the-fact filtering, as the way to join safety with steady online learning.
arxiv-2606-31420:
Huang and five colleagues present BP-TTA, a test-time adaptation method for streams where classes arrive unevenly. Test-time adaptation updates a model on unlabeled test data as domains shift. In live streams, class imbalance and domain shift arrive together and feed each other, yet most methods handle drift alone.

BP-TTA builds balanced adaptation batches by mixing current samples with high-confidence past instances, which curbs bias toward common classes. It also keeps evolving class prototypes during inference and uses prototype similarity to discipline the updates, making pseudo-labels safer. Across dynamic streaming tests the method beats leading rivals steadily. The pairing of balanced batches with prototype guidance keeps online learning stable when both the world and the class mix keep moving.
arxiv-2606-32020:
Nguyen and thirteen colleagues tackle a mismatch that blocks efficient image generation: strong diffusion teachers and compact student models often live in different latent spaces. One-step distillation methods assume teacher and student share latent resolution and the same variational autoencoder. Modern teachers such as SD 3.5 and Flux break that assumption for small deployable students like SD 1.5, so their knowledge cannot transfer directly.

The team formalizes this setting as Cross-Space Distillation and adds a lightweight interface called Bridge. Bridge maps student latents into teacher space using a frozen student decoder as a spatial prior plus a small learnable projector, leaving the student backbone untouched. Distilled this way, SD 1.5 improves from 5.4 to 9.4 on the HPSv3 quality score while keeping one-step inference.
arxiv-2608-00020: Krishna sharpens a set of known numerical radius inequalities for quaternion matrices. The base results come from Kittaneh, published in Studia Mathematica in 2005. Those results were described as a breakthrough in the field. Krishna shows a more restrictive version holds for certain classes of matrices over the quaternions. Readers get tighter bounds, but only within the stated matrix classes.
arxiv-2608-00120:
Cadeddu and co-authors test lepton wave function factorization in germanium-71 electron capture. Capture ratios give precise checks of atomic wave functions. They can also reveal non-factorization effects in nuclear capture. The team uses exact leptonic wave functions for their tests. Their frame predicts capture rates for germanium-71.

They treat the transition matrix element without factorization. That links the nuclear transition density with the leptonic wave functions. Constrained transition densities let them size the non-factorization effect. Rates for L/K, M/K, and M/L capture follow from it. They compare those ratios with current world averages from experiment. Readers get an up-to-date view of theory and data for this capture.
arxiv-2608-00220:
Wei and co-authors name a failure mode in on-policy optimization with verifiable rewards. Training can lift the current objective while harming later ones. Successful behaviours for future goals may grow too rare to sample. They call this verifier-induced support reshaping. Effective rewardable support is what a fixed rollout budget can reach.

Across two model families, they track the effect with repeated sampling and two-way training. Math training raised mean instruction success but cut prompts with any success at best-of-32. Instruction training shifted math replies from stepwise openings to direct answers. Those changes concentrate in the first few response tokens. Tested constraints and distillation preserved cross-task support only partly. Endpoint gains do not guarantee future trainability, they warn.
at-sunwich-port-part-4-contents-chapters:
Part 4 of W. W. Jacobs's seaport novel holds chapters sixteen through twenty, with drawings by Will Owen. News arrives that stops conversation: Captain Nugent, the autocrat of Equator Lodge, has gone as a stowaway aboard the Conqueror, the ship of his ancient enemy. His daughter and Mrs. Kingdom can only gasp at the scandal sure to follow when Sunwich hears.

Mr. Hardy's information spreads consternation through the family circle. In a lighter vein, Mr. Wilks ends a bar-room argument by smashing a glass on the floor, and the landlord grips him round the middle and pilots him out into the sea air. Jacobs lets wounded pride, strong drink, and town gossip drive these middle chapters toward the family's reckoning.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-20:
The twentieth and last volume of Michael L. Rodkinson's set completes his History of the Talmud. Volume nineteen told the story through the Mishnah and the Babylonian schools. This second history volume carries the tale into print, persecution, and the modern age.

Rodkinson follows the Talmud through its first printings, the burnings ordered against it, and the censors who cut its pages. He weighs the great commentators, above all Rashi, whose notes made the text readable. The volume closes his twenty-book labor, the first full English Talmud ever made. It is both a history and the translator's own defense of his work.
beaumont-fletcher-philaster-1620:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher wrote Philaster together for the King's Men, the leading acting company in London. The play mixes romance and danger in the style called tragicomedy. It was first printed in 1620 and stayed popular on stage for decades.

Prince Philaster has lost his rightful throne to a usurping king. He loves the king's daughter, while a false friend spreads lies about her honor. A cross-dressed page named Bellario adds confusion and pathos to the love plot. Wounds, trials, and last-minute pardons bring the story to a tense, happy close that early audiences clearly loved.
belzoni-narrative-operations-1820:
Giovanni Battista Belzoni told of feats no tale smith would dare invent in his Narrative of 1820. Belzoni was a strong man from Italy who showed feats in fairs ere he dug in Egypt. There he hauled a vast head to a ship, broke into a heap at Giza, and found the bright tomb of Seti the First.

Each feat is told in plain, bold prose. He had foes, funds ran low, yet he pushed on. His finds fill great halls in London to this day. The book is the first great tale of the dig.
bergson-mind-energy-1920:
Mind-Energy, published in English in 1920, gathers Bergson's lectures and essays on the mind's powers, translated with care by H. Wildon Carr. The pieces were given across the years of his greatest fame, to audiences that filled Paris halls.

Bergson speaks on dreams, memory, false recognition, and the effort of the intellect, always returning to one theme: mental energy pressing against matter's habits. His celebrated lecture subjects show the same method at playful work. The book is the most approachable of his later writings in English. It catches a philosopher-performer thinking aloud before his public.
boccaccio-decameron-florio-1620:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron in plague-time Italy, and John Florio gave it to England in 1620. Florio's was the first English version of the famed tale set. Ten young people flee Florence and pass ten days telling tales.

Their one hundred tales mix love, wit, trickery, and sharp turns of luck. Merchants, priests, wives, and fools all get caught in clever plots. Some tales praise quick minds, and some mock greed and lust. Florio's rich prose helped shape how English writers told short tales. Boccaccio set the frame tale form for centuries of writers.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-3-:
Edward G. Browne devoted the third volume of his Literary History of Persia, from 1920, to the Tartar Dominion, the years 1265 to 1502. The Mongol storm had wrecked the land, yet Persian letters rose again under the Ilkhans and Timur. Browne ends his tale with Jami, the last master of the classical age. The main text here is complete; the index is missing from the scan.

Hafez sings in these centuries, and the historians Rashid al-Din and Juvayni write the Mongols into Persian memory. Browne weighs court poetry, history, and Sufi verse with his usual sympathy. His extracts let the poets speak in English dress. The volume bridges the classical world and the modern one.
budge-hieroglyphic-dictionary-vol-1-1920:
E. A. Wallis Budge gave learners their key to the script in Vol. 1 of An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary, out in 1920. Budge had kept Egypt's hoard in London for years. Each sign word here gets its sounds, its forms, and its sense in English. The tome runs through the first great span of the word hoard.

Two crops of learners cut their teeth on Budge's lists. Sages now fault some of his sounds and senses. Yet for its age the work was a boon no fan could skip. This tome opens the pair.
budge-hieroglyphic-dictionary-vol-2-1920:
E. A. Wallis Budge caps his word work in Vol. 2 of An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary, out in 1920. The first tome gave the words in script form. This tome gives the key from the flip side. An English word list points fans to the script terms they need. Lists of kings and place names from the Nile world stand here too.

Such lists sound dry, yet they are the tools of the trade. A fan with a name could find its age and kin here. The pair served learners for years. This tome ends it.
bury-idea-progress-1920:
J. B. Bury published The Idea of Progress in 1920, a history of the idea of progress itself. Bury, a noted historian of Rome and Byzantium, asks when humans first believed their future would improve. He traces the notion from faint Greek hints through Bacon, Descartes, and the Enlightenment. The idea, he argues, is modern, not ancient.

Thinkers such as Fontenelle, Turgot, Condorcet, and Comte receive clear chapters. Bury ends by asking whether progress is a faith that evidence can support. The book founded the study of progress as a topic in its own right. Its calm, exact style suits its theme. It remains the classic meta-history of a ruling modern idea.
bygone-beliefs-being-a-series-of-excursi:
H. Stanley Redgrove wrote a set of essays on old beliefs, as trips through side paths of thought. His past books line the front pages: a work on thermo-chemical constants of 1909, and Matter, Spirit, and the Cosmos of 1910. Truth hid in odd old forms is his plea.

Old creeds hold truths in image form, he holds — bent and vague, yet true. We have lost some of them, or risk their loss. Past thought, in its most wild shapes, can still teach the modern mind. One trip in the set treats the Cagliostro tale, as the part in view shows. Library stamps mark this copy as a scanned loan book. The set's method is plain: take a dead belief, walk round it with care, and weigh what grain of sense made men hold it so long.
cather-youth-bright-medusa-1920:
Youth and the Bright Medusa, published in 1920, collects Willa Cather's stories about artists: singers, sculptors, painters, and the small towns that formed and starved them. The Medusa of the title is art itself, beautiful and dangerous to look at directly.

The collection holds 'Paul's Case', her famous tale of a Pittsburgh boy who steals money for one week of luxury in New York. 'The Sculptor's Funeral' and 'A Wagner Matinee' weigh what the prairie gives its artists and what it takes. Cather writes with pity for both the escapees and the left behind. These stories made her reputation in short fiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphael-1483-:
Raphael, painting's most famous name, was born at Urbino on 6 April, or 28 March, 1483, and died at Rome on 6 April 1520. This very long encyclopedia entry places him in the Umbrian School. Raphael is only a Christian name; his full name was Raffaele Santi, and Sanzio is simply wrong. His father Giovanni Santi held a vague but important post at Urbino's court under Duke Frederick.

That court made Urbino a leading art centre, served by Piero della Francesca, Melozzo and Justus of Ghent, and Castiglione's Cortegiano, the handbook of the man of the world, was written there. The entry's heart lies in the Vatican frescoes. They show the three theological virtues, Civil Law with Justinian bestowing the Pandects, and Canon Law with Gregory the Ninth, wearing Julius the Second's features, publishing the Decretals. Parnassus shows Apollo playing among the Muses while Homer sings.
chekhov-chorus-girl-1920:
The Chorus Girl and Other Stories, in Constance Garnett's 1920 translation, gathers some of Chekhov's earlier successes. In the title story a chorus girl named Pasha is accused by a wronged wife of stealing her husband's gifts. Pasha, who received almost nothing, gives up her own small treasures to end the scene.

Verotchka tells of a young official who fails to answer a girl's honest confession of love. The failure haunts him on his walk home through the summer night. These stories are shorter and lighter than the late tales, yet the sting is already there. They show the young Chekhov learning to say much in few pages.
cia-0000009920:
A prisoner of war camp at Hong Het leads a January 1962 item, followed by notes on Vietnamese communist presence in an area the title cuts off. The date matters: 1962 stands at the very start of America's deep involvement in Vietnam and Laos. Prison camps already existed to be reported.

Early items like this one show the captivity record beginning before the big war. A camp at Hong Het in 1962 predates the famous prisons' full growth. Analysts then could not know the system would run for another decade. The file preserves the record's first page for this corner of the war.
cia-0000011620:
An untitled CIA item from August 1964 touches on Charles Klusmann, Air America, and rumored plots in Laos. Klusmann was an Air America pilot, and Air America was the airline the CIA secretly owned and ran across Southeast Asia. The file was never given a proper title, which is common for working papers in the Laos secret war.

The item preserves fragments about the pilot, the airline, and plots said to be forming around them. Such scraps show the daily business of a covert war fought far from public view. For readers, it is a glimpse of the shadowy margins where airlines, pilots, and conspiracies met.
cia-0000012420:
A transcript survives for meeting number forty-two, held in Paris on October 14, 1961, late in the run. The record notes the transcript of the session taken from the tapes that day. Most meetings in the series survive as summaries; a transcript preserves the spoken words themselves. Historians prize such pages, because they let the colonel's voice come through across the decades, careful and precise in every answer.

The forty-second session's record thus carries more than its high number. It holds tone, hesitation, and emphasis that summaries flatten into prose. For readers, the page is the closest the file comes to sitting in the room.
cia-0000013220:
Rach Gia province, in the Mekong Delta, had its own Viet Cong policy for handling prisoners. A CIA report from October 1971 sets that policy out in full. It covered American and Vietnamese prisoners alike under one set of rules. Local directives show how headquarters policy bent to fit provincial realities. The available cages, guards, and boats all mattered. So did the habits of the men who ran them on the ground.

The report gives the Delta's chapter of the prison system. Rules varied from province to province in telling ways. For readers, the page shows doctrine at ground level, where captivity was actually lived.
cia-0000013620:
Brazil's outlook under military rule is surveyed in a CIA paper from July 1966. The regime was consolidating its grip by then. Generals rotated through the presidency by their own rules. Parties were remade by decree, and congress sat tamed. The economy was being readied for the growth spurt boosters later called a miracle. Beneath the order, the analysts noted, the politics stayed brittle, held by force rather than consent.

The paper weighs the dictatorship's durability two years after the coup. It tests the miracle's shine against the regime's hard base. For readers, it is the Brazilian outlook as Washington filed it then.
cia-0000014620: An amnesty movement for Morton Sobell is the subject of a CIA file dated April 1, 1963. The file names a group, cut short as FCP in the title, that meant to launch the drive. Sobell had been in prison since his 1951 spy conviction. Supporters who called his trial unfair kept his name in public life for years.
cia-0000014820: Soviet reactions to certain U.S. courses of action on Cuba fill a CIA paper dated September 5, 1962. The paper forecast how Moscow might answer American moves on the island. It was written weeks before the missile crisis broke into the open. Reading it now shows the agency bracing for a clash it could feel coming.
cia-0000015320: A letter to George Popowitch from an unknown writer fills a CIA file dated November 2, 1958. The letter thanks Popowitch for his letter of November 19, per the clipped title. Unknown writers on agency letterhead turn up often in these files. Popowitch was one more citizen whose saucer mail earned a formal reply.
cia-0000021520: A dead American pilot was sighted in Bac Thai Province, North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated in 1973. The catalog notes the publication date is unknown, so 1973 is the file's dating. Bac Thai lay north of Hanoi, under heavy bombing routes of the war years. Sightings of the dead were logged as gravely as sightings of the living, for the sake of families.
cia-0000028820:
A CIA record dated October 3, 1983 carries the blunt title Why Is the World So Dangerous. The title alone captures the mood of the early 1980s, when Cold War tension was rising again. The memorandum came from Herbert E. Meyer, vice chairman of the National Intelligence Council. American and Soviet forces faced each other across Europe, and fears of a wider war were common.

Readers get the question as officials framed it at the time, in the plain terms of the title itself. The record is useful less for one answer than for what it shows about official thinking in a tense year. It preserves the sense of danger that shaped policy debates in Washington and far beyond it.
cia-0000029020:
In February 1981, COSEP said it saw totalitarian signs in the government, and a CIA record dated February 4 kept the warning. COSEP spoke for much of Nicaragua's business community. Its charge was a public break between private business and the ruling authorities.

The record holds the business group's reading of the government's direction, stated in strong terms. Warnings like this marked a turning point, as groups that once held back began to speak out. Readers can see how economic leaders framed their fears in the revolution's second full year. The warning came from a group whose members owned much of the country's trade and farming.
cia-0000049020: The investigation into the murders of the American churchwomen in El Salvador had stalled by 1981, and a CIA item from that year records the standstill. Four women had been killed the previous December, and Washington pressed hard for arrests that held. A stalled case, noted plainly, told its own story about Salvadoran justice.
cia-0000049120: Background on the assassination of Archbishop Romero fills a CIA item from 1987, kept with the Truth Commission records. Seven years after the murder, officials still needed the story set out whole: the threats, the shot, and the stalled case. Backgrounders like this one were written so a new reader could start from the beginning.
cia-0000049220: Congressmen Zschau and Kostmayer and their staffs received a briefing in 1983, preserved in a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Members who voted on aid to El Salvador were briefed in a steady stream, each session tilting the debate a little. This record shows two of them being schooled on the war.
cia-0000049320: El Salvador: Cleaning Up the Military heads declassified CIA document 0000049320, dated April 5, 1990, a Truth Commission-noted paper. It concerns efforts or proposals to reform the Salvadoran military. The file preserves the agency's own phrasing for that cleanup effort. It gives readers a brief dated glimpse of the topic. Military reform in El Salvador is described there in the agency's own terms.
cia-0000098720: Transfer of Soviet antisubmarine warfare technology to Warsaw Pact countries is an intelligence assessment in declassified CIA document 0000098720, dated July 6, 1981. The sample shows its cover, with information current as of August 1, 1981, from the Office of Scientific and Weapons Research. The body text in the sample is too garbled to summarize safely. The record's stated scope is the transfer named in its title.
cia-0000102920: Organization of the Panel System, with dates of information 1959 to 1978, is declassified CIA document 0000102920, dated February 3, 1981. The heading gives the subject a twenty-year information span. Readers find a short organizational record opening the forced-labor cluster in this catalog, its panel system subject distinct from the camp records that follow.
cia-0000107420: Trends in South Africa's Nuclear Security Policies and Programs is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107420, dated September 5, 1984. The heading promises trends, a look at direction over time, in one country's nuclear programs. Policies and programs are both named in the title itself. The brief record is a nuclear trends item on South Africa from 1984 reporting.
cia-0000112820: Catherine Queszuweit-packheiser Mrs. Meisinger is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112820, dated August 6, 1945. The title is a woman's name in two forms, with Mrs. Meisinger added in brackets in the heading. No topic or charge is stated in the title itself. The brief record is a name file from the summer of 1945 as released there.
cia-0000124320: An October 1951 CIA document covers conditions for American prisoners of war in the West Pyongyang camp, the year in the heading breaking off mid-number. The capital's prisons held captives close to the regime's center. The paper records those conditions as they were reported. Camp condition reports rested on smuggled word and returnee accounts, and each fresh detail helped negotiators press claims about how prisoners were being kept.
cia-0000132420: A neutralist foreign policy actively pursued by Cuba is the subject of item 9 in the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated January 4, 1960. Its headline misspells actively as activitely, a slip kept from the original. Havana claimed a neutral course while leaning steadily toward Moscow. The short item notes that posture and the claims made for it.
cia-0000135620: This Spanish text, dated 2 February 1961, belongs to the declassified document set of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force assembled by the CIA. The date falls in the brigade's final training period before the Bay of Pigs landing in April. The catalog record is bare: no subject, no author, no unit. What the document says must be taken from the Spanish text itself. It is held here as released, one of a large run of similar exile records from that winter.
cia-0000135820: An attempt on the life of Somoza is the subject of a CIA cable dated March 3, 1954. The cable went to Guatemala and to Lincoln, the code name for the Guatemala operation's base. Somoza ruled Nicaragua and stood as an American ally in the region. He was also a marked man for his foes. The short cable reports the attempt and its outcome.
cia-0000136220: The declassified CIA cable dated 2 May 1954 takes up the WSBURNT regime rallying labor unions and a peasants federation, its base called out. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136620: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961. Even the catalog title is imperfect here: it misspells the unit as the 2506 Bigade. The brigade itself, the CIA's exile force, was in training for Cuba. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, a small reminder that these files were assembled and scanned in bulk, errors included.
cia-0000136920: The owner of the ship Alfhem has agreed to cooperate. This April 1954 cable from Stockholm reports it for SKILLET. The owner was interviewed that day. He agreed to cancel the charter. He will order his captain by radio to sail at once. The ship will go to New Orleans or Tampa. There the captain will aid American authorities. He will furnish all details of the voyage. The owner already gave key papers. They include the bill of lading and the loading sheet from Stettin.
cia-0000137320: Latin American communist parties got new instructions in Moscow and Peking. This April 1959 NSC briefing reports it. The source is a long-term CIA penetration agent. He is a high official in his own party. Before the Soviet congress, Moscow circulated a document. It urged cutting the Soviet directing role from party literature. The congress adopted a formula of equal, independent parties. Latin American parties then set new tactics in Moscow. A People's Congress was planned in defense of Latin American resources. Its communist promotion was to stay concealed.
cia-03003520:
Communist China's aid ledger opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 8 April 1958, in the later daily-brief format. Peiping had budgeted 185 million dollars for foreign aid in 1958. About a fourth would meet free-world pledges of at least 107 million, mostly in South and Southeast Asia. Grants to bloc countries over four years came to roughly 740 million.

Indonesia follows: central government forces are reported preparing an air, sea, and land assault on the Padang-Bukittinggi area of Central Sumatra. Israel agrees to pause its Lake Hula drainage digging for a few days, while United Arab Republic aircraft have flown reconnaissance over Israel. EOKA steps up sabotage in Cyprus. French nuclear officials oppose a test ban that leaves production free. Peru's president reshuffles his cabinet under public pressure.
cia-03185120:
Peru opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 July 1956. Military and civilian elements reportedly plan a revolt on 16 July to nullify last month's elections. The war minister's trip to Arequipa, whose commander is close to him, draws notice. Attachés doubt a revolt would win wide support. Success may hinge on the all-military cabinet ruling while President Odria lies hospitalised.

That cabinet worries over president-elect Prado's good relations with the outlawed APRA. It may be fomenting revolt to stay in power, though other reports expect the 28 July installation to proceed. France may seek August trade control talks. The American legation dissects Hungarian factionalism: Moscow currently backs careful relaxation under Rakosi's firm hand. A Burmese leader discusses bloc relations, possibly shading his views to help an American loan. Japanese propose a mission on the Okinawa land problem.
cia-06407620:
General voucher form names David H. Petraeus, listed as DCIA, as the claimant for official travel. The form describes a manual travel accounting voucher for a trip to New York, New York. Dates in the main section are given as 10-12 November 2011. Its purpose is stated as taking part in New York City's Veterans Day Parade and conducting official business for the United States government.

Sections of the printed form cover disbursement type, acknowledgment of receipt of funds, and authority for an agent to pick up funds. Amount fields in the scan are left blank or redacted, so no sum can be read from this copy. A later description line confirms meals were checked with the agent in charge and an executive assistant. Header stamps in the file are dated 17 November 2011.
cia-06628020:
Latin America Review dated 14 February 1983, numbered ALA LAR 83-05 and marked Secret, carries one listed article on Argentina. The article's summary states that the Catholic Church was actively criticizing regime policies. It had taken a firm stand demanding a return to civilian rule.

The article warns that this course could lead to a confrontation with the military if the planned transition were aborted. It recalls Church caution rooted in the Peronist ban on Church activity in the 1950s after a direct clash. Pronouncements were growing more liberal in tone, it reports. Civilian discontent after the Falklands debacle brought broader Church criticism. Complaints centered on conservative economic policies and on the military's refusal to give information about persons who had disappeared.
cia-06907720:
Intelligence memorandum dated August 20, 1974, Cyprus Situation Report Number 16, is timed as of 0700 EDT with all other times in Nicosia time. Its military section states the situation on Cyprus remained quiet. Turkish forces were expected to continue consolidation on the Karpas Peninsula, where they had met little resistance.

A second section covers Cypriot reaction to the death of Ambassador Davies. A Nicosia spokesman said the government would not let the tragic incident affect relations with America, and blamed irresponsible troublemakers. EOKA-B is reported completely discredited throughout Cyprus, according to a Unified Party leader, for two reasons. It had encouraged belief that Greece would intervene in any crisis, and it failed to distinguish itself in the fighting. Turkish policy under the Ecevit government had hardened, the memo states. Strong reprisals were threatened if killings of Turkish Cypriots did not stop.
clare-poems-descriptive-1820:
John Clare was a farm laborer from Northamptonshire who wrote poems about the fields where he worked. A London publisher brought out his first book in 1820. Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery made the so-called peasant poet briefly famous.

Clare describes birds, nests, flowers, and farm work with a closeness few poets match. He names local places and uses the speech of his village without apology. London readers were struck by how exact his nature writing was. The book began a short, bright career that later sank into poverty and asylum years, but the poems kept their freshness.
conrad-rescue-1920:
The Rescue, published in 1920, had the longest birth of any Conrad novel: he began it in 1896 and set it aside for twenty years. It returns to Captain Lingard, the hero of his first books, in the Malay shallows.

A yacht with an English couple aboard grounds on the coast, and Lingard's plans for a native prince collide with his duty to rescue them. Love for the yacht's lady, Mrs. Travers, paralyzes the man of action at the critical hour. The novel completes the Lingard trilogy begun in the 1890s. Its long making shows, but its sea passages remain splendid.
constitution-algeria-2020:
Algeria revised its constitution in 2020, and that revised text is what is hosted here. It opens with general principles governing Algerian society, then parts on the people and the state. Islam is the state religion, and Arabic is an official language, joined by Tamazight. A long title covers fundamental rights, public freedoms, and the duties that go with them.

Executive power sits mainly with a president, working with a prime minister and government. Parliament has two chambers, the People's National Assembly and the Council of the Nation. Later titles handle the courts, independent oversight bodies, and how the constitution can be amended. The 2020 changes followed mass street protests demanding reform.
constitution-armenia-2020:
Armenia's constitution was adopted in 1995, and the hosted text carries the deep changes made in 2015, with amendments through 2020. Those changes moved the country from a presidential system toward a parliamentary one. Chapter one lays out the foundations of the constitutional order. Chapter two lists the fundamental rights and freedoms of the person and the citizen.

Real executive power now sits with a prime minister chosen by the National Assembly, the single-chamber parliament. The president remains head of state with a narrower, mostly ceremonial role. Later chapters cover the government, the courts, the Constitutional Court, local self-government, and the human rights defender. The text reflects Armenia's effort to spread power after years of strong presidents.
constitution-italy-2020:
Italy's constitution took force in 1948, after voters ended the monarchy and chose a republic, and the hosted text includes changes through 2020. Opening articles give basic principles: work, equality, and the rights of the person. A long part then covers the rights and duties of citizens, sorted into civil ties, ethics and society, the economy, and politics.

A president heads the republic and names the prime minister, who must win the trust of Parliament. Parliament joins a Chamber of Deputies with a Senate of the Republic, the two holding nearly equal power, a design few states share. Later parts cover the regions, a Constitutional Court, and the courts. Changes in 2020 cut the size of both chambers sharply.
constitution-kosovo-2020:
Kosovo adopted this constitution in 2008, the year it declared freedom from Serbia, and the hosted text includes changes through 2020. Chapter one gives basic provisions. Kosovo is a republic, and Albanian and Serbian are both official languages, with other community tongues guarded as well. Chapter two protects basic rights and freedoms, and a further chapter guards the rights of communities and their members.

A president serves as head of state, while a prime minister leads the government. The Assembly makes laws and chooses both the president and the government. Later chapters cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, local rule, and the security forces. The text was shaped with heavy input from Western mediators and bars Kosovo from joining any other state.
constitution-liechtenstein-2020:
Liechtenstein, a tiny principality between Switzerland and Austria, works under a constitution from 1921, hosted here with changes through 2020. Early chapters cover the principality and the Prince Regnant, the ruling prince. Power is shared, by the text's own design, between the prince and the people. That sharing is real: voters can launch laws and force votes of their own.

The prince can veto laws and dismiss the government, powers a 2003 public vote chose to keep and even widen. The Landtag, a parliament of twenty-five members, makes laws with the prince's assent. A prime minister leads the government. Later chapters cover the courts, local towns, and state duties. German is the official language. Few charters give a monarch so much live power.
constitution-sudan-2020:
Sudan's hosted text is not a full constitution but the Constitutional Declaration of 2019, with changes through 2020, written after protests and the army ended Omar al-Bashir's thirty-year rule. Its early chapters give general provisions and set a short transitional period with its own bodies, meant to lead the country to elections and a permanent charter.

Power during the transition was shared in a Sovereignty Council joining soldiers and civilians, with the chair set to pass from the military side to a civilian. A transitional cabinet, led by a prime minister, ran the state day to day, and a legislative council was promised. Later chapters cover rights in a full bill, the courts, and the armed forces. War in 2023 tore the transition apart.
contemporary-american-novelists-1900-192:
Contemporary American Novelists, 1900–1920, by Carl Van Doren, sorts two decades of fiction into old style and new. Old style begins with local color, the mode that had Bret Harte for its prophet and spread after the Civil War until it had followers in every county. Its practitioners, Van Doren argues, were episodic rather than epic, and hardly one advanced past his earliest important volume.

New style brings emergent types: Ellen Glasgow, William Allen White, Ernest Poole, Henry B. Fuller, Mary Austin, and the immigrant novelists. Then comes the revolt from the village, with Edgar Lee Masters, Sherwood Anderson, Sinclair Lewis, Zona Gale, and F. Scott Fitzgerald among its names. A passage on Booth Tarkington's Ambersons shows the manner: the traveled young Indianian returns with a secret condescension toward the loyal peasants of the old chateau.
czechoslovak-constitution-1920:
Czechoslovakia adopted its constitution in February 1920, founding the republic of Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš. The new state had been carved from the fallen Austrian empire and joined Czechs, Slovaks, Germans, and others in one democracy. Its National Assembly wrote the charter to Western models, above all the French.

The text builds a parliamentary republic with a strong president, full manhood and womanhood suffrage, and guards for national minorities. In a region sliding toward dictatorship, Czechoslovakia kept free elections and a free press for two decades. It was the freest and most stable democracy between Germany and Russia. Munich and the Nazi seizure tore the country apart in 1938 and 1939, ending the charter's rule. The founding law of interwar Europe's democratic miracle is still honored in Prague and Bratislava.
defoe-captain-singleton-1720:
Daniel Defoe published Captain Singleton in 1720, his pirate novel of Africa and the high seas. The tale gives a crossing of Africa and a pirate republic in the Indian Ocean world. It is a source-text of pirate literature, before Stevenson gave the genre its classic form in English.

Bob Singleton, stolen as a child, goes to sea and is marooned on Madagascar by mutineers. He and his mates trek across Africa, a route no English novel had mapped before in fiction. Rich and restless, he turns pirate, raiding in the Indian Ocean with Quaker gunner William beside him. William's calm counsel steers Bob toward repentance and a quiet, wealthy end in England at last. Defoe mixes geography, trade lore, and moral debate in one restless adventure yarn.
defoe-memoirs-of-a-cavalier-1720:
Daniel Defoe published Memoirs of a Cavalier in 1720, a military memoir in a found-manuscript frame. The tale covers the Thirty Years' War and the English Civil War in one soldier's life. Many call it the founding historical novel in English, decades before Scott made the form famous.

The Cavalier, a Shropshire squire's son, fights under Gustavus Adolphus in Germany as a young volunteer. Home again, he serves Charles I at Edgehill, Marston Moor, and Naseby in the royal cause. Battles are told with a plain soldier's eye for ground, error, and sheer chance in war. He blames the king's counselors more than the king, and mourns a ruined cause with restraint. Defoe's fake memoir fooled some readers into treating it as a true record.
desaguliers-remarks-perpetual-motion-172:
John Theophilus Desaguliers was the Royal Society's chief man for trials of new machines. In 1720 he wrote this paper for the Philosophical Transactions, the Society's own journal. His theme was the wheels that men said would turn for ever. The claim was old, but fresh wheels still came to the Society each year with bold words.

Desaguliers took the best known wheels of his day and tested their claims by maths and by trial. He showed that loss and drag must stop each one in the end. The paper gave the learned world's first firm no to the whole quest, in print.
dewey-reconstruction-philosophy-1920:
Reconstruction in Philosophy, published in 1920, grows from lectures Dewey gave in Japan and China on his long Asian tour. It is his program for rebuilding philosophy itself: turning it from a spectator's quest for certainty into an instrument of social intelligence.

Dewey traces how philosophy arose from religion and tradition, and how science has changed its task. The modern philosopher, he argues, should help men judge values and direct change, not chase absolute truth behind experience. The book is compact, clear, and programmatic. It served a generation as the manifesto of pragmatism's second, public phase.
diaries-court-ladies-omori-doi-1920:
Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi translated Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan in 1920, the first English version of three Heian classics. The Sarashina Nikki, the Murasaki Shikibu Nikki, and the Izumi Shikibu Nikki speak in women's own voices from about a thousand years ago. Pilgrimages, poems, loves, and court service fill their intimate pages.

Heian Japan prized the diary as high art, and these three show why. Murasaki, author of the Genji, watches her court with a novelist's eye even in private notes. The translations opened a whole literature of Japanese women's writing to the English world.
doe-osti-3022786-arm-aerosol-measurement:
An Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report, DOE/SC-ARM-25-025, records the 2024 strategic planning workshop of ARM's Aerosol Measurement Science Group. It was edited by A. G. Hallar with fifteen co-authors from universities, laboratories, and instrument firms. The group, chartered in 2015, coordinates ARM's aerosol and trace gas observations with user needs. This third workshop, held July 9 and 10, 2024 at the University of Utah, focused on external partnerships.

Recommendations run for five years and are written as action items with owners. Sessions covered links with external sampling networks and modeling communities, choosing core and new aerosol measurements, and presenting measurement uncertainties, calibration protocols, and data products clearly. One thread pushes better discovery tools, such as maps for each measurement type and mining data download and citation patterns to steer users toward the products they actually need.
doe-osti-3376013-system-study-auxiliary-:
Report INL/RPT-25-89607 from Idaho National Laboratory, by Zhegang Ma and dated December 2025, grades the auxiliary feedwater system across the U.S. reactor fleet from 1998 to 2024. The work was done for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's risk analysis arm. Auxiliary feedwater is the backup that feeds steam generators when main feed is lost. The study covers sixty-two commercial reactors. It uses the newest SPAR risk models and failure data from the industry's IRIS reporting system.

Two grades are tracked year by year. The first is start-only failure odds. The second covers a full day of run time. For the most recent ten years, start-only odds show no clear trend up or down. The day-long grade tells a better story: its failure odds fell by a margin the stats call significant. Long data tables give the year-by-year sums for each pump and valve class.
dospassos-one-mans-initiation-1920:
Doran issued One Man's Initiation in a 1922 printing, dedicated to comrades from a road in France. Dos Passos names the road from Erize-la-Petite to Erize-la-Grande in that dedication. He had served as an ambulance driver in France during the war.

Chapter one opens in a huge wharf shed piled with crates and baggage. A band plays thin music as ships wait on either side. A young and tender American then faces the bewildering violence of 1917. Slimmer and more personal than Three Soldiers, the tale of lost innocence helped announce a major new voice in war writing.
dubois-wadjak-1920:
Eugene Dubois, the Dutch army doctor who found Java man, issued this second memoir on the Wadjak skulls in Dutch in 1920. The skulls came from a cave at Wadjak in Java, dug in 1888 and 1890. Dubois kept them back from the world for some thirty years.

He calls the Wadjak folk proto-Australian, a first form of the race of Australia. In his scheme, Java links the ape man he found at Trinil to the men of Australia. The late show of the skulls fed his long feud with the learned world of his day.
eddington-space-time-gravitation-1920:
Arthur Eddington published Space, Time and Gravitation in 1920, the first clear English account of Einstein's general relativity. Eddington had led the 1919 eclipse expedition that tested Einstein's prediction. Starlight bending near the sun matched the theory, and Eddington became its chief English champion. The book explains curved space-time without heavy mathematics.

He uses diagrams, analogies, and careful prose to guide lay readers. Chapters cover the principle of relativity, gravitation as geometry, and the tests of the theory. The book brought Einstein to the English-speaking public. It remains a model of science writing: exact, humane, and clear. Historians still cite its role in relativity's triumph.
einstein-relativity-lawson-1920:
Albert Einstein wrote Relativity himself to explain his theories to general readers. Robert W. Lawson's English translation appeared in 1920. The book covers both the special theory and the general theory in plain stages. Einstein uses trains, clocks, and falling lifts as his teaching tools.

Readers learn why moving clocks run slow and why gravity bends the path of light. Einstein builds each step on simple cases before the math grows harder. No popular book on the subject carries more weight, since the founder wrote it. It carried relativity to the wider world. The clear voice surprises many first time readers.
eliot-ara-vos-prec-1920:
Ara Vos Prec, published in London in 1920, gathers the poems Eliot wrote in the lean years before The Waste Land. The title, from Dante, means 'Now I pray you', and the book holds some of his sharpest short work.

Alongside French poems, it includes 'Sweeney Erect', 'A Cooking Egg', and 'Whispers of Immortality'. Sweeney, the coarse modern brute, stalks through several pieces, set against Donne, Webster, and the ghosts of a finer past. The verse is bitter, funny, and tightly made. Readers can watch Eliot's voice harden here into the one that would soon shake poetry.
eliot-poems-1920:
T. S. Eliot published Poems in 1920, gathering the short works that had first made his name in London and America. He was then working at a bank and editing a literary journal. The slim volume is the complete set of his early poems in book form.

The poems are cool, witty portraits of modern city people. Prufrock worries through a drawing-room evening, and Portrait of a Lady watches another social visit go thin and sad.
