Short satires mock hollow manners with clipped, musical lines. Readers in 1920 met a new kind of poetry here: ironic, learned, and quietly bleak about modern life.
eliot-sacred-wood-1920:
T. S. Eliot gathered his early criticism in this 1920 volume, and it changed how English poetry was read. These essays, written while he worked at a bank and taught evening classes, argue for a new standard of taste.

The famous piece, 'Tradition and the Individual Talent', claims a poet must absorb the whole past of literature and then surrender the self to it. 'Hamlet and His Problems' introduces the objective correlative, his test for whether a work's feelings are truly earned. Other essays rank poets and clear ground for modern verse. Few slim books of criticism have carried this much force.
europmc-pmc10817020:
Zhang and Dhalla review how swelling signals drive heart and vessel disease in this 2024 paper. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of illness and death around the world. Certain cytokines, which are small proteins that carry signals between cells, stir up swelling, called inflammation. Three of the most studied are interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor, and the interleukin-1 family.

The review traces how these signals interact with cell stress and calcium handling inside heart cells. It covers their roles in blocked arteries, blood clots, heart attacks, and heart failure. It also covers rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heartbeat. Proof from lab and clinic work shows these signals matter, the authors say. Whether they can serve as warning markers or drug targets is still unclear, so they call for more research.
europmc-pmc11126520:
GBD 2021 Causes of Death Collaborators break down 288 causes of death worldwide from 1990 to 2021 in this 2024 study. Regular, detailed reporting on why people die is fundamental for public health choices. Such counts also show how each cause lifts or drags life expectancy. They matter most after large death spikes such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

The analysis drew on 56,604 data sources in total. They included death registration, verbal autopsy, surveys, and cancer registries, the team reports. Verbal autopsy means interviewing families about a death's symptoms. Most cause-specific death rates were fitted with an ensemble model that blends several models. Counts cover 204 countries and 811 subnational locations by age and sex. Years of life lost were estimated for each cause. The authors say the comparisons reveal each cause's true weight.
europmc-pmc1308820:
Abernethy and co-authors validated a revised performance scale for palliative care in 2005. The Karnofsky scale is the standard for patient function. A community-focused variant suited palliative settings better. Their Australia-modified version blends both scales for any care setting.

All three scales were scored for 306 trial patients in South Australia. Ratings totaled 1,600 timepoints across settings. The median score was 60 on all three scales. The new scale agreed with the original in 87 percent of ratings. Most disagreements sat within one level on the 11-level scale. Kappa values backed the strong agreement between scales.
europmc-pmc1326220:
Fournier and co-authors compared genomes of a drug-resistant hospital bacterium in 2006. A. baumannii was drug-sensitive in the 1970s. It is now a major hospital infection threat worldwide. Two strains were sequenced: an epidemic resistant strain and a susceptible one.

The resistant strain genome measured about 3.9 million base pairs. It held an 86,000-base resistance island, the largest then known. Forty-five resistance genes clustered inside that island. The susceptible strain, linked to body lice, lacked the island. Fournier shows resistance arrived as one large acquired block. The work used full genome reads of both strains.
europmc-pmc1351920:
Hotez and co-authors argued for joining tropical disease control to big disease programs in 2006. Global funds had surged for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. Together those three cause 5.6 million deaths yearly. They also drain 166 million disability-adjusted life years per year.

Neglected tropical diseases overlap the same poor populations. Three billion people live on under two dollars a day. The authors propose a rapid-impact package delivered alongside big-three programs. Shared delivery could cut costs and widen reach. Hotez argues success against the big three may require fighting neglected diseases too.
europmc-pmc1440920:
Some RNAs do work in the cell rather than code for proteins. Pedersen and co-authors swept the human genome for such folded RNAs in 2006. They compared our DNA with that of seven other species, from chimp to puffer fish. Their method scores shapes that stay alike across species, a sign the shape does a job.

The sweep found about 48,000 candidate structures. It caught many known working RNAs, plus 169 fresh candidates for microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune genes. Some hits may guide chemical edits to RNA or help insert a rare building block. Pedersen warns some hits are false, but the list gives labs clear leads to test.
europmc-pmc1464820:
A gene tree and a species tree can tell different stories. Degnan and Rosenberg explored that clash in 2006. As species split, gene copies sort by chance, so a gene's history may not match the species path. They used a chance-based model of that sorting.

Their proof holds for any species tree with five or more species. For some branch lengths, the most likely gene tree differs from the species tree itself. Degnan warns that picking the most common gene tree can thus give a wrong answer with growing data. The pair close with ways to dodge this trap in genome studies.
europmc-pmc1538620:
Claudins seal the gaps between cells, and their levels shift in cancer. Hewitt, Agarwal, and Morin surveyed the whole family in 2006. They tracked all 21 human claudin genes across 266 normal and cancer tissues, using a large public database plus lab tests.

Most claudin genes spoke more softly in cancer. Three, CLDN3, CLDN4, and CLDN7, spoke louder in many cancers, including pancreas, bladder, ovary, and colon. CLDN5 ran high in blood vessel lining, a possible target for drugs that starve tumors. Hewitt flags CLDN18 as a candidate marker for stomach cancer. The survey covered the whole claudin family, in healthy tissue and in cancers.
europmc-pmc1550420:
Tiny gene tuners called microRNAs go awry in colon cancer. Bandrés and co-authors measured 156 of them in 2006, comparing tumors with nearby healthy tissue. Only a few microRNAs had known jobs, yet changed levels had been tied to cancer growth.

Thirteen microRNAs differed clearly between tumor and healthy tissue. The strongest shifts hit miR-31, miR-96, miR-133b, miR-135b, miR-145, and miR-183. Levels of miR-31 also tracked the tumor's stage. Bandrés suggests the microRNA pattern could help predict how colon tumors behave and how patients fare.  Such profiles may also help separate tumor subtypes that behave in unlike ways.
europmc-pmc1637120:
Grouping proteins into working modules from interaction webs is a crowded craft. Brohée and van Helden benchmarked four clustering algorithms in 2006. Interaction data carry false links and missing links, so tools must be robust.

They built a test web from 220 known yeast complexes, then made 41 warped versions by adding or cutting links. Four methods, MCL, RNSC, SPC, and MCODE, were run at varied settings. The team measured how sensitive each was to its parameters and to noise. Brohée gives users a grounded guide for picking settings instead of trusting defaults.
europmc-pmc1851020:
Turner, Mamo and Karlsson reviewed in 2007 how heat-loving microbes and their enzymes could power biorefineries. A biorefinery turns plant biomass into chemicals and fuels using microbes and enzymes. Hot processes mix better, dissolve feedstocks faster, and resist contamination, but most enzymes fail when heated.

Thermophiles are microbes that thrive at high temperatures, and their enzymes keep working where normal ones unfold. The review covers their use in converting carbohydrate feedstocks, with worked cases for lignocellulose, the woody part of plants, and starch. It also assesses tricks that make enzymes more heat-stable, either by changing the protein or its conditions. A final thread covers genetic vectors, the carrier DNA used to install enzyme genes in heat-loving host microbes for production.
europmc-pmc1895920:
Hagmann, Thiran and co-authors mapped in 2007 the structural wiring of whole living human brains with diffusion MRI. This scan type follows water along white matter bundles, letting researchers trace the cables between brain regions without surgery. A full connection map is a long-standing goal in neuroscience.

Their method builds large, individual connection datasets for a whole brain, usable in living or dead, human or animal subjects. For two human volunteers, the resulting networks followed an exponential pattern in how many connections each node holds. A few nodes carry many links, but the numbers fall off smoothly rather than in a long tail. Globally, both brains showed small-world organization, with short paths between any two regions. The pipeline turns one scan session into a complete network dataset per person.
europmc-pmc1978520:
Körding and co-authors asked in 2007 how the brain decides whether two senses report the same event. Seeing a movement and hearing a sound nearby may share one cause. Or they may be separate. The team built an ideal-observer model, a maths model of the best possible judge. It infers whether cues share a source and where that source lies.

Human subjects did two tasks locating sounds and sights together. The model closely predicted their non-linear way of combining cues. People integrated cues when they were close, and split them when far apart. The results show people infer causal structure during basic perception. This happens constantly and without conscious effort, not only in high-level thinking.
europmc-pmc2124920:
William S. Halsted, professor of surgery at Johns Hopkins, described his bulkhead suture of the intestine in 1912. Joining gut end to end, he argues, should be the method of choice if it were as safe as the side-to-side join. Sometimes it is the only possible join. Spillage of bowel contents, he notes, feeds the deaths that follow the circular suture, above all in the large bowel.

His goal was a truly clean join. In the winter of 1909 and 1910, with Dr. Willis D. Gatch, he ran dog experiments toward a device that would seal the gut while it is sewn. Gelatin stuck to the mandrels; firmness failed; licorice, turned into perfect cylinders, came back. Readers get a famous surgeon thinking aloud through failures toward a cleaner operation.
europmc-pmc2125120:
B. S. Kline and M. C. Winternitz of Johns Hopkins reported on pneumonia immunity in rabbits in 1913, the sixth of their series. Rabbits that recover from an attack of experimental pneumonia, they found, carry an active immunity. Such animals can then withstand repeated, increasing doses of pneumococci blown into the windpipe.

Death can still follow a later injection, but its character changes. Fatal first attacks always run with germs flooding the blood. Later deaths usually do not; they seem tied to chronic damage in the heart and breathing apparatus left by earlier disease. Their tables count germs per cubic millimeter in the blood of fatal cases, from forty thousand to millions. Readers get immunity built dose by dose, and then bottled and passed on.
europmc-pmc2131120:
Bernhard Steinberg and E. E. Ecker raised an antiserum against the soluble poison of the colon bacillus and used it to save rabbits from peritonitis. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926. Colon bacilli injected into a rabbit's belly cavity kill within hours, yet the peritoneum shows only slight change.

That mismatch points to a soluble toxin as the lethal factor. The fluid from young colon bacillus cultures, spun free of germs and heated, reproduced the whole fatal course by itself. A quiet hour or so passed, then symptoms ending in death. The toxin's potency varies, partly with the material and partly with each animal's resistance. Serum from immunized rabbits, given into a vein, can avert death in animals already dosed with lethal amounts of culture. Death here is poisoning, not invasion, and poisoning can be met with an antidote.
europmc-pmc2140420:
John Northrop studied the meaning of acidity for pepsin digestion in a 1920 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Pepsin digests proteins fastest at one best acidity for each protein. Northrop measured digestion rate and electrical conductivity of protein solutions side by side across the acidity scale, to test whether the two curves are one.

Digestion rate and conductivity ran very closely parallel. For gelatin, the best acidity for digestion and the peak of ionization were the same, and the two curves hugged each other throughout. Adding a salt sharing the acid's anion depressed digestion just as the same amount of extra acid did. All the facts fit the view that the amount of ionized protein present decides the digestion rate.
europmc-pmc2140720:
Thomas Morrison, at Princeton and the Nela Research Laboratories, studied the light of luminous bacteria in a 1925 paper, part two of his series. Part one had given a way to measure the glow's intensity in numbers. Here the temperature is varied and the brightness tracked, to learn what kind of process makes the light.

The temperature coefficients for light intensity do not follow the van't Hoff rule. They run higher than that rule predicts and change from one ten-degree interval to the next. The glow is no simple process: the observed curve is the sum of several reactions running at once. Near the optimum temperature, a coagulation of the enzyme's colloidal particles may bend the curve further from the chemical norm.
europmc-pmc2140820:
Otto Warburg, Franz Wind, and Erwin Negelein, at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Biology in Berlin-Dahlem, studied tumor metabolism in the living body in a 1927 paper. Tumor cells gain energy two ways: by respiration, burning material fully, and by fermentation, splitting glucose to lactic acid. The question was whether that fermentation, first shown in cut tumor pieces, holds inside the body, and how tumors are fed.

Blood leaving a tumor carries less glucose and more lactic acid than blood entering it, in hens, rats, and a human arm tumor alike. Fermentation runs strongest where capillary blood enters and fades along the vessel, averaging about half its top rate. Raising the blood glucose raised tumor consumption close to double, as predicted. Tumors of all kinds tested behave fundamentally alike in this.
europmc-pmc2323620:
Husain and Nachev reviewed the parietal cortex in 2007, a brain region at the top and back of the head. Standard theory split brain processing into two streams, one for space and action and one for objects. Damage to the right lower parietal lobe often causes spatial neglect, where patients ignore one side of space.

The authors argued that this simple split does not fit the lower parietal lobe. They summed up brain scans and lesion studies showing plainly non-spatial jobs for this region. Those jobs include holding attention over time and spotting key events in a stream of events. Upper parietal zones do handle space and guide action. Lower zones, they concluded, do something that fits neither classic stream.
europmc-pmc2394820:
Terwilliger and colleagues described an automated structure-building wizard in 2008. In X-ray crystallography, scientists build an atomic model into an electron-density map, a cloud showing where atoms sit. They then refine the model, use it to sharpen the map, and rebuild, cycling many times.

The PHENIX AutoBuild wizard runs that whole cycle on its own. It belongs to the PHENIX software project for crystallography. The wizard works from starting phase information obtained by any of the standard routes: comparing similar crystals, using heavy-atom signals, or molecular replacement with a known structure. The authors noted that rival automated tools still struggled at low resolution and at finishing partial models. AutoBuild was built as a second-generation answer to those gaps, aiming at complete, accurate models with little manual work.
europmc-pmc2467420:
Kramer and colleagues, writing for the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Board of Trustees Task Force on Standardized Protocols, set standard scanning protocols for heart MRI in 2008. Cardiac magnetic resonance can measure heart size, blood flow, and scar tissue, but each centre scanned differently, making results hard to compare.

The document lays out shared modules: safety and stress-test equipment, left and right heart function, contrast dye dosing, and first-pass perfusion, which tracks dye through heart muscle. It then gives disease-specific protocols. For blocked-artery disease these cover fresh heart attacks, long-standing damage and viability checks, and two drug stress methods. Further sections cover vessel imaging of the limbs and chest, abnormal coronary arteries, and lung vein checks. Valve disease, heart muscle diseases, congenital defects, and heart masses each get their own protocol.
europmc-pmc2467520:
Hooft, Straver, and Spek presented a statistical method for pinning down a molecule's absolute structure in 2008. Crystallographers can often solve a molecule's shape but not its handedness: which mirror-image form it takes. Handedness matters because the two forms of a drug can act very differently in the body.

Their approach uses Bijvoet differences, tiny intensity gaps between paired X-ray reflections that carry the handedness signal. Rather than forcing a yes-or-no call, they apply Bayesian statistics in a maximum-likelihood framework. That yields a probability for each possible structure, including the standard Flack parameter used to report the answer. The method was aimed at biologically active molecules, where weak signals are common. A probability statement, they argued, is more honest than the sharp verdicts older methods gave on thin evidence.
europmc-pmc2518220:
Curia, Longo, Biagini, Jones, and Avoli reviewed in 2008 the pilocarpine model, a standard animal model of temporal lobe epilepsy. In this model, injecting rodents with the drug pilocarpine triggers a long seizure episode. A quiet latent period follows. Finally, spontaneous recurring seizures begin. That sequence mirrors the human disease, which often follows an early injury and involves scarring in the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory.

The authors compared methods across many laboratories, since results shift with rodent species, strain, sex, age, dose, and drug combinations. They weighed death rates, timing of the first spontaneous seizures, neuron damage, and how brain networks rewired under each protocol. They conclude the model stays valuable for studying how epilepsy develops, especially if standardised to cut deaths and reduce variation.
europmc-pmc2527820:
Beckermann and colleagues asked in 2008 whether stem cells from bone marrow help pancreatic tumours grow their blood supply. These mesenchymal stem cells travel through the blood and settle in wounds and tumours, but why tumours attract them was unclear. The team tracked the cells in dishes and in mice carrying human pancreatic tumours.

The stem cells moved toward growth signals the tumours release, including PDGF and VEGF, and blocking drugs could stop that migration. Within hours they entered tumour-like spheres grown in the laboratory. Labelled cells injected into mice gathered in the tumours and interacted with vessel walls. Crucially, the cells released VEGF themselves, and tumours given them grew denser blood vessel networks. Silencing VEGF in the stem cells removed that boost.
europmc-pmc2535620:
Kan and colleagues studied daily deaths in Shanghai from 2001 to 2004 to see who is most harmed by dirty air. Four pollutants were tracked: fine particles, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. The team asked whether season, sex, age, and schooling changed how strongly pollution tracked with mortality across the city's four years of daily records.

All four pollutants were linked to deaths from all causes and from heart and lung disease. A standard rise in particle levels, for example, came with a 0.25 percent increase in daily mortality, and the other gases showed larger effects. Pollution bit harder in the cool season than the warm one. Women, older people, and residents with little schooling proved more vulnerable than others facing the same air.
europmc-pmc2565420:
Groenewegen reviewed the basal ganglia and motor control in this 2003 paper. The basal ganglia are a set of deep brain structures, including the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and subthalamic nucleus. They connect with the cortex and thalamus in a series of parallel loops that stay largely separate from one another.

Those loops serve not only movement but also thinking and emotion. Groenewegen argues a main job of the basal ganglia is learning and selecting the most fitting motor or behavioural programme for the moment. Their internal wiring suits such selection in children and adults alike. He also weighs whether childhood clumsiness partly reflects basal ganglia dysfunction, comparing their role with the cerebellum's in developing motor control.
europmc-pmc2575520:
Covington, Maloof, Straume, Kay, and Harmer combined several genome-wide data sets in 2008 to measure how much of a plant's genome its body clock controls. Earlier microarray studies of the model plant Arabidopsis disagreed wildly, putting clock control at anywhere from 5 to 15 percent of genes. The team reanalysed the experiments with standardised methods to find the true scale.

Combining data sets proved far more powerful than any single run. The unified analysis found 3,975 clock-regulated genes, and between 31 and 41 percent of all expressed genes showed circadian, roughly daily, rhythms in abundance. Clock-regulated genes clustered in hormone and stress-response pathways, suggesting the clock steers how plants answer nearly every hormone and stress. The authors also identified DNA elements in gene promoters that set the time of day each gene peaks.
europmc-pmc2630720:
van de Sande-Bruinsma and colleagues confronted antibiotic use with resistance across Europe in 2008. They reported for the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System Group and the European Surveillance of Antimicrobial Consumption Project Group. Drug effectiveness is a shared resource being eroded by overuse, and new antibiotics were drying up. The study merged the continent's two big tracking databases. One covers drug use, the other drug resistance.

They compared outpatient drug use, adjusted for population size, against resistance trends. The check covered three drug-and-germ pairs in 21 countries over 2000 to 2005. The routine tracking data did show a link. Higher national use went with higher national resistance. The authors present the joint analysis as support for steps that cut drug use at national level. They caution that country-level data cannot untangle how prescribing and resistance truly connect.
europmc-pmc2631520:
Ma and Huang proposed a statistical method in 2009 for picking reliable cancer genes by pooling several microarray studies at once. Single studies measure thousands of genes in few patients, so the marker genes they select are unstable. Pooling raises power, but studies differ in design and gene counts dwarf sample sizes. Their method, called Meta Threshold Gradient Descent Regularization, was built for exactly this setting.

The method lets each experiment keep its own settings while selecting one shared set of cancer-associated genes across all of them. It also accounts for genes acting jointly rather than one at a time. In simulations and in real pancreatic and liver cancer data sets, it outperformed existing approaches at recovering dependable markers. The authors offer it as an effective route to robust gene selection.
europmc-pmc2638020:
Barr and co-authors mapped the shapes of a large family of human proteins in work published in 2009. The proteins, called tyrosine phosphatases, remove chemical tags from other proteins and so help control cell signals. Faults in them are tied to many diseases, which makes them targets for new drugs.

The team solved the three-dimensional shapes of 22 family members and compared them with shapes known before. The basic fold was shared, yet the surfaces differed a great deal from one protein to the next. Many carried an extra pocket beside the main working site, a spot that could help drugs pick one member only. Tests of working speed also varied widely. Three members, named PTPD1, PTPD2, and HDPTP, proved unable to do the chemistry at all.
europmc-pmc2656620:
Brisse and colleagues sorted in 2009 the family lines of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ that lives harmlessly in many people yet causes hospital infections of urine, lungs, and blood. Some rare lines cause distinct diseases, such as a liver abscess illness spreading in Asia. Knowing which lines are dangerous could sharpen control.

The team typed 235 samples from patients and the environment, checking their genes, capsule coats, and power to sicken mice. Clear clones emerged, each tied to its own source and behavior. Two clones wearing the K1 coat linked to liver abscess and lung infection. Two nose and throat diseases each matched a single narrow clone, so those named subspecies count as clones too. One K2 clone was fiercely virulent in mice, the other not. Coat genes, it turned out, can jump between lines, blurring the coat as a danger sign.
europmc-pmc2667420:
Guh and colleagues pooled 89 studies in 2009 to measure how often overweight and obese people go on to develop other diseases. Extra weight was known to raise many risks, but firm numbers for each illness were scattered. The team searched two large databases for solid forward-looking studies and merged their results.

Eighteen linked illnesses met their standards. Overweight raised the odds of type II diabetes, most cancers, heart and vessel disease, asthma, gallbladder disease, joint wear, and chronic back pain. The strongest single link was diabetes in women, at nearly four times the risk of normal-weight women. Obesity raised the same risks further in nearly every case. Two cancers, of the food pipe and prostate, showed no clear link. The numbers give doctors and planners a shared scale for the harm done by extra weight.
europmc-pmc2771920:
Brennan and co-authors showed in 2009 that glioblastomas, the most common malignant brain tumors, fall into subclasses defined by which signaling pathways are active. Tumors grouped under one name differ widely, and sorting them by switched-on pathways could guide targeted drugs. They ran targeted protein analysis on twenty-seven surgical glioma samples, then checked the patterns against genome and expression data from two hundred forty-three tumors in The Cancer Genome Atlas.

Three subclasses emerged in roughly equal shares. One ran on EGFR signaling, with receptor amplification and mutation plus strong Notch activity. A second was driven by PDGF signaling, mostly through excess ligand. The third had lost NF1, a brake on the RAS pathway, and showed lower overall MAPK and PI3K activity. Each class matched a known gene-expression subclass, tying protein signals to signature gene changes.
europmc-pmc2791220:
Fellay and a large team, including the NIAID Center for HIV/AIDS Vaccine Immunology (CHAVI), scanned the genomes of two thousand five hundred fifty-four people with HIV-1 in 2009. They sought common DNA variants that help some people keep the virus at low levels without treatment.

The scan strongly confirmed three links found in an earlier, smaller study, and all sat in one genome region tied to immune defense. Added effects from both common and rare variants appeared in that same region, plus a cluster for virus entry receptors on chromosome three. No variant outside those areas held up, which narrowed where control of HIV-1 seems to be written in DNA.
europmc-pmc2799520:
Chen and a large team tested in 2010 whether one short DNA stretch, called ITS2, could serve as a standard barcode for naming medicinal plants. A barcode here means a short gene region whose spelling differs enough to tell species apart. The group compared seven candidate regions across medicinal species.

ITS2 copied most reliably, showed a clear gap between variation within and between species, and beat the other candidates. Tested on more than six thousand six hundred samples from four thousand eight hundred species, it named the right species in more than nine of ten cases. The team proposes ITS2 as a standard barcode for medicinal plants and a wider plant naming tool.
europmc-pmc2832020:
Khanna and colleagues found in 2010 why diabetic wounds stay inflamed instead of healing: their cleanup cells fail at eating the dead. Wound macrophages must clear away apoptotic cells, meaning cells that died on schedule, before inflammation can end. The team took macrophages from wounds of diabetic mice and tested that eating job, called efferocytosis.

Diabetic wound macrophages cleared dead cells poorly, leaving a heavy burden of them in the tissue. The same burden appeared in wound tissue from diabetic patients. Forcing extra dead cells into wounds stoked inflammatory signals and muted calming ones. When cleanup worked, macrophages switched into an anti-inflammatory mode, tying the eating job directly to healing.
europmc-pmc2841820:
Livshits and colleagues followed middle-aged British women in the Chingford Study for fifteen years to test whether blood markers of inflammation predict knee osteoarthritis seen on X-rays. Osteoarthritis, the wearing breakdown of joints, lacks any accepted early warning marker. Nearly a thousand women gave X-rays and blood at set visits across the study.

The share with clear knee damage rose from about fifteen percent to nearly half over the period. Women who developed it ran higher body weight and higher levels of two inflammation markers, CRP and IL-6. Higher IL-6 at year five independently forecast damage at year ten, alongside age and starting weight. Women in the top IL-6 quarter faced nearly triple the odds of the bottom quarter.
europmc-pmc2856220:
Hedström, Svensson, Bergström, and Michno charted every fracture treated in children and teenagers around Umeå, Sweden, in 2010, using a hospital injury database running since 1993. Over ten thousand fracture events appeared in the records through 2007. The team mapped which bones broke, how the injuries happened, and how patterns shifted with age, sex, and calendar year.

Falling caused most fractures, and the far end of the forearm was the commonest break. Rates peaked at eleven to twelve years in girls and thirteen to fourteen in boys, with boys breaking bones half again as often as girls. Fracture incidence rose about thirteen percent over the decade to 2007, which the authors partly blame on changing activity patterns in children.
europmc-pmc2877420:
Limmathurotsakul and colleagues tracked in 2010 a rising tide of melioidosis, a severe soil-borne infection, in northeast Thailand. The culprit is Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium living in soil and water that enters through skin cuts. They counted every culture-confirmed case admitted to the region's main hospital across a decade.

More than twenty-two hundred cases gave an average rate near thirteen per hundred thousand people a year. The rate climbed steadily, from about eight to over twenty-one per hundred thousand across the study years. Men, people over forty-five, and people with diabetes, known or hidden, faced the highest risk. Deaths ran above forty percent, making melioidosis the region's third deadliest infection after HIV and tuberculosis by 2006.
europmc-pmc2901520:
Egecioglu and co-authors showed in 2010 that the hunger hormone ghrelin also drives craving for tasty food through the brain's reward hub. They targeted the ventral tegmental area, a midbrain node that feeds dopamine to reward circuits. Mice missing the ghrelin receptor and rats given a receptor blocker both ate less of a rewarding food when offered a free choice against plain chow.

Rewarding food normally triggers a dopamine surge in the accumbens, a reward center, and that surge vanished in receptor-free mice. Injecting ghrelin straight into the hub boosted one-hour intake of rewarding food but not of chow. Blocking the receptor also killed the learned place preference for the tasty food. Hunger chemistry thus sets how much pleasure food is worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc2912920:
Arain, Campbell, Cooper, and Lancaster asked in 2010 what a pilot or feasibility study actually is, after finding the terms used loosely across medicine. A 2004 review had urged that such small preliminary studies stick to description and sample size planning rather than testing treatments. The team re-screened seven major journals for 2007 and 2008 and also surveyed trial registries, funders, and editors.

Fifty-four pilot or feasibility papers turned up, about half of them pilot trials of interventions. Practice had barely budged: many still ran hypothesis tests their small samples cannot support. Worse, registries, grant bodies, and journals each defined the terms differently, and some had no policy at all. The authors press for shared definitions so pilots do the sizing and feasibility work they exist for.
europmc-pmc2919420:
David and colleagues, working in Cynthia Kenyon's laboratory, reported in 2010 that ordinary proteins clump with age in the worm C. elegans, not just the disease proteins famous for aggregating. Sticky clumps define Alzheimer's and similar illnesses, yet whether normal aging itself is clumping-prone was unknown. Using systematic proteomics, the team separated the insoluble fraction of young and old worms and named its contents.

Several hundred normal proteins became insoluble and aggregation-prone as the worms aged. The set was not random debris: it was rich in proteins that influence how other proteins fold and clump. In tests, these age-clumped proteins nudged disease-linked proteins toward aggregation and worsened their toxicity. Aging itself tilts the whole protein pool toward clumping, which may explain why age is the master risk factor for aggregation diseases.
europmc-pmc2919520:
Cornuet, Ravigné, and Estoup upgraded in 2010 DIYABC, software that infers population history from genetic data using approximate Bayesian computation. The approach simulates millions of datasets under competing histories, like splits and admixtures between populations, and keeps the histories whose simulations resemble the real data. Version 1.0 widens what the software can digest and, crucially, lets users check whether a chosen model actually fits.

It now accepts DNA sequence data alongside microsatellites and handles five locus types, including sex-linked and mitochondrial markers with balanced or skewed sex ratios. Simulated tests showed mixing data types can sharpen scenario choice and parameter estimates. The new model-checking step, long neglected in this field, flags histories that merely win a contest without truly explaining the data.
europmc-pmc2949620:
Drummond and Suchard introduced a Bayesian method for dating family trees when evolution speeds up and slows down across branches, in a 2010 article. Strict clock models assume one steady rate, an idea real lineages often break.

Their approach lays many local clocks over different parts of a tree and averages over the possible placements using computer sampling, while estimating the tree itself at the same time. That setup lets users test the single-rate idea directly against a huge range of alternatives. Worked examples cover mammal, primate, and influenza histories, with new ways to display the resulting rate patterns.
europmc-pmc2954820:
Huang, Lee, Marcotte, and Hurles mapped genes where losing one copy matters, a state called haploinsufficiency, in a 2010 genome study. One working copy is not always enough, and such genes cause many dominant diseases.

They contrasted several hundred known sensitive genes with over a thousand genes repeatedly damaged in healthy people, so judged tolerant. Sensitive genes tended to be longer, more conserved, busier in early development, and more connected in gene networks. A model built on those traits scored all genes, and high scorers indeed clustered among dominant disease genes and mouse lines with faults from a single lost copy.
europmc-pmc3009720:
Globisch and co-authors measured a sixth DNA base, hydroxymethylcytosine, across mouse tissues in a 2010 study. They also hunted for further bases. Such bases would prove an active removal pathway for methylation marks. The new base forms from the classic methyl mark, and its job was unknown.

Using an ultra-sensitive isotope method, they found the base in every tissue and cell type, richest in brain nerve cells. The expected follow-on bases of a stepwise removal chain were essentially absent, arguing against that demethylation route. The base looks more like a stable feature of nerve cells than a passing step.
europmc-pmc3117820:
Ralf Hass and colleagues compared human repair cells drawn from adult and newborn tissues in a 2011 mini-review in Cell Communication and Signaling. These versatile cells, found near blood vessels in most tissues, can renew themselves, turn into several cell types, and calm immune responses. Sources range from bone marrow and fat to placenta and cord tissue.

The review contrasts the sources on growth speed, surface markers, and range of cell types they can form. Neighbouring cells, low oxygen, and small regulatory RNAs all shift how each population behaves, so cells from different tissues are not interchangeable. For doctors hoping to use them in healing, the paper maps which source suits which job and what still needs testing.
europmc-pmc3139420:
Craig Johnson and colleagues found a hidden protein in a pig virus in a 2011 paper in the Journal of General Virology. The virus causes the most costly swine disease worldwide, harming breeding and breathing, yet its protein set was thought complete. Suspecting a missed reading frame, the team purified virus particles and searched them for unknown pieces.

A small protein of about fifty building blocks turned up inside the particles, read from an alternate frame overlapping the gene for the main coat protein. Infected cells make it, and infected pigs raise antibodies against it. The same hidden frame appears in every member of the virus family. The finding adds a target for vaccines and drugs and hints the protein matters across the whole family.
europmc-pmc3212920:
David Clark described England's Improving Access to Psychological Therapies programme in this 2011 article in the International Review of Psychiatry. The programme was a large national effort to make recommended talk therapies for depression and anxiety widely available through the National Health Service. Clark explains why it was launched and how it was organized.

He covers the arguments behind the programme, its therapist training scheme, and the model its clinics follow. At the halfway point of the national rollout, progress matched expectations, and many people who would otherwise have received no evidence-based therapy had been treated and benefited. Clark closes by outlining planned developments and the challenges the expanding service still faces.
europmc-pmc3271020:
Ali Zomorrodi and Costas Maranas introduced OptCom, a framework for modeling the metabolism of microbial communities, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. Microbes rarely live alone, yet what each member contributes to a community's chemistry, and who trades what with whom, remains poorly understood despite abundant sequencing data. Existing models typically optimized a single goal, which misrepresents real communities.

OptCom instead sets up nested optimization: each species pursues its own fitness inside, while the outer problem maximizes a community-level goal, exposing the trade-offs between the two. It handles any mix of cooperative and competitive interactions and any number of species. The authors applied it to a well-studied two-species partnership, to light-harvesting microbial mats, and to a model community. They measured how much metabolites and electrons move between members. They also tested what happens when a new member joins.
europmc-pmc3272020:
Ian Holmes, Keith Harris, and Christopher Quince introduced Dirichlet multinomial mixtures, a statistical model for microbial community data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Metagenomic surveys produce tables counting how often each organism appears in each sample, tables that are sparse and uneven in size. Older clustering methods ignored those quirks, so the authors built a generative model that respects them.

Each community is described by a probability profile over taxa, drawn from one of a few mixture components; the components act as community types, sometimes called enterotypes. Applied to gut microbe data from obese and lean twins, the model favored four clusters, two dominated by Bacteroides and two more variable. Body mass did not map onto a distinct community type. Obese twins were, however, more often found in the variable clusters. The authors call this an Anna Karenina pattern, and they verified it in Crohn's disease data.
europmc-pmc3284220:
Annette Michalski and colleagues introduced the Q Exactive, a benchtop mass spectrometer for proteomics, in this 2011 paper in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. Protein analysis by mass spectrometry demands speed, sensitivity, and resolution at once. The new instrument couples a quadrupole mass filter, which selects ions almost instantly, to an Orbitrap analyzer, which weighs them with high precision, a pairing not reported before.

An improved ion lens delivered high currents, and parallel filling and detection kept cycle times near one second. In standard ninety-minute runs on digested cell extracts, the instrument found more than twenty-five hundred proteins, a clear step beyond earlier Orbitrap models. Its fast switching also enables multiplexed modes, selecting and fragmenting several precursors in quick succession for joint analysis. The authors present the robust benchtop design as an advance for proteomics and for chemistry at large.
europmc-pmc3331820:
Abrantes, van der Loo, Le Pendu, and Esteves reviewed a fast killing rabbit disease and the virus behind it, in a 2012 article. The virus first appeared in China in 1984 and swept the world, killing adult European rabbits within two to three days of infection. Australia and New Zealand even released it on purpose to control pest rabbits.

Infected rabbits die mainly of acute liver destruction, with bleeding in lungs, heart, and kidneys from runaway clotting. All deadly strains form a single type, though two subtypes circulate, and harmless relatives may have come first. No other species is known to die of it. Control in rabbit farms rests on vaccination and strict hygiene, which are hard to apply to wild rabbits. The review gathers what is known about the virus's spread, evolution, and possible future use as a medical tool.
europmc-pmc3352820:
Lawrence and colleagues ran tests to see whether living with other species changes how a population adapts to a new setting. Most lab studies of adaptation use one species alone, yet in the wild organisms always adapt in company. The team therefore grew bacterial communities side by side with matching single-species cultures and watched how each changed.

Species changing together did not follow the path they took alone. Community members shifted toward split, complementary use of resources, carving up the setting rather than all chasing the same solution. Those shifts also changed how the whole system worked. The results say adaptation in nature cannot always be foretold from single-species tests.
europmc-pmc3403920:
Francisco and colleagues released software in 2012 to make sense of the flood of sequence-based typing data used to track bacteria. Such typing has become the standard for watching outbreaks locally and worldwide. Its databases hold rich strain profiles and case details, but no friendly tool existed to explore them together.

Their program, PHYLOViZ, runs on any platform and links typing results with outbreak data in one view. Built-in algorithms draw family trees and minimum spanning trees showing how isolates likely relate. Results appear as annotated graphs that can be layered with any other case information. The free tool aims to help labs turn stored profiles into population insight.
europmc-pmc3424120:
Ferreira and colleagues tested in 2012 whether a magnetic scan method called T1-mapping can spot fresh swelling in heart muscle without injected contrast. The standard T2-weighted scan detects such edema but with limits. The team scanned healthy controls and patients with acute heart swelling from Takotsubo syndrome or regional injury, all within a week of symptoms.

Segments of heart wall with abnormal motion, and even those moving normally, showed clearly raised T1 values in patients. Judged by accuracy curves, T1-mapping beat both dark-blood and bright-blood T2 methods by a wide margin. A single cutoff value separated swollen from normal segments with high sensitivity and specificity. The authors propose T1-mapping as a sharper, objective partner to the older scans.
europmc-pmc3536620:
Long-term fear memories live in a network, and Anne L. Wheeler leads a ten-author team mapping that network in mice in 2013. The team reads Fos, an activity marker, across 84 brain regions after mice recall an old fear memory. They then find which regions switch on together, rather than cutting or recording one region at a time.

The recall network shows a clear thalamus-hippocampus-cortex pattern. Its wiring is both tightly knit and split into modules, a small-world layout, with hub regions in prefrontal cortex and thalamus. The layout shifts as a memory ages. In mutant mice that forget early, the network is changed. The result is a network-level portrait of how a remote memory is stored and brought back.
europmc-pmc3562220:
Karan Uppal and colleagues presented a software package named xMSanalyzer in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. The package serves metabolomics, the study of small molecules in samples such as blood plasma, measured by liquid chromatography joined to mass spectrometry. Standard extraction tools, tuned to avoid false peaks, tend to miss scarce chemicals and ones present in only a few samples.

xMSanalyzer re-runs extraction under several settings and merges the results, balancing sensitivity against reliability. Further modules grade sample quality, check feature consistency, find overlap between data sets, and match measured masses against chemical and pathway databases. On plasma samples, the package more than doubled the features found while improving how reliably each was measured. Spot checks with a second method confirmed that many newly found peaks were real metabolites. The tool is aimed at large, untargeted studies.
europmc-pmc3584320:
Jacques Fantini and Francisco Barrantes mapped how cholesterol docks onto membrane proteins in Frontiers in Physiology in 2013. Cholesterol stiffens cell membranes and tunes the proteins embedded in them, but its grip is picky: it favors certain short patterns in a protein's membrane-spanning parts. Two named patterns, CRAC and its mirror twin CARC, plus tilted segments that lean in the membrane, anchor the review's tour of binding sites.

Despite their variety, these sites share habits, the authors show. A small set of amino acids turns up again and again wherever cholesterol binds, whether the site reads as a simple line of letters or a folded pocket. Forces such as weak stacking attractions help seat the rigid cholesterol frame against its two faces, one smooth and one rough. Examples reach from nerve receptors to proteins tied to Alzheimer disease, giving structural biologists a common grammar for a widespread interaction.
europmc-pmc3598720:
Stephenie Chaudoir, Alicia Dugan, and Colin Barr inventoried the measuring tools of implementation science in Implementation Science in 2013. Good treatments often fail to reach patients because clinics cannot adopt them smoothly. Researchers who study that adoption gap lacked both a shared list of what drives success and a catalogue of questionnaires that measure those drivers. The review searched four databases and one journal for every such measure published to August 2012.

Sixty-two measures surfaced. Sorting them by a five-level framework showed plenty of tools for organizations, providers, and the innovation itself, but few for wider structural forces or for patients. A second, sharper finding: very few measures had proven they actually predict implementation success, the test called criterion validity. The paper hands the young field both a shelf of instruments and a warning about how untested most of them are.
europmc-pmc3620520:
Anthony Levasseur and colleagues expanded a major enzyme database in Biotechnology for Biofuels in 2013. The CAZy database catalogues enzymes that build and break carbohydrates, sorted into families. A surprise finding forced a reshuffle: two families filed as binders or sugar-cutters turned out to be lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases, enzymes that attack tough plant fibers with oxygen chemistry. Lignin, the woody glue always mixed with those fibers, pointed the way to a broader fix.

The team created a new top class, Auxiliary Activities, gathering the fiber-attacking enzymes together with the lignin-degrading families. Comparing the new class across forty-one fungal genomes split the fungi into meaningful groups that matched both family trees and feeding style, white rot against brown rot. The wider net, the authors argue, finally covers the full machinery fungi use to dismantle plant cell walls, a process biofuel makers want to copy.
europmc-pmc3621820:
Mora Murri and colleagues compared gut bacteria in children with type 1 diabetes in BMC Medicine in 2013. A rat study had found the gut community differing at diabetes onset, hinting the microbes help steer the disease, in which the immune system destroys insulin-making cells. Sixteen Spanish children with type 1 diabetes and sixteen healthy children gave stool samples, profiled by two DNA methods, and the patients' sugar control was set against their bacterial counts.

The two groups' gut communities barely overlapped in overall similarity. Diabetic children carried fewer Actinobacteria and Firmicutes, more Bacteroidetes, and a flipped ratio between the two big groups. At finer levels, familiar helpful genera such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium ran low, while Clostridium, Bacteroides, and Veillonella ran high. Some counts, including Bifidobacterium, moved in step with blood sugar control. The authors stop short of claiming cause, and frame the pattern as a lead for mechanism studies.
europmc-pmc3650620:
Fat tissue that swells with immune cells helps drive insulin failure, McArdle, Finucane, Connaughton, McMorrow and Roche explain in a 2013 review in Frontiers in Endocrinology. In obesity, fat tissue calls in immune cells with signal proteins and leaks fatty acids into the blood. The mix sparks more swelling signals, which draw more cells in and block insulin's message, in a loop that ends in type 2 diabetes for many.

Drug plans that target the swelling carry safety worries for long use, the authors note. Food-based plans may suit long care better, even if weaker than a drug. The review walks through how obese fat tissue turns hostile, step by step. It then tests how anti-swelling food parts and special nutrients might break the loop, giving a map from body process to plate-level choices.
europmc-pmc3793920:
Edward Archer, Gregory Hand, and Steven Blair published a validity study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on United States nutrition surveillance data. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey underpins dietary guidelines and policy, and it asks people to report what they eat. The team checked those reports against basic physiology for 28,993 men and 34,369 women surveyed from 1971 to 2010.

Reported energy intake fell far below estimated energy use: the average shortfall was about 281 kilocalories a day for men and 365 for women, and far larger for obese respondents. Across the survey's 39-year history, the intake data of most respondents, about 59 percent of men and 67 percent of women, were not physiologically plausible. Protocol upgrades trimmed under-reporting only slightly. The authors judge the data a very weak base for tracking intake trends.
europmc-pmc3928520:
Andreas Krämer, Jeff Green, Jack Pollard, and Stuart Tugendreich describe the causal reasoning tools built into a commercial gene-analysis platform in Bioinformatics in 2014. Gene-expression experiments list thousands of changed genes, and prior biological knowledge is what turns such lists into explanations. The Ingenuity Knowledge Base stores cause-and-effect links between molecules, hand-curated from the published literature, as one large causal network.

Against that network, their algorithms work out which upstream regulators best explain an observed expression pattern, build step-by-step mechanistic networks, and predict downstream effects on cell functions and diseases. The paper presents four tools, Upstream Regulator Analysis, Mechanistic Networks, Causal Network Analysis, and Downstream Effects Analysis, and validates them on example datasets. The tools ship inside the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software.
europmc-pmc3975420:
Anna Mietelska-Porowska and colleagues review the tau protein in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. Tau normally steadies the microtubule rails inside nerve cells, above all in their long axons, and helps with signaling in branches. Chemical decorations added to tau, and its partnerships with other proteins, tune that work. When the decorations go wrong, tau leaves the rails, piles into the cell body, and forms toxic clumps and tangles.

Those tangles mark a family of dementias called tauopathies. Without working rails, the transport of cargo up and down the neuron falters, synapses lose their supplies and support, and signaling fails. The review connects tau's normal regulation to each step of that breakdown, giving a reference on why this one protein sits at the center of so many brain diseases.
europmc-pmc3990520:
Jared O'Connell and a large team of co-authors set out a broad method for working out haplotypes, in PLoS Genetics in 2014. A haplotype is the set of gene variants a person carries on one copy of a chromosome. Guessing it from test data, called phasing, is a core step in many gene studies, but study groups often mix close and distant kin.

Using data from eight study groups, six from isolated places and two from open ones, the team compared phasing tools. A tool called SHAPEIT2 gave far fewer switch errors than rivals, and near-perfect results where shared DNA stretches were long. They then added a new step, duoHMM, which uses family data to fix errors and spot cross-over points and test faults. The combined route fits groups with any mix of kinship, for human, animal, and plant work alike.
europmc-pmc4013820:
Dao-Fu Dai, Ying Ann Chiao, David J. Marcinek, Hazel H. Szeto, and Peter S. Rabinovitch review oxidative stress in mitochondria and ageing, in Longevity and Healthspan in 2014. A long-held theory blames ageing on harm from reactive oxygen species, unstable by-products of cell chemistry. Mitochondria, the cell's power units, are both the main source of these species and a prime target of their harm.

The record is mixed: many attempts to boost antioxidant defences in rodents did not extend life, and human trials of antioxidant pills mostly fell flat. Still, mitochondrial reactive oxygen clearly shapes the health of ageing organs. The review covers the heart, blood vessels, muscle, brain, and sugar control, plus age-linked cancers. It also weighs drugs built to guard mitochondria, among them two targeted antioxidants and a protective peptide. The piece aims to sort where the theory holds and where it fails.
europmc-pmc4189020:
Yukiko Kimura, Shin-ichi Higashijima, and two co-authors reported a cleaner way to build transgenic zebrafish in Scientific Reports in 2014. Zebrafish are a workhorse for watching development, and fish carrying glow or driver genes in set cell types are prized tools. Older methods for inserting such genes at a chosen spot were slow and hit-or-miss.

Their recipe injects embryos with Cas9, guide RNAs that cut both the fish genome and a donor plasmid, and the plasmid itself, which carries a heat-shock switch. The cuts line up so the donor drops into the target site. The team made stable knock-in fish at four gene locations, with success at over 25 percent of attempts. They propose the method as a standard route to reporter and driver fish.
europmc-pmc4230920:
Yiji Li, Xiao-Guang Chen, and nine co-authors measured city effects on a dengue mosquito in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito, breeds in small water containers and spreads dengue and other viruses. Guangzhou, China, offered rural, suburban, and urban districts to compare in one study.

Surveying from May to November 2013, the team found the urban district held the most larva-positive water habitats. It also held far denser mosquitoes, with about twice the pupae and three times the adults of the other districts. Urban larvae also grew faster, survived to adulthood more often, and lived longer as adults. Water depth, clearing, surface type, and shade all shaped where larvae thrived. The results say city growth itself manufactures mosquito habitat, a planning point for dengue control.
europmc-pmc4286720:
Jasmine Lee and Lianhui Zhang map the layered signal network that the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses to sense its own numbers. Their review appeared in Protein and Cell in 2015. The bacterium causes stubborn infections in people with weak immune systems and in cystic fibrosis lungs, and it resists most standard antibiotics.

Its quorum sensing system rests on at least four linked signal pathways arranged in a hierarchy. The network controls toxin output and the forming of biofilms, the sheets that shield the bacteria from drugs and stress. Because the system sits at the center of virulence, the authors present it as a target for new treatments that disarm the bacterium instead of trying to kill it outright.
europmc-pmc4326520:
Michael R Tucker and nine co-authors review how powered leg prostheses and orthoses are controlled. Their review appeared in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation in 2015. Motors can now assist or replace lost leg function, yet a device only helps if it moves in step with what the wearer intends, step by step through daily life.

The review sorts control schemes by how they read user intent, from muscle signals and joint sensors to gait phase rules, and by how they blend with the wearer's own motor system. Practical gaps remain in safety, comfort, and switching between walking, stairs, and standing. A shared classification scheme lets engineers compare designs and spot where the field should push next.
europmc-pmc4374920:
Poonam Tyagi and co-authors tested how curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, kills bacteria, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Curcumin I, a main part of store-bought curcumin, is known for antioxidant effects, but its antibacterial action was less clear. The team exposed four disease-causing bacteria, two Gram-positive and two Gram-negative, to curcumin I and checked what broke inside the cells.

Curcumin I killed all four test species strongly, despite their different cell walls. Two dye tests that reveal leaky membranes both showed leakage after exposure. Electron and fluorescence microscope images confirmed visible membrane damage in the treated cells. The killing thus runs through membrane harm, a broad route that works across bacterial types. The authors suggest the finding could spur work on curcumin I against fast-spreading resistant pathogens.
europmc-pmc4384020:
Ivica Letunic, Tobias Doerks, and Peer Bork reported the 2015 status of SMART, a protein domain tool, in Nucleic Acids Research. SMART identifies domains in proteins and annotates them richly, using hand-curated models. The current version holds models for more than 1,200 domains, about 200 of them new since the prior update. Its underlying protein sets were synchronized with UniProt, Ensembl, and STRING, pushing annotated features past 100 million.

The genomic mode, which annotates every protein of a sequenced species, grew from 1,133 to 2,031 species. Results pages were redesigned with links to new information sources. A vector-based drawing engine renders protein diagrams crisply and exports them at print quality. Taxonomy displays were reworked around an integrated search. After more than 15 years, the tool remains a daily stop for protein researchers.
europmc-pmc4385920:
B. Ye, X. Liu, X. Li, H. Kong, L. Tian, and Y. Chen reviewed T-cell exhaustion in chronic hepatitis B, in Cell Death and Disease in 2015. Hepatitis B virus is a leading cause of liver inflammation, and clearing it depends on sustained T-cell attack. In chronic infection that attack fades: virus-specific T cells kill poorly, make few signal proteins, and carry many inhibitory receptors on their surface, including PD-1. Both helper and killer T-cell classes are affected, through distinct routes.

Blocking those inhibitory receptors can restore antiviral function, as already shown in hepatitis C, HIV, and cancer settings. The review gathers what is known about the exhaustion state in hepatitis B and the pathways behind it. Reviving exhausted cells is presented as a promising route to new immune therapies and vaccines for a stubborn chronic infection.
europmc-pmc4393120:
Russell Corbett-Detig, Daniel Hartl, and Timothy Sackton tested a classic puzzle of evolution across many species, in PLoS Biology in 2015. Neutral theory predicts that harmless genetic diversity should scale with population size. In practice, species with hugely different population sizes hold similar diversity, a mismatch called Lewontin's paradox. One explanation is that natural selection in large populations drags down diversity at linked neutral sites. The team tested that idea directly using genomes and genetic maps.

Where recombination is rare, selection reaches more neutral neighbors, so diversity should dip predictably. Modeling that pattern across 40 species of sexual eukaryotes let the team size selection's drag in each. The drag grew with population size, estimated from body size and range. Selection thus caps diversity in big populations, reconciling the paradox without abandoning neutral theory's core.
europmc-pmc4424520:
Ashok Agarwal, Aditi Mulgund, Alaa Hamada, and Michelle Renee Chyatte surveyed male infertility around the world in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology in 2015. Infertility touches a large share of couples, and men alone account for a sizable part of cases while sharing in about half overall. Yet solid counts for men, region by region, are scarce.

To fill the gap, the team studied reviews and population reports and, where male figures were missing, estimated them from female infertility data using stated shares for male, female, and mixed causes. Their regional estimates varied widely. The article gives doctors and planners a rough world map of male infertility and shows how much direct data are still missing.
europmc-pmc4509720:
Mark G. Stokes wrote a solo review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2015 on how the brain holds things in mind. Working memory keeps a phone number or a planned move alive for a few seconds. The classic view says cells in the prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain, keep firing the whole time to hold the trace.

Recordings at the level of cell groups tell a more restless story: activity shifts and can even go quiet while the memory still works. Stokes argues the trace may sit in changing patterns of links between cells, an activity-silent state, rather than in steady firing. His framework aims to reconcile the old delay-firing findings from monkey studies with the newer dynamic picture.
europmc-pmc4604320:
In 2015, John R. Kelly and colleagues' review linking the gut microbiome, gut barrier leaks, and stress-related mental disorders appeared. Signals between gut and brain travel by immune, hormone, and nerve routes. A weakened gut barrier may open an extra channel for those signals. The review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology.

The authors gather animal and human evidence that gut microbes help maintain the gut lining. When the barrier fails, low-grade inflammation follows, a pattern also seen in depression. Microbes may thus shape brain function partly by guarding or loosening the gut wall. The review sets out what is known, what is still guesswork, and which microbe features matter most for a healthy barrier.
europmc-pmc4634220:
In 2015, Damien Hanlon and colleagues' study making thin sheets of black phosphorus by peeling the crystal apart in liquid appeared. Few-layer black phosphorus is a promising two-dimensional material, but it degrades quickly in air and water. The team used a solvent called CHP to exfoliate it under normal room conditions. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

The solvent forms a protective shell around the sheets, so they survived far longer than expected. Computer simulations showed reactions start only at sheet edges. The sheets could be made in quantity with controlled size and visible light emission. Trials pointed to uses in fast optical switches, gas sensors, and strengthening fillers for composites, well beyond the electronics uses first imagined for the material.
europmc-pmc4643120:
Ole Ellegaard and Johan A. Wallin published a 2015 analysis of bibliometrics, the field that measures scholarly output with citations and counts. Bibliometric methods now shape research evaluation and university rankings. The authors turned the field's own tools on its literature, drawn from Web of Science. The work appeared in Scientometrics.

They split the literature into library science journals and subject-field journals. Citations grew almost linearly from 1994 onward in the subject-field group. Multidisciplinary articles earned the highest impact. Keyword analysis showed the field's favourite topics, and the map of contributing countries shifted over time. A self-reinforcing citation pattern also appeared. The study asks how much weight the growing numbers game should carry in judging science.
europmc-pmc4655320:
Ulla Sovio, together with colleagues, released a 2015 cohort study testing routine third-trimester ultrasound for finding growth-restricted babies. Small babies face higher risks around birth, but screening must separate healthy small babies from starved ones. The Pregnancy Outcome Prediction study followed first-time mothers in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Research scans at twenty-eight and thirty-six weeks stayed hidden from clinicians. The work appeared in The Lancet.

Universal scanning was judged on how well estimated fetal weight below the tenth percentile predicted babies born small for their age. Extra markers, including growth speed and blood flow measures, were tested for spotting true growth restriction. Babies flagged by those markers carried different risk than babies who were simply small. The study informs the debate over scanning every pregnancy late in term versus scanning only when clinically indicated.
europmc-pmc4671520:
Dipak P. Ramji and Thomas S. Davies published a 2015 review of cytokines in atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind most heart attacks and strokes. Cytokines are immune signalling proteins involved at every disease stage. The review appeared in Cytokine and Growth Factor Reviews.

Risk factors activate the vessel lining, and chemokine signals recruit immune cells into the wall. Macrophages swallow modified fats and become foam cells, forming the early fatty streak. Later, smooth muscle cells build a fibrous cap while macrophage enzymes weaken it; rupture triggers clots. The authors describe each cytokine family's role and assess therapies that adjust cytokine action, including trials testing anti-inflammatory treatment to cut cardiovascular events.
europmc-pmc4728620:
Lotte Lauritzen, Paolo Brambilla, Alessandra Mazzocchi, and three colleagues reviewed the fatty acid DHA in brain development and function, in Nutrients in 2016. DHA is a building block of brain cell membranes. It piles into the fetal brain during the last trimester of pregnancy and keeps accumulating fast until a child's second year. Because the body makes little of its own, diet may decide whether the brain gets enough. The team surveyed evidence across the whole lifespan.

Cell and animal work supports roles in neuron growth, branching, and signaling. Human data are strongest for infant visual development. Hints suggest effects may differ by sex and by the genes a person carries for making DHA. Later-life studies raise possible roles in thinking decline and major psychiatric illness, though proof is thinner. The review gives parents and clinicians a balanced map of a popular supplement's real evidence.
europmc-pmc4795320:
David Bakker, Nikolaos Kazantzis, Debra Rickwood, and Nikki Rickard review mental health phone apps in JMIR Mental Health in 2016, and set rules for building better ones. Hundreds of such apps crowd the stores, promising help for low mood, worry, and stress. Few rest on proof: trial testing of most apps is absent, and many lack the features that make an app work or carry features set up poorly.

From literature across mental health, prevention, and app design, the authors draw sixteen recommendations, each rated by the strength of its proof. A good app, they argue, needs a behavior plan and design hooks that keep users engaged; no single app need carry all sixteen. They close by calling for proper trials of the next wave of apps.
europmc-pmc4796320:
Christina M. Sloan-Heggen leads a team of many co-authors in Human Genetics in 2016 running full genetic testing on 1,119 people with hearing loss. Hearing loss is the most common sense deficit, striking one in five hundred newborns, and its many gene causes long blocked a single test. The team offered broad panel sequencing to every patient in line, whatever their story or past tests.

Testing named the cause in 440 patients, about four in ten. Faults spread across 49 genes, from single-letter changes to large missing chunks. Yield ran highest where loss ran in the family or was present from birth on both sides, and the gene mix shifted with ancestry. The authors argue the pattern should guide clinics toward test plans that spend resources where answers are likeliest.
europmc-pmc4810120:
Vita Golubovskaya, Lijun Wu, and Samuel C. Mok review T cell types in Cancers in 2016, with an eye to improving CAR-T therapy. In that therapy, a patient's T cells are fitted with a synthetic receptor that steers them onto tumor cells. Which T cells go into the product turns out to matter as much as the receptor itself.

The review sorts the helper and killer T cell families, and the memory and effector states within them, by their surface marks, inner switches, gene programs, and fuel use. Memory-like cells persist and expand better after infusion, while worn effector cells hit hard and fade. One helper family, regulatory T cells, actively damps the therapy, and the authors review ways to keep them out or down. Tuning the mix, they argue, is the next gain in CAR-T design.
europmc-pmc4846320:
Pei-Qian Liao, Wei-Xiong Zhang, Jian-Ping Zhang, and Xiao-Ming Chen reported a metal-organic framework that purifies ethene by trapping ethane, in work from 2015. Ethene is a top industrial chemical, and splitting it from ethane, a near twin, is both vital and hard. Most filters grab ethene and need repeated cycles. Their porous crystal instead grabs the ethane impurity.

One liter of the material took a standard cracked-gas mix and gave back 56 liters of ethene at over 99.95 percent purity in a single pass, the grade polymer plants require. Crystal studies and simulations show the pore walls grip ethane through many weak hydrogen bonds. A one-pass route could cut energy use in a huge industry.
europmc-pmc4868820:
Christopher J. Tape and co-authors showed in 2016 that a cancer-driving KRAS fault signals through nearby support cells, not only within tumor cells. Mutant KRAS is a classic engine of pancreatic cancer. The team tagged proteins by cell type and read thousands of signal marks in tumor and fibroblast cells grown together, tracing who tells whom.

Tumor KRAS woke the fibroblasts, which then sent signals back that doubled the tumor cell's active signal nodes and used extra enzymes. The returned signal boosted growth, survival, and cell energy through a named growth axis. Oncogene action is thus a two-way street between cell types, and drug plans should treat it that way.
europmc-pmc4892920:
George D. Thurston and co-authors linked long-term fine particle air pollution to heart disease death in 2016, asking which particle sources do the harm. Fine particles, PM2.5, are a known global threat, yet mass alone hides unlike chemistries. The study followed 445,860 adults in 100 United States metro areas from 1982 to 2004, with personal risk data and national air monitors.

Death from ischemic heart disease tied more strongly to some parts and sources than others, with coal burning a flagged source. Particle mix, not just particle mass, shapes risk. Cleaner air rules can thus target the worst sources first. The cohort, drawn from a cancer prevention study, gives the size needed to split such fine effects.
europmc-pmc4958120:
Torbjørn Torsheim and six co-authors, with a study group, validate a shorter Family Affluence Scale for surveying young people. Their paper appeared in Child Indicators Research in 2016. The scale asks teens about household goods instead of income, which families often will not report. The team tested 16 candidate items on 7,120 students in eight countries, from Denmark and Greenland to Romania and Slovakia. Item screening looked for weak or redundant questions.

A strong general affluence factor ran through all countries. Six items survived the cuts: computers, cars, own bedroom, holidays abroad, dishwasher, and bathrooms. Three items behaved the same across countries, which anchors the scale to a shared metric. The short scale matched parent reported income groups in six of the eight countries. The authors recommend the six item version for comparative studies of youth health and inequality. They note it can also serve research well beyond health.
europmc-pmc5015320:
Yuxiang Jiang and a very large group of co-authors report the second Critical Assessment of Functional Annotation in Genome Biology in 2016. The contest, called CAFA, tests computer methods that guess what a protein does, a task lab work alone is too slow to finish. Teams had a set time to predict functions for 3,681 proteins from 18 species, scored against standard gene and disease vocabularies.

In all, 126 methods from 56 groups took part, a much wider test than the first round. The best new methods beat the best old ones head to head on shared proteins. Gains came from both better methods and the growth of lab-made reference notes. Which method wins depends on which vocabulary is used, the authors warn, so users should match the tool to their question. The contest now serves as the field's shared yardstick for progress.
europmc-pmc5075620:
Palanisamy Arulselvan and six co-authors review antioxidants and natural products in inflammation, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016. Inflammation defends the body, but when it runs long it feeds diabetes, cancer, heart disease, arthritis, obesity, and bowel disease. Free radicals, produced when natural antioxidant defenses fall behind, damage tissue and keep the cycle going. The review maps the process and its cell machinery.

Standard anti-inflammatory drugs carry real costs: aspirin and its kin can injure the stomach, and immune-blocking biologics raise infection risk. That gap drives interest in gentler compounds from natural sources. The authors survey how antioxidants counter free radical damage and how plant and other natural products dampen inflammatory pathways. Their aim is practical: a clear account of the mechanisms, so drug hunters can build safer treatments for chronic inflammation from natural starting points.
europmc-pmc5159420:
Anna Skubacz, Agata Daszkowska-Golec, and Iwona Szarejko reviewed a plant stress factor in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Daszkowska-Golec leads with her first surname in the hyphenated byline. The factor, ABI5, is a gene switch in the signaling of abscisic acid, the plant stress hormone that governs seed germination and early seedling growth.

ABI5 turns on stress adaptation genes and sits at the center of the hormone's core pathway. But its own level and activity are tuned by many other switches. Chemical edits after the protein is made play a part too. It also acts as a meeting point where signals from auxin, cytokinin, and four other plant hormones cross. The review covers ABI5's roles in development and in drought, salt, and other stresses, and what is known about its counterparts in grain crops.
europmc-pmc5316720:
John Taylor, a surgeon at the Royal Infirmary in Dundee, placed three cases on record in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1925. Each case was a sudden burst ulcer of the small intestine. The cause of such ulcers was still obscure, and Taylor hoped fresh notes would help. His first patient was a weaver of fifty-three, sent in during November 1923.

She had been seized at work by fierce pain below the navel, with vomiting and a belly that had not moved for days. Taylor operated and dealt with what he found inside. The other two cases follow the same close pattern of history, signs, and surgery. He closes by weighing causes. Sharp swallowed objects, he argues, can pierce the gut wall, and a hard strain of the belly muscles may drive the point through.
europmc-pmc5332920:
Anne Zufferey, Rick Kapur, and John W. Semple reviewed a platelet disease in the Journal of Clinical Medicine in 2017. In immune thrombocytopenia, the body's own defenses drive blood platelet counts low. Low platelets raise the risk of bleeding. The disease can strike adults and children of both sexes, though its roots may differ by age.

The review sorts the attack paths. Antibodies mark platelets for ruin, killer T cells destroy them directly, and the bone marrow cells that make platelets also falter. Off-balance T cells and signal chemicals add to the mix. Care aims not at normal counts but at counts safe enough to stop bleeding. First care blocks antibody making and platelet loss. Later steps calm the immune system, remove the spleen, or push the marrow to make more platelets.
europmc-pmc5345220:
