One shared gene in gut and brain autoimmunity hints at common roots beneath very different symptoms. Shared roots matter practically: drugs aimed at the CD40 pathway might serve both diseases. The study also strengthens the case for comparing autoimmune diseases together when hunting their genes, rather than searching each alone.
plos-pone-0011620:
Majid Eshaghi and co-authors mapped stress defences in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2010. When hydrogen peroxide attacks these yeast cells, a stress switch called Sty1 activates a partner protein, Atf1, which turns defence genes on. Whether every peroxide-induced gene is directly controlled by that pair was not yet clear.

The team profiled where Sty1 and Atf1 bind across the whole yeast genome during the attack. Their maps separate genes directly controlled by the pair from genes switched on by other routes. That distinction gives a fuller picture of how a simple cell organises a genome-wide emergency response.
plos-pone-0011720:
Rosanna Capparelli and co-authors found a surprise vaccine lead against staph infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When germs face bacteria-killing viruses called phages, resistant mutants show up fast. Away from the phage, though, those mutants often grow less well than normal germs, paying a fitness cost for their resistance.

The team tested a phage-proof Staphylococcus aureus mutant in mice. Far from merely staying alive, the mutant gave broad protection against staph disease. A weakened, phage-proof germ that doubles as a vaccine opens a backdoor route to guarding against a germ that shrugs off many drugs.
plos-pone-0011820:
Fernando Sepulveda and co-authors tested a physical view of Alzheimer's harm, in PLOS ONE in 2010. What sets off Alzheimer's is still largely unknown, which slows work on drugs that could change its course. One working idea holds that excess amyloid beta breaks cell membranes by forming pores, which then upsets the cell's ion balance.

The authors argue that the protein's harm to synapses, the links between brain cells, can be explained by this pore-forming power. Framing amyloid as a membrane puncher, not just a sticky clump, points drug work toward blocking the puncture itself.
plos-pone-0011920:
Attila Szücs and colleagues recorded in 2010 from a small rat brain area tied to anxiety and stress, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis. Neurons vary widely in the ion channels they carry, so a brain area can contain several distinct firing types side by side. The team used dynamic clamp, a method that adds virtual channels to living cells.

Their recordings show both consistency and diversity in how these neurons fire spikes. Some shared patterns mark the area's basic wiring, while the differences suggest specialized roles in stress responses. A careful catalog of firing styles is groundwork for understanding how this region helps turn stress into lasting anxiety.
plos-pone-0012020:
Merrin Rutherford and colleagues put in 2010 a blood test for TB to a real-world trial in Indonesia. The test, sold as QuantiFERON-Gold, looks for immune memory of the TB germ in a tube of blood and is used to find hidden infection. As part of a formal check, the team set its hit rate next to that of the older skin test in adults whose TB was sure.

Cases with germs seen in sputum stood in as the mark of true infection the blood test ought to catch. How often the test misses sure cases tells health programs how far to trust a clear result. In lands where TB is rife, that trust level decides if the blood test can take the place of the skin test, which needs two clinic visits to read.
plos-pone-0012120:
Alexis Morice, Béatrice Charreau, Bérangère Neveu, and co-authors studied killer T cells raised against herpesviruses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-lasting virus infections are linked to organ transplant rejection, but clear cases of one T cell attacking both a virus target and a donor organ target are rare. The team grew virus-specific T cell lines and tested whether they also react to foreign tissue markers.

Some of these cells did cross-react with tissue markers from other people. That means a cell trained by a common virus could also strike a transplanted organ carrying those markers. The finding helps explain why past infections can complicate transplants, and why matching and drug plans may need to account for a patient's virus history.
plos-pone-0012220:
Maciej Chichlowski, Greg Westwood, Soman Abraham, and co-authors studied mast cells in inflamed gut tissue in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammatory bowel disease is thought to arise when the immune system attacks the gut's own bacteria in a susceptible host. Mast cells, sentinels packed with alarm chemicals, sit just under the gut lining, perfectly placed to start or feed that attack.

Using mice that lack a calming immune signal and develop gut inflammation, the team tracked mast cells' part in the disease and in the colon tumors that chronic inflammation can spawn. If mast cells drive both, drugs that quiet them, already common for allergies, might find a second use in bowel disease care.
plos-pone-0012320:
Erin McElvania TeKippe, Irving Allen, Paul Hulseberg, and co-authors tested immune sensors in chronic tuberculosis infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A family of internal alarm proteins guards against acute infections, but what they do in a slow, years-long infection like tuberculosis was unknown. The team focused on one sensor, its adaptor partner, and the enzyme the pair activates, in mice infected with the tuberculosis bacterium.

Forming granulomas, the walled-off nodules that contain the bacteria, and defending the host required the adaptor but not the named sensor or enzyme. Untangling which alarms matter in chronic infection redirects drug and vaccine work toward the live wires. It also explains why a sensor famous in acute disease can be a bystander here.
plos-pone-0012420:
Francesca Setiadi, Nelson Ray, Holbrook Kohrt and colleagues counted and mapped immune cells in lymph nodes near breast tumors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Pathologists usually judge tissue by eye, without exact counts or maps of where cells sit. Nodes that drain a tumor are where immune defense is organized, so their layout may reveal how the battle is going.

Using quantitative imaging, the team measured immune cell subsets and their positions in patient nodes and healthy nodes. The tumor-draining nodes showed a distinct layout. Hard numbers on tissue geography could one day help predict which cancers spread and which patients need stronger treatment after surgery.
plos-pone-0012520:
Jian-Guo Ren, Pankaj Seth, Peter Everett and colleagues drained an enzyme from leukemia cells and watched them mature, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The mitochondrial enzyme malic enzyme 2 helps feed energy and building blocks to fast-growing cells, and its levels run high in some cancers. Human erythroleukemia cells are blood cancer cells stuck in an immature state.

Depleting the enzyme pushed the cells toward red blood cell differentiation, as if a growth brake had been released. Forcing cancer cells to mature is a proven treatment idea in some leukemias. The result nominates this metabolic enzyme as a target worth testing in blood cancers.
plos-pone-0012620:
Kochzius, Seidel, Antoniou and co-authors tackled a basic problem in the world fish trade: telling species apart. Fish must be named correctly at every stage, from eggs and larvae to the fillets sold in shops. Their 2010 paper tests two lab tools for the job, DNA barcodes and DNA microarrays.

A barcode reads a short stretch of DNA that differs between species, while a chip checks many samples at once. Together they can expose fraud and protect stocks that are fished too hard. Reliable naming also helps scientists track which fish live where.
plos-pone-0012720:
Pericolini, Gabrielli, Bistoni and co-authors traced how a fungal sugar coat harms T cells through the CD45 pathway. The coat, galactoxylomannan, comes from a yeast that attacks people with weak immunity. Earlier work showed it trips both of the cell's death pathways after meeting receptors on T cells.

Their 2010 study pins down the role of CD45, a major T cell surface signal protein, in that damage. Knowing the entry route may let doctors shield T cells during this infection. It also deepens the picture of how fungal products disarm immunity.
plos-pone-0341920:
Spotting strange traffic on a computer network early can stop attacks before damage spreads. Debiao Luo and co-authors combine several techniques into one detection system, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper on network safety.

Raw traffic is first broken into smoother waves to remove noise. A hybrid network then reads the signal two ways at once: attention heads catch far-apart links, while a memory network reads the sequence in both directions. A firefly-inspired search tunes the system's settings automatically. On standard test data the combined model beat earlier methods on both error rates and detection scores, with gains the authors checked statistically.
plos-pone-0343920:
Imane Bagheri, Atena Dadgari, and Naiire Salmani interviewed palliative care staff in 2026 about death doulas, non medical companions for dying people. Cancer patients at the end of life and their families often need more support than clinical teams can give.

Fourteen staff members described what must exist before the role can work: drivers pushing for it, proper recruiting and training, and basic structures to host it. Challenges included families not knowing the role and officials not recognising it formally. The study gives planners a grounded checklist for introducing doulas without confusion about who does what at the bedside.
plos-pone-0345620:
Juliana Amorim and colleagues hunt for new antibacterial compounds in nature's chemistry library, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer study. Their target is an enzyme Staphylococcus aureus needs to make its golden pigment, which shields the bacterium from immune attack; blocking the enzyme should weaken the germ rather than kill it outright.

Starting from nearly three hundred thousand natural products, shape-based screening and then activity models narrowed the field to about two thousand strong candidates, with a few dozen predicted to bind extremely tightly. Five finalists held stable grips on the enzyme in molecular simulations. The list gives chemists concrete starting points for lab testing against a pathogen known for drug resistance.
plos-pone-0345720:
Md Yasin and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on predicting two key measures of knitted cotton fabric before it is finished. Mills need to know a fabric's final width and its weight per square meter, yet both shift during production. The authors built a fuzzy logic model that takes stitch length, yarn fineness, and machine diameter as inputs.

The model was trained on more than thirty thousand real production records and then checked against fresh factory data. Its predictions landed very close to the actual width and weight values. Because the system rests on proven factory data rather than lab trials alone, the authors present it as a practical planning tool for textile mills that want fewer surprises in finished cloth.
plos-pone-0346820:
Mian Li and co-workers simulate, atom by atom, what happens when a common clay mineral soaks up water. The mineral, illite, is plentiful in oil shale, and its swelling can weaken rock. Their 2026 study runs computer models that vary heat, pressure, and water amount to watch the mineral's size, density, and stiffness change.

Water pushed the crystal to swell mostly along one direction. Pressure held the swelling back, while heat and more water sped it up. The mineral grew stiffer under pressure and softer as heat or water rose. Knowing these micro-level rules helps engineers judge rock stability for oil work and building projects where wet clay can cause trouble.
plos-pone-0347020:
Nasser A M Barakat and co-authors built a new electrode material in 2026 for turning urea in wastewater into energy. Urea is a common pollutant from farms and factories, and breaking it down with electricity can clean water while recovering power.

Thin carbon fibers were spun with nickel particles, plus phosphorus and nitrogen from a cheap starting chemical. Heat treatment tuned the nickel surface into a form ready for the reaction. In alkaline tests the best mix started working at low voltage and carried a strong current. Pairs of dirty water treatment and energy recovery make such catalysts worth developing further.
plos-pone-0348220:
Fanwei Meng and Bing Chen review infections picked up in hospital by children kept alive on heart-lung machines after heart surgery. The machines, known as ECMO, support children born with heart defects while they heal. Their 2026 study covers fifty-four children at one Chinese heart hospital over five years and compares those who caught infections with those who did not.

Fourteen children developed infections, mostly lung infections from tough Gram-negative bacteria. Having a breathing tube placed before surgery stood out as the one clear risk factor in the final analysis. Longer intensive care stays also appeared more often in the infected group. Death rates did not differ clearly. The results urge extra infection care around airway tubes in these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0348520:
Sangjin Lee, Sunggon Kim, and Yongseok Son build a faster defragmentation tool for flash-based solid-state drives. Even fast drives slow when heavy editing scatters a file's blocks across the chip, and the standard tool works through files one by one. Their 2026 system first collects file maps for everything, then runs many defragmenters in parallel, each owning one file and issuing requests without waiting.

On a common multi-core machine with a consumer drive, the tool finished cleanups up to nearly four times faster than the standard one. Throughput rose across workloads, and a program running alongside suffered less slowdown. Data centers juggling huge shared drives could tidy storage in shorter, less disruptive windows.
plos-pone-0348720:
Md Talha Jubaer and colleagues put a local scorecard for healthcare quality through tough math checks. The scorecard is used with left-out groups in Bangladesh. Their 2026 study drew on ratings from 311 local scoring groups. The groups spanned nine left-out communities. Each group rated fourteen items by consensus. The team tested the tool with classic stats and a modern item response model.

The scorecard held up. Ratings fell into three themes: access and fairness, how well offices respond, and mother and child health support. Together they explained over half the spread. The ratings also hung together well. One main thread backed a single overall score. Proof matters because scorecards steer real policy debates. Groups can now wield numbers shown to measure what they claim.
plos-pone-0348820:
Hung-Chun Huang and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE building a sideline triage score for lower-back, pelvis, and hip dysfunction in college athletes. These problems often precede back pain, but expert assessment is scarce, so teams need a field tool flagging who needs priority care and who can self-manage. Over eight hundred athletes from ten universities completed standardized history and functional testing, and experts judged each case as the reference.

Just over half needed priority assessment. The final score combined fourteen factors: a dozen raising concern, such as local pain, weakness, and higher body mass, and two safety-related findings that lowered it. The score separated the groups well, kept its accuracy under bootstrap re-checking, and calibrated nearly perfectly. A cutoff caught most priority cases while clearing most self-managers. The tool is presented as ready for prospective testing in team settings.
plos-pone-0348920:
Haruna Moshi and three colleagues examine why school-based deworming against schistosomiasis is delivered unevenly in Ghana, in this 2026 qualitative study. Preventive chemotherapy through schools is the main weapon against this parasitic disease, yet delivery in many districts falls short of World Health Organization targets and transmission persists. The researchers interviewed coordinators, head teachers, and school health teachers in two endemic districts of the Central Region.

Fidelity suffered where families feared the drugs or doubted the program, where supplies and money ran short, and where frontline teachers lacked training or incentives. It rose where awareness campaigns engaged the community, implementers felt motivated, and health and education sectors worked closely together. The authors conclude that faithful delivery is a system property, not a checklist, and must be built district by district.
plos-pone-0349020:
Javier Silva-Valencia and colleagues tracked lung exercise testing across Ontario over the years spanning the time before COVID-19 hit, the crisis itself, and the recovery since. These tests, such as the six-minute walk test, help doctors judge breathing problems and decide who needs long-term oxygen. The team used province-wide health records covering 2015 to 2023.

More than half a million tests were recorded, yet by late 2023 testing rates were still about a fifth below pre-pandemic levels. Recovery was uneven, lagging more for men and for some other groups. The shortfall matters because delayed testing can delay treatment decisions for people with chronic lung and heart disease.
plos-pone-0349120:
Maguy Saffouh El Hajj and colleagues reviewed why drug errors happen in local pharmacies, where most people collect their medicines. Hospital safety has drawn more study, yet busy counters carry real risk too. Thirteen studies, mostly from the United States and England, were woven together with a method that builds new themes from interview based research.

Five broad causes emerged from the weaving. Workload, staffing, and time pressure ran through many accounts, along with poor handoffs and weak safety habits. Checks confirmed fair trust in most themes. Local pharmacies need system fixes, like calmer workflow and better double checks, rather than blame aimed at single staff members working under strain.
plos-pone-0349220:
Nicholas Behn and colleagues gathered thirteen earlier studies to describe what life feels like when brain injury disrupts the thinking side of communication. After such injuries, people may struggle to follow conversation, find words, or read social cues, even when speech itself sounds fine. The review pools the voices of more than one hundred people with brain injury and sixty-six family members and friends.

Across the studies, eight themes emerged, starting with the plain fact that communicating is no longer easy. Participants described lost confidence, strained relationships, and services that overlook the problem. The authors argue that care should treat communication partners as part of the picture, since spouses, parents, and friends carry much of the daily repair work that keeps conversation going.
plos-pone-0349820:
Bandar Alghamdi and Sonia Rocha searched for low oxygen related genes that forecast lung adenocarcinoma outcomes in 2026. Tumors short of oxygen grow more aggressive and resist treatment, so their gene marks could guide care.

Comparing tumor and normal data, the team found hundreds of oxygen linked genes switched up or down. Up genes clustered in cancer and signalling pathways; down genes tied to immunity. Hub genes included known cancer players on both sides. Survival modelling then picked out genes whose levels track patient outcomes. Such marks may one day sort patients by risk and hint at drug targets in oxygen starved tumors.
plos-pone-0350020:
Charumita Vasudev and colleagues spoke at length with eighty six households in Uttar Pradesh and Goa, India, about food hardship during and after COVID. Field work ran from late 2022 into early 2023, with hundreds of interviews. Households mixed migrant and settled families, town and village homes, and varied caste and family types.

Everyday fixes came first: swapping foods, shrinking portions, and pooling what kin could share. Harder shocks forced harsher steps, like mothers eating last, selling goods, taking debt, pulling children from school, and delaying care. Settled village families leaned on kin and state food support. Migrants often lacked both, so place and movement shaped survival more than income loss alone.
plos-pone-0350120:
Mahunan Sossou and Dieu donné Gnonlonfoun reviewed intensive care records from Benin's national referral hospital for adults admitted with impaired consciousness. A dimmed or lost consciousness is common, dangerous, and little studied in low-resource intensive care. Records for four hundred sixteen patients admitted over two and a half years were used to estimate survival and find traits tied to death.

Two of every three patients died in the unit, half of the deaths within five days. Older age, deeper coma, low blood pressure, high temperature, and lacking oxygen therapy each raised the risk, while head injury cases fared comparatively better. The authors say simple admission readings can flag who needs attention first, and they make a plain case for reliable oxygen and basic monitoring before fancier equipment.
plos-pone-0350720:
Duc Quy Hoang and co-authors build a mammography reader that forces itself to look at suspicious spots, not just the whole breast image. AI readers can cheat by leaning on background patterns, which makes their answers hard to trust. Their hybrid system blends a compact local-detail network with a transformer that scans wider context, plus a branch that gathers evidence from the regions most likely to hold a lesion.

On a large public mammography collection, the full version topped strong rival systems on accuracy and balanced scores while using fewer resources. Its chosen regions often overlapped the lesions human experts had marked. Hoang and colleagues argue that showing its evidence makes the system easier for radiologists to check, a key step toward clinic use.
plos-pone-0350820:
Kanae Kondo and colleagues tracked cigarette sales and household tobacco spending in Japan across the COVID pandemic with national data stretching from 2014 onward. Sales series, spending surveys, and smoking rate data were modelled around the first emergency declaration and the later downgrade of COVID to a routine illness class.

Cigarette sales kept falling after the emergency, but more slowly than before. Price adjusted monthly tobacco spending jumped in the first emergency month, though later checks weakened that finding. Male smoking eased down year by year while female rates barely moved. Crises do not reliably cut smoking, the authors warn; stress and home time can blunt tobacco control.
plos-pone-0350920:
Farming shapes Vietnam's carbon footprint crop by crop, and An Thinh Nguyen and colleagues trained a neural network on three decades of data to weigh each land use. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered twenty-one farm product types from 1990 to 2019.

Most types moved with higher carbon dioxide emissions, including bananas, beans, cassava, coffee, and coconuts. Five moved the other way, among them rice, soybeans, and sesame. A four-layer network captured the links despite their tangled, non-linear shape. The authors say such product-level evidence helps policymakers target emission cuts where they count, instead of taxing all agriculture alike.
plos-pone-0351120:
Yao Zhao and Haoyu Zhou followed college students' sleep across all four undergraduate years in this 2026 study. Most earlier work measured sleep at single moments. These authors instead treated each student's nightly pattern as a smooth curve that changes over time. They used records from the NetHealth Project at an American university.

Wearable trackers produced more than sixty thousand daily sleep records for seventy-six students. Sleep grew longer across the four years, with clear seasonal swings tied to the academic calendar. Better grades and longer sleep went together throughout college. Each step up in grade average came with roughly twenty-seven extra minutes of sleep. Social activity levels also lined up with distinct sleep patterns, which argues for treating student sleep as a moving process, not a fixed habit.
plos-pone-0351220:
Heghine Gevorgyan and three colleagues probe how gut bacteria manage acid stress. Their 2026 study works with Escherichia coli fermenting sugars at an acidic pH. A protein switch called FhlA turns on the formate hydrogen lyase complex. That machinery converts formate into hydrogen gas, consuming protons as it goes. The team compared normal bacteria with mutants lacking the switch. They tracked the cell's main energy turbine, proton flows, and membrane properties at two growth stages.

Mutants showed weakened turbine activity and slower proton flux. The two systems, acid disposal and energy generation, clearly lean on each other. Older cultures of both strains carried more protective membrane groups and leaked fewer protons. Membrane voltage in the mutants stayed stubbornly unchanged. Bacteria, the authors conclude, balance their proton budget by coordinating several systems at once. Understanding that bookkeeping helps anyone fermenting microbes industrially, or fighting them medically, at low pH.
plos-pone-0351320:
Machines that tumble samples slowly can fake weightlessness on Earth, helping biologists rehearse space experiments. Andrada Pica and colleagues measured how well one such random positioning machine actually performs, in this 2026 PLOS One study combining motion sensors, computer modeling, and living nerve cells.

Sensors rode the frames while the machine ran in three modes. Modeling showed average gravity fell to between a hundredth and a thousandth of Earth's, with sideways spin forces staying tiny. Nerve cells grown under each mode reacted to the treatment. The authors offer the numbers as a reference so other labs can judge whether the simulation suits their experiments.
plos-pone-0352020:
Noumou Keita and seven colleagues reconstruct COVID-19's path through Mali from the virus's own genome. Their 2026 study is the country's first comprehensive genomic account. Mali recorded over thirty-three thousand confirmed cases between 2020 and 2025. The team analysed five hundred forty-eight Malian viral sequences. A high-quality subset, combined with close global relatives, powered time-resolved family trees. West African data are scarce in global surveillance, which makes every reconstructed introduction valuable.

Five distinct epidemic waves emerged. Early lineages gave way, wave by wave, to the dominant variants of 2023. Introductions traced mainly to Europe and North America. After each arrival, local transmission sustained itself. Viruses also flowed back and forth with neighbouring African countries. Molecular clock analysis dated the movements. For Malian health authorities, the reconstruction shows their epidemic was repeatedly reseeded from abroad, then homegrown. Border awareness and local genomic capacity both follow from that picture.
plos-pone-0352120:
Haeun Hwang and colleagues tested whether a cancer drug, omipalisib, can help brain cells clear out the tangled tau protein behind a family of dementias. Tau tangles grow when the cell's recycling system, autophagy, falters. The drug blocks a growth switch called mTOR, which normally holds recycling back. The team tried it in human cells engineered to make a mutant tau and in mice bred to develop tau disease.

In the cells, the drug loosened the mTOR brake, raised recycling markers, and lowered both a recycling backlog protein and the harmful modified form of tau, without killing the cells. Mice received the drug for two months starting at six months of age. The work supports the idea that freeing the cell's cleanup crew can cut tau buildup, a strategy now open to further testing in animals.
plos-pone-0352320:
Ahmad Sarraj and colleagues ran a small trial on whether brain stimulation adds anything to an intensive rehab method for people with long-standing paraplegia from spinal cord injury. The base method pairs imagining movements with strong sensory stimulation of the legs. Fifty patients were split among usual care, the method alone, and the method plus mild electrical stimulation of the scalp, over ten days.

Patients on usual care gained nothing measurable. Both active groups improved substantially and by the same amount on touch and pinprick sensation. So the sensory recovery seems to come from the peripheral method itself, with no extra gain from the brain stimulation on those measures. For clinics, that simplifies the recipe: the cheaper, simpler half of the pairing appears to carry the sensory benefit.
plos-pone-0352420:
Sandani De Vass Gunawardane and seven colleagues investigate a herbal capsule called Vernolac in this 2026 study. The product blends five Sri Lankan medicinal plants, including black seed and Indian sarsaparilla. Each plant has shown anti-cancer activity on its own. The team asked how the mixture might act against cancer as a whole.

Computer databases yielded one hundred fifty-five drug-like compounds from the blend. Their predicted protein targets overlapped with cancer-related targets at one hundred thirty-seven points. Network analysis highlighted fourteen hub proteins, many central to cell growth and death. Chemical profiling of the extract confirmed a rich mix of active plant compounds. The work maps plausible routes for the formula's effects, while stressing that laboratory and clinical proof must follow.
plos-pone-0353020:
Yusuf Başkıran and three colleagues compare three ways of performing a hysterectomy and their after-effects, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Turkish hospital. Records covered four hundred and sixty-six women whose wombs were removed for non-cancer reasons between 2020 and 2023, by the open abdominal route, by keyhole surgery, or through the vagina. The team measured vaginal length and sexual function scores before and after surgery.

Vaginal length shrank most after keyhole surgery, yet women's sexual function scores ended up similar across all three routes. Their partners' scores dipped after surgery, a finding the authors flag as tentative. The practical reading: surgical route changes anatomy measurably without clearly changing women's early sexual wellbeing.
plos-pone-0353120:
Bilgilisoy Filiz and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 on gel injections for knee osteoarthritis. More than one hundred adults with moderate knee wear will receive either a high-dose gel injection or salt water, then swap after three months, with neither patients nor assessors knowing the order. Pain, function, strength, and quality of life will be tracked for a year.

The crossover design lets each patient serve as their own comparison. Three-month results will judge benefit, while the full year watches safety. Gel injections are widely sold but unevenly proven, so a blinded trial with a dummy injection offers unusually firm evidence for patients weighing cost against relief.
plos-pone-0353420:
Marcos De Andrés Montero and seven colleagues present a method for untangling mass graves where bones from many people lie mixed together, in this 2026 PLOS ONE archaeology paper. Reassembling individuals is the necessary first step before any identification, yet field guidance has been thin. Their approach records the exact position of every bone in mapping software and adds a new coding system that tracks how complete each skeleton is.

Applied to a crowded sixteenth-century burial in southwestern Hungary, the method substantially increased the number of fully reassembled skeletons and suggested matches for many loose elements. Working spatially first, they argue, makes later bone-sorting techniques far more effective — a step toward naming the dead.
plos-pone-0353520:
Anggeriyane and colleagues published a plan in 2026 for mapping what is known about emotional and behavioral troubles in preschool children. Young children who struggle to manage feelings and behavior can face lasting harm later in life. Yet past studies are scattered across fields and use very different ways to measure the same problems.

Under the plan, the team will search six large databases for studies from the year 2000 onward, with no limit on language. Two reviewers will screen and chart the studies on their own, then group the linked factors into body, mind, family, and wider life domains. Readers get a clear map of what has been studied and where the gaps still sit.
plos-pone-0354020:
Agazhe Aemro and five colleagues count how often women across nine sub-Saharan African countries have ever tested for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of national health surveys. The sample covers nearly one hundred and sixty thousand women aged fifteen to forty-nine. The average woman had tested about two and a half times in her life, but the typical woman — the median — had never tested at all.

Testing rose with age, education, wealth, employment, and knowledge about HIV, and varied enormously by region, with southern Africa far ahead. Having more partners, perhaps through antenatal and clinic contact, sharply raised counts. Over half of women had never tested, a gap the authors say needs community-level, region-specific campaigns.
plos-pone-0354120:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 study, race six inflammation scores drawn from routine blood counts to see which best predicts peritonitis in people on peritoneal dialysis. This infection of the belly lining is the Achilles heel of home dialysis and can end the treatment. More than two thousand patients from ten centers were followed.

About seven in every hundred patients developed peritonitis during follow-up. Three scores, built from ratios and products of blood cell counts, each more than doubled the estimated risk when high, and each separated future cases from non-cases moderately well. The relationships were curved rather than straight, rising steeply past certain levels. No score dominated the others. The authors suggest these free scores, computed from blood tests patients already get, could flag who needs closer watching and earlier teaching on sterile technique.
plos-pone-0354520:
Janet Antwi led a team of seven authors on this 2026 pilot study of a produce prescription program at a historically Black university in the United States. Fifty-five students received nutrition classes and cooking demonstrations; half also got personalized bags of fresh produce every two weeks. Intake was tracked with screeners, day recalls, and food questionnaires.

The produce group showed favorable shifts in how often several fruits and vegetables were eaten, though most group-to-group differences missed statistical significance. Antwi reads the patterns as promising and calls for a larger, fully powered trial.
plos-pone-0354920:
Femke W Overbosch and colleagues staged two table-top drills of a bird flu outbreak sweeping out of the Netherlands. Experts in health, society, and money sat first in split teams, then mixed. Their 2026 study had about forty experts across the drills. The team studied the written advice each setup produced. It also spoke with the experts before the drills. The goal was hunting for blind spots in how governments get outbreak advice.

Split teams disagreed on urgency. They disagreed on how bad things could get, and fiercely on school closures. Mixed talks showed each field's blind spots and built shared grasp of the problem. They also exposed tangled gaps in the rule books and basic systems. The authors suggest merging the advice teams for real. Gluing split memos together at the top, they argue, is worse.
plos-pone-0355020:
Rachel D Gordon and colleagues interviewed eleven adults with sickle cell disease who hope to have biological children. They explored what the adults know about fertility. They also explored what help they have been offered. Their 2026 qualitative study covered participants aged eighteen to thirty-five at an American center. It used open interviews analyzed for themes. The backdrop is evidence that the disease and some treatments impair fertility.

Five themes surfaced. Doctors rarely raised family building. Women felt unprepared for what pregnancy with the disease involves. Partners seemed to share the planning burden unequally. Costs shut down serious consideration of assisted reproduction. Above all, participants asked for earlier, repeated conversations. The authors urge sickle cell care to treat reproduction as routine, not taboo.
plos-pone-0355520:
Correction notice. Xin Pang and co-authors correct two figures in their published study of immune suppressor cells in oral cancer progression. After publication, readers flagged panels that appeared to overlap across different cell lines and conditions. This 2026 notice replaces the faulty panels with originals from the reported experiments.

The authors state that all three starting-time panels in one figure were incorrect and supply a corrected figure with its underlying data files. One panel in a second figure was likewise incorrect and is replaced. A panel said to show one cell line had overlapped a panel from another article showing a different line. The notice documents each fix so the experimental record can be checked.
plos-pone-0355620:
Cui Lin and colleagues followed rectal cancer patients home to test whether caregiver skill predicts stoma complications. A new ostomy demands careful daily care, and the family caregiver usually provides it. Their 2026 prospective study rated caregiver skill at discharge against set standards, then checked patients one month later.

Just over a third of patients developed a complication within the month, most often skin irritation or leakage. The skill gradient was steep. About three quarters of patients with low-skill caregivers had complications, against about one fifth in the high-skill group. Lin and colleagues argue discharge training should be tested against a clear skill standard, not given as a leaflet and a hope.
plos-pone-0355720:
Zehra Narlı Özdemir and coauthors published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on fatigue in people with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. That is an ultra-rare blood disorder in which red cells are destroyed by the body's own complement system. Fatigue is the complaint patients say never resolves, even on the standard drug eculizumab. Clinicians at eighteen Turkish centers surveyed just over a hundred treated patients face to face with a standard questionnaire.

More than a third of patients scored in the severe fatigue range despite treatment. Those patients had lower hemoglobin at diagnosis and at survey time, and they had spent longer on extra medications. In adjusted analysis, being female, having other illnesses, longer extra-medication use, and lower starting hemoglobin each tracked with severe fatigue. The results suggest that controlling the blood disorder alone does not lift fatigue, and clinics should track and treat it as its own problem.
plos-pone-0356220:
Naveen Kumar B and Aslam Abdullah Mohammed built a classifier in 2026 that helps detect when a drilled borehole has wandered off course. Borehole deviation matters in oil, gas, and water drilling because a crooked hole can miss its target and raise costs. Their method reads conventional well log data, the standard measurements recorded in every drilled well, and looks for the signature that the rock formation's response leaves when deviation occurs.

Using data that drillers already collect means the tool can be applied without new instruments down the hole. Catching deviation early lets drilling teams correct course before a small drift becomes an expensive sidetrack. The study applies machine learning classification to a stubborn, practical problem in field geology.
plos-pone-0356620:
Huiling Chen and five colleagues mine twelve years of United States food recall records to find what makes a recall high-risk, in this 2026 study. Their source is the Food and Drug Administration's enforcement reports from 2012 to 2024, covering nearly twenty-seven thousand food recall events. They classified each recall's hazard, product, reach, and region, then modeled which features accompany the most serious category, Class I, meaning a real chance of serious harm.

Yearly counts swung widely without a steady trend. Two hazards dominated: microbial contamination and undeclared allergens. Bacterial contamination recalls were classified as high-risk at consistently high rates across food categories, while allergen recalls varied much more. Once hazard type was accounted for, region, product category, and distribution scope added little. The authors say the classification system is driven mainly by the hazard itself, as its rules intend.
plos-pone-0356720:
Birhane Alem Berihu and seven colleagues measured folate levels in pregnant women in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, reporting in 2026. The region records some of the world's highest rates of neural tube defects, birth defects of the brain and spine that folate prevents. Four hundred women in their first trimester at five public hospitals gave blood samples and answered questions about their diets.

The results were stark: nearly ninety-nine in every hundred women fell below the blood folate level recommended for preventing these defects. Four in five also ate too narrow a range of foods, yet even women with varied diets were almost all deficient. Older mothers fared slightly worse, while dietary variety helped only a little. The authors argue that advice and occasional supplements cannot fix a gap this wide, and they call for mandatory fortification of staple foods at national scale.
plos-pone-0356820:
Tanchun Wang and five colleagues ask whether fatty liver disease simply speeds up normal liver aging, using large public gene-activity datasets in this 2026 study. The disease, now called MASLD, is common and worsens with age, but its molecular path over a lifetime is poorly mapped. The team combined well over a thousand liver samples from healthy donors and patients across a wide age range.

Healthy and diseased livers shared surprisingly few age-related genes, and some genes even moved in opposite directions with age. In healthy livers, aging genes centered on the cell cycle. In diseased livers, the changes instead involved protein cleanup systems, stress responses, and a pathway tied to cell death, and many tracked with scarring severity. The authors conclude the disease follows its own aging route, not just a faster version of the normal one, which matters for age-aware treatment.
plos-pone-0356920:
Shiho Hansen, Snefrid Møllersen, Anna Rita Spein, and Anne Cecilie Jávo present a protocol, published in 2026. It covers a survey of every upper secondary student in Finnmark, Norway's far northern county. The topic is problematic internet use. The study is designed for a multiethnic region. It will compare Sámi Indigenous adolescents with their non-Sámi peers. These groups are rarely examined side by side on digital behavior.

A bilingual questionnaire, in Northern Sámi and Norwegian, will measure compulsive internet use. It will also cover family, peer, and school norms. Strength of ethnic identity and experiences of ethnic discrimination are included. The analysis plan tests whether norms and identity protect against unhealthy use, or feed it. No results exist yet. The finished study should guide culturally fitting prevention in Arctic schools.
plos-pone-0357020:
Jiyoung Emily Lee led a team of eight authors studying the tear film of the eye, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A thin lipid layer floats on tears and keeps eyes moist; its thickness varies more than doctors once assumed. The team ran a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of that variability and its clinical meaning.

Lee's findings help eye doctors read this subtle marker of dry eye disease and tailor treatment to it. Dry eye is common, uncomfortable, and often treated by trial and error. A measurable trait like lipid thickness, properly understood, can sort patients by cause. The study's care in describing normal variability is what makes abnormal readings meaningful in the clinic.
plos-pone-0357920:
Yan Nee Gan and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on preparing a pharmacy-led HIV prevention service for Malaysia. The prevention pill PrEP works, yet only a few thousand Malaysians took the free government supply in 2024, against hundreds of thousands who could benefit. Private pharmacies could widen access. This study reports a one-day Kuala Lumpur consultation where twenty-eight stakeholders stress-tested the model before its pilot.

The group worked through the barriers their earlier research had surfaced. They drafted fixes: build awareness and demand, protect privacy and confidentiality, keep it affordable, and fold in HIV self-testing. They also proposed digital checklists, simpler lab requirements, and a practical workflow guide, plus serious training. Training needs ran from drug basics to eligibility judgments and referral drills. The refined model is presented as ready for pilot testing, with cross-sector cooperation as its glue.
plos-pone-0358120:
Khomsan Yooyen led a team of six authors studying anemia in diabetes patients in northeastern Thailand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Anemia and type 2 diabetes often occur together, and the pairing raises risks for the heart, kidneys, and eyes. The team ran a cross-sectional study to measure how common anemia is in this group and what drives it.

Yooyen's findings tell local doctors whom to screen and which factors to watch. Anemia is easy to miss because its tiredness looks like diabetes itself. Routine screening of the highest-risk patients can catch it early and cheaply. The study's value is local precision: national averages would hide the pattern in this region's clinics.
plos-pone-0358720: Mohammadi and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on guayule, a desert shrub grown as a source of natural rubber. They treated the plants with salicylic acid, a hormone-like chemical, and tracked changes in growth form. They also tracked how active the key genes for rubber making became. The work bears on efforts to grow more rubber at home instead of relying on rubber trees abroad.
plos-pone-0359620: Onyango and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE policy study set in Kisumu, Kenya. They read COVID-19 rules through a lens that weighs overlapping traits like sex, income, and social role. The focus was women who sell food in open, informal markets. The study asks how pandemic rules landed on this group in daily life. Its lessons apply when governments write emergency rules that hit informal workers hardest.
pmc-10652620:
Bryan Chow and co-authors review how Singapore used a digital tracing system to slow the spread of COVID-19, in a study from 2023. The system, called TraceTogether, used phone signals and tokens to log close contact between people. The team studied its role during the Delta and Omicron waves, from late August 2021 to mid February 2022.

The authors compared full digital tracing on its own with manual tracing backed by the digital system. They counted how many close contacts each method found, how many of those contacts later tested positive, and how much time each method saved. They also looked at who used the app or tokens. The work helps judge what digital tools add to classic tracing work.
pmc-10655320:
Nina Teske and co-authors study in 2023 whether cells that wrap small brain blood vessels help protect against bacterial meningitis. These cells help control blood flow and keep the blood brain barrier tight, and they may also react to infection. Evidence in live animals was scarce, so the team tested the cells in the lab and in two animal models of the disease.

Human and mouse cells were exposed to the bacteria that cause the disease, with and without blockers of key sensors. In fish embryos, removing these cells changed the course of infection. In mice bred to lack them, disease patterns also shifted. The authors conclude the cells help by shaping white cell entry and barrier function.
pmc-10656820:
Patience Afulani and co-authors test two scales that measure person centered care in pregnancy and birth. Their 2023 study is set in Fresno, California. It uses survey data from a trial of antenatal care for low income mothers. Most respondents, at seventy eight percent, identified as Latinx. Surveys were given in English or Spanish, as each person preferred.

One scale, with twenty six items, was given at thirty to thirty four weeks of pregnancy. It went to 315 people. The second, with thirty five items, was given ten to fourteen weeks after birth, to 286 people. Each scale showed one dominant factor, explaining more than sixty percent of variance. Items also fit three sub scales: dignity and respect, communication and autonomy, and responsive care. Scores run from zero to one hundred.
pmc-10657520:
Regaieg and nine co-authors work a hard breath path for a new-born's mouth lump cut in this twenty twenty-three case report. The girl, not yet a month old, bore a big roof lump and a wide cleft. Such lumps can block the breath path and bar tube place at birth.

Inside, scans warned that tube place could fail, so the team braced for it. A hard-case cart and a throat cut hand stood by in the room. Gas sleep kept her breath free while a plain scope slipped the tube in. The lump then came out in full with no breath crash in the run. The team backs crew-wide drills for such rare birth lumps.
pmc-10659620:
Tianzhi Song and co-authors review in 2023 how one signal pathway shapes brain injury after a stroke is treated. Restoring blood flow can itself harm the brain, a problem called ischemia-reperfusion injury. The JAK/STAT pathway helps drive the inflammation behind that harm.

The review traces how the pathway switches on immune cells that release inflammatory factors, pushing brain cells toward death. The same signals also guide neuron growth and stem cell fate, so the pathway cuts both ways. Many traditional Chinese medicines act on parts of this pathway in lab studies. The authors gather that evidence to guide future clinical work on herbal treatment for stroke injury.
pmc-10659720:
Fulin Tao and co-authors test, in a 2023 study, whether printing a patient's broken pelvis in three dimensions before surgery improves the repair of old, deformed fractures. Such inveterate injuries, left weeks before treatment, heal crooked and resist standard planning. Seventeen patients had their operations planned on a printed model of their own pelvis; twenty matched patients had conventional surgery.

The printed-model group spent less time in surgery, lost less blood, and needed fewer X-ray checks during the operation. Their pain scores after surgery were also better. Yet the honest limits matter: hip and pelvis function recovered the same in both groups, and the final alignment on imaging did not differ. The authors conclude that printing earns its place in preparation and in a smoother operation, but does not by itself buy a better-working joint.
pmc-10669620:
Florian Baletaud and co-authors compared fish communities on coral reefs and seamounts off New Caledonia using DNA traces and baited cameras, in a study published in 2023. Seamounts, underwater mountains, are often called diversity hotspots and refuges, yet hard data are thin. Five settings from shallow reefs to deep seamounts were surveyed.

Depth drove most of the pattern in both diversity and total fish weight. Species counts fell steadily with depth, but total weight peaked at the shallowest seamounts rather than on reefs. Large predators such as sharks weighed three times more at fifty meters on seamounts than on reefs. Each setting held a fairly distinct community, linked mainly by wide-ranging predators. The authors conclude seamounts are not diversity hotspots, but shallow ones are biomass oases worth protecting.
pmc-10675120:
Ella Ewens and co-authors evaluate Meat-Free Mondays in New Zealand hospital cafes in a 2023 paper. Cutting meat serves both human health and the planet, yet few policies push it. Hospitals, as health exemplars, are a natural test bed.

Three health boards stood at different stages: one not considering the policy, one that had trialed it, and one rolling it out. A staff survey drew 194 responses, and eleven managers were interviewed. About half the staff were already cutting back on meat, and most viewed the campaign positively. Four themes emerged around choice, execution quality, health leadership, and local food culture. Price and taste decided whether the idea survived contact with the lunch queue.
pmc-10675720:
Yonggang Guo and colleagues study the friction and wear behaviour of cotton fabric resin composites reinforced with four flat nanomaterials. Their 2023 study tests the laminated materials under dry rubbing and water lubrication for bearing-type uses.

Graphite-filled composite performed best dry, cutting friction by about a quarter and wear by over three quarters versus the unfilled material. Under water, no filler changed friction much, but most reduced wear at sensible loadings. One sulphur-based filler at ten percent content cut wear by over half in water. Microscopy and surface chemistry analysed the transfer films formed during rubbing. Computer simulations compared how two composites grip the opposing surface under both conditions.
pmc-10687520:
Ganesha and co-authors build a sensor from flower-shaped sheets that can spot hydrazine, a toxic chemical, at very low levels. Their 2023 study mixes a conducting polymer with a layered mineral-like compound, with the help of a soap-like aid. The blend forms thin sheets bunched like petals.

The team checked the blend's build with X-rays and light-based tools, and viewed its shape with fine scopes. Spread on a carbon electrode, the sheets gave a strong, near-reversible signal. In pulse tests the sensor read hydrazine across a wide band, with a floor near half a micro-unit and high sensitivity. In a real water sample it found near all of a spiked dose, which backs field use.
pmc-10692120:
Jie Bai and five colleagues build a prediction chart for which liver failure patients will go on to develop cirrhosis, in a 2023 study. No score existed for hepatitis B patients whose sudden-on-chronic failure struck a still unscarred liver.

Two hundred seventy-four patients were followed for a year; about forty-five percent developed cirrhosis. A muscle measure, the psoas index from scans, protected against that outcome: more muscle, less risk. The final chart combines muscle, age, an inflammation ratio, and a clotting measure. It scored well in both the building and testing groups, with calibration to match. The authors suggest muscle-preserving care may matter for long-term liver fate.
pmc-10692220:
Diego Subero and co-authors report, in a 2023 experiment, a supercurrent that hides from ordinary electrical tests but betrays itself through heat. A Josephson junction, quantum circuits' basic link, was long predicted to turn insulating when shunted by a large enough resistance. Recent microwave work clouded that story.

The team placed a tiny junction in a noise-driven setup and probed it with heat, barely disturbing its balance. By direct current measures the junction indeed blocked charge, its critical current gone, as theory said. Yet heat flow showed it still acting as an inductor at high frequency, proof a supercurrent survives. The two faces coexist: insulating to slow probes, superconducting to fast ones. The result reframes an old prediction about how environment strangles quantum coherence.
pmc-10693120:
Pouria Samadi and four co-authors scan a little-studied RNA strand across 33 cancer types to judge its value as a marker. The strand, called HAND2-AS1, does not code for protein, yet earlier work tied it to cancer growth and immune activity. The team charted its levels, chemical marks, and mutations in tumor data, and built networks of genes that rise and fall with it. In most tumors its levels ran low, and low levels tracked with worse survival.

Its activity linked to tumor growth paths and to immune traffic inside tumors. Higher levels came with more immune cells of several kinds, both attackers and suppressors. Tests on colon tumor samples backed the data patterns. The authors cast the strand as a possible tumor suppressor and a candidate for prognosis and immune therapy planning.
pmc-10693620:
Hamid Mohammadi and co-authors test a growth compound on lentils under dry and watered field conditions in this 2023 study. Lentils are a key plant protein across three continents. Drought and other stresses cut their yields. The compound, called ALA, is a building block for green pigments. Sprayed on leaves, it can raise stress tolerance in crops. The team ran a split-plot field experiment.

Some plots got extra irrigation, others only rainfall. Spray levels varied across the plots as the second factor. Growth, yield, and body measures were recorded. Results show how the spray interacts with water supply. Rain-fed farming dominates lentil regions, so the dry arm matters most. The paper is an agronomy field study.
pmc-10694120:
Puskar Bhattarai and co-authors published a research paper in 2023 on predicting thinking problems in mild cognitive impairment from brain scans of amyloid, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid gathers in a known sequence of brain regions, and its pattern may foreshadow decline. The team trained learning algorithms to estimate test scores from regional amyloid alone.

Both a regression method and a neural network predicted cognition well, the network better. Impaired participants carried more amyloid, most tellingly in mid and late spread regions. An explanation tool named the memory-linked regions that drove the predictions. The approach could support earlier detection before full dementia sets in.
pmc-10694820:
Hengzhi Ruan and eight co-authors build a gelatin gel that fights germs and does much more in this 2023 paper. Plain gelatin gels are weak and melt easily, which limits their medical use. The team stirred in dopamine and a zwitterionic compound, triggered inside the gel with zinc sulfate present.

The finished hydrogel killed essentially all Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria tested, a top mark for its class. It also sticks to surfaces, heals its own cuts, resists freezing, conducts electricity, and survives flexing across a wide span from deep cold to hot. The authors pitch the material for wearable health sensors and antibacterial coatings, where one gel that does many jobs could replace several single purpose ones.
pmc-10695920:
Minhui Ke and co-authors build a rat model of internal haemorrhoids for use in research, in work published in 2023. A good animal model is needed to test treatments, since the disease is hard to study directly in people. The team combined a croton oil mixture with standing and swimming stress to trigger the condition.

They compared one week and two weeks of model building in 48 rats. Both schedules produced swollen tissue in the haemorrhoid area. Microscopy showed swollen blood vessels and immune cell influx, and blood-flow imaging showed raised flow in the area. The changes persisted after two weeks of normal feeding. One week of building matched the human disease most closely. The authors offer the model as a simple, stable base for haemorrhoid research.
pmc-10696020:
Mi Hee Kwack and four co-authors built, in a 2023 study, matched cell lines from the front and back scalp of patients with androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss. Frontal follicles tend to shrink in this condition, while occipital follicles resist, but frontal cells are hard to grow in the lab. No such matched pair of lines had been reported before.

The team immortalized frontal and occipital dermal papilla cells by introducing two genes, SV40 large T antigen and human telomerase reverse transcriptase. The lines kept the marks of their zone, in gene expression and response to androgens. Fluid from the frontal line slowed hair growth and pushed skin cells toward death. In 3D culture, the frontal line clumped less well than the occipital line and lost hair support genes. The pair gives laboratories a tool to probe why loss hits the front of the scalp.
pmc-10696820:
Keiko Kan-o and eight co-authors published a pediatric study in twenty twenty-three on steroid treatment during asthma attacks triggered by rhinovirus, the common cold virus. Such attacks fill children's wards, yet how steroids interact with the virus was unclear. The team followed school-age inpatients across two years.

Nasal samples from fifty-four children were tested for viruses; about eighty-three percent carried one. Rhinovirus types A and C each appeared in about thirty percent of patients. Maintenance inhaled steroids were checked against which species showed up. In virus-positive children, lung function three months later was compared by how long steroid courses lasted. The study gives rare prospective data on a very common childhood emergency.
pmc-10697620:
Thit Kronborg and a large team run a placebo-controlled trial of a statin in liver cirrhosis. Their trial from twenty twenty-three treats patients with high portal pressure. Statins may lower that pressure and calm liver inflammation. Fewer complications and deaths are the hoped-for outcomes.

Seventy-eight patients were randomised to drug or placebo for six months. About sixty patients completed the full intervention period. Gut blood flow measurements tracked pressure-related changes. Blood markers and fat profiles were measured before and after. Admissions and survival were recorded throughout the trial. The design tests statins beyond their cholesterol role. Cirrhosis care lacks drugs that change disease course.
pmc-10698320:
Motoya Sato, Akiyoshi Takami, and Misato Makino recorded muscle activity in patients with severe stroke paralysis as therapists walked them with a full leg brace. Posterior gait assistance with a knee-ankle-foot orthosis is a staple of early rehabilitation, yet which muscles fire, and when, was not well documented. Thirty patients in the acute phase took part.

Electrodes tracked four leg muscles through the stance phase, split into halves. Activity patterns were compared with standard scales of consciousness, recovery stage, balance, and independence. Knowing which muscles the brace walk truly recruits helps therapists set goals and spot compensation. Severe hemiplegia leaves few chances to rebuild walking; each should be used well.
pmc-10698920:
James Wachira and co-authors train rural Kenyan health workers in obstetric ultrasound in a 2023 paper. Ultrasound saves mothers and babies, but machines and skills are scarce where need is greatest, defying world guidance for universal pregnancy scans. A partnership supplied handheld devices and trainers.

Five-day workshops reached five hundred fourteen mid-level providers in three months, most in eight counties with poor birth outcomes. Five scan topics covered danger signs from breech presentation to fluid problems. Trainers watched skills directly, and test scores jumped after training. The scale-up shows short intensive courses can spread scanning skill fast across rural systems.
pmc-10699020:
Maryrose Bauschka and co-authors present a 2023 study on a fear that can block treatment in severe anorexia. Atypical antipsychotic drugs sometimes help the anxiety and distorted thinking of the illness, but in other patients they reliably cause weight gain, which terrifies people with anorexia. No drug is approved for the condition, so every option carries this tension.

The team reviewed records of patients with extreme anorexia in a case-control design. Their hypothesis was that this group, unlike other psychiatric patients, does not gain extra weight from these drugs. The comparison bore that out: weight restoration proceeded at the same pace with or without the medication. The finding may ease a hard conversation at the bedside. Clinicians can offer symptom relief without promising a side effect that does not appear.
pmc-10699320:
Julien Rousseau, Tarik Slaoui, and François Bergeron report a case of stroke in a young man tied to syphilis in the brain, in a French-language paper from 2023. The patient was thirty-six, HIV-positive, and came in with sudden slurred speech and weakness on his right side. Stroke in young adults has many possible causes, from heart flaws to vessel swelling. Pinning down the cause shapes the care that follows.

The authors explain that syphilis can inflame brain arteries of all sizes and trigger strokes. A special high-detail scan of the vessel wall gave the key clue here. It showed a ring of contrast in the wall, a sign of an inflamed or infected vessel rather than plain hardening. They urge matching scan signs with tissue checks when that is possible. The case shows the worth of wall imaging in young stroke.
pmc-10700620:
Textile making uses vast energy and water and releases large amounts of greenhouse gases. Imran and nine co-authors build a method to measure three footprints for textile products: carbon, energy, and water across a product's life. They apply the method as a baseline for the sector, with Asia's large textile trade in mind.

The total carbon footprint of the products studied came to about 42,600 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent. Indirect emissions, from bought energy and materials, far outweighed direct ones. The energy footprint reached about 248 petajoules, mostly from electricity, and the water footprint about 81 billion liters. Spinning was the heaviest stage for carbon and energy, and energy use drove all three footprints. The authors say such measuring, and even carbon labels, can help buyers and makers cut the sector's impact.
pmc-10702020:
David Romero and co-authors set sage word next to field logs to map where toads and frogs thrive in Uruguay, in a study from 2023. Sages hold range lore in their heads; logs hold dots on maps. The two speak unlike tongues, till fuzzy math gives both one coin: how kind a spot is to a kind.

Kind by kind, the team built both maps and read their meet. At-risk kinds, kinds sages call wide-spread, and plain kinds each got the pair. The cross of the two maps gave one joint call of kind spots. Sage lore, oft waved off as soft, turns out to hold hard worth when writ in the same coin as the dots.
pmc-10702320:
Yu-Yun Gao and co-authors build a jelly-like scaffold for growing nerve cells in this 2023 study. Gelatin is kind to cells, and the team had earlier found that nerve cells thrive when a building block in gelatin takes a certain chemical form. They shaped that insight into a three-dimensional gel meant to host neurons.

The new gel mixed gelatin with a partner polymer carrying the favored chemical groups. Inside it, neurons lived better, grew longer fibers, and formed more junctions, while support cells that can crowd neurons grew less. Rival gels with other partners did not match these results. Tests in living tissue agreed. The authors credit the special chemical group, not the gel's stiffness or stretch, and offer the design as a base for nerve repair work.
pmc-10703320:
Lois Choi-Kain and co-authors present a 2023 protocol for a pilot trial in borderline personality disorder. Tailored therapy beats generic therapy for this condition in past trials. Gold standard care is intense, long, and scarce, which leaves a wide supply gap. Psychoeducation is a cheap, light part of most effective care for the condition. It alone relieves symptoms in past work. The team tests online video lessons as the first step of care.

Digital assessments join the videos in the pilot design. The trial checks safety and feasibility before any larger run. Patients get plain facts about their diagnosis and care path early. That early clarity may cut dropout while people wait for full therapy. Health systems get a low-cost bridge for a long queue. The protocol paper sets the design in public, so later results can be judged against the plan.
pmc-10703820:
Kazusa Miyahara, Misako Tatehana, Takako Kikkawa, and Noriko Osumi report a two thousand twenty-three mouse study on father's age and sperm. Older fathers link to higher autism risk in children. Tiny RNA molecules in sperm may carry age effects.

The team profiled sperm microRNAs from mice at three ages. Dozens of molecules changed between young and old groups. Their target genes clustered around cell death pathways and the nervous system. The pattern suggests ageing sperm could pass risk signals to offspring. Readers get a possible biological route behind a well-known statistical link.
pmc-10705720:
Tamara Ordonez Diaz and co-authors compare test pain and mind strain in adults with joint wear at the thumb or knee. The study appeared in 2023. It draws on over four hundred adults from two city areas. Each did health forms, pain tests, and body task checks.

Groups split by pain site were set next to a pain-free group. The both-sites group felt pain at lower push loads and summed pain more than lone-site groups. That group also told of the most pain and the most loss of function. The knee group bore heat pain less well than the thumb group. Wear at two sites hit harder than at one.
pmc-10707020:
Xiaoqiang Zhao and co-authors show a spray of serotonin helps maize shoots stretch past deep seed stress. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Deep sets past twenty counts down help maize rise in dry lands, yet the spray's role was not tried. Two maize lines were sown deep and plain, with split spray doses, and growth, body marks, and gene use read.

Deep sets stretched shoot spans and a growth call while lignin fell. The spray fired growth call genes, curbed lignin genes, and cut stress waste, so spans grew more. Best dose was cast the same for both lines. Rise rates rose with the spray.
pmc-10707520:
Haim Breitbart and co-authors review how sperm are protected from firing too early in a 2023 article. To fertilize an egg, sperm must first mature in the female tract, then release enzymes from a cap called the acrosome at the right moment. If that release happens early, before reaching the egg covering, fertilization can fail.

The review describes built in safeguards during the maturation process. A key step builds a scaffold of actin protein inside the sperm, which is later dispersed before the proper release. Several chemical changes during maturation help hold the cap in place. The authors sum up how these mechanisms keep the reaction timed correctly.
pmc-10709320:
Seven authors wrote a review in two thousand twenty-three on living, engineered bacteria as treatments for skin. The skin's microbe community guards its health, and imbalance in that community links to many skin disorders. Antibiotics carry side effects, so interest has turned to live biotherapeutic products that restore a healthy balance.

The review covers products built from single engineered cells, tuned by gene or metabolic editing to target specific cells and deliver healing agents. Early studies show promise for repair and disease care. Yet the authors stress that moving into clinics is still hard, with practical scale-up a major open problem.
pmc-10709620:
Mie Rath Refn and co-authors report a 2023 study of DNA methylation change over 15 years. Methylation is a chemical tag on DNA that helps steer gene activity and shifts with age. Forensic teams use set tag sites to guess age, so how steady those sites are matters.

The team read genome wide tags in 64 people at two points 15 years apart with a large chip assay. A mixed model found 2,821 tag sites tied to age, with a median drift of 0.18 percent per year. Baseline levels varied a lot between people of like age, and the drift path was not uniform. Of 23 sites used in forensic age models, only one site shifted in the same path for every person.
pmc-10709920:
Park and co-authors test a neural network that sorts tooth decay from fluorescence images of live teeth. The images come from a light-based tool that makes decay stand out. Smarter image tools could help dentists spot decay more evenly.

The team gathered 2,814 mouth images from 606 clinic patients over two years. Images were split into training, checking, and test sets for the model. They used the Xception network and also made masked images to judge tooth area tracing. Results were split by tooth type, with 1,143 premolar and 1,441 molar images compared.
pmc-10710320:
Vasiliki Bountziouka and three co-authors ask whether adult life got fairer for people who grew up with poor sight, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. They used three British birth cohorts, born in nineteen forty-six, nineteen fifty-eight, and nineteen seventy, more than fourteen thousand people in all. Sight was checked in the teen years, and health, work, housing, and social life were tracked into middle age. The span covers decades of new disability law and policy.

The trends were mixed, not a simple march of progress. In the youngest cohort, those with poor childhood sight faced worse odds of poor physical health, crowded or poor housing, and joblessness than their peers. Some gaps shrank, others grew. The authors say laws alone have not leveled adult life for this group.
pmc-10711820:
Linda Birt and co-authors set out a protocol in 2023 for a study of dementia courses at Recovery Colleges in England. Such colleges run short courses co-produced by staff and people with lived experience. Support after a dementia diagnosis varies widely, and how this model fits dementia care is little understood.

The evaluation uses a realist approach, asking what works, for whom, and why. Five case sites across health trusts will host observation of course co-production, interviews with people with dementia, supporters, and staff, and review of course documents. The findings will feed resources, co-produced with stakeholder groups, to guide future dementia courses tied to post-diagnosis services.
pmc-10711920:
Daniela Fortuna, Luana Caselli, Elena Berti, and Maria Luisa Moro measure the indirect toll of COVID-19 on chronic disease patients in a hard-hit Italian region, in a 2023 study. The region is Emilia-Romagna. About one point eight million adults with chronic conditions were tracked. The study covers 2020 and 2021. It compares deaths and care use with pre-pandemic expectations. Non-COVID deaths are the focus.

Overall non-COVID mortality barely exceeded the expected level. Only the first wave, in March 2020, spiked sharply. Later phases stayed at or below the threshold. Care patterns shifted a great deal. End-of-life hospital stays fell while home care rose. Hospital admissions, major procedures, and emergency visits all dropped. Outpatient services collapsed during the first lockdown, then partly recovered. The authors give a full regional account of collateral damage. Planners can use it to protect chronic care in future crises.
pmc-10712120:
Fekih-Romdhane and eight co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three validating an Arabic version of a short perfectionism scale. Perfectionism links to many mental health symptoms across cultures. Arab research in this area has lagged behind other regions. The team translate the sixteen-item scale and test it in Lebanese adults. Over five hundred adults answer through a web survey. Factor checks confirm the scale's three-part structure in Arabic. Those parts cover rigid, self-critical, and narcissistic perfectionism.

All three parts show strong reliability scores in the sample. The scale measures alike across men and women in their tests. Scores track with distress in the expected direction and against well-being. The authors offer the scale for research and clinical screening.
pmc-10712220:
Tiedong Liu, Xiwen Zhang, and Shengqun Liu map how blue and red light steer the cell cycle in maize. Their transcriptome study was published in twenty twenty-three. Light color is a master signal for plant growth, but its grip on division genes was little charted.

Plants grew under red, blue, and switched light regimes. Twenty-three genes changed across conditions. Four unnamed genes stood out by their links to known cycle genes. Sequence and structure comparisons identified them as relatives of known regulators, tied to stress defense, phosphate hunger, and cycle control. Network building placed them in the machinery. The identifications convert anonymous genes into named suspects for light breeding.
pmc-10713320:
Hyewon Seo and co-authors examine what wheezing signals in patients with chronic lung disease, in a 2023 study. The disease, COPD, narrows airways over time. Some patients also have asthma features, a blend called overlap. The team used a large Korean cohort study. Patients were sorted into four groups by overlap status and self-reported wheezing. Symptoms, lung function, and flare-ups over one year were compared.

About fifty-six percent reported wheezing in both the overlap and non-overlap groups. Wheezing patients had worse symptoms and lung function in both groups. They also faced higher flare-up risk. Blood cell counts tied to allergy did not track wheezing. The overlap-with-wheezing group flared most often. More frequent wheezing meant higher risk. The authors call wheezing a marker of severe disease in its own right. It should not be read as proof of the overlap blend.
pmc-10714520:
Yue and co-authors hunt genes tied to term sugar ill in Han Chinese dams. The ill, GDM, bends sugar work in dam and child past birth. Gene traits drive much of the risk, and links shift by stock. Gene clues for Han dams had stayed thin in past hunts. The team ran a broad gene sweep on 398 Han dams. Half the set had GDM, and half did not. Hits were checked next to sugar traits in world banks.

Five fresh marks hit the broad bar for GDM ties. Two marks sat in the TRPV3 and PRMT6 genes in the sweep. Those two tied to sugar reads at one and two hours. Sifted marks were then checked with ward facts from the term. Dams with GDM got tracked past birth for sugar shifts.
pmc-10714620:
Two common dementias leave distinct marks in the fat molecules in the blood. Xin Ying Chua and co-authors profile those fats in a 2023 study of 526 people, comparing healthy minds, early impairment, Alzheimer disease, and vascular dementia.

The team used a lipid-testing platform to measure the sphingolipid family. These fats play a role in cell signals, yet past work on dementia has mostly skipped them. One chain-length family rose in Alzheimer disease while another fell in vascular dementia, a clean contrast. Two specific molecules tied most strongly to Alzheimer disease. Panels made from several fats sorted each type better than single markers did. Blood panels of this kind could one day help doctors tell the two dementias apart without brain scans.
pmc-10714920:
Filip Kolesar and five co-authors test a new way to pull americium out of nuclear waste liquid in a study from 2023. Americium is a long-lived radioactive element in spent fuel waste, and sorting it from look-alike elements eases waste handling. Their variant of a known process swaps the usual oily solvent for an ionic liquid, a salt that is liquid at room temperature.
