Tests tracked how acid strength and ligand dose affect each step, then ran both variants on a fake waste mix. The ionic liquid version split americium from light lanthanides and strontium more cleanly. Stripping ran slower, but the team found workable fixes for the snags.
pmc-10715920:
Junjun Liu, Haibo Xie, Mengfan Wu, Yidan Hu, and Yunsi Kang review the role of cilia in building organs in zebrafish in this 2023 paper. Cilia are hair-like parts that stick out from the surface of nearly all human cells. They carry signals, guide organ development, and keep tissues in balance.

When cilia form or work badly, a group of diseases called ciliopathies can result. Zebrafish serve as a model for this research since their cilia match ours closely in structure and function. The review sums up the types of cilia found in young and adult zebrafish. It sets out why the fish is a strong stand-in for human biology in this field. Then it walks through recent work on what cilia do as each organ forms. The authors close with the prospects they see for cilia research in fish.
pmc-10716120:
Qian Li and co-authors test whether a drug called IOX1 can make lung cancer cells easier to kill with radiation. Their study, published in 2023, looks at non-small cell lung cancer in cells and in animals. IOX1 blocks enzymes that remove marks from histones, the proteins that pack DNA.

Treated cells opened their packed DNA less at genes that repair damage, so repair slowed and harm from radiation grew. One repair-linked gene, PIF1, dropped sharply, and blocking it on its own also raised radiation damage. A protein called MAZ bound less near PIF1 after treatment, which helps explain the drop. The findings point to a possible drug partner for radiation therapy.
pmc-10717920:
Nine authors tie hepatitis C marks to liver harm in rural Cameroon in a 2023 clinic study. World goals aim to wipe the virus by 2030, yet RNA tests stay scarce in poor lands. At one rural center, 306 adults free of two kin ills gave blood for germ and liver checks.

About 16 percent held the virus mark, with women and those over 50 hit most. Liver harm sat near 30 percent of the set at large. Mark holders showed harm at 62.5 percent against 24 percent for the clear, which backs enzyme checks as sentry marks.
pmc-10719320:
Alice Teghil and co-authors map time perception across the Alzheimer's continuum in a 2023 study. Timing faults appear early in the disease, even at mild impairment. A still earlier stage, where people sense decline that tests miss, had never had its timing checked.

Groups with subjective decline, mild impairment, Alzheimer's, and healthy aging took a battery of timing tasks. Alzheimer's patients faltered at judging future durations and placing events in time. Subjective experience of time passage did not differ across groups. Learning from outside cues versus inner cues split the groups in telling ways. The authors name two tasks as candidate early markers of decline.
pmc-10720120:
Doctors lean on what they already know, and shared data systems may help them bring the right knowledge to mind. JunYi Yuan and co-authors study that link in this 2023 paper, comparing more than three hundred Chinese medical institutions, some with remote consultation platforms and some without.

Shared public-level data resources directly aided knowledge recall in both settings. Institution-level resources behaved differently depending on the platform, sometimes helping only through indirect routes involving technology and services. The authors say the patterns should guide governments and hospitals as they design data environments meant to sharpen clinical thinking.
pmc-10720220:
End-of-life care in China grows as the land ages and cancer spreads, and its quality rests on what ward staff know and feel. Meng Ling and five co-authors survey that ground in Sichuan in 2023. Their poll reached 1,591 health workers from the summer to the autumn of 2022.

The state has seeded pilot hospice wards and plans training bases in big hospitals. The poll maps where knowledge runs thin and where hearts resist, so the training can aim true. Hospice staff lead the service, so their grasp is the service. The study hands planners a base line: teach to the gaps this map shows, then poll again to see the shift.
pmc-10720520: Baker, Colston, Hervey, and Bird report in twenty twenty-three the full genome of a bacterium taken from soil tainted by so-called forever chemicals. These man-made chemicals break down very slowly and linger in soil and water. The bacterium was found living in soil heavily hit by them, which makes its gene set of interest. Its genome holds one large chromosome and one small plasmid, a ring of extra genes. The team read it with a long-read method and shares the sequence for further study.
pmc-10720920:
Yuchu Xiang and co-authors review research on a mitochondrial chaperone as a cancer target in a 2023 paper. The protein, mtHsp90, steadies many client proteins inside mitochondria and is abundant in tumors. Blocking it destabilizes those clients and disrupts several tumor pathways at once.

The review covers the protein's structure and function, then the inhibitor pipeline. One specific blocker, gamitrinib, has passed preclinical safety and efficacy work and is in clinical trials. Starving cancer's power-plant management is an elegant strategy; this paper maps how far the idea has traveled toward the clinic.
pmc-10722920:
Tsuyoshi Tajika and eight co-authors describe a joint replacement in a patient with hemophilia in this two thousand twenty-three case report. Repeated bleeding had wrecked the man's left elbow, leaving it stiff and bent. Total elbow replacement can ease pain and restore motion in such joints. But in hemophilia, surgery risks heavy bleeding and other complications. The patient was fifty years old and had a severe fixed bend.

During surgery, part of the upper arm bone cracked and had to be managed. Strict clotting factor replacement, guided by blood specialists, kept bleeding in check. Thirty months later, the elbow's range of motion had grown from a narrow arc to a wide one. Patient-rated scores also improved. The case shows careful planning can make this surgery pay off.
pmc-10727320:
Jennifer Stancati and fifteen colleagues summarize the 2022 Resuscitation Science Symposium, the American Heart Association's annual gathering for cardiac arrest research, in a 2023 review. The meeting in Chicago drew an international community working to improve survival after the heart stops.

The narrative review walks through the program: awards, special sessions, and scientific talks organized by theme and plenary. Beyond the core science of restarting hearts, the meeting ranged widely. Topics included survivorship, the long road after discharge; disparities in who gets timely care; and community programs that put bystanders and defibrillators in the right places. The authors present the summary as a field update for clinicians and researchers who missed the sessions. Their through-line: resuscitation now spans from the first compression to months of recovery, and from the hospital to the street.
pmc-10729020:
Marta Velázquez and co-authors report a clean way to build a family of nitrogen-rich ring compounds with the correct handedness. Their method dearomatises flat phthalazine rings — breaking their aromatic stability on purpose — through catalysis by anion binding. A catalyst derived from an amino acid grips the chloride partner of a reactive intermediate, steering the attack of a silicon-based partner to one face.

The products, dihydrophthalazines, form selectively and in high yield. Further steps convert them into several related families: more saturated rings, phthalazones, and piperazic acid relatives. Those skeletons appear in biologically relevant molecules, which is the point of the exercise. The authors present the route as a straightforward entry to chiral building blocks that asymmetric synthesis previously reached only with difficulty.
pmc-10729120:
Sofyan Sufri and eight co-authors study smoke-free areas in Banda Aceh, Indonesia, in a qualitative study from two thousand twenty-three. Rules ban smoking in set public areas, but enforcement there is weak. The team asked what blocks the policy and what could help it work.

They interviewed seventy-three people, from policymakers and enforcers to community and religious figures, and reviewed ten documents. Barriers included conflicts of interest, weak monitoring, poor public communication, and confusion over what counts as an enclosed area. On the plus side, schools promote the rules and religious teaching opposes smoking. The authors urge stronger communication, enforcement, and evaluation. They note the findings may apply to other Muslim-majority settings.
pmc-10729220:
Jinlong Zhang and co-authors lay out the plan for FLAVOUR II, a trial of two ways to guide heart stent work. One way reads blood flow from a plain vessel film, with no wire in the heart. The other peers inside the vessel with an ultrasound probe. Both beat film-alone care in past work, yet which leads for major blockages was not known.

The trial will split 1,872 patients with a major blockage in a main heart vessel, half and half. Set rules tell when to stent and how to refine the stent in each arm. The main mark at 12 months joins death, heart attack, and a repeat fix. Their 2023 paper is a plan and a rationale: it gives the rules, the marks, and the ethics path. Results will come when the trial ends.
pmc-10729520:
Katekani Shirindza and two co-authors pin down what home-based postnatal care means, since the term is used with loose edges. Such care brings mother and baby checks to the home in the weeks post-birth. The team read wide sources and ran the term through a set concept sieve. Case tales of full, edge, kin, and anti kinds helped fix the shape of the term.

Home skill care by lead carers, town voice and drive, and firm links to clinics form the core marks. What comes before and what flows from the care were mapped in the same pass. Culture shades how the care is lived, the read also notes. Midwife rule books can now gauge the term with set marks.
pmc-10733920:
Kai Zhou and co-authors published a geochemistry study in 2023 on coal-bearing mudstones from the Qaidam Basin in northwest China. These rocks record ancient climate and store organic matter for fuel. Samples from two Jurassic formations were put through carbon, sulfur, isotope, and element tests. Three layers emerged with differing organic richness.

Plant debris fed the lower layers, while the top layer mixed plant and water organism remains. Climate swung from warm and wet, to warm and dry, to hot and dry across the layers. Oxygen levels in the water governed organic buildup early on; later, sheer productivity took over. The authors map how climate shifts steered carbon storage.
pmc-10735420:
Amaanali Fazal, Kahir Lalji, and Barbara McMillan speak in 2023 on the special needs of older adults when disaster strikes. Older people face more harm in pandemics, storms, floods, fires, and heat waves, and they need more help to respond and recover. Recent crises in British Columbia made that plain.

A network plan, run by United Way British Columbia, now links senior-serving groups across the province. It has boosted contact, joint work, peer learning, and the spread of know-how among agencies and partners, the team reports. The talk makes the case for building such a web before the next crisis, not during it. Prepared groups can reach frail elders faster when roads, power, and phones fail.
pmc-10735620:
Jana Nikitin and Fiona Rupprecht study how time spent in nature links to care for future generations, in a paper from 2023. Generativity means acting for those who come after us, in politics, society, and care for the planet. The team tracked 115 adults of wide ages for a week. Each person reported nature contact up to eight times a day.

People who met nature more in daily life also scored higher on generativity. The link was not even across the group. It ran strongest in adults who felt their remaining lifetime was short. That flips a common belief that the young care most about climate and the future. The authors read the pattern through goal choice: a short time horizon favors aims with deep meaning. Nature contact may feed exactly those aims.
pmc-10735720:
Demitri Constantinou and Konstantinos Kastanos present a 2023 case report on an injury so rare that no playbook exists for it. The latissimus dorsi and teres major, two big muscles anchoring the arm to the back, can tear in elite throwing athletes, and surgeons sometimes repair them. Tearing both at once is rarer still, and its surgical outcomes were unrecorded.

Their patient was a forty-five-year-old man hurt while water-skiing. The authors describe his combined tear, the surgical repair they performed, and his favorable recovery, alongside a review of the scattered literature on these injuries. The report gives surgeons a first reference point for deciding whether to operate when both tendons give way together.
pmc-10735920:
Marti DeLiema and Laura Hemmy present a research group's work on money decisions in later life in a 2023 presentation. Handling money well calls for problem solving, clear thinking, and knowing key facts. Those skills are among the first to fade with aging and brain disease, which puts older adults at risk of fraud and loss.

The Financial Decision Making Special Interest Group joins researchers from social work and neuropsychology. Members pool distinct skills: testing cognition, working with patients, and tracing how poor decisions harm financial security. The presentation shares how the group built its membership and found samples to pilot new measures. Their shared agenda aims to chart how money skills change with age.
pmc-10736020:
Carey Wexler Sherman and Joseph Gaugler introduce a symposium on keeping dementia caregiver programs alive in this 2023 paper. Proven programs help family caregivers of people with dementia. Their benefit fades if host organizations cannot run them faithfully over time. The symposium gathers four papers on one program, called Savvy Caregiver.

The first paper reports interviews with 25 staff in nine organizations that deliver the program. Teamwork across organizations and regions helped keep quality high. The second paper describes an online training course for program leaders, built from those findings. Later papers extend the structure further. The aim is a reusable model so decision makers can sustain proven programs, not just launch them.
pmc-10736220:
Barb Nicklas and co-authors reported in 2023 on Walk On, a church-based walking program that kept older adults moving. A large past study showed walking guards against mobility loss, but gains faded once the program stopped. Walk On runs group walks twice a week for twelve weeks, for a fee, with stamina as the aim. Ten rounds ran from late 2017 to early 2020.

Most guests were over seventy-five, female, and slow walkers, and a third used a walking aid. Near two thirds signed up for at least one more round, and showing up stayed near seventy-seven percent. The team calls the safe, social, low-barrier setup one way to keep gains alive, and plans work on who sticks best.
pmc-10736320:
Older adults often leave the hospital with new risks at home, from missed drugs to weak follow-up. Karen Hirschman and co-authors report what it took to run a nurse-led care model for that move in a 2023 study. The model, tested in a large trial, pairs each patient with a skilled nurse who guides care from hospital to home.

The team studied 167 work meetings held at three health systems during the trial. The top hurdles were patient and family factors, staff gaps, and weak teamwork across groups. Sites fixed them in local ways, such as clear role rules, care plans fit to each case, and video visits in place of home calls. The lessons can guide any group that adopts a complex care model.
pmc-10736620:
Saraswathy Battar and Michael Silverman wrote a 2023 paper on teaching medical and pharmacy trainees to cut unneeded drugs. Older patients often take many medicines, and the pile up can cause harm, confusion, and poor adherence. Their program, called VIONE, sorts each drug by five filters, from vital to not indicated.

The method runs inside the health record and is used in veterans' facilities across the United States. Doctors and pharmacists review lists together, agree cuts with patients, and track results. Over seven years, the system dropped more than a million unneeded prescriptions and saved large sums each year. Battar and Silverman describe how trainees at their center learn the method through real cases, so the habit carries into later practice.
pmc-10736820:
James Iveniuk and seven co-authors probe racial bias in a thinking test used on older Americans in a 2023 study. The test, a short version of a standard screen, sits inside a big national aging survey. If some questions favor one group over another, decline can be over- or under-called by race.

Using two survey rounds with thousands of adults, the team checked whether the questions hang together the same way across white, Black, and Hispanic groups. Seven of the 18 items formed a scale that held up across groups. They tested that short scale against dementia signs and death records to confirm it still predicts what it should.
pmc-10736920:
Mitochondria lose power as people age, but lab models rarely capture that slow decline well. Howard Phang, Stephanie Heimler, and Anthony Molina profiled skin fibroblast cells from donors across the adult lifespan in 2023, hunting for an age pattern in their energy output.

Skin cells keep many donor traits in culture, including signs of age, which makes them a useful stand-in for the body. From a San Diego aging study, the team tested eleven cell lines from healthy adults aged twenty to over eighty-five. The cells' peak breathing capacity and spare capacity both fell steeply as donor age rose. The result supports using such cell lines to study age-related energy decline and to test treatments.
pmc-10737320:
Dementia that starts before old age hits people in their working years, when family duties are heaviest. Xiaoyan Cui and co-authors review help programs for those patients and their families in this 2023 paper. Drug care is limited, so support services carry much of the load. Standard dementia services often miss the special needs of younger patients, the authors note.

The team searched four databases and screened the results with care. They kept twelve studies of non-drug programs for younger patients. The programs aimed at daily life support, slowing mental decline, and keeping people socially active. Nine of the studies dealt with family members as well as patients. Sorting what has been tried can guide better matched services for this group.
pmc-10737520:
Reem Waziry compares measures of biological aging taken from saliva and blood in this 2023 study. The question is whether easy saliva tests can flag older adults at risk of stroke and heart disease. Data came from the Health and Retirement Study, a large survey of Americans aged fifty and over.

Saliva gave a measure of telomere length for 5,808 people, while blood gave chemical aging clocks and body-based scores for 9,934. The saliva measure showed no link with stroke or heart disease. Blood measures told a stronger story: people scored as biologically older had about three times the odds of stroke and well over twice the odds of heart disease. Waziry concludes that saliva and blood capture different sides of aging, and that blood measures work better for flagging these two risks.
pmc-10737720:
Jonathan Rush and co-authors track in 2023 how daily stress reactivity changes over twenty years of adulthood and links to functional health. Stress reactivity is the within-person jump in negative mood on stressful days. It predicts later inflammation and chronic conditions in prior research based on single measurement bursts.

Data came from a national daily study with three bursts ten years apart, totaling many thousands of days. Close to three thousand adults took part. Rising stress reactivity over time predicted worsening ability in daily living tasks. The models handled short-term and long-term change at once.
pmc-10738020:
Maria Monserud asks how free time acts link to how well older adults in Mexico think and recall. She asks if group acts and solo acts count in not the same way for wed and unwed men and women. Her data come from the 2018 wave of the Mexican Health and Aging Study. That study holds a fair cross cut of Mexicans aged fifty and up.

Both group acts and solo acts link to better thought and recall, she finds. Some links shift by wed state and by sex, while some stay the same. Poor health and low mood can block the gains from some acts. Yet some acts still help thought in spite of poor health. That point counts for plans to stop loss of thought with age.
pmc-10738320:
Yuekang Li studies how neighborhood setting shapes low mood in older adults across urban and rural China, in work from 2023. Depression is a major burden in later life. Surroundings may act through social capital, the trust and belonging a place builds.

Panel data covered over seven thousand adults aged sixty and up. Models split city and countryside and tested middle paths. Community social capital partly carried the link between built surroundings and fewer symptoms in both settings. When wider society trust ran low, the community path mattered more, though clearly only in cities. Li urges care in splitting levels of social life. Walkable, safe, well-served blocks may lift mood.
pmc-10738520:
Krishna Sapkota, J Scott Brown, and Jennifer Kinney tracked body mass index in older Americans across the pandemic years, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Lockdowns and isolation may have changed eating, activity, and daily habits. The team used a large national health survey to compare trends before and during the outbreak.

Body mass kept rising in both middle-aged and older adults, but at different speeds. In older adults the rise slowed over time, while in middle-aged adults it sped up during the pandemic. Patterns also differed by sex and by race. The authors conclude that the pandemic sped up weight gain most clearly in middle age.
pmc-10738820:
Kelly Parker and co-authors test whether eating a Mediterranean style diet forecasts memory change over nine years in a 2023 study. Data came from a national midlife cohort: 816 adults, average age forty six, whose diets were scored once and whose thinking was tested twice, nine years apart. The diet score used an American adapted version with dairy and whole grains.

Closer adherence predicted better change in episodic memory, though not in executive function, after adjusting for age, sex, race, income, and blood sugar markers. The memory link showed mainly in younger and middle aged adults, women, and White participants in exploratory checks.
pmc-10738920:
A 2023 study examines whether childlessness in later life means more loneliness, and whether the reasons behind childlessness change that link. Having children reshapes a person's social world, and rates of childlessness are rising worldwide. Research often splits the childless into voluntary and involuntary groups, though many fall in a gray zone between.

The authors surveyed five hundred adults aged sixty or older, half of them childless. Two standard scales measured social and emotional loneliness. The study describes how lonely each group is and catalogues the reasons people give for having no children. It then tests whether those reasons soften or sharpen the link between childlessness and loneliness. The aim is a finer picture than the usual two-box split.
pmc-10739220:
Gayoung Choi and Haena Lee study why some South Korean retirees take bridge jobs, in a 2023 paper. Bridge employment means working after formal retirement, often in a new or reduced role. Koreans born from 1945 to 1955 lived through rapid industrial growth and mid-career economic crises, which sets them apart from the baby boom cohort that followed. The authors ask whether social, demographic, psychological, and health factors drive bridge work differently across these cohorts.

Data came from seven waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, spanning 2008 to 2020. The analysis weighs money, health, and mindset together inside one framework. Knowing which forces matter for which generation helps pension and labor policy match the real reasons older people keep working.
pmc-10740620:
Yu Chen and co-authors study how a lack of selenium, a trace mineral, harms the udders of dairy cows through tiny packets shed by cells. Cows short on the mineral lose immune strength around calving. Cells grown without it made more harmful oxygen waste, shed more packets, and released more swelling signals.

When those packets were fed to healthy udder cells, the healthy cells began to die, their defenses fell, and stress paths in their protein-folding compartment switched on. A growth path that normally guards cells dimmed instead. Gene reads of the packets showed wide shifts. The team links this chain to how mineral shortage can spark udder infection.
pmc-10741520:
Pan Wang and co-authors build a chip sensor that sniffs out traces of a veterinary antibiotic in minutes, in a 2023 paper. Enrofloxacin is used widely in farm animals, resists breakdown, and builds up as residue that threatens health and the environment. Their sensor pairs gold nanoparticles with aptamers, short DNA strands that grip the target drug.

Light bouncing off the particles shifts color as drug binds, a signal read on the chip. The device measured the drug from 0.01 to 100 nanograms per milliliter, and could sense as little as 0.001. Tests of interference, repeat use, and selectivity all passed. The authors pitch the chip as a cheap, steady field tool for residue checks in food and water.
pmc-10742020:
Kevin Tong and co-authors use tumor organoids to show how the gene SMAD4 holds back invasion in serrated colorectal cancer. Colon cancer is a top killer, and up to a fifth of cases follow the serrated path, driven by MAPK pathway mutations. Loss of SMAD4 marks most late-stage cancers and goes with aggressive spread. The team needed a model that shows invasion as it happens.

Organoids grown from a mouse tumor model that lacks Smad4 and carries mutant BRAF behave like invaders: they crawl through 3D gel and push through filter membranes. When SMAD4 was put back, the invasion stopped. Gene activity reads showed SMAD4 acts fast, switching transcripts tied to the extracellular matrix and to secreted proteins. The picture is of a brake that works by policing the cell's surroundings, the matrix it must cross and the signals it sheds.
pmc-10742420:
Haoqi Zhou and five co-authors studied in 2023 how other chronic diseases changed the course of fatal COVID-19 in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The data covered 104,753 confirmed patients over twenty months. Patients with comorbidities died much sooner after symptoms began than those without, with the time cut by about 84 percent on the study's measure. The effect depended on which diseases combined.

Among single conditions, chronic lung disease shortened the span most, ahead of hypertension and diabetes. Among pairs, hypertension with diabetes gave the shortest time to death. The authors say the pattern can guide triage when hospitals are strained. Knowing which combinations turn fatal fastest helps target monitoring and early treatment. The study is among the largest of its kind from the region.
pmc-10742520:
Lucia Francesca Lucca and co-authors report three cases where a common spasticity treatment briefly worsened swallowing and speech. The patients had severe acquired brain injury and were in speech therapy to regain those skills. Each had received botulinum toxin shots to ease stiff muscles. After the shots, their swallowing trouble and slurred speech grew worse for a time.

The 2023 report walks through each case and weighs why the toxin may have spread its effect beyond the target muscles. Such worsening raises the risk of food or fluid entering the lungs, which can cause pneumonia. The authors aim to alert clinicians so they can watch for the effect and act early.
pmc-10742820:
Zhou and co-authors study how table salt changes mung bean starch and the jelly sheets made from it in this 2023 food science paper. Salt is known to improve the jelly when dosed right. The team tested salt from 1.5 to 8 percent by weight against a salt-free control.

Salted starch gelatinized at higher temperatures with stronger pasting behavior but lower gelatinization energy. Dried jelly toughness and cooked jelly acceptability rose steadily with salt. Cooking properties improved while cooked hardness fell, and the jelly's elastic range narrowed. Salt also reduced the starch's structural order. Quality tracked closely with the starch's molecular and layered order, giving makers a lever for texture control.
pmc-10743220:
Cheeranan Sriphuttha and co-authors brew oil and pigment together from biodiesel waste using a red yeast, in this 2023 paper. The yeast stores both fat and carotenoid color as it grows. Fed crude glycerol, the leftovers of biodiesel making, it performed best at a set feed strength found by systematic tuning. The team scaled the run to a five-hundred-liter fermenter under three feeding styles.

Fed-batch feeding won, filling over a third of the cell mass with lipid and reaching high pigment levels. A chemical-free extraction using pressure machines was tuned as well. The pigment proved to be mostly beta-carotene under three kinds of analysis. The authors frame the setup as a way to raise the value of a cheap waste stream.
pmc-10743620:
Alexey Kalinkin and co-authors published this cancer study in 2023. It looks at triple-negative breast cancer, the type with the worst outlook and, for years, chemo as the only whole-body drug. The team hunted for gene switches that might mark a group of these tumors. They read chemical tags on DNA in 110 breast tumors and six healthy samples.

A subset of the tumors had lost tags near two genes that sense a fat-based signal in the body. Loss of tags near a gene often means the gene runs hot, and data from a large cancer bank backed that link here. Women whose tumors ran one of these genes hot lived shorter lives. Since drugs that block this signal path already exist, the authors say a simple tag test could pick out patients who might gain from them.
pmc-10743820:
Whitney Tang and a large team test a pedaling test for endurance in people with spinal muscular atrophy who cannot walk, in a 2023 study. The disease weakens muscles over time, and trials need fair ways to track stamina in those most affected. An assisted six-minute cycling test, done with the arms on a supported ergometer, was borrowed from other nerve diseases.

The team gathered data from 38 people with the disease, aged 5 to 74, both sitters and non-sitters. Scores were compared with upper-limb function scales, a neuromuscular test battery, and self-rated fatigue. If the cycling test tracks the established measures and stays tolerable, it could serve as a standard endurance yardstick in clinics and drug trials for this group.
pmc-10743920:
Lei Hao and four co-authors compared two fat families as treatments for diet-induced obesity in a 2023 mouse study. Dietary guidance urges swapping saturated fat for unsaturated fat but does not say which kind. Omega-6 and omega-3 fats behave very differently, and Western diets already run heavy on omega-6. Mice were fattened on a high-fat diet for ten weeks, then split into three groups for ten more.

One group stayed on the plain high-fat diet, one swapped half the saturated fat for omega-6, and one swapped it for omega-3, at equal calories. The omega-6 group kept gaining weight and fat, with insulin resistance and fatty liver. The omega-3 group lost weight and fat, with barely any liver disease, and fat-building genes in the liver switched down.
pmc-10744020:
Chen Chen and co-authors test whether a plant hormone shields kiwifruit from salt. Their 2023 study grows the Hongyang variety under salty water, with one group also fed a brassinosteroid hormone. Salt stress is a rising threat to orchards as soils degrade.

Salt cut the plants' food-making rate and loaded leaves and roots with harmful peroxide. The hormone group kept more of its food-making power and held less peroxide. Its salt-to-potassium balance also stayed closer to healthy levels. Gene reads pointed to sugar paths and hormone signals at work. Two genes tied to salt defense rose sharply. The team credits better ion balance and lower oxidative harm in leaves and roots.
pmc-10744120:
Alberto Barchi and co-authors make the case for intestinal ultrasound in ulcerative colitis care. Their 2023 review notes the disease inflames the colon surface layers, so wall-crossing scans were long sidelined for this condition. Crohn disease got the ultrasound attention instead.

Studies now tie ultrasound markers closely to colon inflammation. The method is cheap, bedside-ready, and quick, which speeds treatment calls. Wall healing on scans links to better long-term outcomes. One blind spot remains: the rectum, where a perineal scan route may fill the gap. Emergency and post-surgery uses are growing as well. The authors urge leaving the surface-only mindset behind and scanning the whole wall as a routine part of colitis care.
pmc-10744320:
People with spinal cord injury face many secondary health problems, and follow-up clinics exist to catch them early. Julia Tijsse Klasen and co-authors describe changes to one such clinic. A pre-visit questionnaire on functioning and health problems came first, with added blood pressure and oxygen measurements, and visits with either a specialized nurse or a rehabilitation doctor. They tracked what the design changed and how visitors rated it.

The clinic produced more recommendations than before, and their focus shifted from body complaints toward psychosocial functioning and the use of devices. The added measurements found high average systolic blood pressure, prompting more referrals to family doctors. Weight and lung function held steady. Participants reported high satisfaction, which the authors credit to the questionnaire: it let visitors prepare and let professionals tailor advice. They judge the adaptations an improvement in catching secondary problems.
pmc-10744420:
Marcin Różycki and co-authors developed a thin, strong concrete panel reinforced with woven textile instead of steel bars. Their matrix is a reactive powder concrete mixed with lightweight aggregate, which leaves it porous but light. Glass fibers and a textile fabric were added to fix the matrix's natural brittleness and raise its bending strength. Panels were cast from one to four millimeters thick and tested for strength and water passage.

Thicker panels failed in the usual staged pattern, while the thinnest bent flexibly. Microscopy showed the fibers bonded well to the matrix. Despite the pores, water passed through far faster than a reference material, an effect the team traces to the aggregate and curing. As a proof of concept they built a working canoe from the material.
pmc-10744720:
Padmassun Rajakareyar and co-authors widened a computing method in 2023 for predicting the stiffness of spongy, repeating materials, such as lattice foams. Engineers need those bulk traits to design light parts, but many lattices are skewed rather than neatly aligned, and older tools assumed alignment.

Their framework handles any of the classic lattice symmetry types, including skewed unit cells. A fast neighbor search sets the repeating edge conditions on a blocky mesh. The authors study where errors creep in, from the mesh and from the edge conditions, and show finer meshes tame them. Tests on hexagon lattices and several other shapes yield charts that link density to stiffness for designers.
pmc-10744820:
Desk workers ache in the neck and shoulder, and a shoulder blade that moves wrong may be part of the story. Seong Eun Moon and Young Kyun Kim examine that link in a 2023 study of about one hundred computer office workers. Standard tests checked blade motion and slide, alongside pain and disability questionnaires.

Nine in ten workers showed the faulty blade pattern, a strikingly high share. Those with it reported more neck and shoulder disability and pain, and their blades slid measurably farther on testing. The authors suggest that screening and retraining shoulder blade control belongs in office health programs.
pmc-10745920:
Yinuo Sun and co-authors map, in a 2023 review, what helps and what blocks a child nutrition powder program. The powder, a mix of vitamins and minerals called micronutrient powder, is one of the best-value buys in child health. Many countries use it, yet large rollouts still snag. The team read fifty studies through a standard framework that sorts rollout factors into five domains.

Most studies came from lower-middle-income countries, and most programs gave the powder free. The local setting domain loomed largest. Spotty supply, thin stocks, and poor training of front-line staff were the top blocks. Taste issues and side effects put caregivers off too. Wins came from firm supply chains, state-led free models with shop paths in the mix, and steady monitoring. The authors urge local production and strong staff training as the core fixes.
pmc-10746020:
Giada Ballarin and co-authors study bullying victimisation, physical fitness, and how young people see themselves, in middle-school students with overweight or obesity. Their 2023 study sets those students next to peers of normal weight.

One hundred twenty-eight youths did tests of fitness and filled in checked questionnaires on fitness as they saw it, on how they saw themselves, and on victimisation. About sixty-two percent had overweight or obesity. Teasing and verbal offences took place more often for those students, and teasing on how they looked was tied to body mass index. Being shut out of groups was tied to how well they did in jumping. All types of victimisation were tied, in a reverse way, to how well they saw their place with others. Students of normal weight did better on some tests, but gave lower marks for grip and muscular strength as they saw it.
pmc-10746520:
Rui Wu and co-authors published this education study in 2023. Sustained reading habits matter for high school students, but the psychology behind them is complex. The team surveyed six hundred students, guided by theories of self-efficacy and achievement motivation. They modeled how reading motivation flows into reading satisfaction. Two middle factors were tested: confidence in one's reading ability, and social support from others.

All four factors linked positively to one another. Motivation predicted satisfaction both directly and through each middle factor on its own. The two factors also worked as a chain, with confidence and support passing the effect along together. The authors say the chain helps explain why some students keep reading with pleasure while others drift away. Schools aiming at lasting reading habits, they argue, should build motivation, confidence, and support together rather than in isolation.
pmc-10747220:
Aniello Cammarano and co-authors map twenty years of work on drugs through the skin, in a count study from 2023. Skin patches and gels dodge the gut and the needle, and the field is now a hot tech race. The team counts papers and patents to chart where the race runs.

From 2000 to 2022, yearly papers grew fivefold, from 131 to 659. The United States, China, and India led the press. Patents told the same tale, with near three thousand groups, a tenth of them granted, led by the same lands plus Europe. Hot themes and team webs are charted too. The map, the team says, can steer grants and firm picks, and save lost work in a fast field.
pmc-10747320:
A vaccine built for animals against the coronavirus was tested in cats in a 2023 study by Igor Morozov and co-authors. The vaccine is a recombinant subunit product, carrying just the virus's spike protein rather than the whole germ.

Two groups of cats received two doses, three weeks apart, of vaccine or placebo. Seven weeks after the second dose, all were exposed to live virus through the nose and mouth. Researchers tracked illness and virus shedding for two weeks, then examined tissues for damage. Vaccinated cats mounted strong antibody responses, which jumped further after exposure. Shedding from nose and mouth fell significantly compared with placebo. The preliminary result supports the shot's promise for protecting cats.
pmc-10747520:
Selina Khan and co-authors present a 2023 safety study on a covid vaccine in rabbits. A very rare clotting disorder in humans has been linked to this vaccine. One theory blames accidental injection into a vein, rather than into muscle. The team gave rabbits the vaccine by vein and by muscle and compared the results in depth.

Both routes were well tolerated, with no signs of low platelets or clots. Blood, clotting, and immune measures did not differ by route in a meaningful way. Tissue checks showed no clot damage. One marker of swelling rose more after muscle dosing than after a control vaccine. The authors note the animal count was small. The data suggest vein dosing may not raise the risk.
pmc-10748020:
Ricciotti and three colleagues review printing buildings and parts from geopolymer goo in twenty twenty-three. Geopolymers are stone like binders made without cement's heavy carbon cost. The review tracks the young field from mix design to print settings. Fresh and hardened traits are weighed by recipe, fiber, curing, and printer shape.

Two part and one part mixes get compared for ease and strength. Early age behavior, key for stacking layers, gets close study. Sample products show where the method stands. Gaps and next steps close the survey. The team sees a green path for printed construction.
pmc-10748420:
Nataliia Rozumna, Vita Hanzha, and Elena Lukyanetz published a 2023 cell study of memantine, a drug that blocks NMDA receptors, against two toxins tied to Alzheimer's disease. Overactive NMDA receptors can excite neurons to death, a process suspected in the disease. The team cultured rat hippocampus neurons and exposed them for a day to NMDA itself or to amyloid beta, the protein fragment that builds up in Alzheimer's brains.

Either toxin more than doubled the share of dying neurons. Adding memantine alongside kept many more cells alive. The authors say the result supports memantine's protective role against this kind of excitotoxic damage. They also praise hippocampal cultures as a handy testbed for screening Alzheimer's treatments. The work is early and in dishes, not patients.
pmc-10748820:
Zhiyong Hu and nine colleagues published a 2023 study on a pine pollen extract that may guard the kidneys from cadmium. Cadmium is a toxic metal found in soil, water, and food. It builds up in the body and harms the kidneys most of all.

The test extract comes from Masson pine pollen and is known for antioxidant power. Rats with cadmium-caused kidney damage got the extract as treatment. The team then read gene activity and small-molecule profiles in the rats to trace how it helps. Damage markers and cell stress signals were tracked as well. Plant extracts that blunt metal harm could matter for people in polluted areas.
pmc-10749920:
Claudia Mierke introduces a journal research collection on how cancer cells stick, spread, and face the immune system. Her 2023 editorial frames the theme for a section of a cell biology journal. The collection gathers five papers: two original studies and three reviews, spanning many disciplines.

One study follows cervical cancer's shift into a mobile, invasive state and its self-eating process. The other takes a pan-cancer look at whether splicing defects sway cell function and therapy outcomes. The reviews cover the tumor surroundings and immune therapy, a protein-cutting enzyme that reshapes cancer cell behavior, and one sticky receptor's role in prostate, kidney, and bladder cancers. Mierke argues that only such a mix of fields and tumor types can give a full picture of how cancers progress.
pmc-10752420:
Marianne Helleseth, Andrew McAleavey, and Christian Moltu present a dual case study of clinical feedback in psychotherapy. In routine outcome monitoring, patients regularly report how they are doing. Therapists then use those reports to steer care. Trials of the method have given mixed results, and how feedback actually helps inside sessions is little explored.

The cases follow two patients. One is a young woman with a trauma history and deep distrust, treated for eight months. The other is a middle-aged man whose past trauma led him to hide his own needs, treated for nineteen months. Feedback records, health notes, and therapist notes form the material. The authors find feedback worked as a shared tool. It helped the pairs talk about their alliance, name progress or stuck points, and voice the unspoken.
pmc-10753420:
Pravesh Sharma and co-authors set out, in a 2023 protocol, a community-built plan to help rural smokers quit through a faith-based Facebook group. Smoking remains the top preventable killer in the United States, and rural adults smoke at some of the highest rates. Distance, cost, and scarce local programs block their access to proven quit help.

The FAITH-CORE project will build and beta test a private, moderated Facebook group. Inside it, peers support each other while faith-based messages steer members toward existing proven resources like state quitlines. The design grows out of community partnership, so the tone fits the people it serves. If the pilot works, the model could carry quit help anywhere phones reach, at low cost.
pmc-10753720:
Chuanjin Yao and five co-authors tested super-hot pressurized water as a way to cook oil out of shale, in a 2023 paper. Shale with low to medium maturity holds huge oil potential. The team built its own apparatus for the tests. Both ground particles and solid core pieces were heated in the water.

Core samples lost a clear share of mass, and many tiny cracks formed. Those cracks raised how well the process worked. Oil yield under the special water reached a high level at set heat and pressure. It beat dry heating by over half. The water also cut the share of oxygen-bearing compounds in the oil. Light, medium, and heavy oil fractions all rose versus dry runs. The authors judge the method feasible and advantageous for such shale.
pmc-10757220:
Ruoyu Liu, Yun Zhou, and Yongtong Cao present a 2023 review of circular RNAs as regulators of ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped molecules once dismissed as splicing noise; ferroptosis, death by iron-fed lipid rusting, now sits at the center of many disease stories. The review gathers evidence that specific rings raise or lower ferroptosis by steering the proteins that control it.

The links appear across cancers, brain, heart, and other systems. Tuning a ring could push diseased cells toward death or shield healthy ones. The authors map the known ring-ferroptosis pairs and mark the gaps for drug hunters.
pmc-10761120:
Lan Nguyen, Masaru Mori, Yuji Yasuda, and Josephine Galipon study shifting gene transcript boundaries during glucose starvation. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses fission yeast. A sudden sixty-fold glucose drop rewires gene activity fast. Transcript ends also move, changing the proteins cells can make.

Three sequencing methods pinned down transcript starts and ends precisely. Protein measurements then checked the functional consequences. Paired sense and antisense genes opposed each other more with time lag counted. Transcript tails shortened early in starvation, then start regions shortened later. Those shifts added or removed protein domains in places. The work shows starvation reshapes messages, not just their amounts.
pmc-10761320:
A rare clotting disorder can follow vaccination, leaving the blood with too few platelets to stop bleeding. Miguel Rodriguez Guerra and four co-authors report in 2023 on a sixty-one year old woman who reached an emergency room three weeks after her second Pfizer COVID-19 shot. Her platelet count had fallen to a dangerously low level.

Doctors began antibody infusions and a steroid at once. Her count rose within a day and kept climbing after the second infusion. The authors stress that fast spotting of this vaccine linked disorder is what allows treatment to start in time. They present the case as a reminder to check platelet counts when warning signs appear after a shot.
pmc-10764220:
Park and co-authors test whether pairing a mild laxative sugar with probiotic strains eases constipation better than either alone, in this 2023 mouse study. Constipation was triggered with a drug that slows the gut. The team then tracked stool traits, gut transit speed, and gut chemistry.

Two partners stood out: a Bacillus strain and a yeast strain, each combined with lactulose. Both mixes restored stool number and water content and sped transit beyond the untreated pattern. They also raised levels of helpful short-chain fatty acids in stool more than lactulose alone. A mix with magnesium hydroxide helped as well. The authors credit the acid boost for much of the relief.
pmc-10765320:
Lecordier leads a large team studying two proteins that control cell membrane dynamics, in work from twenty twenty-three. Apolipoproteins L1 and L3 sit at the Golgi, the cell shipping hub, with factors that split membranes. Changes in either protein disturb that system.

Truncated or deleted forms lowered a key enzyme activity and reshaped the cell skeleton. One protein proved to control the enzyme directly through partner proteins. Both appear in vesicles tied to autophagy, the cell recycling route. Faulty forms cut recycling of worn mitochondria and raised harmful oxygen species. The work links these proteins to mitochondrial quality control, with disease relevance.
pmc-10769520:
Caroline Corbett and a large German study group gauged how widespread non-tuberculous mycobacteria are in lungs across Germany. These germs, kin of the tuberculosis germ, cause a grown share of lung ill in Europe. Firm counts for Germany were lost. A set of 22 labs gave test data from 2016 to 2020. The set held 11,430 samples from 5,998 lung patients.

Those cases stood for near 30 percent of all told cases in the land. Since tuberculosis counts in Germany are near full, they set the base for the sums. The team worked out year rates for how wide and how new the ill was, mapped zone splits by type, and checked drug test scores. The 2023 study gives German staff and health chiefs their first firm land wide view of this germ group.
pmc-10782220:
Soma Dey, Neha Rai, Akash Bansal, Bandana Kumari, Bankim Das, and Alka Kumari surveyed nurses at a large hospital in Patna, India, about blood drawing practice, in a study published in 2023. Drawing blood is the first step of lab testing, and slips at that stage force repeats and can mislead care. The team used a thirty-question survey based on World Health Organization guidance.

Knowledge scores came out satisfactory overall, with a few weak spots. Attitudes were strongly positive, and about eighty-seven percent of nurses showed good practice on the items checked. The authors recommend a dedicated teaching program on blood drawing to close the remaining knowledge gaps and lift sample quality across the hospital.
pmc-10786220:
Verónica Cervigón-Carrasco and co-authors test how games, pornography, and TV series warp people's sense of time, in this 2023 paper. Distorted time sense is known in substance disorders, but its role in problem online habits was unclear. Losing track of time is a hallmark complaint in binge behavior.

Two hundred fifty volunteers across three samples watched short clips of each content type plus documentaries as a control. They judged how long clips lasted and how fast time felt. Men understated time with pornography and series, while women overstated it. Scores for problem gaming, pornography use, and binge-watching were set against the distortions to map the links.
pmc-10793620:
Damian Mikulski and co-authors test a simple blood based score as a guide in blood cancer care, in a 2023 study. The cancer is multiple myeloma that has come back or stopped responding to past drugs. The score, built from counts of three blood cell types, tracks the balance between swelling in the body and immune strength.

The study covered 54 patients treated with a two drug plan at one center from 2018 to 2022. A high score before treatment went with much worse results: free survival and total survival were both far shorter than in the low score group. The authors say the cheap score could help guide next steps in care.
pmc-10803620:
Silvio Ligia and co-authors report a hard case of polycythemia vera in a study published in 2023. The blood disorder struck a girl who was three when diagnosed in 2001, flooding her with red cells and enlarging her spleen. Bloodletting, hydroxyurea, and older interferon each failed to hold her counts or ease her symptoms.

Genetic work found the standard driver mutation plus a rare second variant in the same gene, a pairing that may explain the stubborn course. In 2023 she started a modern long acting interferon. Her blood values improved and symptoms eased. The authors argue the second mutation deserves attention in young, treatment resistant patients, and that the new drug merits wider use.
pmc-10824920:
Abd El-Hamid and co-authors feed rabbits a black seed compound in nano drops and test growth and germ defense in work dated 2023 in the text. Plant based nano mixes are eyed as antibiotic stand ins that lift farm animal health.

Two hundred forty rabbits ate plain feed or three dose levels, then faced a drug resistant lung germ at sixty days. Higher doses sped growth and gut enzyme action. Antioxidant and immune markers climbed, while fats and tissue cholesterol fell. The work sizes up the mix as a growth and shield booster.
pmc-10840420:
Noreen Grace George and co-authors test free-floating DNA ratios as an early warning in acute leukemia in a study published in 2023. Blood cancers shed DNA fragments into the bloodstream, and their levels may forecast relapse sooner than standard residual disease tests. The team sampled patients at diagnosis and after induction therapy.

Twenty-five patients with either major acute leukemia type were tracked, most classed high risk. How much the DNA level fell between the two draws strongly predicted poor outcomes in high-risk patients. A ratio at or above a set cutoff beat the standard flow test for accuracy, regardless of its result. The pilot suggests ratio scoring as a cheap prognostic add-on.
pmc-10854220:
Yumeng Gan and six co-authors review how gut microbes shape the growth of the brain and nerve system, and how they link to related disorders. The gut and brain talk both ways through a path called the brain gut axis. The review was published in twenty twenty-three.

Brain growth is long and complex, so it can be swayed by inner and outer factors. Gut microbes affect new nerve cell birth, insulation of fibers, immune cell work in the brain, pruning of links, and the brain's blood barrier. The authors trace these links before and after birth, then turn to disorders such as autism and two rare syndromes, with an eye to early spotting and new care.
pmc-10859920:
Bernhard T Baune and a large team set out a plan to build a tool that forecasts who will respond to drugs for major depression. Their paper is dated two thousand twenty-four in the pack, while its text head says the year before. Only about a third of patients respond to the first drug, and a like share end with hard-to-treat depression.

The PROMPT project first studies past patients at the two extremes, responders and the hard to treat. Deep clinical, gene, and RNA reads feed a new algorithm that blends those with sex-linked data. A fresh group of patients then tests the tool in real care. The plan also asks patients and staff how they view such tests.
pmc-10876020:
Davide Orsini and four co-authors argue that stigma may harm mpox patients as much as the virus itself. Their essay traces the disease historically and socially, from its long endemic presence in Central Africa to the global alert of July twenty twenty-two. Only when cases crossed Africa's borders, they note, did worldwide alarm ignite.

Public discussion quickly tied the disease to patients' sexual lives, echoing older patterns of blaming groups for epidemics. Incomplete information, amplified after the COVID-19 experience, fed that framing. The authors examine the ethical stakes and the practical damage stigma does to control efforts. Their call is for communication and policy that treat patients without moralizing the infection.
pmc-10903320:
Zahra Esfandiari and co-authors review in 2023 how often a gut germ that causes severe diarrhea turns up in meat, and how well drugs still work on it. Meat and meat products are a known source of this germ, which can pass to people through food. The team searched major health databases for studies from 2007 to 2022.

Their search found 278 papers, of which 54 from around the world fit the rules. They pooled the results to get an overall rate for the germ in meat and for its drug resistance. Pooled rates like these help food safety staff judge the scale of the risk. They also show where checks are weak. A germ that resists drugs and spreads through food is a double concern for public health.
pmc-10907020:
Ruijie Cao and co-authors send sound swirls down a line to haul more facts per wave. Swirl beams can take endless twist grades in math, a vast shelf of channels. Part grades, not just whole twists, could swell that shelf more. The rub is read: part beams blur and shake in noise. Their 2023 plan reads a phase tear unique to each twist grade as the true flag.

Pairs of part beams ride as one pack. A ring of few pick points, far less than a full grid, feeds a learn net built to shrug off shake and tilt. Tests send a ten-bit word on the rig with sound reads at a sparse ring. Sound lacks the photo troves optics trains on, so the math-first flag does the heavy lift.
pmc-10909120:
Rokia Masoud, Ahmed Eladl, Shaimaa El-Ashwah, Ahmed Abbas, and Wageeha Kandil studied immune checkpoint proteins in a slow-growing lymph cancer in 2023. Blocking the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair has reshaped care for many tumors. How often these proteins appear in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and in its shift to a fast lymphoma was little studied.

Records held ninety-six cases across three groups: the slow cancer, its transformed form, and the fast lymphoma arising on its own. PD-1 appeared in the slow cancer, mainly in growth centers. It was far more common in transformed cases than in the fast lymphoma group. PD-L1 on tumor cells appeared in a few fast lymphoma cases and in none of the other groups.
pmc-10915920:
Parnian Parvin and co-authors asked whether screen time in the teen years shapes how young adults rate their own health. The 2023 study drew on the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study in Iran. It tracked 642 teens aged 13 to 19 years and checked their health again at ages 22 to 28 years.

About one third of both boys and girls had high screen time as teens. Young men rated their health higher than young women in both body and mind scores. For young men, high teen screen time linked to weaker mental health and social scores years later. The link did not show the same clear pattern for young women in the study.
pmc-10922920:
Patrick Healey and eight co-authors study how rank shapes the use of sensitive words at work, in work whose text is dated 2023. Rank brings power, but it also brings watchful eyes. Those forces pull in opposed ways on whether staff use words tied to race, faith, or politics. The team mined a large set of work emails with standard word-count tools.

Senior staff used sensitive words about three times less often than junior staff. That care held whether or not peers used such words in the same thread. It also held whether or not the words sat in a touchy context. The authors say exposure and answerability, more than power, seem to tame word choice at the top.
pmc-10994620:
The chemotherapy drug cisplatin saves lives but scars kidneys, partly by stoking inflammation. Saja Kareem Abd Alhusen and Ali Faris Hasan tested whether a blend of omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 fatty acids could shield mouse kidneys. Five groups of mice compared the blend at two doses against the drug alone, a plain control, and vitamin E.

Mice given the fatty acid blend showed lower levels of two inflammatory signals. Their kidney markers, urea and creatinine in the blood, also improved. The protection looked real across both doses. The authors, writing in 2023, conclude the blend fights the drug's kidney damage through its anti-inflammatory action. Human relevance remains to be tested.
pmc-11001320:
Xiang Xiao, Shuming Ji, Junlin Zhang, Deying Kang, and Fang Liu test a body-energy measure as a warning sign in diabetic kidney disease in this 2023 study. Resting energy use can be estimated from formulas, and the team asked which formula best foretells kidney failure. Patients all had biopsy-proven disease.

One disease-specific formula won the comparison. Splitting one hundred twenty-four patients by its cutoff, the low-energy group later reached kidney failure far more often. Adjusted models put their risk at about six times the high-energy group's. The authors propose the simple estimate as an independent risk marker that clinics can compute from routine data.
pmc-11126520:
Members of the GBD 2021 Causes of Death group report on deaths from nearly three hundred causes worldwide. Their counts cover more than two hundred countries and territories, plus many smaller regions within them, from 1990 to 2021. Regular reporting on why people die guides public health choices.

Alongside cause-by-cause deaths, the team shows how changes in each cause raised or lowered life expectancy. That breakdown reveals which gains came from fewer heart deaths, fewer infections, or other shifts. Leaders can use it to see where progress is real and where it is stalling.
pmc-11215220:
Benedict Calys-Tagoe and colleagues published a health study in 2023 comparing COVID-19 patients in Ghana. The setting was a major treatment facility in the country. The team compared people who had been vaccinated with those who had not. They looked at how illness presented and how patients fared.

Hospitalized patients were less often vaccinated than clinic outpatients. Vaccinated patients were far more likely to be managed without admission. Death rates also differed between the two groups in the data. The comparison used records from routine care at the facility. The authors' findings support vaccination as a protection against severe disease. The study adds West African evidence to a mostly Western literature.
pmc-11271220:
Ming Bai and co-authors report a phase Ib trial pairing two antibody drugs in metastatic colorectal cancer, in work the head dates to 2023. Patients had tumors without RAS or BRAF mutations and had already had more than two lines of care. One drug blocks a growth receptor, the other releases an immune brake.

Twenty-one patients were enrolled across centers in an open-label study. The main goals were tumor response and safety. Other measures included disease control and survival times. Pairing a growth blocker with immune therapy is a strategy for cancers that resist standard drugs. The small early-phase design tests whether the pair is safe enough and active enough to study further.
pmc-11532420:
Farzaneh Mohammadi and seven co-authors test a planet-friendly diet score against colon cancer in a 2024 study. Diets heavy in plants seem to protect the bowel, and a planetary health index scores eating for both body and environment. Its link to colorectal cancer in Iran had never been checked.

Seventy-one cancer patients were compared with 142 hospital controls in Tehran. A food questionnaire fed the index, which runs to 150 points. Regression models adjusted for other risk factors. The highest third of scores carried about sixty percent lower odds of cancer than the lowest. Sub-scores for adequate healthy foods and moderation showed similar protection. The results support plant-forward guidance in cancer prevention advice.
pmc-11533420:
Qing Zhang and co-authors study how a regulator protein manages energy in a soil bacterium, in a 2024 paper. The protein, AbrB, acts during the shift between growth phases, a time when energy supply matters greatly. Little was known about how energy levels fluctuate in that window.

Deleting the gene for AbrB slowed cell division and cut stored energy early in the shift. Lab assays mapped the genes AbrB controls directly. It boosts two routes that make energy, one by direct chemical steps and one using oxygen, while it restrains a third route based on nitrate. It also shapes four other regulators tied to energy supply. The authors present a full network map of AbrB control over the cell's energy budget.
pmc-11534620:
Heather MacDonald and Sarah Young introduce new search guidance for Campbell Collaboration systematic reviews, in an article from twenty twenty-four. Searching for studies is a critical step that lays the foundation for the remaining stages of a review. Social science searches face added complexity across a rich diversity of evidence sources. The guidance supports both review authors and information specialists.

The guide updates a document first published in twenty ten and revised in twenty seventeen. It reflects current Campbell practice and the collaboration's updated methodological expectations. New sections explain who the guide serves and how to work with an information specialist. Templates, lists, and checklists help authors meet conduct and reporting expectations. The authors highlight key changes and additions throughout. Their aim is searches that find and organize evidence more reliably.
pmc-11535220:
Yuanpeng He and co-authors study a way to quiet low frequency noise from concrete railway bridges in this 2024 paper. Box girder bridges on urban viaducts radiate rumble between 20 and 200 hertz. That rumble disturbs nearby residents. Most fixes rely on isolating vibration or absorbing sound.

Their idea cuts holes in the bridge wings to create acoustic short circuits. Air pressure equalizes through the holes, which cancels part of the radiated sound. Modeling first showed which bridge parts contribute most noise. With the holes, noise fell by up to 6.8 decibels at standard measurement points. A design rule based on a 3 decibel effectiveness distance is proposed. It aims for stable reduction across sites.
pmc-11536220:
Kalyani Sonawane and co-authors examine how often United States clinicians talk with high risk patients about lung cancer screening in a 2024 study. Screening with low dose scans can prevent lung cancer deaths, and guidelines cover about 13 million adults aged 50 to 80 with a smoking history. Yet in 2022 only 4.5 percent of those eligible were up to date.

Talking with a clinician is a first step toward uptake, but how often it happens was unclear. The study used a national survey from 2022 with a response rate near 28 percent. It breaks down screening talks by smoking status and by social, economic, and health traits, to find where the conversation gap lies.
pmc-11536820:
Jinliang Deng and co-authors ask when a gene sequencing test of spinal fluid is worth using for suspected brain infections, in a research paper from 2024. Finding the germ is key to precise care, and the test is a strong tool for that task. Used on every patient, though, it adds cost for patients and for society.

Records for one hundred seventy-five inpatients were reviewed. Patients split by whether the test found the germ in charge. The team compared symptoms, fluid tests, scans, and brain wave results between groups. From split factors they built a scoring system. The score aims to flag, early, the patients most likely to gain from the test.
pmc-11538320:
Ocio and co-authors report a phase 1b study, published in 2024, testing whether a myeloma antibody can be infused in just thirty minutes. The drug targets a marker on myeloma cells and is usually given over hours. Shorter infusions free chairs, nurses, and patients' days. The study enrolled patients with newly diagnosed disease receiving the antibody within standard combination regimens. Fast delivery must not raise reaction rates or lose effect.

The analysis reports the shortened schedule's safety and early results. Antibodies like this one already anchor treatment for relapsed patients and are moving earlier into care. If a half-hour infusion proves safe, clinics everywhere can adopt it. The study is an early-phase step, so numbers are small and caution applies. Still, time is a real toxicity in cancer care, and this work attacks it.
pmc-11538420:
Marco Luppichini, Giada Vailati, Lorenzo Fontana, and Monica Bini forecast river flow. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses machine learning in small catchments. Climate change calls for new tools to cut flood risk.

Small basins react fast, so warn times can be short. Deep learning models guessed water height hours ahead. Errors were just a few centimeters in most of the tests. Extreme events were guessed hours early as well. A model that gives a trust range did best at long leads. Local bodies could use such tools in alarm phases.
pmc-11539820:
Amirabbas Mollaei and co-authors test in 2024 whether clinical nurses accept QR codes as a microlearning tool at work. Microlearning delivers short lessons that fit busy care settings. Selected medical devices in hospital wards were labeled with codes linking to educational content for staff to scan.

After two months, 185 nurses and head nurses completed an acceptance questionnaire. Most were women with bachelor's degrees on rotating shifts. Acceptance came out at a moderate level overall. The authors argue acceptability testing should precede wide rollout of such tools. The study took place in hospitals tied to a medical university in Guilan.
pmc-11545920: Albert Raizner wrote a 2024 short column on a hard diagnosis in heart care: a heart attack with normal coronary arteries. Most heart attacks come from a blockage. Here the arteries read clear, so the cause must be hunted from a list. One cause is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, a stress condition where the tip of the heart swells and stops squeezing. The case in the column was diagnosed as that condition. The marks were the bulge of the tip, the clear arteries, and wall motion recovered within a short span.
pmc-11548520:
Deshan Yang and co-authors wrote in 2024 about smart farming with low flying platforms. Sensors spread over vast fields can track crops, but many fields are hard to reach and cloud links add delay. The team put small servers on low-altitude platform stations, craft that hover above the fields. Each farm task is split into linked sub-tasks that the near servers can run at once.

They set the task as cutting total delay while honoring task order, rank, and power limits. A step-by-step method with rank choice solves it in fair time. In tests, the near-server plan beat both past plans and on-site computing. The work aims at fast, exact crop care over large areas.
pmc-11568520:
Aminath Shiwaza Moosa and co-authors ask new mothers how they feel about video visits for care after birth, and whether they would pick a mix of video and in-person care. Video care spread in the pandemic, yet what women make of it for this stage of life had not been well studied.

Twenty-five mothers took part in deep interviews, with survey data beside them. Mothers prized the ease, reach, and personal touch of video care for the small worries that come right after birth. They saw it as good for advice and for trust in their new role. The lack of a hands-on exam was the main flaw they named.
pmc-11569120:
Navideh Khodadadi and co-authors run, in twenty twenty-four, a randomized trial of flaxseed, a fasting mimicking diet, and both together in fatty liver disease. The disease, MASLD, is fat buildup in the liver tied to metabolic dysfunction. Each intervention alone had shown benefit; the combination was untested. One hundred patients were split into four groups for twelve weeks: lifestyle advice alone, flaxseed powder daily, a diet with sixteen-hour daily fasting, or both combined. Body measures, blood lipids, sugar control, inflammation, liver enzymes, and liver fat and stiffness were tracked.

Triglycerides, cholesterol, fasting glucose and insulin, inflammation, and liver enzymes fell in all intervention groups. Liver fat scores fell in the intervention groups too, the head text reports. The trial weighs whether combining the two adds benefit.
pmc-11569220:
Masao Nakamura and colleagues demonstrate that excitons can drive photocurrent directly in a copper iodide film, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Excitons absorb light strongly but carry no charge. Conventional solar processes must split them before any current flows. A nonlinear interaction offers another route.

The film's photocurrent surged at exciton resonance energies, even below the bandgap. Polarization tests identified it as shift current. That current arises from a geometric phase change during optical transitions. It exceeded the above-bandgap current and pointed the opposite way. Calculations tied its sign and size to strain in the film. The study reveals excitons as amplifiers of nonlinear optical response. Strain becomes a dial for manipulating the effect.
pmc-11570320:
Nadine Muller and six colleagues published this commentary in twenty twenty-four on Germany's growing leadership role in global health. Germany invests heavily in global health initiatives and holds active roles in bodies such as the World Health Organization. Its universities and technical institutions produce research that shapes policy worldwide. The authors argue this leadership cannot be fully realized while gender disparities persist at home.

In twenty twenty-one, the authors report, men held seventy-seven percent of professor positions in German global health research. Women grow scarcer at each higher career stage, a pattern called the leaky pipeline. The commentary notes that diverse leadership improves performance, satisfaction, and innovation. Closing the gap is framed as a strategic need, not only a matter of fairness. The piece lays out a gender equity roadmap for German global health.
pmc-11570920:
Dahlia Stott and five co-authors link how well people eat with how close they feel to nature, in a pilot study published in two thousand twenty-four. Eating in ways that spare the planet tends to help health, so the team looked for traits that go with better diets. Adults across the United States filled out an online survey in the fall of two thousand twenty-three, reporting their food intake and their bond with nature.

Diet quality was scored with a standard healthy eating index. People who felt closer to nature scored higher on diet quality, even after age, sex, race, and schooling were counted. The bond was measured by a scale with parts for self, outlook, and direct time in nature. As a small pilot, the study cannot prove cause, but it marks nature bond as a trait worth testing in diet programs.
pmc-11571320:
Poor medical students in China who face hardship with a hardy outlook report better mental health. How they cope carries much of that effect, finds a 2024 survey by Huan Liu and co-authors. Questionnaires from 1,280 students at private universities measured hardiness, coping style, and mental health together.

Hardiness predicted better mental health directly. Facing problems head on strengthened the link, while avoidant coping dragged health down. Both styles carried part of the effect between hardiness and health. Gender also shifted how coping related to health. The authors aim the findings at campus mental health workers serving struggling students.
pmc-11573520:
Lijun Zheng, Yi Xu, and Liangsheng Guo show in a 2024 study that stressing a dangerous yeast's inner membranes can accidentally breed drug resistance. The yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, is a top-priority pathogen with few working drugs. A chemical that stresses the endoplasmic reticulum pushed cells to gain or lose whole chromosomes.

Some of these aneuploid strains resisted fluconazole, and some shrugged off a second drug as well, with whole batteries of resistance genes switched on. Without the stress, the extra chromosomes were shed again. Genome wobble itself, the study warns, is a resistance engine clinics must reckon with.
pmc-11574020:
Li and a large team summed up proof in twenty twenty-four on how social and cash rank links to cancer. Rank shapes who gets care, who gets screened, and who gets sick. Proof is vast, so they ran an umbrella review of past pooled works plus a burden count.

Firm proof backed just a few links in that large set. Low-rank folks had less reach to new immune care, gene tests, and aimed drugs. They also had less breast screening and more lung cancer. Lands with high growth scores bore more cancer in all, most so for men. The team urges care that closes those gaps.
pmc-11575020:
Melanie Loix and co-authors review a fat-processing enzyme as a drug target for brain diseases in a 2024 paper. The enzyme, SCD1, converts saturated fats into the monounsaturated kind that cell membranes prefer. Blocking it calms brain inflammation and guards neurons in models of multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's disease. Benefits run from regrown myelin sheaths to rescued memory and less toxic protein clumping.

One inherited disease, though, gets better when fat traffic through the enzyme rises, which warns against blanket blocking. The review maps the cell-level paths behind both the help and the harm. Context decides whether this enzyme is a target or a lifeline, and the authors chart that context disease by disease.
pmc-11575120:
Low blood counts and low iron are common in kidney disease, and both may drag down daily life. Reiko Okubo and co-authors examine that link in a 2024 study of more than two thousand patients in Japan.

The patients, drawn from 31 sites across the country, all had advanced kidney disease but were not on dialysis. Each filled in a survey on quality of life. Those with the lowest blood counts scored worse on kidney, mental, and physical scales. People with a strict form of iron shortage also scored worse on several scales. The findings support checking and treating blood and iron problems as part of routine kidney care.
pmc-11575220:
Ten researchers survey views on healing architecture in child psychiatry buildings in a paper from 2024. Building design can support or hinder therapy, a notion called healing architecture. The team used a questionnaire built for child and adolescent psychiatry settings. Senior doctors and architects across Germany answered it between 2020 and 2022.

Thirty-six department heads and eighty-eight architects completed the survey in full. The two groups agreed on the design value of most of the ninety-three items.
