They split on only four points, covering grounds, building structure, floor labeling, and visible cleanliness. The authors say those gaps should be aired early in hospital planning. Shared views can then guide new builds.
pmc-11575720:
Abdul Hadi and co-authors design and test new compounds against leishmaniasis in a 2024 paper. The disease, spread by sandflies, harms people in many warm regions and has few good drugs. The team built thiourea-based compounds and screened them against three forms of the parasite.

Three compounds stood out, killing parasites at very low doses in dish tests. The best one also hit the parasite stage that lives inside human cells. Lab tests showed the compounds block two parasite enzymes, and adding folic acid undid their effect, which confirms the route. The compounds spared normal human kidney cells fairly well. Readers get promising leads for a neglected disease.
pmc-11576220:
Finsterer wrote a letter to the editor in twenty twenty-four about a study of long-lasting symptoms after COVID-19. The study he discusses compared twenty-nine patients with lasting symptoms to twenty-eight without them. It measured virus material and immune signals in the blood one and three months after infection.

Finsterer raises five concerns about the study. He asks whether high levels were present before infection, and whether new infections, other illnesses, or drugs were ruled out. He notes the groups were small, and that some diagnoses rested on less exact antigen tests. He also asks which organs the virus had hit. His point is that these gaps must be closed before firm claims are made.
pmc-11578420:
Mo Lin and co-authors published a study in 2024 on a lightweight acoustic diaphragm, the thin sheet in a speaker that moves to produce sound. Their diaphragm has a hyperbolic paraboloid shape, a curved saddle form, built from a plastic polymer network combined with graphene oxide layers. It was fabricated by spray coating, a simple and cost-effective method for making large curved diaphragms.

The researchers compared their diaphragm's acoustic performance with a commercial diaphragm made from banana pulp, a known lightweight material. The new diaphragm matched the commercial one in sound performance. It was, however, fifteen times thinner and eight times lighter. Such reductions matter where weight and size are critical, as in portable audio devices and acoustic sensors. The work shows that self-assembled nanoscale structures can perform a professional job at a far lower weight.
pmc-11578920:
Hongjuan Liu and co-authors check whether a simple blood ratio can forecast recovery after an ischemic stroke. The ratio divides blood urea nitrogen, a waste marker, by albumin, a blood protein tied to nutrition. Earlier hints suggested it might predict poor outcomes. The team re-analyzed records from a Korean hospital cohort of 1,850 stroke patients.

About twenty-eight percent of the patients had a bad outcome three months after the stroke. A plain statistical model found no straight-line link between the ratio and outcome once other factors were counted. A flexible model, though, revealed a bend in the curve. Below a ratio of about 2.86, the ratio carried no signal. Above that point, each step up in the ratio raised the risk of a bad outcome by roughly nine percent. The authors say the ratio may still help doctors judge risk, but only past that threshold.
pmc-11579420:
Shiya Cheng and Melina Schuh study how mouse egg cells stay on pause in this two thousand twenty-four paper. In mammals, egg cells rest in an early stage of meiosis for long spans of time. This arrest lets eggs grow to full size before they mature. It was known that a blocked kinase helps hold the pause. Whether control of protein building also plays a part was not known.

The team found that dormant copies of the cyclin B1 message are kept silent by two means. First, a group of RNA-binding proteins grips the message and blocks its reading. Second, other proteins soak up the cell's protein-building machinery, starving short-tailed messages. Together these blocks keep cyclin B1 low and the arrest firm. The work adds a new layer to how fertility is guarded.
pmc-11579720:
Zhe Bai, Hui Li, and Baoping Jiao test a mustard-family plant compound against chemically induced liver cancer in mice. The compound, sinigrin, occurs in Brassica plants and has drawn interest for anticancer effects. Tumors were triggered by injecting young mice with diethylnitrosamine; in the final four weeks of a ten-week study, treated mice received daily sinigrin by mouth at two doses.

Sinigrin shifted the blood picture toward health: liver enzymes and a tumor marker fell, while protein levels rose. It boosted the liver's own antioxidant enzymes and cut markers of oxidative damage. Levels of inflammatory signals dropped, and a growth-driving pathway chain, PI3K-Akt-mTOR, quieted down. At the same time the compound switched on the cell's internal death program, raising pro-death proteins and lowering their blockers. The authors conclude the protective effect works through antioxidant and pro-death actions together.
pmc-11582320:
Plastic films used in packaging burn easily and offer little protection from sunlight or germs. The authors make tiny round particles from dried molokhia leaves, a renewable plant source, using a simple one-pot ball-milling method. The particles average 8.5 nanometers across and mix evenly into polyvinyl alcohol films. Lab checks with spectroscopy and microscopy confirm what the particles are and how they look. The team then tests the loaded films for fire, light, and bacteria.

Plain film burned at 125 millimeters per minute, while films with the particles did not burn at all in the test. The films also blocked far more ultraviolet light, with protection over 900 percent better than plain film. Against two common bacteria, the loaded films produced clear zones of 9 and 7.6 millimeters where growth stopped. The authors also explain how the particles resist fire and judge the cost of making them at scale.
pmc-11582620:
Stefan Stenfelt, Mehrnaz Zeitooni, and Elina Mäki-Torkko present a two thousand twenty-four hearing study using bone conduction sound. They tested how well people with inner-ear hearing loss use two ears together. Sound delivered through the skull may behave differently from normal headphones.

Two groups took part: people with balanced loss in both ears, and people with uneven loss. Tests covered speech in noise, loudness differences, and judging sound direction. Both groups gained from two-sided stimulation, with balanced loss doing better. Air conduction gave about double the benefit, yet true two-ear processing survived through bone conduction.
pmc-11585620:
Zhenyu Ma and co-authors present a 2024 study on an enzyme that helps bacteria resist antibiotics. The enzyme takes a building block from the cell membrane and attaches it to the outer coat, which blunts drug attack. Using too much of that building block can wreck the membrane and kill the cell, so the enzyme's activity must be kept in balance.

Computer simulations at atomic detail showed the enzyme flips between open and closed shapes. That flipping orders the steps of its work. The share of the building block in the membrane steers the flipping: rich conditions hold the enzyme open and active. The study reveals a built-in control for resistance.
pmc-11586120:
Zijun Hu and three colleagues present a 2024 review of a cell-free therapy for lung diseases. Mesenchymal stem cells release tiny vesicles loaded with proteins and RNA that calm injury and guide repair. Because the vesicles carry the benefit without transplanting living cells, they dodge many risks of cell therapy.

The review explains where these vesicles come from and how they act. It then walks through evidence across many lung conditions. These include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, infectious lung damage, and lung cancer. Scarring disease, high lung blood pressure, and acute respiratory distress also feature. For each, it weighs promising animal and early human results against the limits of today's treatments. The authors see vesicles as a broad new avenue for respiratory medicine.
pmc-11586420:
Ziynet Kesimoglu and Serdar Bozdag fused layered networks in 2024 so that standard graph learning tools can read them. Real networks, from biology to social media, carry several kinds of nodes and links at once, and most learning methods expect just one of each.

Their framework learns two levels of importance: which neighbors matter to each node, and which network layer matters overall. Edges are then rescored by those importances and the weakest are cut, leaving one clean fused network. A graph convolutional model runs on the result for tasks like node labeling. Across four data sets from different fields, the fused approach matched or beat leading rivals, and the learned weights can be read back for meaning.
pmc-11589120:
Veronika Loncar and co-authors survey in a 2024 study the genes of common terns across Europe. The migratory seabird is losing breeding pairs in several regions to habitat loss and disturbance. Broad sampling across three zones set up a test of how split the population is.

Eighteen fast markers plus a mitochondrial stretch were read in the sampled birds. Diversity ran high in both marker types, lowest in the southern marine group. Signs of past bottlenecks appeared in all three groups despite the high diversity. Structure between groups proved weak or absent, pointing to strong gene flow. Distance between colonies mattered little, so migration routes likely shape the pattern more.
pmc-11589620:
Minkyu Kim and Panjin Kim present a 2024 paper testing whether quantum algorithms for noisy learning problems truly beat classical ones. The problems, with names like ring learning with errors, rest on adding noise to linear equations. An earlier team had built a fast quantum method using quantum samples. The pair re-examine that work under the same assumptions.

On one side, they widen the quantum method's reach, settling an open case about its Fourier step. On the other side, they show that if the same quantum samples are handed to a classical computer, efficient classical algorithms also exist for two related problems. The upshot is a fairer map of where quantum advantage may lie. The paper speaks to the cryptography built on these noisy problems, whose safety depends on such comparisons.
pmc-11590520:
Ji-won Hwang published this review article in 2024. It concerns chronic aortic regurgitation, where a leaky heart valve lets blood flow backward into the left ventricle. The chamber stretches and thickens to cope, then slowly scars and weakens. Hwang traces that progression from compensation to failure, and asks how doctors can spot damage early enough to time surgery well. Standard ultrasound measures can look normal while the muscle is already deteriorating.

The article focuses on strain imaging, which tracks how heart muscle fibers shorten. Global strain already flags hidden dysfunction in patients without symptoms, and guidelines endorse it when pumping fraction is borderline. Hwang's interest is regional: whether strain loss in the wall area struck by the leaking jet tells more than the global number. Evidence on the jet's local impact is still thin, the review notes. It sets out why that question matters for predicting recovery after valve surgery.
pmc-11591020:
Junhwi Moon and colleagues ask whether fatty acids from seafood change how dietary antioxidants relate to depression, in a 2024 cohort study. They followed 2,564 Korean adults aged 40 to 69 for eight years, using food questionnaires and the Beck Depression Inventory. Over that time, 165 men and 224 women developed depression.

Women who ate more seafood had a 42 percent lower risk of depression than women who ate the least. Among women with high intake of n-3 fatty acids, higher antioxidant index scores also tracked with lower depression scores. The pattern did not show up in men, which the authors note as a limit on how far the finding reaches.
pmc-11592520:
Children's skin care is hard to reach, since few specialists serve them and waits can be long. Daniele Zama and co-authors reviewed the state of telemedicine and artificial intelligence in pediatric dermatology in 2024, and the problems that still block wider use.

From the last fifteen years of studies, the review kept 76 papers. Remote visits matched in-person diagnoses in about 70 to 89 percent of cases for common childhood skin diseases, and they cut waiting times for families far from clinics. The authors note limits such as language barriers and poor image quality, which AI tools may help ease. They also flag the care needed before such tools are trusted with children.
pmc-11592920:
Falls from height can tear the heart, and an old surgical scar may change how that tearing unfolds. Gabriele Napoletano and co-authors report a forensic case from 2024: a twenty-nine-year-old man who died in an eleven-meter fall. He had undergone heart surgery as a child for swapped great vessels, and his blood held a high level of alcohol.

Autopsy found an extensive rupture of the heart, wider than the usual pattern in such falls. The authors argue that fibrous adhesions from the old surgery had anchored the heart to its sac, so the impact pulled harder on the tissue. They call for more study of how post-surgical changes in heart tissue shape injury in later trauma.
pmc-11593920:
Stine Lehmann, Mari Hysing, and Børge Sivertsen compare foster care alumni students with peers in Norwegian higher education, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Degree completion is low among young adults with foster care history. A national student health survey supplied self-reports. Five hundred eight alumni were compared with nearly sixty thousand general students.

Twice as many alumni reported receiving or needing special study assistance. They carried substantially higher economic burden, working more and worrying more about money. Parental financial support was scarcer for them. They also bore more informal care responsibilities. Mental and physical health, loneliness, and life satisfaction all fared worse. Yet grades and study progression matched their peers. The authors call for policies protecting care-experienced students' completion chances.
pmc-11594320:
Josué Lacerda de Souza and co-authors studied gene variants in an inflammation switch among patients with a skin form of leishmaniasis in the Amazon, in work published in 2024. The catalog byline is shorter than the head byline, so team framing is used. The parasite disease varies widely between people, and host genes may explain part of that spread.

Single variants showed no clear difference between patients and healthy controls. One four variant pattern, though, came with a nineteen percent lower chance of disease. A combined pattern across two genes cut risk by about a third. Blood levels of the related signal protein did not track with the variants. The authors call the gene a possible modifier of the disease.
pmc-11595120:
Laipan Liu and co-authors breed a strain of fall webworm moths that resist a bacterial toxin used on poplar trees. The toxin, Cry1Ab, comes from a soil germ and is built into the trees to kill the pest. The team raised a lab strain that withstood forty-five times the dose that kills normal moths.

The resistance passed to offspring as a hidden trait on regular chromosomes, and it covered a sister toxin but not a third. Life table checks found the resistant strain bred as well as the normal one, with no clear cost in growth, weight, or egg output. That lack of cost raises the risk that resistance could spread in the wild, the authors warn.
pmc-11595720:
Richard Laflotte and seven co-authors tested cements for sealing radioactive beryllium waste, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Beryllium serves in some reactors as a neutron moderator and reflector. Dismantling those reactors will leave toxic, radioactive metal that must be locked into a stable form before burial.

Cement is a leading option, but beryllium corrodes in wet cement and data were thin, partly because the metal's toxicity makes testing hard. The team compared five cement recipes with electrochemical tools. Two stood out: Portland cement with much silica fume, and a sulfoaluminate cement with a sulfate additive. They cut the corrosion current sharply versus plain Portland cement. The authors name both as candidates for waste forms.
pmc-11595820:
Fabian Walther and co-authors build, in a 2024 chemistry study, a glowing composite that traps a bright dye inside the tiny channels of a zeolite crystal. Dyes with a large gap between the light they absorb and the light they emit are prized, since the signal stands clear of the source. Free dyes cannot be used in every setting, so a solid host helps.

The team made the dye, proved its shape through a sister crystal, then loaded it into the zeolite and sealed the pores. Light tests, gas uptake, and microscopy confirmed the dye sat inside. The solid kept a large glow shift in varied solvents and did not leak, which suits sensing and imaging uses.
pmc-11596520:
Torrico-Lavayen and co-authors test if vessel health marks explain how fine dust thickens neck arteries. Fine dust in air raises the risk of artery disease. The team studied 251 adults from a Mexico City gene study. They gauged dust load over time for each person. Neck artery wall width was read by scan.

Each added unit of dust load linked to about 19 microns more wall width. The link held for both sides of the neck. Two marks, NOx and l-arginine, did not carry the effect. L-arginine did fall as dust load rose. The authors conclude the dust effect runs through other paths.
pmc-11597120:
Yu An and a team of co-authors used gene-based causal methods to test whether B vitamins guard against Alzheimer's disease through gut microbes, in this 2024 study. The head byline is shorter than the catalog list, so the names here stay general. Three vitamin forms and combo pills were tested against disease risk, with 119 gut microbe groups screened as go-betweens.

No vitamin showed a direct causal tie to the disease. Several microbe groups did: four tied to lower risk and four to higher. Three of them fully carried what links did appear between single vitamins and the disease. The authors read this as evidence that the gut sits between diet and brain in this disease, a path worth probing in feeding trials.
pmc-11597220:
Ying Yao and six co-authors wrote this 2024 review on atractylone, a plant compound studied as a cancer fighter. The compound comes from the oil of a plant genus used in traditional remedies, and it has shown a wide range of effects, from calming swelling to guarding nerves. Work on its power against tumors has grown in recent years.

Studies report that the compound slows tumor growth, spread, and invasion, and pushes tumor cells toward death through several pathways. The review gathers those findings and the signals behind them, cancer type by cancer type. The authors judge the compound a hopeful lead for cancer prevention and treatment. They offer the summary as a base for the next steps: firmer lab proof, safe dosing work, and trials in patients.
pmc-11597520:
Danielle Schwartz and co-authors tracked how fast a syphilis blood marker falls after treatment in pregnancy in 2024. Syphilis passed to babies is rising again in parts of North America. The marker, called RPR, is used to judge whether treatment worked.

Records held one hundred twenty pregnant patients and thirty-five infants, each with several measures over time. The marker fell with a half-life of about thirty-nine days in parents and twenty-seven days in infants. The rate was not steady: it varied with the starting level, so simple decay models fit poorly. A model with a saturable recycling path for antibodies fit the data well. It explains why the marker can linger in the blood.
pmc-11599320:
Florian Fuchs and co-authors test cleaning methods on ceramic veneers in a 2024 lab study. Thirty-two extracted human premolars were fitted with veneers. Two ceramic materials were used for the restorations.

Specimens went through five rounds of heat cycling and cleaning. Cleaning used powder air polishing or ultrasonic scaling. Microscopy checked the margin between tooth and veneer. Surface texture and the inner interface were also examined. Cleaning at recall visits is routine, but its effect on veneer edges is unclear. Readers, mainly dentists, learn which method is gentler on the restoration.
pmc-11599720:
Fuel cells make low voltage, far below what an electric vehicle's motor wants, so the power must be stepped up efficiently. Peer Mohamed and co-authors design such a step-up converter in this 2024 paper, pairing a tweaked circuit with coupled coils to reach ten times the input voltage.

A neural network tracker keeps the fuel cell at its best power point as temperature shifts, beating the classic tracking method in tests. The team built a working two-hundred-watt drive and ran it under a real-time controller. Simulations and bench results agreed, supporting the design for fuel cell vehicles.
pmc-11600520:
Andrew Li and five co-authors pooled nasal microbe data to clarify its role in asthma. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the nasal microbiome. Asthma hits millions and mixes gene, immune, and world traits. Small past studies gave split reads on nose microbes. The team used RNA reads from two large public cohorts, one of Puerto Rican heritage children and one of African ancestry adults.

Host reads were cut, and microbe reads were named by a standard tool. They weighed spread and mix of microbes in asthma and control groups. Kind level gaps were then pooled across the sets. Readers get a larger, steadier read on which nose microbes track with asthma.
pmc-11600620:
Lalit Kumar Radha Krishna and a large team of co-authors review what is known about how mentoring support shapes professional identity, in this 2024 scoping review. Mentoring helps trainees, especially in medicine, become members of a profession, not just learn its skills. Its success is credited to personal, lasting relationships, but the support structures behind those relationships are less examined.

The team searched four databases for studies from 2000 to mid-2023, following standard scoping methods. They asked how mentoring support, the guidance, feedback, and timely attention wrapped around the relationship, helps a mentee absorb a program's values and grow a shared professional identity. Mapping this literature matters because programs often launch mentoring without designing the support that makes it work. The review gathers scattered evidence into a single picture for educators building or repairing mentoring schemes.
pmc-11600720:
Makarim Osman and co-authors cataloged a family of plant sensor genes in tomato, using computer analysis of the crop's genome. These genes, called lectin receptor kinases, help plants sense their surroundings and may take part in stress defense. The search found 161 related genes across seven families, and the study focused on the L-type and G-type groups.

Gene copying, both side-by-side and in distant blocks, drove the family's growth, especially for G-types. Under drought, heat, and cold, particular members switched on strongly, including one G-type gene that answered all three stresses. The genes' control regions carry many stress-related switches, and predicted regulators include small RNAs. The authors offer the catalog as a starting point for breeding hardier tomatoes.
pmc-11601920:
Nikita Mani and Samuel Weinberg comment on how male hormones temper a class of immune cells in a 2024 paper. Autoimmune disease strikes the sexes unevenly, and hormones are prime suspects. The commentary discusses new work tying that suspicion to cell metabolism.

The featured study shows androgen signaling rewiring helper T cells of the Th17 type, specifically throttling their glutamine burning. The result is calmer airway inflammation in males. Hormones, fuel choice, and immune force form one connected dial. The findings raise fresh questions: how do hormone swings across life reshape immunity, and could sex-specific metabolic tweaks become therapies for autoimmune disease?
pmc-11603820:
Amy Howk and six co-authors compared outcomes for injured patients moved out of intensive care by day versus by night, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Earlier work linked night moves to more harm, but trauma patients had not been studied on their own. Records came from a top-level trauma center over nearly two years.

Night moves took far longer to complete than day moves. Patients moved at night were readmitted to intensive care more often and had more major complications. After adjusting for injury severity and other factors, a night move still raised the odds of readmission by over half. The authors urge closer scrutiny of transfer timing as bed shortages grow.
pmc-11603920:
Autism risk seems to mix genes with outside triggers such as inflammation in the young brain, but how the two meet is unclear. Bahaaeldin and co-authors used slices of young cerebellum in culture to test one meeting point: Purkinje cells, the large neurons that organize the cerebellum. They added a bacterial compound that sparks inflammation, with and without extra copies of Engrailed-2, a gene tied to autism.

The inflammation shrank the branching of these cells, and the extra gene copies made the shrinkage worse. Blocking microglia growth or one key inflammation signal undid the harm, which names those players as the route. The findings cast Purkinje cells as a place where genes and environment add up.
pmc-11604020:
Ranran Liao and co-authors catalog in 2024 a family of gene switches in a medicinal plant whose roots yield compounds called coumarins. The plant is grown for traditional remedies, and the switches, of the MYB family, steer growth, stress defense, and the making of useful chemicals. Little was known about their roles in this species.

The team found 157 members of one MYB subfamily and mapped their place on chromosomes, their structure, and their shared patterns. Nearly all the proteins sit in the cell nucleus. Gene activity data covered tens of thousands of genes, with hundreds tied to the pathway that builds the plant's scented compounds. Chemical tests measured eight coumarins in root, stem, and leaf before and after the plant bolts. Two switch genes rose and fell in step with several coumarins in the roots, which marks them as likely drivers of coumarin output.
pmc-11604820:
Dominique F Leitner and co-authors study brain tissue in a 2024 paper on sudden death in childhood. Some children over one year old die suddenly with no cause found at autopsy. About thirty percent of those children had past fever seizures, a far higher share than in children at large.

The team measured proteins in three brainstem zones that steer body functions such as breathing. Tissue came from nineteen children: eight with no seizure history and eleven with one. A label free mass method counted proteins in tiny cut samples. Protein gaps tied to seizure history could point to a faulty control system shared with related sudden death syndromes.
pmc-11605820:
Nikhil Shah and six co-authors check whether irrigating the rectum soon after a delicate infant bowel operation is safe, in a two thousand twenty-four pediatric surgery paper. The laparoscopic Swenson pull-through for Hirschsprung disease leaves a fresh low anastomosis that instrumentation might tear.

Thirty-seven children operated on over six years were reviewed. Eleven, nearly thirty percent, needed irrigations for obstructive symptoms, starting a median of forty-six hours after surgery and lasting about three days. Leak rates were statistically identical between irrigated and non-irrigated children, about nine versus eight percent. The authors conclude early irrigation treats obstruction without endangering the anastomosis.
pmc-11605920:
Carlotta Valensin and co-authors set out the protocol for INSIGHT-2 in this 2024 paper, a cohort study of pregnancy and its complications. The study will follow 1,700 pregnant women over five years and their children to age two. Recruits include healthy pregnancies, women with prior conditions, and those at risk of complications. Staff will gather clinical and lifestyle data plus many biological samples.

The aims reach from prediction markers to the roots of disease in mother and child. A biobank will hold samples for future work beyond the first five years. The varied population should capture many complication types and support checks of health gaps. The authors expect the resource to serve joint studies across sites and to guide better care in pregnancy.
pmc-11606120:
Petter Viksveen and co-authors review teen involvement in mental health care in a 2024 systematic review. Taking part in one's own care is a basic right for adolescents, yet how much say they get, and in what form, varies widely and was little mapped. The review updates earlier work across personal treatment and service design.

Searches across six databases and expert tips yielded thirty-six eligible studies, most of them qualitative. Quantitative work stressed personal support and online tools as aids to involvement. A few studies linked shared decision-making with better self-reported mental health and satisfaction. No study addressed safety issues, a noted gap. Themes at the personal level and the organizational level organize the rest of the findings.
pmc-11607220:
Linrui Li and co-authors build a forecast tool for throat cancer in a 2024 study. The cancer sat high in the esophagus, the tube that carries food to the stomach. All 170 patients came from two sites and had chemo plus radiation as their main care. The team mined scans for fine image traits, a method called radiomics, to guess who would fare well or poorly.

Five learning methods were tried. Models that read the rim around the tumor did best, and a model that joined rim and core beat all single-area ones. A chart that mixed image traits with clinical facts beat a chart based on facts alone. Gene checks hinted that fat handling in cells may sit behind the image traits that marked poor outlook.
pmc-11607820:
Dry mouth is one of the quiet miseries of cancer treatment, wrecking taste, speech, and sleep. Mohammad-Salar Hosseini led a team that reviews why it happens and everything doctors have tried against it. Radiation and drugs damage the saliva glands, and once the flow dries up, teeth, gums, and comfort all suffer.

The candidate fixes are many: saliva substitutes, gland-stimulating drugs, gland surgery, gentler radiation plans, electric stimulation, oxygen therapy, light therapy, acupuncture, and diet changes, among others. None is approved as a definite cure, and the proof behind most is thin or contested. The team offers a guide for tailoring care patient by patient, and a map of the trials now running.
pmc-11607920:
Naveed Siddiqui and five co-authors report a boy whose narrowed windpipe was mistaken for severe asthma, in a case report from 2024. Windpipe narrowing after a breathing tube is a known complication, but it appears late and mimics asthma's wheeze and breathlessness. The confusion can delay the right fix.

A 10-year-old boy arrived with cough, wheeze, and labored breathing and did not respond to asthma treatment. Placing a breathing tube proved difficult, forcing an emergency surgical airway. Closer examination then found advanced grade three narrowing of the trachea. The authors urge doctors to consider this diagnosis in wheezing children with any past intubation.
pmc-11608220:
Kentaro Maejima and fourteen colleagues report a porous crystal that flexes without collapsing, held together only by the weakest glue in chemistry, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Porous crystals earn their keep adsorbing and separating molecules, and flexibility usually boosts performance. But crystals bound purely by van der Waals forces were thought too fragile to flex.

Their crystal keeps permanent micropores while its molecules change shape. Electron and X-ray crystallography pinned down the structure and its transition as it drinks water vapor. As humidity rises, aromatic rings around each molecule's rim rotate like paddles, opening the architecture. The crystal then releases its water ultrafast, a handy trait for humidity control and water harvesting. A flexible, permanently porous solid built from such feeble bonds was not supposed to exist. Demonstrating one widens the design space for soft porous materials.
pmc-11608320:
Agata Kubisiak and co-authors show how the COVID virus reshapes the inner frame of human blood vessel cells, in a 2024 study. Heart and vessel trouble follow the infection even in mild cases. The team used lung vessel cells that let the virus in but do not copy it.

Infected vessel cells lost their spring, and their actin fibers grew thicker as inflammation rose. Lung surface cells that do copy the virus moved the other way and grew more springy. The Alpha, Beta, and Delta variants all dulled vessel spring. The authors argue that this quiet damage, without virus spread, may help explain vessel failure in patients.
pmc-11609120:
Ralf Jäger and seven co-authors match a coffee-wake drug's main child compound with the drug itself, for mind gains in rats. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four.

The child compound had shown gains in thought, recall, and speed in past work, but no lab test had matched it to its parent. Young and old rats got two doses of the child, one high dose of the parent, or none. A water maze read recall by swim time. Brains gave counts of mind marks: mood wires, growth marks, and rust shields. Both drugs cut maze time in the young. The child form did more in the shown reads.
pmc-11610120:
Federico Visinoni and colleagues cross two yeast species and read the children's drug resistance to find its gene addresses, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Antifungal resistance is a rising threat, and natural hybrid yeasts often shrug off drugs well. Hybrids shuffle two gene sets, which can create resistance neither parent owns.

The team screened the offspring of a wine yeast and a cold-loving cousin against six antifungal drugs. Resistance varied widely from child to child. Comparing the gene pools of the toughest and weakest offspring located the controlling regions for three major drugs. Many had never been tied to resistance before, and some regions served several drugs at once. One doubled-up super-region held two linked genes, both proven causal by swap tests. The work shows how hybrid genetics can map resistance before it emerges in clinics.
pmc-11610220:
Karin Hugelius, Jason Murphy, and Karin Blomberg survey health problems among responders to the twenty twenty-three Turkey-Syria earthquake. Their 2024 cross-sectional study uses an online questionnaire completed by over five hundred local and international responders.

Nearly half reported physical or mental health problems during or after deployment. Fifteen percent needed medical care during the mission and seven percent needed medical evacuation. During missions, feeling unsafe, sleep problems, and headache were commonest. Afterwards, fatigue, sleep problems, and feeling depressed led. Local responders reported significantly more problems than international ones. About eleven percent could not return to ordinary work afterwards due to infections or mental health issues, underlining duty-of-care needs.
pmc-11611820:
Hui An and co-authors follow blood platelets and immune cells in patients recovering from COVID-19 in this 2024 study. During the illness itself, platelets are overactive and help drive clotting. What they do weeks later, during recovery, was much less clear.

The study tracked 298 patients who were unvaccinated, most with moderate illness, from admission to day forty-eight after symptoms began. About five percent of the moderate group still had high platelet counts at that point. Those patients also showed higher levels of several T cell groups, including helper, killer, and regulatory cells. Platelet counts also rose in step with B cell counts in this subgroup. The share of each T cell type stayed in balance, pointing to a steady rebuild of the immune system. The authors suggest platelets help steer immune recovery and could be a treatment target.
pmc-11612020:
Yihui Wei and co-authors study body image in Chinese survivors of sarcoma in work from 2024. Adolescent and young adult survivors often live with visible treatment effects, and how they see their bodies may shape behavior and mood.

Of 116 survivors surveyed about fifteen years after diagnosis, about forty percent were dissatisfied with their body image. Being female, having surgery, and poor family functioning raised the risk. Dissatisfaction linked to depression and avoidant personality problems. It also carried part of the path from weak family function to avoidance. The authors urge early psychosocial support for survivors.
pmc-11612520:
Mamoun Mardini and six co-authors sharpen frailty prediction for heart valve patients by mining doctors' free-text notes alongside standard records, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Candidates for catheter valve replacement are mostly older adults, and frailty strongly shapes their outcomes. Fourteen thousand patient records from one university hospital fed the analysis.

Models using only structured records predicted frailty modestly. Adding topic patterns drawn from clinical notes lifted accuracy sharply, to a clearly stronger level. The top warning signs were heart failure management, back problems, and an irregular heartbeat condition. Seven note topics emerged, several tied to specific treatments. The authors show unstructured writing carries frailty signals that coded fields miss.
pmc-11613720:
Kashvi Sheth and co-authors pair wavelet cleaning with a featherweight neural network to spot heart attacks on ECG traces, in a 2024 paper. Myocardial infarction demands fast, accurate calls, and automated reading could help. Their pipeline decomposes the heartbeat signal into frequency bands, thresholds away high-frequency noise, then classifies the cleaned trace as infarction or normal.

Trained with five-fold cross-checks on the large PTB-XL dataset, the model reached 96 percent accuracy, 97 percent precision, and a 95 percent F1 score. On a second public ECG database it held 91.18 percent accuracy. Variants with resampling tackled class imbalance. The authors pitch the small model for settings where heavyweight systems cannot run.
pmc-11615120:
Sarah Schrempel and a large team identify a major altered amyloid form across dementia types. Their brain tissue study from twenty twenty-four compares several dementias. Amyloid clumps define Alzheimer disease, but modified forms may drive harm. Different dementias might carry distinct modification fingerprints.

Post-mortem brains from controls and dementia cases were analysed. Many amyloid variants were measured side by side. One variant, changed at a single amino acid position, stood out. It ranked as a major form in Alzheimer and related dementias. Lewy body and vascular dementia shared that prominence. Such fingerprints could sharpen diagnosis between dementia types. They may also point to new treatment targets.
pmc-11615320:
Nerve cells release their cargo when calcium gives the signal, and a protein called synaptotagmin-1 is thought to hold loaded vesicles clamped until that moment. Seven authors watched single molecules of the protein gather on artificial membranes, filming the clusters form and dissolve in real time.

The protein assembled into two set sizes, small rings of about five units and large ones of about fifteen. Each size grew at a steady rate scaled to its final size, yet both fell apart at the same unit rate. When calcium arrived, both cluster types burst apart explosively, matching the clamp-release story. One targeted mutation erased the large class while sparing the small. The authors conclude the measured behavior meets what a vesicle clamp must do, with numbers attached.
pmc-11616320:
Katie Curran and co-authors study eye screening attendance among young people with diabetes in Bangladesh, in a 2024 paper. Diabetes can damage the eye's retina and blind without warning signs, so regular screening matters. The team tracked patients aged 12 to 26 at a Dhaka hospital and asked what helped or blocked attendance.

Attendance was high, at 88 percent, over the study window from mid-2019 to mid-2020. Children under 15 came more reliably than those aged 16 to 26. Boys and young men were less likely to attend than girls and young women. Those with worse blood sugar control were, in fact, more likely to show up. Distance to the hospital was the top reason given for missed visits. The authors weigh these patterns for screening programs serving the young.
pmc-11616420:
Yang Yang, Yuanji Zhao, Huan Lei, and Xiaohong Tan test a probiotic strain against movement trouble caused by antibiotics in mice. Antibiotics can upset the gut and, through the gut-brain axis, the body. Their 2024 study built the condition with a sterile antibiotic mix, then dosed mice with the strain Limosilactobacillus fermentum ZS09. Running and swimming endurance served as the main motion tests.

Treated mice swam and ran longer than untreated model mice. Inflammation markers fell in brain and blood, while protective enzymes rose. Gut barrier genes switched on more strongly, and brain growth factor paths gained activity. Helpful gut bacteria grew, and harmful ones shrank. The authors see a base for future probiotic work on motor function.
pmc-11616520:
Xiuxue Feng and co-authors single out a proteasome part, PSMD2, as a warning sign and possible target in pancreatic cancer, in this 2024 paper. Most proteasome subunit genes ran hot in tumor tissue from a large atlas. Two of them tracked with worse survival when highly expressed. The team profiled how the pair relates to immune signals, drug response, and tumor pathways.

Cell tests separated the twins. Silencing PSMD2 slowed cancer cell growth, raised cell death, and made the standard drug gemcitabine bite harder; boosting it did the reverse. The protein works by switching on the AKT growth pathway, and an AKT blocker hit high-PSMD2 cells hardest, undoing its push. The authors propose PSMD2 as a marker for who might benefit from AKT drugs.
pmc-11617720:
Sakura Sato and five colleagues measure one peanut protein's antibody levels to judge its clinical weight in allergic Japanese children, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Peanut allergy management leans more and more on component testing. The protein Ara h 6 is a sibling of the well-known Ara h 2. It lacked quantitative evaluation in Japan till this work was done.

Records came from two hundred seventy-three children who ate measured peanut doses. Antibodies against peanut and both components were quantified in the lab. Most children were sensitized to both proteins at once, as a pair. Ara h 6 antibody levels tracked the probability of reactions in a strong way. They also tracked the probability of anaphylaxis. Thresholds for a high predicted probability were worked out from the data. Numbers like these help clinicians pick who needs a supervised food challenge.
pmc-11618020:
Shuruq Albushi and co-authors report a rare skull bone disorder in this 2024 case report. Fibrous dysplasia swaps normal bone for weak fibrous tissue, leaving bone fragile and prone to break. It can strike one bone or many, and its course varies by person.

The case centers on the parietal bone, the plate at the skull's side and top. Diagnosis rests on imaging and tissue study, with biopsy the surest test. Care is often watchful, since the growth is benign and slow. Surgery steps in to guard function or prevent harm. A review of past reports rounds out the paper.
pmc-11618520:
Pierpaolo Falco and a large team of co-authors published this 2024 study of the winter ocean along the Ross Ice Shelf. The shelf floats over a hidden sea cavity where some of the coldest water on Earth forms. Winter there is nearly impossible to visit, so its processes had only been guessed at.

From 2020 to 2023, robot floats programmed in a new way drifted along and under the shelf front all year. Their readings track salt and heat through the dark season. The team measure how much dense, salty water the winter polynya produces, how much heat the cavity holds, and how fast the shelf melts from below. Such numbers feed forecasts of sea level and deep ocean flow.
pmc-11618620:
Ahmed Adam and co-authors present a predictive control scheme for a three-port power converter. Their 2024 study uses single-phase shift tuning, a simple way to steer power flow among ports. The converter is valued for high efficiency and compact size, but linked ports make control design hard.

The controller uses a cost function to hold voltages steady and split port power cleanly. Math conditions yield closed-form settings for the best control values. A hardware-in-loop test rig checked the design in real time. Comparisons with past work back the claims. Results show faster response and clean port decoupling. The authors offer the scheme for uses that need tight, flexible power control.
pmc-11619620:
Linghong Wu and co-authors published a study in 2024 developing and validating a nomogram model to predict prolonged hospital stay in patients undergoing spinal fusion surgery. A nomogram is a chart tool that turns a set of risk factors into a single clear score. A prolonged stay costs more and can signal a difficult recovery.

The researchers analyzed the records of 6,272 patients who had spinal fusion surgery. Two tools screened the candidate factors: one that prunes weak predictors, and a random forest ranking the rest by importance. Two prediction models were built and compared on how well they distinguished patients who stayed long from those who did not. The best model included factors such as blood transfusion during care, the type of surgery, a drug that reduces blood loss, diabetes, and electrolyte imbalances in the blood. The model held up in internal and external validation checks.
pmc-11620620:
School board service fires up some Texans for higher office and drives others out, Kelly Bergstrand, Beth Anne Shelton, and Rebecca Deen find in a 2024 study. Texas board meetings drew national heat, so the team surveyed elected trustees statewide. Three hundred eighty replied with ratings and comments.

City trustees swung hardest in both directions, more than rural peers. Newcomers, the self-assured, and Democrats voiced higher ambition on average. The inspired cited making a difference and representing others. The discouraged blamed party warfare, personal attacks, and unruly constituents. Local service acts as both ladder and warning sign, shaping who seeks power next in state politics.
pmc-11620720:
Lázaro Cárdenas-Camarena, María Teresa Guerrero-García, and Julio César Diaz-Barriga published a 2024 surgical series reporting twenty seven years of lip feminization and rejuvenation for patients assigned male at birth with gender dysphoria. Demand for facial gender affirming surgery is rising, yet combined lip work in this population is rarely documented.

The clinic included all such patients treated from 1997 to 2023, grouped into four age bands. Combined techniques aimed to make lips both more feminine and more youthful. Outcomes were scored three months after surgery with global improvement and satisfaction scales, and complications were recorded. In total, 988 patients had 1,789 procedures. Most were under fifty, though patients over sixty five averaged the most procedures. The series offers rare long run data on satisfaction and safety.
pmc-11620820:
Andrea Lecchini-Visintini and co-authors introduce a journal special issue on the pulsing brain in a 2024 editorial. The issue gathers work from a Royal Society meeting held in Brighton in June 2024. The brain pulses with each heartbeat, and that motion matters for disease and health. Four fields meet here: MRI, ultrasound, and math models of tissue and fluid flow.

Part one mixes imaging, modeling, and clinical work. Early papers map how brain tissue shifts with the heartbeat at high field strength, and how vessel maps can be drawn from pulsing signals. The editors aim to spark joint work and lay ground for a lasting research community in this area.
pmc-11621120:
Xiaoze Zhao, Xiaoli Li, and Weidong Xie published a materials study in 2024 on predicting how mortar made with desert sand and ceramic sand flows. In China's Ordos region, hazardous soft sandstone and desert sand are plentiful, and both can form light aggregates for mortar. How particle density and shape steer flow was unknown. The team measured particle roundness, roughness, and proportions by image analysis, then tied those to viscosity.

Lighter particles proved less round, rougher, and more elongated. As density fell, the mortar's yield stress and thickness dropped, with shear-thickening behavior. Two classic flow models were modified with a coupled density-shape term, and the revised versions predicted the mortars' flow traits more accurately.
pmc-11621220:
Jiarong Yu and co-authors review how coronaviruses interact with cell cleanup in 2024. Cells digest worn parts and invaders through a process that keeps them in balance. A targeted form of that process can destroy viruses inside cells.

Coronaviruses can trigger the cleanup path and bend it to aid their own copying. The review lays out how different members of this virus family steer that path. It draws heavily on the virus behind the recent pandemic for the newest data. The authors aim to ground work on vaccines and drug targets in this picture of virus and host.
pmc-11621320:
Artificial fish raised in virtual tanks can grow up social, Joshua McGraw and co-authors show in this 2024 study. The team built neural network fish and let them swim in tanks mimicking the rearing of real fish. Given deep reinforcement learning plus a curiosity reward, the artificial fish began acting like real ones on their own.

They schooled together and preferred their own group over outsiders, just as young fish do. The behavior carried over to richer, ocean-like virtual worlds. The authors argue that social behavior can grow out of general learning rules plus a drive to explore, with no special social wiring. The setup offers a lab for reverse-engineering how social life develops.
pmc-11621420:
Falls shadow Parkinson's disease, and spotting who will fall years ahead could change care. Charalampos Sotirakis and five co-authors asked in 2024 whether a two-minute sensor test could predict falls five years out, using data from 104 patients who had never fallen.

Six wearable sensors recorded a short walk and a thirty-second standing sway task, and five machine learning classifiers mined the movement data. A random forest did best at sixty months, with seventy-eight percent accuracy, while most models topped ninety percent area scores at two years. Variability in walking and posture carried the signal, and adding age helped. The authors pitch sensor screening as a practical upgrade over slow, subjective clinic assessments.
pmc-11621720:
Tatsuya Akitomo and co-authors (2024) put three AI chatbots through Japan's national dental licensing examination. Artificial intelligence is spreading into dental education, but its command of the field's tested knowledge needed measuring. The team took 349 of the 400 compulsory questions from the past five years of exams. They posed them to ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4o mini, and Gemini, and scored the answers across thirteen topic categories.

ChatGPT 4o mini met the passing standard in two of the five years and earned the highest total score of the three systems. Its scores in society and dentistry and in cardinal signs were significantly higher than those of ChatGPT 3.5. The authors read the result as evidence that such tools could already help in dental teaching, while noting that scores still vary by topic. Further gains, they suggest, would widen the tool's role in training future dentists.
pmc-11622420:
Pongpawan Chienvichai and colleagues pool trials of a hormone shot meant to lift success in frozen embryo transfer, in this review and meta-analysis from twenty twenty-four. In these IVF cycles, a thawed embryo is placed in the womb, and a single dose of a GnRH agonist has been proposed as a booster. Reports disagreed, so the team gathered the randomized evidence.

Of nearly sixteen hundred papers found, only six trials qualified. Clinical pregnancy ran a little higher with the shot than without, about fifty-two percent against forty-seven. The gain concentrated in natural cycles, where the body runs its own hormones; in artificial cycles it vanished. No other outcome, from implantation to live birth to miscarriage, differed clearly. The authors call the benefit marginal and cycle-dependent, and imply routine use in artificial cycles lacks support.
pmc-11622620:
Yu Liang and seven co-authors study how a sulfur amino acid steers immune cells toward a harmful state in artery disease, in a 2024 lab paper. High blood levels of homocysteine are a known risk factor for atherosclerosis, the fatty buildup inside arteries. Recent work hints the harm runs through epigenetic tuning, including a common RNA tag called m6A.

The team profiled that tag across the RNA of macrophages, the immune cells that gorge on fat in artery walls, with and without homocysteine treatment. Treated cells shifted their tag pattern and leaned toward the inflammatory cell state. Two surface receptors, CD209 and CD163L1, stood out as tag targets. Cell counts confirmed fewer of the calming cell type after treatment. The chain gives drug hunters a fresh angle on a classic risk factor.
pmc-11623120:
Anila Hashmi, Alexander Papachristos, Stan Sidhu, and Gyorgy Hutvagner test a protein as a marker for a rare adrenal cancer in this 2024 paper. Adrenocortical carcinoma is uncommon but fierce: hard to diagnose, quick to return, and often deadly. Better markers would help on all three fronts.

The team examined the machinery that processes microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, in tumor data from large public atlases. They also measured the proteins directly in banked tissue. One part stood out: AGO2, the enzyme that carries out microRNA silencing, ran far higher in cancers than in healthy adrenal tissue or benign lumps. Patients with higher AGO2 also fared worse in survival analysis. The authors propose AGO2 as a candidate marker to flag the cancer and to warn of a harder course.
pmc-11624120: Barsha Baral and five co-authors summarize the essentials of aconite poisoning, a fast moving emergency caused by toxins in monkshood plants, in this 2024 paper. The poison can trigger dangerous heart rhythms that kill quickly if missed. Early recognition is the hinge of survival. Two intravenous drugs, magnesium sulfate and amiodarone, can stabilize severe rhythm disturbances when given promptly. Close monitoring and treatment tailored to the patient's course improve recovery. The authors stress that speed and vigilance, more than any single drug, decide outcomes in acute cases.
pmc-11624720:
Jennifer Schlecht and three co-authors track how special health needs shape third grade marks in German children. Kids with long health needs oft lag peers at school, but timing of need may matter. A town cohort was screened before school and at the end of first and third grades, with marks in three subjects.

About one in five kids ever had such needs. Those kids scored worse on the average mark than never need peers. Current need in third grade hurt most, and new or lasting need hurt, while past need alone did not. Regular school age checks and early aid are urged.
pmc-11625320:
Bamdev Subedi, writing alone, argues that Nepal's mix of medical systems is plural in name but unequal in fact. This 2024 paper notes that most countries let biomedicine and traditional medicine share official space. In Nepal, though, traditional systems lag far behind in buildings, budgets, staff, schools, and research output, and popular healers outside the scholarly traditions lack any official standing at all.

Working from published data, Subedi compares the two worlds on money, facilities, workforce, training institutions, and publications. On every count biomedicine dominates, which makes the pluralism exclusionary and undemocratic in practice. The paper then proposes measures to level the field: real institutional support and legitimacy for traditional practice, scholarly and popular alike. The goal named in the title is a medical pluralism that is both inclusive and democratic, where coexisting systems stand on something closer to equal footing.
pmc-11626620:
Annabelle van Gils and a large team compare two ways to prevent early birth in a 2024 trial report. Women who had a prior early birth face high risk of another. A cervical stitch, called cerclage, is the standard step, but a removable ring, called a pessary, may be gentler.

The trial ran in 21 hospitals from 2014 to 2022 and enrolled women with a single pregnancy and a cerclage indication. Women were assigned at random to pessary or cerclage in equal shares. The main outcome was birth before 32 weeks. Secondary outcomes covered other birth timings and health results for mother and baby.
pmc-11626720:
Heavy metals slip into beer from grain, water, equipment, and storage, and drinkers take them in glass by glass. Niwaeli Orgenes Eliaza and three co-authors measured six metals in ten top-selling beer brands in Tanzania in a 2024 study. A standard spectrometer read the levels of copper, cadmium, lead, chromium, iron, and zinc.

Cadmium and lead showed up in none of the samples. Zinc and copper sat below World Health Organization guideline levels, in that order of size, while iron and chromium ran above them. Daily intake estimates for iron and zinc stayed under the joint FAO and WHO tolerable cap. Chromium intake, though, passed its recommended value, hinting at risk for steady drinkers. The authors ran the standard hazard and lifetime cancer risk scores to complete the picture.
pmc-11626820:
Ochuko Erukainure and a team including Priyanka Banerjee test whether HIV drugs might be reused against the Omicron form of the COVID-19 virus. Their computer-based study was published in twenty twenty-four. Omicron carries many changes in its spike protein, which raised fears about how bad the illness could be.

The team compared the spike gene of Omicron with the Delta and Wuhan forms. They then modeled how four HIV drugs, among them dolutegravir and lamivudine, might bind the start and stop signals of the changed viral proteins. The thinking is that these drugs could jam the making of the spike. The study is purely on the computer, with no lab or patient tests. It offers a low-cost lead for drug reuse that later lab work would need to check.
pmc-11627220:
Kexin Zhong and eleven co-authors review how the cleanup of worn out mitochondria may drive functional dyspepsia, in this 2024 paper. The condition brings chronic stomach discomfort that shows no clear damage on standard tests. Attention has shifted to the duodenum, the first stretch of small intestine, where subtle faults are now documented. The review centers on mitophagy, the process that recycles the cell's power plants.

The authors trace how faulty cleanup could harm the gut lining's barrier, stir inflammatory signals, and scramble the wiring that controls movement and sensation. Two cell types in the duodenum, eosinophils and mast cells, are already known to rise or fire more in patients, matching the sensitivity and motility complaints. The paper offers the mechanism as a base for new treatments, while calling for deeper pathway work.
pmc-11628520:
Haiqing Chen and co-authors present a 2024 study searching for immune markers of atherosclerosis, the artery-clogging process behind most heart attacks and strokes. The team combined three public gene datasets. They covered whole artery tissue and single cells from plaques. Their pipeline layered several methods: network analysis to find gene modules, machine learning to nominate markers, and a neural network to validate them.

Single-cell data revealed restless monocyte groups inside plaques, and their communication patterns shifted over time. The pipeline converged on marker genes that separated diseased from healthy tissue. It also sorted patients into immune subtypes. The authors present the framework as a route to molecular diagnosis and immune-aware treatment of atherosclerosis, pending experimental confirmation.
pmc-11628620:
Karthikeyan Dhamotharan and six co-authors map a core residue web inside the COVID virus's pack protein that keeps it whole and choosy about RNA, in a 2024 journal article. The protein readies the viral genome for new copies. Its head domain grips RNA, yet clear views of that grip were lacking.

The team used crystal views and magnet based scans to test how changes in the domain bend its shape and grip. Both traits hang on a small web of building blocks kept across the virus family. The web steadies the fold and lets flex loops talk to each other as they pick RNA. Changes since 2019 were also weighed. The authors say the web makes the domain hardy yet able to shift shape for its many jobs.
pmc-11629020:
Aine O'Reilly and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, the two faces of reactive oxygen species in cancer care. These sharp oxygen forms can both feed a tumor and kill it. Cancer cells make more of them than sound cells, which helps the tumor grow. Push the level higher still, or cut the cell's shields, and the same forms can kill cancer cells first. Chemo and radiation gain part of their force that way. At the same time, such forms from swollen tissue can mute the immune cells that hunt tumors.

Care that shifts these levels can thus help or harm, based on which cells it hits. Short bursts of antioxidants may free the immune system to work with immune drugs. Long use can feed the tumor in its place. The team maps paths to aim the shift at the right cells.
pmc-11629320:
Giovanna Caparello, Fabrizio Ceraudo, Francesca Meringolo, Giuseppina Augimeri, Giuseppe Morino, and Daniela Bonofiglio published this pilot study in 2024. It compares children who eat lunch at school with children who eat at home, focusing on diet quality and a skin marker of vegetable intake.

The study covered 132 pupils. Those eating school meals also joined activities that praised fruit and vegetables. A handheld meter read the pigment level in each child's skin, a stand-in for how many vegetables they eat. The school lunch group scored clearly higher on that pigment measure. Daily vegetable eating and being a girl also raised scores. Diet quality scores overall sat mid-range, and pigment levels ran low across the whole group. The authors back school meals as a lever for healthier habits.
pmc-11629820:
Liver cancer often hides from the immune system, and a metabolism gene may hold one of the keys. Qianlong Kang and co-authors combined single-cell and spatial data in 2024 to screen metabolism genes tied to outlook in this cancer. Six genes carried prognostic weight, and one, SLC16A3, stood out for its link to immune suppression.

The gene ran high in tumor-promoting macrophages and at the tumor's invasion edge. Tumors with high levels showed fewer active killer T cells nearby, and the gene's presence went with more immune-dampening proteins. In tests, blocking the gene slowed cancer growth and revived T-cell killing. The authors propose it as a fresh target for restoring immune attack in liver cancer.
pmc-11630520:
Marschall and co-authors reported this heart case in twenty twenty-four. A seventy-year-old patient had a narrowed stent treated with a drug-coated balloon. The balloon leaves medicine behind without adding new metal. The first result looked excellent, with no tear and little remaining narrowing.

Three months later the patient arrived with a major heart attack. The treated segment had slammed shut, a complication not previously reported for this therapy. Doctors prepared the lesion and placed a drug-eluting stent with a clean final result. The patient went home two days later and stayed symptom-free at six months. The authors say the rare event does not undo the strong safety record of the balloons.
pmc-11630820:
A research team used a light-based ruler to watch a cell channel change shape, in a 2024 study. The channel opens when small ring-shaped signals bind to it, and it helps set cell excitability. The team worked with a bacterial version that serves as a clean model for the family.

They placed a glowing tag and metal tags at set spots on the channel's tail region. By timing the glow, they measured distances within the protein with and without each signal. One signal, cAMP, drove large shape changes and strongly favored the open state. The second signal, cGMP, nudged the channel only weakly. The study also tested how grouping and salt levels shift the balance of states.
pmc-11630920:
A clot in the lung often wears the mask of heart disease, and heart wards miss it. Doudou Yao, Wenjuan Cao, and Xiaoyan Liu looked back in 2024 at seventy-four such cases in one heart ward, set against a larger group cleared by scan. Chest tightness, short breath, sweats, and chest pain filled both groups alike. That likeness is the trap: the signs give no clean tell.

Two traits stood out as strong lone flags: a clot in the leg veins and ropey leg veins. Crackles in the lungs, blue lips, fast pulse, low pressure, and two blood marks also tracked with the clot. The team urge heart staff to rescan folk whose picture mixes breath and belly signs. A missed lung clot can kill where a caught one can be cured.
pmc-11631820:
Rachit Sharma and co-authors sweep the evidence on air pollution, temperature, and seizures, in this 2024 scoping review. Dirty air and heat may stir brain inflammation and stress, yet studies had never been gathered in one place. The team found thirty-four studies, most from East Asia, that drew exposures from outdoor monitors and cases from medical records.

Sixteen studies covered pollution, twelve covered temperature, and six covered both. Common suspects included fine particles, traffic gases, and daily mean temperature. Results were mixed across the board, with no consistent link for any single exposure, the authors report.
pmc-11631920:
What fat a broiler chicken eats reshapes the microbes in its gut, and those microbes feed back on the bird's health. Vidya Jadhav and co-authors fed groups of broilers seven fat-supplemented diets in 2024. The fats were canola, coconut, fish, flaxseed, and olive oils, lard, and a poultry-fat control. The team sequenced the microbes in the cecum at days 41 and 55.

Two bacterial phyla made up 99 percent of the community throughout. Age moved the microbiome more strongly than diet alone, though the two together mattered too. Butyrate-making species, prized for gut health, clustered with the fish-oil diet early and with flaxseed later, and the flaxseed group's predicted microbial functions hinted at health benefits by day 55. The authors recommend polyunsaturated fats as the more promising direction for feed design.
pmc-11632420:
Gerhard Hamilton and eight co-authors profile a lung cancer cell line that carries a rare switch-on fault in the SOS1 gene. Their 2024 study starts from a puzzle: about thirty percent of lung cancer patients have no known driver fault, so they miss targeted drugs. The cell line, grown from fluid around a patient's lung, reacted to an SOS1 blocker in early screens.

Deep gene scans found the fault, a small rewrite near a known hot spot. The cells proved sensitive to three SOS1 blockers, more so in three-dimensional growth than flat. The blockers also quieted key growth signals inside the cells. Partner drugs from three other classes boosted the effect. The authors offer the line as a test bed for SOS1 drug research.
pmc-11632920:
Matthias Schmidt and three co-authors survey how bone and joint surgeons view generative AI tools, in a 2024 mixed-methods study. The team sent a theory-based survey to surgeons and then interviewed a small group in depth. One hundred seventy-seven surgeons replied to the survey, and seven sat for interviews. Use and know-how varied widely across the group.

Surgeons used the tools more for research and self-training than for direct patient care. Younger and older surgeons differed in how easy they found the tools, which points to a need for tailored training. Barriers included thin proof of benefit and fear of dulling their own judgment. The authors call for a careful, field-aware path to adoption. They say schools and hospitals must weigh the mix of personal, tech, and workplace factors.
pmc-11633020:
Arjun Nair and co-authors present a teenager whose spinal canal outgrew his cord in a 2024 case report. Chiari malformation type I, where brain tissue dips into the spine canal, often travels with a fluid cavity in the cord and a curving spine. The links among the three are still being worked out.

Their thirteen-year-old patient had all three. Four months after successful skull-base decompression, he bled around the brain with no vessel flaw found. His neck canal measured wider than norms. A spinal drain relieved his symptoms and no bleed returned. The cord shrank dramatically as the cavity collapsed, while the bony canal stayed wide. Four years on he does well. The team floats canal width as a clue.
pmc-11633420: Lei Zhao and three co-authors report the full chloroplast genome of Dendrobium hainanense, an orchid, in a 2024 paper. The genome runs 151,367 bases with 37.46 percent GC content, split into large and small single-copy regions and a pair of repeated sections. It holds 127 genes in total: 81 that code for proteins, 38 for transfer RNA, and 8 for ribosomal RNA. A family-tree analysis placed this orchid closest to Dendrobium parciflorum. The authors present the sequence as a help for studying diversity in the genus.
pmc-11634420:
Otto van Leeuwen and co-authors describe the bumpy arrival of liver perfusion machines in American transplant practice, in a commentary published in 2024. Donor livers can now be kept alive on machines that pump warm, oxygenated blood through them, rather than resting on ice. United States practice has swung toward this normothermic approach after device approvals and strong trial results.

The authors contrast continuous perfusion, where the machine travels with the organ from donor hospital to recipient, with the back-to-base style that starts perfusion only after cold transport. Trials almost always used the continuous version. Moving from trial conditions to everyday logistics, staffing, and cost is the hard part, and the piece maps what American centers must solve to make the technology routine.
pmc-11635220:
Qiuming Hu and co-authors analyze in 2024 outcomes of chest muscle flap surgery for deep sternal wound infection, a dangerous complication after heart surgery. The flap method is simpler than many rivals but its risk factors were unclear. They reviewed 785 patients treated at one Beijing hospital over a decade and followed them for a year after surgery.

About ninety percent healed fully. Overall death rate was under four percent. Diabetes, obesity, smoking history, anemia, and chronic infection raised the risk of delayed healing or death. Longer delay before treatment also hurt outcomes. The analysis guides which patients need extra caution and closer follow-up.
pmc-11635320:
Lee Valentine and co-authors study how young people experienced a phone app for looping negative thoughts, in a 2024 paper. Such loops feed both depression and anxiety. Youth mental health needs are rising while services are stretched thin. The app, Mello, steps in at the moment with support tuned to real-time data.

Fifteen users aged sixteen to twenty-five gave deep interviews. The study is qualitative, focused on lived experience rather than scores. Users described what helped, what annoyed, and what felt personal or generic. Apps that act across diagnoses are a growing bet in youth care. Honest user accounts can show whether moment-by-moment design truly lands with the young people it targets.
pmc-11636120:
Mozaffar Vahedi and six co-authors compare three common insecticides against the German cockroach in a 2024 study. The pest fouls homes, spreads germs, and triggers allergies, so knowing which poison kills it at the lowest dose guides control programs. The team tested fenitrothion, malathion, and deltamethrin under the World Health Organization's standard bioassay.

Adult male cockroaches were exposed in coated jars for one hour, then watched for three days, with deaths counted across a ladder of doses. Malathion proved the most potent of the three, killing half the insects at the lowest dose measured. The analysis also weighed sublethal doses, the amounts that sicken without killing, which matter for resistance and for how survivors behave. The authors present the ranking as practical guidance for pest managers choosing among widely used sprays.
pmc-11637520:
Arjee Restar and eight co-authors wrote a 2024 guide for health researchers on measuring sex and gender. Surveys and studies often blur these two ideas into one box. That blur can hide real health gaps and skew results. The authors speak to epidemiologists, who track health patterns in large groups.

The primer sums up past critiques and offers rules that teams can apply at once. It urges clear terms, careful question design, and respect for how people describe themselves. The authors argue that sharp measurement serves the field's aims of better health and less disease. They frame the work as part of an ongoing talk, not a final word. Better data on sex and gender, they say, leads to fairer health action.
pmc-11640020:
Pragati Lodha and co-authors review how the lymphatic system helps tumors spread their influence, in a 2024 paper. Tumors shed tiny parcels called vesicles that carry messages to other cells and can prep distant sites for spread.

The review explains that lymph vessels drain fluid from tissues, so they form the main route for these parcels. Parcels ride the lymph first to nearby nodes, then through the body. In those nodes they can blunt immune attack and ready the ground for tumor growth. The authors map open questions: how parcels enter lymph vessels, how they act on node cells, and where new drugs might block the path.
pmc-11640620:
Łukasz Kaczyński (2024) studies how goat cheese should be stored once opened, following the product's water and shine. Two cheeses were tested: a soft feta-type salad cheese and a hard goat cheese. During storage in different wrappings, the author measured water activity, which governs spoilage and drying, along with gloss and color. The question came from shoppers themselves, who had reported trouble after repackaging cheese at home into whatever container was handy.

The results sort the wrappings by cheese type. For the soft salad cheese, aluminum foil kept quality best. For the hard cheese, the producer's own packaging won. The practical upshot: one-size advice is wrong, and labels may need to tell buyers the right way to rewrap each cheese. The study links lab measures, water and gloss, to a daily kitchen habit.
pmc-11640720:
Hongki Gwak and co-authors ask whether having several small breast tumors at once worsens outlook in a 2024 study. Reports of such multiple cancers vary widely, and better scans now find more of them. The team reviewed 45,881 patients who had surgery for invasive breast cancer between 2004 and 2016.

Patients were grouped by tumor count on the same side: one, two, or three or more, all at the small T1 stage. Survival and breast cancer survival matched between the one and two tumor groups. Those with three or more fared clearly worse on both counts, and tumor count stayed an independent risk factor after adjustment. The authors suggest stronger treatment for that group.
pmc-11640820:
Sai Xu and co-authors review ways to keep farm product quality testing steady when the test does no harm to the goods. Hand testing is slow, biased, and can spoil samples, so farms turn to vision, spectral, and bio inspired sensors. In real use, though, results wobble for many reasons.

Their 2024 review sorts the causes into three groups: the samples, the setting, and the gear itself, which ages and picks up noise. The authors then gather fixes from recent work for each cause. They close with advice for future studies. The goal is tests that stay accurate and fast as the food sector grows more automated.
pmc-11641120:
Yujiao Chen and co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, how the farmed red seaweed Neopyropia yezoensis copes with phosphorus shortage, and whether an organic phosphorus source can rescue it. This valuable seaweed suffers as phosphorus runs low in many growing regions.

Long phosphorus starvation stunted growth and dulled photosynthetic pigments and antioxidant enzymes. Feeding glucose-6-phosphate, a sugar-bound phosphorus form, gradually reversed the damage. Gene activity shifted under both conditions: starvation and nutrient-sensing pathways switched on while photosynthesis and defense genes quieted, less strongly when the supplement was present. The results map how this seaweed taps organic phosphorus.
pmc-11641320:
Emilia Gruszczyńska and co-authors propose a new way to guess the time of death from a chemical found in the body, in a 2024 study. Guessing that time is hard, and current methods have clear limits, so forensic work needs fresh tools that do not harm the body. The team turned to light-based tests of tryptophan, an amino acid that shifts as a body breaks down.

First, the team checked how the chemical acts under light at varied acid levels. Its light traits stayed stable as those levels changed. Early trials with 15 healthy volunteers then showed that amounts in fingerprint samples sat within the range their light method could detect, a first step toward later tests on the dead.
pmc-11641820:
Bi-Tian Zhang and co-authors probe links in 2024 between a brain tumor, COVID-19, and vitamin D. Glioma is an aggressive brain cancer with poor survival, and the pandemic added risk for such patients. Whether the virus can nudge tumors back, and whether vitamin D plays a protective role, were open questions.

Comparing gene activity in tumor and virus data, the team found two hundred three shared altered genes and five key ones after crossing with vitamin D targets. The key genes sit in a growth pathway and appear to bind vitamin D in docking tests. The authors suggest the vitamin might improve outlook for infected glioma patients, pending real trials.
pmc-11642020:
Irzal Hadžibegović and co-authors follow heart patients who arrived with an acute coronary syndrome and were found to have a fully blocked artery beyond the one causing the attack. From a two-centre registry of 1,950 treated patients, 171, about 9 percent, had such an extra blockage. These patients were older, more often diabetic, and left hospital with weaker heart function and worse disease scores. They were also less likely to take their prescribed medicines faithfully.

Over a median follow-up of 49 months, cardiovascular death struck 18 percent of the blockage group against 8 percent of the others.
