After adjustment, though, the blockage itself faded as an explanation. Weak heart function, poor kidney function, diabetes, and low adherence to medication carried the risk, with poor adherence the strongest factor, tripling it. Death also came sooner when the extra blockage was left unopened.
pmc-11642120:
Christina Karakosta and co-authors compare lens proteins in three kinds of cataract, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A cataract clouds the lens of the eye. Paths in cells that handle fats joined with sugars may help that clouding start. The team took samples while surgeons worked to fix the cloudy lenses.

They took lens skin and fluid from 11 people whose cataract was tied to diabetes, 12 whose cataract was tied to age, and 7 whose cataract came after a vitrectomy. A mass-based lab tool weighed and named the proteins in each sample. The age-linked group stood out, with the biggest shifts in the fat-and-sugar paths. One protein, GLA, ranked near the top of the list of changes. The team reads this as a sign that age-linked cataract runs on its own chemistry.
pmc-11642520:
Liyue Xu and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, a ginseng compound that may ease gut damage from a common cancer drug. The drug, 5-fluorouracil, often inflames the gut lining, a side effect called mucositis. The compound, ginsenoside Rc, is known for calming swelling and oxidative stress. The team tested it in mice and in gut cells in the lab. They tracked weight loss, diarrhea, gut leakiness, and tissue damage in mice. Network analysis of drug targets hinted at the pathways involved.

The compound cut weight loss, diarrhea, and gut damage in treated mice. In cells, it lowered inflammatory signals, cell death, and leakiness. A pathway that controls swelling and survival was implicated by protein tests.
pmc-11642720:
Neftalí Guzmán and a large team of co-authors build in 2024 a tool to predict which patients hospitalized with COVID-19 are most likely to die during their stay. Many such tools exist, but each one works better in some populations than in others, so local data matters.

Working from records of two hundred one patients treated at one clinical center, the team tested which factors tracked with survival over time. They used survival curves to follow outcomes through the hospital stay and built their model from what the data showed. A well-fitted local model can help doctors make hard calls about care and resources.
pmc-11642820:
Malgorzata Ponikowska, Joanna Zebrowska, and Piotr Skowron build a heat-stable antibacterial enzyme that sticks to cellulose, in a 2024 paper. The enzyme comes from a bacterial virus and digests the cell walls of its host bacteria. Keeping such enzymes at the site of action is hard because they diffuse away.

The team fused the enzyme to a cellulose-binding part and produced it in lab bacteria. The fusion kept full activity after heating across a wide range and stayed active near its melting point. It attacked several heat-loving bacteria and reduced biofilms. Binding to cellulose could load it onto wound dressings, valves, or food packaging.
pmc-11643420:
Limei Fan and co-authors test a plant compound in a 2024 cancer study. The source plant, a relative of the daisy used in Chinese medicine, is rich in coumarins, a family of compounds with reported anti-tumor effects. The team isolated seven compounds from the plant and screened them on four cancer cell lines.

One compound, cyclobrachycoumarin, stood out against bowel cancer cells. It drove the cells to self-destruct and halted their division cycle, in step with dose. Stress markers rose inside treated cells, while survival proteins fell. In mice carrying human tumors, the compound slowed tumor growth by the same routes. The authors identify it as the plant's key active ingredient and a lead for further drug study.
pmc-11643520:
Ondřej Patloka and co-authors review how gut microbes, diet, and obesity shape each other. Their 2024 paper sums up recent findings on this three-way link. Obesity is a complex disease that raises the risk of other illness. Gut microbes are seen as one factor that can shift its course.

The review describes what lives in the gut and how it is measured. It covers products made by microbes, like short-chain fatty acids, and their effects on the gut wall and immune balance. Diet types get close study, from high-fat plans to low-carb plans. Fiber and resistant starch get special stress for how they feed helpful microbes. The authors close with a joint view of these links.
pmc-11643620:
Andrea Asensio-Grau and co-authors watched gut microbes change as six breast-fed babies with cystic fibrosis met solid food, in this 2024 study. Early microbes shape immunity and metabolism, and chronic illness raises the stakes. Stool samples were taken before and after each new food.

Each baby's gut looked different from the start, led by a different main genus. One common gut group was missing in all six. Adding foods shifted each gut in its own way, with no shared pattern. The authors call for larger work to learn which foods steer the gut best for these infants. Personal plans, they suggest, may beat one-size rules.
pmc-11643720:
Maja Dorfner and co-authors swap single amino acids in plant enzymes to learn how heart drug pathways evolved, in a 2024 study. The enzymes, called PRISEs, serve two chemical roads in plantain species: one toward iridoids, one toward cardenolides. Two plantain versions share ninety five percent of their sequence, yet one processes progesterone seventy times faster than the other.

Structural models blamed two spots near a twin phenylalanine clamp that grips the substrate. Mutating those residues tested the claim. The authors read the swap as a fossil of how plants widened one enzyme family into new chemistry.
pmc-11643820:
Mayindza Ekaghba and a large team tested in twenty twenty-four a plant bark brew used in Gabon to treat loose stools. The tree is Pentadesma butyracea, and its bark is boiled for this use in folk care. They checked what is in the brew and how it acts in rats.

Lab reads found pairs of plant compounds as the main parts, and the brew showed no harm in tests. Its shield strength rose with its plant compound load. Bark picked in the wet season calmed gut strips in a dose-linked way. In rats dosed with castor oil, the brew cut wet stools, which backs its folk use.
pmc-11644020:
Paulina Gwóźdź and six co-authors study iron-doped perovskite ceramics as catalysts for cleaning ammonia from exhaust, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The ceramics blend two titanate bases in varying ratios, with small iron additions. Such materials could help convert ammonia pollution into harmless nitrogen.

Scans and spectroscopy found no separate iron phases, so the iron sits inside the crystal structure, its oxidation state shifting with dose. Heating tests showed the materials partly bounce back after reduction. The highest-iron samples were tested in two ammonia reactions. They performed strongly and selectively in the reduction route, forming nitrogen, but showed no activity in the oxidation route. The work maps how iron settles into these ceramics.
pmc-11644220:
Yu-Xuan Xian and co-authors present a 2024 materials study on a honeycomb panel that soaks up microwaves while bearing load. Such panels serve stealth and shielding work, but older versions drank in only a narrow band of radar waves and crushed too easily. The team married a honeycomb core to a patterned surface layer that selects which waves pass.

The plain honeycomb drank well across a band of about eleven gigahertz. The enhanced panel widened that band to about fourteen gigahertz, a gain of about a quarter, and the authors explain the split of labor between low and high waves. A crush test gave the panel a strength of 17.10 megapascals. The whole build costs about 271 dollars per square meter, which the authors cite as a practical plus.
pmc-11644320:
Prayook Jatesiktat, Guan Ming Lim, and Wei Tech Ang calibrate camera arrays that surround large three-dimensional capture volumes. Their tool pairs a wand carrying two LED markers, waved through the space for far-range data, with chessboard images captured close up during each camera's own calibration. A bundle adjustment fuses both data sources.

Benchmarking against an independent ground-truth trajectory exposed an overfitting problem in wand-only calibration. Adding the chessboard constraints fixed it, substantially improving three-dimensional accuracy and consistency. The authors also show a ray-distance triangulation formula beating the standard direct linear transformation. They release a benchmarking workflow and dataset so future calibration methods can be compared fairly.
pmc-11644520:
Xianda Sun and co-authors model leftover oil in rock pores in a 2024 paper. Polymer flooding is widely used to push more oil from reservoirs. Where the remaining oil sits at pore scale is still unclear.

A digital pore network was built from mercury intrusion data. Three-dimensional software rendered the pore structure for viewing. Flooding was simulated across polymer strength, molecule size, and tension settings. Moderate rises in polymer concentration improved the sweep. Other settings shifted which pores kept their oil. Readers in petroleum engineering learn how pore-level patterns can guide smarter recovery design.
pmc-11644720:
Mei Fu and co-authors trace a gene from a purple Chinese cabbage that deepens plant color when moved into a model plant. Their 2024 study deals with B-box factors, proteins that steer light responses and pigment making. The team found eighteen relatives of one such gene across five Brassica species. One cabbage gene matched the model plant's version most closely. It codes a protein of 319 amino acids and sits in the nucleus.

Plants overproducing that gene built up more anthocyanin, the purple red pigment, in leaves and seeds. Gene activity scans compared the altered plants with normal ones. Over 7,500 genes changed activity between them. Whole pathways shifted, including hormone signaling and pigment routes. The authors present the gene as a lever on color traits. Such traits matter for the look and nutrition of leafy crops.
pmc-11644920:
A neural network small enough to live on a chip can still hear a failing bearing, report Yu-Pei Liang and co-authors in a 2024 hardware paper. Their design squeezes a one dimensional convolutional network with separable convolutions and aggressive number rounding, then runs it on a standard programmable chip board.

Fed raw current signals from a public bearing dataset, the system reached 96 percent accuracy in telling fault types apart. The whole model fits in about 22 kilobytes and sips half a watt. The authors aim the work at factory floors, where diagnosis must happen on the machine, not in a data center.
pmc-11645020:
Ducsun Lim, Inwhee Joe, and Hai Dong present a smarter way to share computing power at the edge of a network, in a research paper from 2024. In edge computing, nearby servers do tasks for users so replies stay fast. The network can be split into virtual slices, each set up for a kind of service.

Their method, called MAARS, splits the job in two. One part shares resources across servers, and the other adjusts them as conditions change, moment by moment. Both parts learn from trial and error. In tests, MAARS finished more user tasks and used resources better than older methods.
pmc-11645520:
Justin Bellavance, Laurence David, and Michael Hildebrand build an open source tool to compare gene activity in spinal cord cells of male and female mice. Chronic pain differs by sex in type, prevalence, and severity, yet spinal cord gene data had not been compared by sex at single cell scale. The team merges three large single nucleus datasets.

Machine learning classifies more than 37,000 cells into predicted types. Standard tests then find genes that differ by sex in all cells, in neurons, and in surface dorsal horn neurons that process pain. Differences are large, and stronger in inhibitory than in excitatory pain neurons. All results sit in a free web app, with enrichment analysis to guide new pain research.
pmc-11646120:
Carla Julia S P Vieira and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study tracking mosquito-borne viruses in Brisbane, Australia. Watching viruses inside caught mosquitoes is a cheap, sensitive surveillance tool. Standard tests, though, reveal little about virus diversity.

Mosquitoes were trapped in five urban parks over more than a year. Pools were screened for two virus families with standard molecular tests. Positive samples then had their full viral genomes sequenced. Several viruses were found circulating together over the long term. The combined pipeline gives public health teams both early warning and detailed strain information.
pmc-11646620:
RSV hospitalizes many older adults, but standard testing misses cases, blurring the virus's true burden. Evan Anderson and co-authors enrolled in 2024 adults over fifty with respiratory illness, plus heart and lung patients, at two hospitals across two seasons. Beyond the usual nose swab, they tested throat swabs separately, collected sputum, and drew paired blood samples for antibody rises.

Ninety-two of 1,558 participants proved positive by some method. Testing nose and throat separately added a fifth more positives, and adding paired serology lifted detection by over forty percent among those fully sampled. The authors urge layered testing when accuracy matters for burden estimates.
pmc-11647320:
Aoibheann Brennan-Wilson and nine colleagues, for the World Health Organization, sift what research on violence against women during COVID-19 taught us, and what it failed to ask. Reports of such violence rose so much in lockdowns that many called it a shadow pandemic.

Of 419 papers kept from over twenty-five thousand found, more than ninety-five in a hundred only counted the harm. Just six in a hundred tested ways to help, and one in a hundred looked at how to stop the violence in a crisis. Online abuse, femicide, forced marriage, and acid attacks stayed near-invisible. The authors urge a sharp turn toward trials of support and prevention, above all for women hit by more than one form of bias.
pmc-11647920:
Kei Hirai and co-authors sort the public by radiation views in a 2024 survey paper. After the 2011 Fukushima plant accident, fear of radiation drove stigma and heavy avoidance, even where doses were low. Facts spread widely, yet what people actually knew and felt stayed blurry.

A survey of 2,400 people sorted respondents by attitude, knowledge, beliefs, and anxiety. Seven groups emerged from the sorting. Groups differed in how they think and act when faced with radiation questions, such as claims about disease clusters. Knowing which group a message reaches should help officials talk past fear without talking down to it.
pmc-11648220:
Autism shapes how people sense and act, and older theories each caught only part of that picture. Pratik Raul and two co-authors review in 2024 a brain based idea that may tie the parts together: that autistic brains carry high neural noise, a background hiss from unbalanced signals. About fifteen years ago, researchers proposed that such noise could sometimes help, by a quirk called stochastic resonance, where a dose of noise sharpens a weak signal.

That quirk could explain why autistic people do better on some tasks and worse on others. The authors gather the proof for and against the noise idea and judge it the best placed guide for new studies. They say it could also shape better support services.
pmc-11652320:
Leticia Rosevics and co-authors report Crohn's disease striking a tonsil in a 2024 case paper. Crohn's can inflame any stretch from mouth to anus, though mouth cases are less common. Their patient was a forty-nine-year-old man with eighteen years of gut Crohn's.

His right tonsil had grown large with a fleshy growth, and tonsil pain brought him in. A biopsy showed the granuloma pattern typical of Crohn's, with deep ulceration. Cancer and opportunistic infections had to be ruled out first, the authors stress. His drug was switched to infliximab. Three months later his gut symptoms were gone and the tonsil lesion had healed. The case reminds doctors that Crohn's can surface far from the gut.
pmc-11652520:
Ibrahim Ahmed Saleh Murshed and co-authors review bloodstream infections in children treated for blood diseases and cancer at one center in Wuhan in 2024. Such infections are a grave risk during chemotherapy or stem cell transplant. They lengthen hospital stays and raise the chance of death.

The team looked back at just over two hundred infections in a group of children, most of whom had blood cancers. They recorded patient details, which germs caused each infection, and which drugs still worked against them. Gram-positive germs were the most common, followed by gram-negative germs, with fungi rare. Most infections struck during treatment. The findings help local doctors pick first drugs wisely while lab results are pending.
pmc-11653120:
Austin Wesevich and five co-authors study biased wording in patient handoffs in a 2024 paper. When care passes from one clinician to the next, sloppy or slanted language can seed errors and unequal treatment.

Trainees at two medical centers heard three recorded handoffs based on real ones about Black patients. Each handoff came in either a biased or a neutral version, with bias of one of three kinds: stereotype, blame, or doubt. After each, the listeners answered questions on the clinical facts, their attitudes toward the patient, and their main takeaways. Comparing the paired versions shows whether slanted words warp what clinicians remember and how they judge the person in the bed.
pmc-11653820:
Charlotte Ibsen and co-authors build a support program for heart patients in this 2024 paper. Cardiac rehabilitation helps people recover after heart trouble, but many drop out. Patients in tough life situations drop out most often. The team co-designed the Heart Priority Programme with patients and health staff in Denmark.

The program first flags patients at risk of quitting, using a form with thirteen risk factors. Flagged patients then get a named contact person, steady communication, and active follow-up. In a six-month test, 260 patients joined and about a third were flagged. Staff found the program easy to fit into daily work. Patients spoke well of the extra support.
pmc-11654320:
Nadieh Taks and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on reforms in Dutch public health training. Institutes faced two changes at once: structured rotations for trainees, and a shift to a single national employer. Public health postgraduate training is multidisciplinary and scattered across organizations. It had drawn little research compared with hospital specialties. Fourteen leaders from eight institutes described the change in interviews.

Three themes decided whether the reforms stuck: influence, communication, and motivation. Participants mourned their shrinking say over their own programs. They also flagged tangled communication lines between institutes, trainees, and the new national structure. Where ownership survived, implementation held; where it drained away, the innovations wobbled. The study reads implementation as an organizational story, not a curriculum one.
pmc-11654420:
Beibei Hu, Guohui Yin, Jialin Zhu, Yi Bai, and Xuren Sun build a cheap way to guess a tumor trait in a 2024 study. The trait counts how many gene changes a tumor holds. High counts can flag patients who may gain from immune drugs, but the gene tests that count them cost a lot.

The team used gene activity data from four gut and stomach cancers held in a large shared bank. High-count tumors drew in more immune cells and showed more cell growth checks. A trained net built on just 31 genes then guessed the count with strong match to true values. The tool could help clinics screen patients at low cost.
pmc-11655520:
Marcel Wilhelm and five co-authors check a German version of a vaccine attitudes scale, in a 2024 study. The scale, called VAX, sorts anti-vaccine views into four groups, such as distrust of benefits and fear of side effects. The team translated the scale and gave it in online surveys twice: once before the COVID pandemic, with two hundred ninety-seven people, and once during it, with two hundred sixty.

Math checks backed the four-group shape of the German scale, with good fit. Scores were steady over time and lined up with other measures of vaccine doubt. Average scores split people who had taken vaccines from those who had refused them. They also predicted who planned to vaccinate later. The authors offer the scale as a sound tool for German studies of vaccine hesitancy.
pmc-11655820:
Huafeng Liu, Xuewen Liu, and Yanjun Lu review what is known about CARMN, a long non-coding RNA, and its part in cancer, in a review published in two thousand twenty-four. CARMN was first found in heart tissue. Its levels are now known to shift in tumors of the cervix, breast, colon and rectum, and gullet.

Across these cancers, changed CARMN levels track with tumor growth, spread, and how well patients do. In cervical cancer it acts like a brake on cell growth. In breast cancer it helps cells change shape and spread, and low levels can make drug treatment work better. The review also links CARMN to immune cells in and around tumors. The authors see it as a possible test marker and drug target, but say its workings still need proof in the clinic.
pmc-11655920:
Sara Lojo-Lendoiro writes a pointed essay on lung blood clots and the teams that treat them. Her 2024 piece covers a grave illness that needs fast, exact care. In theory, heart doctors, radiology doctors, and others work as one team for each patient.

In practice, she argues, pride and turf fights often shape who leads the care. Heart doctors stress risk scores, heart strain, and drugs that thin blood or break up clots. Radiology doctors bring a different focus and set of tools. Response teams were built to join these views, yet she asks if joint work is real. The essay calls for care that puts the patient first.
pmc-11656020:
Xiao-Feng Zhang and three co-authors weigh graft choices in 2024 for rebuilding a torn knee ligament. Surgeons can take the graft from the thigh tendon, from the kneecap tendon with bone ends, or from the hamstring. Which source works best has long been debated.

The team pooled twenty-one studies with close to three thousand patients. The thigh tendon graft failed less often than the hamstring graft. It also caused less pain at the harvest site than the kneecap tendon graft, and fewer kneecap complaints during sport and work. Knee looseness measures favored it too. The authors call it a safe, sound option, while noting that strong trials are still needed to prove it best.
pmc-11656220:
Cyniak and Kasprzak review green making of molecular receptors. Their review from twenty twenty-four deals with mechanochemical synthesis. It is a growing field in applied organic chemistry.

Grinding based making avoids much solvent waste in the lab. The review sums up gains for many receptor types. Groups covered range from Schiff bases to rhodamine types. Such receptors can spot ions and small molecules in tests. How they sense their targets is also set out. The work shows the scope of this green route.  Such work aims to cut solvent use in labs.
pmc-11656420:
Josef Finsterer questions a hopeful dementia case report in a 2024 letter. The report described one patient with probable frontotemporal dementia who improved after ten weeks of home brain stimulation paired with computer training: test scores rose, and family saw better language and self-care. Finsterer finds the study impressive but presses several objections.

His first target is the outcome test itself. The Mini-Mental State Examination, he notes, is easily disturbed and captures deficits only roughly. It can miss disease in the highly educated and can fake it in others. It also cannot separate one mental ability from another. Stronger batteries exist. The letter argues that a single case measured with a blunt tool cannot carry the claim that the treatment truly helps.
pmc-11656720:
Ying Li and Yan He review the use of exosomes from stem cells to treat lung injury caused by radiation, published in 2024. This injury is a common complication of radiotherapy for chest tumors, and effective clinical treatments are still lacking. Exosomes are tiny parcels that carry proteins, lipids, and small RNAs between cells.

Exosomes from stem cells keep much of the repair ability of the cells themselves, with better stability and safety, the authors argue. The review sets out the pathology of radiation lung injury and its current therapies. It then focuses on how these exosomes might help and the mechanisms proposed for their effect. Limits that slow clinical use, from science to regulation, are also discussed, along with future directions for exosome-based treatment.
pmc-11656820:
Jialiu Luo and co-authors review how a brake on immune cells, a molecule called Tim-3, goes wrong in sepsis and how blocking it might help. Sepsis is a runaway response to infection that kills millions each year. After an early storm of swelling, many patients sink into immune suppression. In that late stage, they catch new infections easily and die at higher rates.

Tim-3 sits on many immune cells and, when engaged by its partners, helps switch them off. In sepsis it is part of a wider pattern of exhausted defense cells and excess calming signals. The review gathers evidence on its partners and paths. It weighs drugs that target the pathway as a way to revive immunity.
pmc-11657120:
Mingyan Shi and seven co-authors compare gut microbes and muscle proteins in cattle with high and low marbling, the fat flecks that grade beef quality. Their study came out in 2024. Gut microbes shape how animals turn feed into body fat, so the team looked for links across the digestive tract and the meat itself.

High-marbling cattle carried more diverse gut microbes, with more of some groups and fewer of others than low-marbling animals. Their gut microbes leaned toward fat-making pathways, and their stomach fluid held more of the fatty acids that feed fat synthesis. Muscle proteins in the high group were richer in fat transport and metabolism roles. The authors conclude that gut differences supply more building material for marbling. The findings could inform feeding strategies for better beef.
pmc-11657220:
Emma Di Carlo and Carlo Sorrentino wrote this 2024 review of CRISPR tools for finding and treating cancer. CRISPR lets scientists cut or change DNA and RNA with great care. The best known system is Cas9, and newer ones are called Cas12 and Cas13.

The review explains how the tools can target genes that drive cancer and genes that help tumors hide from the immune system. It also covers tests that spot mutations, screens that find genes linked to drug resistance, and cell work that may lead to treatments matched to each tumor. Two test platforms, DETECTR and SHERLOCK, get close attention.
pmc-11657420:
Lingyan Wu and a large team survey how fully China’s family medicine teachers actually teach residents in clinics, in a 2024 national study. Clinic-based training is a core part of residency for general practitioners. Yet there is worry that supervising doctors, pressed by their own patient loads, lack the will or the skill to teach well at the bedside.

The cross-sectional survey asked preceptors across China how they run routine outpatient teaching and what they think of it. It then searched for factors tied to stronger engagement, such as training, workload, and rewards. Knowing what lifts or sinks teaching effort lets program leaders target fixes, from protected teaching time to faculty development, rather than exhorting everyone equally.
pmc-11659220:
Heping Xu and co-workers study a blood-based index and death risk in ICU patients with sepsis-related kidney injury, in a 2024 paper. The index combines a sugar-lipid measure with body mass, and it reflects insulin resistance. Its link to outcomes in this patient group was unclear.

Using a large ICU database, the team analyzed more than three thousand patients. Higher index values went with lower death rates at one, three, and six months. A curve analysis showed an L-shaped link, where risk fell as the index rose from low levels. A feature search ranked the index as an important predictor. Subgroup checks supported the finding.
pmc-11659720:
An introduction from 2024 opens a special issue of a food safety journal devoted to a European fellowship program. The program trains fellows in food risk assessment across Europe, and this issue collects the work from its seventh cycle. The introduction is signed on behalf of the program team by Victoria Villamar, whose name appears at the close.

The editor congratulates the new graduates and praises their professionalism and engagement during twelve months of training. Fellows deepened their knowledge of food risk assessment and contributed to their host areas. Thanks go to agency management and staff, member states, partner organizations, and the training consortium. The editor hopes graduates stay active as alumni in the community.
pmc-11661020:
Szymon Szemik, Maksymilian Gajda, and Małgorzata Kowalska track medical students' quality of life in a 2024 Polish study. Training loads press hard on students, above all in the first years. The POLLEK cohort follows students at a medical university in Katowice across graduation. Quality of life was scored with a short World Health Organization survey, taken at two time points.

Following the same students over time shows how well being shifts as training ends, not just how it looks in one snapshot. The team also weighed what drives the scores up or down. Such findings can steer schools toward support placed where the strain peaks. For future doctors, protecting their own health during training may shape how well they later care for others.
pmc-11662920:
Chris Lievens and co-authors report a 2024 study of comfort in a monthly soft contact lens made for astigmatism. The lens is worn for long days, from morning to midnight, over a full month. The team wanted hour-by-hour comfort data, not just one score at a clinic visit.

Forty-seven adults with mild symptoms wore the lenses and sent comfort scores by text through each day. Comfort held steady at each hour across the month, but it fell as each day wore on. Even so, few wearers called the lenses uncomfortable, even after sixteen hours, which points to steady, predictable comfort.
pmc-11664220:
A team including Fiona Bennin and Linda-Gail Bekker describes how young people helped shape Fast-PrEP, an HIV prevention service in Cape Town, South Africa. The service offers daily pills, a vaginal ring, and long-acting shots to people aged fifteen to twenty-nine. A youth group formed in twenty twenty and helped plan, run, and judge the service.

Group talks and staff talks in twenty twenty-three showed young members felt heard and proud when their ideas reached real campaigns. Good practice meant youth input at every stage, flexible meeting times, and safe, easy places to meet. Staff also gained from training youth members in health facts and confidence.
pmc-11665920:
A five-carbon ring molecule found in space may seed larger carbon structures, Yang and co-authors report in a 2024 study. The ring is a building block for curved carbon sheets and balls seen in deep space. How it forms from simple chains at low temperature was unknown.

The team crossed beams of two small carbon gases in the lab and tracked the products. A simple two-carbon radical hit a four-carbon chain and closed the ring in one facile path. Rate sums and models of a cold space cloud match the route well. The find explains how ring molecules arise in cold clouds, a step toward the large carbon forms that telescopes detect.
pmc-11666820:
Seaweed extracts are sold as antioxidants, but how they protect cells at the molecular level is often unclear. Andreas Goutas and co-authors studied an extract of the red seaweed Hypnea musciformis in human mesenchymal stem cells. Chemical analysis found amino acids, organic acids, sugar alcohols, fatty acids, and other compounds in the extract. Bench tests showed it could neutralize several kinds of free radicals and protect DNA from breakage.

In stem cells facing hydrogen peroxide, the extract lowered fat and protein oxidation, cut reactive oxygen levels, and limited DNA damage while raising glutathione. The protection ran through NRF2, a master switch that turned up six antioxidant proteins. The authors say the pathway evidence supports using the extract in foods and supplements.
pmc-11666920:
Munazzah Ejaz and five co-authors develop in 2024 dental filling materials made from ingredients sourced inside Pakistan. Standard composites rely on pricey imported parts, which pushes up the cost of tooth repair and puts it out of reach for many patients.

The team built new composites from local materials and tested their cost, strength, and lasting power. Their study also involved three hundred eighty-five patients, aged eighteen to sixty-five, who received fillings made from the new materials. A home-grown composite that holds up in real mouths could widen access to restorative dentistry across the country.
pmc-11667120:
Reham Afify and co-authors review in 2024 how antigen-showing immune cells shape brain decay diseases through display molecules on their surface. These cells bridge body defense and nerve health, and their signals can steer disease course. Most work covers two classic display classes, while rarer display types get less study.

The review sums recent findings on both classic and rare display molecules, with a focus on brain immune cells. Rare types that show fat-like or vitamin-linked targets to T cells may hold untapped roles. Gaps in that knowledge block new care ideas. The authors map where immune display meets nerve loss to guide future drug work.
pmc-11667620:
Nirosha Ramesh and seven co-authors review ways to clean dye from waste water in a 2024 review paper. Dyes from cloth mills harm water and pose risks to health. The review looks at a light based method that uses a common white powder to break dyes down.

Plain powder works poorly in sun light and loses power fast. Adding small bits of silver helps it catch more light and work for longer. The review covers how the mix is made, what speeds or slows the clean up, and what still blocks wide use.
pmc-11668420:
Tammineni Ruchita, Surada Chandrika, and Manchu Kalyani present a 2024 study that screens adults in an Indian city for their risk of type 2 diabetes. A simple score, built for Indian populations, can flag people at risk cheaply and early. It uses facts such as age, waist size, family history, and activity.

The team surveyed 145 adults aged twenty to sixty in the practice area of a medical college in Visakhapatnam. People who already knew they had diabetes were left out. Each person got a risk score, and the team sorted them into risk bands. They also looked at which risk factors were most common in the group.
pmc-11669120:
Attila Keresztes and co-authors connect how well older adults sleep with the size of memory-related brain structures, in a study published in 2024. The hippocampus and entorhinal cortex shrink faster after about age sixty, with consequences for everyday memory. Rather than asking people how they sleep, the team recorded brain waves at home over several nights in sixty-one volunteers, and scanned 112 of the 118 participants.

Objective sleep efficiency, the share of time in bed actually asleep, tracked with entorhinal cortex volume once age was accounted for. Self-reported sleep showed no such link. Age-related differences across hippocampal subfields also followed measured sleep efficiency. The findings argue that how aging brains fare may partly ride on measurable sleep quality.
pmc-11669320:
Xinghai Yue and co-authors ask whether eating yogurt is linked to slower aging, in this 2024 study. They used a large United States health survey from 2003 to 2006, covering more than four thousand adults. Aging was measured with a score based on blood and body markers that estimates how old a body seems, compared with its true age.

People who ate yogurt at least once a year showed a lower risk of fast aging than people who never ate it. The link followed a U shape, with moderate intake looking best. Yogurt eaters were also less likely to be overweight. The authors urge care, since survey links cannot prove cause.
pmc-11671520:
Bedsole and co-authors check whether a one-sided glue strip on fungal spores is shared across Colletotrichum species. This fungus group causes anthracnose disease on many crops worldwide. One maize species makes sickle-shaped spores that stick to leaves and then punch inside.

That species carries glue on only one side of each spore, matched with an actin array. The strip aids attachment and sprouting, and may also help spread. Some spores skip the first landing spot thanks to the uneven glue. The study found the one-sided glue across nine species checked. The trait looks widespread in the genus, not a lone quirk.
pmc-11672920:
Six researchers led by Jianhua Guo built a stronger form of elemene, a plant compound already used against tumors in China, and tested it on colorectal cancer. The base compound needs high doses and works weakly. Their new version carries added chemical groups meant to sharpen its punch.

In dishes, the new compound slowed growth and spread of two colon cancer cell lines. It raised harmful oxygen byproducts, cut the cells' energy making, and pushed them into programmed death. Gene and protein hunts named the switches it flips. In zebrafish carrying human tumors, growth shrank as well. The authors present it as a lead for kinder bowel cancer drugs.
pmc-11673020:
Jacobo Rodríguez-Sanz and co-authors review the body effects of percutaneous electrolysis, a needle therapy that passes current into tissue, in a 2024 paper. The method draws growing use in physical therapy, yet its cell-level effects needed a map. Seven studies passed the screen from three databases. Effects were sorted into swelling, cell death, and tissue rebuild groups.

In chronic tendon states, the method sparked a brief pro-swelling wave that settled by about day thirteen. Cell death marks rose in the first week, with signs of matrix teardown and rebuild. In acute injury states, it instead raised anti-swelling marks early. Growth signals for new vessels rose in both states. The authors call the profile controlled and short-lived.
pmc-11673220:
Chunjie Jiang and co-authors test whether berberine, a natural plant alkaloid, can shield diabetic skin from a kind of cell death called ferroptosis. Sugar damaged proteins, known as AGEs, harm skin cells and slow wound healing in diabetes. Whether they trigger this iron linked death, and whether berberine blocks it, was unknown.

In lab skin cells, the sugar products cut survival and raised damage markers, reactive oxygen, and iron, while two guard proteins fell. Berberine pretreatment reversed much of that harm. Knocking down the NRF2 gene erased most of the shield, which names its path. In diabetic mice, berberine also cut fat oxidation buildup in the skin.
pmc-11673420:
Yurun Li and co-authors test how well crash test dummy skin mimics human soft tissue, in a 2024 study. Dummies stand in for people in car crash tests, and their skin's give shapes the injury readings. Human tissue comes in layers with complex behavior, which makes a faithful fake hard to standardize.

The team pressed samples of real single- and multi-layer tissue and of dummy skin materials, slowly and at varied speeds. They fit math models for stretchy and time-dependent behavior to each sample. The comparison showed current dummy skin misses how real tissue stiffens with speed of loading. Better skin models would sharpen the injury numbers that car safety rules rely on.
pmc-11673520:
Yibin Zhang and co-authors review diabetes drugs for protecting cognition in a 2024 paper. Type 2 diabetes raises the risk of cognitive decline. A drug class aimed at the kidney shows gains beyond sugar control. Heart and kidney protection from it is already shown.

Cognitive protection is the newer claim under review. Mechanisms span metabolism, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Brain growth factors and a block on an enzyme also feature. Mild impairment, Alzheimer's, and vascular dementia all appear. Trial and meta-analysis results are mixed so far. Some show a clear gain, others none. Blood vessel effects may guard in a special way against vascular impairment. That subtype point gets a special stress. The authors compile mechanisms beside clinical evidence. Optimal drug choice and dose per patient remain open. Future trials must target cognition head-on. Doctors who prescribe should watch this space rather than act yet.
pmc-11674620:
Riccardo Forni and co-authors report a ten-year exercise case in a 2024 paper. Muscle loss with age, called sarcopenia, fills muscle with fat and frailty follows. One man began a full-body gym program done in bed at home at age seventy, and kept it up for a decade. The team measured what that persistence did to his muscles with detailed CT scans.

One analysis compared his leg scans from 2013 and 2023. Leg muscle volume grew over the decade, while density fell more slowly than expected, a sign of preserved quality. A second analysis compared his 2023 thigh scan with scans from 2,500 older adults in an Icelandic cohort. The case suggests long, steady home exercise can hold back age-related muscle decline.
pmc-11674720:
Connor Beck and co-authors test how magnetic tugs shape the firing of brain cells, in a 2024 paper. Tiny magnetic grains, pulled by a steady magnet, can press or pull on cells from afar with fine control. The team grew cortical nerve cells with coated grains, then applied forces from two to one hundred sixty piconewtons and watched with both electric and light recorders.

Gentle forces sped up firing for a spell, then firing eased after two minutes of steady pull. Stronger forces lifted activity for up to four hours before the cells fell silent. Calcium rushes into the cells played a part, but the team could also steer the reply without them by tweaking how the grains grip the cells. The work maps how force size writes the cell's answer.
pmc-11674820:
Kseniya Serebrennikova, Nadezhda Komova, Anatoly Zherdev, and Boris Dzantiev review sensors built on natural materials for catching pesticide residues in farming. Their 2024 review notes that unchecked pesticide use harms the environment and health. Standard lab analysis is costly, slow, and labor-heavy, which delays action when residue limits are breached.

The sensors use surface-enhanced Raman scattering, a light method that reads molecular fingerprints with high sensitivity and no destruction of the sample. The review covers substrates grown from natural micro and nano structures, flexible films from biopolymers, and treated surfaces tuned for farm use. It also discusses herbicide effects on photosynthesis and detection prospects. The focus falls on substrates drawn from nature, not factories.
pmc-11674920:
Anna Planas-Ballvé and co-authors report long-term, real-world experience with safinamide, an add-on drug for Parkinson's disease, at one movement disorders unit. Trials had shown the drug helps, but everyday practice over years tells more. The team reviewed 180 patients treated between 2016 and 2022.

After a median follow-up of forty months, only eight percent had stopped the drug, suggesting it is well tolerated. Among those who stayed on it, motor scores held steady. The daily dose of levodopa, the main Parkinson's drug, rose over the years, as expected as the disease advances. Doses of a drug class, dopamine agonists, did not climb. In patients who never needed agonists, motor scores were stable. The authors conclude that safinamide keeps working and stays tolerable in routine care over the long term. They present the study as a real-world check that should accompany trial evidence.
pmc-11675020:
Ki-Beom Kim, Sang-Ho Kim, and Seung-Min Yoo review a class of tiny sensors in a 2024 paper. The sensors pair aptamers, short strands that grab a chosen target, with metal nanoclusters, specks of metal just a few atoms wide. The clusters glow and react in ways that shift with their size and coating, which makes them handy for tests.

The review explains how adding an aptamer changes the light a cluster gives off, and how that shift can flag a target. It then walks through fresh uses in illness checks and other lab tasks, with case studies. The authors close with the strong points, weak points, and open problems for these paired sensors.
pmc-11675220:
Francesco Dondi and co-authors present a systematic review from two thousand twenty-four on a PET imaging tracer for lymphomas. PET scans use radioactive tracers to reveal disease, and the standard sugar tracer is not the only option. A tracer based on methionine, an amino acid, has shown promise for judging these blood cancers.

The team searched three major databases for studies of this tracer in lymphoma care. Eighteen studies met their criteria. Uses included judging disease extent, checking response to therapy, forecasting outcome, and telling lymphoma apart from other conditions. Results across the body and in the central nervous system were broadly like those of the standard tracer. The authors see a real, if still uneven, evidence base for the method.
pmc-11675720:
Stewart and coauthors study how school closures shaped bullying in Ontario youth. Bullying is a large concern for school-age children. The pandemic closed schools in waves and moved class online. The team asks how those shifts changed bullying reports.

They used records for 22,012 children aged 4 to 18. All were referred to mental health services in Ontario. Data ran from early 2017 to early 2022. Spans were split into pre-pandemic, remote class, and in-person class. Home, personal, and mental health facts were also logged. The team weighed which facts tracked with bullying in each span.
pmc-11675820:
Shameran Slewa-Younan and co-authors explore mental health stigma through a gender lens in two migrant communities in a 2024 study. Arabic- and Swahili-speaking Australians face higher mental illness risk yet use services at low rates. Stigma is a prime suspect, and it may not weigh on men and women alike.

Five focus groups and 18 interviews were held online in Sydney. Three themes stood out: fear that illness would be exposed to the community, different ways men and women confront that shame, and the calculations behind choosing a source of help. A 'what matters most' reading explained the gender split. The authors urge services to design outreach with those values in mind.
pmc-11675920:
Concrete crews hurt the same body parts in the same tasks again and again, and a risk map could target protection better. Jiseon Lim and co-authors built that map in a 2024 study. Work was split into ten tasks across rebar work, formwork, and concrete placement. Six body parts, from head to ankle, were scored for each task. Over twenty-two hundred accident reports fed the chance scores, and expert surveys set the severity scores.

Wrist and hand injuries during rebar cutting and shaping topped the risk list. Scores were placed on one scale so tasks could be compared fairly. The map points safety spending at the worst task-body pairs first. The authors offer the frame for wider site use.
pmc-11676120:
Eun Kyung Choi, Jongyoon Baek, and Kyu Jin Chung compare two pain drugs in a 2024 surgery study. Patients having broken noses reset received one of two drugs by drip during the operation: lidocaine or magnesium. The team then asked how well each group felt the next day, using a forty-item recovery survey.

Seventy-four patients took part. Overall recovery scores a day after surgery were about the same in both groups. Pain half an hour after surgery was lower with lidocaine, and that group needed less extra pain relief. At later checks, pain levels matched. Rates of nausea, vomiting, and sleepiness also showed no clear gap. The authors read the two drugs as broadly even, with an early edge for lidocaine.
pmc-11676220:
Stripe rust, caused by the fungus Puccinia striiformis in its wheat form, is a major threat to wheat in Xinjiang, China. Hong Yang and co-authors compare the rust population between 2021 and 2022 to track changes in virulence and race mix. They test hundreds of isolates from spring and winter wheat against wheat lines carrying known resistance genes.

Virulence shifted markedly in one year. Some attack traits grew more common while others fell sharply, and race diversity rose, with 90 races among 354 isolates in 2022. One race, CYR34, became prevalent, while another group vanished. Two resistance genes still held against all local races. The authors warn that fast race turnover demands steady monitoring and fresh resistant varieties.
pmc-11676420:
Van Thi Nguyen and co-authors published a plant protection study in twenty twenty-four on a marine bacterium that fights crop diseases. The lactic acid bacterium Pediococcus strain M21F004 came from the gut of a starry flounder and beat fifty other marine isolates for antimicrobial power. Chemical analysis fingered oleic acid as a key weapon it produces.

In dishes, the broth and its oleic acid suppressed fungi and bacteria attacking cucumbers, turfgrass, tomatoes, and cabbage. Greenhouse tests confirmed real protection, strongest against tomato bacterial wilt. The strain also lowered disease severity in the other crops. The authors present this fish-gut microbe as a promising biological alternative to chemical sprays.
pmc-11677020:
David Vasquez and co-authors show that pairing two light-based probes reads colon tumors better than either probe alone. Their study appeared in 2024. Colonoscopy finds colon cancer but often takes biopsies that prove needless. The team built fiber probes for use inside the body: one reads Raman scattering, a chemical fingerprint, and one images tissue layers by reflected light. In removed tissue samples, each method first classified cancer versus healthy tissue on its own.

Merging the two verdicts with a Bayes rule lifted the discrimination score to 0.93, up from 0.77 for the chemical probe alone. The imaging probe alone also trailed the pair. The authors say combined probes could one day guide doctors during the exam itself, cutting needless biopsies while missing fewer cancers.
pmc-11677720:
Paige Snider and co-authors show that losing one enzyme's activity is enough to cause male infertility in mice, in a 2024 study. The enzyme, tafazzin, works in mitochondria, and its loss causes Barth syndrome in people, a rare disorder of heart and muscle.

The team studied mice carrying a patient-like mutation that leaves the protein in place but inactive. The males' testes stayed small and made no sperm. Sperm formation stalled before the cell division that halves the chromosome count. Mitochondria in the testes looked abnormal, and cell death ran high. Key DNA-damage markers were missing. The work pins fertility on the enzyme's action itself, not just its presence.
pmc-11677920:
Xiaoqin Tang and co-authors design new collecting chemicals for zinc ore processing, using theory to skip a copper step. Their 2024 paper concerns sphalerite flotation, where ore is floated off with the help of chemicals that cling to the mineral. The standard route activates the surface with copper before collection.

Guided by coordination chemistry, the team designed dozens of sulfur-bearing compounds and screened them with quantum simulations. A dozen candidates emerged, and one structure with two sulfur grip points showed the strongest reactivity. A related real compound with the same grip pattern also performed well in simulations. The strong grip traces to overlap between zinc and sulfur electron clouds. A direct collector could simplify plants and cut copper use.
pmc-11678020:
Fangyi Ju and co-authors build a genetic transformation system for a root-rot fungus so its glowing-tagged strains can be watched inside plants. Fusarium acuminatum rots the roots of many farm and forestry plants and has lately hit Chinese pink flowers hard. To study how it infects, researchers need to insert genes into the fungus reliably.

The team used protoplasts, cells stripped of their walls, to carry in a gene for green fluorescent protein. The method proved easy, cheap, and efficient at producing high-quality protoplasts from their study strain. Microscope checks showed the glow switched on inside the transformed fungus, and gene tests confirmed the insert. The system now gives researchers a platform for testing what individual fungal genes do during infection.
pmc-11678120:
A sea alga makes a prized orange dye and rich fats at once, and the food it gets can tilt how much of each it makes. Ning Zhang and co-authors vary one food, phosphorus, in a 2024 study of the alga. They grow it at set phosphorus grades and read dye, fats, and cell growth.

Cell count and dye marks peaked at a mid grade of the food. Dry weight and fat marks, both plain and rich kinds, peaked one grade up. The top fat grade also gave the most of one prized fat. Since dye and fat peak at unlike grades, growers can pick the grade that fits the good they want most. The work guides joint runs of both goods.
pmc-11678420:
Stefania Petrini and a team of co-authors published a 2024 cell study on two proteins inside the nuclei of cells from patients with laminopathies. These genetic disorders stem from faults in the nuclear lamina, the mesh that lines the nucleus and senses mechanical force. The team focused on lamin A/C and Src, a signaling enzyme known to modify lamina proteins.

Using advanced microscopy, including a super resolution method and lifetime imaging, they compared skin cells from two patients with cells from healthy donors. The two proteins were found together far more in patient cells, and sat closer than in healthy cells. The tight pairing suggests Src joins the altered lamina in driving disease features. Imaging based evidence of this kind can flag new drug targets.
pmc-11678520:
Di Gong, Tingting Yan, and their co-authors studied moldy smells made by a fungus that rots stored fruit. Their 2024 study concerns Penicillium expansum, which spoils apples and makes a toxin called patulin. The fungus uses oxygen using enzymes to make scent compounds that act as signals inside the fungus itself.

The team removed two of those enzyme genes, one at a time. Both mutant strains grew slowly, formed damaged spores and threads, and turned down genes that guide spore growth. The scent compounds nearly vanished in one mutant. Both mutants also harmed apples less and made less patulin, in dishes and in fruit. Signal pathways inside the cells ran lower as well. The work links scent making to the fungus's power to cause rot.
pmc-11678720:
Jangho Lee and colleagues review plant and microbe compounds that switch on a cell sensor tied to eczema care, in a twenty twenty-four article. The condition, atopic dermatitis, is a long-term itchy skin disease with immune faults and a weak skin barrier. The sensor, called AhR, helps tune immune responses and keep the barrier sound. When its pathway fails, the disease worsens.

Compounds such as curcumin, resveratrol, and quercetin can switch the sensor on and calm swelling. They tend to carry fewer side effects than standard drugs, which may help patients stick with care. The authors present these natural agents as partners to standard care that also repair the barrier.
pmc-11679120:
Daniel Pierce and a team of co-authors test a new electrical method for detecting DNA in water in a 2024 paper. The method uses glowing molecules parked near a film of metal nanoparticles. When the glowing molecule is excited, it couples with the film, brightening its glow and, under the right conditions, generating a small electric current tied to the molecule's traits.

The team checked whether this current based sensing, already used for ions, could measure DNA using probes that switch on in its presence. They varied DNA amount, probe amount, and probe type to map how the signal develops. The study lays groundwork for a sensor that reads DNA concentration from current rather than light alone.
pmc-11679220:
Maria Iliadi, Maria Varveri, and Dimitrios Tsitsigiannis wrote a study in 2024 on a toxic mould in Greek grapes. The mould Aspergillus carbonarius makes ochratoxin A, a strong cause of cancer that ends up in wine. Ways to hold it back with sprays and with live agents had not been tried for years at a stretch.

Six spray goods and eleven live goods were tried for four years on two white grape types, both on their own and in mixed plans. Some live mixes worked well on sour rot and on toxin growth. Mixed plans stopped the toxin in full in the best cases. Most mould strains could still be killed by the pure spray parts. Scores changed from year to year, which the team puts down to how live plans shift. They urge joint plans.
pmc-11679320:
Erica Phillips and co-authors compared ways to measure adherence in a child feeding trial in Tanzania in a 2024 paper. The trial gave low-aflatoxin porridge flours and promoted feeding practices across fifty-two health facility clusters. How well families followed the plan could shape the trial's results.

Caregiver surveys at several points were compared with detailed day-long dietary recalls in a smaller cohort. Reported use of blended flours was high by both methods, between about three quarters and nearly all families. Results also agreed on breastfeeding, feeding frequency, and diet diversity. Only the amount of porridge fed differed by method, higher in recalls. Either method can serve, they conclude.
pmc-11679420:
Perna and co-authors tested, in a 2024 field study, whether tractor-mounted sensors can see olive canopies change after pruning. Ten trees in a Tuscan grove were scanned before and after cutting, with a multispectral sensor and a two-dimensional laser scanner riding the vehicle.

The light-based sensor barely noticed the pruning: leaf color signals stayed flat despite real losses of wood and leaf. The laser, by contrast, rebuilt each canopy's volume, height, and width from its point cloud, and those measures could be checked against hand measures and the weight of cut branches. Laser scanning thus gives growers an objective way to log pruning work and tree shape. Paired sensors, the study suggests, are not equal witnesses.
pmc-11679720:
Volf, Vučemilović, and Dobrović propose a data-driven model for managing pollution threats to ecosystems and human health, in this 2024 review. The human body itself can signal contamination in the environment. Linking specific pollutants to specific disorders, though, can take decades of study.

Their model joins monitoring data on contamination with medical data on failing body functions, across places and times. Artificial intelligence tools handle the scale and support strategy choices. The paper walks through the human health case in detail. The same design, the authors note, extends to plants and animals. They present it as a way to speed up both protection and cleanup decisions.
pmc-11679820:
Duncan Kibet and co-authors build a fall detection model for older people, based on how fast key body points move. Falls can cause grave harm when help comes late, so care homes and home monitors need fast, sure alerts. Their 2024 model watches video and tracks body points with a common pose tool.

Speed changes at those points, read in real time, signal a likely fall. A transformer model, good at spotting subtle shifts, reads the pattern. It reached accuracy above ninety-seven percent, with far fewer false alarms than older methods. The authors pitch the system for elder care wards and home use, where a quick alert can change the outcome of a fall.
pmc-11680320:
Wojciech Miazga and co-authors compared how European Union countries run national vaccination programs against human papillomavirus, in a 2024 study. The virus causes cervical cancer and other diseases, so the shots are a front line of prevention. Rules for access, vaccine choice, and buying differ by country. The team reviewed official government and health sites for all twenty-seven member states. They also searched a public tender database for the terms used to buy vaccines.

All twenty-seven states fund the shots in public money. All but one offer them free to both girls and boys. In most states, the broadest vaccine is the only free option. Two states give a single dose of that vaccine as their scheme. The authors map where schemes converge and where they split. The map is meant to help late or low-coverage states copy the parts that work elsewhere.
pmc-11680420:
Ibrahim Khalil and nine co-authors track chicken disease and antibiotic use in Bangladesh through a web-based reporting system, in a study from 2024. Sonali chickens are widely farmed there, but disease checks and drug control are weak. Vets logged 1,690 cases from 2020 to 2021 in one district known for dense Sonali farming, based on signs and post-mortem findings.

Growing birds and small flocks were hit most often, and summer brought the most cases. Newcastle disease was the top diagnosis. One antibiotic, tylvalosin, made up nearly four in ten prescriptions. The authors say a central web system could anchor national poultry disease surveillance.
pmc-11682320:
Taishiro Kamasaki and nine co-authors test whether long sitting tracks with weaker physical function in older adults living at home. Their 2024 study uses Japan's Kihon Checklist, a national frailty screen, and a standard activity questionnaire for sitting time. Cutting sitting may be an easier public health sell than pushing exercise targets.

The final group held 79 adults, averaging 75 years, drawn from a preventive care project. After adjustments for grip strength, walking speed, muscle mass, pain, and more, longer sitting still tied to poorer scores on the checklist's physical function part. The link survived every control the team applied. The authors say a simple sitting question can flag elders whose function needs support. Trials that swap sitting for light movement come next.
pmc-11683320:
Yoon Hyung Kang and co-workers introduce a new sphincter-preserving operation for anal fistula, in a 2024 paper. Many preserving techniques exist, but none has proven clearly best. Their method ties off the anal duct and closes the muscle, aiming to heal the tract without harming continence.

Records covered more than five hundred patients treated over fourteen years at one Korean hospital. Many had complex fistulas above the sphincter, and over a quarter had prior fistula surgery. Recurrence occurred in about six percent, delayed healing in about seventeen percent, and incontinence in about two percent. The authors judge the method safe and feasible, above all where sphincter preservation matters.
pmc-11683620:
Hanfi and co-authors published a 2024 review of experiments making hydrogen inside heavy oil reservoirs. The gas promises cleaner energy than natural gas, and oil fields could become sources of it if burning part of the oil underground frees it up. The review sorts the lab literature into catalytic and non-catalytic routes. Reservoir clay and formation water themselves can act as catalysts and boost output.

The authors weigh how added catalysts compare with the rock's own materials. They also examine formation damage from the underground burn, and how that damage feeds back on gas output. The review aims to guide a young field: which reservoir conditions and additives actually raise yields. It frames in-situ production as a low-carbon option worth testing at scale.
pmc-11685020:
Daniel Huebner and co-authors test ultraviolet light on cannabis plants in a 2024 study. Growers hope light can raise valued plant compounds without harming yield. The team varied both the mix of ultraviolet bands and the strength of the light.

Three light mixes were tried at up to five strengths, and flower yield and chemistry were measured. No mix changed the cannabinoid profile. One mild mix did lift three scent compounds, linalool, limonene, and myrcene, by roughly a quarter over controls. Growth and form effects are also reported. Growers get a sober guide: light tuning helps scent, not strength, in this setup.
pmc-11685120:
Victorita Sorodoc and co-authors review how to give blood thinning therapy to people with morbid obesity who face venous thromboembolism, clots in the veins. Published in 2024, the review is, to the authors' knowledge, the first to cover both preventive and treatment doses for patients with very high body mass or weight. Extreme weight can change how these drugs act.

The review covers all drug classes used for this purpose, from vitamin K antagonists and heparins to direct oral agents, weighing proof of benefit and harm for each. It also treats special groups, such as patients with cancer, kidney trouble, or weight loss surgery. The authors find the proof base thin and urge tailored dosing with close monitoring.
pmc-11685920:
Bidkar and five co-authors compare two nose paths for a flexible scope that inspects the throat, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The scope exam is a routine office test for airway complaints. Doctors can steer the scope under one nose ridge or along another. The team asked which path gives smoother passage and less harm.

One hundred eleven patients were split at random into two groups. First-try smooth passage rates were much the same in both groups. One path caused less surface bruising, while the other bled a bit more often. Pain spiked most when the exam had to be repeated. The authors say either path works for a first pass. Gentle technique matters more than path choice.
pmc-11686220:
Johanne Brunet and John Kelly wrote a 2024 editorial that opens a set of six papers on plant mating systems and inbreeding harm. When plants mate with close kin, their offspring tend to be weaker, a cost that shapes how mating habits evolve. Self-mating gives a gene-spread edge, yet it also raises that cost.

The papers in the set bring new theory and field work on how the cost forms and how it steers mating change. One review finds weak proof for the idea that inbred lines purge their harmful genes over time. The editors also note that no crop papers made the cut for the set.
pmc-11686520:
Wei-Lin Yang and colleagues measure the burden of low back pain in China and chart how Chinese scholarship has responded to it. Low back pain is a global problem, and China's experience, including its traditional therapies, may offer insights. The burden analysis uses the Global Burden of Disease twenty twenty-one data, examining incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years.

Prevalence rose from roughly seventy million people in nineteen ninety to about one hundred three million in twenty twenty-one. New cases and disability burden also grew, though China's increase in disability rates was slower than the world average. A bibliometric analysis of the same period shows Chinese publications on low back pain rising steadily. Domestic collaboration among scholars increased significantly, while international and solo work declined, with a recent dip in domestic collaboration.
pmc-11688020:
Chengjia Li and Huijun Chen use Mendelian randomization to test whether COVID-19 causes cardiovascular disease in a 2024 study. The method uses genetic variants as natural instruments to infer cause. Past common pneumonias serve as a comparison, to see whether any effect is specific to COVID-19.

Genome wide data covered COVID-19, bacterial and viral pneumonia, and six heart conditions. Sensitivity checks found no pleiotropy problems. Neither common pneumonia type contributed to the heart conditions. COVID-19, in contrast, raised risk for stable and unstable angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but not for two other conditions studied.
pmc-11688320:
Dan Qin, Xiaobo Wang, Jun Pu, and Houxiang Hu present a 2024 review on tiny parcels that heart cells use to talk to each other. These parcels, extracellular vesicles, carry proteins and small RNA messages between cells. After a heart attack, they can spread harm or help repair, depending on which cells sent them.

The review surveys vesicles from heart muscle cells, vessel lining cells, immune cells, and several stem-like cell types, and explains how their cargo reports the state of the parent cell. Vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells stand out for aiding heart regeneration in experiments. The authors argue these parcels could become both warning markers for heart injury and treatments in their own right after infarction.
pmc-11688520:
Taku Kikuchi and four co-authors report the first grave brain-toxic case tied to elranatamab, a drug for hard-to-treat myeloma. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-four. In the key trial of the drug, just mild forms of this brain harm were seen. Risk marks for the grave form were not yet known.

Their patient showed the most grave grade of the harm, with just mild body-wide fever signs at the same time. The patient had a past brain bleed with no lasting loss, and brain scans showed no new flaw. High-dose steroids were needed to curb the harm. The team urges close watch of nerve signs for all who get the drug.
pmc-11688920:
Jonathan Suen and seven co-authors ask whether comfort with smartphones changes how much good a hearing aid does, in this 2024 analysis. Hearing loss among older Americans is set to grow by seventy percent by 2060, yet few who need amplification get it. A community trial called HEARS delivers hearing care with affordable over-the-counter devices to low-income older adults.

Re-examining that trial's 151 participants, the team split them by prior technology use: those already at home with smartphones and computers, and those who were not. The tech-connected group gained far more, cutting their hearing-related communication difficulty by an extra fourteen points against controls. The less connected participants gained less. The finding cuts two ways: modern hearing care rides on digital confidence, so trials and clinics that ignore it risk widening the very gaps they aim to close.
pmc-11689320:
Emma Gay and seven co-authors profile fatigue in older adults in a 2024 paper. They combine two measures: how fatigued people feel and how much their performance actually drops. Using a large aging study sample, they grouped people by both scores and compared body traits across groups. Muscle energy was measured by scanner and biopsy, fitness by treadmill testing, and activity by wrist trackers.

People low on both fatigue measures were younger, more active, and faster walkers than those high on both. Their muscle energy, lung fitness, and walking economy were all clearly better. The authors say the combined grouping exposes targets for healthy-aging interventions.
pmc-11689420:
Eric Klopack and Eileen Crimmins use biomarkers to study how aging at the cell level and across body systems links to death risk, in a 2024 conference abstract. Aging seems to be a joined decline across many systems, but how general and system-specific aging interact is unclear. Social exposures may also speed decline in some systems more than others.

They draw on a national study of about 4,000 United States adults over age fifty-five. Machine learning models built risk scores from biomarker sets for systems such as the immune and heart systems, plus cell aging clocks. Those scores were tied to death, multiple illness, and limits on daily function. The work aims to separate kinds of aging.
pmc-11689520:
Angela Perone and Brian Lindberg host, in twenty twenty-four, a policy talk on AI in aging. AI can scan vast data to find patterns in how people age. Machine learning may also flag who will get age-linked disease, and when to act. These gains could reshape study, teaching, and care for older adults. Yet they raise ethical issues that now draw policy focus, the hosts note.

The session is a joint talk across fields. Panelists come from all six sections of a national aging society. Two advisory panels, on minority issues and on arts and culture, also take part. The aim is to weigh gains against risks in plain policy terms.
pmc-11689620:
Lauren Chrzanowski, Elisabeth McLean, and Jonathan Singer study in 2024 whether family caregivers feel pain that mirrors the pain of a loved one who is dying. Such empathetic pain had not been studied in aging groups. Their sample held one hundred family members of people with advanced cancer and thirty eight of people with dementia, with scales for grief before death and for caregiver burden.

Grief before death clearly predicted empathetic pain, accounting for about a fifth of the variation. Burden also predicted it, though more weakly. Care recipient age and diagnosis were held fixed in the tests. Readers who support caregivers get evidence that grief itself, not just workload, can show up as physical pain.
pmc-11689720:
Alex Bishop, Tonya Finchum, and Melinda Heinz study oral stories from very old people of Indigenous descent. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses the Oklahoma 100 Year Life Project. Sixteen people who had lived to one hundred took part. The team read their life stories for themes that show cultural roots and identity.

Four themes stood out. One was passed-down trauma, tied to forced moves, slavery, and race. A second was mutual aid and sharing. A third covered play and sport in youth. A fourth was love of learning across a whole life. Quotes from the elders ground each theme. The study shows how story can rebuild a sense of who one is.
pmc-11689920:
Shinae Choi, a solo author, studies wealth gaps in later life in a 2024 paper. The study asks how far gaps by race, sex, and age persist among older adults in the United States. Wealth is split into housing wealth and other, liquid wealth, with income counted as well.

Data came from a 2018 national retirement study, with 4,472 older adults in the part used here. Math models with interaction terms tested whether a sense of meaning and purpose in life softens the gaps. Health and background traits were held steady in the models. Gaps across race, sex, and age groups were found to persist in old age.
pmc-11690020:
Soomi Lee, Christopher Kaufmann, and Daniel Buysse mark ten years of the sleep health idea in a symposium summary, from 2024. In 2014, Buysse argued that sleep health means more than the lack of a sleep disorder. Health rests on several sides of sleep at once, not just hours slept. Four talks in the session take stock of the shift.

One talk weighs the ways sleep health can be measured, with their gains and flaws. Another links a multi-part sleep score to heart and brain aging in two adult groups. A third shares population data from the United States and Brazil, with gaps by sex and race. The last ties sleep health to decline in thinking and dementia. The session closes with a call to carry the frame into new studies.
pmc-11690220:
Xiayu Chen and Wan Wen survey research on chatbots that support older adults' mental health, in a 2024 scoping review. Conversational agents now offer psychoeducation, symptom checks, and self-help coaching at scale. Modern language models make them warmer and more personal — yet most were designed for younger users.

Older adults bring different eyesight, hearing, habits, and trust, and studies focused on them are scarce. The review maps what exists: which tools were tried, for which problems, and with what designs and results. Gaps in the map show where tailored features — larger text, simpler flows, carer links — are missing. The overview gives builders and clinicians a starting grid for age-fit mental health chatbots.
pmc-11690320:
Jason Flatt and four colleagues synthesize studies of dementia caregiving in sexual and gender minority families, in a 2024 paper. Such caregivers often look after chosen family, not just blood relatives, and research has rarely separated the two.

Across the team's studies, between a tenth and a fifth of minority caregivers tended chosen family members with dementia. Over half did not live with the person they helped. Compared with other caregivers, more of them cared for a grandparent. Chosen-family caregivers gave fewer years and hours of care, yet their physical and mental health looked no different from blood-family caregivers. The authors flag divergent support needs as the next research and policy question.
pmc-11690420:
Lauren Moo, Elizabeth Chamberlin, Victoria Ngo, and Steven Shirk surveyed family caregivers of older veterans across the United States about what shapes their quality of life. Caregiving strains body and mind, and knowing which burdens matter most helps target support. Five hundred eleven informal caregivers answered the national web survey.

The more the veteran depended on the caregiver for daily tasks, the poorer the caregiver's quality of life, and living in the same home also weighed it down. Caring for an extra person, surprisingly, did not. Caregivers who still made time for their own medical care and social lives fared better. Protecting the caregiver's own health visits may be a lever services can pull.
pmc-11690520:
Caring for older adults takes a team, yet students in the health professions rarely train as one. Katherine Bennett and co-authors plug students into Project ECHO-Geriatrics, a video-based learning community built for practising clinicians. Their 2024 paper reports the first two years of the programme at the University of Washington.

Forty-four students from nine programmes — nursing, medicine, pharmacy, physical therapy, social work, dentistry, and more — joined at least three ECHO sessions with debriefs. Every one of them called the programme meaningful and worth the time. Scores rose on all measures, most sharply for confidence in age-friendly care, which nearly doubled. More students also said they might aim their careers at geriatrics. The authors conclude that an existing clinician network can cheaply widen into student training.
pmc-11690720:
Aneeka Ratnayake and seven co-authors study exercise among older adults in rural Uganda in a 2024 paper. Benefits of activity are well proven in rich countries, but little is known for older rural Africans living with HIV. The team followed two similar groups, one with HIV and one without, over yearly visits.

Almost all participants met world activity guidelines at the start. Still, those who were older, living with HIV, frail, or carrying other illnesses moved less. People with higher quality of life moved more. Meeting the guidelines went with lower odds of frailty and other illness. The authors say frail and ill elders may be missing the gains activity offers.
pmc-11690820:
Amber Miller-Winder and co-authors sorted older adults into planning styles for future Alzheimer's care, in a 2024 study. Many elders who will need help at home are unprepared for it. The team followed two hundred and ninety-three people in a long-term study of care planning, surveying them every six months on thinking, social life, function, and support preferences.

Four styles emerged. Deniers overlook the chance of the disease and plan least, especially when their thinking still tests normal.
