Do-gooders plan to spare their families, often finishing legal directives. Defeaters want to plan but are blocked by outside limits, with low health confidence as a marker. Dumpers leave the planning to family, leaning on strong social support. The authors say naming the style early could help clinicians prompt the right kind of help.
pmc-11690920:
Lena Thompson, Steffi Kim, and Jordan Lewis report a 2024 study on resilience among Alaska Native Elders who age in their home villages. Elders face hard limits on care and travel, yet many choose to stay, drawing joy and connection from village life. As wisdom keepers, they guide families and communities through hard times.

The team interviewed 72 Elders from 11 communities in Southeast and Interior Alaska. Elders told of lifelong trials, from racism to inherited trauma and swift change between generations. They met those trials with teachings, gathering, hunting, and a native way of life. Elders also felt a duty to pass knowledge to the young, sparing them like hardship. Eldership, the authors argue, binds youth, tribes, and towns in mutual gain.
pmc-11691020:
Oleg Zaslavsky and four co-authors pilot an online aid for family carers in a 2024 study. Carers of people with Lewy body dementia face more stress and deeper low mood than carers in other dementia kinds. Their aid, called VOCALE LBD, runs on the web with no set meeting times, over eight weeks.

Thirty-nine family carers took part in the pilot. The program mixed peer chat in text, staff-led talks, lessons, and drills in solving care problems, all shaped for this dementia kind. The team tracked mood, burden, stress, and backing before and after. Readers learn whether the aid eased strain.
pmc-11691120:
Ying-Ling Jao, Julian Wang, Shevvaa Beiglary, and Yo-Jen Liao published a study in 2024 on measuring lighting with a wearable sensor in nursing home residents with dementia. Light exposure can shape sleep and mood in dementia, but it varies widely across places and times of day. A sensor worn on the body can track the light one person actually receives.

The team clipped a small, lightweight sensor to the collar or shoulder of twenty-seven residents. It recorded light every fifteen seconds, all day, every other week for thirteen weeks. Reminder signs, a monitoring station on site, and twice-weekly checks kept the plan on track. Even so, fifty-two sensors were lost or damaged, and some data went missing each day. The detailed data stream was still sufficient to work with. The authors conclude that the method works for daytime light, while night wear needs rethinking.
pmc-11691220:
Anthony Molina spoke in 2024 on marks of aging in the blood and body that can guide care for older adults. Teams world-wide hunt for firm, countable signs of how fast a person ages. Such signs can sort a person's true body age from the years on their birth record. They may also flag who faces the highest risk of age-linked ills.

Molina summed up the most sound marks so far and how trials now use them. Changeable marks can show in weeks whether a health plan helps the body age more slowly, a span that would take decades to see in plain terms. He also traced joint world work to test and compare marks across labs. The talk casts the marks as tools for care tuned to each older adult.
pmc-11691420:
Catherine Mann, Norine Masella, and Suzanne Sullivan published a 2024 study of how palliative care teams guide patients into hospice care in the community. Palliative care supports people with serious, progressive illness, and hospice takes over when the goals of care shift to comfort. Little research describes how teams manage this transition outside hospitals.

Using a grounded theory approach, the researchers explored the processes teams use with patients and caregivers in home care settings. They collected data on how conversations, timing, and coordination unfold in practice. Their aim is earlier acceptance of and admission to hospice, so families get its support for longer. The findings describe patient-centered transition work step by step.
pmc-11691620:
Care hours and the mind of the person cared for are linked in a 2024 study by Valerie Luskey and co-authors. Care strain can harm both the giver and the receiver of care. The team used a large United States survey of older adults from 2014. Just over seven hundred people who gave care facts and took a memory test were kept in the study.

More care hours tied to more hopelessness in the receiver, and that in turn tied to worse short-term memory. More hours also cut the receiver's sense of control, though that path did not reach memory. Care hours cut memory scores on a direct path too. Backing carers may guard memory.
pmc-11691820:
Charity Lewis and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on caregiving for older adults who live with both dementia and hearing loss. The two conditions often occur together, and hearing loss leads to communication problems. Its impact on such caregiving, however, had not been studied.

The researchers linked two national surveys from 2022. They covered 1,445 caregivers assisting 942 older adults. Close to nine in ten care recipients with dementia also had hearing loss. Three in ten of them assisted a person with both conditions. For those caring for people with dementia, worse hearing in the older adult was linked to many more hours of care each month. No firm association appeared with how hard they found the work physically, emotionally, or financially. The findings point to hearing as a major unmet need in this population.
pmc-11692120:
Carlotta Grünjes and co-authors study couples' daily reports in a 2024 paper on older adults. Time spent with a partner tends to lift daily wellbeing, but partners may not agree on how much time they shared. The team asked whether those gaps in reporting matter for mood.

End-of-day diaries came from one hundred thirty-six older Canadian adults and a close partner of each. Early results confirm that longer shared time tracks higher wellbeing. Reports of shared time did differ between partners. The study tests whether painting a rosier picture of shared time lifts one's own mood, and whether partners who judge time alike also feel alike. The work treats small daily mismatches as a window on relationship health.
pmc-11692220:
Peter Sun, Nancy Morrow-Howell, Mary Click, and Kendra Minch measure health gains for older adults who tutor children in a 2024 study. The pandemic shrank volunteering, raising the question of whether its health links still hold. Tutors aged 51 and over in the Oasis program were surveyed before and after two years of service.

Three matching methods paired them with non volunteers from a national retirement study, for a merged sample of 518. By every method, tutors showed lower depression and fewer functional limits than the comparison group. One method also gave tutors better self rated health. The results back tutoring as health promotion after the pandemic.
pmc-11692420:
Yanjun Dong, Kun Wang, and Victoria Rizzo measure racial gaps in health care use among older Americans in a 2024 study. Little was known about how race combines with gender, income, and education to shape use. The team analyzed six waves of a national retirement study covering over twenty six thousand people from 2010 to 2020.

Older adults of color consistently used fewer services than others across hospital stays, prescriptions, outpatient surgery, home health, doctor visits, and dental care. Low income adults of color were especially unlikely to get prescription drugs, though more likely to use home health and physician services. Women of color used nursing homes less. The authors call for policies that cut money barriers and build culturally competent care.
pmc-11692620:
Hyebeen Sim, Jinhee Shin, and Kennedy Diema Konlan review in 2024 digital health tools to reduce burden for older adults with cancer during chemotherapy. Such tools may help patients manage symptoms at home. Their benefits and parts were not well defined for this group before this review.

Following standard guidelines, they screened more than five thousand articles and kept thirteen. Tools included mobile apps, remote monitoring, and games on phones, tablets, and watches. Benefits covered symptom control, activity, nutrition, and quality of life. Hospital visits and treatment side effects also fell in the intervention groups, the review reports.
pmc-11692720:
Idiatou Diallo and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on depressive symptoms, sleep disturbance, and quality of life in adults with chronic conditions. The participants had diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease. These problems influence one another, yet how they unfold over time was not well understood.

The researchers used a large United States survey with 17,283 adults aged fifty or older, followed from 2014 to 2018. Within the same person, greater depressive symptoms at one wave predicted greater sleep disturbance at the next, and the reverse also held. Poor sleep also predicted lower quality of life later. Depressive symptoms, in turn, predicted lower quality of life in every period examined. The authors call for more research on how these relationships play out over longer periods.
pmc-11693020:
Haley Hentnik and four co-authors test whether the way older adults walk can help screen for cognitive impairment. Their study came out in 2024. Walking speed and steadiness have been proposed as early warning signs alongside standard thinking tests.

Just over a hundred older adults took a telephone-style cognitive screen and an attention test while their gait was measured. Walking speed, symmetry, and smoothness each tracked the screening score. Smoothness tracked attention and processing speed even more strongly than it tracked the screen itself. That fits earlier work linking visual-spatial processing to unsteady walking. However, smoothness also rose and fell with walking speed, so its independent value is unproven. The authors call for work on how specific these gait signals really are.
pmc-11693220:
Collin Sakal and Xinyue Li link sleep quality to survival in older adults in a 2024 conference abstract. Most past work counts only sleep length. Their cohort holds 33,428 UK Biobank elders with wrist sensor data over about nine years of follow-up. A hidden Markov model scores sleep efficiency and its night-to-night swing.

Poor average efficiency and high swing both tie to higher death risk at first, they report. Once daytime activity enters the model, both links vanish. Activity itself shows a bent curve: low movement raises risk, high movement lowers it. The authors suggest that daytime movement, not sleep efficiency alone, drives the survival pattern.
pmc-11693320:
Cooking over wood, dung, or crop waste fills homes with smoke, and Mani, Gupta, and Elo ask whether smoke reaches the mind in old age. They used aging surveys from India and four other low- and middle-income countries to link polluting cooking fuels with later-life cognition. They counted the fuel a person's household used and how common such fuels were in the neighborhood.

Both layers hurt. People in homes using polluting fuels scored lower on cognitive tests, and so did people whose neighbors used them, even if their stove was clean. Women in homes with polluting fuel, in areas where fuel use was highest, had the lowest predicted scores; men in clean-fuel homes in clean areas had the highest. Money and schooling differences could not explain the gaps. The authors argue the spillover harm strengthens the case for moving households to clean fuels.
pmc-11698020:
Chen Hu, Boris Freidlin, and Edward L Korn reviewed cancer trials that pause enrollment midway to decide whether a treatment deserves a full large test, in a paper published in 2024. These combined phase II and III trials can spare patients from weak treatments, but the pause can drag on while early data ripen.

The authors gathered twenty-two such trials run by a national cancer network and its forerunner groups. Most planned a pause, and every finished trial's pause ran longer than planned, by three to twenty months. They discuss a calendar backstop: a fixed date by which the go or no-go call is made with whatever data exist. One trial is used to show the trade-offs plainly.
pmc-11698920:
Iman Soodmand and co-authors wrote a 2024 review on computer models of the human jawbone. Engineers simulate the jaw to plan implants and surgery. A model is only as good as its material settings, and real bone varies in stiffness from place to place. The review asks how studies assign that variation from medical scans.

Following standard review rules, the team searched three databases for work published before July 2024. They kept seventy-seven simulation studies and found twelve distinct ways of mapping scan brightness to bone stiffness. The models came from lab tests or from calculations, and they do not agree. The paper also grades the studies for bias. A shared standard would make jaw simulations easier to trust and compare.
pmc-11699520:
Six authors led by Kowmudi Maddineni poll primary school teachers in India on bad mouth habits in children. Habits such as thumb sucking start at school age and can push teeth out of line over time. Teachers see these habits in class hours, when they peak, so their grasp of the harm matters. The study ran in Nellore, with a paper poll handed out and picked up the same day.

All 150 teachers asked took part in the poll. Scores were split by topic: what teachers know, how they feel, and what they do when they spot a habit. Rates per question fill the report in plain shares. Gaps in teacher grasp mark where dentist-led talks in schools could help most. Early spotting by teachers can send a child to care before teeth shift far.
pmc-11699620:
Zhenqi Yang, Guoyong Yin, Shuyang Sun, and Ping Xu survey medical uses of polylactic acid, a plant-based plastic that breaks down in the body. Their 2024 review covers a material prized for safety, low tissue reaction, and vanishing over time so no second surgery is needed. New nano methods and 3D printing add fine structure at micro and macro scales.

Drug delivery systems lead the survey, followed by bone repair work. Tissue engineering uses the material as a scaffold that fades as real tissue grows. Surgery and medical devices round out the clinical map. The authors weigh future prospects for each use. Their verdict favors wider clinical adoption as printing and nano design mature.
pmc-11700520:
Aisha Siewe and a large team describe the Performance Monitoring for Action panel surveys, an open cohort for contraceptive research. The platform runs repeat surveys with the same respondents plus fresh cross sections. It tracks how contraceptive use changes over time and what drives supply and demand.

Data are nationally representative in Kenya, Niger, Uganda, Burkina Faso, and Ivory Coast. Subnational coverage includes parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, and India. Resident enumerators revisit households, which supports high quality longitudinal data at modest cost. The profile explains sampling, measures, and access, so other teams can use the data for family planning research and policy.
pmc-11704420:
Anis Chaba and co-authors read, in a 2024 study, how grave high blood sodium grows in an intensive care unit. The state is a known harm of grave illness, but its path was not mapped in depth. The team screened 11,642 stays in a 40-bed unit of a teaching hospital. They found 109 patients whose sodium hit 155 or more. Their median age was 57, and near two in three were men. On day one, most were on breath help and blood-flow drugs; a fifth had kidney harm.

Peak sodium hit a median of 158, at a median of four days in. Few had urine salt checks: just eight patients. The team tracked fluids, water care, fix speed, and wild thought states.
pmc-11704920: Rachel Jimenez, editor of a radiation oncology journal, thanks the peer reviewers who served the journal through 2023 and names its outstanding reviewers for the year. The editorial appeared in 2024. Reviewing is unpaid and often invisible, yet the journal's quality depends on it. Jimenez notes how fast medical knowledge now grows and credits reviewers and editors for keeping the journal current amid clinician burnout. A table lists the honored reviewers and their institutions.
pmc-11706520:
Pasquale Viola and six co-authors develop and validate an Italian digit in noise hearing test. The test measures the speech reception threshold by asking listeners to repeat digit triplets heard in noise. Digits from zero to nine are recorded in Italian and equalized so each is equally easy to recognize.

A phone and tablet app administers the test to each ear independently with a new adaptive procedure that shortens the run. Normative data come from 45 normal hearing subjects and 62 subjects with varied hearing loss, beyond the equalization group. Thresholds for normal hearing match prior literature, and values align with World Health Organization hearing loss grades. Users can self test on a standard personal device.
pmc-11709520:
Sheng-Min Wang and co-authors link two hormones to Alzheimer's disease stages and brain amyloid, in a 2025 study. Women face higher Alzheimer's risk than men, and sex hormones are suspects in that gap. The team studied women past menopause, sorted into normal, mildly impaired, and dementia groups. Blood levels of a pituitary hormone and of estrogen were compared across the groups.

The pituitary hormone ran higher in the dementia group than in both other groups. Estrogen levels, by contrast, did not differ clearly across groups. Higher hormone levels also tracked with worse thinking scores on most subtests. In a scanned subgroup, the hormone ran higher in brains with amyloid deposits and tracked deposit levels in several regions. Estrogen showed no such links. The authors single out the pituitary hormone for more study.
pmc-11709620:
Sithara Vivek and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on lung function and blood markers of Alzheimer's disease. Blood markers are entering clinics and trials, so factors that shift their levels matter. The team used a national retirement study to test whether weak lungs move marker levels and help explain later dementia.

Data covered 3,801 adults surveyed in 2016, with 142 new dementia cases over four years. People in the weakest lung group showed higher levels of an astrocyte marker in both sexes. Women in that group also showed higher levels of a nerve damage marker. No link appeared for amyloid ratio or a tau marker.
pmc-11709720:
One brain disease stiffens movement and steals balance, driven by clumps of a protein called tau, yet its root triggers stay unclear. Kristen Whitney and co-authors probe a stress-response system inside cells in a 2025 study. They read gene activity cell by cell in donated brains and grew mini midbrains in the lab from patients' own skin cells.

In the donated tissue, the stress system ran hot in exactly the regions the disease hits hardest, and cold where it spares. Its heat tracked with the tau load in the same cells. The lab-grown mini brains echoed the pattern, with more of the harmful tau forms and altered stress markers. The team frames the stress system as a candidate driver worth testing as a drug target.
pmc-11709820:
Luana Heimfarth and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on irisin, a hormone released during exercise. Irisin has already been shown to guard synapses and memory in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease. The team asked whether it acts through astrocytes, the brain's support cells, by changing the helpful factors those cells release.

In cultured astrocytes, irisin raised two growth factors, BDNF and GDNF, and briefly switched on a signaling protein. In mice given toxic amyloid pieces, irisin eased memory loss and shifted growth factor signals in the living brain. The results suggest astrocytes help carry the hormone's protective effect.
pmc-11709920:
Jennifer Bruno and co-authors test whether hormone therapy links to lower Alzheimer harm in women, in work from 2025. More than two-thirds of Alzheimer patients are women. The drop in estrogen at menopause may play a role, but past therapy studies disagree.

The team used three large data sets covering brain checks after death, brain scans, and memory scores. One set held over three thousand women, and another held over twenty thousand records. Both scan and fluid markers of Alzheimer change were also tested. Early results point toward a protective link in these groups. The authors weigh timing and therapy type as likely keys to the mixed past record.
pmc-11710020:
Jae Won Oh and co-authors study in 2025 how two protein buildups in the brain relate in people who had both Alzheimer's disease and a second age-linked brain change. Tau and TDP-43 are the two proteins at issue, and the paired state is more common than either one alone. The team used data from two long studies of aging and memory.

They measured protein loads in many brain regions for more than fourteen hundred people who had died. A third protein, amyloid, was linked to TDP-43 at first, but that link vanished once tau was counted. Tau in outer brain regions seemed to carry the link, while TDP-43 and that tau each tied to faster loss of thinking skill on their own.
pmc-11710220:
Daniel K Mori-Fegan and co-authors present a 2025 study of a gene variant that tunes the brain's own cannabis-like signalling, and its links to Alzheimer's disease. The gene makes an enzyme that breaks down a calming messenger called anandamide. One common variant weakens the enzyme, leaving more of the messenger active, and has been tied to lower trauma disorder risk but higher addiction risk.

Whether that variant also shifts Alzheimer's risk was unknown. The team set out to test the link, given the signalling system's hand in brain inflammation. A clean answer would add a genetic thread to how this internal system shapes late-life brain disease.
pmc-11710320:
Tiffany Petrisko, Shu-Hui Chu, and Andrea Tenner study what brain immune cells eat when one immune protein is cut just in those cells, in a 2025 study. The work uses mice bred to model Alzheimer disease. The protein helps mark bits for the cells to clear.

Mice lacking the protein in these cells ate less of the sticky brain plaques. They also ate less of the nerve links that the disease puts at risk. A second brain cell type ate less plaque too, though its own gene was left whole. The trade off shows why broad blocks of this path are hard to judge.
pmc-11710620:
Five researchers ask why some people keep clear thinking even when their brains show heavy disease in a 2025 paper. They study donors whose brains held the protein clumps linked to Alzheimer's disease, yet whose minds declined very little. The team joined three large studies of brain tissue taken after death.

They sorted brain cells by type and looked for groups tied to this strength. Two types of microglia, the brain's immune cells, stood out in distinct ways. One type was more common in people who resisted one protein, and less common in those who resisted another. A group of nerve cells in one brain layer also ran higher in some resilient donors.
pmc-11710820:
Jun Lin and Jiong Shi study vessel growth factors in spinal fluid in a 2025 Alzheimer's report. New vessel growth seems to rise in the disease, but its role is unclear. The team measured twelve such factors in two hundred people, half with very mild scores and half with worse ones.

Higher tau damage tracked higher levels of several of the factors. Many factors also tracked vessel leak signs, white matter damage, thinner cortex, and lower test scores. The amyloid effects looked weaker once tau was accounted for. The authors suggest tau may drive the rise in these factors. They raise the idea of calming excess vessel growth as a treatment path.
pmc-11712120:
Arshia A Khan and co-authors test a smart living space for dementia care in a 2025 feasibility study. Their test room joined a humanoid robot, wearable sensors, and wall and chair sensors. The robot, Pepper, could talk, tell jokes, and offer medication. Thirty-two healthy volunteers spent ninety minutes in the room.

Volunteers took a placebo pill from the robot, walked a treadmill test, did thinking tasks, made a small meal, and folded towels. Chair pressure sensors and the robot's mood reading matched self-reported mood in ninety-five percent of cases. Door sensors caught every exit, and wall sensors flagged wandering. Body sensors logged pulse and skin signals throughout. The authors say the joined system can support safe, personal care at home.
pmc-11712220:
Sarah Gothard, Nathaniel Rodrigues, and co-authors test if old folks can set home sense kits by mail in a mind study, in a 2025 study. Home kits catch day acts in true life, a plus for mind work. Staff trips to set kits blocked wide use of that path in past runs.

A guide book with clips and steps ships to a score of homes. Some folks set all kit lone, while most need phone help for one step. All snags clear by phone with no staff trip at all. Data take and snag rates match staff set homes in full. Watch, mat, and pill box data run as good or best.
pmc-11712320:
Cynthia Felix and co-authors test memory scores in healthy older adults with brain scans in a 2025 conference study. People with no thinking complaints can still carry the two hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's disease. Finding early signs in such people matters, since treatment may work best before symptoms grow.

Eighty eight unimpaired adults had scans for both proteins plus a standard thirty point thinking test. Those positive for both proteins scored lower overall than those negative for both, and delayed recall of a word list drove the gap. The result suggests that even a brief clinic test can flag subtle change in at risk adults. The work comes from a multi site study of brain aging.
pmc-11712420:
Xiaoqing Huang and co-authors move Alzheimer's subtype labels from brain data to blood data in living patients, in a 2025 paper. Some patients decline out of step with their tangle load, forming atypical groups found so far only after death. Living patients cannot give brain tissue, so the team trained on a cohort holding both brain and blood gene data.

Four groups were defined there, from control to typical disease. An optimal transport method then carried those labels into blood data from two fresh cohorts. Genes that stayed consistent for each subtype across all three cohorts were kept. A pseudo time study ordered the gene changes, sketching how each subtype unfolds.
pmc-11712720:
Rasheed Abdulraheem and six co-authors test whether polyphenols from sorghum grain can slow the amyloid plaques tied to Alzheimer's disease. Approved drugs have not managed to change the course of the disease, so food-based options draw growing interest. Sorghum is cheap, widely grown, and rich in antioxidants, yet its brain effects had not been studied.

The team extracted polyphenols from three sorghum types, with black, reddish-brown, and red outer grain layers. Computer docking showed the compounds could bind the amyloid protein and hinder its clumping. In cell tests, treated cells survived better. In tiny worms bred as an Alzheimer's model, the extracts improved movement and feeding, signs of less damage. The black sorghum extract worked best, then reddish-brown, then red. The authors propose black sorghum polyphenols as a candidate ingredient for a dietary supplement, with more study to come.
pmc-11712820:
Emily J Rogalski and five co-authors report a global telehealth trial in this 2025 paper. The trial served people with primary progressive aphasia, a rare dementia that harms speech and language. Care came by video chat, so patients joined from home with a communication partner. One group got a joint program built on taking part in daily talk. The other group got a solo program built on word drills.

Ninety-five pairs took part across four countries, and fewer than one in ten dropped out. After the first block, the joint group beat the control group on a goal based participation score. Both groups gained on word and script tasks. Talks after the study showed the format was easy to use at home. The team sees telehealth as a real path to bring this care to more families.
pmc-11712920:
Christan Monge Ortega and eight co-authors review talk based and brain based care to slow dementia in Alzheimer disease, in a 2025 review. After a dementia finding, thinking skills and mood often slip. Drugs help some, but non drug care is in high demand.

The review sums tests of talk therapy, memory rehab, and brain wave training, alone and in pairs. Gains were most clear in early stages of the disease. Talk care plus brain training beat talk care alone on test scores in one study. Gains from computer drills were weaker and often faded by one year, so more firm tests are still needed.
pmc-11713520:
Samira Maboudian and co-authors find that tau linked cortex thinning gathers in the depths of brain folds, in a 2025 paper. Past work hints that folds wear faster than crowns in aging and Alzheimer's disease, but the tie to tau protein was unmapped. The team joined thickness maps with amyloid and tau scans from eight hundred nine people across health states.

Spots where high tau met thin cortex overlapped folds far more than crowns. The deepest five percent of fold points matched most of all, and one early forming fold stood out against a control fold. The pattern held across both brain halves. Fold depths, which act as wiring hubs, may be where tau does its worst thinning.
pmc-11713720:
Lalit Sharma and Yogesh Gupta present a 2025 study on a plant compound against Alzheimer's disease. The disease brings memory loss, inflammation, and failing cell powerhouses. A pore in those powerhouses can swing open and damage neurons. The compound, from a famed Ayurvedic herb, has shown nerve-protective signs before. The team tested it in cell and mouse models of the disease.

Treated mice did better on maze and field tests of memory. Their brains held less of the toxic protein that marks the disease. The compound blocked the pore from opening, which kept cell voltage steady and cut harmful oxygen radicals. Energy output held up as well. Inflammation signals fell and growth factors rose. The authors back the compound as a candidate worth more study.
pmc-11713820:
Chinmayee Athalye and co-authors describe a 2025 method for linking brain scans to tissue samples after death. Studying donated brains is the surest way to confirm a dementia diagnosis. The team uses scan images to guide where tissue is cut, so each sample sits close to the spot the scan measured. They test whether closer sampling gives stronger links between scans and disease.

The work uses 29 brain halves from patients with Alzheimer's disease. Staff mark nineteen regions on high-detail scans, then print a mold of each brain to guide the cuts. Stains show tau protein in each sample, and software turns the stain into numbers. The setup could make scan-and-tissue studies more exact.
pmc-11714120:
Jonathon White, MD Azaharuddin Ansari, and Nafia Al-Mutawaly describe a lighting system built to run around the clock for people with dementia, in a 2025 conference paper. Most people with dementia sleep poorly, and more than a quarter fall due to weak sight. Good light has been shown since the 1980s to ease both troubles.

Code tunes the color and strength of light from standard LED strips across the day. The light turns warm and bright fast in the morning, then softens toward night. A small controller runs four strips in a room, with one low strip for night. The system passed Canadian safety checks and was put in six bedrooms at a memory care home. Staff and users gave mostly kind reviews.
pmc-11714320:
Jose Bernal Moyano and a large team of co-authors track tiny fluid spaces around brain vessels in a 2025 paper. These spaces can grow large enough to see on brain scans, but why they enlarge is debated. The team follow their size over three years in more than five hundred people at varied stages of thinking health.

The spaces grew over time even in healthy aging, and growth in one brain region tracked growth in another. People with more white matter damage at the start tended toward faster growth deep in the brain. Those positive for both Alzheimer markers tended toward faster growth in an upper region. Aging itself looked like the main driver.
pmc-11714420:
Elena Guseva and co-authors review studies that use wrist motion sensors to spot behavior symptoms in people with dementia, in a 2025 conference paper. The sensors track body movement all day, which may flag symptoms tied to motion. The review covers six such symptoms, from restless pacing and agitation to apathy and wandering.

The search swept nine databases and found more than twelve thousand records, of which 84 reports stayed for review. Only eight reports held data fit to test how well the sensors spot symptoms. Most work covered agitation and apathy. Combined results gave modest links between sensor data and symptom scores. The authors say the tools show promise but need far more proof before clinics can trust them.
pmc-11714520:
Trevor Meyer and co-authors analyze eye movements and speech together while people take the Stroop color-word test, aiming to characterize Alzheimer's disease more objectively, in a 2025 paper. Standard rating scales miss detail in the disease's early stages and lean on judgment. Behavior during the test may carry finer signals than the final score alone.

Seventeen patients and 24 matched healthy controls took part at a university memory center, with some patients returning for repeat sessions months later. A head-free eye tracker recorded gaze while spoken answers were captured. The team studies how patients interact with the task across both channels, hunting patterns that separate the groups.
pmc-11714620:
Zahinoor Ismail and three co-authors test a cheap way to spot early Alzheimer's disease for trials, in a 2025 paper. New drugs work best early, but the spinal fluid tests that confirm the illness cost much and hurt. The team asks whether a lasting change in conduct, called mild behavioral impairment, can flag who is likely to test positive.

They studied 984 older adults without dementia from a shared US data set. People with the lasting conduct change had more than twice the odds of positive results for the two hallmark proteins of the illness. Brief or passing symptoms showed no such link. The authors say screening for the conduct change could help trial teams pick whom to test first.
pmc-11714720:
Liling Dong and co-authors describe the genetic makeup of a large dementia group at a Beijing hospital, in work published in 2025. More than twenty five hundred patients had history checks, thinking tests, brain scans, and gene tests. Over half had early onset disease, before age sixty five.

About six percent carried a clearly harmful gene variant tied to dementia. The most common such gene was NOTCH3, followed by two others known for early Alzheimer type disease. A common risk gene variant was carried by about a third of patients. The authors say the group shows wide genetic diversity, with a notably high rate for the top gene.
pmc-11714920:
Yian Gu and co-authors ask whether heart ills add to mind loss in older adults with low blood marks for Alzheimer's disease. The study appeared in 2025. Blood marks for the disease have moved fast into clinic use. The team used a long city aging study with near one thousand adults.

Mind loss share rose step by step as heart ill counts grew, from a fifth to seven in ten. More heart ills did not tie to mark status, sex, age, or school years. The count held four ills in view, from sugar ill to stroke. The team sorts adults by a pair of blood marks to set low and high groups.
pmc-11715220:
Nelson Roque and co-authors report on a phone-and-sensor study of cognitive aging in a diverse older cohort, in a 2025 paper. Older adults, especially from minority groups, are often assumed unwilling or unable to join mobile health research. The Einstein Aging Study has supported such participation since 2017. In 2023 it added multiple wearable sensors.

Beyond clinic testing and blood draws, participants complete fourteen days of app surveys. Brief thinking tasks arrive five times a day, from wake-up to bedtime. The paper asks whether this heavy protocol is feasible in a varied population. Showing that it works widens who aging research can honestly claim to represent.
pmc-11715320:
Caroline Dallaire-Théroux and co-authors, with the CIMA-Q group, probe links between body metabolism and Alzheimer's disease. Blood markers of fat and sugar control may hint at how the disease grows. The 2025 study drew on 288 older adults sorted into four groups: healthy, mild worry about memory, mild impairment, and Alzheimer's. Blood, spinal fluid, brain scans, and thinking tests were compared across the groups.

Two markers, FGF21 and IGFBP2, rose with age. IGFBP2 ran high in the worry and Alzheimer's groups and tracked worse memory scores plus signs of brain shrinkage. Signs of obesity and insulin trouble linked to lower IGFBP2 but higher FGF21. The authors call the pattern complex and urge more work.
pmc-11715420:
Setthanan Jarukasemkit and co-authors argue that brain networks, not single regions, are the right level for reading tau pathology in dementia. Published in 2025, the pilot study assessed thirty patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia. Blood markers, clinical scores, and tau PET scans were mapped onto the standard network atlas.

Tau PET signal across all networks tracked blood tau levels, with the limbic network showing the strongest link. Cognitive scores told a different story: their ties sat mainly in the dorsal attention network, at moderate to strong levels. The split suggests blood tests and bedside scores each reflect a different network's burden. Network level analysis, the authors say, adds what region level reads miss.
pmc-11715520:
Yongjun Lee and five co-authors ask which video messages best persuade volunteers to stay signed up in a research recruitment registry. Registries hold the names of people who may join future studies, but they lose value when members drift away. The registry here is run by a California university campus and sends a yearly renewal. Four short videos each stress one reason to stay: payment, helping science, a match to one's own health, or new research built on shared data.

Members saw pairs of videos drawn from combinations of the four themes and picked the one that moved them most. A ranking model then weighs which themes win, alone and in blends. When the report was written, responses were still coming in. The team plans to use the ranks to shape a full trial of ways to keep members enrolled.
pmc-11715620:
Malavika Pillai and co-authors examine, in a 2025 study, how Alzheimer imaging markers shift across diabetes stages in a diverse Texas cohort. Diabetes raises Alzheimer risk and hits Mexican American and Black communities hardest, yet how brain markers differ by diabetes stage within each group was unclear.

Scans measured amyloid, tau, and brain shrinkage in about two thousand adults sorted into non-diabetic, pre-diabetic, and diabetic groups by blood sugar records. Thinking scores were compared alongside. The analysis weighed each marker across stages and tested whether ethnic group changed the pattern. Results from this disparities-focused cohort guide fairer dementia screening in mixed communities.
pmc-11715720:
Matthew Cohen and five co-authors test Brain-WISE, a short group program that aims to cut dementia risk in older adults. The name is short for Brain Wellness Information, Support, and Empowerment. The program runs as six group sessions of 90 minutes each, led by speech-language therapists. Each session pairs a lecture on brain health with individual and group activities, plus health goals set by each person.

The team ran two pilot waves with 49 adults aged 64 to 93 and refined the program between waves. Attendance stayed high, at 97 percent and then about 93 percent, and most members rated the program as worth their time. After the second wave, knowledge rose, diet scores and exercise improved, and perceived barriers to change fell. Self-efficacy, the sense of control, did not move. The team now calls for a full trial.
pmc-11715820:
Jason Russell and co-authors link a brain chemical system to thinking in adults with Down syndrome in this 2025 study. People with Down syndrome carry an extra copy of a gene that raises Alzheimer's risk. The cholinergic system, a network of brain signaling, fades in Alzheimer's and supports memory.

The study scanned 188 adults from a Down syndrome research cohort. Brain imaging measured a cholinergic hub's volume, and PET scans tracked a related marker. Scores on cognitive tests were set against both measures. The links found may flag who declines earliest. Early flags matter because prevention trials need the right volunteers.
pmc-11715920:
Shana Stites and co-authors published this 2025 study on asking the same life-circumstance survey twice in an Alzheimer's research cohort. Health is shaped by schooling, money strain, work, stress, and support. To see how those forces steer dementia over time, they must be measured again and again. The team repeated a long survey about eighteen months apart.

The sample held 135 cognitively healthy older adults at a university center. Eighty-one, or sixty percent, completed the follow-up. Most answered nearly all of the roughly 225 items. Completion dipped most on a health literacy scale and a stress scale. The pilot shows repeat surveying is workable, and it flags which items tire respondents. Such data can link lived experience to later brain outcomes.
pmc-11716120:
Ravi Mahalingam and co-authors found in 2025 that a monkey chickenpox kin virus sparks amyloid build-up across organs. The human virus hides in nerves in most adults and wakes as shingles, which lifts dementia risk. Since the human virus infects only people, the team used its monkey twin in rhesus macaques, following them from first illness through hiding to shingles under immune suppression.

At peak virus in blood, a clot-prone, amyloid-friendly state rose in serum. Virus marks sat with amyloid in gut, pancreas, artery, and smell tissue. Amyloid also turned up in brain arteries. The team reads this as a route by which such infection may speed Alzheimer disease, and a model to test it.
pmc-11716220:
Clive Ballard reviews psychosis in Alzheimer's disease. It is a common and upsetting feature of the illness, and no treatment is approved for it. Delusions and hallucinations in these patients track with worse outcomes and a higher chance of moving into care. New criteria now help doctors spot the condition. In some patients, the signs show up even before memory problems appear.

The review looks at fresh work on genes and brain scans. It also looks at post-mortem tissue, and at how this work sharpens ideas about how the symptoms arise. Drugs that may help include pimavanserin, which is licensed in the United States for psychosis in Parkinson's disease. Other options are escitalopram, muscarinic agonists, and cannabidiol. Ballard also covers better targeted talking therapies. He covers the harder problem of psychosis in related dementias, and the near lack of work on vascular dementia.
pmc-11716320:
Annika Baumeister and co-authors poll folk in three Euro lands on whether they would want their mind loss risk told, in a study from 2025. Blood marks may soon let labs call that risk ere signs show. Polls ran to set shares of the whole in each land, near a thousand souls per land.

Most in each land said yes to the tell, from two thirds to past three fourths. Blood draws beat spine taps and scans as the path of pick. GPs are the told source of pick in all lands. Cure and ward off odds sway the pick most. Folk read the tell as a chance to plan, with mind load grants.
pmc-11716520:
Claudio Del Percio and nine co-authors published a study in 2025 on resting brain rhythms in people whose mild memory loss stems from Alzheimer's disease. When patients rest with eyes closed, one rhythm at the back of the brain often weakens. The team asked whether that weakening is stronger when Alzheimer's is the true cause, and whether it tracks spinal fluid markers.

They compared seventy patients with Alzheimer's-linked impairment, forty-five whose impairment had other causes, and forty-five healthy elders. The rhythm was most reduced in the Alzheimer's group. In that group, weaker rhythm also went with higher levels of a tau marker in spinal fluid. A simple resting recording may help tell causes of memory loss apart.
pmc-11716620:
Giuseppe Piga and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on a blood marker called BD-tau, short for brain-derived tau. Most tau in blood comes from outside the brain, which blurs the signal; this form is made in the brain itself.

The team used patient cohorts from a Paris hospital, covering healthy people with amyloid, Alzheimer's patients at many stages, and people with other brain diseases. BD-tau rose only in people with symptoms from Alzheimer's disease, whether it was the main illness or a second one. People with Alzheimer's biology but no symptoms had normal levels. Levels tracked memory scores and rose over time only in the symptomatic group. The authors say BD-tau could stage the disease by how far symptoms have gone, not just whether the biology is present.
pmc-11716720:
Cong Chu and co-authors compare two MRI strengths for measuring age-related brain shrinkage. Brains lose volume and thickness in places as they age, and stronger 7-tesla scanners give sharper images than common 3-tesla machines. Whether that sharpness changes what aging studies find, person by person, was unknown. The team scanned 351 healthy adults on both machine types.

After quality checks, 279 matched scan pairs were analyzed. The stronger scanner found age links in more brain regions and with stronger correlations than the standard one, including extra regions the weaker scans missed. Ventricle size, which grows with age, also tracked more strongly at high field. The authors conclude that 7-tesla imaging can shrink the sample sizes aging studies need while sharpening their statistics.
pmc-11716820:
Juliet Nnenda Olayinka and ten co-authors published early results in 2025 from a Nigerian study of memory in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, and standard tests for that risk are costly or invasive in Nigeria. The team also asked whether saliva could serve as a simpler sample for testing.

They recruited twenty patients and forty healthy controls at a hospital in Nigeria. Everyone took a standard mental test and gave blood and saliva samples. The blood work covered sugar control, stress markers, and inflammation, while saliva was checked for an amyloid protein. These early results set up a larger multi-centre study of diabetes and memory.
pmc-11716920:
Chinedu Udeh-Momoh and a large team of co-authors describe a study of women's brain health in Africa in twenty twenty-five. The study is called FemBER-AFRICA. It seeks targets for stopping Alzheimer's disease in women of African ancestry. Those targets span hormones, daily habits, mental and social life, and culture.

The team notes that very little dementia research has been done in Africa so far. Yet early stages of Alzheimer's may be the best time to act. A study built with African women can find risks that work done elsewhere would miss. Readers get the aims of the study and the range of factors it will track over time.
pmc-11718520:
Hira Lal and co-authors tested whether a mix of ultrasound methods can track the health of a transplanted kidney without repeated biopsies, in a 2024 study. Biopsy is the trusted check for graft trouble, but invasive and unfit for routine follow-up. One method measures stiffness, which tends to rise when a graft struggles. The team followed seventy-one recipients over two years in Lucknow, India.

Stiffness readings in stable grafts and in failing grafts sat close together at the start, with no gap. Readings dipped over the first three months after surgery, then climbed toward the one-year mark. Patients with biopsy-proven trouble did show higher stiffness than those with clean biopsies. Still, no reliable cutoff separated stable grafts from failing ones. They call the method promising for monitoring but not yet a biopsy stand-in.
pmc-11726720:
Loic Lesobre and co-authors check the genes of a captive flock of Eurasian stone-curlews in Morocco. The 2024 study asks whether the flock, bred to boost wild numbers, still matches wild birds of its North African type. The founders' origins were unknown, so the team compared captive birds with wild ones from west and east Morocco.

Gene tests on two kinds of markers found like levels of variety in all groups. Captive birds showed low kinship with each other and little split from wild birds. Those results confirm the founders came from Morocco. The team ends with advice to keep variety high in this flock and in like breeding plans for other rare birds.
pmc-11727220:
Yaling Hew leads a team in a review of artificial intelligence in IVF labs, with Nina Smolinska among the pack-listed authors. The paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Lab work for in vitro fertilization leans on fine hand skill and steady checks. Smart tools promise more exact picks and fewer slips.

Neural nets and deep learning can grade embryos and sperm, run quality checks, and flag patterns that guide a plan fit to each patient. Gains in success rates are claimed in case studies. Yet the shift raises hard points on data safety, bias in the tools, and how staff and machines share calls. The authors call for more study and firm ethical watch.
pmc-11728020:
Polona Peclin and co-authors study how anesthesia choice affects timing in urgent cesarean births, in a 2024 paper. The optimal anesthetic technique for category two and three cesarean deliveries is still debated among birth teams. Concern persists about impacts on the decision-to-delivery interval and on outcomes for mother and baby alike, at a moment when each minute can shape how both of them fare.

The prospective cohort study at a tertiary perinatal center took in women in these urgent deliveries and tracked them through their care, step by step. It set epidural, spinal, and general anesthesia against each other for delivery speed, for surgical and postoperative complications, and for neonatal outcomes in the newborn. Clear evidence of this kind helps teams pick the fastest safe one when minutes matter most.
pmc-11728220:
Islam and co-authors published this mouse study in twenty twenty-four on gut microbes and allergy. Lab mice raised in very clean rooms have immature immune systems, which can skew test results. The team moved gut microbes from wild mice into lab mice. They then exposed the mice to house dust mites, a common trigger of airway allergy.

Mice with the wild gut microbes showed less lung damage and lower levels of a key inflammatory signal. Their gut genes also shifted in ways tied to a calmer immune response. Microbe and chemical profiles in the gut differed clearly between the groups. The authors suggest drug tests should use both clean lab mice and mice with wild-type gut microbes for fairer results.
pmc-11728720:
Andrea Macejova and co-authors compare ketamine with a sedative in depressed teens in this 2024 study. Treatment-resistant depression is rising among adolescents, and few options act fast. Ketamine lifts adult depression quickly, but teen data are thin.

The trial gave intravenous ketamine to 27 girls and midazolam, a calmative, to 28. All had depression that standard care had failed to move. Three rating scales tracked depression and anxiety. Scores were taken two hours after the first dose and a day after treatment ended. Within-group changes were compared at both points. The study tests whether a fast adult remedy helps the young.
pmc-11729520:
Maria Alejandra Diaz and co-authors tune wearable device settings using muscle signals instead of gas analysis, in work published in 2024. Wearable robots aim to lower the energy cost of walking, but that cost is usually measured with breathing equipment that is slow and awkward. Muscle signals from the legs may offer a simpler proxy.

The team built a score from muscle signal strength and patterns of muscle coordination. In offline tests, the score tracked the true energy cost of walking well. They then used an online search algorithm to tune step frequency so the score fell. The search settled near each user's own preferred pace and cut energy cost. The method could help set exoskeleton support for each user with fewer test rounds.
pmc-11734020:
Sumon Roy and three co-authors present a 2024 case report on removing a large mass from the heart through a catheter instead of open surgery. An eighty-five-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation had a mass over four centimeters wide in her left atrium. Through a vessel, the team advanced an aspiration cannula and sucked out the bulk of the mass.

A fragment broke free and traveled downstream, lodging in the leg artery. Surgeons opened the groin artery and pulled the piece out. Lab analysis showed the mass was a complex blood clot. The case shows catheter aspiration can extract even large atrial masses, with a plan needed for stray fragments.
pmc-11735120:
Kip and co-authors pool past studies to gauge mental illness after natural hazards in poorer countries, in a 2024 analysis. Storms, quakes, and floods hit such countries hardest. Yet most research on the mental toll comes from rich countries. The team set out to sum up what is known where the burden is greatest.

They searched three databases for studies of at least 100 adult survivors. Each study had to use a sound test for mental disorders, at least one month after the event. Countries were classed by a United Nations index of human development. The pooled rates cover both short-term and long-term shares of disorders. The work gives aid planners a firmer base for mental health support after disasters.
pmc-11759120:
Appendicitis care changed during the COVID-19 pandemic, and this single-center study from Zagreb, Croatia checks how. The authors compare patients treated before the pandemic with those treated during it, from September 2019 to October 2020, at one university hospital. They track how many patients came in, how long symptoms lasted before arrival, the surgical approach, lab-confirmed diagnoses, and hospital stay. The study covers the pandemic's first year.

Two shifts stand out as statistically significant. Open surgery, rather than keyhole surgery, becomes more common during the pandemic. Perforated appendicitis, the burst form of the disease, also rises in share. By contrast, the time from symptom start to hospital arrival does not grow significantly, and the small rise in postoperative stay is not significant either. The authors present the pattern as a real change in practice and case mix, not a delay story.
pmc-11775520:
Zubair Abdullah-Vetter and co-authors give in 2024 a deep learn tool to read sun cell yield marks with no hand fit work. Such marks bare loss at the cell's faces and key power traits. Hand reads take long, and fast ways were built for the main cell stuff, not for the rarer gallium mix.

Their net calls many traits at once from the yield curve. Calls held true across the full trait range in tests. Noise in the reads bent the calls just a shade. The team aims the tool at wide cell sorts past the main kind.
pmc-11782220:
Hip fracture patients who wait too long for surgery fare worse, and Rui Gong and six co-authors built a predictor of the wait in a 2024 paper. They mined records of 1,116 patients with intertrochanteric fractures treated at one Chinese hospital over seven years. Delay meant passing 48 hours before the operation.

A logistic model trained on 728 patients surfaced five predictors: age, sex, a leg-vein clot, the injury's location, and blood markers. Drawn as a nomogram, a point-scoring chart, the model separated long waiters from prompt ones with fair accuracy. The authors offer the chart for triage: flag the likely delayers on arrival, and the scheduling fixes can start before the clock becomes a complication.
pmc-11784820:
Xiangting Shi, Yakang Zhang, Manning Yu, and Lihao Zhang present a system that predicts which phone customers are about to leave. Their 2024 paper notes that older customer systems react slowly because their models stay fixed while customer habits keep changing.

The team joined three learning methods into one model and fed it a large telecom data set. The combined model sorted customers with high accuracy and beat simpler approaches. Plugged into a support tool, its output can guide staff toward offers that keep at-risk customers. The authors also weigh privacy and fairness, since such systems judge people from their data. They argue a churn tool must stay open about how it reaches each call.
pmc-11789720:
Rafail Ibragimov and co-authors check hepatitis B vaccine protection in Tashkent health workers in a 2024 study. Health workers face high exposure to the virus. Uzbekistan ran staff vaccination drives in 2015 and 2022 but does not test immunity afterward, unlike world guidance.

They sampled 334 workers from drive records in 2023 and tested their blood. Most recalled all three doses. About 5 percent had active infection and 4 percent a past one, while 91 percent carried vaccine-made antibodies. Among those, 71 percent held protective levels, rising with dose count. Clinic staff lagged hospital staff. The authors urge help to finish the series and routine immunity checks.
pmc-11790020:
Yuan Guan and co-authors built a live-cell imaging system for human liver fibrosis in 2024. Liver scarring is hard to study: lab systems and animal models capture it poorly, and treatment options are few. Their system grows tiny human liver organoids with several cell types in a microwell.

A growth factor turned support cells in the organoids into scar-like cells much like those in human fibrotic liver. Drugs that block single growth pathways only stopped scarring driven by that same pathway, which hints at narrow use. Gene and signal analyses pointed to two other drug targets with broader effect. The authors say the system can now be used to hunt for more candidate therapies.
pmc-11790620:
Maciej Nowak and eight co-authors characterize a food-poisoning germ found in soil under organic carrots in Poland, in a study listed as 2025. The germ spreads through food such as raw produce and can cause severe illness. Natural fertilizers used in organic farming can carry it into soil and onto crops.

From 250 soil samples they isolated twenty-seven strains of the germ. Tests covered genetic similarity, drug resistance, ability to invade human gut cells, clumping with another germ, and slime layer growth. They also checked how disinfectants act on those layers. The results inform food safety for crops eaten by children and older adults.
pmc-11794120:
Yuye Li and co-authors ask, in a study published in 2024, whether a count of marker cells in the womb lining affects pregnancy chances for infertile women. The cells carry a marker called CD138, used to spot a long term womb lining inflammation. Women in the study had not been diagnosed with that inflammation, and had not taken antibiotics for it.

The team looked back at 664 infertile women treated in the first eight months of 2018. They stained lining samples for the marker, and compared counts at two points in the monthly cycle. Women were split into three groups by how many fields held clusters of the marked cells. Pregnancy outcomes were then compared across those groups for women pursuing fertility care. The aim was a finer rule for when the cell count matters, beyond a simple yes or no diagnosis.
pmc-11794320:
Ludivine Aubry and Mats Küssner review why some musicians dread the stage, tracing performance anxiety back to early life and personality, in a 2024 mini-review. The condition, classed as a subtype of social anxiety, can cripple talented players. Its definitions vary across studies, and its causes stay tangled.

The authors sort the literature on formative experiences and traits, arguing the field under-studies three things. These are the weight of early events, how personality channels their effect, and the protective factors that shield some musicians. Knowing which childhoods and temperaments breed stage fright, they say, would let teachers and clinicians intervene earlier and tailor help, rather than treating anxiety only once it erupts on stage.
pmc-11802420:
Xuejiao Yan and co-authors wrote a pilot study, dated 2024 in its text, on sex differences in plaque buildup inside brain arteries of diabetic patients after a stroke event. Plaque in these arteries is a main cause of stroke. The team used high-resolution magnetic resonance scans to count plaques in patients with type 2 diabetes who had suffered a stroke or a brief stroke-like attack.

One hundred twenty patients carried nearly five hundred plaques between them. The culprit plaque sat in the nearer stretch of its artery in most patients of both sexes. After adjustment, men carried a higher total and near-artery plaque load than women. Among patients on blood-sugar drugs, the male excess in near plaques was sharp. Among untreated patients it vanished. The team reads the split as an effect of sex and treatment, and urges care plans that weigh both.
pmc-11813920:
Alice Azoicai and colleagues review what is known about COVID-19 vaccination in children, in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Vaccines were built at pandemic speed, and children, from infants to eighteen-year-olds, were folded into programs as evidence allowed. The review asks how well the shots work in the young, and how safe they are.

Across trials worldwide, vaccinated children mounted a sustained immune response, and most studies judged the schedules effective and safe in their age bands. Harder questions stay open. Whether vaccinating children protects the wider population enough to outweigh individual risks has not been settled. Long-term side effects still need monitoring, so that the next pandemic's vaccines can be safer by design. The authors present pediatric immunization as proven in the clinic, and still unfinished as public policy.
pmc-11814220:
Tereza Hornikova and co-authors show how genes and gut germs shape skin driven food allergy in mice in a 2024 study. Food allergy can start when allergens cross broken skin before the gut learns tolerance. Two mouse strains got egg protein through stripped skin, then by stomach tube. Germ free mice joined the test to isolate microbe roles.

One strain fell ill with fever drops and diarrhea, while the other stayed well. The sick strain mounted stronger antibody and helper cell responses. Its gut lost acid making bacteria after treatment. Germ free mice spiked worse fever drops yet skipped diarrhea. Strain choice thus matters greatly for allergy models, the authors conclude.
pmc-11816320:
Shi-Heng Wang and co-authors (2024) used Taiwan's health records to ask how a father's age at birth shapes his children's health. The cohort covered two and a half million singleton births from 2001 to 2015. A million and a half children had full siblings in the data. Comparing siblings is the key move: the same family supplies different father's ages, which strips out shared family background. Plain comparisons showed a U shape for deaths before age five.

After adjustment, that curve faded toward nothing. Children of fathers over thirty-five did face more early birth, low birth weight, and low Apgar scores. The sibling comparisons surprised: younger siblings, born to older fathers, had lower risks of early death, low weight, small size, and birth defects. Only early birth and large size ran the other way. The authors conclude that family background explains much of what raw statistics blame on paternal age.
pmc-11821620:
Zhou and six co-authors test a teaching program for patients who have both narrowed brain arteries and heart disease. The program follows a knowledge, attitude, and practice model, building understanding first, then habits. Sixty patients who had vessel-opening treatment joined the study, split evenly into two groups.

The taught group reported higher satisfaction with care. Their confidence rose, and their anxiety and depression scores fell at discharge and in the months after. They also scored higher on knowledge, attitude, and practice measures at every check. The authors conclude that structured teaching of this kind supports both mood and self-care in these patients. The study appeared in 2024.
pmc-11825520:
Kaori Nishigaki and six colleagues wrote a 2025 scoping review on telenursing for children with disabilities. Telenursing means nurses check in and give care from afar by phone or video. The pandemic made home visits hard, so remote care drew fresh interest.

The review gathers past reports on remote nursing for children from birth to age 18 and their main family caregivers. It covers checks, monitoring, teaching, consults, and mentoring by nurses using digital tools. Studies in English or Japanese with any design were included. Few reports exist for this group, the authors note. Their map of the field shows what has been tried and where gaps remain for home care teams.
pmc-11839220:
Aleksandr Reznik and a large team of co-authors track symptoms and social function in schizophrenia under three forms of one drug, in a 2024 study. Long-acting shots have grown fast in Russian care. The forms are a daily pill, a monthly shot, and a quarterly shot of paliperidone. One hundred fifty-five patients in early remission were followed for twelve months, with checks five times.

All groups eased in positive symptoms. Hallucinations yielded more than stubborn delusions. Shot groups finished the program far more often than the pill group, with the quarterly shot on top. Flare rates were like across groups. The authors read the shots as an adherence win that frees time for social work.
pmc-11841420:
Rinawati Rohsiswatmo and co-authors survey how Asian hospitals revive very early babies, and how practice splits by national wealth, in a paper whose head dates it to 2024. The first minutes of an extremely preterm life shape survival and brain outcomes, yet recommended resuscitation steps vary in real delivery rooms. A six-question online survey went to facilities in the Asian neonatal network in 2021, covering babies born before twenty-nine weeks.

Answers from rich and poorer countries were compared practice by practice. Gaps found this way point at training and equipment needs that guidelines alone cannot fix. A network that measures itself can then target help where the delivery room reality lags the textbook most.
pmc-11888720:
Pragathi Yatham and four co-authors review gene studies linking gum disease with heart disease, in a 2024 paper. Gum disease is a long-running inflammation, and heart disease is a leading killer. Shared genes might explain part of the overlap between them.

The team searched three major databases and kept sixteen studies that fit their rules. Variants in genes that steer inflammation, including two toll-like receptor genes, were tied to worse gum disease and to higher risk of blocked arteries, heart attack, and stroke. The authors argue that gene screening could one day join dental and heart care plans. They also note that the studies varied in quality, so stronger work is needed before clinics act on the findings.
pmc-11897720:
Aikeranmu Kadeer and co-authors knock out a gene in a photosynthesis bacterium and find the mutant grows faster when fed sugar. Their 2024 study uses Synechocystis, a model cyanobacterium. The missing gene makes methylglyoxal, a reactive by-product of sugar breakdown, and the team wanted to know what that pathway is for.

Under light-only growth, mutant and normal strains grew alike. Under mixed feeding, with sugar added, the mutant pulled ahead. The genes of the methylglyoxal pathway also switched on more strongly in light-only conditions, a hint the pathway matters most when the cell makes its own food. The result reframes a supposed waste route as a growth brake with a purpose.
pmc-11936320:
Laura Edison Kallen and co-authors published this commentary in 2024 on digital health tools. Digital and data technologies are being rolled out to strengthen health systems, raise efficiency, and widen care coverage, above all in low- and middle-income countries. Yet hard numbers on what these tools do for health, and what they cost for each unit of gain, remain scarce. Standard ways to measure those effects are also few.

Without such proof, governments and funders have little ground for backing the tools over the long term, and weak backing in turn threatens the tools' survival. The authors call for dedicated funding and planning aimed at building this evidence base. Better measurement, they argue, would let decision-makers hold providers to account. It would also help scarce money flow to the digital tools that earn it.
pmc-11971820:
Abiodun Ipadeola and co-authors survey what Nigerian health workers know about mosquito- and tick-borne virus infections, in a 2024 study. Arboviral diseases are often mistaken for malaria or typhoid, delaying the right care. The cross-sectional study sampled health workers in Lagos State and the Federal Capital Territory with a staged design. Three hundred ninety-five workers answered semi-structured questionnaires about the diseases and how they diagnose them.

Findings were tested for significance at the five percent level. Knowing where frontline knowledge breaks down matters because the first clinician a feverish patient meets sets the path. The survey gives training programs a map of the exact gaps, in the two most populous health systems of the country.
pmc-11975520:
Yang and co-authors test whether an anti-inflammatory protein can slow melanoma spread in living mice in this 2024 study. Malignant melanoma spreads early and kills often, so blocking metastasis matters. The protein IL-37 calms inflammation and has shown anti-tumor hints.

The team engineered mouse melanoma cells to overproduce IL-37, with empty-vector and untreated controls. They injected the cells into the veins of C57 mice, three per group, to seed lung metastases. After one month they weighed the mice and harvested lungs and other organs for counting and staining. Blot tests confirmed the engineered cells made the protein. The design isolates IL-37's effect on spread in a whole animal.
pmc-11978420:
Lucchiari and six co-authors described a case in twenty twenty-four where a return to exercise after COVID lockdown exposed a hidden muscle disease. The condition, myotonic dystrophy type 2, causes stiffness, pain, and weakness, yet it can stay silent for years.

A young woman came to an emergency room with cramps and severe muscle pain after a seven-kilometer walk that followed months of lockdown inactivity. Tests showed broad weakness, stiffness in her hands and feet, and a sharp rise in a blood marker of muscle damage. Gene testing confirmed an expansion linked to the disease, and her family was screened as well. Regular exercise, the authors argue, can mask this condition by keeping muscles conditioned. A long layoff followed by sudden effort can then trigger heavy damage. They call for care advice tuned to such hidden cases.
pmc-12008320:
Sandeep Shinde and co-workers test a multi-component exercise program for breast cancer survivors, in a 2024 study. Treatment for breast cancer can leave women with weaker muscles, poorer fitness, and worse sleep. The team asked whether a broad exercise program improves daily functional performance.

One hundred thirty-two women were split into an exercise group and a support group control. Both programs ran for a year, with tests before and after. The exercise group improved clearly on a sit-to-stand test and a twelve-minute walk test. The authors conclude the program enhanced physical performance in survivors and back its use in recovery care.
pmc-12052420:
Jerzy M Behnke and Joseph A Jackson untangle two confused names for gut nematodes of wood mice and bank voles, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The worms infect rodents used widely in disease ecology. Two species names have been muddled for over a century. Literature, host records, and naming precedence supply the evidence.

One name proves valid: a worm with a long spicule living in the small intestine of many rodents. The other name lacks any proper establishing description. It should be suppressed as a bare name or junior synonym. The stomach-dwelling morphotype in voles needs a different name entirely. A nineteen twenty-four description under another genus fits it. The authors recommend that older name for the vole stomach worm. Their ruling cleans up identification for ecologists using these hosts.
pmc-12121320:
Brian Benitez and co-authors ran a 2024 exercise study on whether men's and women's leg muscles tire in unlike ways. A surface sensor can pick up the tiny shakes muscles make as they work, and those signals shift as fatigue sets in. Older readouts caught only still parts of the signal.

Eleven men and ten women held a hard leg extension with the weaker leg until they failed. A wave-based method tracked how the signal's tone mix changed over time. Both sexes showed the same fall in mean tone and the same fade in signal strength. Time to failure did not differ by sex. When the data were pooled, the wave view showed fresh detail on how low and high tones trade off in fatigue.
pmc-12368520:
Zhihao Yue and co-authors design glue-like binders for a heat-proof glowing protein in a 2024 paper. Green fluorescent protein is a workhorse of life science, used to tag and track molecules in cells. A coral version, TGP, withstands far more heat than the classic jellyfish one. It lacks the rich toolbox of the classic version, though, including nanobodies, tiny binders cut from heavy-chain antibodies.

The team solved the crystal structure of TGP bound to a synthetic nanobody, mapping exactly where it grips. With that map and a second known complex, they placed sulfur bridge bonds between protein and binder by design. Two bridged pairs were confirmed in the lab. One pair resisted chemicals that usually break such bridges. The authors say the work widens the TGP toolkit and should spread its use.
pmc-12660320:
Reaching deep brain areas without surgery would open new ways to study and treat reward-related illness. The authors test focused ultrasound aimed at the nucleus accumbens, a small reward hub, in 26 healthy adults. Each person receives ultrasound to that hub, to a control region, or a sham treatment, then plays a probabilistic learning game inside a brain scanner. The team compares brain responses and choices across the three conditions.

Ultrasound to the accumbens changes activity tied to reward expectation in and around the hub. It also shifts behavior: how often people repeat rewarded choices, how fast they learn from rewards, and how their learning curves rise. Direct electrical stimulation of the same hub in earlier work disturbed the same features, which supports that the ultrasound hit its target. The authors present the method as a workable non-invasive route to deep-brain modulation.
pmc-12661220:
Oladé Charles Sansan and co-authors drought-test fourteen elite onion varieties in a greenhouse to find which shrug off dry spells, in a 2025 study. Onion yields suffer under water shortage, and tolerant breeding could protect dry regions. Drought was imposed at three growth stages, longest and latest at bulb development.

Growth and yield traits sagged as stress lengthened, most sharply after 25 days during bulb filling, when yield fell by about a third. The stress chemical proline rose, as expected. Three varieties, Goudami, Prema, and Red Jewel F1, held up as tolerant, while Red Creole, AVON 1074, and Safari wilted as sensitive, and three more sat between. The tolerant lines, the authors say, are breeding stock for thirstier futures.
pmc-12663220:
Piotr Szkodziak and five co-authors measure insulin resistance across the four forms of polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2025 study. The syndrome mixes hormone, ovary, and weight-related drivers. Insulin resistance ties them together. Excess male hormones, high insulin, and low levels of a binding protein feed each other in a vicious cycle that worsens every symptom.

The team reviewed 200 women aged 18 to 36 seen from 2018 to 2022. Cases were classed by standard criteria into the four forms, from the full form with all three traits to milder ones. Insulin resistance was gauged with a standard index from fasting values. Comparing the forms shows where metabolic risk concentrates, which can guide screening and weight care.
pmc-12666020:
Callum Forbes and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 that urges two health causes to join forces. One cause tracks how a warming climate harms health, using set gauges to follow the harm. The other cause builds stronger surgical systems in poor lands. Health care itself adds a large share of the gases that warm the planet, and surgery carries a heavy share of that load. Strong surgical systems can also help towns cope when climate harm strikes.

The authors propose gauges tuned to surgical care, such as the carbon cost of an operation. They call on surgeons to refine the gauges and to join national plans that build surgical care. Joining the two causes could also open funding that each cause now struggles to reach. They frame the link as a chance to cut harm from care while making care itself more able to withstand a warming world.
pmc-12669620:
Ruimin Liu and co-authors propose in 2025 a forecasting model for financial time series that blends several feature types. Prices, trading volumes, and technical indicators are combined to capture market patterns. Existing methods struggle with nonlinear links and volatile conditions, and they often lack clear explanations.

Their model turns windowed data into image form, then applies a convolutional memory network. A fuzzy control mechanism reshapes the network's input gate. Explainable AI tools are added so users can see what drives each forecast. The authors aim for better accuracy and stability in rough markets, plus clearer reasoning behind predictions.
pmc-12679720:
Marion Ludwig and co-authors report a claims study from two thousand twenty-five on the burden of three rare genetic diseases in Germany. Rare diseases are hard to study one by one, yet together they affect many people. Insurance claims offer a way to count patients and costs at national scale.

Using an anonymized claims database from two thousand seventeen to two thousand twenty-three, the team tracked Huntington's disease, beta-thalassemia, and spinal muscular atrophy type one. Rates per hundred thousand people ranged from about one to thirteen. Common side conditions matched each disease's known pattern, such as depression in Huntington's patients. Yearly direct costs per patient were near ten thousand euros for Huntington's, lower for thalassemia, and far higher, near one hundred forty-five thousand, for infantile muscular atrophy.
