The authors say claims data robustly identify such populations.
pmc-12684220:
Nicole Dorfer, Ross Bailie, and co-authors review how floods strain health care in Australia, in a 2025 review. Floods harm health in clear ways, but how they hit clinics, hospitals, and staff is less well mapped. The team searched seven large data bases for past work.

Just twenty eight works fit the review from thousands found. Most dealt with hospitals and travel blocks, and with staff who could not reach work. Less than a third dealt with groups at high risk. Gaps were large for local doctors and allied care. The team gives a frame to sort flood harms for future plans.
pmc-12690220:
Blister beetles make a toxin used in medicine, and their sense of smell guides how they find food and mates. Feng Zhou and nine co-authors cataloged the smell-related genes of one such beetle, Lytta sifanica, in a 2025 study of its antennae.

The team sequenced the active genes in adult antennae and found 70 chemosensory genes in total. The set includes binding proteins that carry odors, plus several families of receptor genes that detect them. Tests across body parts such as the head, legs, and wings showed where each gene is switched on. The catalog gives researchers a parts list for studying how this beetle reads chemical signals from its surroundings.
pmc-12691920:
Kamila Korzekwa and co-authors weigh the two faces of hyaluronic acid in infection, a sugar chain found across body tissues, in a review from 2025. The chain keeps tissues wet and whole, yet germs make it too.

Germ coats of this chain help bacteria stick, hide from immune attack, and spread. Broken chain bits, by contrast, fire up swelling signals and feed long term inflammation. The chain also shapes biofilms that shield germs from drugs, a worry for filler injections. New forms that carry germ killers may keep the gains with less risk.
pmc-12692520:
An Andean tuber called mashua could move from folk food to modern product, and a 2025 review by William Vera and co-authors surveys its promise. The review pulls together work on the tuber's nutrients, active compounds, and food uses, drawn from a broad search of the Scopus database covering 2000 to 2025.

Mashua carries glucosinolates, phenolics, and color pigments tied to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects. Methods such as freeze-drying, microencapsulation, and 3D printing can protect those compounds while shaping new foods. The tuber is hardy and underused, yet its strong taste and low profile hold it back. The authors map both the science and the hurdles for food makers.
pmc-12693020:
Agnieszka Kublińska and co-authors tune laser printing settings for a strong steel in a 2025 study. The printer fuses metal powder layer by layer with a laser. Power, speed, and layer depth together set the energy each spot gets. Samples printed under varied settings were tested for strength and flaws.

Well matched energy raised density and cut defects in the parts. Too much energy, though, made the steel brittle in the tests. Hardness and strength tracked the energy settings closely across samples. The results guide printing this steel for planes, cars, and building parts.
pmc-12694320:
Vanessa Nadia Dargenio and a large team use celiac disease in kids as a lens on gut-based poor nutrition. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. In celiac disease, the gut fails to take in food well, and a strict no-gluten diet adds its own gaps. Key gaps can last even when the gut wall heals.

Kids on the diet took in more fat and plain sugars, but too little fiber and key micro foods. No-gluten goods held less protein, spiked blood sugar more, and were less enriched than wheat goods. Gaps hurt growth, slowed teen change, and raised health risk. The team urges set blood checks, one-to-one diet help, and better no-gluten goods.
pmc-12696020:
Ines Rodrigues Lopes and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 mapping which bacterial genes Staphylococcus aureus needs to live inside ordinary body cells. The germ is famous for surface infections, but it can also hide inside cells, dodging immunity and antibiotics. The team screened a library of nearly two thousand mutants in epithelial cells over two days.

Seventy-three factors strongly shaped invasion, growth, persistence, or host damage, most never linked to the indoor lifestyle before. One enzyme stood out: it tunes a master virulence switch through the cell's redox state. The catalog gives drug hunters fresh targets against the sheltered bacterial population that standard treatment misses.
pmc-12696120:
Paula Valdés-Chiara and co-authors improve the delivery of DNA into Streptomyces, bacteria famed for making natural medicines. Their 2025 study works on the standard route: mating with a stripped-down Escherichia coli strain that passes plasmids across. The passing gear includes a helper plasmid and a gene called traJ, which builds part of the transfer machine.

Some carrier plasmids already hold an extra copy of traJ near the transfer origin, while many common ones lack it. The team rebuilt two lacking plasmids to include the gene and measured how much better they transferred into the test species. The result guides labs that struggle to edit these valuable but stubborn bacteria.
pmc-12696320:
Gil Bashe, writing from a caregiver's view in 2025, tells how his family spent decades seeking the right diagnosis for his child. The child was at last found to have three linked conditions, among them a connective tissue disorder and a pinched artery syndrome. On the long road there, doctors again and again brushed off or misread the symptoms.

Bashe works in health communications, and he argues that listening to patients is not a courtesy but a core part of care. He lays out the roadblocks that slow the hunt for rare diseases, called zebras in medical slang. His advice, drawn from lived experience, is aimed at care providers and policy makers.
pmc-12698620:
Chengxin Liu and co-authors build a gene activity atlas of the developing human brainstem, in a 2025 study. The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and runs many basic functions, yet how its genes switch on and off before birth was poorly mapped. The team cut 18 fetal brainstems, from week 9 to week 33 of pregnancy, into 107 blocks and read each block's active genes.

A network method grouped the genes into 22 modules with known roles. The team charted where and when each module runs hot, and sorted genes by the shape of their rise and fall over time. Genes tied to developmental brain disorders were confirmed as active in the tissue. The authors offer the atlas as a base resource for studying how the brainstem is built and where its disorders begin.
pmc-12699320:
Queiroz and a team including Sousa and Júnior ran a trial in twenty twenty-five on a plant gel for mouth sores in folks who get stem cell grafts. Such sores hit most graft folks, with pain, germ risk, and low life quality. Care now mostly eases pain with no heal aid.

Folks were split by chance to the gel or to a low laser care, with near two dozen in each arm. The gel group healed in near five days, less than half the laser group's time. A mild burn feel came up in some gel users but did not cut use. The gel looks safe and sound, they find.
pmc-12699720:
Jiasen He and co-authors chart immune therapy in melanoma patients young enough that data are rare: adolescents and young adults. The cohort held 136 patients, median age thirty-three, treated between 2013 and 2023. Combination checkpoint therapy hit harder than single drugs on every harm measure: more side effects overall, more severe ones, more delays and hospital stays.

Rechallenge after side effects was common, seventy-one patients, and the same organs, colon and liver, flared again most. Survival was favorable, five-year rates from 77 to 88 percent by setting, and response rates held up on rechallenge. Curiously, developing colitis or hepatitis tracked with better survival, a pattern seen in older adults too.
pmc-12699820:
Xinfang Zhang and co-authors study in 2025 how tobacco leaves react when farm waste and factory made plant food are used as one. Past work looked more at soil traits and soil life than at leaf chemistry. The team uses tobacco as a test crop to trace gene and chemical shifts in the leaf.

One mix, with cattle manure and a high carbon compost, gave the best growth of leaf hairs that guard the plant. Hair counts rose well past the food only group, and two key leaf oils rose too. Gene and chemical scans show the paths that drive those shifts in the leaf.
pmc-12699920:
Yubo Wang and co-authors build in 2025 a model that predicts a key gene fault in lung cancer from MRI trait mining. The fault guides drug choice, so a scan-based call could aid patients who cannot spare tissue. Ninety one patients split into training and check cohorts for the build.

More than seventeen hundred image traits come from two scan types per patient. Screen steps cut the pool to a core set that feeds a score. Clinic traits join that score in a chart model for the final call. Curve and calibration checks grade the tool for clinic use.
pmc-12700720:
Shahar Dubiner, writing alone in 2025, reports a striking sight from a sea survey in the Galápagos. At least fifty Elliot's storm-petrels gathered on open water to feed on a drifting piece of blubber. Scavenging at mammal carcasses is poorly documented for small seabirds. The birds pattered at the surface, picking up oil droplets rather than tearing flesh.

Dubiner suggests small-bodied birds may exploit the liquid fat fraction, a more efficient meal than tissue. The note raises questions about what senses guide the birds to such feasts. It also argues for the value of plain natural history observation in catching rare, meaningful events. The birds were Elliot's storm-petrels, among the smallest of their order.
pmc-12700820:
Lauren Babb, Maria Kulapurathazhe, and Joel Collier review in 2025 engineered materials that calm chronic inflammation where the body meets the outside world: gut, mouth, airways, and skin linings. Such materials can ferry calming drugs or actively coach immune cells. Mucosal sites fight back with barriers that shed, wash, and digest.

The review sorts recent designs by disease and by how each slips past those barriers to reach the right immune cells. Tissue specific tricks matter more than generic carriers here. Gaps in proof and delivery are flagged for the next round of work.
pmc-12703120:
Shaghayegh Moradi Alamdarloo and colleagues published a case-control study in 2025. They studied ovarian health in women with lupus. Lupus is a long-term autoimmune disease. Even moderate illness may reduce fertility over time. Ovarian reserve was measured in two standard ways. A hormone blood test gave one measure. Ultrasound follicle counts gave the other measure. One hundred fifty patients were compared with matched controls. Disease activity was scored with a standard questionnaire.

Hormone levels were clearly lower in lupus patients. Follicle counts were lower on both sides too. Average counts showed the same strong pattern. Differences were large and statistically clear throughout. The team also compared active and controlled disease. Findings support direct effects of lupus on ovaries. Fertility counseling may need to start earlier. Doctors should not wait for severe illness.
pmc-12704120:
Xinming Pan and co-authors showed in 2025 how a pig pathogen uses a toxin system to win a home in the tonsils. Streptococcus suis infects people as well as pigs, and its tonsil colonization is thought to seed later infection. How it outcompetes the local microbes there was unknown.

The focus is a large wall protein, WapA, a distant cousin of proteins other bacteria use to poison rivals with varied toxin tails. Tests using sequence analysis, protein blots, and head-to-head bacterial contests showed a toxin form tied to two partner proteins. That form reshaped the tonsil microbe mix in the pathogen's favor, in the team's results. Readers get a mechanism for a quiet first step of infection: clear the neighborhood, then settle in.
pmc-12705420:
Intrinsic capacity, the sum of a person's physical and mental abilities, anchors the World Health Organization's healthy aging plan, yet India had no tested measure of it. Arokiasamy Perianayagam and co-authors build one in this 2025 study, using a national ageing survey of 60,591 adults aged 45 and up. Fourteen items spanning thinking, movement, mood, senses, and vitality feed a scoring model.

The average score came to 69.7 out of 100, ranging from 63.4 to 77.8 across states and territories. Higher scores went with better self-rated health and fewer limits in daily life, even after accounting for wealth, schooling, and chronic illness. The authors offer the score as a ready tool for ageing research and policy across India.
pmc-12705920:
Ashenafi Betrie and eleven colleagues test whether a sedative used around heart surgery changes kidney vessel behavior in sheep, in a 2025 paper. Heart-lung bypass often injures kidneys, and dexmedetomidine had been both praised and blamed for kidney outcomes. The team's earlier work found more tubular injury with the drug, prompting a vessel-level look.

Fourteen ewes underwent two hours of bypass, half with the drug infused and half with saline. Living measurements tracked kidney blood flow and oxygen during surgery. Afterward, small kidney arteries were tested in the lab: vessels from drug-treated sheep were over twice as sensitive to a constricting agent, though maximum squeeze and relaxation stayed normal. Vessel lining looked intact in every group. The authors conclude the drug heightens constrictor sensitivity in kidney arteries without damaging their lining, a clue to the focal injury pattern.
pmc-12706220:
Maja Skov Kragsnaes and co-authors set out a 2025 plan for a review of gut-based treatments for autoimmune and inflammatory joint and tissue diseases. Gut bacteria are out of balance in many of these diseases, and the gut wall can leak more than it should.

The planned review will search major databases for trials in people with such diseases. It will cover probiotics, fecal transplants, live microbe products, and drugs meant to change gut bacteria or disease activity. The main goal is to weigh health gains against harms. The team follows standard review reporting rules, and the results should guide both care and future trials.
pmc-12706520:
Roholla Hemmati and colleagues study how body mass index influences electrocardiogram measurements in healthy people and cardiovascular patients. Their 2025 cross-sectional study was conducted at a hospital in Ilam, Iran.

Nine hundred sixty-four patients had twelve-lead heart tracings analysed alongside age, gender, height, and weight. Height and weight changes related differently to specific intervals on the tracing. One interval stayed stable with height but shortened slightly as weight rose. Other intervals lengthened modestly with body size changes. The authors conclude heart tracing parameters are influenced by body mass and may relate to cardiovascular risk. They stress maintaining healthy weight when interpreting these measurements.
pmc-12706920: Hong Jiang and co-authors present an AI platform for epidemic control in a 2025 paper. The platform, DeepSeek, is cast as a driver of early warning, trend forecasts, care tuning, and public advice. It fuses live data from case counts, social posts, and movement records, and deep learning models power the forecasts. Clear decision frames aim to keep the advice open to check. The authors flag privacy and accuracy as live challenges, yet rate the platform's promise for world health resilience as large.
pmc-12708620:
Yang Wang and six co-authors test a reshaped badminton course for school children, in a 2025 trial in China. Standard sports classes often drill one skill at a time, which may limit gains in fitness and focus. The new course was built around the fast, varied play of the sport itself. Two groups of fifth-grade pupils took part for ten weeks, three times a week. One group got the new course, and the other got the standard one.

Pupils in the new course gained more in speed, stamina, and steady focus than the standard group. Gains in bend, balance, and strength did not differ between groups. Test scores for simple reaction speed also matched. The authors urge schools to design classes with more varied, game-like play. Such designs, they say, can lift both body and mind.
pmc-12709020:
Shawahna and six co-authors compare two ways of placing dialysis needles into patients' arm shunts. One method reuses a small area, the other climbs along the vessel like a rope ladder. Their study followed 309 patients at two centers in a resource-limited health system.

About one in five patients had a complication, most often a bruise-like hematoma. Infection clustered with the area method, while high venous pressure clustered with the rope-ladder method and jugular shunts. Clots linked to female sex and rural residence. The authors call for standard protocols, better staff training, and fixes to system barriers. Careful technique choice, they argue, should match each patient's risks.
pmc-12709720:
Ruling Yang and co-authors compare two antibiotics for stubborn Mycoplasma pneumonia in children in a 2025 study from China. Cases that fail to respond to first line macrolide drugs are a growing worry, and data on backup drugs were limited. The hospital study covered children admitted in the second half of 2023. Those who failed first line treatment were grouped by the backup drug they received.

Two thirds of cases were unresponsive to the first drug, and those children had more rapid breathing and high fever. Fever after switching lasted a median of zero days in both backup drug groups, far shorter than in children kept on the first drug. Adjusted and age based checks agreed, with no clear gap between the two backups. Readers see both options perform alike.
pmc-12710720:
Shu-min Chen and co-authors report that a member of the Schlafen gene family, SLFN14, can block a key step in how HIV-1 copies itself. The family shapes cell growth and the defense against viruses, yet how its members work has stayed largely unclear.

The team show that SLFN14 grips a factor that HIV-1 needs to switch its genes fully on. By holding that factor, it stops the virus from drawing it to the viral start site, which halts viral copying. The same grip lets SLFN14 tune a set of the cell's own genes, which widens its role in cell life.
pmc-12710920:
Zehua Yan and co-authors present a 2025 study of how trace antibiotics in food help a drug-resistant staph germ settle in the human gut. Residue-level drugs and resistant germs both reach the gut through food, but their combined effect on where the germ takes hold was unclear. The team used a lab simulator of the human intestine.

They took a resistant strain of the germ from edible fish raised in aquaculture and exposed the simulated gut to it with and without residue-level drug. The study tracked how the germ colonized the gut wall lining against the free-floating space. The work speaks to food safety risks that sit below current residue limits.
pmc-12711120:
Hilal Kurt Sezer, Sibel Kucukoglu, and Murat Konak survey new parents in Turkey in a 2025 study of faith in their own skill at breastfeeding. Data were gathered face to face from one hundred fifty mothers and the same number of fathers.

Mothers scored higher than fathers on the skill scales the team used. A father's faith in his own skill was closely tied to the mother's faith in hers. Income, training on feeding, and how soon feeding first started shaped the mothers scores. For fathers, work status, past feeding practice, and whether the pregnancy was planned mattered most. The authors urge training that brings fathers in.
pmc-12712020:
Elissa Khadra and co-authors mapped this 2025 layer of gene control in acute myeloid leukemia. After a gene is read into RNA, further steps decide how much protein gets made. That layer's global role in this blood cancer was poorly known. The team paired RNA and protein measures from 44 leukemia samples to study the protein-to-RNA ratio for each gene.

Over a thousand related features fed models that explained the ratios. The patterns matched those in healthy tissues, hinting at universal rules. Some genes long invisible to protein scanners turned out to simply make little protein per RNA copy. The team released a tool, POSTCODE, that tags data sets with these features. It lets other researchers spot this hidden control layer in their own cancer data.
pmc-12713220:
Shiwei Chen, Wenling Gou, and Renzhi Gao pool studies on walking patterns after ACL reconstruction in a 2025 analysis. Surgery rebuilds the torn knee ligament, but whether gait returns to normal was unsettled. Five databases gave 5,251 records, and 21 studies with 861 people passed screening for a three level pooled model.

Six gait measures were compared with healthy controls. Only one differed clearly: the peak knee straightening angle while standing on the leg, with a large effect size. Bending angle, knee moments, stride length, and walking speed all matched controls. That angle also improved with time since surgery in a trend analysis, hinting at slow recovery.
pmc-12715220:
Noura Nayel and co-authors test whether adding electrical stimulation sharpens exercise therapy for back pain. Their 2025 trial randomized fifty young adults with chronic nonspecific low back pain to core stability exercises alone, or the same exercises plus Russian current stimulation, three times weekly for six weeks.

Both groups improved, but the combined group improved more on nearly every measure. Pain scores fell further, disability ratings dropped by about ten extra points, and spinal stability rose more. Ultrasound showed greater thickening of two deep trunk muscles that brace the spine. The authors conclude that pairing the current with core work buys extra relief and function beyond exercise alone, at least in young patients over a short program.
pmc-12716720:
Shulong Zhuo and five colleagues built a lightweight vision network that spots surface defects on phone screens, in a 2025 paper. Tiny flaws on screens are easy to miss, and heavy models run too slowly for factory lines. The team reworked the YOLOv8 detector for small targets on weak hardware.

Their version adds a context-guided feature pyramid for multi-level detail and a local attention module for sharper positioning. A new loss function steadies training, and a shared, detail-rich detection head trims size. Pruning and knowledge distillation shrank the model further. On a public phone dataset it beat the base detector by clear margins on both accuracy measures. Parameter count fell by eighty percent and computing cost by nearly two thirds. The system was deployed on an RK3568 edge device for line use.
pmc-12717420:
Six authors, led by Shahid Ganie, build in 2025 a computer model that spots and sorts breast cancer in ultrasound scans, and can show its reasons. Early finds save lives, yet reading scans by eye is slow and uneven. The team first trained six known image models on a public scan set.

Their new model stacks the three best of those models into one. Extra steps cleaned the images, masked the key area, and tuned the settings. The stacked model scored best on the test measures. A heat map method shows which part of each scan drove the call, so doctors can judge the result rather than trust it blindly.
pmc-12717820:
Eman Elayeh and colleagues review multi-omics prediction of immunotherapy response in lung cancer. Their review from twenty twenty-five spans genes, proteins, and metabolites. Checkpoint drugs help only a subset of lung cancer patients durably. Single biomarkers have not predicted responders reliably enough.

Thirty-three gene studies met the inclusion rules. Nine protein and nine metabolite studies qualified too. Each was scored on a standardised evidence rubric. Certain gene changes predicted poor response consistently. Fusion genes and mutation partners shaped outcomes as well. Combining data layers promises sharper prediction than any alone. The field still lacks large validated combined models.
pmc-12718820: Yoonjeong Na and co-authors report, in a 2025 case paper, a rare muscle problem that followed a whole body seizure in a 52 year old man. Psoas syndrome is an irritation of the deep hip muscle that causes pain and weakness in the leg. The man came to an emergency department after a seizure, with weakness in his left leg. A CT scan showed thickening of the left psoas muscle that later reversed, which fit the syndrome. The authors discuss its traits and other causes to rule out.
pmc-12719020:
Li, Cao, Yang, and Chen present a study from twenty twenty-five on gut acids that may ease depression-like behavior in rats. The acids, made by gut germs, are called short-chain fatty acids. Rats under chronic mild stress form the model for low mood. One group got the acids, one got stress alone, and one stayed as control. Behavior tests and gene-based germ surveys ran after four weeks. Treated rats showed fewer depression-like behaviors than stressed peers.

Germ mixes shifted in both mouth and gut across the groups. Treated rats had lower gut swelling and a stronger gut wall protein. Helpful germ genera rose in the treated gut as well. The authors say the acids restore balance along the mouth-gut line. They propose the acids as a base for future mood treatments.
pmc-12719220:
Simin Jamshidi and co-authors showed in 2025 that two minutes of resting brain waves can forecast which Parkinson's patients will die within three years. Death in this disease is hard to predict, since courses vary so much. Their algorithm reads a single EEG channel with a predictive coding method tuned for Parkinson's.

In ninety-four patients, several scalp channels classified three-year survival perfectly in cross-checks. The algorithm's scores also tracked time to death closely, even after accounting for age and thinking and movement scores. In fresh tests, the best five-channel mix averaged about eighty-three percent accuracy. The authors pitch cheap, short EEG as a practical prognostic tool. Such forecasts could guide care planning and trial design.
pmc-12720420:
Wei Dong and eleven co-authors review the role of DNA methyltransferases in diseases of the urinary system. These enzymes attach methyl marks to DNA, a chemical editing process that can change how genes are read without changing the code itself. Such marks shape cell behavior in health, and they go wrong in fibrosis and cancer.

The review explains how the enzymes drive gene expression changes in conditions such as kidney scarring and prostate cancer. By raising or lowering methylation at key spots, they can switch genes on or off and push disease forward. The authors also weigh the clinical promise of these enzymes as drug targets. Blocking or tuning them might one day slow these diseases. The paper sets out open questions for future research on the urinary system.
pmc-12721120:
Qiaofang Yan and co-authors hunt for early warning signs of diabetic kidney disease in a 2025 study. The disease, also called diabetic nephropathy, is the hardest complication of diabetes to manage, and doctors still lack sharp tests and strong drugs for it. Odd copper handling in the body has been tied to diabetes, so the team focused on genes linked to copper.

Working from public gene data sets, the team found five copper-linked genes that behaved differently in diseased tissue. Used together, the five markers picked out the disease with good accuracy, and some tracked how well the kidneys still filtered blood. The markers also lined up with immune cell patterns in the tissue. A drug database search turned up fifteen compounds that act on these genes, giving future treatment studies a place to start.
pmc-12721520:
Redolen Dhar and co-authors test prompt sheets that help tribal cancer patients in Meghalaya ask their doctors more, in work from 2025. Question prompt lists are short menus of questions patients may want answered. Tribal patients face language and custom barriers that mute their voice in the clinic.

Sixty patients with head, gut, or lung cancers took part. Half got the prompt sheet before visits, and half got standard care. Satisfaction with the talks was scored over two follow-ups. The sheet group rated doctors' answers and their own say higher on several counts. The authors present the cheap tool as a step toward shared decisions in tribal care.
pmc-12722220:
Peng Yuan and co-authors ask how much a bent spine segment should be straightened in a 2025 study of a common back procedure. The procedure injects cement into a crushed vertebra to ease pain from bone thinning fractures.

Records of 204 patients were split into four groups by the curve angle left after surgery. All groups started alike. Patients left with the smallest angles saw their pain and disability scores fall the most, and the group straightened to between zero and five degrees did best of all. That group had essentially recovered full function one month after the operation. The authors conclude that aiming for a nearly straight segment speeds and improves recovery.
pmc-12722320:
Yuke Liu and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 reading sun cycles in the layered muds of a Cretaceous lake in northeast China. The Songliao Basin's shale and carbonate couplets, laid down about ninety million years ago, preserve fine bands tied to oil-bearing rock. The team measured element levels and nano-scale hardness across the layers and hunted for repeating periods. Climate wiggles at these scales are blamed on the sun, but hardness had rarely joined the evidence.

Cycles near twenty to forty-eight years and seven to fifteen years matched the sun's Hale and Schwabe rhythms. A shorter rhythm near three to five years resembled the ocean-atmosphere swings of ENSO. The picture: solar shifts steer climate, climate steers the lake, and the lake writes chemistry and strength into the rock. The weak seams between layers matter, since cracks follow them during shale oil fracking.
pmc-12722720:
Hiroshi Ueno and co-authors asked whether a mother's nearby presence after weaning can shield young mice from the harms of social isolation, in a study published in 2025. Lab mice are normally weaned at three weeks, and what a watchful parent nearby does for later behavior was largely unexplored. The team housed some pups in a cage beside their mother and others without her.

After weaning, pups were raised either with littermates or alone until eight weeks, then tested for movement, anxiety, social behavior, and low mood signs. In group-raised mice, the mother's presence changed nothing. In isolated mice, it softened several changes, including overactivity and odd social responses. The authors offer the simple setup as a model for studying parental watchful presence.
pmc-12723620:
Amamnkwah and Ibrahim report a rare lymphoma that looked like a breast armpit abscess in a 31-year-old woman. Both lymph and tissue cancers can present as abscesses, which delays diagnosis. Her tumor was an anaplastic large cell lymphoma, a rare T cell type marked CD30 positive.

She first got abscess care, with repeated antibiotics and scans, yet the lump grew and hardened. A first biopsy showed only chronic inflammation, missing the cancer. Drainage surgery later gave tissue that showed odd lymph growth. Stains confirmed ALK-positive disease. Scans found a dead-tissue mass of six centimeters and a large spleen.
pmc-12723920:
Dario D'Asaro and co-authors model, in a 2025 study, how DNA copying reshapes the folded genome inside a yeast cell's nucleus. Copying and folding are each well studied, but how they influence each other in three dimensions remains unclear.

Their computer model joins a realistic genome layout with the timing of copying along each chromosome. It shows paired sister forks gathering into fountain-like shapes around early copying start sites. Fresh contact maps from living cells in early copying phase show the same shapes, and they vanish when copying is blocked. At larger scale, forks cluster at one pole of the nucleus early on, then spread out later.
pmc-12726820:
Jamie Nam and co-authors ask stroke survivors how they feel about a wrist activity tracker in a 2025 study. Wearable monitors can follow recovery at home, cheaply and minute by minute. Their value depends on patients actually wearing them. Sixty-five people with stroke wore a Fitbit Inspire 2 for three months, then rated it on a standard acceptance questionnaire.

Scores ran high across all seven dimensions, from usefulness and ease to privacy and social pressure. The median answer was agree for nearly every statement. Participants found the device helpful, simple to put on, and no burden on daily life. Yet warm ratings did not predict actual wear time in the weeks before the survey. The authors note the gap between stated acceptance and habit. They still judge the device well accepted by this group.
pmc-12726920:
Katherine Parkin and colleagues built an expert-agreed framework of risk factors for mental health problems in young people, meant to guide prediction models. Machine learning tools are only as good as the risk information fed into them, so the team drafted a prototype from the literature and stakeholder talks. They then ran three voting rounds with specialists from many fields. Experts judged the overall structure, marked when in life each risk matters most, and ranked factors inside each domain. The authors report the framework in twenty twenty-five.

The agreed framework holds several hundred risk factors across eight domains and five life stages. Social and environmental factors and psychological factors were ranked most important. Rated lists and heat maps show where each factor bites hardest across childhood and youth. Equity concerns were kept in view throughout, and the authors offer the framework as shared ground for model builders.
pmc-12727720:
Felix Snoodijk and co-authors study fossil deer from Crete that grew to very different sizes on their island, in a 2025 paper. Island life, with few predators and scarce food, often slows an animal's life pace. This slowdown was known in dwarf island deer, but not tested in island deer that grew giant instead.

The deer genus Candiacervus held dwarf, medium, and giant forms side by side. By reading growth layers in fossil bone, the team found all three sizes matured late compared with mainland deer of like size. Even the giants kept the slow pattern. The authors say this is the first such report for giant or mid-size island deer, and it widens what we know about how islands reshape a species' life history.
pmc-12727820:
Beatrice Orso and co-authors review why dementia with Lewy bodies looks so different from patient to patient, in a 2025 paper. The disease mixes thinking decline with movement and sleep symptoms, and its protein clumps can start in brain or body and spread along unlike paths. Other pathologies often ride along, including Alzheimer type plaques and tangles and vessel damage.

Genes such as APOE and GBA further shape each case. Sleep behavior disorder, mild impairment, and psychiatric first forms all appear. Brain scans help split the disease from Alzheimer's, the authors note, but reading mixed pathology stays hard, and better markers are needed.
pmc-12728420:
Benedikt Gasser, Alain Dössegger, and Martin Flück presented in 2025 a case where genetic testing solved one elderly woman's stubborn high blood pressure. She suffered repeated hypertensive emergencies during supervised exercise sessions. Several standard drugs were stopped for severe side effects or simple lack of effect. Testing two genes changed the picture.

One gene variant pointed to a higher share of fast-twitch muscle fibers. Such fibers squeeze blood vessels harder during effort, the authors reasoned. A beta-blocker, chosen on that basis, finally controlled her emergencies on its own. The authors argue that genetic information can guide drug choice when routine options fail, a common problem in older patients.
pmc-12728920:
Wei-Tse Hsu and co-authors ask whether AI predicted protein drug complexes can train scoring models that estimate binding strength, in work from twenty twenty-five. Machine learning scorers need many example complexes, and measured structures are scarce. Co-folding models can mint synthetic ones, but quality varies.

The team found that gains from synthetic training data hinge on the structural quality of the added complexes. Poor predictions drag the scorer down rather than lift it. They set simple heuristics that flag high quality predictions without any reference structure to check against. Those filtered predictions can stand in for experimental structures in training. The study guides future augmentation plans that lean on co-folding.
pmc-12729120:
Stem cells grown in the lab age as they multiply, which limits their use in medicine. Jianjian Zhuang and co-authors tested a ginseng compound, ginsenoside Rh2, against that aging in 2025. They watched the cells' power plants and recycling sacs under microscopes and tracked aging-related genes and proteins.

The compound slowed the aging of mesenchymal stem cells by switching on a protein called SIRT1. That switch tuned the cleanup of worn power plants and curbed the release of inflammatory signals that aging cells broadcast. It also steadied the recycling sacs and cut the shedding of tiny vesicles. The authors offer the compound as a practical way to keep lab-grown stem cells younger for longer.
pmc-12729320:
Joanna Slowik and six co-authors ask what makes stroke survivors' mouths, and their quality of life around them, worsen in the first three months. They followed 392 patients from a Polish stroke project who filled in a fourteen-item oral health questionnaire during the acute hospital phase and again three months after their ischemic stroke. Thirty-seven candidate factors, from scans and blood tests to mood, were tested against who deteriorated.

Nearly half the patients, 189 of 392, worsened. The strongest signals were mental rather than dental: persistent anxiety roughly tripled the odds of decline, and worsening anxiety or depression after the stroke carried similar weight. A higher platelet count also nudged risk up slightly. The authors argue that protecting oral health-related quality of life after stroke means watching mood at least as closely as teeth, since anxiety and depression track the decline so strongly.
pmc-12729820:
Shaohui Geng and co-authors test whether alternating current can speed the healing of broken bones, in a 2025 study in rabbits. Broken bones are a heavy burden for patients, and faster healing would ease it. The team broke bones in rabbits, applied the current, and tracked healing with X-rays, fine scans, and tissue stains. They also treated bone-forming cells in dishes.

By two weeks, treated bones showed more new bone and better shaping, with gains visible in the first days. Treated tissue held more of two proteins linked to bone growth and blood vessel growth. In dishes, the current pushed cells to mature and lay down mineral. Gene tests pointed to shifts in key bone genes, which the authors read as a sign the method could help patients heal faster.
pmc-12730020:
Mario Candela Andrade and co-authors dissect the joint capsule of dogs with two common inherited knee problems: a slipping kneecap and a torn cruciate ligament. Their study appeared in 2025. Capsule tissue came from dogs having corrective surgery, with healthy comparison tissue from dogs treated for unrelated problems. Under the microscope the team counted lining cell layers, villi, and the state of the capsule's three layers, then linked the patterns to disease type, duration, sex, age, breed, and weight.

Diseased joints showed extra lining cell layers. Chronic cases grew fewer villi, and a missing middle layer tracked with kneecap disease and long lameness. The authors say the capsule quietly records the joint's history, and reading it may refine how these dogs are staged and treated.
pmc-12730720:
Dev Pradeepkumar Nayak, Ali Tarokh, and Muhammad Saif Ullah Khalid compare active and passive tails in swimming robots in work from 2025. Fish swim by body and fin motion, but whether a freely pitching tail helps was unresolved.

Simulations varied joint stiffness, damping, and inertia at two flow speeds. Active tails gave more thrust overall. Passive tails used less power at the low speed, and a few passive cases did well even at the high speed. Larger swings helped only with higher beat frequency. The authors draw design rules by swimmer size.
pmc-12731020:
A team led by Abdulmohsen Ahmed Alhussaini studied liver cancer care at one center. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at a treatment called TARE. It asks if a faster way of running care helped patients live longer. The new way is called the Order-Map-Treat plan. It puts the whole path from the first choice to treatment into one stay.

The team looked back at one hundred eighty-five patients. Eighty-eight had care before the plan began, and ninety-seven had care after. The new plan cut the wait from choice to treatment by a large amount. Readers learn how a change in how care is run can shape the time patients wait for cancer treatment.
pmc-12732220:
Yeji Lee and co-authors study how a plant compound kills skin melanoma cells in 2025. The work uses team framing since the head byline is shorter than the catalog list. Melanoma spreads fast and resists many drugs. The compound is a natural product found in grapes and berries. It targets two enzymes that drive sugar burning in cancer cells.

In two melanoma cell lines, the compound cut both enzymes in level and activity. Energy output fell, and sugar based metabolism slowed. Two death paths switched on at once: a planned cell death and a burst form. Cell growth paused in an early phase. Effects were stronger in one cell line, tied to its sugar traits. The authors propose the compound as a metabolism based therapy lead.
pmc-12732420:
Kuzan and nine co-authors measured the mineral content of placentas in this two thousand twenty-five study from Lower Silesia in Poland. The placenta feeds the baby during pregnancy and is normally discarded, yet its chemistry can reveal how mother and child were nourished.

The team analyzed thirty-three placentas for ten elements, from calcium and iron to heavy metals, and compared levels with mothers' blood results and newborn measures. Element levels moved together in clear pairs, and some tracked blood values like hemoglobin. No heavy metals were found, and mineral levels did not track smoking, diabetes, or birth weight. The authors advise watching several minerals, not just iron, to guard against anemia in pregnancy.
pmc-12732620:
Four authors present a first lab study in two thousand twenty-five on a plant extract against a hard-to-treat bacterium. The plant is Arnica montana, long known for varied effects on living tissue. The bacterium, Acinetobacter baumannii, resists more and more antibiotics and forms biofilms, slimy layers that protect it.

The team tested alcohol-based and water-based extracts of the flowers. They found the lowest doses that stopped growth and that killed the bacterium. They also checked whether the alcohol extract kept biofilms from forming. Last, they measured how genes tied to biofilm building changed after doses too low to stop growth.
pmc-12732720:
Ching-Feng Cheng and co-authors published this liver study in 2025. Fatty liver tied to poor metabolism is spreading with obesity, and good drugs are scarce. The team tested a compound called ST32db, which switches on a gene named ATF3. They asked whether that switch could cut fat build-up in liver cells and in mice.

In dish-grown liver cells fed a fatty acid, the compound cut stored fat and muted genes that build fat. It also raised a gene for an enzyme that breaks fat down. In mice fed a rich diet for eighteen weeks, treated animals had lighter livers and less fat in the blood and liver. Two energy-sensing pathways in the liver ran hotter. The authors say the compound may shield the liver through those pathways.
pmc-12733020:
Alexander Haide Joechner and co-authors published a review in 2025 on modular CAR T cells, a flexible form of cancer cell therapy. Approved CAR T treatments rearm a patient's own T cells against a tumor, but each design is fixed to one target. Modular versions split the job: the cell carries a receiver, and a separate adaptor molecule connects it to the cancer.

Because adaptors can be swapped or mixed, one batch of cells can aim at several targets or follow logic rules. The review walks through the design choices that matter, from binding strength to adaptor size and shape. It also weighs safety and control gains against direct designs. The field matters beyond cancer, with autoimmune disease in view.
pmc-12733220:
Anastasia Mutovina and seven colleagues study how a history of aggression changes the way mice handle inflammation, in a 2025 paper. Male mice with long aggressive experience, about a third of whom turned pathologically aggressive, received repeated doses of LPS, a bacterial compound that triggers inflammation. The team tracked blood counts, activity, brain immune cells, and gene expression.

The aggressive mice cleared inflammation from their blood within five days, while control mice stayed inflamed. Their brain microglia also settled back to a resting state faster, and genes tied to resolving inflammation rose. The aggression itself did not change. The authors link the pattern partly to dopamine signaling in two brain regions.
pmc-12733520:
Federica Lo Muzio and seven co-authors test pomegranate peel extracts against a stored-grain pest in a 2025 study. The granary weevil eats into wheat stocks worldwide, and chemical sprays raise safety and resistance worries. Pomegranate peel, a juice-industry waste, is rich in active plant compounds that might do the job more gently.

Peels were extracted with three solvents and tested on adult weevils for killing power by touch and by feeding, plus repellent and feeding-deterrent effects. The acetone and hexane extracts killed half the weevils at low doses within a day. At the highest feeding dose, the acetone extract cut feeding by about 80 percent and slashed food intake. Waste peels could thus yield a store-room protectant.
pmc-12734020:
Shanti Narasimhan leads a team of eleven in a 2025 study on virtual reality for heart defects present at birth. Some defects sit outside the heart itself, in the great vessels or nearby parts, and flat scans can be hard to read. The team turned scans into 3D models that staff could walk around in.

Nine child patients were covered, with faults such as double aortic arch, vessel rings, and growths near the heart. The models were shown at weekly heart center meetings. In a staff survey, all who replied called virtual reality a useful tool, and it stood alongside standard scans in daily work.
pmc-12734420:
The thin separator inside a lithium battery keeps its poles apart while letting ions through, and today's plastic versions melt too easily and drink electrolyte poorly. Chi Chen, Boqiao Li, and Chong Zhao review a renewable challenger: separators woven from biomass fibres such as cellulose. These plant-based sheets wet better, tolerate more heat, and come from abundant natural sources at lower material cost.

The review gathers recent work on making and testing such separators in working batteries. Their promise rests on matching the plastic incumbents' strength while beating their safety and sustainability. The authors look ahead to development paths and offer the survey as a reference for researchers steering battery parts away from petroleum.
pmc-12734720:
Alberto Pasetto and co-authors tested how shaking bases affect piezoelectric wind energy harvesters in a 2025 study. These harvesters flex in the wind and turn the motion into small amounts of electricity, with no rotating parts. In real placements, from bridges to poles, the base itself also vibrates, sometimes randomly.

Working with co-authors as a team, the study combined wind excitation with band-limited random base vibration. It varied the bandwidth of the shaking to see when it helps output and when it hurts. Harvesters powering remote sensors need every microwatt, so knowing whether ambient shaking is friend or foe shapes mounting design. The results fill a gap between clean lab tests and messy field sites.
pmc-12734820:
Metal foam soaks up sound, but plain aluminum foam has a weak band in the middle frequencies. Bei Huang and co-authors wove stainless steel fibers through the foam's pores to fix that dip. They grew the fibers inside a salt template, then infiltrated the structure with aluminum and washed the salt away. The result is a network where fibers and pores interlock.

The composite absorbed sound far better across the speech and machinery range. Its weakest point still absorbed most incoming sound, and averages rose about ten percent over plain foam. Simulations showed why: fibers reroute air flow, add surface area, and strengthen the friction and heat effects that drain sound energy. The design suits noise control panels.
pmc-12734920:
Valentin Mishev and co-authors sprayed atom-thin layered coatings onto stainless steel and tested their toughness, in a 2025 study. The stack alternates chromium with chromium-and-carbon layers, laid by magnetron sputtering onto two steel grades. Total thickness stayed under two micrometers. Chemical checks confirmed the recipe, and indentation tests probed adhesion and hardness.

Spectroscopy suggested a diamond-like carbon phase forms inside, explaining the strength gains. The coated steels came out harder than the bare metal. Such skins could armor parts against wear while adding almost no bulk. The work details growth settings and the test evidence side by side.
pmc-12735220:
Polyimides are heat-proof plastics used in microelectronics, and their glass transition temperature decides where they can serve. Cui and co-authors build a model that predicts this temperature from molecular structure, and just as much, explains itself.

From a curated dataset they used a genetic algorithm with linear regression to pick seven molecular descriptors, numbers that summarize shape and charge. The model predicted well on new cases and passed strict statistical checks. The authors then read the descriptors through free volume theory: some, by branching the molecule, open gaps that lower the transition point, while charge-related ones act through forces between chains. The paper turns those readings into design rules for making polyimides that run hotter, or that process more easily.
pmc-12735320:
Guna Bīlande and co-authors report six-month results after weight-loss surgery in Latvia in a 2025 study. Such surgery treats severe obesity well, but local outcomes had not been studied. Seventeen adults at one Riga centre were checked before surgery and again half a year later.

Body mass index fell from about forty to about thirty-two, a total weight loss near twenty-three percent. Quality of life scores rose clearly over the same span. Reports of high blood pressure and sleep apnoea dropped, and every patient with reflux symptoms saw them end. Hair loss was the most common side effect. The authors call the findings exploratory, given the small, single-centre sample.
pmc-12736120:
Zaihui Zhang and co-authors run the first human trial of an AXL-blocking cancer drug, SLC-391, in a 2025 study. The AXL receptor helps tumors grow, spread, dodge immunity, and resist therapy, making it an inviting target. The oral drug had already shown punch in lab models.

Thirty-five patients with advanced solid tumors took rising daily or twice-daily doses in three-week cycles. The drug was generally well tolerated, and no maximum tolerated dose was reached. A few severe side effects clustered at the highest doses. Blood levels rose with dose and steadied by the third week. Twelve patients held stable disease, some for nearly a year. A mid-range twice-daily dose looked cleanest for further trials.
pmc-12736320:
The authors explore in a 2025 article whether white-rot fungi can clean farm soil amendments made from animal waste before they reach fields. Such amendments feed crops but can carry dangerous germs, and dust from nearby feedlots adds risk, with crops beside one feedlot shown to pick up a harmful strain traced to the cattle. Little is known about how these germs behave in amended soil.

Filtering water through fungal mats, called mycofiltration, is their candidate fix. White-rot fungi digest a wide range of pollutants and have curbed that same germ in reactor tests. A cheap fungus filter on farms, they argue, could cut the routes by which germs reach the edible crop.
pmc-12736520:
Elena Krivina and co-authors test how to split kinds in a green microalga clan in a 2025 paper. The clan is well dug yet its true spread of kinds stays dim, as does its use in trade. One strain from far north soil in the Russian north was the test case.

Its shape, its place on the kin tree from a long gene span, and the folds of two spacer spans all set it apart. One matched base swap in a kept fold sealed the case. The team names it a new kind. Alga teams gain a check on which tests draw true lines.
pmc-12736820:
Hilário Júnior de Almeida and co-authors test whether silicon softens ammonium stress in young maize plants, in a 2025 study. Heavy nitrogen feeding can pile up ammonium, which harms tender seedlings, and silicon has been floated as a shield.

Seedlings grew in nutrient solution at five nitrogen levels, with or without added silicon. The team tracked growth, leaf area, root shape, and how well plants took up and used nitrogen. Silicon lifted a key enzyme's activity, greened the leaves, and widened leaf area. It also eased a stress marker in roots and shoots. A mid-high nitrogen level paired with silicon gave the best uptake and growth.
pmc-12737120:
Yu Zou and his team compared two types of japonica rice grown with low nitrogen in two thousand twenty-five. Nitrogen is a key plant food, but too much farm use harms soil and water. Rice types also differ in how well they use what little nitrogen they get.

Low nitrogen cut root growth and slowed key root enzymes in both types. One type, HJ753, kept higher enzyme levels than the other, DJ8, in both low and normal feeds. Gene reads from the roots found over five thousand genes that changed with low nitrogen. The changed genes sat in paths for growth, defence, and nitrogen use. The authors say these gaps may help breed rice that needs less feed.
pmc-12737220:
Radar can measure heart rate without touching the body, but sorting out several people at once is hard. Dong and co-authors propose a full scheme for that case. A precise range method locates each person, an antenna array with a root-MUSIC algorithm finds their angles, and a chained signal-cleaning method pulls out each heartbeat.

A faster version of an interpolation method then reads the heart rates with about 60 percent less compute time. In six test setups, including people packed close and blocking each other, the scheme kept its average error under 2.6 beats per minute. The authors see uses in health monitoring and other fields.
pmc-12737520:
Haesung Jeon and Choongho Lee review a protein that can help or hinder viruses depending on the setting, in a 2025 paper. The protein, A20, edits ubiquitin tags and mainly reins in inflammation and cell death through a central signaling pathway. During infection it cuts both ways. Sometimes it dulls antiviral defenses and lets a virus thrive; other times it shields the host by preventing immune damage.

The review gathers findings on what tips the balance. The virus's own makeup matters, as do the cell type infected and the stage of infection. Early and late roles can even oppose each other. The authors propose a framework that treats A20 as a dynamic regulator, balancing pathogen clearance against tissue protection. They aim the synthesis at researchers designing therapies that touch this pathway.
pmc-12737620:
Zhaoxing Sun and co-authors test a cancer-killing virus against liver cancer cells grown in the lab. The virus, an adenovirus, was engineered in earlier work to carry apoptin, a protein from a chicken virus. Apoptin is known for forcing cancer cells to die while leaving normal cells unharmed.

The team treated Hep3B liver cancer cells with the virus and ran a battery of tests. Treated cells grew more slowly, moved less, and invaded less than untreated cells. Many showed signs of programmed cell death, and their inner power stations lost strength. Levels of proteins tied to stem-like behavior and to spread also fell. The effects grew stronger with higher doses and longer exposure. The authors say the virus shows promise as a future treatment for this cancer, though the work so far is in cells only.
pmc-12738620:
Amado and co-authors test a plasma device on wheat seeds in this 2025 study. Cold plasma is a stream of charged gas that can wake seeds up without heat or chemicals. Their setup dips the electrodes in salt water and adds double glass insulation. Spring wheat seeds were treated for set times at three voltage levels.

Short bursts of twenty to thirty seconds lifted sprouting to near ninety-eight percent. Untreated seeds sprouted at under half that rate. Longer bursts or the highest voltage cut the gains, likely from too much oxidative stress. The plasma made seed coats wetter and easier for water to enter. The design could scale up as a clean seed treatment for farms.
pmc-12740920:
Yanan Ji and co-authors review how macrophages, a type of immune cell, shift form, in a 2025 paper. These cells can lean toward attack or toward repair, but the review stresses that their states form a spectrum, not just two poles. Local signals around the cell steer which way it leans.

Signal paths, fuel use, and gene marks all work together to set and hold each state. Attack leaning cells burn sugar fast, while repair leaning cells favor other fuels. When the balance goes wrong, many diseases follow. The review sorts drug ideas that aim to push the cells back toward a healthy mix, from small drugs to fuel based tools.
pmc-12742120: A correction notice fixes two vaccine prices in a study of how China finances new additions to its national immunisation programme. In the China 2024 column of the prices table, the BCG vaccine should read US$0.69 per dose instead of US$3.44. The diphtheria-tetanus vaccine should read US$0.09 instead of US$0.36. Both errors stemmed from a miscalculation. The notice states that the mistakes are confined to that table and leave the study's main findings, analyses, and conclusions untouched.
pmc-12743020:
Seven authors describe a simple surgical technique to stop internal hernias after colon surgery in this 2025 paper. An internal hernia, where bowel slips through a gap left by surgery, is rare after keyhole colorectal resection but can block the bowel and threaten life.

Their method frees the upper small intestine fully. It then aligns it and stitches it to fatty tags on the rebuilt left colon lining, closing the risky gap by layout rather than by suturing the defect shut. In twenty-five patients treated from November 2024 to February 2025, follow-up scans at three to six months found no hernias. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the gain.
pmc-12743620:
Olorunleke Arokoyo, India Rees, Lauren Bolton, and Frank Agada review in 2025 hospital stay length after full or completion thyroid removal at one United Kingdom center. First-time half removal is lower risk and often done as day care. Full removal carries more risk and more often needs a hospital stay.

The review covers one hundred thirty seven cases over four years at a district hospital. Stays were grouped from under one day to three days or more, and problems within thirty days were tracked. Nineteen patients left in under a day, while the largest group stayed one to two days. The data help the center judge safe discharge timing.
pmc-12744320:
Mahmoud Mersal and co-authors audited how well a Birmingham hospital followed its own rules for infection-blocking drugs after hip surgery, in a 2025 study. The surgery replaced the hip joint in patients with a broken thigh bone near the hip. Rules called for three doses of a set drug after surgery, with a swap for patients who cannot take penicillin. The audit covered two months of care in late 2023.

The team checked records for one hundred seventy-nine patients. About five in six got drugs after surgery, and one in six got none. The main drug was used most often, and about seven in ten of its users got all three doses. The audit shows a clear gap between the rule and daily practice, which the authors link to the risk of joint and skin infection after surgery.
pmc-12745020:
Thi Thu Tra Vu and co-authors survey rabies knowledge in Hung Yen province, Vietnam, in a 2025 study. Rabies kills nearly 59,000 people a year worldwide, and almost all cases come from dog bites. Vietnam aims to reach zero human deaths by 2030, a goal that depends on what dog owners know and do.

The team asked 210 people in three districts about rabies and how they keep their dogs. Most had heard of rabies, and most knew that dog bites spread it. Gaps showed too: many did not know scratches can infect, and over half held at least one wrong belief. The authors use the gaps to point One Health programs at the habits that most need to change.
pmc-12745320:
Sihan Wang and co-authors select a DNA strand that binds a mold toxin in 2025. The toxin, patulin, can spoil fruit juices, and it is hard to raise antibodies against it. A short DNA strand that sticks to it could form the base of a quick test.

After twenty rounds of selection, the best strand bound the toxin well and ignored nine other drugs. The team built a glow-based test with no labels that could sense the toxin in juice. The test worked in blended juice despite other compounds present. The authors show the approach suits targets that resist antibody methods.
pmc-12747120:
Pywell S and co-authors present a 2025 study on teaching nature-based social prescribing to allied health students. In this approach, clinicians link patients to outdoor and community activities that support health. Health workers in the United Kingdom need grounding in public health, fairness, and connection with nature, yet teaching guidance is thin.

The team used a group concept mapping method with thirty-eight stakeholders. Together they sorted statements about what the training should contain and how it should be taught, in person and online. Forty of one hundred statements were rated highly relevant. Stakeholders stressed direct time in nature for students, plus work with community groups, alongside classroom teaching. The study produced checklist items for course design.
pmc-12748620:
Bahatdin Daşbaşi modeled in 2025 how nine school problems feed into Turkish students' scores on the international PISA tests in math, science, and reading. Two modeling styles faced off: a neural network and a system of differential equations tracking twelve variables over time. Both were fit by least squares and judged by standard error scores.

Both approaches fit the national data closely, as expected for smooth, aggregated series. The neural network edged ahead with slightly lower errors. A fancier fractional-order version added nothing. Sensitivity analysis through the network ranked which school problems sway each score most. The equations then projected short-term score paths for Türkiye. Daşbaşi presents the forecasts as math extensions of past trends, not promises.
pmc-12748820:
N Ikken and co-authors design a two-way quantum teleportation scheme in a 2025 physics paper. Standard teleportation sends a quantum state one way. Their protocol lets two users swap states at once, driven by a quantum walk on a three-part system with position and coin parts.

States are encoded in light-like coherent forms, recast into an even-odd basis for clean fidelity math. Closed formulas give the fidelity in both directions. A discrete-event simulator then stress-tested the scheme on large networks with photon loss, memory decay, and swapping wear. Two-way swapping kept strong fidelity on high-capacity, large networks, at greater resource cost than one-way sending. The authors weigh that trade for future quantum networks.
pmc-12748920:
Xudong Peng and co-authors report a solid-state lithium metal battery cell that stores far more energy per kilogram than today's lithium-ion cells, in a 2025 paper. Such energy density matters for electric aircraft and ships, but pushing lithium metal cells past 600 watt-hours per kilogram has proved hard. The team pairs a gel-based solid electrolyte with a treated lithium surface.

Their gel forms in place and traps loose solvent molecules that would otherwise attack the cell. A graded polymer coat on the lithium guides smooth metal plating and shields it from air and moisture during handling. The resulting pouch cell, at a practical 11 amp-hour size, reached about 604 watt-hours per kilogram. It ran more than 100 cycles while keeping about 93 percent of its energy, on a lean supply of electrolyte.
pmc-12749120:
Won-Taek Oh and co-authors describe in 2025 a keyhole repair for torn wrist cartilage and report one-year results. The torn part, at the wrist's edge, steadies the forearm joint. Their method passes two suture strands through a single bone tunnel, with no anchor hardware.

Forty-eight patients were followed for at least a year. Pain scores fell from 7.2 to 1.9 on a ten-point scale. Grip strength and wrist function scores rose clearly, and no joint looseness could be felt on testing. No surgery-related complications occurred. Waiting longer before surgery and a tilted bone measure predicted slightly worse function. The authors note that longer follow-up is needed to judge durability.
pmc-12749720:
Jiahao Fang and three co-authors build a one-kilometer map dataset that traces the full gradient from city to wild land across Southwest China. Older datasets split land into just urban and rural, missing suburbs and natural areas and their roles. The team fused built-surface and farmland data, then applied a pattern analysis to class each cell as urban, suburban, rural, or natural, year by year.

Checks against published products showed strong agreement, with average fit scores above 0.8, and cleaner spatial wholeness than a three-source reference set. Suburban cells matched social and economic data less tightly than urban ones, reflecting suburbs' mixed nature. Natural areas aligned well with nature reserves. The authors offer the dataset for tracking how landscapes change and for judging sustainability goals with finer grain.
pmc-12750820:
Yang Lu leads a team on work values, pay, and health in China. Their study from twenty twenty-five surveys health care workers. Staff there face low pay and poor health at once.

The survey spanned many hospitals and thousands of workers. Work values guide good practice, but pay gains were less known. Strong values went with higher pay in their models. They also went with better self rated health by a lot. Extra stats tools checked that the links were not false. Gaps by age and job type are also probed.
pmc-12751420:
Jiahao Li and nine colleagues tested lab-made reproductive hormones for improving pig breeding efficiency. The team synthesized pig follicle-stimulating hormone and human chorionic gonadotropin. The combination was tried for inducing puberty in young gilts and for triggering estrus and ovulation in sows. Standard commercial hormone products served as comparisons. Hormone blood profiles checked whether treated gilts matured like naturally cycling animals.

At the tested doses, about seventy-seven percent of gilts reached puberty between 160 and 175 days of age. Ovarian cysts were significantly less frequent than with the standard products. In sows, estrus induction matched the standards, again with fewer cysts in one comparison. Litters grew larger and piglets needed fewer nursing days. A higher dose for ovulation induction raised farrowing rates. The twenty twenty-five results favor the synthetic pair.
pmc-12751520:
Zhihao Wei and four co-authors study immune clusters in breast tumors and what they mean after chemotherapy, in a 2025 study. The clusters, called tertiary lymphoid structures, are small lymph-like groups that form inside tumors. The team counted them in tumor samples from hundreds of patients, some treated with chemotherapy before surgery and some not. They also checked paired samples taken before and after treatment in a small group.

The clusters grew more common after chemotherapy. Patients with many clusters had less cancer left in the armpit lymph nodes after treatment. Gene scores for the clusters ran higher in patients whose armpit disease fully cleared. Vessel growth near tumors tracked with cluster counts as well. The authors tie the clusters to a stronger local immune response after treatment.
pmc-12751620:
Xi Zhang and a large team trace a chain of gene control that helps an eye cancer spread, in a study published in 2025. Choroidal melanoma often metastasizes, and its cells' membrane fluidity, set by fat metabolism, influences how invasive they are. The chain starts with a factor called MAFG, which switches on an enzyme that tags RNA, which in turn raises SCD1, an enzyme that shapes fatty acids.

Profiling patient samples and cells showed SCD1 driving progression through membrane lipid pathways, with more SCD1 making membranes more fluid and cells more invasive. In mice, blocking SCD1 with the drug aramchol, combined with a stearate-rich diet, markedly suppressed distant spread. The axis gives drug developers three linked targets in one pathway.
pmc-12751720:
Dilara Pirhan and four co-authors review outcomes after surgery for cataracts present at birth, in a 2025 study. Long term data on vision and eye movement after such surgery are limited. The team drew on their clinic database covering 143 children and 233 eyes.

Children were followed for a median of six years after surgery and lens implantation. Final vision was far better in children with cataracts in both eyes than in those with one affected eye. Crossed eyes became more common after surgery in both groups, and a shifting focus toward near sight occurred in over a third of eyes. Sticking with glasses or contact lenses was higher in the both eyes group. The analysis searches for factors that predict final vision.
pmc-12751920:
Che-Yuan Wu and co-authors compare dementia risk across three diabetes drug classes in a 2025 population cohort study. Adults over sixty with type two diabetes were followed in United Kingdom primary care records. Three pairwise comparisons pitted the drug classes against each other, with matched initiators in each pair.

Tens of thousands of matched pairs entered each comparison. The main outcome was new all cause dementia, analyzed by intention to treat, with a secondary analysis for continuous use. In the main analysis, dementia risk did not differ between the first pair of drug classes. Full pairwise results and follow up analyses are reported.
pmc-12752120:
Morag J Andrew and co-authors set out a trial plan in a 2025 protocol on feeding for high risk newborns. Babies born very early, before 28 weeks, and full term babies with brain harm from low oxygen face higher risk of later learning problems. Early feeds with key fats and nutrients might support brain growth in that window.

The UK trial, called DOLFIN, will test a long term feed supplement across many centers. Babies are placed at random into groups, with staff blind to who gets what. Growth of thinking and learning skills is the main outcome of interest. The protocol spells out who joins, what is fed, and how results will be judged.
pmc-12753520:
Ying-ping Hu, Guo-dong Lu, Dong-mei Lin, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It finds two bacteria living inside upland rice that can battle Fusarium head blight fungus, a major cereal enemy, with chemical weapons of their own.

The team screened the rice's inner microbes against the fungus in paired dishes. Two strains, a Pseudomonas and a Bacillus subtilis, blocked fungal growth by about seventy and seventy-six percent. Their suspensions also rescued infected seedlings within a week. Chemical analysis credited two arsenals: fatty lipopeptide extracts that stunted the fungus's threads, and volatile compounds drifting through air that did the same. Microscopy showed the damage up close. The authors present the pair as seedling bodyguards for breeding and biocontrol programs, potentially cutting fungicide use in the field.
pmc-12753620:
Anjana Jadhav, Aravind J, and Trupti Patel review how viruses can be turned into cancer drugs in 2025. Some viruses kill cancer cells while doing far less harm to healthy tissue than standard care does. Doctors have long noted tumors shrinking after a viral illness, and new tools now let labs shape viruses for care.

The review explains how these viruses attack tumors and how labs tune them to be safer and more exact. It covers ways to boost their effect and pairs them with other forms of care. Early trial results for some viruses are noted, along with newer work such as plant virus particles used in mammals.
pmc-12753820:
KyungYi Kim and seven colleagues modeled whether artificial intelligence makes lung cancer screening pay off in South Korea. AI can sharpen screening accuracy, but its economic value was unproven. The team built a decision model comparing five strategies: no screening, chest X-ray alone, AI-assisted X-ray, low-dose CT, and AI-assisted CT. Hypothetical cohorts of ten thousand people were followed over a lifetime. Costs and quality-adjusted life years were projected.

AI-assisted chest X-ray cost between about eighty-seven hundred and ten thousand dollars per quality-adjusted life year gained. That sat comfortably below the national willingness-to-pay threshold across all age groups. Plain X-ray looked worse, and CT strategies exceeded the threshold. The twenty twenty-five analysis supports adding AI reading to X-ray screening as a scalable national option.
pmc-12753920:
Jiating Sun and co-authors wrote this 2025 review on using a bird virus to fight cancer. Newcastle disease virus can infect and burst tumor cells while also waking the immune system against the cancer. The natural virus, though, works unevenly, so researchers have rebuilt it with genetic tools.

Engineered versions drop unneeded viral genes or gain added genes that boost the attack. These versions stir stronger immune signals in and around tumors. The review covers design strategies, how the viruses kill cancer, clinical use so far, and pairings with other treatments. It also lists open problems, from delivery routes to tumors that dodge the virus.
pmc-12754820:
Khaled El-Atawi and four co-authors measure what a workshop on the newborn golden hour did for staff knowledge at a large Dubai maternity hospital. Their 2025 study explains that the first hour of life is a critical window: warmth, breathing support, glucose checks, and early feeding in that hour steady the newborn and cut complications. Guidelines exist, but knowledge gaps among providers still vary the care babies get.

Nurses across the hospital took the workshop between February and November 2024 and were tested before and after. The share with good knowledge rose from twelve percent to seventy-six percent, with a further quarter reaching the top bands after training. Staff in intensive care and emergency units scored highest, as did those in their late thirties and forties. The authors read the result as proof that structured workshops raise readiness for this vital hour.
pmc-12754920:
Why did some patients fall far sicker with COVID-19 than others? Yongjie Xu and co-authors check one suspect: blood group. Their 2025 study looks back at patients held in a hospital in Fujian, China, during a two-month wave from December 2022 to January 2023.

Staff pulled records on each patient's blood group, lab tests, illness level on arrival, and final outcome. The team then compared health profiles and risk traits across the blood groups to see whether any group fared worse. Blood type has drawn wide interest as a trait that might shape both the chance of catching the virus and the course of the illness. The study adds local data to that debate, drawn from a single centre and a short window.
pmc-12755820:
Ian C Murphy and co-authors audit how deeply America's veterans hospitals sedated ventilated patients during COVID-19, in this 2025 evaluation. Early pandemic reports suggested COVID patients needed far heavier sedation than guidelines recommend. Practice drifted, and this study measures how far, across 13 VA intensive care units.

Charts of patients ventilated at least two days were compared before and during the pandemic. Use of fentanyl, midazolam, and propofol all rose. Median fentanyl doses climbed from 1,575 micrograms before COVID to about 1,900 in each pandemic year. Antipsychotic add-ons crept upward too, and most patients started on them in the unit stayed on them after the breathing tube came out. Mortality rose from 26.9 percent to roughly 36 percent. Among COVID-positive patients, fentanyl use was nearly universal.
pmc-12756220:
Qing Li and Jianxia Yin present a study from twenty twenty-five on how to rank swimming strokes with a formal decision method. Tech has sharpened swim training, yet the best stroke stays hard to call. Experts clash and hedge in their views. The team builds a frame that holds both hedged and two sided views, then ranks by grey relational scores.

Five strokes face four tests: speed, energy use, smoothness, and breath ease. Experts in the frame ranked butterfly as the most fit stroke. The authors say the frame makes sports calls less vague and more open to check. Gaps named are reliance on expert views and stale data as gear shifts fast.
pmc-12756920:
Dmitry Lapkin and a large team of co-authors watch defects move and heal inside supercrystalline nanocomposites, in a two thousand twenty-five materials paper. These materials assemble nanoparticles into crystal-like superlattices with unusual properties, and heat cross-linking makes them very strong.

X-ray analysis and in situ electron microscopy tracked each step of the work. Pressing pellets warped the superlattice; emulsion assembly created supraparticles with stacking faults. Heating then migrated and healed those faults, backed by molecular dynamics model runs, while grain boundaries shifted through moving disconnections. The authors show how processing writes, moves, and erases defects at the tens-of-nanometers scale, knowledge needed to make these composites reliably.
pmc-12757420:
Zhen Tian and co-authors measured, in a 2025 study, how common frailty is among hospital patients with Sjögren's disease. The autoimmune disease dries the eyes and mouth and can inflame the whole body. Frailty, a state of weak reserve, had not been charted in this group.

At one Beijing hospital, 180 patients were graded on five signs: weight loss, exhaustion, low activity, slowness, and weakness. Twenty-seven percent counted as frail and 49 percent as pre-frail.
