Blood inflammation, disease activity scores, and patient-reported burden each raised frailty odds on their own. The authors urge routine frailty checks in this clinic population, above all when inflammation runs high. Early action may protect strength and independence.
pmc-12764820:
Tunahan Haciimamoglu and three co-authors study how climate change affects tea yields in Turkiye. Tea is a key crop for the eastern Black Sea region and for rural incomes there. The study covers five tea growing provinces from 2004 to 2022.

Two methods are combined for the first time in this setting, a quantile regression method and machine learning. Both point to the same broad pattern. Higher temperature and rainfall raise yields in the data, while higher humidity lowers them. Farmed area is the strongest factor in the machine learning results, and humidity is the weakest. The authors urge joint farm policies for the five provinces, with a focus on moisture control.
pmc-12765320:
Marking points on a 3D face scan by hand is slow and varies between experts, yet clinics need those points to plan tooth and jaw care. Yongwei Wu and co-authors built an automated system in 2025 that marks 68 facial landmarks at once. It uses deep learning and computer vision, with a standard face template that can be adjusted for each patient.

The system was tested on 55 patients in China, including some with severe jaw deformities. Its marks landed within about one millimeter of expert marks on average, and most points met clinical standards. Templates made for each deformity type cut error further. The authors present the tool as a faster way to support facial shape studies.
pmc-12765920:
Wen Qian Jian and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-five, three delivery methods when a baby's heart rate drops for a long spell in late labor. That event is called prolonged deceleration. It can signal distress, so speed matters. The team reviewed one hundred fourteen single, full-term births with the baby head-down, from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four. Methods were vacuum extraction, forceps, and cesarean section, a surgical birth. Outcomes covered mother harm, blood loss, hospital stay, and newborn health marks such as cord blood acidity and intensive care admission.

The cesarean group had higher fetal position and longer wait to delivery. Mothers in that group lost more blood, stayed longer, and cost more. Newborn outcomes were alike across all three groups.
pmc-12766120:
A stubborn form of eczema driven from inside the body, rather than by outside triggers, can be hard to treat. Fiorella Yori, Carlos Sarmiento, Javier Gimeno Beltran, and Ignacio Umbert tested a skin treatment mixing mineral salts with natural antioxidants. Thirty-four patients used it for fourteen days, and doctors scored their skin before and after with four standard scales. Patients also rated their own itch and life quality.

Every score improved sharply. Skin samples showed a thinner outer layer and far fewer immune cells of several kinds after treatment. No side effects appeared. The team concludes the mix cut the disease's severity a great deal in this short trial, and was easy for patients to tolerate.
pmc-12766820:
Stephen James Walsh, Aisling O'Leary, and Matthew Lynch interview primary care workers in Ireland in a 2025 study on green health care. Health care leaves a large mark on the planet, and primary care accounts for up to a quarter of it.

Twenty pharmacists, dentists, doctors, and practice nurses were interviewed in depth. Most saw climate action as important, yet many felt unable to turn concern into change in their daily work. Blocks included low knowledge, little guidance, and weak system support. Workers asked for focused training, handy tools, and clear leadership. The study adds the voice of front line staff to a field often led from above.
pmc-12767420:
Pregnant women who caught COVID-19 faced risks beyond their own lungs. Abdulrahman Wasel Koja and co-authors review how such pregnancies fared at a military hospital in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, in a 2025 study. Records of one hundred thirty-eight infected women were examined, most diagnosed late in pregnancy.

About four in ten women had no symptoms and another four in ten had mild illness; about one in fifteen became severely ill. Outcomes included preeclampsia in about five percent, early births in about twelve percent, and low birth weight in about fifteen percent. Severe disease stood out: women with it had clearly higher rates of preeclampsia and intensive care admission, and their babies needed intensive care far more often. The authors tie outcome to illness severity rather than infection alone.
pmc-12768620:
Raymond Matey studies what happens when a hospital pharmacy cannot supply prescribed drugs and patients must buy them outside. The work took place at the University of Ghana Medical Centre and focused on blood pressure drugs. Such referrals can burden patients, harm health, and drain hospital income and workflow.

Over two months in late twenty twenty-three, nearly half of prescribed drugs were not dispensed in house. Lost income on blood pressure drugs alone topped forty-three thousand Ghana cedis. Interviews with three hundred sixty-seven patients showed extra travel and time costs, plus high rates of frustration and stress. Matey argues that fixing supply would aid patients and the center alike, with lessons for other health systems.
pmc-12768720:
Rachele Busca and Jana Boleckova wrote a 2025 study on why European countries judge the same medical devices in different ways. High-risk implants, such as heart devices, are reviewed at national or regional level in Europe. Even with the same clinical proof, verdicts can differ a lot, which changes patient access from place to place.

The team searched the websites of review agencies in 13 countries for 2023 reports on heart devices for structural heart disease. They found 80 reports from 11 countries, with 23 on structural heart topics from four of them. Most dealt with heart valves, wall defects, and heart failure. Some tools were judged again in later years, with shifts in the verdicts. The authors argue for a flexible shared approach that cuts needless gaps between countries.
pmc-12768820:
Selai Akseer and co-authors wrote a 2025 study on the cost of special care planning for older adults with cancer. The approach, called geriatric assessment and management, checks the health, strength, and needs of an older patient to shape cancer care. Guides back the approach, but its value for money was unclear.

The team built a model from pooled data of four trials run in several countries. They compared the approach plus usual care with usual care alone over six months. Costs were counted from the payer's view, with Canadian prices as the base case. The team also tested each trial on its own, a one-year span, and United States prices. The study helps health systems judge when this extra planning is worth its cost.
pmc-12770920:
Amit Baumel, Or Brandes, and Chen Saar test a fully remote parent training program for childhood oppositional defiant disorder, run before and during wartime in Israel. Digital programs promise care at scale with fewer hurdles, but their reach to untreated families, and their grit in a crisis, were unproven. Parents got guided training with human support. Child behavior and parenting were rated before, after, and three months later, next to platform use data and clinician checks.

In all, 55 families took part, 25 before the war and 30 during it. Most, 62%, had never had any help for their child's behavior before. Parents reported clear gains in child behavior, with large effect sizes, and in their own parenting. Families spent about 139 minutes in the program over 31 logins, backed by about 39 minutes of human contact, mostly by message.
pmc-12771820:
Brigit Hatch and co-authors report a large trial to raise HPV vaccination in rural clinics, in a 2025 paper. The vaccine prevents cancer, but rural teens in the United States lag behind. Clinics in Oregon joined a five-year trial with support to pick and run fixes that fit local needs.

Forty-five clinics joined and 36 finished the plan. Most worked on completing the vaccine series, using tools such as reminders and staff training. Rates of starting and finishing the series rose over time in all clinics. Yet the support plan added no clear gain beyond that trend, though clinics' skill at quality work grew a lot, most in care coordination.
pmc-12772220:
Yangyi Zhang leads a team of nineteen authors exposing a feedback loop that helps prostate cancer hide from natural killer cells. Immune-cold tumors resist immunotherapy, and the suppressive environment behind that resistance is poorly mapped. In prostate cancer cells the team found a loop centered on the enzyme PSAT1 and the regulator YBX1.

PSAT1 boosts YBX1's phosphorylation through a kinase, sending it into the nucleus, where it switches on both PSAT1 itself and the NK-dampening molecule HLA-E. The loop thus sustains its own activity while blunting killer cell attack. Blocking loop members restored NK killing of tumor cells in culture and in animals. The authors propose the loop as a drug target for NK-based therapy.
pmc-12772420:
Shichun Chen and colleagues reported an eye case in 2025 involving a two-month-old baby boy. Objects stuck on the cornea are rare in infants. They are easy to miss and hard to remove. The parents noticed a small dot on the baby's left cornea. The baby showed no pain or other symptoms. A slit lamp exam found a small oval plastic piece. It sat in the surface layer of the cornea. The piece came from an ornament on the babysitter's clothing.

The family refused sedation for the removal. Flushing with salt water failed to move the piece. A cotton swab alone also failed. Doctors then added numbing drops to the eye. A fine needle helped free the piece from the surface. The cotton swab then lifted it away. The authors propose this office method as low risk. They warn that silent cases like this are easily ignored.
pmc-12772620:
Michael Parker presents an essay, published in 2025, on how bioethics should handle deep moral disagreement. Its scholars work amid intense value conflict and sharp division, from end-of-life care to new biotech. Parker argues the field is well placed to help society argue well, but only if it moves beyond its usual methods. He proposes adversarial cooperation: structured work between opponents that fuses the rigor of adversarial collaboration in science with the cultural breadth of cooperation across difference in the humanities.

Such work faces real hurdles: misinformation, the pull between fixed values and fair process, and the need to decide while disagreement continues. Parker casts the bioethicist as a facilitator of trustworthy, inclusive deliberation, skilled in mediation and the arts as well as philosophy. Training and practice, he says, must change to match, with humility and voices too often left out at the center.
pmc-12774920:
Jae Kyu Lim and co-authors compare microbes living on a stalked barnacle from two deep-sea vent fields in a 2025 study. The barnacle, Neolepas marisindica, lives only near vents on the Central Indian Ridge, and its microbe partners were little known.

Samples came from the Solitaire and Onnuri fields, which sit close to each other but differ in water chemistry. Both sets were dominated by one large microbe group, yet the mix differed by site. One site held more methane-using microbes, while the other held more sulfur-using ones. Predicted microbe jobs also split by site. The work shows that local vent chemistry shapes the barnacle's microbe community.
pmc-12780020: Nannini and co-authors compare two targeted multigene panels used to characterize GIST, a tumor of the gut wall. Molecular analysis is required care for this cancer, since gene results guide drug choice. The study weighs how each panel performs in routine practice and how much clinical value each adds, so labs can pick the panel that best balances breadth, accuracy, and cost.
pmc-12780420:
Jiagen Li and co-authors test a surgical technique for partial lung removal in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Removing less than a full lobe can preserve lung function, but cutting the lung plane with energy devices rather than staplers is debated. The team reviewed outcomes for patients treated this way.

Sixty-nine patients had surgery through a single small port with video guidance. Operations averaged about two hours with little blood loss. About thirteen percent had complications, most often a prolonged air leak. Drainage and hospital stay were short. By six months, nine in ten checked patients had full expansion of the remaining lung. The authors call the technique safe and feasible for selected patients.
pmc-12780520:
Asif Khaliq and a large team published a global analysis in two thousand twenty-five on overlapping forms of malnutrition in young children. Children can be underweight, stunted, and wasted at once, and these combined forms are deadlier than single ones. Their worldwide scale in poorer countries was the target.

Health survey data covered over five hundred forty thousand children under five in sixty-two countries from two thousand six to two thousand twenty-four. Overall malnutrition touched about forty-four percent; combined forms hit about twenty-one percent. Underweight with stunting was the commonest overlap. South and Southeast Asia carried the heaviest burden, and Timor-Leste the highest national rate. Toddlers aged one to three faced two to three times the odds.
pmc-12783320:
Ting He and co-authors published this immunology study in 2025 on virus-like particles built from the SV40 virus shell. Such particles, empty of genetic material, are promising carriers for vaccines and cancer immunotherapy, but their safety and immune effects inside the body are under-studied. The team injected the particles under the skin of mice and tracked immune cells across key organs.

Imaging showed the particles traveling between lymph nodes. In the spleen they raised the counts of helper T cells and natural killer cells, and helper T cells also rose in gut lymph nodes. Lungs, liver, and kidneys showed no significant changes, and blood chemistry and clotting stayed normal. The particles alone did not treat tumors, but they homed to tumor tissue and raised an inflammatory signal in the spleen. The authors call them a promising, safe platform for further engineering.
pmc-12784020:
Sum Kim and co-authors measure hoarseness after spine surgery in a 2025 interim report. A hoarse voice can follow surgery under general anesthesia, but self-reports carry bias. Objective voice measures were needed to pin down how often it happens.

The plan covers more than four hundred patients; this report covers one hundred sixty-two with full data. Hoarseness struck thirty-five percent on surgery day, falling to about five percent by day thirty. Two sound measures, pitch and jitter, tracked the handicap scores early on. Cutoff values for three sound measures at day thirty were derived for future screening.
pmc-12784920:
Chao Fang, Hang Cao, Lingling Liu, and Wujun Liu study a jaw defect in Dolang sheep in a 2025 paper. In this defect the lower jaw sticks out past the upper jaw, the face looks concave, and chewing suffers. It shows up far more often in this flock than is normal, so the team looked for a cause in the genome's three-dimensional shape.

They checked 959 sheep and found the defect in about one in ten. They then built a case-control group of 200 affected and 200 clean sheep. Maps of folded DNA from jaw bone showed the broad fold pattern was much the same in both groups. A few short zones stood out, with more fold borders near genes linked to face growth.
pmc-12785120:
Maria Pagoni and co-authors published a 2025 meta-analysis of one gene variant and prostate cancer risk in men of European ancestry. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, and its rate varies by ethnic group. The gene in view, CYP3A4, helps the body process drugs and hormones, which makes it a plausible suspect.

The team searched the field and kept ten studies, with more than three thousand cases and three thousand healthy men. One gene variant was examined under six genetic models. In the two strictest models, where the variant was inherited from both parents or dominated the pair, risk ran at nearly twice that of the ordinary form. In looser models the increase was less firm. The variation across earlier work was wide, and tests for publication bias were run. The team calls the variant a real, if uneven, marker of risk.
pmc-12785420:
Head and neck cancers often resist treatment and come back, and the tissue around the tumor helps explain why. Abhinav Bagchi and Ratna Ray reviewed that tumor microenvironment in 2025, with a focus on squamous cell cancers of the mouth, throat, and voice box. Risk factors include smoking, alcohol, and infection with human papillomavirus, and the review stresses cancers without that viral link.

Cancer and non-cancer cells in the tumor's surroundings together shape response to surgery, radiation, drugs, and immune therapy. Differences in tissue type and virus status change that mix a great deal. The authors survey current and experimental treatments that aim at resistance itself, hoping to improve outcomes in advanced disease.
pmc-12785720:
Aurelijus Pūkas, Deimantė Stankutė, and Jūratė Gudaitytė report in 2025 the sleep care plan for a man with Marfan syndrome during planned hernia surgery. The syndrome weakens connective tissue across the body, and heart and vessel risks loom largest. Longer lives now bring such patients to routine surgery more often.

Their patient, aged thirty seven, had severe high blood pressure, a past heart valve swap, a curved spine, and a stiff jaw that threatened airway access. The team tilted him head up, placed an artery line before sleep, and dosed drugs in small steps. The report shares the full plan for like cases.
pmc-12786220:
Palmira Bernocchi and co-authors published this 2025 study on whether sick, older patients can actually run a home telemedicine kit. Their six-month program served people living with both heart failure and type 2 diabetes. It paired nurse teleassistance with devices: a wearable heart tracer, a step tracker, and an app for logging readings and video calls.

Forty-three patients, averaging 71 years old, took part. Use was heavy: 95 percent logged into the app daily, nurses made nearly 900 video calls, and the group recorded over 900 ECG traces. Walking sessions averaged about six per week. Usability questionnaires at the end let patients grade the system. The authors judge the setup applicable and welcome in real homes, not just in trials.
pmc-12786420:
Clémence Peufly and co-authors compare knee measurements in a 2025 study of teenagers with torn knee ligaments. The slope of the shinbone's top surface is a known risk factor for such tears in adults, but in teens the measure is unsettled. X-ray and MRI give different numbers, so the team tested how they relate.

One hundred eight injured knees were measured both ways by two reviewers. X-ray read higher on average, with a steady bias over MRI, and single knees could differ by up to five degrees. The two methods still tracked each other well. Using the X-ray danger line, the matching MRI cutoff came out near nine degrees with strong accuracy. The authors warn that thresholds cannot be swapped between methods.
pmc-12786820:
A research team pooled past studies on a rare harm of atrial fibrillation, the common heart rhythm fault, reporting in 2025. Clots from the heart can block blood flow to the gut, spleen, or kidneys, yet these events are often lumped in with stroke counts and stay poorly tracked.

The team searched four large databases through September 2024 and found 12 studies with 329,128 patients. They scored study quality and grouped results by how each study defined the events, since pooled rates varied a great deal. New European scoring rules that drop sex as a risk factor frame the review. Clinicians gain a clearer map of how often these clots strike and who faces the most risk.
pmc-12787220:
Ko and co-authors check the real-world safety of cyproheptadine-based appetite stimulants in this 2025 hospital records study. Korea has used these stimulants for over 30 years. Older adults face malnutrition risks, but the drug's antihistamine effects raised safety questions for them.

The team used Seoul National University Hospital records from 2004 to 2022. They compared patients given the stimulant with those given megestrol or other antihistamines, matching groups by propensity scores. They tracked dizziness, sedation, and low blood pressure within 30 days. Against megestrol, hazard ratios sat near one for dizziness and below one for sedation and low blood pressure, with wide intervals. No clear safety penalty appeared.
pmc-12787420:
A nine-herb formula used in Korean medicine may touch many Alzheimer's pathways at once, and network methods can map that reach. Hyein Jo, Joonyoung Shin, Hyorin Lee, Gi-Sang Bae, and Sungchul Kim mapped the formula, Mecasin, in a 2025 study. Active parts from the nine herbs were screened in public databases. Their predicted targets were crossed with close to nine thousand disease-linked genes.

Six core genes sat at the hub of the shared network. Paths around them cover cell survival, swelling control, and stress response. Docking models suggested some formula parts can grip hub targets directly. All results are computer-based, with no lab or patient tests yet. The authors offer the map as a guide for later bench work.
pmc-12787620:
Fomichev, Briggs, and Sokoloff trace how flowers form in a restiad plant in this twenty twenty-five study. The plant group has many species with split male and female plants, yet its flower growth is still not well known. The team picked a species that sits near the base of one branch of the family.

Inside, both sexes grow branched flower heads built from small spikes of blooms. Male spikes hold far more blooms than female spikes, and each bloom starts with parts for both sexes. One set of parts then stops growing, which leaves the bloom as male or female. The team uses these growth steps to rethink how a close kin species builds its more complex female unit.
pmc-12787720:
Wei Liu and co-authors build a light detector for rice leaf disease that can run on field devices in a 2025 study. Rice disease cuts yield, and field photos are hard, with tiny spots, uneven light, and cluttered scenes. A model must be both accurate and small enough for edge hardware, so the team reworked a known detector.

They swapped in a lighter backbone, added a part for fine detail at many scales, and added a head that finds small spots better. They then pruned parts and used teaching from a larger model to regain quality. The shrunk model took little storage, scored high on a public data set, and ran fast in their tests.
pmc-12788020:
Yingying Wang and colleagues reviewed flexible light devices in two thousand twenty-five. Atom-thin materials suit bendable electronics well. They keep working under bending and stretching. Three material families headline the review. Graphene, layered metal compounds, and MXenes each bring strengths. Uses span detectors, lights, and solar cells.

Gas sensors and optical modulators also feature. The review explains why bands stay stable under strain. Efficient light conversion under flexing gets special attention. Wearable systems are the obvious application home. Self-powered platforms could follow from this work. Challenges and future prospects close the survey. Engineers gain a broad, critical map.
pmc-12788420:
Raghunathan Natarajan and co-authors follow 150 dental patients after root canal treatment, in a 2025 study. Success in that treatment is often judged by the tooth alone. The team instead tracked three gains at once: less pain, better chewing, and less worry. They call that trio a frame for patient-centered success.

Pain scores fell steeply over thirty days, and most patients had mild pain or none by the end. Chewing scores near doubled, and worry scores dropped by a large step. Better chewing was the strongest driver of patient contentment in their model. Early pain and worry before treatment pulled contentment down. The authors urge care for both body and mind.
pmc-12789520:
Pooja Sadalagi and co-authors model hair-driven flow of smart fluids in a sloped, narrowing micro-channel in a 2025 paper. Tiny hairs line the channel and sway to push fluid, while an electric pull also drives flow. Heat shifts the fluid's thickness and heat spread, which the model counts in full.

Longer hairs slow the core flow but ease the push needed to keep it going. The electric pull speeds the fluid and offsets hair drag, the team finds. Mild blocks help flow and heat shift when fluid traits vary, a guide for drug and chip tools.
pmc-12790120:
Tessa Parkes and co-authors set out a trial of peer guides for homeless people with substance problems in a 2025 protocol. This group often cannot reach the care it needs. An earlier pilot showed guides with lived experience could build trust, lift service use, raise uptake of opioid swap therapy, and cut risky use. A full trial now tests whether the gains hold at scale.

Twenty Salvation Army service towns will be split by coin toss into guide and plain arms. Adults who are homeless or at risk and report problem substance use will be recruited. Cost and value reads ride inside the trial, with a process study alongside. Outcomes span mental health, life quality, and linked service marks. The authors will judge both effect and worth.
pmc-12795620:
Shivangi Yadav and Chiranji Lal Goel present a 2025 audit of workstation ergonomics in radiology departments. Radiologists spend long hours at screens, and surveys report high rates of muscle and joint disorders plus eye strain. The audit checked whether reporting workstations met the national college's ergonomic standards.

Staff at two hospital sites answered a questionnaire in two cycles, 25 replies in 2023 and 21 in 2024. The questions followed the Royal College of Radiologists guidance on correct workstation use. Between cycles, targeted fixes were applied to the setups. The closed-loop design then measured whether compliance improved. The report shows how a simple repeat audit can lift staff wellbeing. Better setups also guard diagnostic accuracy during long reporting sessions.
pmc-12797820:
Xiaotian Yuan and eight co-authors published a single-cell study in twenty twenty-five on why the solid type of adenoid cystic carcinoma, a salivary gland cancer, is its deadliest form. The solid tumors are rich in blood vessels and fibroblasts, and the study asked whether the two facts are connected. Sequencing individual cells sorted the fibroblast population.

Solid tumors were dominated by one fibroblast subtype, marked by the adhesion molecule MCAM, which churned out vessel-growing factors at high levels. In culture and in animals, these cells proved strongly pro-angiogenic, feeding the tumor's blood supply. Upstream controls on those growth factors were traced in follow-up experiments. The fibroblast subtype becomes both a marker of the aggressive form and a targetable accomplice.
pmc-12800020:
Bin Liu and co-authors present a 2025 mouse study on how a mutant gene in support cells speeds breast tumor growth. The gene, a famed tumor suppressor, often mutates in the fibroblast cells around breast tumors, and patients with that pattern fare worse. What the mutant support cells do to the tumor was unclear.

Mice with the mutation only in fibroblasts grew tumors sooner than matched controls. Gene readouts showed a surge in growth signal paths in their tumors. Fifteen genes for secreted factors stood out between the groups. Two of them also ran high in human breast tumors with the mutant gene. Adding those factors to tumor cultures in dishes sped growth, which backs a signal spill route.
pmc-12800220:
Senthilkumar and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a learning system that estimates free-space optical channels. Optical links through open air offer huge bandwidth and license-free use, but turbulence, misalignment, and wavelength-dependent fading make their channels hard to predict. Classic estimators adapt too slowly when conditions swing.

Their network, SWALNet, uses a sparse attention encoder that stays aware of wavelength. It learns how each wavelength fades and how modulation distorts the signal, then maps the received waveform to channel coefficients. Training data simulated standard turbulence models plus pointing errors across several wavelengths. The network's channel error beat conventional baselines in simulation. Robust channel estimates keep optical links viable in bad air. The authors pitch the system for next-generation optical wireless networks.
pmc-12800520:
Minhee Hwang, Youngjun Kim, and Changryul Claud Yi published a 2025 study of eye socket fractures across thirteen years in Korea. A blowout fracture breaks the thin wall of the eye socket while the rim stays intact. The team asked how injury causes changed over time, and whether eye movement problems at arrival changed with them.

They compared records from two major trauma centers: a 2011 series of 150 patients and a pooled series of 50 patients from 2019 to 2023. Only CT confirmed fractures of the inner or lower wall were included. They logged injury cause, fracture site, double vision, and eye movement limits. Statistical models then tested trends by year and whether differences between centers survived adjustment for patient mix.
pmc-12800820: Jorge Rodriguez-Gil and co-authors issue a 2025 guidance note on a rare inherited disease. Niemann-Pick disease type C harms the brain and nerves, and two drugs now target those signs. The note, from a medical genetics college panel, is meant as a teaching aid for doctors who treat such cases. It rests on the facts known when it was accepted, and it urges each doctor to judge every case on its own rather than treat the note as a strict rule.
pmc-12801420:
Ding, Xie, Zhang, Jiang, Wang, and Wan describe in twenty twenty-five the traits of severe near-sightedness that starts very early in Chinese children. Such early, strong cases often hide other eye or body problems. The team enrolled over two hundred young children, measured their vision and eye shape in detail, and read the full gene sets of some.

Just over half of the children had the severe early form. More than half of those had another eye or body condition as well. A slipped eye lens was the most common extra problem, followed by inherited decay of the light-sensing layer. Every child whose genes were read carried a variant tied to inherited eye disease. The authors urge careful checks for hidden problems in such children.
pmc-12801620:
Eva Caly-Simbou and co-authors publish the first full genome of a plant-wilting bacterium strain from Mayotte island. The bacterium belongs to a complex that causes bacterial wilt, a disease that ruins many food crops. One lineage in the Indian Ocean region has proved highly destructive. Their 2025 data report sequences a strain gathered on the island.

Two reading methods were joined to build the complete genome, just under six million letters long. It holds one chromosome plus two extra DNA circles, which is uncommon for this group. The smaller circle carries gene sets for two secretion systems, tools bacteria use to move proteins out. Those genes may help explain the strain's epidemic success, the authors note, and the genome gives a base for tracking its spread.
pmc-12804820:
Radim Šumbera and nine co-authors measure bite strength across breeding and non-breeding mole-rats, in a 2025 study. These African rodents live underground in families where usually one pair breeds. Bite force matters for feeding, dominance, and defense, and so for reproductive success.

The team measured live bites, head width, and incisor width in 404 animals from 75 families across four social species. Breeding males bit hardest in every species. Non-breeding males bit about twelve percent weaker, and non-breeding females about twenty-two percent weaker. Breeding females were the surprise: their bites ran about thirty-one percent below breeding males, and many refused to bite at all. Head and tooth measurements matched the pattern. The authors argue breeding males need strong bites to repel unrelated rivals seeking entry, while females face little such competition.
pmc-12805320:
Fereshteh Baygi and six co-authors test whether three-way video consultations make cancer patients feel their care is better coordinated. In the trial, 278 patients were randomized to usual care or to video meetings joining the patient, the oncologist, and the family doctor, with perceptions measured at baseline and seven months.

Delivery faltered: only eighty patients, under thirty percent, actually received the video consultations, held back by technical and administrative problems. Among those who answered the questionnaires, no measure separated the groups. Changes in coordination scores and information satisfaction were small and statistically indistinguishable between arms. The authors report the null result plainly, and the gap between the intervention as designed and as delivered hangs over the findings. A coordination tool that cannot reliably reach patients cannot show its worth.
pmc-12805720:
Mehreen Fatima and co-authors grade a medical school's new mentorship program in this 2025 study. Mentoring is meant to grow students professionally, but a program only works if it is checked and fixed. The team judged the program with the CIPP model, which weighs context, inputs, process, and product, mixing surveys with group talks.

One hundred eighty-two mentees and twenty-nine mentors took part. Only a small share of mentees strongly agreed the program hit its goals, and most mentors rated it merely good. The talks exposed the friction: aims were unclear, pairing of mentors and students felt off, each side found the other hard to reach, and mentors had no training. The authors list fixes in exactly those areas.
pmc-12807120:
William Singer and a large team review how gene work can make soybeans more nourishing for food and feed. Soy is a key world crop, yet some seed traits hold back its food value. Breeders have long chased better protein, oils, and sugars and fewer harsh traits.

The review maps what is known about the genes behind each prized trait. It also covers new gene edit tools that can make fresh seed forms. Plans for next steps close the piece. Growers, food makers, and buyers all gain from seeds bred with clear food goals in mind.
pmc-12808420:
Md Jawadul Hasan and co-authors review machine learning methods that detect mental health states from data. Published in 2025, their systematic review responds to a hard setting: mental illness is rising worldwide, yet stigma keeps many people from speaking openly, which delays help. Automated detection from text, voice, or behavior offers a quieter first door.

The review sorts the techniques in use, gathers the studies that predict mental health states, and lists the data sets available for training. It also counts which algorithms appear most often in the field. The authors aim to give newcomers and clinicians a single map of a fast-growing, scattered literature.
pmc-12812620:
Ning Sun and nine co-authors lay out a trial protocol testing electroacupuncture for thinking problems after stroke. Such problems are common and slow recovery, and iron mishandling in the brain is one suspected driver. Their 2025 protocol describes a single-blind randomized trial of seventy-two patients with cognitive impairment after ischemic stroke. Half get real electroacupuncture and half a sham version, both on top of standard care. MRI scans will track iron deposits in the brain alongside thinking scores.

A protocol paper fixes the design in public before results exist, which guards against quiet changes later. If the needles help, the iron link may explain how. The authors aim at an early window, when treatment could matter most. The trial is set to test a traditional therapy with modern imaging discipline.
pmc-12812720:
Corn stalks are farm waste that cattle could eat, if fermentation made them softer and richer. Jianwei Wei and co-authors test in 2025 a combined treatment: friendly microbes plus a cellulase enzyme mix, against each alone and a plain control. They tracked the silage over twenty-eight days, simulated rumen digestion in glass, and finished with feeding trials in Yanbian yellow cattle.

The combined batch fermented best, with lower acidity markers of spoilage, less fiber and lignin, more kept protein, and higher digestibility. Cattle on it gained faster and converted feed better. The authors offer the pairing as a workable route to turn field waste into feed.
pmc-12813420:
Tyler Harrison and four co-authors track bonding hormones around mother and baby play in a study first published in 2025. Postpartum depression shadows both mother and child, yet its hormone story is thin. Oxytocin and vasopressin shape mood and care, so the team sampled both around a set play bout in mothers with and without the depression.

Twelve mothers, five with the depression, played with their babies for fifteen minutes. Blood and spit were drawn before, during, and after. Maternal oxytocin rose across the bout in all, and infant levels rose by the end. Mothers with depression climbed more slowly and, after play, their levels stayed up while peers settled back to base. Vasopressin dipped mid bout. The authors offer the paths as groundwork for bigger studies.
pmc-12813720:
Nicole Vernot-Jonas and Alfred Kwesi Manyeh evaluate a disease control program in Ghana in a 2025 study. Schistosomiasis, a worm infection spread in fresh water, persists around the Volta Basin despite years of mass drug drives. A local authority teamed with a university to improve how the drugs reach villages. The study grades that effort with the RE-AIM framework, which scores reach, effect, uptake, delivery, and upkeep.

Surveys before and after, plus interviews and group talks, fed the grade. Infection rates fell by about eighty-eight to ninety-one percent across three districts. Training levels and health worker satisfaction ran high, and villages received the program well. Side effects from the drug and lost work time may still hold some people back.
pmc-12816220:
Xukai Liang and co-authors tested whether dusting maize with silicon nanoparticles helps the crop yield more while using less water, in field trials the head dates to 2025. The trials ran in the dry northwest of China. Three maize varieties grew under full watering or under a mild, planned water shortage. Half the plots got the silicon spray and half got plain water, so the team could isolate the spray's effect.

Shortage alone trimmed yield a little but raised water savings. The spray lifted yield and water productivity in every variety, under both watering plans. Leaves turned greener, breathed better, and caught more light as the canopy reshaped itself. The yield gain tracked the better light capture and photosynthesis, not lower water loss. The authors offer the spray as a practical tool for dry farming regions.
pmc-12816620:
Abdelmoneim Ali, Zain Najjar, and Mutamed Ayyash review the tiny regulatory RNAs dissolved in breast milk and baby formula, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Milk microRNAs survive digestion and can regulate infant genes. They are among breastfeeding's least visible active ingredients.

The review surveys what is known about these molecules in human milk versus manufactured formulas. Their roles in development and immune maturation anchor the discussion. Formula composition differs, raising questions about what bottle-fed infants miss or receive differently. Understanding milk microRNAs could seed diagnostics and improved formula design. The authors frame the topic as both basic biology and a practical agenda for infant nutrition science.
pmc-12816720:
Wei Ge and co-authors build a privacy-safe cancer detector in 2025 for pancreatic cancer, a disease usually found too late. Fewer than one in ten patients live five years, and early tumors hide on standard scans. Their answer trains AI across hospitals without pooling patient data, a method called federated learning.

Two network types split the work: one reads long-range patterns in scans, the other pulls local detail with a light build. Inputs span CT and MRI scans, tissue, genes, and clinic records, for spotting, subtyping, and forecasting the disease. A twin animal-inspired search tuner speeds the setup. Trials across five to seven mock hospital sites form the test bed. Keeping data home while still learning jointly is the core promise here.
pmc-12817420:
Brenna LaBarre and six colleagues present a 2025 study on sex differences in the brains of people with progressive multiple sclerosis. The disease strikes women about three times as often as men, yet men often fare worse at diagnosis. The team mined public single-nucleus gene data from MS and control brains, focusing on the cells that make myelin and their parent cells.

In women with MS, these support cells switched on genes that stayed unchanged in men. The changes included immune-related genes and a set of energy-producing mitochondrial genes previously tied to other brain diseases. The authors suggest male and female support cells answer myelin damage with different programs, which could eventually guide sex-aware treatment planning.
pmc-12817520:
Niecky Fruneaux-van Amerongen and co-authors evaluate a program that trains nursing home teams to weave spiritual care into daily work. Their 2025 study starts from the move itself: entering a home shakes a resident's sense of meaning, and daily staff meet those questions first. A Dutch guideline exists, yet many staff feel unsure in this area.

The program mixed group training, one-on-one coaching on the job, and team reflection meetings. The team measured how staff rated their own spiritual skills before and after, read the questions they brought to coaching, and watched how the skills showed up in daily practice. The design mixed surveys with close reading of the coaching record.
pmc-12817720:
Xingxing Jiang, Yongping Gui, Yu Yang, Jie Li, and Aijun Liang hunt in 2025 for core genes that could mark or help treat glioma, the most common malignant brain tumor. The disease has a bleak outlook and a tangled molecular profile. The team merged five public gene data sets, covering about five hundred samples, and cleaned the batch differences between them.

Several screening methods, from network analysis to machine learning, all pointed to the same six genes. All six ran low in tumor tissue, backed by outside data sets and tests on sixty-nine patient samples. Low levels went with a faster cell cycle and immune upset. Single-cell data placed the genes mainly in a stem-like tumor cell group, with levels dropping in the tumor core. The authors also mapped control networks and screened drugs that might act on them.
pmc-12819420:
Huseyin Topcu and co-authors test how wobbling the back foot changes muscle work during a split squat, in a study from 2025. The Bulgarian split squat is a one leg strength staple for athletes. Training on unstable surfaces is said to wake muscles up more, but the rear foot's role in that effect had barely been studied.

Twenty three trained male football players did body weight split squats in four setups: a stable platform, two kinds of balance balls, and a suspension strap for the rear foot. Wired sensors on six thigh and hip muscles recorded activity during both the lowering and rising phases. The design crossed each player through all setups. Results speak to coaches choosing gear for strength and balance work.
pmc-12819820:
Oded Shamriz and a large team show that one part of the cell’s power plant is vital for immune T cells, in a study published in 2025. The part, called NDUFS4, sits in the first complex of the chain that makes energy in mitochondria. How much each single part matters for T cells was not clear.

The team bred mice whose T cells lack the part and studied T cells from a patient whose loss of it causes Leigh syndrome. Without it, the energy chain faltered: energy output fell, backup sugar burning rose, and chemical balance slipped. The mouse and human results match closely. The work ties a single power-plant part to how well T cells guard the body.
pmc-12821720:
Papadopoulos and four co-authors report a rare cyst hidden in a tonsil, in work from twenty twenty-five. Lymphoepithelial cysts are uncommon benign lesions of the head and neck. They are rare in the mouth and exceedingly rare in the palatine tonsils.

Their patient was a woman of sixty-eight with four years of a foreign body feeling in her throat. The cyst sat at the top pole of the tonsil, in a crypt, hence the title phrase en crypto. Nonspecific symptoms and mimicry of commoner lumps make such lesions easy to miss. The case reminds clinicians to keep rare benign causes in the differential.
pmc-12821920:
Wentrell Bing and eleven colleagues published a school health survey in two thousand twenty-five on alcohol and drug use among Ugandan teenagers. Little firm data existed for pupils in school, as most studies focus on adults. The team surveyed secondary schools in central and eastern Uganda.

They questioned one thousand eight hundred thirty-three pupils aged ten to eighteen in eight schools. Rates of heavy use were low: about three percent for alcohol, under two percent for tobacco, and about two and a half percent for marijuana. About six percent reported real harm from some substance. Boys had higher odds of marijuana use than girls. A past mental illness also raised the odds. The authors call for school-based prevention.
pmc-12822020:
Jiaming Lu and ten co-authors use an extra-strong MRI scanner to watch migraine harden into a daily condition. Migraine is now seen as a disorder of whole brain networks, not one spot. The shift from occasional attacks to chronic migraine is the key change this 2025 study hunts in the brain's wiring.

Scans from 122 people — 30 healthy, 66 with episodic migraine, and 16 with chronic migraine — fed two kinds of network maps. Both maps showed the brain's main ordering gradient flattening step by step across the three groups. Changes centered on visual and body-sensation networks. Flatter ordering also tracked with more anxiety and worse scores on related clinical scales.
pmc-12822120:
Tetsuya Kokabu and co-authors chart, in a 2025 study, anemia and iron shortage in Japanese women treated for gynecologic cancers. Low blood counts are common in cancer and can worsen outlook, yet the local picture for these cancers was unclear. The team reviewed patients at one center from 2022 to 2024, before and during treatment.

Of 103 patients, about twenty-nine percent were already anemic before treatment began. A blood measure of iron availability, called TSAT, sat below twenty percent in nearly half the group. Among those who went on to chemotherapy or combined treatment, over ninety percent became anemic within six months. Patients who started with low TSAT sank to lower blood counts during care. The authors propose TSAT as a warning sign that can trigger early iron support.
pmc-12822220:
Katrine Damgaard Skyrud, Siri Rostoft, and Astri Syse report a registry study from two thousand twenty-five on care for older Norwegians after sudden hospital stays. Aging populations strain public care budgets, so knowing who moves into home care or institutions matters. The team tracked a full population of people aged seventy-five and older in two thousand twenty-one.

About fifty-three percent already received formal care at admission, mostly home health care. Four weeks after discharge, the institutional share had risen to about a third before settling near fourteen percent at six months, while home care recovered. Moves into care tied to older age, female sex, living alone, and poor function. Trauma, stroke, and geriatric diagnoses especially predicted institutional uptake.
pmc-12822320:
Jiahua Liang and co-authors test a blood index as a death risk sign in a 2025 study. The index mixes blood fat and sugar values, and variants add waist or weight measures. Their patients had an advanced syndrome that spans heart, liver, kidney, and metabolic health, a group where the index was untested.

Records of 1,384 adults from a national survey were followed for about 56 months, with 360 deaths. Risk formed a U shape: lowest at mid values, higher at both ends. The plain index predicted death as well as its dressed-up variants. The authors give cut points where risk turns, to guide care for each patient.
pmc-12822520:
Muhammad Awais and eight co-authors review the growing use of immune-tuning treatments in heart and vessel disease. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five. Heart disease is the world's top killer, and inflammation plus immune disorder now stand beside classic risk factors as drivers.

Cancer-born tools such as checkpoint inhibitors and engineered T cells are being weighed for heart use, while their own heart harms need watching. The review traces how cytokine signals, autoimmunity, and vessel injury set both benefit and toxicity. It also covers landmark trials of anti-inflammatory drugs, including interleukin blockers. The field where immunology meets cardiology is young but moving fast. The authors map its promise and its safety traps.
pmc-12824320:
Chengzhi Ruan and six co-authors squeeze more air and efficiency out of the fan inside an oolong tea shaking machine. Their 2025 study treats the centrifugal fan's blade shape as the lever. Blade curves were fitted through a few control points set by key measurements, and forty-five candidate designs were sampled evenly across the design space and tested by flow simulation.

A surrogate model learned from those simulations, and a multi-objective swarm search then hunted for the best compromise between air volume and efficiency. On the winning design, swirling backflow between the blades calmed down, and the strong turbulence at the inlet, outlet, and tongue of the housing eased. Air volume rose by a measured margin over the original fan. The authors note that tea machinery fans have long been designed by rule of thumb, and offer the method as a template for multi-parameter tuning.
pmc-12825220:
Pivovarova and five co-authors study opioid treatment programs inside Massachusetts jails, in work from twenty twenty-five. Medications for opioid use disorder are increasingly offered in carceral settings across the state. Most research focuses on drug delivery or on outcomes after release into the community.

Less is known about side effects on other jail services and daily operations. Thirteen jails gave qualitative data on how the medication programs affected mental health services and substance use counseling inside. New programs can strain or strengthen neighboring services. Hearing staff perceptions helps administrators expand treatment without quietly hollowing out mental health care.
pmc-12826820:
Shigeki Matsubara wrote a 2025 letter on writing with smart software tools, drawn from a French word, apprivoiser. In the novel Le Petit Prince, the word means more than to tame. It means taking time with something, building a bond through shared work, until it becomes precious and hard to replace.

Matsubara argues that a paper should be treated that way. Long nights spent shaping words are not wasted time; they are how a writer makes a paper truly their own. He notes a split between those who see papers as mere records and those who see them as the fruit of a personal path. His advice is plain: draft alone, revise until the work feels fully yours, and only then let a tool check grammar. If its phrasing feels foreign, go back to your own words.
pmc-12828920:
Jacob van der Ende and co-authors hunt for silent malaria infections in Ecuador's Amazonian Putumayo region, in a 2025 study. Ecuador nears malaria elimination, but this border area sits next to high-transmission zones in Colombia and Peru. People can carry the parasite with no symptoms, seeding new cases while routine checks miss them.

The team tested 293 healthy people in four river communities during the 2023 rainy season. Rapid tests found no infections at all. Microscope checks found three, and sensitive gene tests found five, all at very low levels. The study warns that elimination plans need molecular surveillance to catch this hidden reservoir. The infections clustered in the mid-to-late rainy season, mostly in males.
pmc-12830920:
Jing Li and co-authors present a measurement method for rapid-fire guns in this 2025 study. When many barrels fire at once, several shells cross the same test plane, and old methods cannot tell them apart. Their sensor uses seven planes of light beams, built from two triple-plane units plus one angled single plane.

As each shell breaks the beams, the timing data feed a math model of its flight. The model yields impact point, speed, and flight angles for every shell. A check based on straight-line paths then sorts out which timings belong to which shell. In tests, impact points were found with error under five millimeters, half the error of older methods. The authors say the setup suits range testing of multi-barrel guns.
pmc-12831420:
Mousa Barboura and co-authors report, in a 2025 case study, a twisted gut pouch in a sixteen-year-old Syrian boy that was first read as appendicitis. The pouch, a Meckel's diverticulum, is the most common birth variant of the small bowel and is usually silent. Twisting is a very rare twist of fate that mimics other belly emergencies.

The boy arrived with a day of severe lower belly pain, vomiting, and two days of blockage. With the scanner out of service, doctors operated on the clinical picture. The appendix was normal, but a large dead pouch was found twisted near the bowel's end. It was cut out and the bowel rejoined, with a smooth recovery.
pmc-12836520:
Cammarota, Kamarajah, Markar, and Smyth meta-analyze PD-L1 as a response marker in operable stomach and esophagus cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Adding immune checkpoint drugs to chemotherapy before surgery is under study. Fifteen randomized trials with over six thousand patients are pooled. Pathological response and survival links are quantified.

Chemo plus immune drugs triple the odds of complete pathological response. Response predicts survival weakly overall but better in recent trials. PD-L1 level five or higher significantly predicts complete response. Stratifying patients by PD-L1 is supported by the pooled evidence. Biomarker-selected trial designs are the recommended next step.
pmc-12836920:
Yinkang Mo and five co-authors pool the scattered literature on the triple infection of HIV, hepatitis B, and tuberculosis, which together carry a worse prognosis than any alone. Searching three databases for studies from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-four across Asia, South America, and Africa yielded seven studies totaling over sixty-four hundred participants and two hundred fifty-nine triple infections.

The pooled prevalence was about four point four percent of the enrolled populations. South American samples ran significantly higher, near nine percent, and patients on antiretroviral treatment showed about seven percent. The authors call the burden underestimated, arguing that single-disease programs systematically miss the people carrying all three infections at once.
pmc-12837220:
Chang Liu and Qing-Xing Qu study how phone news design affects mental load for older users in China. Their 2025 study joins eye tracking with self-rated load scales. Prior work left gaps on human factors for this age group in news apps.

Test screens varied three design traits drawn from top Chinese news apps, in a set grid of combos. Older users viewed each version in turn while their eyes and replies were logged. Visual complexity raised load in a clear way. Keyword color strongly shaped that effect. The authors turn the findings into design advice for fairer screens. Simpler layouts with careful color use, they argue, can ease reading for older adults.
pmc-12837720:
Yingtan, Yaxuan, and Qiuming ask if higher health payouts must lead to waste in care in this twenty twenty-five study. They use payment data from a large city in China where a pooled hospital payout rate changed. A sharp cut-off in the rules lets them gauge cause more cleanly than a plain match would.

Inside, a higher payout rate went with a five percent drop in mean cost per stay, not a rise. Patients picked more cost-wise care inside the plan list, and wards reshaped care paths to fit. Patients also picked higher-grade wards more, and repeat stays fell as a result. Gains were largest in top-grade wards and in the most ill patients.
pmc-12838020:
Skin and ear infections bring many dogs to clinics in Serbia, and drug-resistant germs make them harder to cure. Isidora Prošić and co-authors reviewed lab records from Belgrade covering 2017 to 2024 to map which bacteria appear and which drugs still work.

The review covered 422 swabs from sick dogs. One staph species dominated both ear and skin samples, while a second germ was common in ears. Resistance was high to many first-line drugs, and over a quarter of the staph samples shrugged off methicillin. Multidrug resistance was frequent in both main germs. The authors urge testing before treatment and tighter control of drug use in pet care.
pmc-12838420:
What counts as quality in an intensive care unit depends on who is asked. Maksym Barsa and Valentyna Anufriyeva survey anesthesiologists in Ukraine on that question in a 2025 study, gathered as the country reforms care during wartime.

Responses came from 114 doctors in late 2024 and early 2025. Most framed quality as the quality of the care process itself. Nearly all ranked preventing blood clots in veins at the top of clinical indicators. Preventing pressure ulcers and ventilator-linked pneumonia followed close behind. Answers to open questions were sorted into a set framework and tested with statistical models. The authors hope the results help Ukraine, and like systems, build fairer quality scorecards.
pmc-12838720:
A heart attack raises a protein called myoglobin in the blood within hours, and catching it fast can steer emergency care. Yikai Wang and five co-authors built a chip-sized test for it in a 2025 paper. Their platform joins a magnetic sensor with tiny fluid channels on one device.

Magnetic beads tagged to the protein are caught by antibodies on the sensor, and the sensor's resistance shifts in reply, turning a chemical event into an electrical reading. The chip handles sample prep, the immune reaction, and signal capture in one flow. After tuning bead size, antibody load, and the coupling chemistry, the setup detected myoglobin at 75 nanograms per milliliter. Rival proteins barely registered, showing the test reads its target cleanly. The authors aim it at fast, bedside heart attack screening.
pmc-12838820:
Věra Daňková, Andrea Exnerová, Hana Vágnerová, Vojtěch Pavlík, and Kristina Nešporová wrote a 2025 paper on a cell-free treatment for animals. Stem cells from dog fat calm inflammation and aid repair, mostly through the mix of signals they release. The team grew such cells in a stirred tank rather than flat dishes, hoping the more natural setting would yield a stronger signal mix.

Both cell batches grew with low oxygen and an added blood product. The tank-grown mix carried more of two key signals tied to healing and blood vessel growth. In lab tests it calmed inflammation better, drew repair cells faster, and fought scarring more than the flat-grown mix. A treatment with no cells at all would be easier to store and dose in clinics.
pmc-12839620:
Mary-Pat Schlosser, Lea Stelter, and Mike Stelter share a child's brain tumor case. Their report from twenty twenty-five is told by family and doctor alike. The tumor was a high grade glioma with two gene faults.

Care used surgery, radiation, chemo, and a targeted drug. None of it stopped the tumor in the end. High grade gliomas in kids still have a grim outlook. Choices for care and trials are few for such kids. Families want new cures and a chance to join trials. Hope rests on future work doing far better.
pmc-12840620:
Andras Guttman and Felicia Auer review a lab method that sorts large charged molecules by size inside hair-thin tubes. Their 2025 review covers the version where pore size shifts along the tube, which sharpens sorting of proteins and nucleic acids. Half a century of growth made the base method a workhorse for complex mixes.

Chapters lay out how gradient pores form, how pore spread steers molecule speed, and why stable gradients in narrow tubes are hard to keep. Gear choices such as wall treatment, filling, heat and voltage control, and sensors all shape results. Uses span gene tests and protein checks. The review suits labs that need fine splits across a wide size range.
pmc-12842820:
Nour Regaig and co-authors catalog a family of stress genes in oat and test one of them in depth, in work published in 2025. These genes carry zinc finger parts and help plants respond to many stresses, but they had not been studied in oat. The team found eleven such genes in the oat genome.

Most of the genes switched on under salt, drought like stress, heat, and metal stress. A plant hormone strongly raised nine of them in leaves and roots. When the first gene of the family was made in bacterial cells, those cells tolerated salt and water stress better. The authors say the work opens the way to deeper study of stress defense in oat.
pmc-12843920:
Dandan Wang and eight co-authors report a 2025 study on deep reactive ion etching, a key step in carving fine structures into silicon. Two flaws limit the method: trench walls that lean instead of standing straight, and a cap on how deep a narrow trench can go. The team mapped how the main process settings shape the etched form.

Raising the bottom power step by step made walls lean one way, while lowering it made them lean the other way. More etch cycles alone hit a depth ceiling, though pairing them with rising power broke past it at the cost of uneven trench width. Tuning the ratio of coating time to etch time gave the best control. In the end, the team etched a trench 112.2 micrometers deep and only 5 wide, with a small width gap from top to bottom.
pmc-12845020:
Otilia Elena Frasinariu and co-authors review gut clues to early puberty in a 2025 paper. Early puberty of the central type may be nudged by gut microbes through their chemical products and by how the gut recycles estrogen. The review gathers human and animal studies on this link.

Children with early puberty tend to lose helpful fiber-eating microbes and gain others, with matching shifts in gut chemicals. Animal work suggests the imbalance can speed puberty, while microbe-targeted care can slow it. Some patterns overlap with obesity, yet hormone-linked changes look distinct. Readers get a candidate early-warning system, still needing proof.
pmc-12845420:
Valentina Mangano and co-authors report eight years of blood donor screening for two parasite diseases in Tuscany, Italy, in a 2025 study. Malaria and Chagas disease can pass to patients through donated blood, so Italy screens donors with travel or birth links to regions where the parasites circulate. The Pisa lab ran these checks from 2016 onward.

Of 3,754 donors tested for malaria antibodies, 6.8 percent came back positive, with the highest rates in donors from sub-Saharan Africa. None of the positive donors who took a DNA test had a live infection, and many lost their antibody signal within a year. For Chagas disease, 0.7 percent of 4,285 donors tested positive. Rates dipped in 2020, when travel fell during the pandemic. The results show screening can catch past exposure while live infection stays rare.
pmc-12847720:
Landslides kill people across India each year, and Khan and co-authors map where they are most likely in a 2025 study. The team built a national map at fine detail, using a list of more than one hundred thousand past slides. Three scoring methods weighed slope, rain, and other causes picked with expert help.

All three methods mark about a tenth of the land as high or very high risk zones. Field checks show the maps predict well, with the best method near nine in ten correct. Small gaps between methods show why using more than one guards against bias. Planners can use the maps to guard roads, towns, and rescue plans.
pmc-12848020:
Rujia Si and fifteen co-authors find a chain of molecules whose suppression makes stubborn lung tumors open to cisplatin once more. KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma resists platinum drugs in part through strong antioxidant defenses. To force the cells into ferroptosis, an iron-driven death that bypasses blocked apoptosis, is the detour put forth here.

In cell lines and mouse models, the deubiquitinase OTUD7A controls the demethylase KDM5B. When that chain is suppressed, a repressive histone mark rises, the mitochondrial transcription factor GABPA falls, and reactive oxygen species surge till ferroptosis triggers. In organoid models, cisplatin-induced ferroptosis paired with GABPA inhibition beat standard platinum treatment. The axis offers fresh drug targets for a resistant cancer subtype.
pmc-12848120:
Yanyan Cai and co-authors amplified quantum squeezing with a weak device in a 2025 study. A squeezed state cuts noise in one measure by piling it into another, which sharpens quantum sensors and aids error care. Strong squeezing has called for strong nonlinearity, which brings decoherence that eats the gain.

Their device is a superconducting microwave cavity with only weak Kerr nonlinearity. A cleverly set off-tune drive made the squeezing grow and swing in a cycle in their tests. That path yields large squeezing without the usual noise tax. The work may ease the build of sharp quantum sensors.
pmc-12849420:
Panpan Hai and co-authors report results for a keyhole surgery to fix pelvic organ prolapse in a 2025 study. In prolapse, pelvic organs slip from their place, and the surgery anchors them to a chest-wall ligament through small cuts. The team reviewed forty women treated at one Chinese hospital in 2022 and 2023.

All surgeries finished with no problems during the operation. Later issues were few: one case of trouble passing urine, one mesh exposure, and two cases of lasting pelvic pain. Success rates, by both exam and patient report, stayed near ninety percent at one year. Scores for quality of life and sexual function improved a lot after surgery.
pmc-12853620:
Gregor Toporowski and co-authors compare COVID-19 variants in older hip fracture patients after surgery, in work from 2025. Hip fracture is a top injury of old age, and infection with the pandemic virus adds real risk. Whether each virus variant changed surgical outcomes was unclear.

Registry data covered over twelve thousand patients in 119 German hospitals from 2021 to 2022. Patients were grouped by the variant dominant at their surgery date. Each group split further by infection status on admission. During the Alpha period, death rates and stay length were alike for infected and clean patients. Later periods are compared in the same way. The scale supports fair variant contrasts.
pmc-12853920:
Zhang C, Fan Y, Li P, and Su M tested three nerve blocks for pain control after hip arthroscopy. Ninety patients were split at random into three groups. One group got a fascia iliaca compartment block. One got a pericapsular nerve group block with 20 milliliters of local anesthetic. The third got the same block with only 10 milliliters. The team compared leg muscle strength, pain scores, opioid use, and recovery quality after surgery.

Pain relief was much the same in all three groups, two hours and one day after the operation. The clear difference was muscle strength: patients who got the low-volume block kept far more strength in the thigh muscle. Their recovery quality scores were also the best of the three. The authors conclude that the small-volume block gives equal pain control while sparing muscle strength.
pmc-12855920:
Fahd Alhamdan, Stefano Gianoli, Koichi Yuki, and Sophia Koutsogiannaki published this 2025 study on how sepsis disrupts B cells in children. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, often drains these antibody-making cells, worst in severe cases, but the mechanism was unclear. The team read the gene activity of single blood cells.

Samples came from six children with sepsis, three mild and three severe, plus four healthy controls. Immune cells fell across the board, but B cells dropped most and best separated mild from severe disease. Severe cases lost whole B-cell subsets and rewired the rest, with signs of self-destruction pathways, stalled development, and restless movement. The authors frame the pattern as a fingerprint of severity that could guide care.
pmc-12859920:
Jacobson, Spitzer, and Edelstein survey vaccine views among Ultra-Orthodox Jewish parents in Safed, Israel, in twenty twenty-five. This group is often treated as one block, yet it holds subgroups with unlike norms. The city has low vaccine uptake and repeat outbreaks. The team asked parents of young children about shots, trust, and information sources in twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four.

Three hundred eighteen parents took part, two thirds of them Ultra-Orthodox. Coverage for key shots ranged from full in one subgroup to about three fifths in a fringe subgroup. Trust in rabbis and in health workers also split by subgroup. The authors urge local services to plan for each subgroup, not the label.
pmc-12860020:
Yuwei Jia and seven co-authors cataloged the YABBY gene family in wheat, a set of plant-only switches that steer growth, leaf shape, and stress responses. Working from the Chinese Spring reference genome, they found twenty-one YABBY genes and sorted them into four subfamilies. Promoter analysis turned up control elements tied to seed endosperm development, and variant scans mapped the family's natural diversity.

Expression data showed the genes switching on in different tissues at different times, as befits developmental regulators. To test one member directly, the team overexpressed a gene called TaYABBY4A in a model plant. The engineered plants bolted and flowered late, with fewer, narrower leaves and smaller seeds. The authors conclude the family carries real weight in wheat development and grain formation. They offer the catalog as a starting map for breeders and biologists who want to tune these switches.
pmc-12860120:
Adhishree Nagda and Mukesh Meena profile in 2025 how a fungus attacks potato leaves. The fungus makes two toxins, called TeA and AOH, and leaf spot from this pest is a major threat to potato crops. The team asked how the fungus and each toxin harm the leaf in their own way.

Under the microscope, the fungus and TeA wrecked leaf tissue, bursting membranes and breaking cell parts. AOH did milder harm, mostly warping the green parts that catch light. All three stresses raised the leaf's defense enzymes and damage markers. Defense genes switched on most strongly a day or two after exposure. The authors say AOH's harm has been underrated until now.
pmc-12861920: Hamid Tizhoosh opens a 2025 collection of ten poster abstracts from a Mayo Clinic summit on artificial intelligence in medicine, held in Rochester, Minnesota. His foreword welcomes readers and frames the shared aim of the meeting, to use AI to advance care and health. The posters span radiology, pathology, cancer at the molecular level, and kidney care, with stress on fitting tools into clinical work and keeping patient outcomes at the center.
pmc-12866520:
Hengchen Liu and fourteen co-authors test whether tiny packets shed by fat-derived stem cells can heal acute tendon tears, and which cell subgroup makes the best packets. Sequencing and data analysis pointed to a subgroup lacking a marker called TNFAIP6. Packets from that subgroup healed tendon stem cells better in dish tests of growth and movement. A small RNA carried in the packets, named let-7c-5p, was present at high levels and drove much of the effect.

Animal tests backed the dish work, with tissue checks and strength tests showing better repair. The RNA acted through a chain of signals inside the cells, running from CRCT1 through JAK2 to STAT3. The authors propose building tailored packets from the chosen subgroup to strengthen their natural healing effect.
pmc-12868820:
Xiaobing Wang and co-authors map the cells of a medicinal herb's embryos one by one, hunting for the switches that guide its growth. Their 2025 study grows Pogostemon cablin embryos in culture through four shapes, from round to cotyledon stage. Single-cell sequencing of the first and last stages sorts the cells into eight types.

Tracing their paths over time singles out one regulator gene, PcNAC048. Tests in a model plant show it promotes side root growth. Binding assays then show the same factor latches onto the promoter of the gene for patchouli alcohol, the herb's prized scent compound, and turns it down. Turning the factor up or down in the herb confirms the brake. One switch thus steers both root shape and scent output.
pmc-12870120:
Kaihu Huang, Bo Gao, Lijiao Zhang, and Manhua Xiao measure the global burden of newborn jaundice in this 2025 study. The condition, tied to blood breakdown in newborns, causes avoidable deaths and long-term brain harm, mainly in poorer regions. The team used a global disease study to track its burden from 1990 to 2021.

Standardized prevalence rose by about 42 percent over that span, while the death rate fell by about 57 percent. Total years of healthy life lost fell, but case counts rose as population grew and survival improved. Burden was higher in boys and in low and middle income regions. Main risk factors were low birth weight, early birth, and air pollution. Forecasts see prevalence rising to 2050.
pmc-12872820:
Xiaochen Luo and Mengsen Zhang introduce a method for tracking change inside psychotherapy in this 2025 paper. Therapy shifts moment to moment, but most tools average those shifts away. Their method, Temporal Mapper, comes from topological data analysis. It maps a session's data into a network of stable states, called attractors, and the transitions between them. As a test, they applied it to sessions coded for interpersonal behavior and alliance ruptures, the strains that can break a therapy bond.

Therapist warmth steadied the pair's interpersonal states, both inside one session and across sessions. Confrontation ruptures did the opposite across sessions: states scattered and destabilized, even while holding steady within a session. The network picture makes such patterns visible at a glance. The authors offer the method for any high dimensional process data where the governing rules are unknown.
pmc-12890020:
Matthew Hoffman presents a 2025 review of low-dose aspirin use in pregnancy in the United States. US birth outcomes trail those of peer nations, driven by harms such as preeclampsia, early birth, stillbirth, and poor fetal growth. Most of these harms trace to the placenta and start early in pregnancy. Aspirin at low dose cuts the risk, yet uptake stays low and uneven across groups.

The review names open questions on dose, who should get the drug, and blocks to prescribing and steady use. A Delaware quality group then tackled the blocks: it set one screening rule for all, fed results back to hospitals, and taught patients more. Apt prescriptions rose from 10 to 65 percent under that push. Hoffman urges joint work by researchers, doctors, officials, and families to close the rest of the gap.
pmc-12903420:
Yu and Dev present a 2025 study on the reliability of sensor-based mobility tests in older women. Falls hit about a third of older adults each year, and women fall about twice as often as men. The timed up and go test gauges mobility, but its plain stopwatch form can miss subtle gait flaws. Wearable motion sensors add rich detail to the same test.

Twenty-five healthy women near seventy years old repeated the test in plain and dual-task forms within two days. Sensors yielded twenty-one measures, from total time to turning traits. Core gait measures proved steady across repeats. Variability and turn measures, though, bounced too much to trust. The authors sort which numbers clinics can rely on.
pmc-12924320:
Jiancheng Ye and co-authors use machine learning to map how coaching strategies for clinics relate to clinic traits and quality gains, in a 2025 study. Practice facilitation, where an expert coach helps clinics improve care, is common in primary care, but which strategies work where is murky. The team structured its data with a logic model from implementation research.

Twenty context factors were selected across five domains, and factor checks showed they hung together well. Modeling then linked all five coaching strategies, from doing tasks to teaching and coaching, with how many quality changes clinics actually adopted. The authors present the combined method as a way to study implementation with both theory and data pulling together.
pmc-12940120:
Kazuki Funahashi and eight co-authors forge one gas-read way to count gut waste parts of five kinds at once. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such parts are oft split tween two read ways since their forms clash. A tag step let one gas way count short fats, bile salts, chain parts, kin parts, and sugars in stool in one run, sixty-five parts in all.

The fly risk of short fats was curbed by the stool ground it self. Mouse diet runs matched known marks: one diet raised short fats, one raised bile salts. The team pitch the way for gut work.
pmc-13083620:
Wrinkles, folds, and creases in soft stuff were once read as flaws, but they can be made on plan to give a skin new tricks. Qiuting Zhang and co-authors review that craft in a 2026 sweep. Their base case is a thin film on a soft bed, the seed of most such marks.

The review sets out how each mark kind forms and how to steer its size and place, in stacks and zones. Made marks then serve wide work: stretch skins that feel touch, power from rub, bend light tools, and fake proof tags that can not be cloned. Wet shift skins and cell scaffolds join the list. Next steps wed smart stuff with AI design.
pmc-13086220:
Keeping disease out of pig barns depends on daily habits, yet farmers often claim stricter routines than they practice. Benti Gelalcha and co-authors interviewed Midwest swine experts in 2026 about what blocks stronger biosecurity and where it succeeds. They mined the transcripts with word counts, topic models, and theme analysis, and seven themes emerged.

Human behavior was both the weakest link and the best hope: training, communication, and workload shaped compliance. Sow and boar farms ran stricter routines than finishing farms. Trucks, shared equipment, manure handling, and plant visits stood out as risky contact points. Success stories included air filtration that kept one virus out for years and farms with dedicated biosecurity managers.
pmc-13104220:
Cheng Chen and Yong Guo review, in twenty twenty-six, the use of melanin and its engineered nano forms in tumor radiotherapy.
