Radiotherapy, the use of radiation to kill tumors, is a core cancer treatment. It is held back by harm to healthy tissue and by tumors that resist radiation. Melanin is the dark pigment in skin and hair. It can shield tissue from radiation by soaking up rays and mopping up harmful free radicals.

Yet in dark tumors such as melanoma, too much melanin makes tumors resist treatment. New work engineers melanin into tiny platforms that flip that resistance into sensitivity. They add atoms and drug loads to boost energy uptake in the tumor. The review maps both roles and the design tricks.
pmc-13105720:
Artur Rebelo and co-authors study large cancer operations that remove the pancreas with neighboring organs, in work from 2025. Such wide resections are the only hope for some advanced abdominal cancers. They also carry high risk in the weeks after surgery.

Data came from a large international collaboration of specialist centers. The study logs illness and death soon after surgery across many hospitals. It also hunts for traits that predict a hard recovery, such as age, fitness, and tumor extent. Past small series hinted results can be acceptable in picked patients. Large pooled data can now guide who should be offered the operation and how to prepare them.
pmc-13115720:
Luminita Labusca, Teodor Gheorghevici, and Bogdan Puha review mitochondria networks in ageing tissues. Their narrative review from twenty twenty-six goes beyond the powerhouse slogan. Mitochondria form shifting networks that fuse, split, and recycle. Cells even pass mitochondria between each other through tiny tubes.

Ageing disrupts network shape, placement, and quality control. Damaged DNA inside mitochondria adds to the decline. Heart, skeletal muscle, and nervous tissue get detailed coverage. Weak networks cut energy flexibility and stress resilience. Regeneration capacity falls as the network frays with age. The review frames ageing partly as a network communication failure. Therapies may aim at restoring those connections.
pmc-13117920:
Katharina Jäckle and co-authors present a 2026 study of long-term results after surgery for spine fractures. The breaks sat where the chest and lower back meet. Surgeons can rebuild the front of the spine with a metal cage, a body replacement part, or a graft of the patient's own pelvic bone. The team asked how patients felt long after each kind of fix.

The study followed 91 patients treated from 2008 to 2018 at one center. Of these, 63 filled in score forms at least a year after surgery. The forms rated pain and daily function on a set scale. The authors weighed age and sex in their math and read the gaps between groups with care. Results of this kind help surgeons pick a rebuild method with the patient's long view in mind, not just the first months of healing.
pmc-13123520:
Yuko Tashima, Masamichi Nagae, Jiaoyang Jiang, and Tetsuya Okajima solve the structure of an enzyme that tags proteins with sugar, in a 2026 study. The enzyme works inside the cell's folding compartment. It attaches a single sugar unit to a class of protein domains. The team froze the enzyme with its sugar donor bound. X-ray crystallography revealed the pair's shape. Key contact points were then tested by mutation.

Three residues form a signature grip on the donor. One is an asparagine and two are arginines. The grip needs no metal ions, breaking a common pattern. The same trio appears in a close enzyme relative. It is conserved across animals and green plants. That spread suggests an ancient shared mechanism. The structure helps explain disease-linked mutations in the enzyme. It also frames how this enzyme family evolved. Sugar-tagging enzymes matter for protein quality control across life.
pmc-13128620:
Haibo Li and co-authors mapped melanoma tumors cell by cell to find a small group of cells that may drive the cancer's spread. They studied single-cell data from ten tumors at early and later stages. One subpopulation, marked by the gene ID4, was much more common in stage III tumors. These cells divide fast, show stem-like traits, and seem to quiet the immune response, which helps explain why melanoma often resists immune therapy.

The team traced the signals these cells trade with neighbors and found a growth-factor pathway at the center. A gene switch called ETV5 appeared to run the program. When they knocked that switch down in lab cells, the cells moved and grew less and died more. The authors suggest ETV5 as a possible drug target for tumors rich in this high-risk group.
pmc-13135420:
Atsuhito Tanaka and Yuka Kamitani report an unusual emergency case in a 2026 paper. An eighty-eight-year-old man arrived with altered mental state and shock from a urinary tract infection. A CT scan showed the cause: his ureter, the tube that carries urine from kidney to bladder, was trapped in a small gap in the lower back wall called the Petit triangle.

Hernias through that gap are rare on their own. The authors say they know of no prior report with the ureter as the trapped part. Specialists in urology were called, and the hernia was pushed back into its proper space without a full operation. The paper also notes that image-guided reduction by radiology can be an option. The case warns doctors to check for this rare cause when scans show a trapped ureter.
pmc-13136220:
Liu and six co-authors ran a pilot trial in twenty twenty-six of a body-mind-spirit group cure on sleep and life quality in folks with poor sight. The cure blends east grateful thought with west talk care. Thir-ty adults took part, with one group getting ten weekly long sessions and the rest plain care.

Life quality rose in the cure group, with the clear-est gain in body health. Wrist-tracked sleep marks did not shift, yet that group said they fell asleep faster and felt more pleased with sleep. Longer sleep tied to better mind well-ness in the reads. The cure looks usable, though wear-able trust and age gaps need care.
pmc-13136520:
Jant Cres Caigoy and three co-authors test extracts of bluestem grass against the cholera bacterium and the slimy biofilms that protect it. Their 2026 study starts from a hard fact: biofilms help Vibrio cholerae resist drugs and the immune system. Plant compounds are a growing source of anti-biofilm leads.

Two extracts, rich in a pair of flavonoid compounds, killed the bacterium outright in lab tests. Below killing doses, they still blocked biofilm growth and broke down formed films. Gene checks showed the extracts turned down the bacterium's biofilm control genes and matrix building genes. The pattern hints the extracts jam the chemical chatter bacteria use to coordinate films. The authors note the grass itself is an invasive plant, turning a weed into a drug lead.
pmc-13137120:
Li and eight co-authors test ear nerve stimulation after brain injury in mice, in work from twenty twenty-six. A hard brain injury can trigger a second wave of harm from oxidative stress. That stress worsens nerve function over time.

Mice got a controlled impact injury, a standard model. Some then got stimulation of the vagus nerve through the ear skin. pmc-13137220:
Smell loss in children drew little attention before COVID-19, yet clinic patterns shifted sharply during the pandemic. Yuji Kishimoto and co-authors review patients under 18 seen at a tertiary smell clinic in Japan from 2009 to 2024. They compare causes and symptoms before and after the pandemic began.

Children made up 1.5 percent of smell patients before the pandemic and 4.7 percent after. The leading cause flipped from a structural narrowing to upper respiratory infection, and most post-pandemic cases tied to COVID-19. Distorted smell, called parosmia, appeared only in post-COVID children. The authors say pediatric smell care must now plan around infection-driven cases that barely existed before.
pmc-13139720:
Qiong Jiao and eight co-authors present a 2026 study of a low cost gene test for thyroid lumps that look unclear under the microscope. Such lumps pose a hard call before surgery: many are harmless, but some are cancers. Gene tests can sharpen the call, yet broad tests cost a lot.

Ying Zhao and co-authors compare deep and moderate muscle relaxation during keyhole gynecological surgery in a 2026 trial. The deep group reported lower pain half an hour after surgery and used fewer opioids, with fewer needing extra pain relief. Life today depends on molybdenum at the heart of many enzymes. Yet early Earth's oceans held very little of the metal. Aya Klos and co-authors ask when life first learned to use it. They also track tungsten, a chemical cousin with shared pathways. The team rebuilt the family history of the enzymes, transport systems, and cofactor pathways for both metals. Molecular dating then placed their first use in deep time.

The evidence points back 3.4 billion years, and possibly earlier. That reach covers the Eoarchean to Mesoarchean eras. The finding challenges assumptions about how scarce these metals were. It also shows how ancient and adaptable metal-based biochemistry is.
pmc-13144820:
Kevin Moncion and co-authors set out a trial on whether mixed exercise can guard the brain after stroke. Their conference abstract from 2026 notes that over half of stroke patients have lasting thinking loss in six months. One in five gets a dementia diagnosis in five years.

pmc-13145120:
Pádraig Synnott and co-authors test home blood pressure checks tied to fast drug changes after stroke or a mini stroke. Their conference abstract from 2026 notes that blood pressure often stays above target after such events. Readings were sent by phone app, and the care team could act at least once a week.

The gap was clear in the small sample. The study was built as a pilot, to test if a larger trial can work.
pmc-13145220:
Zhihao Zhao and co-authors set out a trial protocol on a pig brain extract drug for thinking after head injury. Their conference abstract from 2026 compares the drug with a known thinking drug, piracetam. Both have shown gains in past work, but proof for the extract drug has a clear gap.

pmc-13145420:
François Fenter, Vincent Dunet, Patrik Michel, and Davide Strambo studied strokes in medium-sized brain vessels. Clot-dissolving drugs are the standard acute treatment for these strokes. Their registry held two hundred twenty-nine patients, most given the dissolving drug. Half showed a fully reopened vessel on scans a day later. The drug strongly raised the odds of reopening. Yet reopening, not the drug itself, tied to better scores at a day and at three months. Patients whose vessels reopened also reached top recovery ranks more often. The study backs reopening as the goal that tracks with benefit.
pmc-13145520:
Anna Zsigmond and co-authors describe a 2026 conference lab study on a compound that may limit a harmful wave of cell stress after stroke. The waves spread through brain tissue and deepen injury. pmc-13145620:
Carl Deaney surveys stroke patients on a risk-lowering drug in this 2026 conference abstract. After a stroke or mini-stroke, patients still face high risk from artery disease even on standard drugs. Guidelines urge fuller risk control in primary care, past the usual cholesterol target.

The drug at stake is icosapent ethyl, given for raised blood fats in rural English practices. Deaney asked patients how well they grasp the drug's role, how confident they feel, and what support they need. The mixed-methods survey centers the patient's view. It aims to shape care that people can actually follow in country practices.
pmc-13145720:
Li Gao and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on long-term death after stroke in Shanghai, split by age and sex. The group was enrolled from 2002 to 2007 and tracked for a median of sixteen years. Knowing who dies late, and why, can guide care long after the first event.

The excess ran highest in older men. Older age at first stroke, high blood fats, and a past warning event each raised the long-term death risk on their own. Younger patients fared better in both sexes.
pmc-13145820:
Magdalena Targosz-Gajniak and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on whether long-term pressure drugs shape how stroke looks at arrival. Which drug class a patient took might sway arrival pressure, stroke weight, or bleed change. Records covered patients who reached hospital within a day of onset.

The authors say acute stroke forces, not home drugs, drive the early picture.
pmc-13145920:
Hanna C Persson and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on long sick leave after stroke among working-age adults in Sweden. Stroke at work age brings lasting disability and heavy costs for society. The team tracked leave from a year before stroke to three years after, against matched peers.

More than fifteen hundred first-stroke patients were set against about six thousand matched controls. Patients were on sick leave far more at every point in the span. Even before stroke, their leave ran about two and a half times the control level. Long leave before stroke, bleeding stroke type, speech trouble, hand weakness, and fall risk each foretold longer leave after. The authors urge rehab plans that weigh prior health.
pmc-13146020:
Bleeding inside the brain is the second most common stroke, and scans sometimes reveal separate ischemic lesions, small zones of starved tissue, in the same patients. They asked how common those lesions are and what predicts them in this multi-ethnic group.

Ischemic lesions appeared in twenty-seven percent of patients. Vessel disease of the amyloid type, bleeding into the brain's fluid spaces, and a surface iron stain each strongly predicted them, as did blood pressure two days in and bleed size. Patients with the lesions stayed longer in hospital and intensive care.
pmc-13146120:
Dustin J Marshall and five co-authors examine why single celled organisms are shrinking as the world warms, and what that shrinkage will do to ecosystems, in this 2026 paper. Microbes underpin food webs and the ocean's carbon handling. Warming already shrinks protists, and the authors show early signs the same holds for bacteria and yeasts.

Much, they argue, hinges on how cell size maps to energy use, and that map has been misread. pmc-13146220:
Kanila Wathsara Thanthrige Perera and co-authors report a 2026 conference post-mortem case linking repeat strokes to a reaction against device coat stuff after clot removal. pmc-13146320:
Peter Orosz and five co-authors report a 2026 conference study on how stroke patients reach specialist care in a large city. The records covered 2,017 patients treated over eight years in a city network with eleven smaller centers feeding one main center. pmc-13146420:
Guoliang Hu and Shujuan Li present a 2026 conference study on how low levels of a harmful cholesterol and high blood pressure act together on death from bleeding stroke. With pressure held low, the low cholesterol link faded away. The pair stress pressure control for people with low cholesterol.
pmc-13146620:
Camila Pantoja Ruiz and co-authors outline a 2026 conference study on why poorer patients often fare worse after stroke. Past work shows the gap in outcomes is real and lasting. What is less clear is which steps along the way drive the gap.

The study uses the South London Stroke Register, which holds first stroke cases from 1995 to 2025. The team compares outcomes at three months, one year, and five years across income groups. It then tests whether health risks, stroke care, drugs, and rehab explain part of the gap. Results were still early when the abstract was written, and the work was ongoing.
pmc-13146920:
Kailash Krishnan and colleagues shared a conference report in two thousand twenty-six using data from the RIGHT-2 trial on bleeding inside the brain. Patients arrived within hours of symptoms. The team asked whether the density of the blood clot on a scan predicts later growth of the bleed or swelling around it.

Clot density was nearly the same in patients whose bleeds grew and those whose did not. After accounting for bleed size and timing, density did not predict growth, swelling, or recovery. pmc-13148320:
Carlos Errazuriz-Henao and co-authors study how carbon rich sediment feeds volcanoes in this 2026 paper. When ocean plates sink, they carry carbonate sediment down with them. That process moves carbon into the deep Earth and shapes long term climate. What happens to the sediment at depth is still debated.

The source seems to include sediment from the Panama Basin, where carbonate builds up fast. The authors argue that partly melted sediment leaves a carbon rich residue. That residue later feeds the mantle and helps explain varied lava types.
pmc-13148820:
Chen and co-authors record brain cells in awake monkeys while one eye's view is hidden from awareness by flashing patterns, in a 2026 study. The trick, continuous flash suppression, lets scientists study vision below consciousness, but how much signal survives in the first visual area was unsettled. The authors conclude that signals surviving in this first area are too weak to feed higher visual thought.
pmc-13150920:
Martin Holmberg and four co-authors publish the design of a Swedish trial comparing two pain strategies for robot-assisted urinary tract surgery, in this 2026 protocol paper. The authors say the head-to-head against an active comparator, not placebo, is the design's point.
pmc-13154720:
Siem van Alfen and co-authors probe in a 2026 study whether iron state and a blood hormone predict cancer in the general public. Iron feeds cell growth, and imbalance has been tied to cancer, though proof is mixed. The hormone erythropoietin may also sway tumor growth over time.

Dropping early diagnoses left both of those links standing in the checks.
pmc-13155020:
Faye Yu and co-authors check shot replies in a 2026 study of a drug that sweeps shield bits from blood. The drug blocks a cell gate that saves those bits from wear, so bad self-bits fall fast. That same sweep could blunt the good bits a shot builds, a fair fear.

pmc-13156220:
Thales de Carvalho Storti and nine colleagues measure old industrial pollutants in the livers of twenty-three Magellanic penguins found stranded on the coast of Brazil in 2017. These pollutants build up through food webs and threaten top predators. The team tested for polychlorinated biphenyls, several banned pesticides, and hexachlorobenzene.

Pollutants showed up in every bird. Biphenyls and DDT compounds were the most common, though biphenyl levels trended lower than in older reports. One DDT breakdown product was still stubbornly present. No oil-related hydrocarbons were found. The authors credit the penguins' fast clearing of those chemicals, not a lack of exposure. They argue checks must go on, above all as melting polar ice may release stored pollutants again.
pmc-13156320:
Mahsa Zabihi and co-authors study why scarred lungs heal and sometimes stall, using a mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis. In this disease, support cells in the air sacs turn into scar-forming cells. The team traced those support cells through scarring and a delayed recovery phase in aged mice.

pmc-13157020:
Eugenio Rastelli leads a large team studying microbes that live on seagrasses, in work from twenty twenty-six. Seagrass meadows support coast life but are shrinking due to human harm. Microbes matter for seagrass health, yet their range and roles stay poorly known.

pmc-13157120:
Dev Patel, Diana Mastellone, Bobby Chhabra, and Michael Franco published this case report in 2026. It describes relief for Buerger disease in the arm: an inflammatory vessel disease, tied to tobacco, that chokes small and medium arteries and often leaves no bypass targets.

Their patient, a forty-six-year-old woman, had worsening left-hand pain, numbness, and fading pulses. Imaging showed the upper arm artery blocked low down, with blocks in both forearm arteries and the palm arch surviving on a side channel. pmc-13157620:
Seven doctors in Morocco report a grave sinus case in a 2026 paper. A 17 year old boy from Senegal came in with fever, headache, and a swollen forehead. The cause was Pott's puffy tumor, a rare state where sinus infection eats into the forehead bone and forms an abscess.

pmc-13158420:

pmc-13159520:

pmc-13160420:
Philip Nash and a large international team ask whether overworking kidneys spell danger after a stroke, in this 2026 study. It had been tied to death in other groups but barely studied in stroke patients.

The team pooled records for 11,175 stroke and mini-stroke patients from many cohort studies. About five percent met the hyperfiltration mark at presentation. pmc-13161720:

Working grafts rose from about two percent on day one to about forty percent at week one, and about eighty-five percent at one month. They settled near seventy-three percent after a year. Transient low function hit about seventeen percent of patients, with no permanent cases.
pmc-13163420:

The review covers mechanical pumps that support the failing heart, catheter ablation that burns away the rhythm's source, and newer treatments still emerging. Electrical storm, a run of repeated life-threatening rhythms, demands fast teamwork above all. The authors trace the shift from a single-specialty response to a multidisciplinary heart rhythm team as the unit's standard.
pmc-13166020:

pmc-13166220:

pmc-13172820:

pmc-13173320:

pmc-13175920:
Xenia Ray and co-authors wrote a 2026 best-practice guide for planning radiation therapy that adapts to the patient each day. pmc-13176220:

pmc-13176320:

pmc-13177920:

pmc-13178720:
Stephanie Shiers and co-authors map a pain-linked channel in the human spinal cord in a 2026 study. pmc-13181320:

pmc-13181520:

The authors link two-handed coordination to the evolution of limb preference in primates.
pmc-13182820:

pmc-13183220:

Their scheme joins adaptive pruning of model channels with multi key encryption.

A dynamic threshold sets pruning rates from accuracy feedback, balancing compression against quality and cutting bandwidth sharply. A distributed key protocol lets the server merge encrypted updates from many sources without decrypting them, and it resists collusion by all but one node. Tests on two image data sets showed large savings in communication.
pmc-13183920:
Erin Aboelnour and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, mouse models of myelin loss with real multiple sclerosis lesions at the single-cell gene level. The disease strips myelin and slowly destroys nerves. Two common mouse models trigger that loss chemically, but how faithfully they mirror human disease was unclear.

The team merged new and published single-cell datasets from both models and from human lesions. One model produced a stressed sheath-cell state that strongly resembled the human one. Both models met at a shared immune-responsive state during repair. Mouse immune cells followed a conserved activation program, though one model pushed it harder and longer. The comparison tells researchers which model to trust for which question.
pmc-13184020:
Five authors map the research on an early orthodontic index in this 2026 scoping review. The index, called IPION, grades how much a child in mixed dentition, when baby and adult teeth are both present, needs early treatment to prevent or intercept problems.

Following standard scoping rules, the team searched several databases in July 2025 and had five reviewers screen the records. Twelve studies from 1999 to 2025, across North America, Asia, and Africa, made the cut. Reported shares of children needing early treatment ranged widely, from 20 to 96 percent. The review also notes changes made to the index and gaps where more work is needed.
pmc-13185020:
Lanyue Zhang and eight co-authors assess community resilience during the first COVID wave after China ended its zero-COVID policy, in a study from 2026. The sudden exit in December 2022 sparked a surge in cases plus medicine shortages. Social media offers a real-time window on how neighborhoods coped.

They analyzed nearly twenty-seven thousand geotagged posts from a megacity of over ten million people across one month. Almost half the posts sought help, and most of those sought medicine. Machine learning sorted posts by content, responder, response type, and time. Response ratio, speed, and sentiment gauged how strongly communities mobilized.
pmc-13185220:
Cats that fall from height form a named injury pattern, and one clinic reviewed one hundred twenty cases to map it. Parisa Haghi and co-authors collected owner accounts of each fall plus X-ray and ultrasound findings. Most patients were under one year old, and most fell from the third floor. Three quarters had shown risky behavior before, such as balcony roaming. Leg fractures led the bone injuries, and bruised lungs led the soft tissue list.

Fall height did not predict injury severity, a surprise for owners who assume higher means worse. Worse injury did track with death, and survival overall was ninety-two point five percent. The authors urge window and balcony guards as the simplest fix.
pmc-13185520:
Costa and six co-authors reported a trial analysis in twenty twenty-six on whether strict oral hygiene eases bad breath and lifts quality of life in people with gum disease. Bad breath weighs on self-esteem and social life, and gum disease is one of its main sources.

Twenty-four patients with periodontitis were split evenly into two groups. One group followed a strict, coached hygiene routine for forty-five days; the other received no guidance in that window. By the end, half of the coached group still reported bad breath, down from all of them, while the uncoached group barely moved. Scores on a breath-focused quality-of-life scale improved clearly in the coached group, including social impact and self-esteem. Gum bleeding and plaque also improved. The authors call the routine a useful add-on to gum care, while noting the trial was small.
pmc-13185920:
Luca Lautenschläger and co-authors found that learned fear thins the nerve supply of the heart's main pumping chamber in female mice but not males, in a 2026 study. Fear conditioning is a standard way to model anxiety states in rodents. The team asked whether its effects reach the autonomic nerves of the heart.

Mice went through two days of habituation, one day of training, and one day of memory recall, with five animals per group. Hearts were then stained to show nerve fibers and measured with a design-based counting method. Females showed a real drop in nerve length density after conditioning, while males did not. The fine build of the heart cells stayed unchanged in both sexes.
pmc-13188120:
Lung researchers in China built a repair kit to fix immune cells that drive scar build-up in stiff lungs. In this disease, scar tissue grows as hurt air sac cells and immune cells egg each other on. One fix is to give the immune cells fresh power units, called mitochondria, from healthy cells. Loose power units fade fast and miss their target, so past tries fell short.

The team first used sick air sac cells as a factory for repair bubbles, a kind of tiny cell packet. They then packed healthy power units inside the bubbles, making a kind of ark that keeps them alive. A sugar tag steers the ark to the right immune cells. In mice with drug-made lung scars, the ark restored cell power balance. It also cut a scar signal and eased lung scar growth.
pmc-13188620:
Yi-Qian Sun and four co-authors linked the speed of aging, read from blood DNA, to death rates in a Norwegian population study, in this 2026 paper. Chemical marks on DNA can estimate a person's biological age and how fast it is advancing. Whether those measures hold steady over time, and what lifestyle factors move them, needed testing in a general population with repeat samples.

The team used 140 cancer-free adults from a long-running health study of Trøndelag county. Blood DNA was measured twice, in the mid-nineties and again about eleven years later, and deaths were tracked to 2023. Four established aging measures proved fairly reliable across the gap. University education went with slower aging, while smoking pointed the other way. The study connects a molecular pace-of-aging score to the hardest outcome of all, in ordinary people rather than patients.
pmc-13190020:
Pengcheng Ma and six co-authors review how gene-control marks shape the oxidative stress that drives a severe lung failure syndrome. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. The syndrome, ARDS, follows widespread injury to the air sacs and blood vessels of the lung, and no targeted drug yet works well.

Care today rests mostly on careful breathing support. Across its many causes, excess reactive oxygen acts as a shared driver, harming cells and keeping inflammation alight. The review lays out three gene-control systems: marks on DNA, marks on the proteins that spool it, and small non-coding RNAs. Each tunes how cells make or clear reactive oxygen. The authors argue these controls could become drug targets for a condition that badly needs them.
pmc-13190720:
What people eat shapes their gut microbes, and a new scoring index rates diets by how friendly they are to those microbes. Yatian Wang, Guoshan Zhang, Shen Lin, and Xiaoyuan Zhuang asked in 2026 whether that score tracks irritable bowel syndrome. Their case-control study covered 350 adults, half with the syndrome and half matched without it.

Patients scored far lower on the gut-friendly diet index than controls. Those with the highest scores had lower levels of several blood markers tied to a leaky gut and inflammation, and they reported milder symptoms. The top third of scores came with much lower odds of having the syndrome. The authors caution that symptoms may change diet rather than the other way round, so forward-looking studies are needed.
pmc-13191220:
Shih-Jen Chang and co-authors describe two patients with a rare birthmark like growth on the face in a 2026 case series. The condition, a verrucous venous malformation, is a slow growing tangle of veins with a warty surface. It usually appears on the limbs.

Facial cases are rarely reported and hard to treat, since the anatomy is delicate and anesthesia tricky. One patient, a woman of twenty six, had purple patches on her forehead and right eyelid since childhood, which thickened over four years into a heavy, drooping lid with occasional bleeding. The second was a seven year old boy with a cheek lesion. Both were treated with surgery, combined in the woman's case with a skin drug and laser work.
pmc-13191720:
Tugba Ozer and co-authors build a phone-linked virus test in a 2026 paper. Point-of-care tests must find tiny amounts of virus genetic material without a full lab. Their sensor targets DNA from the virus that causes COVID-19. The design uses peptide nucleic acid, a synthetic DNA mimic with a neutral backbone, as the catching probe.

Neutral probes avoid the fouling that charged DNA probes attract from sticky body molecules. Probe-coated magnetic beads grab the target, then charged magnetic particles tag the catch. A magnet pulls everything onto a coated electrode, and a voltage reading, sent to a smartphone, reports the amount. Under tuned conditions the sensor detected the target across a very wide range of tiny concentrations.
pmc-13192020:
Patrik Majcen and co-authors map in 2026 the repeated DNA stretches in the mealworm beetle, a widely farmed insect. Such stretches, called satellite DNAs, shape chromosomes and help steer genome change, yet they are hard to chart with one method alone. The team combined gene maps, microscope views, and computer scans of the genome.

The repeats sat in varied patterns, from spread across many chromosomes to confined to a few. Some proved very old, shared across insect orders, while others seem confined to this beetle. Six types also turned up as small free circles of DNA. All were active as RNA at set life stages, with peaks in older male pupae and young male adults.
pmc-13194320:
Avi Gajjar and a large international team quantify how deep venous drainage affects outcomes after surgery for certain brain arteriovenous malformations. Their 2026 multicenter study covers Spetzler-Martin grade two to three lesions.

The retrospective study analysed one hundred twenty-nine patients across nine centers in North America and Europe. All underwent primary surgical resection, and cases with prior endovascular or stereotactic treatment were excluded. Deep venous drainage is considered a negative prognostic factor, but its effect on functional decline was incompletely defined. The primary outcome was poor functional status after surgery. Readers get a multi-center estimate meant to sharpen surgical risk assessment.
pmc-13194520:
Yichen Ma and co-authors built a data-driven method for describing the energy spectra of beta decay, the radiation that radioisotope power sources convert into electricity. Getting the spectrum's shape right matters for designing and tuning these materials. Older curve-fitting can bias the shape, and a common smoothing method, kernel density estimation, uses one fixed width that misses sharp peaks and long tails.

Their method lets the smoothing width adapt to local data and tunes it with an optimization algorithm modeled on a fish swarm searching for food. Tested on nickel-63, sulfur-35, and carbon-14 samples, it matched measured spectra almost exactly and beat fixed-width and other adaptive rivals on accuracy and stability. The authors offer it as a cleaner theoretical tool for the field.
pmc-13194920:
Octavio Reyes-Matte is first author on a 2026 methods paper on measuring bacterial cell size precisely at scale. Bacteria vary hugely in size, and size can evolve quickly, yet comparative size studies are rare because manual measurement is slow and standard imaging segments cells poorly. The team built a pipeline named MEDUSSA.

Deep learning first sharpens fluorescent membrane images, then segments individual cells, corrects errors, and measures each one regardless of shape, chaining, or clustering. Applied to six strains of one bacterial species, the method found over twofold volume differences, driven mainly by cell width. A partly working gene variant explained one strain's narrowness. The toolkit opens comparative study of how bacterial size evolves.
pmc-13196020:
Rizwan Suliankatchi Abdulkader and co-authors mine ten years of laboratory surveillance for brain inflammation across India, in this 2025 study. Acute encephalitis syndrome strikes children hardest. Japanese encephalitis stays a leading known cause despite vaccination. The data come from a national network of 159 diagnostic laboratories.

Close to one hundred and twenty five thousand cases were logged from 2014 to 2023. About sixteen percent tested positive for at least one pathogen, and ten percent were the Japanese form, clustered in the northeast. More tests were run and more cases were found as the years went on, and the cases skewed more toward the young. The authors credit the network with changing how well the country can spot and track these ills. They urge still wider testing, and plans aimed at the zones where spread goes on.
pmc-13197020:
Sima Fansa and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on amyloidosis found through gut symptoms. Amyloidosis is a set of diseases where misfolded proteins build up in organs and harm them. Gut involvement is common but often missed, since symptoms vary a lot.

Their patient was a 68-year-old man with long-term gut complaints. Tests showed AL amyloidosis, a form tied to abnormal proteins from immune cells, along with a slow blood cancer called lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Care combined chemotherapy with support for his gut symptoms. The authors urge doctors to weigh amyloidosis when gut symptoms persist, above all in patients with related blood disorders.
pmc-13197720:
Ritesh Ranjha and co-authors explain in a 2026 review how silent malaria can keep the ill alive in a region. Some people carry the germ with no signs of sickness. Their germ loads are so low that standard tests miss them, yet they can still pass the ill on through bites.

The review shows how the germ hides by changing its coat, clinging to vessel walls, and mixing strains. Host traits such as age, prior exposure, and gene quirks help it linger too. Long silent carriage can still drain blood and slow thought in children. Health teams learn why wiping out malaria means finding people who feel well.
pmc-13198120:
Tuğba Aktemur Özalp writes about heart tracings that change over time, and why shifting patterns can mislead doctors who treat rhythm faults. One case in point is Brugada syndrome, a fault passed down in families that raises the risk of sudden death. Its classic mark is a raised segment in the right chest leads.

That mark does not always stay put. It can fade, move to lower leads, or look normal on one tracing and odd on the next. The author argues that a single tracing should never settle the call. Symptoms such as fainting, plus any family history of sudden death, must weigh in the choice, and close watch is wise.
pmc-13199220:
Pati Aji Achdiat and five colleagues report a fifteen-year-old girl with a rapidly growing giant wart-like tumor beside the anus, a Buschke-Löwenstein tumor. This locally destructive growth, driven by low-risk human papillomavirus types, usually afflicts immunocompromised adults; her immune system was normal and she had no standard risk factors.

Testing identified HPV type 11. The crucial history: she reported a sexual assault about a year and a half earlier. Surgeons removed the mass completely, and at one month nothing had returned. The authors emphasize that giant condyloma in an adolescent should trigger both timely surgery and careful consideration of abuse, which changes the care owed to the patient.
pmc-13199420:
Porntita Sae-li and colleagues surveyed Thai medical students on antibiotic knowledge and self-treatment in a 2026 study. Misuse of antibiotics fuels drug resistance, a major global threat. Future doctors who self-medicate set a poor pattern, so the team measured what students know and do.

More than five hundred students at a public university answered an anonymous online survey. Most knew drug names and the need to finish a course. Fewer than half grasped resistance in gonorrhea or how resistance spreads between people and animals. Senior clinical students scored higher than juniors. Junior status tied to using antibiotics for wrong illnesses and stopping courses early. Teaching should be tailored by year, the authors say.
pmc-13200120:
Hang Li and colleagues pooled studies on decent work among nurses in China in 2026. Decent work means fair pay, safety, dignity, and an equal setting at work, in the labour standards sense. No pooled estimate existed for Chinese nurses, so the team systematically reviewed and combined the available surveys to quantify the level.

Overall, nurses in China scored at a moderate level for decent work. Nurses exposed to workplace violence were among those with low levels. The authors urge policymakers and managers to watch groups scoring lowest, support career development for clinical nurses, and build a good working atmosphere as a base for further improvement.
pmc-13200320:
Older adults often live with two or more chronic diseases at once, and diet is one lever that might hold that count down. Wuchao Tu and co-authors study plant-based eating in 7,551 older Chinese adults from a 2018 national survey. Their 2026 paper scores each diet three ways: overall plant content, the healthful plant share, and the unhealthful plant share.

Higher overall and healthful plant scores went with lower odds of carrying several diseases at once. The unhealthful score, built on refined and sugary plant foods, went the other way and raised the odds. Where people lived and how active they were shaped the links. Checks with missing values filled in and with diabetes cases removed gave the same picture, which the authors offer as a dietary lead for prevention.
pmc-13200420:
Yuanhan Zhong and eleven co-authors trace how a plant compound turns into active forms inside the body, in this 2026 paper. The compound, platycodin D, comes from a medicinal root and fights acute lung injury, but it absorbs poorly by mouth. Its sugar chains suggest gut germs may cut it into the forms that truly work.

The team combined germ-drug interaction tests, computer target prediction, and animal checks. In dishes they found nine stripped forms and nine sugar-chain pieces. In blood, only three stripped forms and five simple sugars showed up. The stripped forms pointed at a target called PTPN2, and the sugars at both PTPN2 and HIF1A. Mouse models of lung injury backed the activity. The authors note, against expectation, that fatty acid by-products were not the active agents, and offer their method for other hard-to-absorb plant drugs.
pmc-13200720:
Yanira Jiménez-Padilla and Brent Sinclair show gut yeasts speed cold recovery in fruit flies in this 2026 study. Microbe research on flies centers on bacteria, while yeasts were assumed to be mere food. The team asked whether gut yeasts change how fast flies wake from a chill coma, a stand-in for cold tolerance.

Females raised germ free recovered forty-two percent more slowly than flies with their normal microbes. Live native yeast species fully restored the speed, while baker's yeast and dead yeasts did not. The rescue arrived within forty-eight hours, appeared only in females, and grew with dose. Gut yeasts were confirmed alive inside the flies, marking a true if passing symbiosis with real effects on stress tolerance.
pmc-13202020:
Saranya Velmurugan and co-authors pooled studies on a blood protein gene and sickle cell disease severity in 2026. The protein, haptoglobin, mops up free hemoglobin and shields tissue from damage. Gene variants of it might explain why the same disease hits some patients harder.

Eight studies were combined, with gene pathway tools adding context. Under a dominant model, the variants linked significantly to disease severity. Splitting results by ancestry, the link held in African and South American groups but not in Asian groups. The authors frame the gene as one factor in the disease's uneven course. Quality checks and pooled statistics were used across five databases.
pmc-13202520:
Di Wang, Aisong Zhu, and co-authors test if cuff based blood flow training boosts gains from skill drills in basketball men, in work from 2026. Twenty six male players were split in two groups for half a year. One group did plain skill drills, while the other added cuff work to the same drills.

Checks ran each month on strength, jump, speed, and shape. The cuff group gained more on half squat strength and on raw speed. Gains in full squat and staying power were shared by both groups. Jump and quick turn gains came with time in both groups, with no clear edge for cuffs.
pmc-13203520:
Sergio Méndez-Cardona and co-authors survey sand flies where the Andes meet the Amazon in southeastern Peru, in a 2026 paper. The flies spread a skin disease that weighs heavy on the region, yet local data are thin. Light traps ran in the wet season across four home types near homes and woods.

More than twenty-six hundred flies from thirty-two species were caught. Home type drove the mix most, with nightly low heat the top weather link. Second-growth woods and home edges held the most flies. Bamboo woods held fewer flies, but near all were possible disease carriers. Home-edge groups mirrored the woods next door, hinting at spillover paths toward houses.
pmc-13204120:
Garrido and co-authors studied how immune cells file certain oxidized fats into their membranes, in a paper published in 2026. Macrophages, the immune system's scavengers, reshape their membranes when activated. The fats in question arise during inflammation and differ subtly by where an oxygen group sits. Whether the cells treat the variants differently was unknown. The team fed three variants to mouse macrophages and tracked where each ended up among the membrane's fat classes.

The variants sorted themselves by class, each family of membrane fats taking a distinct share. That patterned sorting hints the cell is not merely soaking up whatever arrives. Where these fats sit can steer signaling and cargo traffic inside the cell. The findings add a rule to how inflammation chemistry is stored in the membrane. Future work can ask whether the sorting aids or harms the immune response.
pmc-13206120:
Karan Chadda and co-authors propose racehorse lung bleeding as a stand in model for a rare human lung bleeding disorder, in work dated 2026. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage floods the air sacs with blood and often kills. Its mechanics are poorly understood, and no good animal model exists to study it.

Horses develop exercise induced lung bleeding after hard racing, in up to ninety-five percent of thoroughbreds. The damage pattern mirrors the human disorder: capillary stress failure, inflammation, and later scarring of lung tissue. It also links to high lung artery pressure, as in some human cases. The authors argue this common horse condition is an underused research gift.
pmc-13206620:
Saja Alnahar, Mahmoud Alquraan, and Austen El-Osta model how COVID-19 knowledge, attitudes, and behavior relate in Jordanian undergraduates. Their 2026 study starts from a policy point: mandates guide behavior briefly, while knowledge and attitudes can sustain it. Health campaigns during the pandemic aimed at exactly those levers.

More than thirteen hundred students at one university answered a validated questionnaire in 2021. Knowledge was low for most, with only a tiny share scoring high, while reported preventive attitudes ran much higher. Structural modeling linked the three domains in the full data. The authors aim to inform health initiatives and campus programs for future outbreaks. Student populations matter because universities concentrate young adults whose behavior can spread or slow a virus.
pmc-13207620:
Antonino Maniaci and eight co-authors review regional anaesthesia for head and neck surgery, where numbing specific nerves can replace part of general anaesthesia. The region's dense wiring makes such blocks attractive, especially within enhanced-recovery programs that try to spare opioids. The team searched the literature from 2000 to 2025 across three databases and organized it under a narrative review framework.

The review maps the anatomy behind the main blocks, from surface neck blocks to deep and single-nerve ones. The most consistent evidence supports the superficial cervical plexus block, mainly in thyroid surgery: less pain, fewer opioids in the first day, and shorter stays. Ultrasound guidance has sharpened accuracy and safety, though some risks remain debated. The authors call for cleaner trials to firm up guidance.
pmc-13207920:
Kasra Cheraqpour and co-authors open a review series on how spaceflight changes the eye, in a 2026 paper. Long missions threaten vision, and eye trouble ranks among the top health worries for astronauts. Two stressors dominate: weightlessness and cosmic radiation. Weightlessness pushes fluid toward the head, raising pressure inside the skull. That shift is blamed for the neuro-ocular syndrome seen in crew members.

Radiation adds its own harms, from cataracts to retinal spots and nerve damage. Both stressors act through oxidative stress and failing cell power plants, the review argues. The authors also survey the eye checks now done in flight, such as retinal imaging. They call for combined countermeasures and early warning markers. The stakes rise as lunar and Martian missions approach, they note.
pmc-13208020:
Zhenzhen Wu and co-authors test a detoxified version of a blood hormone as a nerve-repair drug, focusing on the support cells that nurse injured nerves, in a 2026 study. Erythropoietin helps nerves recover but also thickens blood dangerously, causing clots. Its carbamylated cousin keeps the protective side without the blood effects. The team studied Schwann cells, the cells that wrap peripheral nerves and guide regrowth.

In dishes, the drug improved Schwann cell survival, growth, movement, and production of nerve growth factor, with a best dose identified. In rats with crushed sciatic nerves, treated animals regained function significantly better by three weeks. The authors argue the support cells are the drug's main lever: energise the nurses, and the nerve's own repair programme runs faster. Clinical translation would need the usual safety ladder first.
pmc-13209120:
Hui Wang and co-authors build sensors into road reinforcement grids so a highway can report its own strain while it is being built and used. They stitch two kinds of fiber-optic strain sensors into the grids on a factory knitting line, then test which kind survives production and paving. A full-scale damage trial followed during expressway construction in Hebei, China.

The steel-armored sensor came through intact, keeping nearly 99 percent of its signal over a 60-meter run, and its readings tracked the grid's stretching in a clean straight line. The bare sensor broke during production. A rubber shielding scheme guarded the sensors against hot asphalt and rollers, giving crews a workable method for live road monitoring.
pmc-13210020:
Sachin Acharya, Satyanarayana Poojari, and Asha Kamath study machine learning prediction of polycystic ovary syndrome, in a research paper from 2026. The hormonal disorder affects fertility and long-term health. Data sets for it are skewed, with far fewer positive cases, and they carry many measures, both of which can bias models toward the majority class.

Data cover forty-one measures for more than five hundred patients from ten hospitals in Kerala, India. Five model types were tested across skew levels made by resampling. Tree ensemble models led at mild skew, while a boosting model led at stronger skew. At high skew, minority class accuracy fell below half. The study guides model choice.
pmc-13210720:
Zhuoxi Chen and co-authors test liquiritigenin, a licorice-root flavonoid, against rheumatoid arthritis, focusing on the joint-lining cells that drive its damage. In this autoimmune disease, fibroblast-like synoviocytes overactivate, invade cartilage, and feed inflammation. The team used a rat model of arthritis and a human joint cell line inflamed in the dish.

In rats, the compound eased joint swelling and bone damage and calmed the thickened joint lining. In cells, it slowed growth, migration, and invasion, cut damaging oxygen by-products, and lowered two inflammatory messengers in both rat blood and cell fluid. Protein tests confirmed it works through a named defense-and-inflammation pathway trio. The authors propose the licorice compound as a candidate for further arthritis drug work.
pmc-13211220:
Gevenois and five co-authors searched for the best sugar blend to protect antibody proteins inside inhalable dry powders, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Antibodies sprayed into the lungs could treat disease at the source, but drying and storage can clump the proteins and ruin them.

The team spray-dried cow antibodies with three protectors: a sugar alcohol, a common sugar, and a starch-like polymer, alone and in mixes. They measured moisture and clumping right after drying and again after ten months on the shelf. A two-part mix of the sugar alcohol and the polymer guarded the protein best across the whole period. A three-part mix that added the sugar handled drying well but faded over time. The powders also flew well in tests of how they would travel into deep lung tissue. Picking partners with matching strengths is the lesson.
pmc-13211720:
Tatjana Munko and four co-authors measured in 2026 why lung tuberculosis gets treated late in Croatia, a low-incidence European country. Records and interviews covered 116 adults at one care center. The median wait from first symptoms to treatment was 85 days. Living in the countryside was the strongest single factor, stretching the wait by about 88 percent over city patients.

People living alone waited about half again as long. Retired patients faced longer delays inside the health system itself. Oddly, lacking chest pain came with shorter waits and lower odds of extreme delay. The authors warn that aging populations and more one-person homes may widen these gaps. They urge outreach aimed at rural, retired and solitary patients. Keeping clinical suspicion alive matters as the disease grows rarer.
pmc-13213520:
HaEun Lee, Camilla Bjelland, Kay Wallace, Donath Asiimire, and Fred Sheldon Mwesigwa published this study in 2026. It records what frontline health workers saw after global aid was abruptly cut in early 2025, focusing on Nakivale, a large refugee settlement in Uganda.

Interviews with twenty-six practitioners across six facilities, held in July 2025, surfaced four broad themes. Services shrank across HIV and tuberculosis care, nutrition, maternal health, and routine visits. Supplies ran short, from medicines to fuel for transport. Staff numbers fell while workloads and burnout rose, though resilience also showed. Workers predicted worse disease patterns and more migration if the gap persists. Their advice: restore funding to high-impact services, strengthen local leadership, and reform policy. The authors frame the testimony as evidence of how fast distant budget decisions land on refugee health.
pmc-13213820:
Sarah Merritt Ryan writes from lived experience about why people stop taking antipsychotic drugs, in this 2026 essay. Ryan is a survivor of schizophrenia who reports full cognitive and emotional recovery. Beyond side effects and lack of insight, she argues, stigma loads these pills with false cultural meanings that feel as real as the illness itself.

She defines emotional recovery as trusting and believing in oneself again, and wanting to be oneself. That self-trust, she says, lets patients spot stigma, reject faulty reasoning, and choose self-care over fear of judgment. She tells her own story: warned by a counselor, she still quit her drug under stigma's pull, then suffered three major breaks. Staying on the drug for life, she concludes, is what let her move forward. The essay asks clinicians to treat emotional recovery as part of adherence care.
pmc-13214220:
Najmeh Davoodian and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Donor heifers give embryos after their ovaries are strongly stimulated. That stimulation creates oxidative stress, which can hurt later fertility. The team tests whether melatonin implants protect the next breeding round. Twenty-four donor heifers took part. Fourteen got implants dosed by body weight before the program.

Blood was drawn at the first breeding after embryo collection. Lab scores measured antioxidant capacity and oxidant load, joined into one stress index. Pregnancy outcomes were then followed for each group. The gap between flushing and breeding was like in both groups. Cattle breeders get a direct test of a cheap implant for donor care. Embryo programs depend on donor fertility after collection, so guarding that window has real cash value for herds.
pmc-13214620:
González-Enríquez and co-authors studied how weather relates to dengue cases in northwestern Mexico. Dengue has resurged worldwide as the climate warms, and the region's seven states report cases year after year. The team matched lab-confirmed dengue data from 2017 to early 2025 with weather station records, and used regression models to test which climate factors predicted case counts in each state.

In Jalisco, temperature in all its forms plus rainfall predicted cases and explained about a fifth of the variation. Elsewhere the links were weaker or absent: rainfall had no predictive value in Colima and Michoacán, and models for the other states explained between 5 and 23 percent. The authors conclude that climate explains only a modest share of dengue patterns, and that mosquito ecology, population immunity, virus types, travel, and control programs must be counted in too.
pmc-13215520:
Jiangxu Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 case study on using AI image generation to renew a traditional Chinese folk art, the New Year pictures of Zhuxian Town. These prints are known for bright colours and strong folk customs.

The team built a checked image dataset, organized keywords into a three-layer thesaurus, and trained a LoRA model on the Liblib platform in two stages. The trained model reproduced the prints' stylistic features while blending in modern design elements. The outputs were applied to cultural and graphic products. The authors offer the workflow as a reference for digitizing other folk arts without losing their character.
pmc-13215620:
Hao Yuan and co-authors propose a 2026 encryption scheme for sharing medical data across the Internet of Medical Things. Wearable and monitoring devices produce sensitive records that many parties need to read under strict rules.

Their design combines blockchain records with multi-authority attribute-based encryption, so no single authority controls all keys. A distributed key generation protocol and threshold signatures verify where data came from, while a hierarchical access tree matches the layered structure of medical files. Proxy re-encryption allows permissions to be revoked without rebuilding the system. Tests on a 100-node network reached consensus in about 280 milliseconds, and security analysis found resistance to common attacks.
pmc-13217520:
Dominika Opala and co-authors present a 2026 case report about a woman in her late thirties. Her severe myalgic encephalomyelitis, also called chronic fatigue syndrome, ended in assisted suicide in Switzerland. The illness followed an Epstein-Barr virus infection and left her progressively disabled.

Over two years, multidisciplinary medical, psychological, and rehabilitative treatment failed to halt the decline, and treatment sensitivities multiplied. Blood tests showed raised cytokines, but the pattern matched no recognized autoimmune disease, and no effective therapy existed for her presentation. Her decision-making capacity was assessed repeatedly and judged intact. pmc-13218120:

pmc-13218220:
Xiao-Miao Han and co-authors grind in a 2026 study buckwheat four ways and test which flour makes the best gluten-free noodles, in bite and in digestion speed. pmc-13218420:

pmc-13219020:
Chagas disease patients are living longer and moving less, which may harm their arteries. Erica Maria Diferenz and co-authors studied 349 patients with chronic Chagas disease. pmc-13220120:
Vincent Peters, with Kayleigh-Ann Clegg, reports on the growing pains of remote patient monitoring in the Netherlands in a 2026 article. pmc-13220220:
Collin Sindt and co-authors study the structure of ultra-thin layers used in solar cells, in a 2026 paper. The layers sit on electrodes and help pull positive charges out of the cell. pmc-13220420:
Tailai An and co-authors compare two stitching methods for closing the common bile duct after keyhole surgery to remove duct stones, in a 2026 study. The running stitch came out ahead on the points reported in the opening results. Readers weighing closure choices after this surgery get a direct head-to-head account from real practice.
pmc-13220820:

pmc-13221620:
Medical chatbots can give dangerous answers, and checking them takes medical, ethical, and legal judgment at once. Lenard Paulo Velasco Tamayo and co-authors built a multi-agent system in 2026 that grades chatbot replies for risk across all three domains together.

The study reports how the staged design performed against simpler setups that rely on one general model.
pmc-13221720:
Martin Zinicola, Reinaldo F Cooke, Juan Manuel Bollatti, and Ramiro Andreola report a two thousand twenty-six trial of a maternal appeasing substance given at castration in feedlot bulls. Intake, growth, hair stress markers, and daily disease checks were recorded for six weeks. The design tests whether a scent signal can ease a routine but painful procedure.
pmc-13222820:
Fengming Zhang and co-authors pool trials of burst-style interval training in young trained athletes, in work from 2026. The training swaps short hard efforts with rest, and coaches use it widely. The team asks how much it lifts fitness in teens who already train.

pmc-13223020:

pmc-13223720:
Shengdan Zhang and co-authors build a two drug microneedle patch for diabetic gum disease in this 2026 paper. pmc-13223920:
Juliette de Klerk and co-authors search blood for early warning signs of kidney disease in a 2026 diabetes paper. Eleven bits tracked with who got sick. Samples from three drug trials showed which bits the kidney drug changed. One bit stood out as a new marker.
pmc-13224320:
Ajay Thomas Joy and Preetha read two classic Malayalam films as a study of masculinity disguised as goodness, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13224720:

pmc-13226220:

pmc-13226820:

pmc-13230220:

pmc-13230520:

pmc-13232920:

pmc-13233220:

pmc-13233520:

pmc-13233720:

pmc-13234720:

pmc-13234920:

pmc-13235520:

pmc-13236620:

pmc-13236720:

pmc-13236920:

pmc-13237220:

pmc-13237320:

pmc-13237920:

pmc-13239320:

pmc-13240320:

pmc-13241520:

pmc-13242020:

pmc-13242120:

pmc-13242720:

pmc-13242820:

pmc-13243220:

pmc-13244520:

pmc-13244820:

pmc-13244920:

pmc-13245320:

pmc-13246420:

pmc-13246720:
