Their method, called CRUSH, uses a set of pattern rules written in a chemical notation.

CRUSH tries its rules at every breakable bond rather than stopping at the first match, opening many more paths. Tested on five data sets, from drugs to natural products and food compounds, it produced more pieces than known methods. Its pieces also reached parts of chemical space the other tools missed, and they were smaller and simpler. The code is free online.
pmc-13267620:
Qianwei Tang and colleagues present a 2026 study of a sticky gel that delivers a healing drug to mouth ulcers. Dexamethasone calms inflammation well, but the wet, moving mouth washes treatments away fast. The team packed the drug into tiny plastic particles, then set those into a gelatin gel. A special linker bonds the gel firmly to tissue.

The bonded gel gripped skin about ten times more strongly than the plain version. It stayed in saliva for over five days, slowly breaking down while releasing its drug particles. In lab tests the particles did not harm gum cells and helped them grow. In animals, one application healed mouth ulcers quickly. The authors offer the system as a step toward longer-lasting mouth treatments.
pmc-13267820:
Jing Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 multi-center study of satisfaction among disabled older inpatients in China. The team surveyed 1,157 residents at seven institutions. They asked whether men and women judge nursing home style care differently, and how illness type changes that judgment.

Men were clearly less likely than women to report satisfaction. The gap held for heart and vessel disease wards and for chronic geriatric disease groups. For nerve disease groups the gap was smaller and less certain. Most residents carried nerve or heart conditions, often both. The authors argue that one-size care misses real differences in what men and women need. They urge care plans shaped by gender, covering social and emotional support as well as medical needs.
pmc-13267920:
Shenglu Xu and Hong Gao wrote a 2026 letter raising doubts about a study of vibration for injection pain. The study gave each person a control shot, then a shot with vibration meant to dull pain. The letter writers say the fixed order is a problem: everyone got the control first, so learning, expectation, and leftover soreness could skew self-reported pain.

They also note the study enrolled people who fear needles but never measured their anxiety with a standard scale. Claims that vibration works better with thicker needles rested on two groups of ten, without a proper interaction test. They found small mismatches in the reported effect sizes and an impossible height value in a data table. The writers ask for clearer reporting so others can check the work.
pmc-13269320:
Chiara Saracini writes in 2026 about cognitive sovereignty and neuro-justice, arguing that brain technology debates ignore the realities of the Global South. Wealthy countries frame neurotechnology around enhancement, privacy, and mental liberty. In the South, she notes, the pressing need is basic health care and brain rehabilitation, and falling behind could drain national brain capital rather than upgrade it.

Artificial intelligence deepens the shift: systems no longer just read brain signals but adaptively interact with users, blurring the line between device and cognitive influence. Southern countries have joined rights debates, led visibly by Chile, yet remain far from the economic and scientific centers driving development. Saracini calls for frameworks built on Southern priorities, not imported assumptions.
pmc-13269620:
Arthur C K Chu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a radioactive form of an antibody drug for breast cancer. The antibody targets a growth receptor found in large amounts on some cancer cells. Two mercury forms attached to it emit short-range electrons that damage DNA up close.

The labeled drug bound strongly, at 87 to 91 percent, to receptor-rich cancer cells and moved into their nuclei. Nuclear dose rose with the number of receptors on each cell line. Survival of the richest cell line fell below 5 percent, while the unlabeled drug did not cut survival. Blocking the receptor restored survival to about 60 percent. Tumors in mice took up the drug on scans.
pmc-13270220:
Ali Keshavarz and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on whole-grain bread eating among university students in southwest Iran. A validated questionnaire was given face-to-face to 567 students at a medical sciences university in the 2024 to 2025 academic year. Knowledge, perceived barriers, and wider diet habits were scored.

Rarely eating whole-grain bread was reported by 42.15 percent of students, while 32.45 percent ate it at least one to three times weekly. Mean knowledge scored 13.88 and barriers 18.53 on the scales used. Eating rose with knowledge and fell as barriers rose, with correlations of 0.196 and minus 0.422. Barriers also tracked with less fruit, vegetable, and dairy intake and more sweet and salty snacks.
pmc-13270520:
Sarah Beatriz de Fucio and co-authors review in 2026 how three-dimensional cell culture is changing the study of protozoan parasites, the single-celled organisms behind malaria, Chagas disease, and other neglected infections. Flat dishes of cells, the field's workhorse, miss the layered architecture of real tissue. The authors survey the newer platforms now in use, from filter-grown cell layers to living tissue replicas.

Spheroids, organoids, engineered scaffolds, and chip devices that flow fluid through miniature organs can now imitate gut, brain, heart, and blood vessel environments. Studies using them follow parasites such as Trypanosoma cruzi, Plasmodium species, and Giardia through infection in near-real conditions. The authors argue these models sharpen understanding of host-parasite contact and should yield better-targeted drugs than flat cultures alone.
pmc-13270820:
Zobaer Akond is lead author of a 2026 genome-wide study of RNA interference gene families in Brassica rapa, an oilseed crop grown for vegetable oil and food. These genes help switch other genes off and defend plants against viruses and stress, but they had not been mapped in detail in this species.

The team found four DCL genes, 13 AGO genes, and six RDR genes spread across the plant's ten chromosomes. Their structures closely matched those of a well-studied relative, Arabidopsis. Analysis linked the genes to virus defence and gene silencing, and traced shared segments that suggest some genes arose by duplication. The authors frame the catalogue as a base for crop improvement.
pmc-13271020:
Nishimura and co-authors report a melanoma that grew inside a birthmark in a twenty-three-year-old woman. Congenital melanocytic nevi are moles present from birth. Giant ones carry a known cancer risk, but medium-sized ones are considered low risk and are usually left alone.

Her mole had been stable for years, then enlarged quickly and bled over two months. Microscope and staining tests confirmed a nodular melanoma with fast-dividing cells and growth into blood vessels, staged as IIc. The case warns that rapid change in any congenital mole, whatever its size, is a danger sign. The authors urge careful monitoring and teaching patients which changes demand a prompt visit.
pmc-13271420:
Xiaoliang Li and Qi Feng report a 2026 case of pneumonia in which lung wash fluid revealed two hard-to-grow bacteria at once. One was Tropheryma whipplei, the cause of Whipple's disease. The other was Chlamydia psittaci, a bird-linked germ that causes psittacosis. Finding both together in a lung infection is rare, and standard cultures often miss such organisms.

The patient was a 69-year-old male farmer with five days of high fever. Flu treatment and then a first antibiotic failed, and chest scans showed patchy shadows with thickened lining. A targeted gene sequencing test on lung fluid identified both bacteria. Treatment switched to two suitable antibiotics, fever fell fast, and scans cleared steadily over six months.
pmc-13271520:
Loema Moshi Buyi is lead author of a 2026 interview study of why intensive care nurses at Tanzania's Muhimbili National Hospital struggle to follow guidelines for suctioning breathing tubes. Suctioning keeps the airways of ventilated patients clear. Guidelines exist for doing it safely, yet adherence is weak in resource-limited settings.

Seventeen experienced nurses were interviewed. Three barrier groups emerged. The first was scarce resources, including too few staff, equipment, and supplies. The second was human and behavioural challenges, such as knowledge gaps and resistance to changing routine practice. The third was guidelines that were hard to access and felt untailored to local conditions. The authors conclude the problem is mainly systemic, not individual neglect.
pmc-13271920:
Jiemei Chen and colleagues pool in 2026 the results of cell therapy using a woman's own regenerative cells for stress urinary incontinence. Leaking with cough or effort affects many women, and standard options do not suit everyone. Injecting the patient's own cells aims to rebuild the weakened closing mechanism of the bladder outlet.

The review gathered 19 studies with 591 patients from five major databases. Pooled cure stood near two fifths of patients, and over half improved by the studies' own measures. Pad tests, leak counts, and quality of life scores all got better. Harm events stayed uncommon, though results varied widely between studies.
pmc-13272120:
Xinwei Ma and coauthors develop in 2026 a CT-based method to estimate immune activity markers inside kidney tumors without a biopsy. Two genes tied to natural killer cell killing, ICAM1 and RAET1E, serve as the targets. Linking scan patterns to gene activity could help judge a tumor's immune environment when tissue sampling is impractical.

Scans from 143 patients with clear cell kidney cancer were measured for thousands of image features, while gene data came from 538 tumor samples in a public atlas. A penalized classifier learned to predict high or low expression of each marker. Tissue staining in 26 separate cases provided an outside check on the model.
pmc-13272220:
Lindsay A. Welikovitch is lead author of a 2026 neuropathological study, an examination of brain tissue after death, of aducanumab, an antibody drug against amyloid beta, in Alzheimer's disease trial participants. Scans and fluid tests already showed such antibodies clear amyloid from the brain; this study checked the tissue itself.

The team compared a key memory region from six treated participants, who died between seven weeks and five years after their last dose, with nine matched untreated patients. Treated brains showed a strong reduction in amyloid burden, with some amyloid redistributed around small vessels. A tau-related measure near plaques fell, but established tangles did not change, and immune cell reactivity matched untreated patients. Plaques appeared to rebuild with time since the last dose.
pmc-13272320:
Zhe Xu and coauthors gather in 2026 trial findings on how cervical cancer patients manage vaginal irrigation themselves during radiotherapy. The practice helps keep the vaginal canal open and clean during treatment, but guidance for patients doing it at home was scattered across small trials. No guidelines or prior syntheses met the review's standards.

Twenty-three randomized trials were included in the synthesis. The authors distilled twelve recommendations across four areas, covering personal care plans, structured health teaching, supervision methods, and psychological support. Because trial quality carried real risk of bias, every recommendation landed as conditional rather than strong.
pmc-13272420:
Lin Tang and coauthors measure in 2026 skin thickness at pressure injury sites with high-frequency ultrasound to test a possible early warning tool. Judging these wounds by eye misses damage forming under the surface. Ultrasound at eighteen megahertz images skin layers finely, but its readings in injured tissue needed validation.

Forty-two bedridden patients had measurements taken at each wound and at nearby healthy skin. Injured skin was substantially thicker than neighboring normal skin, a large and clear difference. The analysis also tested whether injury risk status and body weight changed that gap, toward a scanning protocol nurses could use at the bedside.
pmc-13272520:
Qunling Yang and co-authors tested a new mRNA treatment for chronic hepatitis B in a 2026 mouse study. Current interferon treatment helps only a small share of patients. The team packaged mRNA coding for a fused interferon protein inside tiny fat particles called lipid nanoparticles.

Earlier virus based delivery of the same fused protein had lowered hepatitis B markers safely in mice. A single vein injection of the new particles lowered virus antigens in a dose related way. One dose matched the effect of an approved interferon drug given under the skin. Safety checks showed no organ damage, only brief immune changes. Repeated doses raised antibodies against the human protein in mice, a problem the authors do not expect in people.
pmc-13272620:
Xingyu Yang and five co-authors uncover, in 2026 work, an odd path in a reaction between an excited oxygen atom and a common ether. Such reactions matter for the chemistry of space clouds and of flames. The textbook path has the atom slip into a bond of the other molecule.

Lab tests joined with high-grade sums show that path does not run here. In its place, the atom strikes a hydrogen-carbon bond, wakes it, and the molecule folds into a ring as it reacts. A dip below the start line in the energy path makes the rate rise with heat, a rare twist the sums match to the lab reads. The team expects the same path in kin reactions, which would widen its reach.
pmc-13272820:
Panpan Hu and seven co-authors grow mini-tumors from patients' spinal chordomas to test drug response, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Chordoma is a rare bone cancer with few working drug options, and standard chemotherapy barely helps. Lab-grown organoids can preserve a tumor's traits and screen drugs, but linking pathways to response in this cancer was untested.

Organoids grown from surgical samples matched their source tumors and stayed stable over six passages. Screening a panel of clinical drugs found one, gemcitabine, hit hardest. Silencing the TP53 gene then blunted the drug's killing effect and let cells keep dividing. The authors conclude the drug's power here depends on TP53, a clue for choosing patients.
pmc-13273220:
Qiao Yin and a very large team studied depression in Parkinson's disease in a 2026 paper centered on complement protein C3. Depression is common and early in Parkinson's, and it differs between the sexes. The team suspected that immune pruning of synapses, the links between neurons, plays a part.

Blood protein profiling in patient cohorts showed immune and clotting pathways raised in both sexes, alongside strong sex specific changes. In a mouse model, complement proteins rose in the hippocampus, immune cells in the brain ate synapses, and depressive like behavior appeared. Removing the C3 gene protected both movement and mood and saved synapses. A botulinum toxin treatment also eased behavior, and its benefit depended on the complement pathway.
pmc-13273520:
Muhammad Hassan Saeed leads a 2026 meta-analysis of colchicine, an anti-inflammatory drug, for preventing atrial fibrillation after heart and chest surgery. This irregular heartbeat is the most common rhythm problem after such surgery and links to heart failure, stroke, and death. The team pooled randomised trials published up to September 2025.

Twelve trials with 5,637 participants were included. Colchicine cut the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation, with a risk ratio of 0.73, and both short and long courses worked. Gut side effects rose, including diarrhea, but bleeding, sepsis, and in-hospital death did not increase clearly. The authors support colchicine as a safe, inexpensive add-on, with short courses offering the best tolerability.
pmc-13273720:
Nagham Said and co-authors ran a pilot study of hepatitis A among Palestinian refugees in North Lebanon in a 2026 report. Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water and can be prevented by vaccine. Lebanon has seen recent outbreaks, yet refugee data were missing.

They tested 84 refugees attending a hospital in the Al-Baddawi camp between December 2023 and May 2024. Nearly four in five carried antibodies showing past infection or vaccination, while only a small share showed signs of recent infection. People aged sixteen to thirty stood out with higher antibody rates. Reported vaccination coverage was very high, though the authors warn it may not hold across the wider refugee population. They urge sustained vaccination and better surveillance.
pmc-13273820:
Meng and colleagues write a 2026 letter to the editor about deep learning in gum disease diagnosis. The letter responds to a study by Valente and colleagues. That study used a YOLOv8l model to read dental images.

The writers praise the model's promise for periodontal diagnosis. Periodontal disease affects the gums and bone around teeth. They also raise concerns about class imbalance in training data. Rare disease stages may be underrepresented, skewing results. The letter points to Vision Transformers as another approach. It also urges combining images with other data types. Three-dimensional scans could add useful detail. The authors close with directions for stronger future studies.
pmc-13274120:
Liang Yuan, Xingyi Xie, and Yiqian Wen pool trials in 2026 on AI help in teaching vessel CT scans. Seven randomized trials with 515 learners, all from China, weigh AI teaching against standard teaching. Scores cover book facts, hands-on skill, read speed, and learner joy.

AI teaching lifted hands-on skill and cut image read time in the pooled counts. Book scores and joy also leaned to AI, though spread across studies clouds those two. All trials held bias flags of some grade. The team backs set AI use in scan courses with larger firm trials to come.
pmc-13274420:
Ali Arshad and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on plastic beads designed to pull PFAS 'forever chemicals' out of water. PFAS persist in the environment and harm health, and ion exchange is a standard cleanup route. The team built their beads by a method that forms microscopic channels as the plastic hardens.

The beads swapped ions at a capacity of about one millimole per gram. For two short-chain PFAS, they soaked up the chemicals more than twice as fast at first as a leading commercial resin. Their grip on all tested PFAS was stronger, suiting them to dilute pollution, though the commercial resin held more overall. A salt and methanol wash stripped the beads completely clean for reuse.
pmc-13274620:
Kateryna Murlanova and a large team present a 2026 journal article showing that a gene in star-shaped brain support cells is required for normal thinking in mice. NPAS3 is a gene switch tied to cognitive problems in several psychiatric conditions, and it is strongly active in astrocytes, the brain's support cells. The team deleted it only in mature astrocytes.

The deletion lowered a mitochondrial glutamate carrier, cutting the cells' energy output and their lactate production. Neighboring neurons in the prefrontal cortex then fired less, grew fewer connection spines, and signaled more weakly. The mice performed poorly on a trace fear learning test. Giving lactate, the missing fuel, rescued their learning, tying astrocyte energy directly to cognition.
pmc-13275120:
Binisha H Mishra, Pashupati P Mishra, and Jan Aerts introduced a software tool for finding multi-omic subgroups in a 2026 paper. Modern studies often measure several molecular layers in the same people, which can reveal hidden subgroups with distinct disease paths. Most integration methods average over the whole population and miss subgroup signals.

Their tool, MOBAA, joins biclustering, which groups people and features together, with module finding by hierarchical clustering. It handles several omics at once and needs no assumptions about data shape, using shuffled permutations to judge significance. The output aims to give an intuitive map of how a population splits into molecular profiles. The code ships as a free R package with documents and examples, aimed at precision medicine research.
pmc-13275320:
Sammy H S Chan and colleagues report a 2026 journal article capturing the shapes of proteins caught mid-fold on the ribosome, the cell's protein factory. Proteins often start folding while still being built, pausing in stable halfway forms that vanish once free. Those intermediate shapes could not be predicted by current AI tools and had never been seen in detail.

Using fluorine-based magnetic resonance tricks engineered into the protein, plus computer simulations, the team solved two intermediate structures of an antibody-like domain still attached to the ribosome. Each had a native-like folded core but loose, nonnative ends, letting them grip a helper chaperone in distinct ways. The shapes suggest parallel folding routes and are conserved across the protein family.
pmc-13275620:
Xingyang Liu and co-authors look for a warning sign of confusion after surgery in older patients. Their 2026 study follows 210 patients over age 65 who had planned surgery on the abdomen. The sign they track is blood flow in the neck artery that feeds the brain, watched during the operation.

Delirium, a state of sudden confusion, struck 41 of the patients in the week after surgery. Long spells of low neck artery flow went with a much higher risk of that state. Usual blood pressure readings did not show the same pattern. Flow checks, the authors say, may flag at-risk patients whom pressure checks miss. They call for more trials to test the link.
pmc-13275920:
Mohamed Abdelhamed and co-authors report a 2026 materials article on putting a sugar industry waste to work in plastic. Making sugar from beets leaves behind piles of precipitated calcium carbonate, a chalky powder that can blow into water and air. The team mixed this waste into PVC, a common plastic, at several loadings.

Adding the powder made the plastic resist heat better, losing far less weight when heated. A small loading, about one part in twenty, raised bending strength by roughly a third. Heavier loadings hurt stretch, pulling strength, and impact resistance, though. Microscope images showed the powder spread evenly at low loadings but clumped at high ones, which explains the pattern. Density and water uptake rose slightly as more powder was added.
pmc-13276120:
Sebastian Riemann and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how obesity and asthma feed each other. More than six hundred fifty million adults worldwide live with obesity. People with obesity develop asthma more often, and most asthma patients in trials and registries carry excess weight.

The authors explain that extra fat harms asthma through many routes, not just one inflammation type. Fat tissue sends faulty chemical signals, stirs low-grade inflammation, upsets metabolism, and physically squeezes the lungs. Asthma control is poorer and flare-ups are more common. Losing weight, by lifestyle change, drugs, or surgery, improves symptoms and lung function across asthma types. Modern gut-hormone drugs used for weight loss still need dedicated asthma trials, the authors argue.
pmc-13276320:
Latifa Ou-Skou and co-authors report a 2026 case report on a gallstone that blocked the small intestine. Gallstone ileus is an uncommon cause of bowel blockage, mostly in older patients. A stone escapes the gallbladder through an abnormal channel into the gut, then lodges and obstructs it.

The patient was a sixty-nine-year-old woman with diabetes and heart disease, ill for five days with belly pain, vomiting, and no bowel movements. A plain X-ray hinted at the problem but could not confirm it. A CT scan showed the blockage, air inside the bile ducts, and a layered stone stuck in the lower small intestine. Special reconstructions even showed the channel from gallbladder to duodenum. Surgeons removed the stone through the bowel and deferred gallbladder surgery given her risks. She recovered without complications.
pmc-13276520:
Xue Tian and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on using tobacco straw char to grow safer, better pak choi. Heavy metals like lead and cadmium pollute much Chinese farmland and slip into vegetables. Turning waste tobacco straw into biochar could lock metals in soil while using up farm residue.

In pot trials, three char rates were compared against plain soil. Shoot weight rose by roughly a sixth, and sugar, protein, and vitamin C contents climbed steeply at the best rates. The char loosened the soil, raised its organic matter and key nutrients, and shifted soil bacteria toward greater diversity. Metal levels in the edible shoots fell by about a third for cadmium and nearly two fifths for lead. A middle rate, three percent of soil weight, scored best overall in the authors' combined evaluation.
pmc-13276720:
Matteo Aloi and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping how features of narcissistic personality disorder connect to each other. Modern views hold that grandiosity hides a vulnerable core of shame and rejection sensitivity. Reading one's own and others' minds, called metacognition, may hold the system together.

A network analysis covered two hundred eighty-seven patients with the disorder, using five established surveys and interviews. In the resulting web, that vulnerability sat at the center as the most connected feature. Sensitivity to others and mind-reading integration ranked next. It tied strongly to negative emotions and detachment, while grandiosity tied to antagonism. That integration linked harmful traits with distress between people, acting as a bridge. The authors say the pattern fits a therapy model that targets this integrative capacity.
pmc-13276820:
Paul Schulan leads a 2026 laboratory study of how gas plasma changes a model protein. The protein is ovalbumin, the main protein in egg white, and plasma is a charged gas that makes reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. The team made twelve plasma mixes and mapped chemical changes on the protein.

Using precise mass measurement, they found more than eighty kinds of oxidative change, located amino acid by amino acid. Atomic oxygen and hydrogen peroxide played a large role in the damage pattern. Each gas mix left its own fingerprint, with different hot spots on the protein. Knowing those patterns may help link protein oxidation to disease and to plasma use in medicine.
pmc-13277020:
Júlio Belo Fernandes leads a 2026 interview study of why academics agree, or refuse, to review other researchers' work for journals. Peer review is the check that helps guard research quality, yet little is known about reviewers' own views. The team held recorded interviews with health science academics between June and September 2025.

Twenty-seven academics from seven fields took part. Reasons to review included helping science, learning, career growth, personal satisfaction, and pay. Barriers included heavy workload, weak recognition, doubts about skill, worries about honesty, and poor journal handling. Weighing the two sides shaped each choice. Better recognition and journal support could keep reviewers willing, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278620:
Christina Sauer leads a 2026 mixed methods study of a cancer care app called SOFIA, tested with patients including those in palliative care. The app combines symptom self-reports that patients enter electronically with a coaching component. Interviews at two points in a twelve-week period were paired with app usage data from active users.

Patients valued feeling empowered, supported, and able to communicate better with doctors through the symptom reports. They criticized a rigid design and doctors making too little use of the data. Half of active users read articles, most started guided journeys, and just under half completed exercises. Intuitive design, relevant symptom items, and reliable reminders are the design lessons drawn.
pmc-13278720:
Nazish Tarar and co-authors present a 2026 case of heart failure shock after childbirth from reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Takotsubo syndrome temporarily weakens the heart after intense stress, usually ballooning its tip. The reverse form spares the tip and weakens the base and middle instead.

The woman developed cardiogenic shock around an emergency caesarean delivery. Her heart's pumping recovered quickly, a pattern that fits stress cardiomyopathy rather than blocked arteries. A multidisciplinary team treated her with standard heart failure medicines chosen to stay safe during breastfeeding. The authors stress separating this diagnosis from other pregnancy-related heart conditions, since prognosis and advice on future pregnancies differ.
pmc-13278920:
Caic Figueiredo and a Brazilian team study why some people control a skin parasite without ever falling ill, in a 2026 paper. Leishmania braziliensis causes cutaneous leishmaniasis, yet some infected people in endemic areas never develop lesions. Their immune cells seem to contain the parasite silently.

Macrophages grown from blood of silent-case and ill donors were infected with labelled parasites in the lab. Cells from silent-case donors killed parasites within the first hours and kept control over two days. Those cells also raised a vesicle marker faster, showing quicker formation of the sacs that digest parasites. The authors conclude that rapid phagosome building underlies silent control of the infection.
pmc-13279020:
Suhui Hu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a gut parasite in pigs on large farms. The parasite is Balantioides coli, a one celled germ that can also infect people. Pigs are its main host in farm settings. The team built a new test that reads two genes at once to tell strains apart.

They checked more than twelve hundred pig stool samples from three farms. About eighty eight percent held the parasite, and rates neared one hundred percent by five to six months of age. Gene reads found three types and a new form not seen before. Some types clustered in one region, which hints that farm place and practice shape spread.
pmc-13279320:
Zhihao Li and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of RehabXR, a virtual reality system for balance therapy in service members with chronic mild traumatic brain injury. Dizziness and gaze instability after head injury interfere with duties such as marching and obstacle courses. The system delivers vestibular exercises through low-cost wearable sensors and a virtual environment. Fifteen service members with vestibular complaints completed the program, and the team measured physical performance and brain connectivity at rest.

After the program, participants finished mobility and agility tasks significantly faster. Brain scans showed stronger links within the network joining vision and balance, and weaker links in the default mode network, a system active during rest. The authors read the pattern as improved integration between movement and cognition. They present RehabXR as a promising, cheap route to vestibular therapy. The small single-group sample means larger controlled trials are still needed.
pmc-13279420:
Gabriele Gallo Afflitto and colleagues published a 2026 clinical study of a new eye drop for the dry, irritated eye surface common in glaucoma treatment. The drops combine hyaluronic acid, a standard lubricant, with a modified glutathione molecule against oxidative stress. Sixteen patients with glaucoma or high eye pressure and dry eye symptoms used each drop for four weeks in a blinded crossover design. Lab tests on corneal cells explored the combination.

Fifteen patients finished. The combined drop beat hyaluronic acid alone on symptom scores, tear film stability, and surface staining, with several comparisons reaching strong significance. No treatment-related side effects appeared. Tear samples showed a brief rise in immune mediators that the authors interpret as a controlled repair response. In cell culture it sped wound closure while suppressing one inflammatory signal. They describe the study as preliminary, a first step toward confirming the added ingredient's value.
pmc-13279520:
Yanfeng Jia and colleagues published a 2026 study comparing two knee replacement designs in patients whose kneecap joint had mild to moderate arthritis, without resurfacing the kneecap. One design keeps the posterior cruciate ligament (cruciate-retaining); the other substitutes for it (posterior-stabilized). The comparison covered 107 knees with the retaining design and 109 with the stabilized design, using X-ray angles, pain reports, motion range, and knee scores.

Front-of-knee pain occurred more often in the stabilized group, a significant difference. The timing of kneecap crepitus, the crackling some patients feel, did not differ. Range of motion came out better with the stabilized design. Overall knee scores and alignment measures did not differ between groups. The authors conclude both designs deliver early clinical and imaging results for this patient group. The choice may hinge on how a surgeon weighs motion gains against the higher chance of front knee pain.
pmc-13279920:
Le Van Bui and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study asking which internal resistance setting of the RS01 dry powder inhaler delivers the most consistent lung dose of budesonide. Budesonide is a controlled-release steroid for asthma and COPD. Weak inhalation can leave drug stranded in the device. Using a breathing simulator coupled to an impactor and an artificial throat, the team tested four resistance versions. The breathing profiles spanned typical patient flow rates, volumes, and inhalation times.

The medium-low and medium-high resistance inhalers produced the steadiest fine particle dose across all simulated breathing. Between them, the medium-low version delivered the most stable amount. By contrast, doses from the low and medium resistance devices swung significantly with peak flow rate. Weaker breathers would thus get less medicine. The authors present the design as a practical way to match an inhaler to a formulation while accounting for real breathing.
pmc-13280320:
Chao Wu and co-authors present a 2026 trial of a gel for prurigo nodularis, a skin disease with hard bumps and fierce itch. Few good treatments exist for the disease. The gel holds ruxolitinib, a drug that blocks a signal path tied to skin inflammation. The trial, run at many centers in China, tested the gel against a plain base gel.

Forty-nine adults were split by chance, with more getting the drug gel than the plain one. Care ran once or twice a day for four weeks. Side effects were mostly mild, and drug levels in the blood stayed low. Rates of side effects in the drug groups sat near or below those in one plain-gel group. The early results support larger trials of the gel for this stubborn skin disease.
pmc-13280820:
Han Cao and colleagues published a 2026 engineering study of which forces control oil movement when water or steam is pushed through heavy oil reservoirs. Recovery hinges on a three-way contest among viscous forces, capillary forces, and gravity, and operators need to know which one dominates. Using experiments, the team built a dimensionless framework scoring forces for heavy oil flooded with water and super-heavy oil flooded with steam. They varied injection rate, temperature, rock permeability, steam quality, and well angle.

Water flooding was governed mainly by capillary forces, and recovery fell in a straight line as their capillary number rose. Steam flooding obeyed gravity and heat instead: steam thins the oil and lets gravity organize flow. A model built around their thermogravimetry number predicted steam-flood recovery with a correlation of 0.9692 against experiments. The authors offer the framework as a quantitative basis for setting parameters in heavy oil fields.
pmc-13280920:
Huiyong Liang and colleagues published a 2026 simulation study of how kinetic hydrate inhibitors interfere with gas hydrate growth at molecular scale. Hydrates are cages of water and gas that can plug oil and gas pipelines, and the inhibitors are polymers dosed to delay their formation. Two polymers, PVP and PVCap, were modeled with molecular dynamics, with quantum chemical calculations, tracking cage counts, water ordering, and energy.

The simulations resolve a three-part mechanism. The polymers block growth sites on the crystal surface, interfere with the mass transfer that feeds new cages, and disrupt the hydrogen-bond network the cages need to organize. Together those actions stall early growth and destabilize the forming solid. The authors argue that seeing the mechanism gives formulators targets: a good inhibitor should do all three jobs, not just coat the surface. They offer the findings as design guidance for better flowline additives.
pmc-13281320:
Youssef El Dsouki and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter on pressure spikes inside heart and lung support machines. Blood run through such machines faces fake surfaces and harsh flow. A key part, the oxygenator, adds oxygen but also squeezes the flow. The strain can switch on platelets, the blood bits that form clots, even with no wound. Switched-on platelets stick and clump, and the clumps choke the oxygenator.

As flow meets more blockage, pressure inside the machine climbs. A sharp climb can force staff to swap the oxygenator mid-care. That swap is risky, costly, and breaks the run of support. The authors say a patient's own blood traits may add to the risk. They urge teams to watch pressure trends early and to study how flow strain wakes platelets. Better design, they argue, could cut these events.
pmc-13282220:
Anu Tripathi and co-authors report a 2026 modelling study on whether the folds of the brain's outer layer change predictions of head injury risk. Computer head models help judge mild traumatic brain injury, meaning injury that disrupts brain function without major visible damage, after blunt impacts. Many models smooth away the cortical folds. The team built models with and without folds for eighteen subjects aged nine to eighteen.

Each model faced the same spinning head motion around three axes. Models with folds gave higher strain measures, the measures of tissue stretching linked to injury, in every person and direction. The gap averaged roughly fifteen to twenty-two percent across three injury measures. Where strain peaked also shifted, and some deep brain regions showed rises up to about half. The authors conclude that leaving out folds underestimates risk and misplaces hot spots.
pmc-13282420:
S M Yasir Arafat and Sadeed Hossain wrote a 2026 narrative review on burnout among health care professionals in Bangladesh. Heavy workloads, long hours, and emotional demands make such workers vulnerable everywhere. Bangladesh's constrained health system may add risk. The authors searched four literature sources without date limits, up to February 2026, and thematically combined the eligible studies.

Eight cross-sectional studies covered groups from intern doctors and nurses to intensive care physicians and hospital attendants, with samples from fifty to over two thousand seven hundred. Moderate to high burnout ranged from about twenty percent to over fifty-five percent. Emotional exhaustion hit extreme levels in some cohorts. Women doctors, intensive care staff, and early-career workers showed the highest rates. Long hours, night shifts, workload, poor pay, weak support, and pandemic stress recurred as risk factors. The authors call burnout a structural problem needing organisational fixes, not just personal resilience.
pmc-13282620:
Tatiana Velásquez-Roa and co-authors present a 2026 software paper introducing Rosario, an algorithm and R package for analysing cyclical ecological data. Ecologists study when animals are active across the day or year, and how those rhythms overlap between species. Null models, which shuffle data to build baselines, help reveal real patterns. Rosario preserves temporal autocorrelation, the tendency for nearby times to resemble each other, making its fake scenarios biologically realistic.

The package moves the algorithm from older Windows software into R, the language ecologists widely use. That shift improves access and lets it work alongside other R packages for activity and overlap analysis. Unlike rivals, Rosario can analyse overlap among many identities at once, from individuals to whole communities. The authors say this gives a fuller view of temporal niches. They present standardisation in R as key to the method's continued use in ecology.
pmc-13282920:
Picking the right family donor for a half-matched transplant is the dilemma in Mahtab Mashayekhi's 2026 leukemia cohort work. Such transplants can cure patients who lack a fully matched donor. The best donor age, sex, and family link remain uncertain.

Records covered 159 adults treated from 2015 to 2022 with one drug protocol. Most donors were siblings, then parents, then offspring. Survival and relapse were tracked for three years with adjusted models. Patterns differed between myeloid and lymphoid leukemia types. Offspring donors showed weaker results in some groups. The study helps centers weigh donor choice when several relatives can donate.
pmc-13283220:
Spin waves and lattice vibrations merge into hybrid particles inside a layered magnet, Qili Li's tunneling experiments reveal in 2026. Such mixed waves are called magnon polarons and link magnetism with sound-like motion. Clear proof in metal magnets had been scarce before this work.

Crystals of Fe3GeTe2 were probed with a scanning tunneling microscope at very low temperature. Energy spectra showed spin and lattice bands merging at crossing points. Strong coupling lifted rules that normally block spin wave signals in metals. That lifted rule is a hallmark sign of the mixed waves. The result gives a test bed for tuning spin-lattice effects in thin materials. Future devices may use such hybrids.
pmc-13283920:
Breathing failure tied to severe obesity anchors a 2026 clinical case from Sajedeh Zarghi and colleagues. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome leaves carbon dioxide high and oxygen low in blood. Late recognition can bring long intensive care stays and organ strain.

Hidden malnutrition can worsen outcomes even in patients with excess body fat. The case frames obesity itself as a chronic inflammatory, whole-body disease. Linked harms span heart disease, diabetes, fatty liver, stroke, and sleep apnea. Early team-based care is presented as the way to cut harm and cost. Nutrition support teams play a named role in that early response.
pmc-13284120:
Peng Yu and colleagues tested in 2026 how blocking vision changes leg mechanics in athletes after knee ligament surgery. Athletes who have had an anterior cruciate ligament rebuild often lean harder on sight because joint position sense is blunted. Twenty such athletes and twenty healthy athletes each performed a sharp ninety-degree cutting move with eyes open and with strobe glasses that disrupt vision, while cameras and force plates recorded the body.

Under visual disruption, the rebuilt group landed with greater inward knee collapse and more inward ankle roll, plus a stronger hip extension push and weaker knee extension push. Healthy athletes showed no clear change between the two visual conditions. The authors warn that sight disruption exposes risky movement patterns in the rebuilt group that may raise re-injury risk.
pmc-13284420:
Yin Mo and co-authors share a research update, published in 2026, from the ADVANCE-ID trial network on drug-resistant bacterial and fungal infections. The update gathers highlights from the network newsletter for March to April 2026. It shows how new trial results can guide policy and daily care in varied health settings.

One large trial in rural township hospitals in China cut antibiotic use for chest infections sharply with a digital stewardship program, with no rise in hospital return within 30 days. A trial in England and Wales, by contrast, found procalcitonin-guided rules did not cut early antibiotic starts, though deaths were lower in that arm. The contrast stresses that local setting and delivery shape whether stewardship works.
pmc-13285020:
Emma Bergstedt and Ann-Charlotte Nedlund trace health policy stories in Sweden in a 2026 study covering 1992 to 2024. Governments worldwide urge use of best evidence in health choices, yet real policy is shaped by politics and rival ideas. The team read 132 Swedish government documents and sorted the stories that frame problems and fixes.

Four periods emerged, each ruled by a distinct story about health care ills, fixes, and the role of evidence. Stories also set who counts as part of the problem, what values drive action, and how change should work. The authors show that evidence use is never neutral, since the ruling story decides what proof matters.
pmc-13285220:
Xiaogang Zhou, Qingguo Xiong, Liang Ding, and Bingguo Zhai study in a 2026 paper how digital tools at work link to job results. They ask if staff who feel their firm gives them strong digital support do better work. Work freedom and a drive to act early sit at the heart of the test.

A two-wave survey drew data from 302 staff in tech, factory, and finance firms in China. Staff who felt more digital support also did better and felt more free in their work. That sense of freedom helped carry the gain in results. Staff with a strong drive to act early gained even more from digital support, the team found.
pmc-13285320:
A 50-day-old boy with chlamydial lung infection and a blocked, collapsed lung lobe is the subject of a 2026 case report by Yuan Huang and colleagues. Chlamydia trachomatis passes from mother to baby and usually causes a milder lung pattern in infants. A mucus plug blocking a bronchus, with lobe collapse, is rarely seen.

The full-term baby had coughed for fifteen days. Scans showed pneumonia and collapse in the left upper lobe. Sputum testing found the germ, and fluid from a scope wash backed the call with targeted gene sequencing. Care paired erythromycin with scope clearing of the plug. The baby recovered fully, with no return over two months of checks.
pmc-13285420: Mariam F. Farid and co-authors issue a correction, dated 2026, to a cat study of a cell-free spinal cord treatment for multiple sclerosis. The notice states that control images were reused from a sister study by the same team without clear notice. The authors say reuse kept the studies comparable and cut animal use, in line with welfare rules that favor fewer animals and kinder handling.
pmc-13285920:
Yanbin Chang and co-authors report a family case of Townes-Brocks syndrome in a 2026 case report centered on cup-shaped ears. The rare inherited disorder usually mixes ear, thumb, and bowel defects, but its signs vary a great deal. Here a seven-year-old boy came in only for cosmetic repair of folded ears on both sides, with clean hearing and kidney checks.

A three-generation family tree showed the same ear shape in the boy's father and grandfather, pointing to dominant inheritance. Gene tests found the same damaging change in the SALL1 gene in boy and father, which confirmed the syndrome. Both had ear surgery with good early cosmetic results. The case warns that a family ear shape alone can hide the syndrome, so history taking, gene checks, and long-term watch belong in care.
pmc-13286520:
Esma Cinar, Demet Sengul, and Ilker Sengul stack imaging clues to judge uncertain thyroid lumps in a 2026 retrospective study. Needle samples sort most thyroid nodules cleanly, but the middle categories leave surgeons guessing between watchfulness and removal. Six years of records supplied 838 nodules from 716 patients, scored by size, blood-flow patterns, guideline risk tiers, and stiffness readings from an elasticity scan.

Uncertain-category nodules ran larger than plainly benign ones on average. Richer blood flow inside and around a nodule, higher guideline risk tiers, and the stiffest elasticity grades all clustered in the uncertain groups. Cancer confirmed under the microscope also came more often from those groups. Age and nodule position, by contrast, predicted nothing. Layering the measures together, the authors argue, sharpens the call on which uncertain lumps merit surgery.
pmc-13286920:
Ying Shen and colleagues follow self-care ability in 209 spinal cord injury patients from just before hospital discharge through their first year at home. The 2026 study, based at a hospital in northern China, measured self-care at five time points plus mental health knowledge and perceived social support at the start. Self-care prevents complications and supports life back in the community.

Average self-care peaked one month after discharge, then slid gradually. Modeling found three paths: about a third of patients declined from a low start, two fifths held steady at a middle level, and the rest improved from a high base. Sex, education, mental health literacy, and social support predicted the path. Early gains can fade, the authors warn, so support should follow the trajectory.
pmc-13287020:
Zengrong Ye and co-authors compare five ways of drying a medicinal rhubarb relative from China's high plateau, measuring which method best preserves its looks and chemistry. The 2026 study weighs physical traits such as color and rehydration alongside the plant's active compounds, using metabolite profiling to track hundreds of chemicals through drying. The root serves as both a traditional drug and a functional food.

Vacuum freeze drying best protected appearance and the widest set of key metabolites. Microwave drying kept the most of the headline drug compounds, the free anthraquinones. A combined score across all quality dimensions crowned a different method, labeled SG. Flavonoids, phenolic acids, and amino acids formed the core of the chemical differences between methods.
pmc-13287220:
Desmond Darko Asiedu and colleagues searched the maize genome in 2026 for regions that protect stalks against Fusarium rot, a soil-borne disease that cuts yields worldwide. They crossed 180 lines from an Austrian flint landrace with a tester line and scored disease after deliberate infection at two sites over two years.

Resistance and related traits such as height and flowering time were moderately to strongly heritable. Two regions together explained about a fifth of inherited variation in disease severity, and nearby genes fit known defence roles. Because many small effects shape resistance, the authors suggest selecting on the whole genome may serve breeding programmes better than single markers.
pmc-13287420:
Yohei Takenobu and colleagues present in 2026 a patient whose abnormal blood vessel link at the neck level of the spine caused damage far away in the brainstem, copying a vomiting-centre syndrome. Detailed vessel imaging traced drainage upward from a fistula at the sixth neck vertebra.

Merged three-dimensional scans showed a sharp narrowing where the draining vein passes a skull fissure. The team reads that pinch as a bottleneck that pushed blood into the medulla. Blocking the fistula with a catheter cured the problem on scans and in symptoms. A literature review covers similar remote cases and common diagnostic traps. The authors favour catheter treatment when anatomy suits it.
pmc-13287620:
Ahmed Sobhy and colleagues modelled power supply options in 2026 for Ras El-Hekma, a large coastal project in Egypt with peak demand of 28.8 megawatts and yearly use near 100.46 gigawatt-hours. Six mixes of wind, solar, grid, and storage were simulated over twenty years, both tied to the grid and standalone.

A grid-linked wind setup of 15 megawatts came out cheapest in their runs. Costs and savings figures are given in the study, with green sources covering 68.6% of supply. Carbon emissions fell by 60.45% against a grid-only base. Wind speed and finance terms swayed results most. The authors present the case as a model for other coastal mega-projects.
pmc-13287820:
Mahmood Alawainati and colleagues measure diabetic retinopathy in Bahraini primary care in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Retinopathy is eye damage from diabetes that can lead to blindness if missed. The team invited adults with diabetes at clinics across all primary health centers in Bahrain during late 2025. A specialist checked each patient's retina with a camera that needs no dilating drops.

The study included 594 patients, most with type 2 diabetes and a median age of 61 years. Retinopathy appeared in 88 patients, or about 15 percent, and most cases were the milder non-proliferative form. Longer time with diabetes, high blood pressure, and poor blood sugar control each raised the odds. A simple foot sensation test linked to nerve damage also predicted eye disease. The authors press for yearly eye screening and tighter risk control in primary care.
pmc-13288520:
A blocked outlet at the stomach entrance can return even after scope work and surgery, especially when a pouch forms in the esophagus wall. Laith Baqain and co-authors describe a rescue approach in a 2026 case report. Their patient was a 48-year-old woman with lupus and an overactive esophagus.

She had already had a muscle-cutting scope procedure, then surgery for reflux and a hernia, then a revision that loosened the wrap. Solid food still stuck, and the pouch kept growing. The team used an endoscopic cut through the pouch wall, plus a selective cut of the diaphragm muscle that can squeeze the junction from outside. The report presents the combined move as a less invasive salvage when repeat surgery looks forbidding.
pmc-13288620:
Alexander J Auty and colleagues probe how oxygen content changes light-driven charge behavior in printed graphene films, in 2026. The films are made from graphene aerosol-gel inks rather than perfect flat flakes. Ultrafast laser pulses let the team watch excited charges appear and fade across visible and near-infrared light. Films differed in how much oxygen sat inside the carbon lattice.

Higher oxygen content lined up with more long-lived trapped electronic states after the light pulse. Computer calculations point to oxygen atoms swapped into the lattice as the likely trap sites. Film shape, particle makeup, and carbon bond quality all tracked with the transient signals. Pristine graphene films, studied earlier by the group, behaved differently from these printed gels. The authors frame oxygen as a tuning knob for printed graphene electronics. Adjusting it could tailor films for sensors or light-based devices.
pmc-13288720:
Ziyu Wang and colleagues ask whether caffeine genuinely speeds swimmers in a 2026 systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis. Five databases yielded thirteen randomized placebo-controlled crossover trials in competitive swimmers, contributing 28 performance effects from 144 men and 48 women, pooled with three-level models that handle several results per study.

Caffeine improved performance by a moderate margin, worth about 1.71 percent on race times when effects were expressed as percentage change in their supplementary analysis. Blood lactate after racing also ran higher on caffeine. Bigger doses, at or above six milligrams per kilogram of body weight, looked more helpful than smaller ones, while stroke, distance, form, and athlete level showed no clear splits. Variation between studies stayed substantial.
pmc-13288920:
Andrea N Loes and colleagues compare flu vaccine types against a newly changed H1N1 strain in a 2026 study. The 2023/2024 vaccine updated its H1N1 part to match a new virus clade. Yet the vaccine trended weaker against that very clade than against its parent. The team measured antibody strength in blood from people who got either egg-grown or recombinant protein vaccine. Test viruses covered 58 H1N1 strains from that season.

Egg vaccine recipients showed a smaller antibody boost against the new clade. Recombinant vaccine recipients did not show that gap. The likely cause sits in the egg production seed strain, which had reverted a key surface mutation. That single change, named K142R, made egg-grown vaccine antigen differ from the target virus. The authors warn that production method can quietly reshape which strains a vaccine covers best. Their findings matter for yearly strain selection and manufacturing choices.
pmc-13289020:
Kelsey Hegarty and colleagues build a scale for coercive control in Australia. Their 2026 study deals with partner abuse of women. Past scales miss how abuse acts as a whole. The new scale is called C-CAS. It was built from older scales and expert views.

Data came from 854 adult women. Five survivors and eight experts gave feedback. The scale split into four parts. Mind control formed the largest part. Sex and birth coercion formed one part. Severe control and tech threats formed two more. Scores held up well in tests. Fear rose with more severe patterns. More checks in new groups are still needed.
pmc-13289220:
Geonhui Min and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide cohort study from Korea on bronchiectasis in people with systemic lupus erythematosus, often shortened to SLE. Bronchiectasis means lasting widening of the airways. They used National Health Insurance Service data and matched adults with SLE to controls by age, sex, and coverage.

Follow-up ran for a median of 12.8 years after a one-year lag from enrollment. New bronchiectasis appeared more often in the SLE group, at 374.8 versus 236.2 cases per 100 000 person-years in controls. Age over 40 and asthma raised risk further, while obesity linked to lower risk in the models. People with SLE who developed bronchiectasis also had more deaths, emergency visits, and hospital care, showing a real added burden.
pmc-13289320:
Yuxi Chen and coauthors report a 2026 mouse and lab study linking gut fungi to Pneumocystis pneumonia.
