The habit loosened significantly. Overall preoperative urine culture rates fell from 20.7 percent to 12.9 percent after the program. Orthopedic surgery improved most dramatically, dropping from 18.7 percent to 7.4 percent over the same comparison, while the other specialties moved less. The authors present the package, education made concrete by showing clinicians their own numbers, as a workable tool for diagnostic work hunting similar low-value tests.
pmc-13316020:
Mondeep Gayan and a large team compare in 2026 two ways to teach spinal injury handling skills to undergraduate medical students in India, using a standardized patient versus a video demonstration. Fast trauma care in the golden hour can cut deaths by 20 to 50 percent, so early training matters.

Acted patients allow hands-on practice and build communication skill, but they are scarce, while video is easy and reliable to deliver. The prospective comparison study weighs skill gains under each method within a competency-based curriculum. The result can guide schools that must train many students with few live simulated patients.
pmc-13316220:
Ingrid J. Hickman and colleagues ran a national needs survey in 2026 on implementation science skills in the clinical trial workforce of Australia and New Zealand. Moving trial results into routine care stays patchy, and building worker skill in putting evidence into practice could fix translation much earlier in the pipeline.

An online survey with rating scales and open answers, spread through trial networks, drew 353 responses across regions and professions, including consumers. It measured familiarity with implementation methods, interest in training, and barriers and preferred ways to get support, to guide future workforce programs.
pmc-13316420:
Anna Simonetto and nine co-authors mapped what drives a West Nile virus mosquito across northern Italy in a 2026 study. Nine years of trap data from the Po Valley, a virus hotspot, fed statistical and learning models at several time scales. Population states persisted strongly from month to month and year to year.

Rain before the active season was the top driver of year-to-year swings, making it an early warning sign for summer build-up. Within summers, heat pushed numbers up but extreme heat cut them back. Lasting hotspots sat over irrigated farms, wetlands, and river corridors, while hills and forests stayed poor habitat. The authors say such climate-linked indicators can be turned into action plans for mosquito control.
pmc-13317220:
Satyendra Pratap Singh and co-authors uncover, in a 2026 study, how a crop fungus launches its asexual spores into the air, solving a puzzle in orchard disease spread. These spores were thought to travel only in splashing water, yet disease jumped long distances without the sexual stage ever being seen in Israel.

Field and lab work on the model fungus showed that high humidity swells its fruiting bodies from inside: dissolved sugars and glycerol build pressure near 4.18 atmospheres until the case bursts. As air dries, the glue around spores hardens off and wind carries them, farther at higher wind speeds. The humidity burst and dry release pattern held across related tree pathogens, reshaping how growers should time protection.
pmc-13317420:
Qian Liu and co-authors test a small gene signal in 2026 as a marker for a fungal eye infection that can blind. The infection, fungal keratitis, needs fast and sure diagnosis. The team measured the signal in tears, blood, and cornea tissue from patients with the fungal disease and from patients with a non-infectious eye disease.

The signal ran higher in every sample type from fungal patients, and highest in cornea tissue. Its levels also rose and fell with three swelling factors in all three sample types. The tight link with swelling suggests the signal tracks the disease process. The authors present it as a candidate marker worth further checks for diagnosis.
pmc-13318120:
Pratik N P Singh and co-authors map cell states in small intestine hormone tumours by reading many layers of cell data at once, in a 2026 study. Such tumours grow from hormone-making gut cells that form only a tiny share of the gut lining, which has slowed study. New maps of how those normal cells mature give a fresh yardstick.

Tumour cells looked much like mature hormone cells, yet single cells also carried stem-like gene activity. One switch gene that times normal maturation was shut off and locked down in tumours. Growth-brake genes were mostly silenced too, bar one that is often mutated in these tumours. Deleting that brake changed cell timing in lab-grown gut cells. The authors link the missing switch and brakes to tumour traits.
pmc-13318720:
Qiuyu Jin and colleagues offer a 2026 bibliometric analysis of cognitive behavioural therapy for chronic pain. Few such maps of the field existed. The team charted two decades of publications, from 2005 to 2024. Sources were the Web of Science and PubMed trial records.

They found 1,070 papers from 67 countries and 1,584 institutions. The United States contributed 59.16 percent of publications and led citations. The University of Washington was the most productive institution. Frequent keywords included depression, sleep, anxiety, and quality of life. Hotspots now centre on digital delivery of therapy. Managing linked conditions and tailoring treatment to specific groups also draw attention. The authors frame the map as a roadmap for future trials.
pmc-13318920:
Karina Medina-Jiménez and colleagues present a 2026 study of a prebiotic-based biostimulant, FoliarBlend, on rice growth and yield. The variety was Kitaake, grown under controlled conditions from germination to seed production. Automated imaging tracked seedlings, and manual checks followed plants to day 82. Photosynthesis measures completed the picture.

Treated seedlings showed larger leaf area and longer stems from day 5 to day 14 after germination. Stress markers stayed normal, so the product added no strain. Later, treated plants grew taller with fewer leaves and tillers. They produced more panicles, more biomass above and below ground, and ultimately more grain. Photosystem efficiency and chlorophyll content improved from day 49 onwards. The authors see promise for sustainable rice production.
pmc-13319420:
Jian Liu and co-authors give a broad review of epilepsy in a 2026 article on causes, body changes, and care. The seizure illness affects more than 50 million people worldwide and adds to early death and long term hardship. Near one third of patients still have seizures despite drug care, which shows how much remains unclear about how seizures start.

Gene faults, faulty cell signals, swelling in brain tissue, energy strain, and shifts in cell control are traced as paths that leave brain circuits prone to fire too much. Care now spans exact gene tests, surgery, implanted devices, diet plans, and timed dosing. New gene and immune based methods aim to change the illness itself, not just calm seizures.
pmc-13320420:
Pham Thanh Hieu and Nguyen Kieu Linh present a benchmark data set built from world trade records in a 2026 data article. Trade webs settle into balance states that math models frame as inequality puzzles, yet test sets for solver tools were scarce. A pipeline turns product level trade files into clean puzzle cases with known trade flows as ground truth.

Source files cover yearly flows among lands for 2017 to 2024 at fine product detail. Steps filter live flows, group products into five sectors, pick lead trade lands, and tune a cost and price rule to match real flows. Cases ship in two sizes with feasible sets, tuned rules, flow tables, and check scores, plus solver test results and build scripts for reuse.
pmc-13320520:
Anqi Lin and colleagues offer a 2026 perspective on germs that live inside bowel tumours. Bowel cancer ranks among the most common cancers and a leading cause of cancer death. Past work mostly linked the wider gut germ mix to cancer, but new gene reading and imaging now reveal distinct germ groups inside tumour tissue itself.

Those inner groups differ from germs in nearby healthy tissue and vary from place to place within a tumour. The authors set out the makeup of these groups, how they may help tumours grow or resist care, and how they might open new treatment paths. Their dual role, as both driver and possible target, frames the discussion.
pmc-13321420:
Ali Asghar Maleki and co-authors present a 2026 review of exercise therapy for pain behind the kneecap. Patellofemoral pain is a common joint problem that limits daily activity and quality of life. Neuromuscular training aims to fix faulty movement patterns, yet its overall benefit across outcomes was unclear.

The team gathered randomized trials from four databases through May 2025. Seventeen trials with 871 people, most of them young women, met the rules. Training was compared with no treatment or with plain strength work. Outcomes covered pain, daily function, balance, muscle strength, and leg movement patterns. Pooled results were graded for certainty with a standard tool. The review gives clinicians a single tally of what this training can and cannot do.
pmc-13322620:
Minesh Kapadia, Lorraine V Kalia, and Suneil K Kalia write a 2026 letter on electrical stimulation and protein clearance in Parkinson's disease. The disease kills dopamine neurons as a protein, alpha-synuclein, misfolds into toxic clumps and Lewy bodies. Current drugs and standard brain stimulation ease symptoms but do not slow neuron loss, so boosting clump clearance is a live research goal.

The letter discusses a study by Bechkos and others where direct current stimulation cut clump build-up in cultured neurons and improved cell survival. The writers note that this matches and extends their own group's finding that high frequency stimulation aids clearance. Comparing stimulation styles may shape future disease slowing therapy.
pmc-13322920:
Yujia Wu and co-authors review Chinese herbal formulas for Hashimoto's thyroiditis through the thyroid-gut axis, in a 2026 article. Standard hormone replacement fixes low thyroid hormone but does not reverse the autoimmune attack itself, which leaves room for other approaches.

Searching databases for work from 2015 to 2025, the team kept eight studies of eligible formulas. Their framework sorts action into four nodes: gut barrier repair, microbe reshaping, immune balance and hormone recovery, alone or in combination. Most evidence came from varied animal studies and stayed correlative, with safety reporting uneven. The authors call for randomised clinical trials, causal microbe tests and standard outcome measures before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13323020:
Mina Xu and co-authors trace a shift from virtual pregnancy models to digital twin obstetrics, in a 2026 review. Static checks at set visits miss how pregnancy changes over time, so newer models simulate mother, placenta and fetus as one changing system.

Digital twins extend that idea with live, multi-type data that keep a patient-specific model updated. Inputs include clinical profiles, imaging and radiomics, multi-omics and wearable signals, joined through machine learning. Uses centre on preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, growth restriction and placental failure. The authors weigh promise against proof, noting that personal prediction tools still need strong trials before routine obstetric use.
pmc-13323720:
Younghwan Lee and co-authors tested whether a peptide drawn from human telomerase can slow Alzheimer disease in mice. Their 2026 paper studies GV1001, a 16-amino-acid peptide from the catalytic part of telomerase reverse transcriptase, which had already improved memory with proven safety in a phase II trial in patients. The open question was how it works. The team treated 5xFAD mice, a standard Alzheimer model, and probed microglia, the brain's immune cells, with single-cell RNA sequencing.

GV1001 cut amyloid plaque burden and rescued both synaptic loss and memory deficits, by drawing microglia toward large plaques and boosting their breakdown of amyloid beta. Sequencing showed the peptide pushed microglia toward migratory and phagocytic states, and pulldown work identified bradykinin receptor 1 as its binding target, acting through an mTORC2-dependent route. The authors present GV1001 as a promising disease-modifying candidate, with its mechanism now mapped in microglia.
pmc-13324220:
Clara Fernandez-Cordón and Ignacio Amat-Santos review valve alignment strategies in transcatheter aortic valve replacement, published in 2026. Younger patients now receive these valves more often. Aligning the new valve's posts with the native seams thus matters for lifetime care.

Good commissural alignment eases later coronary access. It also cuts obstruction risk and enables leaflet work in repeat procedures. Flow and durability may improve as well. The authors summarise clinical impact, success rates and limits. They set coronary alignment against commissural alignment as rival targets. Step-by-step techniques for the latest valve systems close the review, for teams weighing present access against future re-intervention.
pmc-13325420:
Dinara Turebekova and colleagues review links between blood markers and life quality in long COVID in a 2026 systematic review. Lasting symptoms drag down daily life, but the biology behind the loss is murky.

Searches of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus gathered controlled studies, yielding ten papers with 1,078 patients and 768 healthy controls. Life quality fell hardest in physical function, energy, daily activity, and breathing comfort. Inflammation and vessel markers such as CRP, IL-6, and D-dimer were measured most often. Few studies tied markers to life quality directly, though inflammation and vessel dysfunction signals recurred. The authors call for uniform tools so future studies can compare cleanly.
pmc-13325720:
Adel S. Alagl and Marwa Madi test antibacterial hydroxyapatite coatings on titanium in a 2026 lab study. Bacterial films on dental implants drive peri-implantitis, a leading cause of implant failure.

Discs of grade 2 titanium were coated by sputtering plus hot water treatment or left bare. After 24 hours with Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, or both, coated discs cut colony counts by 97.9 to 99.7 percent across all setups. Surface type alone explained 74.1 percent of the difference in bacterial survival. The coat hit the Gram-positive species harder than the Gram-negative one. Mouth-like conditions still need testing before clinic use.
pmc-13326120:
Alexander C. Razavi and Roger S. Blumenthal argue that timing is everything in lowering LDL cholesterol. Their 2026 editorial opens with Arnold Palmer's line that timing matters in life and golf, then applies it to cardiology. LDL cholesterol is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. About half of adults sit at or above 100 mg/dL, and roughly 1 in 250 to 300 carry levels at or above 190 mg/dL consistent with familial hypercholesterolemia.

Population LDL and statin gains have stalled since the pandemic, renewing focus on early control under new 2026 American guidance. They highlight adults who gain most from statin therapy and LDL control. These include those with premature family history, high-risk ancestry, high polygenic risk, chronic inflammatory disease, high lipoprotein(a) or swelling markers, persistently high triglycerides, cardiometabolic syndrome, or markedly high LDL or apolipoprotein B. The message is to act early, not to wait for disease.
pmc-13327020:
Fan Yang and team traced knee osteoarthritis burden in China and where it heads next. Their 2026 study used Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. It ran age-period-cohort and ARIMA trend models on new cases and years lived with disability from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts for the next fifteen years. Knee joint wear leads as a cause of disability, hitting women and older adults hardest.

New cases and disability rose a lot over three decades, most among women, with a clear rise by age. The trend model sees a slow fall in new cases and disability after 2021, which may mirror health reforms and guard steps. The team stresses the rising health load. It urges strong guard steps, early finds, and better health care build-out, while noting the hoped gain hangs on reforms and guard steps truly paying off.
pmc-13327520:
Teemu Kuosmanen and colleagues test a fairness idea for microbe communities in a 2026 study. They compare how biomass is actually shared among species with a fair share drawn from game theory, the Shapley value, which credits each species for what it adds. In total 56 community outcomes covered both rival and cooperative growth.

Some communities matched their fair shares closely across settings, while others strayed far from what each species seemed to contribute. The authors then build a fair assembly rule from the Shapley definition and show that even the uneven cases fit the rule once lower-level contest results are known. The work lays groundwork for a rule-based theory of how ecological communities come together.
pmc-13328020:
Martina Gnazzo and colleagues review thinking and development in spinal muscular atrophy in a 2026 scoping review. The disease was long framed as a pure motor neuron disorder, but as new therapies extend life and movement, mental outcomes matter more. The team gathered cohort studies, observational work, and case series on cognition, language, and behavior.

Twenty-three studies qualified, and general intellect looked broadly preserved, above all in the milder type II and III forms. Weak spots recurred in processing speed, executive skills, and language, and children showed behavior and social-emotional strain. Early-onset cases ranged widely, with children treated before symptoms showing brighter paths, though testing was often hampered by motor limits.
pmc-13329020:
Teresa Fontán-Baselga and co-authors test long-term blocking of a brain enzyme in mice bred to model Alzheimer disease in a 2026 study. The enzyme is a receptor phosphatase that is held back by pleiotrophin, a factor that supports nerve cells. Earlier short treatment with the blocker MY10 had cut amyloid plaques and calmed glial cells.

Here mice aged five to seven months were treated for 3 months. Plaque build-up fell, and more microglial cells appeared in one hippocampus area. Fewer star-shaped glial cells gathered around plaques, and pleiotrophin levels dropped after treatment. A gene for Mmp9, an enzyme tied to disease progress, also fell. The authors see the blocker as a possible disease-changing lead.
pmc-13329520:
Doha H Al-Afify and co-authors test added shockwave therapy for carpal tunnel syndrome in women in a 2026 randomised trial. One hundred women aged 25 to 40 years were split into two groups. Both received standard therapy, while one group also received extracorporeal shockwave treatment. Outcomes covered symptom and function scales, pain scores, and nerve signal tests.

The added therapy group improved more on symptom scores, pain, and several nerve measures than the standard group in the reported results. Two outcomes, motor speed and function scale change, showed no clear group gap. The authors conclude that adding shockwave therapy can aid pain relief and nerve recovery in this group, alongside standard rehab care.
pmc-13330220:
Lama Alfehaid and four co-authors test a heart risk tool in a 2026 study of breast cancer care. Some cancer drugs can harm the heart, so guides urge clinics to grade each patient's heart risk before care starts. The tool sorts patients from low to very high risk. The team asked how well that grade split real patients who later had heart harm.

They reviewed 687 women with HER2-positive breast cancer treated from 2016 to 2023. About forty percent had heart harm during follow-up, but cases spread across all risk grades with much overlap. The tool's scores sorted patients weakly, and the grade alone did not predict harm. The authors urge checks during care, not just at the start.
pmc-13330320:
Ion Hong Wong and nine co-authors review in 2026 whether learning by doing improves how healthcare students view dementia. Future clinicians' attitudes shape the care older patients receive, and classroom lectures alone rarely shift them. Hands-on formats range from single sessions to long programs, including art-based work.

Thirteen studies covering 1,861 students were pooled. Learning by doing raised attitude scores clearly, and short and long programs helped about equally. Artistic formats such as storytelling also showed gains. The review supports building real contact with dementia into health training rather than relying on theory alone. Better attitudes early in training can carry into kinder, more skilled care on the ward.
pmc-13330520:
Anne Chalumeau and team engineered a repressor-to-activator motif switch to reactivate fetal globin in sickle cell disease. Their 2026 study replaced the BCL11A repressor-binding site in fetal HBG1/2 promoters with a TAL1:GATA1 motif seen by transcriptional activators. Lasting fetal hemoglobin improves sickle cell disease, and transplant of autologous corrected blood stem cells offers promise, but promoter editing needed testing.

Prime editing nuclease installed the motif well in K562 cells, beating original prime editing, and blocking end-joining boosted editing. The strategy worked poorly in patient stem cells, so the team used CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt the repressor site or install the new motif by homology-guided repair. Edited stem cells kept clonogenic capacity and became red blood cells with raised fetal globin expression and corrected sickling. The team presents the motif switch as a potent route to fetal globin reactivation.
pmc-13330620:
Maha Najdini and colleagues pool studies on substance use across immigrant generations in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Searches spanned six databases for cross-sectional studies from 1990 to 2026. From 157,426 screened records, 51 studies entered the pool, covering about 4.9 million people across more than 9 countries in the reported totals.

Second-generation immigrants showed higher odds of alcohol use, dependence, and abuse than first-generation peers in the pooled values. Drug use gaps were larger still, and cannabis use odds were higher as well. Tobacco showed no clear generational gap. The authors call for prevention shaped to culture and generation, since risk grows as families settle into new settings.
pmc-13331520:
Haemophilia care long meant replacing the missing clotting factor by vein, with peaks, troughs, and immune blockers as costs. Lukas Graf reviews the therapies that skip factor replacement altogether in 2026, an era of factor VIII mimics and rebalancing drugs.

Antibody mimics stand in for factor VIII's helper role and give steady protection from under-skin injections. Years of use of the lead mimic, emicizumab, show durable effect across patients with and without blockers. Newer mimics aim for more potency. Rebalancing agents instead mute the body's own anticoagulants, lifting clotting in both haemophilia A and B, though they demand care against overshoot. Graf also notes the special value of these drugs when the disease is acquired.
pmc-13331920:
Rubén Marciel defends his account of journalism in a 2026 reply article answering critic Carl Fox. Fox had commented on Marciel's earlier piece about private media, public money, and fair democratic sharing of funds. Fox raised two linked objections, one about theory and one about policy.

On Fox's view, tying journalism's worth to a single function, promoting good democratic discussion, is too narrow and yields funding rules that reward only discussion-friendly traits. Marciel answers that one function can serve several values at once: watchdog reporting, for example, can support accountability, fairness, and stability together. He argues that promoting sound deliberation likewise serves stability as well as legitimacy, so his account can absorb Fox's concern without giving up its single-function core.
pmc-13333320:
Beatrice Scagnoli and co-authors functionalise graphene nanocarriers with a cell-penetrating peptide without disturbing how the carriers load aromatic drugs. Drug loading on graphene relies on its flat surface, which peptide coating might block. Their 2026 study attaches polyarginine, an eleven-unit arginine chain, only at the particle edges, where acid groups sit, leaving the flat faces free.

Using a fluorescent test compound and a conjugated cancer drug candidate, the team showed grafting did not change loading capacity or heat-triggered release. Spectroscopy and microscopy confirmed the flat surface stayed intact and accessible. Computer simulations showed the peptide chains forming a flexible charged fringe around the particle edge without interfering with cargo binding. The authors present edge grafting as a design rule for peptide-graphene hybrids carrying poorly soluble aromatic medicines.
pmc-13333420:
Yue-Qin Qian and co-authors sorted dialysis patients in Shanghai by how fully their lives flourish, in a 2026 survey study framed by social support theory. Staying on maintenance hemodialysis for life keeps people alive but often drags down mood and self-worth, and treating all patients as one group hides real differences.

Between October and November 2022, 376 patients completed the PERMA flourishing profiler plus scales for emotional self-belief, perceived support, and coping style. Profile analysis found three groups: a low group of 77 people, 20.48 percent, weak above all in meaning; a middle group of 153, 40.69 percent, low in accomplishment; and a high group of 146, 38.83 percent, low only in engagement. Coping style, social support, and confidence in handling emotions each tracked with group membership. The authors recommend tailoring mental health help to each profile rather than offering one program to all.
pmc-13333820:
A G Lunde and co-authors test whether a gene variant tracks lung decline in sarcoidosis, a disease that often scars the lungs. The variant, rs1800693, sits in the gene for the TNF receptor 1. It mimics the effect of the TNF-blocking drugs used to treat the disease. The team genotyped two cohorts in Germany and Norway, plus two control groups.

Follow-up ran six and a half years in Germany and eight in Norway. In Germany, patients with two copies of the A variant lost lung volume faster than G carriers, whose gas transfer held steady. In Norway, decline was much the same across genotypes, though AA patients started and ended with lower lung volume than GG patients. The variant showed no link to lung function in controls. The signal is real but place-dependent, a caution against one-cohort claims.
pmc-13333920:
Sarah Najah AlJanabi and co-authors tried gene silencing against drug-resistant bacteria, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Their target was Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that often shrugs off strong antibiotics. They loaded short antisense strands onto gold nanoparticles. The strands were built to switch off two genes that help the germ resist key drugs.

Working with 70 samples from Iraqi hospitals, they found the target genes in most drug-resistant samples. After treatment with the loaded particles, gene activity fell sharply and the germs grew sensitive to the drugs again. The early result points to a way of disarming resistance rather than killing the germ outright.
pmc-13334720:
Michelle Wazan and colleagues examine 2026 safe hospital access for OD care in Lebanon. In Lebanon, criminal law on drug use and misuse of ministry orders have led hospitals to report OD cases to police. That scares off people who use drugs from seeking urgent care and raises the risk of avoidable death. The paper treats OD response as a right to health issue, using civil society campaigns in Lebanon to show how police presence in health settings weakens emergency access.

Drawing on repeated countrywide surveys of hospital practices when receiving OD cases from 2016 through 2024. The paper documents patterns of compliance and disobedience with Ministry of Public Health orders prohibiting overdose reporting to police. Sustained campaigns contributed to multiple policy wins, including ministry and syndicate circulars restating hospitals' duty of care without police involvement. Rollout has remained uneven, the paper finds, leaving access to OD care tied to local practice.
pmc-13335420:
Şükran Calp and Pınar Bulut asked primary school teachers how children engage with media on global platforms in a 2026 qualitative case study from Türkiye. Their lens includes platform imperialism, the worry that a few global services reshape local values.

Semi-structured interviews with 71 public school teachers from village, town, and city settings fed a thematic analysis mixing inductive and deductive coding. Teachers described how platform content shows up in children's values and behavior, and how they position media literacy lessons in reply. Concepts of cultural autonomy and pedagogical resistance framed the interpretation. The study gives curriculum planners a ground-level view of what teachers think media education must accomplish when children's media lives run through foreign-owned platforms.
pmc-13336120:
Jing and co-authors study a chemical mark on histones that guides insect growth and egg making. The mark, lysine succinylation, is a key epigenetic signal in many body processes. How it steers insect metamorphosis and reproduction was poorly understood before this work.

Using the migratory locust as a model, the team found succinylation was the most abundant acylation in the fat body. That tissue acts much like the liver and fat stores of vertebrates. Marks at two histone sites, H3K14 and H3K23, changed by life stage. Their timing suggests the marks orchestrate body change and egg production.
pmc-13336420:
Rui Fu and co-authors designed a nanoreactor that starves pancreatic cancer cells into a sulfur-stress death in a 2026 nanomedicine study. Pancreatic tumors rewire metabolism to grow fast and resist therapy, and that rewiring creates exploitable weak points.

The particle targets CD44 on tumor cells and, once inside the tumor environment, releases phloretin, which throttles glucose uptake and the pentose phosphate pathway, cutting the cell's supply of reducing power. Its manganese dioxide shell meanwhile burns through glutathione and amplifies oxidative stress. Caught between too little reducing power and too much oxidation, cells pile up cystine, suffer disulfide stress, and their actin skeleton collapses in the death program called disulfidptosis. Released manganese also lights the tumor on MRI scans.
pmc-13336620:
Jibbe Keulen heads a 2026 team that built a self-running lab chip system for growing human tissue and watching it over weeks. Cameras guide fluid flow, so the system samples on schedule, refills food fluid, and doses drugs by program. Such control lets researchers copy real body patterns, such as insulin pulses or repeated drug doses.

Tests with three-dimensional human liver spheres showed why timing matters. A sharp acetaminophen dose pattern that mimicked overdose caused liver harm, with enzyme release and lost cell energy. The same total amount given steadily caused no clear harm. Protein and imaging checks tied the damage to fat handling problems and loosened cell joints. Exposure shape, not just dose size, shapes risk.
pmc-13336820:
Zi Hao Guo and co-authors add plant pollen to a touch sensor for prosthetic arms in a 2026 study. False limbs restore movement but rarely real feeling, since most systems only remap signals. Their sensor mimics skin by turning pressure into ionic signals inside a water gel.

Pollen microgels give ions anchor points inside the gel, boosting uneven ion flow under pressure. Output rose by up to 12-fold compared with the plain gel setup in the reported tests. Ten sensors fitted to a robotic arm, paired with a learning program, read object contacts accurately. Stronger, more natural touch signals could help prostheses feel less like tools and more like body parts.
pmc-13336920:
Artur Braun and a large team listen to lattice vibrations to learn how protons move through ceramics in a 2026 study. In doped perovskite conductors, protons were long pictured as hopping alone between oxygen sites. Special vibrational spectroscopy on wet, deuterated, and dry barium stannate samples tells a richer story.

Adding water reshaped the tin-linked vibration spectrum and stiffened the whole tin-oxygen network, shifting its first peak by about 0.4 meV in the measured spectra. Swapping hydrogen for heavier deuterium barely changed that spectrum, showing protons ride collective lattice modes rather than vibrating alone. A coupled oscillator model matched the data well. Phonon-aware design could raise proton flow for fuel cells and hydrogen devices.
pmc-13337020:
Xiuyun Liu and co-authors correct a hidden bias in fertilizer accounting across Asian rice fields in a 2026 study. Tracing fertilizer nitrogen is costly, and a soil priming effect quietly skews estimates of how much stays in soil. Their ensemble model maps residue and loss at fine scale across the continent.

Correcting the bias shows priming pushes retained fertilizer nitrogen below 7% while 48% of applied nitrogen escapes to the environment in the central estimates, at a yearly cost near US$98.53 billion from reactive emissions in the modeled total. Three risk patterns cover 42% of world rice fields, led by a high-loss yet high-residue type at 37% of fields in the analysis. Targeted maps could guide fertilizer policy by place, not averages.
pmc-13337420:
Kimiyoshi Okano reports a small veterinary case series in 2026 on closing mouth-to-nose holes in dogs with difficult anatomy. Six dogs covering eight upper canine teeth had oronasal fistulae plus problems like lost gum tissue, weak bone support, and scar-stiffened tissue that defeat a standard single-flap closure.

After tooth removal, a shaped flap was pulled over the hole with a trimmed collagen membrane laid on its nasal side to brace the suture line. In every case, nosebleeds, nasal discharge, and sneezing cleared within 14–21 days after surgery, and no recurrence appeared during follow-up. The membrane supports early healing but does not replace sound flap design or tension release, the author cautions.
pmc-13337920:
Hui Xu and colleagues model choices around crop straw handling in rural China in a 2026 study. Straw is plentiful but spread out, and collection, storage, and transport hurdles limit its use. Poor disposal such as open burning also harms public health.

Government, cooperatives, and farmers are placed in one game model that tracks how strategies shift over time. Subsidies and sales income drove participation most strongly in the reported results. Modest subsidy rises with lower fines encouraged joining, while cheaper oversight improved supervision. Linked choices formed a feedback loop, suggesting policy must move all three groups together to cut burning.
pmc-13338120:
Wearable sensors that sip fluid from under the skin can track body chemistry, but two problems plague them: the needles work loose, and sending data to the cloud drains power. Peidi Fan and co-authors solve both in a 2026 paper with a starfish-inspired patch. Suction cups anchor the microneedles, borrowed from how a starfish grips.

The anchoring cut signal wobble thirty-eight-fold and boosted signal strength more than five-fold over flat devices. Clean signals let a tiny 43-kilobyte algorithm run on the patch itself, reaching about 98.7 percent diagnostic accuracy with a battery life of 120 hours. Tests in pigs confirmed the patch could follow changing body chemistry continuously. The authors present the co-design as a template for wearables that judge metabolic risk on the spot.
pmc-13338420:
Xiaomo Yu, Jiajia Liu, Ling Tang, Jie Mi, and Long Long speed up predictions of influence in large networks in this 2026 paper. Knowing which nodes spread information or disease furthest matters for epidemic control and marketing. Classic spread simulations are far too slow for huge networks.

Their framework teaches a small, fast student model from two teacher models: one trained on many synthetic networks, one tuned to the target network. Only a small share of nodes needs true labels. The student matched simulation accuracy while cutting computing time by nearly ninety percent. Tests on eight real datasets beat leading methods, and networks of half a million nodes stayed practical.
pmc-13338820:
Amaia Torrecilla Ugarte and co-authors published this case report in 2026. A man of thirty-six, with no past health woes, came to hospital with fever, malaise, and yellow skin. Blood tests showed his red cells were breaking apart fast, while his marrow rushed to replace them. Tests ruled out an immune attack on the cells.

Three days before the illness, he had breathed in poppers, a party drug of nitrites. Such drugs can overwhelm the red cells' defenses, above all in people who lack a guard enzyme. Tests proved the man lacked that enzyme, a state called G6PD deficiency. The authors warn that poppers can spark this anemia in healthy people too, and urge doctors to ask about drug use when red cells break down without a clear cause.
pmc-13338920:
Yifang Shi and colleagues study spine fusion outcomes when back muscles have wasted in weak-boned patients in a 2026 review of records. Disc herniation patients with osteoporosis had single-level posterior fusion from 2021 to 2025. Muscle wasting was measured on scans by working area and fat content.

A total of 142 patients entered, with 90 having osteoporosis alone and 52 also showing muscle wasting as reported. Disability, pain, and quality-of-life scores tracked recovery alongside bone density and hospital stay. Comparing the groups tests whether wasted muscles predict poorer healing beyond bone quality alone. Such knowledge could guide rehab and patient selection before fusion surgery.
pmc-13339020:
Marta Sawicka and a large team build blue laser diodes wrapped in air in a 2026 study. Nitride lasers at longer wavelengths trap light weakly because material contrast is low. Replacing cladding with air on both sides is offered as a fix.

A tunnel junction allowed side contacts and a top air gap, while chemical etching hollowed a sacrificial layer below. Wing and membrane forms both resulted, with very smooth undersides as reported. X-ray scans showed slight bending from relaxed strain. Devices lased at 456 nm in pulses with slope efficiency of 0.4 W per amp, matching standard versions and proving the air design works.
pmc-13339220:
Canan Altinsoy, Yagmur Demirel Ozbek, and Isa Celik link eating habits to gut symptoms in young adults in a 2026 survey. Mindful eating and a Mediterranean pattern timed to the day were tested against stomach and bowel burden. Awareness of gut microbes was also measured.

A total of 677 adults averaging about 21 years old took part, mostly women as reported. Higher symptom scores tracked with lower microbe awareness and lower diet scores in the reported correlations. Mindful eating alone did not track with symptoms directly. Adjusted models tied male sex, non-smoking, and mindful eating to diet adherence, guiding campus programs on gut comfort.
pmc-13339620:
Daniel González-Pinardo and Israel Fernández compute the structure and reactivity of nitrilium-type hetarynes in a 2026 study. These strained ring species carry a triple bond plus a charged nitrogen unit. Their Diels-Alder behavior was compared with classic benzyne relatives.

Strain and energy breakdown analysis showed far less repulsion between reacting partners for the new species, explaining faster reactions as reported. Aromatic character and diradical traits were also charted. Groups attached to a neighboring boron atom, and swapping that group-13 element, tuned reactivity further. Results guide chemists seeking highly reactive building blocks for ring synthesis.
pmc-13339820:
Xuejiao Tian and a large team review probiotic-fermented herbal leftovers for weight control in a 2026 article. Chinese herbal production leaves large residue piles once treated as waste. Fermentation with helpful microbes may turn them into anti-obesity preparations.

Fermentation raises active compounds and their uptake while reshaping gut microbes, the review argues. Gut imbalance is tied closely to obesity and metabolic harm. Acting through the gut-liver axis, fermented residues could cut fat storage and improve energy handling. The approach joins waste recycling with metabolic care, though human proof remains the needed next step.
pmc-13341420:
Henry D. Heisey and colleagues reviewed GLP-1 drug stopping and adherence in 2026 through a narrative review framed by an established adherence model for chronic disease. GLP-1 drugs are increasingly used for glucose lowering and weight management, yet many patients stop them. Definitions of stopping, adherence, and persistence vary widely across studies, hampering comparison.

Few qualitative studies focus on why patients stop GLP-1 drugs, while quantitative work often stresses drug factors and superficial socioeconomic and condition factors. Very few studies cover all five dimensions of the adherence framework. The review maps gaps and urges richer, framework based research on why patients stay on or leave these widely used drugs.
pmc-13341620:
Ground-glass nodules often shrink during lung cancer immunotherapy, in a 2026 imaging study by Yuting Zheng and colleagues. The retrospective comparison covered 90 patients harboring 110 extra nodules through 3 to 4 cycles of checkpoint inhibitors, matched against untreated incidental nodules.

By volume change, 23.6% of treated nodules regressed versus 1.8% of controls, and risk category improvements were also commoner under therapy. Treated nodules gained diameter, volume, and mass more slowly per month. For clinicians, incidental hazy nodules in patients on immunotherapy may reflect treatment effects rather than new cancers, changing how aggressively they get chased.
pmc-13341920:
Predicting failure to urinate after prolapse surgery is modeled by Juan Zhang and colleagues, in their 2026 retrospective study. The dataset covered 698 patients, split by time into 505 for training and 193 for later validation, with urinary retention striking 176 of the patients (25.21% of the total).

Ten predictors survived screening, including prolapse severity, bladder neck mobility, comorbidity count, glucose, and surgery type. A gradient boosting model reached an AUC of 0.848 in validation, modestly but significantly beating plain logistic regression. Better net benefit across decision thresholds suggests such scoring could individualize catheter plans and discharge timing after pelvic repair.
pmc-13342220:
Álvaro Vera-López and co-authors describe a 2026 study on detecting breathing disease from voice and cough sounds, using long COVID as the test case. Recordings taken at rest can miss subtle changes, so the team asked whether exercise and modern speech models make the signal clearer.

Using recordings from 154 people, the group captured vowel sounds and coughs before and after walk and sit-to-stand tests. Models that mixed classic sound measures with self-supervised speech embeddings, such as WavLM and wav2vec 2.0, scored best after exercise, reaching an F1-score of 87.7 percent in the combined model. The approach offers a quick, non-invasive aid for screening that still needs wider testing.
pmc-13342520:
After a peripheral nerve is crushed, recovery depends on Schwann cells, the support cells that clear debris and guide regrowth. Chen and co-authors test whether gentle pulsed ultrasound can help those cells survive and work better.

In rats with a crushed sciatic nerve, the ultrasound treatment improved movement, sped regrowth of the nerve fibers and their insulation, and reduced wasting of the calf muscle. The team traced the effect to the cells' power plants: ultrasound eased mitochondrial failure in Schwann cells, which shut down a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. With less of that death, fewer inflammatory signals spilled out, and the cells multiplied, migrated, and cleared debris more effectively. The result was a friendlier setting for repair.
pmc-13343320:
Neil Heron and Steffan Griffin authored a Faculty of Sport and Exercise Medicine UK guide, corrected in 2026, that sets a standard framework for critical incidents in sport. The correction fixes the work's title. It also prints corrected summary and opening passages, which lay out guidance for rare but high-impact emergencies during sporting events.

Sport brings clear health gains yet carries a small risk of severe incidents. The framework covers planning ahead, managing the event itself, and caring for everyone involved afterward. Rehearsed emergency action plans fitted to each setting anchor the approach. Structured follow-up uses the 5Cs approach, built on clear talk, debriefing, and mental health support. Prevention, acute response, and rehab join into one consistent standard.
pmc-13344120:
Zi-Yu Yan and co-authors catalog functional sweet teas of China in a 2026 review, drinks brewed from naturally sweet plants with claimed health benefits. No standard list existed, so the team defined the category and compiled 22 plant species used in China along with 27 sweet components reported from them.

The sweet compounds show promise against high blood sugar, blood fats, blood pressure, and uric acid, plus liver disease, acting through better sugar and fat handling, calmer inflammation, and antioxidant routes. Named targets include AMPK, SGLT, and Nrf2, along with gut flora shifts. The catalog gives the growing natural sweetener industry a shared vocabulary and a research base for metabolic disease prevention.
pmc-13345820:
Xia Sun, Xiang Tang, and Guoyue Yuan review orosomucoid 2, a liver-made blood protein, as a bridge between type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease in 2026. The two conditions share inflamed, disordered roots, and this acute-phase protein keeps appearing at the crossroads of fat handling, insulin action, and immune control.

Lower ORM2 shows up in obesity and insulin resistance, while blood orosomucoid levels track kidney damage and future heart attack risk. Lab work shows the protein curbing liver fat making through AMPK, easing glucose control, and steering liver macrophages, and giving it to animals slowed artery clogging and fatty liver without metabolic harm. Big prospective and genetic studies must now test causality.
pmc-13346620:
Ka Chan and co-authors map how thousands of blood proteins vary with daily life and health in Chinese adults, in work from 2026. Proteins run all cell work, and shifts in their levels can flag disease early. New lab tools can now read thousands of proteins at once.

The platform used reads about sixty-six hundred proteins in blood plasma. The team linked each protein to age, sex, habits, surroundings, and health traits. Known markers for heart, liver, and swelling served as anchors for the scan. Such maps help sort which protein shifts reflect aging, lifestyle, or early disease. The data set gives drug and diagnosis research a rich base in an Asian population.
pmc-13347020:
Yuan Liu and co-authors mine a United States safety database for sex-linked gaps in harms from CAR T-cell therapy in a 2026 study. This cancer treatment retools immune cells to attack blood cancers, but it can cause severe side effects. Whether those harms fall differently on women and men had been little studied.

The team pulled all reports tied to the therapy from the federal database, some seventy-seven hundred cases in all. Women showed higher reporting odds for a strong immune overreaction and for later leukemias, with higher odds across many organ systems too. The pattern did not match sex gaps seen in other cancer treatments. The authors say sex should be weighed when teams plan how to watch for and handle these harms.
pmc-13347120:
Finn Upham, Bilge Serdar, and Alexander Refsum Jensenius study laughter during dance, in an exploratory study from 2026. Three settings were filmed and measured. They were a Norwegian folk session, an amateur line dancing lesson, and professional duo work. The duo work ran in person and remotely. Heart rate and body motion were added to the video.

Laughter marked mistakes, hard moments, joint choices, and shared success rather than pausing the work, and its shared quality shifted with the channels open for contact in each setting. The authors treat laughter as a fast bodily signal that helps dancers stay in sync, handle doubt, and build joint understanding without stopping to talk.
pmc-13348220:
Seung Chul Shin and co-authors told in 2026 of the full genome of Thermus scotoductus AK-1, from an Arctic hot spring site in Alaska. In situ heat reached about 75 degrees Celsius. Thermus species are heat-loving, air-breathing bacteria from one of Earth's oldest lines. They are most often found in hot springs from 55 to 70 degrees.

Read with PacBio HiFi tech, the round chromosome spans 2.21 million base pairs. The genome gives a resource for weighing heat-loving bacteria from polar hot sites against those from temperate hot springs. It probes how heat tolerance, metabolism, and stress replies adapt to cold surrounds. It also widens the list of old bacterial lines for evolution and biotech work.
pmc-13348820:
Jong Won Moon, Sook Hyun Yoon, Geun Woo Lee, and Donghun Lee compare how fast swelling of the optic disc fades in two diseases that can look alike at first glance. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. One cause is a stroke-like loss of blood flow to the optic nerve head. The other is inflammation of the optic nerve itself.

They reviewed thirty-three eyes with each diagnosis, all with proven swelling. Imaging tracked the nerve fiber layer from diagnosis until the swelling settled. The swelling lasted about a month and a half in both diseases. Thickness at diagnosis and the fading rate also matched closely. So timing cannot separate the two causes, the authors conclude. Clinicians must lean on other signs for the early call. That matters because treatments for the two diverge.
pmc-13350020:
Ren Gao and co-authors compared two navigation systems for keyhole screw fixation of chest-to-lower-back spinal fractures in a 2026 study of 105 patients treated between 2020 and 2024. Screws passed through the skin avoid the blood loss and long recovery of open surgery.

One group used a new two-dimensional optical navigation workflow, the other a three-dimensional O-arm system. Operation time, radiation dose, screw accuracy, pain and disability scores, complications, and the learning curve were all compared. Repeated X-ray guidance protects nerves but irradiates staff and patients. Showing a lighter 2D method can match 3D accuracy would make safer surgery easier to adopt.
pmc-13350320:
Rune Johan Krumsvik and Marius Ole Johansen examined a national research funding call in a 2026 article on trust and fairness in evaluation. Norway's AI centre call drew 50 large consortium bids, including education-focused ones, and rejected 88 percent when centres were named in June 2025.

Using one bid as an illustrative case, they ask whether the half work-year teams sink into a proposal can still pay off through learning, provided feedback is thorough and well argued. The piece is a reflective case study, not a standard experiment. It speaks for rejected applicants everywhere: transparent, expert review turns even a failed bid into usable competence.
pmc-13351620:
Xuemei Guo and colleagues present a 2026 case series on a rare gene fusion in childhood B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The P2RY8::CRLF2 fusion can switch on growth pathways, yet data on Chinese children with the change are scarce. Seven newly diagnosed children treated between September 2017 and July 2024 were reviewed.

Median age at diagnosis was 3 years and 11 months, and all children had precursor B-cell disease. Three also had RAS pathway changes and two had PAX5 fusions. Five children cleared measurable disease by day 19 and six by day 46 under current chemotherapy plans, with targeted drugs added for some. All stayed in full remission over median follow-up of 32 months, though the authors urge wider validation.
pmc-13351920:
Edyta Maria Urbanska and co-authors discuss targeting MET amplification in lung cancer in 2026, drawing on the phase II KUNPENG study of vebreltinib. Gene-driven treatments have reshaped care for non-small cell lung cancer, yet MET changes remain hard to treat. Amplification appears on its own in about 1 to 5 percent of cases.

MET amplification is also the most common off-target route by which EGFR-mutant tumours escape osimertinib. Approved drugs already cover a different MET change, exon 14 skipping. The authors review why pairing EGFR and MET blockade makes sense and what vebreltinib results add. Open questions include how to define true MET-driven disease.
pmc-13352620:
Mikiko Tsudome leads a 2026 sensing study that makes chitin breakdown visible on a nanofibre gel. Microbe enzymes that chew insoluble fibres work only at surfaces, which makes their activity hard to spot. The gel is built from N-acetylchitosan nanofibres whose tangled network offers a huge surface for enzymes to attack.

When chitin-eating microbes grew on the gel, their enzymes carved nanoscale dents that grew into pits visible to the eye. Profiling measured amounts down to about 1 nanogram, and the naked eye caught several tens of nanograms. Linking surface form, pit growth, and reaction speed gives enzyme hunters a simple, cheap screen that pairs with data-driven searches.
pmc-13353720:
Shumin Liang and a large team show that RNA capping helps set how a model plant answers its stress hormone in a 2026 paper. Messenger RNAs carry a chemical cap that keeps them stable and working. Capping was long treated as automatic, but it is now seen as regulated. One plant enzyme both removes an alternative cap and, through a separate non catalytic part, switches on the cap adding enzyme.

Plants missing that activating part answered the hormone abscisic acid weakly and tolerated stress poorly, while the enzyme's cutting activity mattered little. Mutants of the cap adding enzyme behaved the same way. Gene activity scans showed the capping pair mainly governs genes for stress, defense, light response, photosynthesis, and transcription control. The authors cast capping as an active control layer in hormone response.
pmc-13353920:
Thais Pimentel and others tested oral dexamethasone after wisdom-tooth surgery in a 2026 triple-blind trial. Removing impacted lower third molars often brings pain and jaw stiffness, known as trismus, and steroids are commonly used to limit swelling. Whether an after-op oral dose meaningfully helps comfort and daily life needed a strict test.

The split-mouth design meant each patient could serve as their own match, with drug and control sides assigned at random and neither people nor assessors knowing which side received the drug. Pain, mouth opening, and quality of life were tracked after surgery. The trial gives dentists firmer evidence on whether this simple steroid regimen eases recovery.
pmc-13354420:
Farhan Ahmed and others surveyed the results on bronchodilators for bronchiolitis in infants, in 2026. Bronchiolitis, most often caused by breathing syncytial virus, is a leading cause of lower breathing illness in babies, yet care remains largely supportive. No drug has always shortened illness or clinic stay, and bronchodilator use remains contested.

The review weighs trials of salbutamol and related drugs, noting short-term score improvements in some studies against pooled results that show little lasting benefit. It gives doctors a balanced summary rather than a simple yes-or-no verdict. Child teams can use it to explain to homes why supportive care, not routine bronchodilators, remains the standard approach.
pmc-13355220:
Marcela Preliasco and co-authors give a full 2026 account of Nierembergia rivularis, a South American plant that poisons sheep and cattle. The plant causes calcinosis, a wasting illness where soft tissues harden with minerals, and farm losses are large. The team describes the plant's shape, growth cycle, flowers, favored ground, and toxic compounds.

The small perennial spreads mainly by underground stems, whose mass can be 15 times that above ground. It favors wet, sunny soil with little rival root growth, and its white flowers drew a beetle and a small bee in spring. Vitamin D-like toxins were found in all parts, a clue for preventing stock losses.
pmc-13355320:
Zhebin Zhang led a 2026 study that builds planned plastic porous skins from nano-crystal lattices. Porous skins with tunable layout and strong workings are hard to make, because built order and firmness are hard to achieve jointly. A general, reliable route would benefit split, sensing, and energy uses.

Two-sized lattices, self-built at the liquid-air edge from guided nanocrystals, served as templates, and thermal annealing activated polymer tangle to lock the plan in place. The confined tangle stabilises the porous structure while keeping its planned layout. Items scientists gain a flexible method for skins whose pore layout can be built rather than left to chance.
pmc-13355420:
Mikkel Lammers Haglund and co-authors reviewed outcomes in 2026 after surgery for meralgia paresthetica, a trapped thigh nerve that causes burning pain and tingling. When simple measures fail, doctors either free the nerve or cut it, but proof was limited. The single-center study covered 101 patients and 128 operations from 2019 to 2024.

Freeing the nerve cut pain by a median of six and a half points on a ten-point scale. Cutting the nerve later, often after freeing failed, gave a like total gain, so neither method won on pain. About 85 percent needed no further surgery at one year. The authors favor freeing first, since cutting always costs feeling.
pmc-13355720:
Eugene Yu-hin Chan and colleagues followed kidney survival in children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome after rituximab, in a 2026 international cohort study. Outcomes after rituximab in this group were unclear, so the team gathered 151 children across 23 centers in 17 countries who had failed calcineurin inhibitors. Children with genetic variants were excluded.

At rituximab start, 48 percent had normal kidney function, 31 percent had stage 2 chronic kidney disease, and 21 percent had stage 3. Nineteen percent later reached kidney failure, and overall kidney survival stood at 82.7 percent at 3 years, 75.8 percent at 5 years, and 72.3 percent at 7 years. Baseline kidney stage strongly predicted survival at 5 years, guiding family counseling.
pmc-13356620:
Yeongrin Kim and co-authors built a 2026 switch to turn CAR T cell therapy up and down in a reversible way. CAR T cells are living drugs that can cause severe side effects, and most safety switches kill the cells for good. Their system tags the cancer-targeting receptor with a mutant protein piece that a designer drug can destroy on demand, while sparing the body's own like proteins.

The designer drug broke down the tagged receptor about tenfold more strongly than a comparison drug on the normal tag, and normal T cell function stayed intact. In animal models, the cells fought tumors as well as standard CAR T cells and could be dialed down by the drug.
pmc-13358520:
Alessandro Garlaschi and co-authors share a long look at breast implant surgery in a 2026 paper. Their method places the implant behind the breast gland rather than behind the chest muscle. Over 14 years they used it in 1,043 cases and tracked both looks and health through scans and follow-up visits.

A questionnaire found 94 percent of patients were pleased with their results, and two outside surgeons rated before-and-after photos at four out of five on average. Problems such as hardening around the implant or rotation were rare. The authors argue that a fixed, standard method helps keep results steady across many kinds of patients.
pmc-13358820:
Kang Li wrote a 2026 letter about how a breathing test result is read in bronchiectasis, a disease where airways stay widened and clogged with mucus. A recent study had linked a strong response to airway-opening drugs with worse lung function and more flare-ups. Li praises the work but raises points that could shift its meaning.

Chief among them: patients who respond may simply be those still using long-acting airway drugs on test day. Guidelines say those drugs should be stopped a day or two before testing, or the response looks smaller than it is. Li argues that how the test is run shapes the very definition being studied.
pmc-13360220:
Małgorzata Zalewska-Adamiec and co-authors report a 2026 case of a heart artery that grew from the wrong place. The patient was a 51-year-old man who felt palpitations when he exercised. A stress test on his heart picked up a risky rhythm problem in the lower heart chambers. Such artery defects are rare but can cause sudden death during sport in people under 35.

A tube test of the heart arteries could not reach the right coronary artery, even with several tools tried. A CT scan then showed the artery starting from the left side, in a high-risk form. The case shows why doctors should think of this hidden defect when exercise brings on rhythm trouble, and why CT imaging can settle the question.
pmc-13360520:
Alharbi and co-authors present a 2026 survey of satisfaction with urgent care centers in Saudi Arabia. These centers give patients a faster option than crowded emergency departments. The team measured how happy both patients and staff were with the service in 2024, and which factors tracked with those scores.

Two validated questionnaires went to 425 patients and 103 practitioners. Patients scored satisfaction at a mean of 72, while staff averaged 68 with a wider spread. Statistical tests compared scores across groups, and regression models singled out the linked factors. Satisfaction is a core gauge of service quality for managers. Staff contentment also feeds system performance. The study gives Saudi planners a baseline for both sides of the counter.
pmc-13360720:
Reynaldo Arellano-Cervantes led a 2026 survey study of pharmacy students and mood at the University of Guadalajara in Mexico. Pharmacy students show fairly high rates of depressive symptoms, which can hurt grades and quality of life. Young adults also take medicines on their own more often than in the past. The team asked whether ongoing self-reported medicine use links to depressive symptoms in these students.

Students in pharmacy programs at one university center filled in a tailored questionnaire. The team then compared medicine use between students with and without depressive symptoms. The concern is that some students may take medicines to cope with body complaints or low mood without guidance. Knowing the link can help universities plan support and safer habits for future pharmacists.
pmc-13361320:
Beata Balla and co-authors present a 2026 case-based review of high-risk gene damage in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. This slow blood cancer varies widely in its genetics, and damage to the TP53 gene is a strong bad sign. The team profiled one patient's cancer with tools that count gene copies and read mutations. The case is rare because several severe faults stacked together.

The patient's cancer had lost parts of two chromosomes and carried two harmful TP53 mutations, wiping out the p53 guard protein. That mix marks a very high-risk profile. Even so, a targeted drug that blocks a B-cell enzyme brought clear improvement in blood measures within six months. The authors stress that TP53 damage outweighs good markers, so full gene checks are a must.
pmc-13362820:
Mu-Chieh Chi, Kao-Shang Shih, and I-Hsin Chen wrote a 2026 review on spinal fractures caused by osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease of older age. These vertebral fractures are the most common break from the disease, yet most are missed: they often cause no clear pain and show up only by chance on scans. The review gathers guidance on finding them, judging future risk, and treating patients after one is found.

A spinal fracture warns strongly of more breaks ahead, even when bone density tests look fair. The authors promote checks built into bone scans, routine CT reviews, and AI scan readers to catch missed cases. Care should pair pain relief and rehab with bone drugs and a follow-up service that keeps patients on treatment.
pmc-13363420:
Eva Greibe and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study on blood levels of intrinsic factor, the stomach protein that lets the body absorb vitamin B12. Tiny amounts leak into the blood, and the team asked whether the level reflects the state of the stomach lining. They tested three groups: patients before and after weight-loss surgery, patients with portal hypertension, and patients checked for suspected pernicious anemia.

After weight-loss surgery, blood levels fell within two months, and over a third of patients dropped below the normal band, matching the known fall in B12 uptake. The other groups gave mixed pictures, with a few strikingly high values in liver-pressure patients and low values in most antibody-positive anemia cases. Larger, longer studies must judge the test's worth.
pmc-13365820:
Tineke Vanderhaeghen and others discussed how TCA-cycle switch-on protects at risk newborns, in 2026. Preterm neonates are highly susceptible to sickness that easily become sepsis, a major global burden with hard finding and care limited to drugs and supportive care. How newborn defence interacts with energy use during illness was poorly known.

In the same issue, Wu and others showed a clear link between body-wide energy use and neonatal defence, identifying tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolites as key regulators linked with reduced illness burden. The commentary places that finding in context for neonatal care. Doctors gain a energy perspective on newborn illness that may eventually yield adjunct care.
pmc-13366120:
Ursula de Matos and co-workers tell in 2026 of a rare, fast cell break ill in a 61 year old man with spread colon cancer. The ill, more known in blood cancers, struck two days after his first drug round. His kidneys fail, and blood salts and waste run wild.

Fluids and two waste cut drugs clear the ill fast. Still, he dies two weeks on from his far gone cancer. The team warns that colon cancer with a huge liver load can spark this ill at first care, and that fast spot and treat steps save the window that counts.
pmc-13366320:
Bastian Engel, Theresa Kirchner, and Richard Taubert reply to a letter about antibody testing in liver disease, in a 2026 journal exchange. The topic is autoimmune hepatitis, where the immune system attacks the liver, in both adults and children. The letter writers had praised the team’s study and urged finer measures of one antibody type.

In reply, the team explains that stored blood samples were scarce, above all for children, so the first study used common assays. With left-over samples from the original group of 202, they then ran a test aimed at the actin-specific form of the antibody. Only one dilution could be run, as stocks were low. The reply shows how added testing can still refine diagnosis when samples are tight.
pmc-13366520:
Wayne Hayes and co-workers give in 2026 a shape only way to guess lost links in huge nets, from friend webs to cell maps. Most guess tools need side facts on each point or stall on big nets. Their tool reads small shape bits round each pair of points and ranks pairs by those counts.

Across 12 real nets, some with a million points, the tool beats 13 past tools on hit truth and runs fast. In tests on next time shots of the nets, its lead holds. Shape alone can guide link hunts in nets too big for deep tools.
pmc-13366820:
Banken and co-authors set out the plan for a Dutch trial on high risk rectal cancer, in a 2026 protocol paper. Care before surgery now often joins drug treatment with radiation. That full course lifts the chance that no tumor is left at surgery, but the best drug mix for high risk cases is unsettled.

The trial will assign close to four hundred patients by chance to a three drug course or a two drug course, each with radiation. Patients have cancer that has not spread to distant sites. The study will weigh tumor response, survival, and the chance to spare the rectum. Its results should guide a choice that clinics now make in varied ways.
pmc-13369020:
Alba Galdón and five co-authors track how often vision faults appear in Spanish school children, in a 2026 report from the CISViT project. Rates of short sight have risen in many places, and the team wanted local figures for the northeast of Spain.

The study checked 1,189 children twice, about a year apart, starting at a mean age under nine. The share of children with short sight rose from about 12 percent to about 17 percent. Fifty-six children developed a vision fault in that year. Children whose eyes were already near the short-sight range faced higher odds of a marked shift. Having a short-sighted mother or father raised the odds a great deal, and spending little time outdoors raised them too.
pmc-13369820:
Train delays follow power laws: most are small, a few are huge, and the tail matters. Tommaso Rondini and co-authors ask how such patterns arise in a hierarchy. They model a railway as levels of agents under priority rules — high-speed trains outrank local ones — and add random wobbles to scheduled times drawn from real data.

Local trains collect far more large delays than high-speed ones, in both the data and the model. A queue-based model tuned on Italian data reproduced the observed power-law exponent for Italian local delays, and comparisons with German data held up. Timetabling policies such as priority assignment and compensation thresholds left visible marks in both data and model. The authors argue that simple layered rules, without any intricate network, can generate the heavy-tailed statistics of real systems.
pmc-13369920:
Xu Liu and co-authors find a missed factor in breaking down PFAS, the hardy chemicals that resist decay, in a 2026 study. The best known cleanup method uses ultraviolet light with sulfite, which frees loose electrons in water that attack the chemicals. Past work blamed success or failure on the shape of each PFAS molecule alone.

The team show the electrons' own water shell matters just as much. When the shell's inner cavity grows wider, the electrons reach the chemicals' weak points more easily and strip off more fluorine. Under strong alkaline settings, one tough PFAS type broke down by over 97 percent. Tuning the water shell around electrons may be a new lever for cleaning water of these chemicals.
pmc-13370720:
Kento Nakagawa and Rieko Osu test in 2026 if ear nerve pulse care in short motor drill shifts brain maps with no gain in skill score. The pulse care is cast as a rehab aid that may wake nerve growth cues. Thirty one adults drill a two ball roll task for a brief span, half with real pulses.

Skill gains run the same in both arms. Yet brain map spread for the hand runs wide more in the pulse arm, while spine gains show in the sham arm lone. Pupils widen on pulses, a sign of a wake cue. Brain shift can lead skill shift, they hold.
pmc-13371120:
Feng-Ping Zhang and colleagues compare flower and leaf pigments across 36 orchid species in the genus Dendrobium in a 2026 study. Chlorophylls and carotenoids drive photosynthesis, attract pollinators, and help plants cope with stress, yet flower and leaf pigments may follow different rules. Pigments were measured in petals, sepals, flower lips, roots, stems, and leaves.

Leaves held the most chlorophyll, while flower lips held the most carotenoids. Flower pigments varied far more across species than leaf pigments, and flower parts tracked each other closely while showing little link to vegetative parts. The pattern suggests that flower colour evolves freely to suit pollinators, while leaf chemistry stays conserved. The work helps explain how orchids diversify their blooms without changing their basic leaf machinery.
pmc-13372920:
Tricking the eyes can soften the misery of hard exercise, Lara Biller and co-authors show in this 2026 study of virtual reality cycling. Riders saw a gentler slope than their legs actually fought, a mismatch built to fool effort sense. Forty-eight healthy volunteers rode in a blinded trial; patients and caregivers also weighed in on the idea.

The mismatched view cut both breathlessness and leg fatigue by the same clear margin. Mood and health anxiety colored the effect somewhat. Nine patients with heart or lung conditions then tried the setup and found it acceptable and easy to bear. The authors see rehab programs, where breathlessness scares patients off exercise, as the natural home for the trick.
pmc-13374120:
Melika Khademi and colleagues test whether a probiotic strain can restore gut barrier function in ulcerative colitis models in a 2026 study. Barrier breakdown is a hallmark of inflammatory bowel disease, yet probiotic benefit varies by patient. Gut cells were exposed to stool fluid from three ulcerative colitis patients, which raised inflammatory IL-8 and lowered barrier genes Claudin-1 and MUC2.

Preparations of Lactobacillus helveticus SBT2171, including live bacteria, cell-free fluid, and debris-containing fluid, were then tested at 24 and 48 hours. Restoration of barrier genes was partial and depended on both patient source and preparation. Live bacteria gave transient or sustained Claudin-1 gains by source, while cell-free fluid gave broader, more durable gains. The work argues for personalised probiotic choices rather than one-size-fits-all dosing.
pmc-13374220:
Khandaker Asif Ahmed and eight co-authors publish a chromosome-scale genome for a biting midge in a study from 2026. This midge, Culicoides brevitarsis, lives close to cattle and spreads viruses that harm animals. Gene data for the species were scarce, which limited work on how it transmits disease and how it evolved.

The genome spans about 130 million letters in three chromosomes and looks nearly complete. Annotation found close to twelve thousand genes, including hundreds tied to immunity. Comparisons across twelve fly genomes showed family and genus level patterns. Many gene families grew or shrank in this species, mostly in metabolism and sensing.
pmc-13374320:
Mahboobeh Asadi, Mahnaz Noroozi, and Mousa Alavi build in 2026 a questionnaire that measures how well women adjust after childbirth. New mothers face body, mind, and social changes, and health workers need a sound tool to spot those who struggle. The team drafted items from interviews and past literature, then tested them on 203 Iranian mothers.

Weak items were cut by standard content checks, and a factor study settled the form at thirty items in five groups. Those groups explained about fifty-seven percent of the spread in answers, and the whole scale showed high internal consistency. The authors judge the tool valid and reliable for clinic use.
pmc-13375320:
Dario Shaw, Hari Ananda Rao, and Pascal Saikaly review how a bacterium called Geobacter can support green technology, in work published in 2026.
