Their method, intuitionistic fuzzy driven retinex, joins a fuzzy index part with single scale retinex. One part sharpens local detail and contrast, and the other part evens out light across the whole image. The cleaned up images show clearer sickle cell edges, a better split of cells that lie on top of each other, higher contrast, and less noise. A DenseNet121 classifier trained on these images reaches an accuracy level that stands up well on a Kaggle data set.
pmc-13402820:
Xiao Han built a hybrid neural net to sort feelings in old Chinese paintings. His 2026 work takes on a culture-bound task: Chinese literati painting follows beauty rules that differ sharply from Western art, so generic feeling models may miss its cues. Computer feeling analysis for this tradition had lacked a tuned design.

The model joins convolutional brushwork detail with transformer layout context through spatial, channel, and cross-attention parts. Tested on 7,842 paintings across seven feelings, from calm to solemnity, it hit 91.4 percent right, beating ResNet, DeiT, and ConvNeXt baselines. Cut-out tests proved the attention part key, and visual maps lined up with old art theory. The work backs culture-aware design for digital humanities, with wider art tests still to come.
pmc-13403220:
Siva Chamarthi and co-authors map soybean genes behind canopy temperature under drought in a 2026 study. Leaf canopy warmth betrays how hard a plant is breathing: cool canopies transpire freely, hot ones shut down. That makes temperature a handy proxy for drought response in breeding.

Two hundred five soybean lines grew across twelve fields, half irrigated and half rainfed. Association mapping found over one hundred loci tied to normalized canopy temperature. Most were new or matched other drought traits rather than earlier temperature hits. Over five hundred nearby candidate genes touch water transport, pore control, and root growth. Stacking the cool-canopy alleles could breed hardier soybeans faster.
pmc-13403420:
Hongze Lin and co-authors ask whether swelling signals link muscle loss to neck artery plaque in diabetes in a 2026 study. Both troubles cluster in type 2 diabetes, and shared inflammation may bridge them.

Seven hundred forty nine patients were scanned for plaque and graded for muscle loss by Asian criteria. Plaque and muscle loss each touched a large share. Two swelling ratios, built from blood cell counts, ran higher with both troubles and rose in straight lines with each. Muscle loss kept its own link to plaque after adjustments. The ratios partly carried the link, the mediation tests suggest.
pmc-13403720:
Yuanyuan Wan led a 2026 study on how heat stress darkens skin by waking pigment cells. Growing clinical signs link heat to dark patches, and warming trends make the question sharper. The team worked with mouse skin, lab pigment cells, and human skin pieces.

Heat pushed skin support cells to release a signal protein called WNT5A. A chemical mark on that protein's message, placed by one enzyme and read by another, kept the message stable. Adding the signal raised pigment in cells and skin pieces alike. Blocking its receiver on pigment cells shut the effect down. Heat therapy may thus aid pale-skin diseases such as vitiligo.
pmc-13404620:
Jorge Ortega-Márquez and colleagues present a 2026 trial protocol on placebo effects in stroke recovery. Placebo responses have produced real gains in movement after stroke, yet the brain activity behind them is poorly mapped. The study contrasts openly given placebo with hidden placebo during brain stimulation.

Fifty-six adults at least six months past stroke, each with a weak arm, will be assigned across four arms. Groups receive open-label placebo tablets, hidden sham magnetic stimulation, no intervention, or active low-frequency stimulation over the motor cortex. The main measure is change in frontal alpha asymmetry on dense EEG after two weeks. Secondary measures cover brain connectivity and arm function on the Fugl-Meyer scale.
pmc-13405020:
Suren Kanayan reports a 2026 low-cost safety project in a Phnom Penh tertiary hospital in Cambodia. Safety problems in low-resource hospitals often go unreported, so fixes arrive late and harm repeats. The project set out to make reporting routine without new technology.

A one-page checklist went to four departments, covering emergency and intensive care, maternity, outpatients and children's wards. Weekly reviews, feedback and department champions kept the system moving through small Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles. Within three months, written standard procedures rose from none to ten, the report states. Resistance to extra work and uneven submissions were handled by simplifying forms and coaching, with a hospital quality committee watching progress.
pmc-13405120:
Lydia S Massae and co-authors explore why vacuum-assisted birth is rarely used at a Tanzanian tertiary hospital, in a 2026 qualitative study. A vacuum cup can deliver a baby safely when labour stalls, sparing some mothers a caesarean. Underuse of the method remains a concern across similar settings.

Twelve clinicians with relevant experience gave in-depth interviews, analysed for recurring themes. Barriers fell into organisational and individual groups. Equipment was scarce or unreliable, and poor teamwork slowed decisions about using the device. Individual barriers, including confidence and training gaps among clinicians, complete the picture the authors draw. Their findings aim to guide training and equipment plans that could revive the technique.
pmc-13405620:
Kely Catarine Matteucci and a large team show how malaria infection rewires energy use in immune cells, in 2026 mouse work. The tumour necrosis factor, TNF, both fights the parasite and causes sickness behaviour such as inactivity and appetite loss. The chain linking those effects was traced in Plasmodium chabaudi infection.

TNF proved necessary for switching on nitric oxide production, stabilising the HIF-1alpha factor and raising glucose uptake in monocytes. Mice lacking parts of that chain showed weaker glucose burning, higher parasite counts and greater tolerance of disease. Liver and spleen took up more glucose under TNF signalling in the reported experiments. The pathway is presented as central to host defence.
pmc-13407720:
Dirk Linke and co-authors chart, in 2026, German hip and knee replacement volumes and project them to 2035. Using federal statistics and hospital quality reports from 2015 to 2024, they tracked first-time and revision operations, patient ages, hospital stays, and how many hospitals still offer the procedures.

First-time operations grew steadily, adding roughly five thousand cases a year for each joint, while revision volumes stayed flat. Patients skewed older over time, with shrinking shares under fifty. Projections show total first-time volume nearly stable to 2035, but hips rising by about eleven thousand cases while knees fall by a similar amount, and revisions climbing, especially past age seventy-five. Hospital stays shortened each year, and hospital numbers fell sharply, signalling centralisation the authors say planning must confront.
pmc-13407820:
Uta Kiltz and co-authors review golimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2026 narrative review. The disease is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune condition that slowly wears the joints down, year by year. It cuts quality of life, work productivity, and daily function, and it brings pain, fatigue, and structural damage to the joints.

Golimumab blocks tumor necrosis factor, one of the inflammatory cytokines that drive the disease. The review draws on the large randomized trials and on studies of real-world care as it is lived day to day. Set side by side, trial efficacy and real-world performance help rheumatologists judge where this long-used biologic still fits among newer options, and for whom it still earns its place.
pmc-13408820:
Yiwang Chen and team rebuilt the long-term evolution of drug-resistant tuberculosis across China from over 18,000 bacterial genomes. Their 2026 work takes on a gap: antibiotics have treated tuberculosis for over 80 years, yet population-level dynamics of resistance under drug pressure had been poorly mapped. Spatial and temporal patterns matter for control plans.

Resistance mutations to varied drugs arose time and again, forming hundreds to over a thousand small resistant clades, mostly arising in the past two decades. Once set, clades spread mainly within provinces, but could widen with human movement and bacterial fitness. Genomic and CRISPRi data flagged mutations tied to resistance rise and spread. The work highlights migration and bacterial adaptation as shapers of local drug-resistant tuberculosis epidemics.
pmc-13409020:
Crystal violet dye colors textiles and other products, and its wastewater is hard to clean. Mansoori and co-authors tested a cleaner way to break the dye down: spark plasma discharge paired with a ferric vanadate catalyst, with no added oxidant chemicals. The plasma itself creates reactive species in the water, and the catalyst's surface helps turn them on the dye.

The pair worked fast. At a near-neutral pH, about 99.4 percent of the dye at a starting level of ten milligrams per liter was destroyed within ten minutes. Trapping tests showed that holes and singlet oxygen did most of the oxidizing work. The breakdown followed a simple first-order rate law. Because the method needs no stored oxidants, the authors argue it cuts cost, removes a safety hazard, and simplifies treatment of dye wastewater.
pmc-13410920:
Ahad Bakhtiari and colleagues explore in 2026 fresh ways to pay for health care for migrants and refugees in Iran. Money is tight, authority is split across many bodies, and displacement has lasted for years. Afghan migrants form the main group affected, with mixed legal and insurance status.

The team combined a literature sweep, national document review, and interviews with 44 people from agencies, insurers, charities, and migrant communities. Fifteen experts also mapped who influences whom in a network analysis. Stakeholders were rated by interest, money-raising power, and policy sway. Findings point to underused funding routes that link existing pots of money more tightly, rather than building parallel systems for displaced people.
pmc-13411120:
Elaheh Dadashi and colleagues examined frailty, health literacy, and pill-taking habits among 210 older adults in Tabriz in 2026. Frailty leaves older people more open to falls, illness, and hospital stays. The team used standard scales to test whether understanding health information lines up with staying strong and taking medicines as directed.

About 42 percent of the group met frailty criteria, while nearly all reported high medicine adherence and about half showed adequate health literacy. Stronger health literacy looked protective against frailty, which points clinics toward plain-language teaching as a practical frailty defense.
pmc-13411320:
Beatriz Bartulic Machado and co-authors assess in 2026 how Brazil's data protection law reshaped research involving human participants. Personal databases have grown fast with digital tools, and the law, plus a 2024 health council resolution, set new guardrails. Document analysis compared the rules before and after the change.

Consent and privacy duties now carry legal weight beyond ethics custom. Researchers must justify data use, protect identities, and respect participants' rights under enforceable rules. Gains in protection come with real operational strain for study teams. The authors weigh that tension: health and science need data, while each person keeps a claim on their own information. Clear procedures, they argue, let both goods stand.
pmc-13412420:
Meng-Hsing Ho and co-authors compare two follow-up chemotherapy regimens after stomach cancer surgery in a 2026 nationwide Taiwan cohort study. Both XELOX, a two-drug pairing, and TS-1, a single-drug option, are guideline choices after D2 gastrectomy, yet direct comparisons in stage III disease were scarce. Insurance and cancer registry records identified patients treated from 2010 to 2019, and matching balanced the groups for fair comparison.

In 490 matched pairs, TS-1 patients survived longer and progressed less overall, with three-year survival near 65 percent versus about 57 percent on XELOX in this dataset. The advantage concentrated in stage IIIA disease, while stages IIIB and IIIC showed no clear difference. The authors label the finding hypothesis-generating and ask for a randomized trial.
pmc-13413520:
Yingwu Shi and co-authors track in 2026 how a friendly bacterium settles inside cotton plants and primes them against Verticillium wilt, a devastating soil fungus. The biocontrol strain, Bacillus velezensis BHZ-29, was tagged with antibiotic resistance so its travels could be followed without changing its behaviour. Pot trials then measured where it colonized, which defence enzymes it stirred, and how well it protected several cotton varieties.

The strain took up stable residence in roots, stems, and leaves, with roots as its stronghold. Treated plants fired up five defence and antioxidant enzymes, gained vitamin C, and suffered less cell damage when the wilt fungus attacked alongside. Greenhouse checks confirmed broad, steady protection across varieties, backing the strain as a green alternative to chemical sprays.
pmc-13413720:
Takashi Nagai and colleagues look in 2026 at whether bone drugs called SERMs lose their punch as women age, using real-world Japanese clinic data. These estrogen-like drugs are a staple for postmenopausal osteoporosis, yet routine practice rarely tests age effects. Records covered women treated for one year between 2017 and 2021, split into three age bands, with density measured at spine and hip and bone turnover tracked in blood and urine.

Spine density rose significantly in every age band across the year of therapy. Hip density improved significantly only in the youngest band, women aged fifty to sixty-four, and gains there were smaller overall. Once baseline density and kidney function were accounted for, age itself predicted nothing at either site. Lower starting density forecast bigger relative gains, the authors note.
pmc-13414720:
Hae-Yeon Cho and colleagues ask whether methyl gallate can soften the side effects of the antibiotic tylosin in weaned piglets, in a 2026 trial. Forty piglets were assigned to salt solution, tylosin, methyl gallate, or both compounds, each drug at 10 milligrams per kilogram. Blood, weight, and gut bacteria were tracked after one injection.

Growth and feed measures stayed similar across groups. Tylosin lowered Lactobacillus counts and shifted immune signals, a pattern suggesting brief gut disturbance. Methyl gallate raised several cytokines linked to adaptive immunity. Given together, the plant compound partly eased the gut bacteria changes, though one major bacterial group stayed unchanged.
pmc-13415020:
Anna Giorgio and colleagues review two decades of work on attaching peptides to gold and platinum cancer drugs, publishing in 2026. Metal drugs kill cancer cells well yet often harm healthy tissue and meet resistance. Peptides, short protein chains, can steer a metal complex toward tumors and change how cells take it up.

Platinum pairs in the common form mostly keep their DNA attack, with peptides improving delivery rather than potency. A higher oxidation form acts as a prodrug, switched on inside cells. Gold pairs target sulfur or selenium sites in proteins instead. Success depends on balancing peptide delivery against the metal's own chemistry, the review concludes.
pmc-13415320:
Şerife Yılmaz Gürbüz, Oğuzhan Yağdı, and Erhan Başar examine two tricky patterns in hepatitis B blood testing, reporting in 2026 from Karabuk. Their records spanned 2021 to 2025. One puzzle is a lone core antibody result, the other a weak surface antigen signal close to the cutoff.

Among 17,356 people screened, 506 showed the lone core antibody pattern, and about three percent of them carried viral DNA. That pattern grew commoner after age fifty. For weak surface antigen signals, a threshold near three times the cutoff caught every DNA positive case in 213 checked specimens. Every specimen below that range tested DNA negative, which could spare needless follow-up testing.
pmc-13415520:
Rongcen Zhao and colleagues recycle spent indium tin oxide, the coating used on display glass, through electrochemistry in 2026. Spent material is the main secondary source of scarce indium. Their method makes the spent oxide the anode in a water based cell, where charge excitation multiplies surface oxygen vacancies.

Weakened metal oxygen bonds release indium and tin ions into the liquid. The ions migrate to the cathode and form a high purity indium tin alloy, separated from impurities by their differing electrical behavior. At hundred ampere scale, current efficiency reached about 71 percent with modest energy use. The electrolyte can be reused, cutting wastewater sharply.
pmc-13415720:
Vanessa Gipson leads a large team testing the RALE score, a numbered grading of lung clouding on chest X-rays, in acute respiratory failure in 2026. Portable films from 814 critically ill adults, 4,259 images in total, were scored by trained clinicians blinded to clinical details. Patient groups ranged from ARDS to heart failure lung edema and airway protection cases.

Scores rose in steps from no airspace disease to limited to diffuse involvement. A cutoff score of seven caught 96 percent of cases with any airspace disease. Scores overlapped heavily among ARDS, heart edema, and lung scarring flare groups, since films look alike. Poor X-ray penetration inflated scores and wrecked accuracy.
pmc-13417720:
Antonello and colleagues reported in 2026 a hard-to-diagnose fever case at a public hospital in southern Brazil. A man in his sixties had high fever for over three weeks and severe leg muscle pain that limited walking. Tests for infection and cancer found no cause, meeting the formal idea of fever of unknown origin.

Blood tests showed many white cells, very high ferritin, a protein linked to inflammation, and strong inflammation markers. That pattern pointed to a body-wide inflammatory disease rather than infection. Rheumatology specialists supported adult-onset Still disease, a rare inflammatory disorder, using standard criteria. A low steroid dose helped partly, and a higher dose ended the fever and muscle pain quickly. The authors stress structured reasoning and careful reading of lab patterns where advanced tests are scarce.
pmc-13418420:
Alice Lacan and colleagues tested diffusion models in 2026 for creating synthetic gene-expression data to ease small-sample problems in precision medicine. RNA data sets often hold too few samples for deep learning, and earlier synthetic generators leaned on variational autoencoders and adversarial networks.

Diffusion models trained on landmark genes predicted better on cancer and tissue reference data, and methods that rebuild the full transcriptome lifted diffusion, autoencoder, and adversarial models alike. Researchers gain a strong new synthetic-data option for training models where patient samples stay scarce. The work matters where gene data are precious and every sample counts.
pmc-13418520:
Roberto C French and co-authors capture brain activity and connectivity together while people watch a social film, in a 2026 neuroscience study. Viewers judged awkwardness, a cue to detecting social blunders and reading minds. Earlier work usually measured local activity or connections separately, and rarely tracked their change over time during natural scenes.

Sensorimotor activity rose with awkwardness ratings, while default network activity fell. Dynamic connections, especially involving the frontoparietal control network, explained extra variation beyond activity alone. Social judgement thus draws on both local firing and shifting network teamwork, the authors conclude, and methods should track both at once.
pmc-13419020:
Ashwag Al Dhuhaibat and colleagues review what is known about the money side of medical scribes in United States outpatient clinics. Scribes take over note writing so doctors can spend more time with patients, yet reports on cost and output gains have been mixed. The team searched nine databases for work from January 2010 to September 2024 on scribe effects in clinic care.

Screening 1,945 records left 20 studies that fit the review, spanning before-and-after designs, cohort work, two randomized trials, and simulations. Only 13 of the 20 studies tried a return-on-investment count, and just 6 of those counted full costs like pay, training, and staff turnover. Gains in doctor output appeared often, but uneven study designs limit firm claims. Clinic managers get a clear map of what the proof does and does not show.
pmc-13419220:
Ayse Bilicioglu Gunes and Serife Zeybekoglu Yesil probe how missing answers and drifting question difficulty distort the matching of scores across test forms. Large testing programs use several forms of the same test, and scores must mean the same thing on each. Their computer simulation built the setting of two unequal groups linked by shared anchor questions.

Each run placed 2,000 test takers on a form, with 500 repeats for each of 25 condition mixes. The mixes varied how many answers went missing, why they went missing, and how far question difficulty drifted. A standard linking method then tried to recover fair score matches under each mix. The results show which mixes testing programs can shrug off and which ones bend scores enough to matter.
pmc-13419320:
Elizabeth Sanseau and colleagues argue that medical simulation should be treated as an implementation strategy, not just as a teaching tool. Simulation already trains clinicians and probes hospitals for hidden safety flaws before new units open. Implementation science, the field that studies how good practices spread, has its own models that simulation rarely uses.

Framing practice runs as change tools could help hospitals roll out new care routines with fewer surprises. The piece gives simulation leaders and change specialists a shared language for joint projects.
pmc-13421320:
Shir Maimon and colleagues recorded place cells in 2026 from bats flying tunnels up to 200 meters long. pmc-13421920:
Kadriyan and colleagues examined in 2026 whether handwash stations in health education institutions help students follow World Health Organization handwashing models. Knowledge alone often fails to change behavior, so they also watched the facilities themselves.

Awareness by itself did not predict how often students used the stations. Station use, however, was strongly tied to actual compliance with the hygiene rules the team measured during the same survey period across the institution's teaching sites. Observers judged the main washing infrastructure sufficient but found the supporting facilities, such as supplies around the sinks, substandard.
pmc-13422120: Correction: Saygin and colleagues correct their 2017 paper on CD55, a surface protein marking self-renewing, drug-resistant cells in endometrioid tumors of the ovary and uterus. Two figure errors are fixed. In one panel, a blot image for a related protein was copied from the wrong film; in another, a control blot was accidentally duplicated from a different figure. The notice shows the original and corrected figures and states that conclusions and legends are unchanged. Corrected versions now appear online; the errors survive only in print and older downloads.
pmc-13424320:

Because embryonic versions of these cells are classic feeders for growing skin grafts, the team tested the state directly: low-collagen cells boosted epidermal stem cell self-renewal. The findings inform expansion protocols and graft production.
pmc-13424420:
Yoshihiro Kishida and eleven colleagues compare scope-only removal with full surgery for early colorectal cancers carrying high-risk features. Their patients were aged eighty or more. Records from 2008 to 2021 covered fifty-nine patients, twenty-three treated by endoscopy alone and thirty-six by surgery.

Tumour features and complication rates were similar in the two groups, near 7–8%, with one surgery-related death. Over roughly five years of follow-up, no cancer recurred and no patient died of the disease in either group. Five-year survival reached 90% after endoscopy and 81% after surgery, a non-significant gap. Poor nutrition scores marked the patients at risk, especially in the scope-only group.
pmc-13424520:
Gil Genuth, Peter Stavrou, and Lukas D Iselin compare heel tendon surgery with and without a bioinductive collagen scaffold. The scaffold is a patch meant to coax healing. It was tested for insertional Achilles tendinopathy with Haglund deformity. Their retrospective study covers thirty consecutive patients treated by one surgeon between 2021 and 2024, fifteen with the scaffold added to the standard repair and fifteen without.

Patients reported function and pain scores before surgery and at six, twelve, and eighteen months, and MRI scans were taken at the start and at one year. Return-to-sport timing and complications were also recorded. Meaningful change thresholds were set in advance for the scores: five to eight points for function, eight to ten for pain interference. The comparison can therefore judge whether the patch earns its cost.
pmc-13424620:

The package includes spike times, average waveforms, patient details, and electrode positions in a standard format, plus quality metrics and demonstrations that single neurons tune to film features. Decoding analyses even predict scenes from population activity. The authors offer the set as ready-made ground for machine learning.
pmc-13424820:
Laaraj and colleagues measured in 2026 how place and ripeness change the fruit of the carob tree, a drought-tolerant Mediterranean species valued for food and health products. A summary analysis captured about eighty-four percent of all variation and grouped samples clearly by stage and site. The findings help growers pick harvest timing and origin for food, drug, and supplement uses.
pmc-13424920:

The app, built on World Health Organization guidance, advised on drug dose changes, lifestyle counseling, and when to consult a physician.

Thirty-two patients were followed monthly for six months. The workers' prescribing matched the supervising doctors' judgment in almost ninety-nine of a hundred cases. Top-number blood pressure fell by about seven and a half points on average, and control rates rose. Eleven app errors occurred across more than two hundred visits, none harming a patient. The authors call the model ready for larger trials.
pmc-13425620:

The focus is the first assessment tier, the screening level used before deeper studies. A formal protocol, though not required, was judged worthwhile given the task's complexity.
pmc-13426020:
Theurich and colleagues published a 2026 study on when Brent geese leave for their breeding grounds. These geese stage each spring in the Wadden Sea before flying north. Leaving on the right wind can save energy and boost breeding success. The team tracked 43 tagged geese across seven spring seasons.

Damp air, by contrast, held birds back from leaving the staging site. Early in the season, geese picked their winds with great care. By early June, urgency grew and birds left on poorer winds. Weather records were matched hour by hour to each bird's position.
pmc-13426120:
Hu and colleagues tested in 2026 a metaverse rehab platform built for people who have survived colorectal cancer. Cancer survivors and family members at a partner hospital used the platform, then rated it with two standard usability surveys and took part in structured interviews.

The overall usability score was 65, which sits near the middle range for such tools, and survey scores did not differ by sex, age, or schooling. Learnability, how easy the system is to pick up, scored lowest, while the quality of interaction scored highest. Interviewees liked the rich content and ease of access but said the controls still felt awkward to run.
pmc-13426320:

Some past work tied these compounds to higher breast cancer risk. The team ran a careful case-control study across several centers in Iran.

The study compared 44 patients with 42 healthy controls of like age. Diet intake of the compounds matched between the two groups overall. Blood and tissue levels of the compounds also showed no real gap. Patients did report far less physical activity than the control group. The authors say their null result argues against a diet-compound link here. Larger studies that follow women over time could still revisit the question.
pmc-13426720:

After temporary external fixation, surgeons used a W-shaped double plate at the front, shaped to the bone. It allowed long screws to grip deep into the front column of the pelvis.

Back screws through the skin into the sacroiliac joint completed the repair. The patient bore full weight at two weeks, earlier than advised, and could squat fully without pain by four weeks. At twelve months, X-rays showed stable alignment with no implant failure and no re-widening of the joint. Bone bridging was incomplete, yet function was excellent. The authors argue reinforced double plating suits very unstable front pelvic injuries.
pmc-13426920:
Cardaras and colleagues published a 2026 study on software that reads bar charts in papers. Bar charts hold key trial results, yet their data sit locked in pictures. Review teams copying numbers by hand waste hours and risk slips. The team built a four-step pipeline that pulls numbers out automatically.

The pipeline sorts chart parts, reads labels, and rebuilds values from the axes. On 28 charts from eye-disease trials, it spotted most chart types correctly. About four in five rebuilt values landed within five percent of hand-checked truth. Most errors traced to misread digits or fuzzy bar edges in scans. The proof-of-concept tool could speed up large evidence reviews greatly. Hand checks used a semi-automated labeling tool as reference standard.
pmc-13427220:
Li and colleagues report a light-driven method that chops lignin and upgrades the pieces in a single pot. Lignin is the tough polymer binding plant cell walls. Together they steer the chemistry toward cross-coupling, instead of the unwanted self-coupling of identical fragments. pmc-13427320:
Navez and co-authors reviewed whether adding stem cells or their secreted vesicles to machine-perfused donor kidneys, organs kept alive on pumps before transplant, can repair preservation damage and improve graft outcomes. Following standard review guidelines, they searched three databases for experiments in animal or discarded human kidneys.

The pooled analysis, however, found no significant benefit for creatinine clearance, urine output, or NGAL levels across studies. pmc-13427420:
Kurt Stange and seven co-authors track gaps in toddler shots in a 2026 study. Shot rates fell in the COVID-19 years and have not fully bounced back. Low rates can let curbed childhood ills flare anew, a risk that falls first on poor towns.

The team read health files from 213 town clinics in ten states that serve low-income families. They counted how many children were up to date at two years of age, from 2019 to 2024. Rates were split by child traits and by whether well-child visits took place. The gaps map where catch-up work should aim.
pmc-13427620:
Setoguchi and Hennessy mapped in 2026 the two-way relationship between climate change and medications. In one direction, extreme heat, storms, and broken supply chains threaten drug stability, access, and safety, from mail-order insulin spoiling in heat to an IV fluid shortage after a hurricane. In the other, making, using, and discarding medicines adds to health care's carbon output, feeding the warming that creates those threats.

The authors note that equally effective drug options can differ widely in carbon cost, so cutting needless prescribing and choosing lower-carbon equivalents are levers clinicians and pharmacists already hold. Warnings about heat and drugs still rest largely on mechanism and case reports. The authors call for studies linking weather exposure data to drug outcomes, with confounding by illness and multiple medicines as the central hurdles. Where greener choices already match guidelines, they urge action now, backed by formulary and guideline reform.
pmc-13428120:
Oriana Awwad and colleagues checked whether an Arabic version of a 23-question heart failure survey measures quality of life soundly in Arabic-speaking patients. The Kansas City questionnaire asks about symptoms, daily limits, and social life in people whose hearts pump weakly.

The study enrolled 331 patients at two centres in Jordan and tested the survey's consistency, stability over time, and structure. Scores held together very well, with a consistency measure of 0.937 on a scale where one is perfect, and repeat answers stayed steady. Patients who were married, active, and faithful to their medication reported better quality of life. Awwad concludes the Arabic survey is fit for clinic and research use across the region.
pmc-13429120:
Manting Hao and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, tiny probes that both image rheumatoid arthritis and treat it in the same package. Such theranostic particles home to inflamed joints, light up disease activity on scans, release therapy on cue, and report back on the response. Rheumatoid arthritis varies a lot between patients, which makes that feedback loop attractive. The review follows the field from joint targeting through imaging to drug delivery and monitoring.

Therapies riding these particles include anti-inflammatory drugs, immune modulators, and light-based treatments. The authors draw a line between truly integrated systems and simple carriers with a dye attached. Translation to patients lags far behind animal work. Safety over time, body distribution, repeat dosing, factory consistency, and regulatory paths all remain open problems, and the review names them without flinching.
pmc-13429220:
Leo Lui and co-authors test, in a 2026 Hong Kong study, a one-step cleaning product for surfaces around patients carrying a resistant staph germ. MRSA spreads partly through bedside surfaces that staff touch all day. Over six months in medical, surgical, and bone wards, each patient's surroundings were split in half. One half got the classic two-step clean, detergent then bleach solution, while the other half got a combined detergent-disinfectant in a single pass.

Both methods cut MRSA detection sharply, from about 69 percent of samples to the low teens. Cleanliness test failures also plunged under both. The one-step method saved about six minutes and about ten wipes per patient. Scaled to public hospitals citywide, the authors project savings above six million Hong Kong dollars a year. Equal cleaning power with less time and waste is the selling point.
pmc-13430820:
Neetha Harisha and co-authors tested in 2026 whether values from dental cone beam scans can flag low bone strength, and how those values line up with heel sound tests and blood markers. Bone thinning raises risks for the skeleton and for dental work. The cross-check study enrolled 86 adults older than forty.

Heel sound scores split the group into normal and low-bone sets. Scan values for both hard outer bone and spongy inner bone ran far higher in the normal set. The two scan measures tracked heel scores closely, and both tracked blood levels of vitamin D as well. Shape-based scan measures fared poorly by contrast. A graded scan index of the jaw cortex moved the other way, as worse grades went with lower heel scores.
pmc-13432020:
Macarena Siri and co-authors probed in 2026 how two fiber types blend to give E. coli biofilms their strength, treating the slimy mat as a tunable layered stuff. Biofilms of this gut germ rest on a shared matrix built from stiff amyloid threads and a changed plant-like fiber, held in water. The stiff threads lend firmness, while the plant-like fiber lends cohesion.

The team grew mats from strains that make both fibers, one fiber, or blends at set ratios. Poking tests, fine scopes, and cold 3D imaging showed mat stiffness tracks both the mix and the layout of the fibers. The plant-like fiber swells, yet stiff threads cage that swell where they touch. The wild strain blends the pair at a tiny scale into a hybrid stuff whose traits beat what each part gives alone. The authors see a route to grown living goods.
pmc-13432820:
Bo Yan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the tiny bubbles that E. coli germs shed from their outer skin, and how those bubbles spread harm, drug proofing, and talks with hosts. The bubbles are balls of skin stuffed with proteins, wall sugars, and gene scraps. Drug-proof and fierce strains of this gut germ pose a rising threat to public health.

The review maps how bubbles form, what they carry, and the jobs they do in illness. Bubbles can ferry drug-proof traits to kin germs and tune how host immune cells react. The authors also weigh fresh uses: bubble-based vaccines, bubble couriers for drug loads, and bubble strikes on tumors. A firm grasp of bubble traits, they argue, can seed new ways to spot, block, and treat infections.
pmc-13433320:
Saman Abbaspoor, Ayman Aljishi, and Kari L Hoffman recorded cell crowds in 2026 in the deep memory hub of free-moving macaques. The monkeys called back item chains from that day, the day before, or weeks past. How fresh learning reshapes old traces without wiping them stays a core puzzle. Sleep replays help firm new traces in many species.

Crowds tuned to old chains drifted less, linked more thickly, and replayed harder in sleep than crowds tuned to fresh chains. Old and mid-age crowds paired into joint teams that held from task to sleep, a tie fresh pairs lacked. In the hub, two cell layers grew more prone to team up as the memory aged. The authors read swift sorting and firming at work.
pmc-13433620:
Maria Laura Diniz Pereira and co-authors tested in 2026 how sour wear on tooth dentin cuts the grip of four filler pastes with tooth-tone mineral traits. One hundred twenty dentin bits from sound human molars split by wear path. Paths ran from a one-day sour soak to a soak plus five more days of wear rounds after the fill. One set took no wear at all. Each set split again by paste thinness and depth style.

Grip tests pulled the fills till they broke, and break kinds faced a scope check. Sour ground and paste kind each moved grip on their own, with no cross play. The long wear path sank grip for every paste against sound ground. Among thin pastes, the deep-fill one gripped harder. The plain thick pastes tied. Wear rounds hurt all bonds, the authors close.
pmc-13433820:
Altalib, Li, and Perelli present a diffusion model that upgrades low-quality radiotherapy scans in this 2026 study. Cone-beam CT guides daily treatment cheaply and at low dose, but scatter corrupts its density values, making dose calculations unreliable. Their model, EqDiff-CT, learns to synthesize standard CT images from cone-beam ones for head and neck patients, using a denoising diffusion process constrained to respect rotational symmetry.

The symmetry constraint, built from steerable network layers, helps preserve fine anatomical detail while stripping noise and artifacts, the authors report. The model was trained and validated on the multi-site SynthRAD2025 dataset. It beat advanced rivals, including CycleGAN and a plain diffusion model. It won on structural fidelity, density accuracy, and quantitative scores. Images showed sharper soft tissue boundaries and more realistic bone, supporting more confident adaptive treatment planning.
pmc-13434420:
Jianping Xu and colleagues build a self running microbe system in 2026 that eats wood waste chemicals. Lignin leftovers are rich in useful ring compounds, yet they poison microbes and jam their inner pathways. The team hardened a workhorse germ and gave it smart gene switches.

Breeding for toughness plus layered controls let the germ sense each feed and adjust on its own. Nearly all feed became one target acid, at a load of 53.40 grams per liter. Two more valued acids were made at high loads from the same stream. The design offers a template for green plants that run with little oversight.
pmc-13434820:
Anran Li and a large team audit how much medical text large language models memorize in 2026. Models tuned on health data may recite training text later, for good or ill. Three tuning routes were tested, including work with more than 13,000 real hospital records.

Memorization runs higher in medicine than in general text. Much of what is learned early sticks through later tuning, up to 87 percent in one check. Recall splits into helpful, dull, and harmful kinds. Harmful recall can leak private patient facts. The authors give steps to keep the helpful kind while cutting risk. Hospitals should test models before use.
pmc-13435120:
Anne Schwarz-Pfeiffer's team reviewed liquid crystal elastomer filaments in 2026, materials that join ordered liquid crystal parts with rubber stretch to give large, reversible motion. Such filaments could serve soft robots, smart cloth, artificial muscle, and adaptive structures, yet moving from lab films to steady, factory-scale threads has been held back by scattered, non-standard methods. The review joins chemistry, flow, alignment, and curing into one path from mix to filament.

Benchmark mixes based on common mesogens and crosslinkers are walked through, with viscosity bands tied to spinning, drawing, and curing choices. Nozzle design, draw ratios, inline curing, and annealing are covered as levers for strength and lasting motion. Engineers get a practical map plus a call for shared measures and greener chemistry.
pmc-13435820:
Ou and Gong use layered gene data to trace how SN-011 protects the brain in ischemic stroke, where a clot cuts blood flow. SN-011 blocks an immune alarm protein. Their 2026 study starts from stroke gene datasets and genetic causal tests. It adds single cell maps of brain vessel cells and cell talk analysis. Lab checks use a docking model and a binding assay in oxygen starved endothelial cells, the cells lining vessels.

The search converged on ADGRE5, a gene that genetic tests mark as protective and that falls in vein lining cells as stroke advances. A switch protein, JUNB, holds ADGRE5 down. The drug bound JUNB, lowered it, and let ADGRE5 recover, which restored a laminin signaling route that vessel cells use to talk with immune and support cells. Inflammatory signals dropped. Blocking that route erased the drug's protection, pinning the mechanism.
pmc-13436820:
Samina Khan and coauthors lift biopsy yield for solid masses at their center through a quality drive in 2026. An audit first found definite diagnosis in just seventy five percent of scope guided needle biopsies. The fix set three or more needle passes, fewer slide makers, and formalin for cell blocks.

In 262 later procedures on 241 patients, yield reached eighty one percent overall. Yield split sharply by half year, at seventy two percent early and ninety percent late. Three pass cases rose from twelve percent to forty seven percent. Slide maker limits alone moved nothing. Steady audit plus reinforcement did the heavy lifting.
pmc-13436920:
Ribes Valles and colleagues tested in 2026 whether insomnia tracks with estimated type 2 diabetes risk in a very large worker sample. They studied 84,898 Spanish workers aged eighteen to sixty-nine during occupational health checks, scoring insomnia severity and estimating diabetes risk with three validated questionnaires that need no blood tests.

Severe insomnia came with roughly two to two and a half times the odds of a high estimated diabetes risk, on every one of the three scales. The link grew step by step with insomnia severity and held for men and women and across activity levels, after accounting for age, class, smoking, diet, and exercise. Adding the insomnia score improved risk prediction modestly but measurably. The authors propose that brief sleep questions could sharpen early diabetes prevention in clinics and workplaces.
pmc-13437320:
Siddhartha Singhal and Kakelli Anil Kumar built a security tool to catch address spoofing in networks of connected medical devices. In such attacks, a hacker fakes address records so traffic flows through their machine, risking theft or tampering with life-critical data. Their 2026 study shaped a random forest model, an ensemble of decision trees, with features tracking behavior over time and penalties tuned to the cost of each error.

Missing an attack is far more dangerous in a hospital than raising a false alarm, so the team forced the missed-attack rate under a set safety cap. On a public medical device benchmark, the tool scored near-perfect marks for accuracy and for catching attacks. It missed forty of more than twenty-three thousand attack cases, a rate well inside the safety cap, and raised only twelve false alarms.
pmc-13439020:
Sazgar Ajeeb Mohammed and Dler Hamad Ismael tested whether theory-based teaching could tighten blood sugar control in patients whose eyes diabetes is damaging. Diabetic retinopathy blinds people whose glucose runs high for years, and structured education is scarce. Their 2026 quasi-experimental study enrolled 200 patients at a tertiary diabetes center in Erbil, Iraq. Half received standard care; half took a three-session program shaped by the theory of planned behaviour, targeting attitudes, social norms, and perceived control.

Three months on, the taught group's key blood sugar marker fell by half a percentage point while the control group's rose by about one point. Knowledge gains were stark: over half the taught patients reached the high-knowledge band, against none of the controls. The authors present theory-guided teaching as a low-cost lever for settings short on specialists. The study links a psychological framework to laboratory numbers.
pmc-13439420:
Fernandes and McCormack published in twenty twenty-six a critical reflection on artificial intelligence and person-centred care. Artificial intelligence is entering healthcare quickly and unevenly. The authors use a well-known person-centred practice framework to judge its effects. They draw on literature and structured dialogue between themselves. Artificial intelligence can advance care in some ways, they find. It can also undermine the human side of care if used carelessly.

Opportunities and challenges are identified side by side. Relational ethics and professional judgment need active safeguarding. Core person-centred values should guide how tools enter daily practice. The authors argue for context-sensitive implementation rather than blanket adoption. Technology should fit the care setting, not reshape it blindly. The piece is a reflective essay, not an empirical study.
pmc-13440220:
Hopkins and colleagues reported in 2026 on oral health in fibromyalgia, a long-term condition marked by widespread pain. The team compared 60 women with the condition, all of whom had past allergy patch testing, against 120 matched controls from the general population. They used a survey on oral symptoms and quality of life, plus clinical and X-ray exams of the mouth.

Hopkins found that gum disease was clearly more common in the fibromyalgia group, with the gap largest in younger patients. Mouth lesions were also far more common, at about three in ten patients versus about one in ten controls. Tooth decay levels did not differ between the groups. Younger patients reported the worst oral quality of life. Contact allergy showed no link to the mouth findings, so its role remains an open question.
pmc-13440620:
Rao wrote this 2026 letter about a study by Du and colleagues on hepatocyte growth factor in the eye's drainage tissue. That study asked whether trabecular meshwork stem cells survive a glaucoma-like environment and protect neighboring cells through secreted factors, identifying the growth factor as a mediator. Rao welcomes the work, which used cells from six human donors and a receptor-blocking drug to test causality, but raises methodological cautions for interpretation.

The letter notes that primary meshwork cells change character between culture passages three and five, yet the experiments used cells up to passage six, and asks for passage-matched comparisons. Donor ages spanned 43 to 69 years. Cell numbers and stress tolerance shift across that range. Rao asks whether age was accounted for. She also asks which donor batches served which experiments. The transcriptomic analysis also draws questions as the letter continues.
pmc-13442320:
Ioakeim Sapantzoglou's team pooled gene-chip testing in 2026 for fetal brain fluid buildup, where extra brain fluid raises questions about gene changes. Older tests miss small gene changes that gene chips can catch, but the added yield by case type was unclear. Sixteen watch-only studies with 2,137 fetuses were pooled under strict review rules, split into alone, non-alone, and mild alone cases.

Gene chips added seven percent overall over karyotype, four percent in alone cases, ten percent in non-alone cases, and two percent in mild alone cases. Prenatal teams get numbers for advice: gene chips add most when other anomalies accompany brain fluid buildup, least in mild alone cases. Single care decisions still need care context.
pmc-13442520:
Shota Enomoto and Kohta Ito model how twist in the Achilles tendon steers force in a 2026 study. The tendon, the largest in the body, joins three calf heads through strands that wind around each other. Computer models with no twist, mild twist, and strong twist took a simple pull at the top end.

Twisted models sent part of the pull sideways and forward at the foot end, a split the straight model never showed. Side force reached about 101 N and front force about 63 N in the twisted runs. Strands also passed force to each other, and that sharing grew as twist grew. The pair reads the twist as a gear that turns one-way muscle pull into three-way force. Such spread may shape how the ankle and foot bear load with each step.
pmc-13442820:
Akilan Krishnamurthy and colleagues probe how a TNF blocker guards bone in rheumatoid arthritis in a 2026 study. Joint lining bits came from 12 patients before drug care and eight weeks after adalimumab began. Lab work then tested the drug on bone cells and on cells that eat bone.

Joint scores fell hard, with a median mark drop from 5.4 points to 3.1 points after drug care. Lining scans showed fewer CD163 macrophages, while T-cell counts held steady. A bone-eat signal, RANKL, fell next to its guard, OPG, so their ratio dropped. Dish tests echoed the shift in bone-forming cells dosed with the drug. In growth assays, the drug slowed the birth of bone-eating cells. The authors tie bone gains to calmer signals plus direct cell effects.
pmc-13443420:
Shin and colleagues report how deucravacitinib, a pill that blocks an enzyme called TYK2, performs for plaque psoriasis in everyday Korean care, not trials. Trials had shown the drug works, but routine practice data were scarce. Their 2026 study follows 42 adults at three hospitals. It scores skin severity at the start, at four to six months, and past ten months. Side effects and time on the drug are logged too.

Severity scores fell steeply. The index dropped by about two thirds within six months, and further by the later check. At ten to twelve months, nine in ten patients still followed had cut their score by at least three quarters. Seven in ten had cut it by nine tenths. A third reported side effects, mostly skin, mouth, or infection issues, and three stopped the drug. Nearly three quarters stayed on treatment at last follow up.
pmc-13444320:
Junhwa Seong and colleagues coat one lens skeleton to serve both ultraviolet and visible light in a 2026 paper. Flat metalenses steer light at nano scale, yet one build rarely spans both bands well. Their silica frame stays fixed while nanometer oxide coats tune its optics.

A low-heat bake at 80 degrees sets titanium oxide for visible work, while zirconium oxide stays glassy for UV clarity. The coats split light modes by direction, which yields mean efficiency marks of 69 percent in the UV band and 75 percent in the visible band. Focus stayed sharp across both bands in their rigs. A pocket UV camera showed sunscreen maps and hidden marks, while a twin build served as a color VR eyepiece.
pmc-13445720:
Gene data tools lean on hash functions, which scramble text into short codes, yet no full survey of those functions existed for gene work. Ke Chen and co-authors fill that gap in work from twenty twenty-six, aimed at people who build gene software. Their survey sorts hash functions into four groups.

One group spreads codes widely, one shuffles inputs, one packs codes with no waste, and one keeps like inputs near each other. For each group the survey gives both broad-use cases and cases built just for gene data. Traits, shared points, and gaps are set side by side. The guide helps builders pick the right scramble for tasks like searching and counting gene reads.
pmc-13446120:
Min Sheng and eight co-authors trace a cucumber mutant's yellow, dying seedlings to a broken transcription factor, in this 2026 study. The mutant, found through map based cloning, carries a jumping gene insertion in the gene for a factor called NF-YB3. Without it, seedlings make far less chlorophyll and photosynthesize weakly, and their chloroplasts grow stunted with underbuilt internal membranes.

Deleting the gene with CRISPR editing reproduced the defect, confirming the culprit. The factor partners with a sister subunit and switches on a gene for importing proteins into chloroplasts. It is most active in young tissues and rises with light. Genome wide expression in the mutant showed photosynthesis genes broadly turned down. The authors establish the factor as a core requirement for building chloroplasts in cucumber.
pmc-13446220:
Guerrero Serrano and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether faults in DNA damage response pathways can guide treatment of urothelial carcinoma, a common and aggressive bladder cancer. These pathways repair broken DNA, and tumors with faults in them may react better to some drugs. Three first-line treatments exist for advanced disease, but no proven blood or tissue test helps doctors choose between them.

The review sums up how often such gene faults occur and what studies link them to benefit from platinum chemotherapy, immune checkpoint drugs, and PARP blockers, which jam a backup repair route. Early data hint at better outcomes for patients with these faults. Studies define the faults in unlike ways and rarely include the comparison groups needed to prove a test predicts benefit. The authors call for shared definitions and forward-looking trials before these markers enter routine care.
pmc-13446320:
Carlos Eduardo Santa Ritta Barreira and colleagues issue a consensus guide for emergency windpipe opening in head and neck cancer, written for the Brazilian Society of Surgical Oncology, published in 2026. Tumors in the mouth, throat, or voice box can close the airway without warning, a crisis that can kill in minutes. Standard tracheostomy guides speak to intensive care, not cancer wards.

The guide joins clinic signs, scope findings, and setting limits into a decision path. Spotting the early window of chance, before full block sets in, is cast as the key move that averts disaster. Awake surgery under local numbing is the favored route for high-risk patients. Plans should also guard the cancer treatment that follows, so the rescue does not spoil the cure.
pmc-13447120:
Tien-Wei Hsu, Chia-Kuang Tsai and Chih-Sung Liang reply in 2026 to a comment on their study comparing two drug groups for tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder linked to some medicines. Critics had questioned how the start of follow-up, called time zero, was set. Fair comparison depends on both groups starting at a similar point in care.

The authors explain that diagnosis and treatment both had to fall in the same recent period, from early 2019 to mid 2025. That window ensured both approved drugs in one group were in routine use. They also reran the work requiring treatment to start after diagnosis. Sample size barely changed, and the risk estimates stayed much the same, which they offer as reassurance about the original design.
pmc-13447220:
Weixing Zou, Lingping Xie and Guoyan Liu study self-injury without suicidal intent among Chinese senior high school students in 2026 work from Guizhou. Acting on impulse and having been left behind by migrant parents are each linked to such behaviour. How the two combine, and whether self-control sits between them, was the focus.

Questionnaires from five hundred thirty-four students, with an average age near seventeen, measured impulsivity, self-control and self-injury. Impulsivity linked to more self-injury, and weaker self-control carried much of that link. The pattern split by background in a striking way. For left-behind students the path through self-control mattered, while for others a direct link dominated. Because the model explained only a modest share overall, the authors present one pathway among several and suggest tailored school support.
pmc-13447820:
Aman Nanda and colleagues design lead-free piezoelectric ceramics through human and artificial intelligence teamwork in 2026 work. Such ceramics convert pressure to charge for sensors and harvesters, yet the lead-based standard is toxic and replacements need complex multi-element doping found by slow trial and error. Language models mined prior literature for hidden structure and property knowledge to propose fresh compositions.

Expert judgement steered which proposals were actually made and tested in the lab. A random starting composition already performed well, and aligning crystal grains plus sintering tweaks pushed performance far higher. The tuned ceramic held steady coupling up to high temperatures despite an off-peak design. A vibrating cantilever harvester built from it beat reported lead-free rivals on power density, proving practical relevance.
pmc-13448120:
Viet Nguyen and a large team remodel ring-shaped sulfone molecules to build diverse three-ring and two-ring aromatic scaffolds in 2026 synthetic chemistry work. Linked aromatic rings anchor many drugs, catalysts and materials, yet most known examples are flat and linear because sphere-like versions with both substituents beside the link are hard to make. A library route into that neglected shape space was the goal.

Their ring remodelling uses paired attacking and leaving partners to open and rebuild the sulfone ring with varied attachments, including amines, phenols, ethers and phosphines. Product variety spans single rings pairs and longer chains in a streamlined sequence. A simple machine learning classifier, newly applied to this problem, predicts which orientation complex products will take. The combined experimental and data approach aims to correct a structural bias in medicinal chemistry collections.
pmc-13448220:
Asad Malook and colleagues present a 2026 low-cost vision system that lets workers control industrial motors with hand gestures in resource-limited factories. A lightweight MobileNetV2 network, tuned by transfer learning, recognizes a binary gesture set on an edge device, sending wireless commands to an Arduino controller driving a variable frequency drive.

Tests showed stable classification with low latency and memory fit for cheap hardware, plus consistent real-time response and safe behavior on a working industrial motor. Small manufacturers gain an affordable path to intelligent interfaces without expensive automation platforms, the authors argue.
pmc-13449320:
Samira Arami led a 2026 study asking whether a simple blood ratio can warn doctors about risk in chronic heart failure. The ratio pairs hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, with the spread in red cell sizes, a measure known as red cell distribution width. Earlier work had linked this combined marker to outcomes in other diseases, but its value in long-term heart failure was still unclear.

The researchers followed 419 patients and checked death and return to hospital over twelve months. A lower ratio went with higher odds of dying, and each unit rise in the ratio went with about a one-sixth fall in mortality odds. The link held for patients with anemia but not for those without it. Rehospitalization showed a different pattern, so the ratio looks most useful as a warning sign for mortality rather than for readmission.
pmc-13449520:
Shurui Wang and colleagues measured frailty among older women with breast cancer in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Frailty means reduced reserve to cope with illness and treatment, and it can shape outcomes, yet its frequency in this group was not well described. The team recruited women aged sixty-five and older from a tertiary cancer hospital.

Among 227 participants, 138 were classed as frail by the Fried phenotype, a standard set of physical signs. Frailty varied with age, job, number of daily drugs, fall history, sleep quality, self-rated health, tumor stage, radiotherapy history, and other illnesses. The high share found argues for routine frailty checks so care plans can be adjusted before treatment strain mounts.
pmc-13450020:
Kunning Wang and colleagues reported a 2026 case of a rare eye syndrome appearing years after lens implantation. Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome affects one eye, starts subtly, and is easy to miss, and reports after implantable collamer lens surgery are exceedingly rare. The case adds a long-term warning for a popular vision-correction procedure.

A nineteen-year-old woman with high myopia received toric implantable lenses in both eyes in 2021. Her right eye showed localized adhesions and slight pupil displacement before surgery, but the cornea was clear and cell counts were normal. Follow-up stayed unremarkable until blurred vision four and a half years later revealed corneal swelling and iris changes typical of the syndrome. Eye surgeons gain a reason to watch implanted eyes closely for years, not just months.
pmc-13450420:
Falge and colleagues reported a one-step route in 2026 to hexafluorophosphate salts, chemicals widely used in batteries and synthesis, made straight from white phosphorus and simple fluoride salts. The usual paths to these salts are harsh or indirect. Adding quinone oxidants, ring-shaped molecules that take up electrons, opened a clean and selective route.

In acetonitrile solvent the method gave the salts in yields up to 95 percent. Nuclear magnetic resonance tests, which track atoms by their magnetic signals, revealed PF3 and a PF5-solvent pair as key steps along the way. The quinone binds fluoride in a donor-acceptor pair, which raises the amount of free fluoride and drives the reaction forward. Changing the solvent changed the product: a glycol stopped the reaction at a PF5 adduct, while dichloromethane favored PF3. The work shows quinone-fluoride pairing as a new tool for fluorine chemistry.
pmc-13450520:
Dor Shwartz and a large team report in 2026 the first known find of a tick-borne fever germ in cattle in Israel. The germ, Borrelia theileri, spreads through ticks and was long known to cause only mild illness in herds. Blood came from beef and dairy cattle at 23 sites across the country.

Gene tests found the germ in six of 439 blood draws, split between beef and dairy herds. Its gene pattern sat close to samples taken from local ticks, which points to a live cycle between ticks and cattle. A few cattle also carried other tick germs, and the authors warn that mixed infections could add to herd losses.
pmc-13451920:
Anahita Hejazi and co-authors test in 2026 two drugs in rats shaped before birth toward autism-like traits. The model uses a dose of valproic acid during pregnancy, a setup tied to brain swelling and cell rust. One drug fights cell rust, the other calms swelling, and the team gave each alone and as a pair.

All treated groups showed better social play, sharper memory, and lower anxiety than untreated model rats. Swelling signals and a rust mark fell, while two guard enzymes rose back toward normal. The pair, though, beat neither single drug. The authors read that ceiling as a hint that one path, hit well, may be enough in this model.
pmc-13452220:
Hilde Stevens and co-authors argue in 2026 that Europe's orphan drug rules need deeper change than the reform bills now on the table. A small slice of rare diseases draws most funds, while most go unstudied and patients wait. New bills trim market solo rights to spur work and cut prices.

The authors grant the bills point the right way yet call them too weak alone. They add planks from a known growth report: a joint health scoring office, a bold research agency on the United States model, and wider test sandboxes. Two more tools follow: joint public-private funds to de-risk high-need work, and joint buying to cut prices and steady demand.
pmc-13452320:
Kevin Lord, Lucas Haase, and Michael Wiater report in 2026 a rare harm after a reverse shoulder swap: a plastic liner broke free and wandered into the armpit. Liner pop-out is known in under one percent of these swaps, blamed on the liner rim striking bone as the arm drops. Open repair is the usual fix.

In this case the loose liner cut a branch of the armpit artery. The bleed pooled, sparked a deep vein clot, and pressed the arm's nerve bundle, a chain the authors say has not been told before. Their patient was a man aged 70 whose swap dated back two years. The case urges fast action once a liner slips.
pmc-13452420:
Hong and colleagues combined in 2026 a network meta-analysis of apple storage treatments with their own storage experiments. Forty-eight preservation methods were compared across past studies for their effects on fruit quality. Two stood out: methyl jasmonate, a plant signal spray, and pullulan, a natural coating polysaccharide, each lifting several quality measures at once.

Hong then tested the pair together on stored apples. The combined treatment cut weight loss sharply and slowed enzymatic browning, the brown discolouring that ruins cut and stored fruit. Sugar, acid, vitamin C, and healthy phenolic levels held up better than in untreated fruit. Antioxidant defence enzymes worked harder, while peroxide and other damage markers built up less. Breathing rate and ripening gas release both slowed. The authors offer the paired scheme as a practical reference for apple storage.
pmc-13452820:
Paula Reyes-Pérez and a large team map two versions of a gene region tied to Parkinson disease across many ancestries. The region holds MAPT, a gene for the tau protein, and comes in two broad forms called H1 and H2. Their 2026 study covers 20,507 patients and 11,841 controls from eleven ancestry groups, drawn from two global genetics programs.

The H1 form backed a higher Parkinson risk in people of European ancestry, with hints of the same link in other groups. pmc-13455520:

pmc-13456820:

pmc-13457020:

pmc-13457220:

pmc-13458620:

pmc-13458920:

pmc-13460520:

pmc-13463220:

pmc-13471520:

pmc-13471620:

pmc-13473020:

pmc-13473120:

pmc-13473920:

pmc-13474320:

pmc-13474520:

pmc-13474720:

Feruzjon Bobosharipov and co-authors present a case report the catalog lists under 2026. A seventy-one-year-old man with chronic constipation gave himself a cleansing enema at home. pmc-13476320:

pmc-13476720:

pmc-13476920:

pmc-13477320:

pmc-13477720:

The authors call for subsidized rehabilitation and support, especially for rural families.
pmc-13478020:

pmc-13478320:

pmc-13478420:

pmc-13479420:

pmc-13479820:

The authors stress team care and close monitoring.
pmc-13480520:

pmc-13490420:

pmc-13491820:

pmc-13492020:

pmc-13492220:

pmc-13494620:

pmc-13495220:

pmc-13495420:

pmc-13495520:
