The phone service links primary care doctors with hospital and community help for complex patients. The team interviewed twenty primary care doctors, three internists, and six project staff over video calls.

Seven themes shaped use. Doctors weighed a health system they saw as broken, plain awareness that the line existed, and whether its services matched their needs. A tool that felt useful and easy won a first try; habit and the effort of change then decided whether use stuck. Feeling heard by the service kept doctors coming back. The authors say such lines help only when doctors feel backed, grasp the gains, and get time to learn the new way of working.
pmc-13499920:
Divya Deodhar and colleagues compare in 2026 bloodstream infections caused by Candida auris, a hardy drug-resistant yeast, with infections from other Candida species at a university hospital in Muscat, Oman. Yeast in the blood is life-threatening and increasingly healthcare-linked. Their retrospective review covered all adults with such infections over five years, from January 2018 to December 2022, comparing risk links, outcomes, and drug susceptibility between groups.

Of 160 patients, 58 carried the resistant species while 102 carried other Candida types. Prior colonisation with Candida species was the strongest link to the resistant infection, raising odds several-fold in the reported ratios, and recent healthcare contact within ninety days also linked strongly. The authors suggest one drug family, echinocandins, as an early empirical choice when these warning links are present, while local susceptibility patterns are confirmed.
pmc-13500420:
Abigail Hui En Chan and colleagues assess in 2026 drug resistance in a gut worm of livestock that can also infect people, sampled in Thailand. Benzimidazole dewormers are heavily used, and resistant worms had been found at high levels locally. Working with 60 adult Trichostrongylus colubriformis worms from Sukhothai and Satun provinces, the team read resistance directly from a tubulin gene, a standard marker. A mitochondrial gene mapped diversity and population structure.

Strong resistance was present, with the mixed genotype carrying one resistant and one sensitive copy forming most worms. Genetic diversity ran high, while Thai worms differed sharply from those in other countries, hinting at limited gene flow across borders. That isolation cuts both ways, since local control measures could likely contain resistance spread, provided watching of this zoonotic worm continues.
pmc-13500720:
Zhiheng Tai and four co-authors report a 2026 study of a titanium composite made by laser directed energy deposition, a form of metal 3D printing. They built samples from the alloy Ti6Al4V, which is strong and light but wears poorly, and tried to grow hard titanium nitride particles inside it during printing. One route deposited the metal under a nitrogen-argon mix, while a second route remelted the surface under pure nitrogen. Dry sliding wear tests ran at room temperature and at 300 degrees Celsius.

The remelted samples grew larger, more densely spread nitride particles. Their friction was somewhat higher, yet wear volume fell by about 44.8 percent at room temperature and 78.8 percent at the higher temperature compared with the plain alloy. The directly deposited samples, with sparser and smaller particles, improved much less.
pmc-13500820:
Lilla Otrokocsi leads a five-author team with a 2026 mouse study of whether vaccines given in pregnancy affect how the offspring act. Pregnant mice received the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2, a flu vaccine, or a control, and pups were tested at four and eight weeks of age. Blood and fetal brain tissue were checked for immune markers: cytokines, the P2X7 receptor, BDNF, and fat oxidation damage. A comparison group received poly(I:C), which mimics viral infection.

The COVID vaccine raised two maternal cytokines modestly without inflaming the fetal brain. Some mild, age- and sex-linked changes in how pups acted appeared, but no consistent autism-like pattern emerged at either age. The flu vaccine caused smaller, passing effects, while poly(I:C) triggered strong inflammation and lasting changes. The authors conclude that prenatal COVID vaccination showed no widespread harm to brain development in this model.
pmc-13501620:
Derya Demirtaş Esmer leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 study of whether low muscle mass blunts chemotherapy response in advanced ovarian cancer. The retrospective study covered 52 overweight or obese women with stage III to IV epithelial ovarian cancer treated between 2019 and 2022 with platinum and taxane chemotherapy before interval surgery. Muscle mass was measured on baseline CT scans at the third lumbar vertebra. Women were split into low and high muscle mass groups at the cohort median, and those combining obesity with low muscle were flagged.

That combined group responded worst: response rates were 46.7 percent against 62.2 percent for the others, and disease control rates were 80 percent against 100 percent. Body mass index alone and low muscle mass alone showed no significant effect. Median disease-free survival after surgery was 19.3 months. The authors propose muscle assessment as a risk marker, while noting overall survival data were immature.
pmc-13501720:
Mais Musleh, Mahmoud Alhamadeh Alswij, and Khaled Omar ALdosh untangle a heart valve growth that looked infectious but was cancer-driven, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. Leukemia can mimic heart valve infection through sterile clot vegetations, a paraneoplastic syndrome. To treat the wrong diagnosis is to waste time that counts.

Their eighty-two-year-old patient arrived with fever, fatigue, and confusion. Scans of the heart showed mitral valve vegetations that pointed to infection. Yet blood cultures, run more than once, stayed negative. And the markers of inflammation were just mildly raised in her blood. Her blood counts were grossly abnormal on the tests. A smear and flow cytometry confirmed acute myeloid leukemia in the end. The vegetations were thrombotic in kind, not infected at all. The case teaches skepticism when cultures stay silent in a deteriorating elder.
pmc-13501820:
Ming Zhou leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of whether the choice of anti-seizure drug changes survival in low-grade glioma, where epilepsy strikes most patients. The team combined lenses: machine learning over 105 targets of ten anti-seizure drugs, molecular docking, a past-records patient cohort, and cell experiments. A thirteen-gene signature predicted prognosis. One sodium channel gene, SCN9A, emerged as a hazard factor, while two glutamate receptor genes, GRIN2C and GRIN3A, acted as protectors.

Three drugs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and lacosamide, were predicted to extend survival by blocking the hazard gene's product. Phenobarbital pointed the other way, shortening survival by suppressing the two protective genes. The cohort check supported those directions, and bench tests agreed: blocking SCN9A curbed malignant cell behaviour, while suppressing the protective pair enhanced it. The authors offer the work as guidance for drug choice.
pmc-13502820:
Longping Chen and others compare two traction methods for hard bile duct cannulation when a periampullary diverticulum distorts anatomy. In 2026, the single-center look-back study covers 193 patients undergoing endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, with propensity matching producing sixty patients per group: clip-assisted versus clip plus rubber band-assisted cannulation.

Success reached 96.7 percent with clip plus rubber band versus 73.3 percent with clip alone, in about half the time, with far fewer rescue methods such as double-guidewire or transpancreatic sphincterotomy. Adverse events were comparable and all resolved conservatively, with no serious events. The merged method offers a safe, faster route through distorted papillary anatomy.
pmc-13503720:
A full genome map for the blacktip trevally fish is built by Mudagandur S. Shekhar and co-authors in work dated 2026. The fish is a salt-tolerant food fish with farm promise, but gene data for it were scarce. The team read its DNA with long-read, short-read, and shape-capture tools at deep cover. They also read full gene messages from seven tissues.

The map spans a large genome in few pieces, with most of it laid on twenty-four chromosome-level frames. It holds more than thirty thousand genes that code for proteins. The maps should aid farm breeding, food value studies, and work on how the fish adapts and how it evolved.
pmc-13503820:
Xiaoyu Xue leads a team showing how a genome-guard complex tags proteins with SUMO, a small modifier, in a 2026 study. Most tagging enzymes work alone, but the Nse2 enzyme only works as part of the larger Smc5/6 complex. How the other parts of the complex help was unclear.

Tests in yeast showed that DNA boosts the complex's tagging action by pulling enzyme and target close. Four partner parts use their grip on DNA to support that boost. Parts that bind ATP, the cell fuel, help the complex latch onto DNA and change shape for the task. The findings frame Smc5/6 as a joint tagging machine switched on by DNA and fuel together.
pmc-13503920:
Alejandro Santos-Mayo leads a team that built an AI model which predicts brain wave responses to words and pictures, in a 2026 paper. Brain waves read from the scalp, called EEG, show how the brain reacts to meaning and feeling. Most AI work decodes those waves; far less work runs the other way.

Their model, Concept2Brain, turns a picture or text into a rich trait vector with a public vision-language tool, then maps that vector into a brain wave space. The fake responses it makes closely match real ones recorded from people. The model is offered as a free web service, so labs can build open EEG data sets for any concept or image. The authors see it as a step toward modeling brain activity with AI.
pmc-13504220:
An 88-year-old woman with back pain turned out to have tuberculosis spread through her whole body, yet standard tests kept missing it. Scans showed destroyed spine segments at T9 and T10 plus the fine nodular lung pattern typical of miliary tuberculosis. At two earlier hospitals, six sputum smears and two blood tests for TB all came back negative. Kabeya and co-authors refused to drop the suspicion.

After admission, three more sputum smears finally confirmed the germ. Their case argues that strong clinical and imaging evidence should outweigh negative first-round tests, and that repeating a simple smear can spare patients invasive procedures.
pmc-13504320:
Xiao-yi Wang and co-authors describe in 2026 a film that shows meat freshness by changing color. The film is built from collagen taken from leather waste, mixed with purple cabbage powder. It is fully biodegradable, unlike many lab tests for freshness that are complex or hard on the environment.

An enzyme linked the film's parts, and a seaweed-based gum gave it extra strength. More cabbage powder made the film weaker and less stretchy, but it also drew water better, so the color shift came faster. The film turned from red to green across a wide acid range. On pork kept at room temperature, it changed clearly once a key spoilage measure passed the set limit. The work turns leather waste into a useful, earth-friendly freshness tag.
pmc-13505120:
Desmond Maada Kangbai and others evaluate Sierra Leone's COVID-19 vaccination program and its role in introducing human papillomavirus vaccination. In 2026, the post-introduction review draws on eighty-four set talks across six districts plus a desk review, adapting the World Health Organization review tool. Sierra Leone launched COVID-19 vaccination in March 2021 and reached 73.2 percent full coverage among ages twelve and older by December 2022.

By October 2023, full coverage reached an estimated 86.7 percent, with over eighty-four percent of doses delivered through surge campaigns. Lessons included bringing adult vaccination closer to clients, retooling current infrastructure, engaging community leaders, strengthening electronic tracking, and integrating giving platforms. HPV uptake exceeded targets, with 119 percent of aimed girls vaccinated, mostly in schools, though surge giving strained staff and disrupted some routine immunization.
pmc-13505420:
Yi He and colleagues built a structural model of apolipoprotein A-II, the second most common protein carried on HDL, the particles that move cholesterol out of tissues. The protein grips lipids more tightly than its better-known partner APOA1, yet its shape on the particle was unsettled. The team combined computer modelling with targeted mutations to test how the chain folds.

Their model wraps the protein's paired chains as a double hairpin belt around disc-shaped HDL. Most charged building blocks sit in the hairpin loop, and internal bridges plus ring stacking hold the fold steady. Two strong lipid-binding stretches appear in each half of the pair, and the hairpin seems built to meet partner proteins. Chemical crosslinking found sixteen links between parts of the chain, and fifteen of them fit the belt model. The result gives lipid researchers a picture for explaining how APOA2 shapes HDL behaviour.
pmc-13506120:
Tony Tannoury and co-authors report outcomes for the longest front-of-neck fusions in their series, spanning four or five levels, drawn from 1,428 cervical fusion patients treated between 2009 and 2021. Twenty-seven patients met the study rules and had at least two years of follow-up. The graft material was the patient's own hip bone, fixed with a front plate and screws.

Function and pain improved markedly: average disability grade dropped by more than half, and neck and arm pain scores fell with clear statistical strength. Neck alignment also improved on imaging, and every patient achieved solid fusion. Swallowing trouble was the commonest early problem, affecting about thirty percent, but it faded to a small share by late follow-up. Three patients developed wear at a neighbouring segment. The authors conclude the extended operation gives excellent results for multi-level cord compression when patients are chosen well.
pmc-13507020:
Anna Piotrowska and colleagues report 2026 mouse tests of cenicriviroc, a drug that blocks two chemokine receptors tied to nerve pain. Mice had a chronic squeeze injury to the sciatic nerve, a standard model of nerve pain. Twice-daily doses were compared with morphine over sixteen days, and spinal tissue was checked for pain-related signals.

On day three, pain relief matched morphine, and on days eight and sixteen the new drug worked better. Mice given cenicriviroc before morphine also lost less response to morphine over time. Spinal readings showed lower pain-driving signals and higher calming ones at key points. Dual blockade may offer a fresh route for nerve pain care.
pmc-13508120:
Sabina Ipembe, Hussein Mohamed, and Elibariki Mwakapeje study malaria in one Tanzanian district in work from 2026. The region has the land's highest rate, which rose in recent years despite a goal to end the disease by 2030. The district keeps passing the illness on despite steady control work.

The team mixed survey counts with deep talks. A staged pick chose 522 people to fill a set survey, and local leaders gave views in person. Land factors, such as standing water, and social habits were both in view. Work that joins counts with local views can show why nets, sprays, and clinics miss some homes. It gives district staff a fuller list of levers, from drains to daily customs, for the next push.
pmc-13508220:
Yuanyuan Yin and four co-authors pilot a seminar-case teaching model for postgraduate students in orthodontics, the field of teeth straightening, in 2026 work. Chinese training in this field leans on lectures and apprenticeships, which can leave reasoning skills underbuilt. Their model mixes seminar debate with real case work. Sixty-four students from 27 dental schools joined a summer program and were split into six small groups. Each group, led by a seasoned teacher, worked through three complex cases.

Surveys before and after showed strong approval of the model. More than four fifths of students rated it better than traditional teaching. Large majorities reported gains in diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical reasoning. Most felt ready to apply what they learned in clinic. Gains varied oddly with experience, dipping for the middle group. The authors present the model as a workable upgrade for specialist training.
pmc-13508520:
Li Ye, Maoting Chen, Qianling Wei, and Yue Wang study whether starting tube feeding within a day of heart surgery helps young children recover, in 2026 work. Feeding timing after congenital heart repair is disputed. Records covered 246 children aged one month to three years operated between 2021 and 2023. The early group, 128 children, began feeding within twenty-four hours. Infection rates, nutrition blood levels, and time in intensive care and hospital were compared.

Early feeding came with far fewer hospital infections, about fifteen percent against twenty-seven percent. Surgical wound infections also ran lower in the early group. Blood nutrition markers a week after surgery were higher with early feeding. Those children left intensive care sooner and went home days earlier on average. Adjusted models named delayed feeding an independent risk factor for hospital infection. The authors back starting feeds within a day when the child's state allows.
pmc-13509020:
Jane Tuckerman and co-authors report the first year of an RSV prevention program in a 2026 paper. RSV is a common virus that can hit newborns hard. New antibody products can shield infants, and programs are launching worldwide. Victoria, Australia, offered two such antibodies through hospitals to the infants at highest risk in 2024.

The team tracked use by checking drug records at five hospital sites. In all, 430 infants received a preventive antibody that year. Follow-up through hospital records noted later visits for breathing illnesses. The study stays descriptive: it maps who got the products and how delivery worked, rather than grading effectiveness. The operational lessons are meant to guide future seasons and other regions.
pmc-13509320:
Walid Atiki, Najia Ameur, Atika Zidouh, Abdelmoula Elouardi, and Latifa Tahri present a 2026 field survey of drug resistance in bacteria taken from broiler farms in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra region of Morocco. The group sampled manure, drinking troughs, farm soil, more distant fields, and well water across 13 farms. In total they collected 543 samples between late 2023 and spring 2025.

Escherichia coli turned up in about a third of samples and Salmonella in about a quarter. Roughly six in ten isolates of each kind resisted drugs from three or more classes. Resistance was most common in manure, troughs, and farm soil. Resistant bacteria also appeared in nearby soil and well water. The authors say the pattern calls for tighter farm hygiene and joint human and animal health monitoring.
pmc-13510020:
Jiang and co-authors optimise the finger bones of a biomimetic robot hand. Their 2026 paper tackles a design tension: compact hands lose versatility. With total finger length fixed, the team asks how to split it among the phalanges. Designs were scored three ways. The criteria were grasp capability in a shared workspace, kinematic dexterity from the Jacobian matrix, and key-press range for typing-like strikes.

A full grid search produced distinct optima per criterion, and Pareto analysis found 117 non-dominated designs balancing the three. Key-press range proved the most sensitive objective, varying by about a quarter across designs. A hierarchical strategy that privileged key-pressing while balancing the rest yielded a recommended compromise. Built and tested, it achieved a 98.8 percent keystroke success rate over 1,000 cross-row strikes without wrist movement. Grasp and dexterity validation remains future work.
pmc-13510820:
Nakao and colleagues tested in 2026 a body composition measure, intracellular water scaled by height squared, as a partner to the standard skeletal muscle index. Both come from bioelectrical impedance analysis, a method that sends a weak current through the body. The standard index can mislead when fluid balance is off, since extra water outside cells inflates it. The team studied 477 hospital patients and split results by sex, weight class, and hydration level.

Nakao found the water-based measure tracked body mass index more strongly than the muscle index in both men and women. The two measures agreed closely in men but only weakly in women. In men, their agreement grew sharply as body mass rose, while hydration status shifted the pattern further. The authors argue the water measure reflects true cell volume and adds useful context beside the standard index in sick patients.
pmc-13511520:
Where a pancreatic tumor sits, and whether a stent was placed before surgery, may change the gut microbes a patient carries into the operation. Marionna Cathomas and co-authors test that idea in this 2026 study of 63 stool samples from patients in Heidelberg. Samples came from 40 patients with head tumors and 23 with body or tail tumors, all sequenced in depth.

Microbe mixes differed clearly by tumor site, with one fiber-loving species richer in body and tail cases. Among head tumor patients, stenting came with lower microbe diversity and losses in several bacterial groups. Stented patients also had more major complications after surgery, 28.6 percent against 3.8 percent. The authors say stenting may matter when judging surgical risk.
pmc-13511720:
Hazal Su Bıçakcı Yeşilkaya and five co-authors design a system that reads emotion and stress from wearable brain and heart sensors, in 2026 work. Results travel over future 6G health networks. A deep learning model with an attention step sorts brain wave recordings into three emotion classes, while an image-style network sorts heart signal traces into three stress states. Radio performance was simulated inside a virtual hospital at two frequency bands.

On standard datasets, the brain wave model sorted emotions with accuracy above ninety percent. The heart model scored lower, with a clear drop from validation to held-out testing. Simulated radio links showed short signal smearing and wide usable bandwidth at both bands, better at the higher one. The authors present the frame as a workable base for personal health monitoring over next-generation networks.
pmc-13512820:
Togzhan Serbatyrova, Gulnar Shalgumbayeva, Assel Tukinova, Gulnara Sarsebayeva, and Laura Danyarova run a case-control study of gestational diabetes in Kazakhstan, where evidence from Central Asia remains thin, in 2026 work. The condition, diabetes first appearing in pregnancy, is rising worldwide and harms mothers and babies. The team compared women with the condition against women with normal glucose tolerance to find tied factors and outcomes.

Obesity before pregnancy and schooling level each held an independent link to gestational diabetes after other factors were counted. Women with the condition faced more high blood pressure problems, more cesarean deliveries, and more oversized babies than the comparison group. The authors say tackling obesity before pregnancy could cut both the condition and its fallout. They call for larger multi-center studies to guide maternal health policy in the region.
pmc-13513020:
Oral lichen planus is a long-term mouth condition that can turn malignant, so timely diagnosis and steady follow-up matter. Keren Martí De Gea, Massimo Petruzzi, and Pia López-Jornet trace the care pathway of 199 confirmed patients at a university oral medicine unit in Spain. They split the wait into patient, primary care, and specialist intervals.

Older patients waited longer at nearly every step. Women came forward sooner than men but then waited longer in primary care. The erosive form of the disease moved slower through the system than the milder mixed and reticular forms. Daily alcohol use went with the longest total delay, and older patients were most often lost to follow-up. The authors map where delays pile up.
pmc-13514320:
Canonico and co-authors looked to kombucha, a fermented tea, as a source of yeasts for new plant-based drinks. Their 2026 study pulled yeast strains from the tea and named each type by its genes. They found fifty-two distinct strains in all. One type, Brettanomyces anomalus, was by far the most common in the mix. The team then put the yeasts through lab tests that mimic the gut.

More than eight in ten yeasts lived through the fake gut tests. Many also stuck to each other and held back two germs that can cause illness. Two strains of one yeast and one strain of a third stood out as the best picks. Mixed pools of these yeasts made drinks with good lab scores and good taste marks. A strain from a wild source also helped brew a kombucha with no bacteria at all.
pmc-13514820:
Lule and colleagues studied in 2026 whether chronotype, a person's natural tilt toward morning or evening activity, links to hidden belly fat and blood fat risk. They enrolled 282 adults with no known chronic disease and no regular medicines at one centre. Each person filled in standard questionnaires on morningness and sleep quality, and the team computed combined risk indices from body measures and blood tests.

Lule found that greater morningness went with lower scores on both a visceral fat index and a blood fat risk index, even after accounting for sleep quality and other factors. Sleep quality itself showed no independent link to either index. Hints that the link ran stronger in women did not survive stricter statistical correction. The link also faded in the subgroup with strictly normal blood sugar. The authors say late chronotype may flag early risk even when sleep feels fine.
pmc-13517320:
Mark Godley and five colleagues review how chronic energy shortage reshapes athletes' bodies in a 2026 article. When training burns more than food replaces, the leftover energy for basic body functions falls short, a state called relative energy deficiency in sport. The authors gathered eighty-five studies since 2000 and sorted the effects across four compartments: bone density, muscle mass, fat stores, and body water.

The patterns differ by sport and sex. Endurance and leanness-focused disciplines carry the highest risk, with up to three-fifths of athletes affected in some estimates. Bone thins, hormones falter, and fat and muscle shift in ways that screening tools can misread. Godley's team appraises what current nutrition and screening advice rests on and where it wobbles. Their synthesis aims at care teams who must spot underfueling early, before performance problems become lasting damage.
pmc-13517420:
Qiaobo Lei and five colleagues feed laying hens a prickly-ash leaf extract in a 2026 trial. Plant additives are sought as antibiotic-free ways to keep layers productive, and the leaves of Zanthoxylum armatum 'Jiuyeqing', a green prickly ash from southwest China, carry antioxidant compounds. Diets with several extract levels ran for eight weeks, and the team tracked laying, egg quality, antioxidant defences, gut structure, and liver chemistry.

Six grams per kilogram of feed gave the best overall response. Hens laid more eggs with deeper-coloured yolks, and their antioxidant protection strengthened. Immune-linked measures shifted as well. Gut structure responded unevenly along its length, a reminder that plant extracts rarely act uniformly. Liver metabolite profiles moved in step with the dose. Lei's team proposes the leaves, often an underused farm by-product, as a feed resource that lifts both output and the value of the crop itself.
pmc-13517720:
German Roev and co-authors sequence the full genome of RSV and trace its entries into Russia. Their 2026 study deals with a virus that causes lower airway infections and is a major global health challenge. Gene sequencing lets experts monitor viral change in detail. That monitoring matters for judging prevention tools. In all, 106 samples from Russia were sequenced, from 2021 to 2025.

Three sequencing platforms were used. A geographic method estimated at least forty five introduction events for one virus type. For the second type, the count was thirty nine. Most events were represented by a single Russian genome. That pattern indicates repeated introductions from abroad. Few introductions led to detectable spread within the country. Limited sampling in Russia is a caveat, the authors note.
pmc-13518820:
Jiejun Luo and six colleagues pin down in 2026 a sea-level rise rate beyond which tidal wetlands worldwide start vanishing fast. Salt marshes and mangroves drown as seas climb, yet proving the link at global scale had been difficult. The team merged several remote sensing sources covering two decades.

Loss sped up in a nonlinear way as relative sea-level rise increased. Past about 9 millimeters per year, the chance of accelerated loss topped 92 percent and the loss rate rose eightfold. Marshes shrank gradually before that point, while mangroves held steady until the threshold, then fell quickly. Edge erosion showed a slightly lower threshold, giving managers a concrete warning benchmark.
pmc-13518920:
Divya Agrawal and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Breast cancer care needs safer, sharper drug targets. The team built a data pipeline to find targets from tumor data. They compared tumor tissue with matched healthy breast tissue from a large cancer atlas. Filters favored surface proteins that drugs can reach. A known marker ranked high, which supports the pipeline's soundness.

From the short list, the team picked one receptor target for lab work. They isolated new human antibodies against it and characterized them. The arc runs from computer screen to bench-made antibodies in one study. Drug teams get both a target list and a first antibody set. Surface targets matter because antibodies cannot reach inside cells. The pipeline can be rerun on other cancers, which gives the work value past breast cancer alone.
pmc-13519020:
Ipsita Kumar Sen and seven colleagues synthesize glowing carbon dots capped with heparin in 2026 and test how they mingle with human blood proteins. Carbon dots are tiny, low-toxicity light emitters suited to cell imaging, and heparin, a blood-thinning sugar chain, served as both cap and stabilizer. Glucose supplied the carbon.

The dots averaged 2.5 nanometers across with a strong negative surface charge. Fluorescence tests showed firm binding to both serum albumin and methemoglobin. Against lung cancer cells in culture the capped dots were slightly more toxic than bare dots, with a half-kill dose near 176 micrograms per milliliter. Red blood cell damage was negligible at high dose, supporting blood compatibility.
pmc-13519420:
Alka Modi Asat and colleagues surveyed homes in Mandsaur city, India, to learn what residents know and do about dengue prevention. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study visited 1,061 households in seven high-risk areas during the monsoon months of July through September 2025. Surveyors asked one adult per home about dengue knowledge and habits, then inspected water containers for mosquito larvae.

Knowledge sat at a middling level while reported habits scored better, yet larvae turned up in 195 homes, nearly one in five. Standing water, low income, and poor water storage each predicted larvae strongly. After the survey, the team gave one-to-one advice and live demos on emptying, cleaning, and covering containers. The work argues for targeted mosquito control aimed at the homes and habits where breeding persists.
pmc-13520020:
Vanessa Lünsmann, René Breuch, Silvia A M Herrmann, and Kostyantin Konstantynovski compare two ways of ionizing explosive traces before a mobility spectrometer reads them, in this 2026 methods study. Security screening and cleanup of old military sites both hinge on spotting nitro explosives like TNT, RDX, and PETN at trace levels. The ionization step decides what the instrument can see.

Their setup paired a differential mobility analyzer with a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. Samples entered as liquid injections or by heating swab filters. Both electrospray and photoionization gave linear, sensitive detection overall. Photoionization proved sharper for the dinitrotoluenes, including a microbial breakdown product of TNT. Electrospray won clearly for TNT, RDX, and PETN, but missed dinitrotoluene entirely when samples were heat-desorbed. Tests on real soil extracts rounded out the comparison, a practical guide for choosing a front end.
pmc-13520220:
Jian Zhao leads a nine-author forensic study in 2026 using skin microbes and metabolites to tell apart two causes of death in decomposing mice: hemorrhagic shock and organophosphate poisoning. Both leave few marks after decay sets in, beating standard autopsy and toxicology. Facial skin was sampled at three decay stages spanning 2 to 16 days.

Shock cases carried lower microbial variety throughout, with other bacteria dominating each cause and stage. Some 237 telltale microbe types emerged, while chemical profiles showed cause-linked molecules that shifted with time since death. Histidine and phosphate pathways split the causes best. Zhao's team argues paired skin signatures could estimate time of death and name its cause at once.
pmc-13520320:
Rui Xie and colleagues describe in 2026 five years of denture care for a boy born without teeth due to a rare inherited condition affecting skin, hair and teeth. A fully digital plan was used so new dentures could keep pace with rapid facial growth.

Care began at age four with scans and three-dimensional planning for a complete denture. Visits every six months checked fit, with relining or full remaking guided by measured growth. Eating, speech and appearance all improved over the follow-up period. The report offers a repeatable, measured workflow for other children who need dentures while still growing.
pmc-13520520:
Jiaqing Luo and Xiaobing Li propose in 2026 three new numbers for describing children's dental arch shape between ages four and twelve, aiming for measures that are repeatable and easy to interpret. Standard alignment scores miss large-scale shape and upper-lower jaw coordination.

Measures capture fine alignment wobble, overall shape departure from population templates, and mismatch between upper and lower arches. Applying them to 473 digital models, covering normal and faulty bites, showed wide individual variation. Fine wobble appeared most often and frequently alone, while jaw mismatch rarely appeared alone. Follow-up measures helped separate temporary wobble from lasting shape differences.
pmc-13520620:
Mike Westmeijer and nine colleagues, with the Dangle Research Group, published this 2026 study on recovery after lower limb salvage with free flap reconstruction. In that surgery, tissue is transplanted to cover leg wounds. Patients from four Dutch academic centres, enrolled in the Dangle study, completed questionnaires on ability, quality of life and discomfort after surgery. The authors modelled which factors tracked with outcomes over time.

Fifty-one participants returned 113 questionnaires between them. Male sex and the absence of diabetes were each tied to greater physical capability, though neither changed the recovery path. Only time since surgery predicted improving quality of life. Foot reconstructions brought more discomfort than lower leg reconstructions. Scores for individual tasks stayed largely flat over time. Most factors cannot be changed, the authors note, but they set expectations and flag patients who may need rehab, mental health and pain support.
pmc-13520920:
Rohit Pardasani and co-authors test whether an AI reader of fetal heart traces matches nurse readers in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Heart and womb traces guide labor care, but human reads vary between and within readers. The algorithm blends deep learning with set rules to label the traces.

Trace data came from five United States hospitals, spanning two thousand thirteen to two thousand twenty-four. A panel of expert nurses accepted or rejected each read, from the AI and from staff nurses alike. Main checks covered the baseline rate, speed-ups, slow-downs, and contraction timing. The test asked whether the AI fell short of nurse reads by more than a set margin.
pmc-13521220:
Zihan Xu and colleagues mapped chemical marks on DNA in the egg-supporting cell layer of chickens that grow too many follicles at once. Published in 2026, the study tracked a trait in which extra follicles mature together, harming egg laying and fertility. Sound scans followed the trait early in laying, and full-genome sequencing mapped DNA marks in small yellow follicle nurse cells.

The work delivers the first nurse-cell DNA-mark profile for this trait. Gene-switch regions that lost their marks pointed to Wnt, calcium, and cell-stickiness routes, suggesting ways gene control slips. The trait itself wavered during growth and cut egg laying. Readers gain a gene-control foothold on a poultry breeding problem, with gene-level leads for future checks.
pmc-13521920:
Naomi Azulay and colleagues test in 2026 whether heartbeat dynamics recorded during a cold-pressor pain test can sharpen ten-year heart disease prediction in Norway beyond the national NORRISK2 model. Recordings came from a population study wave in 2007 to 2008, totalling 6,694 traces.

Pulse variability and baroreflex measures were added to the standard model, while a separate machine learning model used only the time-series signals. Test accuracy hovered near 0.80 for standard variants and reached 0.73 for signals alone. Merging both model outputs brought no gain. Added physiology therefore offered little beyond recalibrated standard risk factors in this dataset.
pmc-13522120:
Jianlan Zhang and colleagues describe a young child's stubborn skin disease cleared by a borrowed drug, in this case report from twenty twenty-six. The disease, classic juvenile pityriasis rubra pilaris, covers the skin in red patches, scaly bumps, and thick palms and soles, with fierce itching. Standard creams and pills often fail it, and proof for stronger drugs in small children is thin.

Their patient was a girl of four whose rash spread fast and resisted steroids, antihistamines, and traditional remedies. With the family's consent, doctors gave adalimumab, a drug that blocks an inflammation signal, as eight injections over about four months. Within three months her skin had cleared, leaving only pale marks. No serious side effects appeared. Eight months after the last dose she stayed clear. The authors offer the case as early support for this drug class in severe childhood cases, while calling for proper trials.
pmc-13522420:
Charlie Albert Smith and eleven colleagues wrote a study in twenty twenty-six on the weight of Huntington's disease on patients and families across Europe. The disease is passed from parent to child and slowly breaks down the brain. Since it runs in families, its reach spans generations: a carer may one day need care too.

The team spoke with people who have the disease and with family carers in six European countries. They traced effects on body, feelings, money, and ties across generations. The disease upends daily life, work, close ties, and long-term plans, the team found. Problems with thinking and mental health added still more strain. Carers spoke of heavy loads on body, purse, and mind, in some cases from a young age. Portraits of this full kind can help health systems build support for whole families, not just for single patients.
pmc-13523020:
Sanduni Dabare and Imalka Munaweera review fertilizers built at the nanoscale to fight crop disease while feeding plants slowly. Farms must raise yields while cutting chemical harm, and these products promise both jobs at once. The particles carry antimicrobial agents, such as zinc, copper, and titanium oxides, silver specks, and plant-derived compounds, packed into structures that release nutrients over time instead of all at once.

Field trials cited in the review found better yields, crop quality, and soil health than with standard fertilizers. Less disease pressure meant fewer pesticide sprays, and slow release cut the nutrients lost to water. The authors stay candid about the barriers: cost, scaling up production, how long the particles persist in soil, and missing rules. They close with the gaps that must close before such products can anchor sustainable farming at commercial scale.
pmc-13523220:
Ahmad Pourmohammadi, Saba Naghavi, and Iman Adibi reported a rare first sign of a blood disorder in a 2026 case paper. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is a quiet plasma cell growth that usually causes no symptoms. It can harm nerves at the body's edges, but strikes on the central nervous system are rare.

Their patient, a healthy 54-year-old Iranian man, suffered repeated optic neuritis, flare-ups of the eye nerve. Testing traced the attacks to the gammopathy. High-dose steroids calmed the flares and rituximab kept them away. The case warns eye doctors to check blood proteins when neuritis keeps returning.
pmc-13523420:
Hakimi Kassim and colleagues test whether data from a dating app track area HIV patterns in Malaysia in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Publicly visible profiles on a place-based dating app were sampled on a grid across all states and federal lands. Per-person user rates and profile traits were compared with area rates of people living with HIV using rank methods.

User density tracked area HIV rates closely. Several profile traits showed initial positive links, yet none survived checks for multiple testing. The authors attribute the weaker result to the small number of regions and widespread non-disclosure on profiles. Grid sampling can therefore map user density in a set pattern, but profile traits cannot reliably show true local rates where omissions are common.
pmc-13523520:
Wenxuan Liu and colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, whether impacted wisdom teeth are linked with root damage on the neighboring second molar. External root resorption, where root tissue is eaten away, is hard to spot on ordinary X-rays and may be found only after lasting harm. Cone-beam computed tomography gives a clearer three-dimensional view.

Six databases were searched for human studies using that imaging method, through June 2025. Twenty-six articles entered the synthesis, most judged at low risk of bias. Pooled prevalence of resorption on second molars next to impacted third molars was 31 percent. Risk rose when the impacted tooth leaned forward, lay horizontally, or crossed sideways, and when it touched the deepest third of the neighbor's root. The findings inform decisions about symptom-free impacted teeth.
pmc-13525020:
Shine Tone and five co-authors test navigation tools for hip replacement surgery in this two thousand twenty-six paper. A good hip replacement restores leg length and the hip's offset, its sideways geometry. Imageless navigation systems guide the surgeon without extra scans. The team compared two systems: a large console unit and a portable handheld one. About two hundred patients were split between them.

Readings taken during surgery were checked against X-ray and CT measures after surgery. The differences gave each system's error. Judging accuracy two ways, flat images and 3D scans, makes the verdict sturdier. Hospitals choosing between console and handheld tools can use the results. Precision here shapes how well patients walk after surgery.
pmc-13525620:
Ramzy and co-authors review the reviews in this 2026 umbrella analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonists, the diabetes and obesity drug class that includes semaglutide, and atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat. Meta-analyses claiming these drugs prevent fibrillation have multiplied quickly. They often recycle the same trials. So the team appraised all of them for quality and overlap. Two questions were covered: new-onset fibrillation and recurrence after ablation.

Ten meta-analyses qualified. Their estimates pointed protective, with odds ratios for new fibrillation spanning 0.54 to 0.83 across reviews, yet confidence ratings were low in five reviews and very low in four, and none scored moderate or high. Overlap was heavy: shared primary studies reached a corrected covered area of 43.8 percent among recurrence reviews, and two reviews using an identical six-study base produced different estimates. The authors conclude the seeming consensus partly reflects repetition, and call for proper randomized trials.
pmc-13526120:
Lauren Geary leads a large group of medical writing leaders in a 2026 review backing lean authoring for medical study reports in the drug industry. Lean authoring means clear, concise, plain content that gives regulatory reviewers fast paths to decision-critical facts and a clean trail from design to results. Industry adoption, the authors argue, lags behind what reviewers want.

Noted benefits include easier reading, content reuse, cheaper drafting, and smoother regulatory review with fewer questions caused by unclear wording. Pushback against change is the main obstacle named. The article lays out benefits plainly, then a step by step uptake path: reviewer needs analysis and change planning. The goal is to prepare reports for future machine drafting while cutting the burden of regulatory review today.
pmc-13526420:
Yaoli Cui and a large team study a fiery form of cell death in blood cancer cells, in a 2026 lab paper. The cancer is multiple myeloma, a disease of plasma cells in the bone marrow. Forcing cancer cells into this bursting death route is a new treatment idea, but the steps that set it off were unclear.

The team found that a protein called IFI27 jumps in level when myeloma cells enter this death route. Adding more of the protein to cancer cells set off the burst, while removing it nearly stopped the burst. The protein harms the cell powerhouses and, with help from a second protein, pulls a pore-forming protein to them. Cells drained of powerhouses barely died this way, which pins down where the action happens.
pmc-13526520:
Atomu Kiriyama and co-authors report a rare tumor that burst while a patient waited for planned surgery, in work from twenty twenty-six. The growth was a solitary fibrous tumor in the pelvis of a man in his seventies. Such tumors are rare, and a burst belly case with infection is rarer still.

Scans first showed a large pelvic mass with fluid, but a biopsy gave no firm answer. A week later the man came back with belly pain and worse scans. Drugs at first held the line, but fever and blood signs worsened. Emergency surgery found a partial tear leaking fluid into the belly. The tumor was fully removed, and tests confirmed the type. He went home about a month later.
pmc-13527220: Koki Yokawa and six co-authors report an emergency aortic repair that, though it could not save the patient's brain, preserved lungs for donation, in a 2026 case report. A catastrophic Stanford type A dissection tears the aorta's first segment and usually kills quickly. Diagnosis and surgery were fast, but neurological recovery proved impossible. The report stresses that the quick response kept the lungs viable, and a successful lung donation followed. Bedside ultrasound made the diagnosis when CT scanning could not be performed.
pmc-13527420:
A routine robot-assisted operation through the anus nearly killed a patient by seeding infection behind the abdominal cavity. Jonathan Tiong and co-authors report the case in this 2026 paper: a 56-year-old man had a small early rectal tumor removed cleanly, with the cut closed by sutures. Within a day he spiked fever, his pressure fell, and scans showed gas behind the bowel.

Emergency surgery found pus and gas in the space, though the operation site itself looked healthy. Swabs grew a drug-resistant gut bacterium. Surgeons diverted the bowel, left the abdomen open under cover, and flooded him with broad antibiotics. He went home fifteen days later. Sudden collapse after such surgery, the authors warn, demands this rare diagnosis be considered.
pmc-13527920:
Merve Yılmaz and three colleagues report a 2026 veterinary study of two small regulatory molecules, miR-21 and miR-93, in ovarian tissue from slaughtered cattle. Cystic ovarian follicles, fluid-filled structures that fail to release an egg, are a common cause of poor fertility in cows. The team compared 35 healthy ovaries with 35 cystic ones.

Microscopy confirmed the thinned, worn layers typical of cysts. Both microRNAs were more abundant in cystic tissue, while a related gene called BMPR2 did not differ between groups. As a test marker, miR-93 separated cystic from healthy tissue well, reaching an area under the curve of 0.899 in the authors' analysis, and it tracked with BMPR2 levels inside cysts.
pmc-13528620:
Abdalrahman Al-Slaimieh and colleagues compare two electric ablation systems for heart rhythm faults on a hidden side effect: burst red blood cells, in this review and meta-analysis from twenty twenty-six. Pulsed field ablation zaps faulty heart tissue with electric pulses instead of heat or cold. Red cell damage can strain the kidneys, so the two catheter shapes on the market were compared.

Eleven studies with fifteen hundred patients were pooled. The five-spine catheter left stronger marks of red cell breakdown in blood tests than the circular one, and the few kidney injuries in the data sat in its group. Total hemoglobin and kidney filtration changes, though, did not differ clearly, and real kidney harm stayed rare. The authors call the lab signal real but its clinical weight unproven, and ask for standard reporting so systems can be compared fairly.
pmc-13528920:
Stefanie L. Moye leads a large team linking dietary omega-6 fats to rogue bone growth after injury in obesity in a 2026 study. The condition, heterotopic ossification, grows bone inside soft tissue. It locks joints and causes pain after trauma or burns. Fat mice on high-fat food grew far more of it. The team traced the fuel to the injury site itself.

Injured tissue in obese mice was rich in linoleic and arachidonic acids. Immune cells turned those into a signal, PGE2, via the COX-2 enzyme. That signal reprogrammed repair cells to build bone and cartilage. A low-linoleic diet cut the rogue bone despite equal obesity. Patient data agreed: obesity raised risk, and COX-2 blockers cut it only in obese patients. Diet makeup, not weight alone, is the actionable lever.
pmc-13529020:
Sharleen O'Reilly leads a large team setting out a Europe-wide study plan on diabetes in pregnancy, in this twenty twenty-six protocol paper. The condition affects about one pregnancy in seven and harms mothers and children over time. Coaching on daily habits can cut the risk, yet such programs rarely reach routine care.

An earlier phone-coaching program helped women at risk from early pregnancy to a year after birth. The new study refines that program and tests how to plant it in clinics across several countries while checking that it still works. The plan blends rollout science with health outcomes in one design.
pmc-13530120:
Jose Borreguero heads a large 2026 team showing that portable low-field MRI can image hard tissues such as bone, tendon, and cartilage. Cheap Halbach magnet scanners promise wider access to scanning, yet their uneven fields block methods that picture dense tissue. The group built a full workaround for that limit.

Calibrated radio pulses, a two-shot mapping method, and model-based image rebuilding formed the core fix. Scans of knees and ankles finished in under 15 minutes and revealed structures that standard sequences miss. Measurements of tissue relaxation in living subjects came first for this scanner class.
pmc-13530220:
Yang and colleagues report a light-driven chemical synthesis in 2026 built around a new high-entropy sulfide photocatalyst, a material that mixes many metals into one crystal. Their catalyst, with the composition NiSnCaZnInS, uses visible light to drive reactions that normally need harsher conditions. The target reaction joins benzyl alcohol and ammonia to form an imine, a useful building block for medicines and fine chemicals.

Under illumination, the catalyst converted benzyl alcohol with ammonia into the imine product at a yield of 1240 micromoles per gram over five hours, and the reaction reached 91.7 percent selectivity for the desired product. Mixing several metals into the sulfide tuned how the material absorbs light and moves charge, which the authors credit for the performance. They present the system as a greener route to imines that avoids high heat and harsh reagents.
pmc-13530820:
Caplan and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 59, a systematic review comparing autologous minced cartilage implantation against microfracture and cell implantation techniques for focal knee cartilage damage. Minced cartilage implantation is a one-stage procedure that dices the patient's own cartilage into the defect.

The review gathered 41 studies with 51 cohorts and 2,116 patients published between 2015 and 2025. Cell implantation cohorts dominated the count, with minced cartilage the smallest and shortest-followed group, averaging about twenty-nine months against roughly five years for the others. Across a battery of standard knee scores, no technique's patient-reported outcomes differed significantly from the others at follow-up. Failure and reoperation rates were generally lowest in the minced cartilage cohorts. The authors judge the newcomer at least non-inferior at short to mid-term, while noting its long-term data are thin.
pmc-13531120:
Jung-Il Kang and co-authors studied how a male hormone drives skin cell death in hair follicles in a 2026 paper. The hormone, dihydrotestosterone, is a known driver of hair loss. Most past work focused on the dermal papilla cells that sense the hormone, while the keratinocytes that build hair shafts got little attention.

Those cells grow and die in rhythm with the hair cycle, so their response matters. Using a human keratinocyte cell line, the team tracked two signal pathways tied to growth, death, and cycle control. They found the hormone switches on one pathway, called ERK signaling, and that this push leads the cells toward death. The finding fills a gap in how hormone-driven hair loss unfolds.
pmc-13531520:
Lucero Martinez-Fructuoso and co-authors (2026) report three new natural compounds from the sea sponge Cribrochalina vasculum. Guided by cell-killing tests, the team separated the sponge extract and isolated three members of the duryne family, durynes G, H, and I. They worked out the structures with spectroscopy and set the handedness of one key carbon with a chemical method. The compounds proved unstable in a common solvent, slowly turning into chlorinated versions of themselves.

The team solved the structures of those breakdown products too and proposed how the chlorine atoms get added. In a standard panel of sixty human cancer cell lines, the three new compounds slowed cell growth at low doses. Adding chlorine to the middle of the chain weakened the activity, and chlorine near the alcohol end weakened it further. The study adds new chemistry and a warning about storing this compound family.
pmc-13531620:
Priscilla Wessly and colleagues measure in 2026 the radiation reaching imaging doctors during catheter heart procedures. These echocardiographers stand close to the X-ray beam while guiding valve and closure work. Real-time badges at chest and pelvis tracked dose across 230 procedures at one center over a year.

Pelvis dose under lead was almost always zero, and a full pregnancy estimate sat far below safety limits, reassuring news for reproductive safety. Chest dose ran far higher and climbed from closure work to mitral to tricuspid procedures. Standing at the bed head and using only a half shield raised dose sharply.
pmc-13531720:
Emily D'Agostino and a large team describe a toolkit in 2026 that helps researchers and communities work as true partners. Health studies go better when the people they affect help shape them, but such teamwork is hard to start and keep. The toolkit, called the Roadmap for Community Engagement, was built with community partners and is free online.

The team tested it over a year with surveys, group talks, and a two-day review event. Among ninety partners, nearly all found it useful and said it would strengthen their links with researchers. They praised how clear and flexible it is. They also flagged hurdles, such as language access, cost, and time. The authors call for full trials of its effect.
pmc-13531820:
Peipei Zhang and co-authors probe in 2026 a stress sugar ratio as a death predictor after open heart surgery on a heart-lung machine. Records for 1,221 intensive care patients came from a large United States database. The ratio compares admission sugar against a long-term average derived from blood testing.

Sixty-three patients died within 180 days. Risk stayed flat at lower ratios, then climbed once the ratio passed about 0.97, forming a threshold pattern rather than a straight line. Missing sugar data excluded many patients, and key operating times were unavailable, so the authors label the threshold exploratory.
pmc-13532620:
Francesco Sergi and eleven co-authors published a study in 2026 on what emergency department patients know and think about the tetanus vaccine. Adults should receive it every ten years, yet many arrive at emergency care unsure of their status. Since emergency visits reach people without regular doctors, the team asked whether the department itself could close the gap.

They surveyed more than thirty-two hundred adults at ten United States departments. Over half were not up to date, and about one in eight had never heard of the vaccine. Lacking insurance or a regular doctor tracked strongly with being behind. Among those behind, about one in five would accept the shot on the spot. Most refusers wanted more information or preferred their own doctor.
pmc-13534420:
Jun Wakabayashi, Seiichiro Higashi, and Masashi Morifuji compare in 2026 NMN taken under the tongue versus by mouth in healthy men. NMN feeds production of NAD+, a molecule that falls with age, and the under-tongue route may bypass liver breakdown. Fourteen men took both forms in a crossover trial with an eight-day gap.

Blood was sampled for 60 minutes after each dose. Two end breakdown products rose faster and higher after under-tongue dosing, while NMN and NAD+ levels showed no clear route gap. No side effects occurred, yet the source of the early rise could not be pinned down.
pmc-13535120:
Mohammad Ali Mahdiabadi, Asma Moghaddam, and Nafiseh Erfanian review how gut microbe products from tryptophan can restore the gut barrier in inflammatory bowel disease. These products switch on the AhR sensor, which sets off protective pathways in the gut lining. Several gut bacteria make the key indole compounds named in the review.

Sensor activation lifts barrier proteins, guards the mucus layer, and calms inflammation through energy, antioxidant, and immune pathways. Animal studies show benefit that vanishes when the sensor is blocked. Human trial proof is still lacking, and some related compounds may carry risks with lasting exposure.
pmc-13535220:
Yannik Vollmuth and co-authors review antibiotic use in children with suspected brain or spine infections, in a 2026 study. Such infections need fast action, yet early signs are vague, so broad antibiotics often start before spinal fluid results return. New rapid panels can name the germ within hours.

The study covered 1,198 children who had a spinal tap at one center from 2016 to 2024. About 61 percent got antibiotics, with use near universal in newborns and lowest in teens. Once panel and fluid results landed, treatment often changed. The team scored how the drug spectrum widened or narrowed around the tap. Their data help hospitals judge where fast testing trims needless broad coverage.
pmc-13535420:
Zayd Tippu and co-authors profile the tumor surroundings in kidney cancer after dual immune therapy in this 2026 paper. Combined immune checkpoint drugs are standard for advanced clear cell kidney cancer, and some patients gain lasting control. No proven test yet predicts who will benefit, and the cell mix around the tumor is a prime suspect.

Tumor samples came from 30 patients in two cohorts who had kidney surgery after treatment with both drugs. Patients were split into durable responders and those who first responded then progressed. Samples taken before and after treatment, from several tumor regions, underwent layered molecular profiling. The study maps cell types, states, and layout linked to lasting response or resistance.
pmc-13536120:
Miriam Retuerto-Guerrero and co-workers review outcomes of GLP-1 drugs in rheumatology patients, in a 2026 single-center study. These drugs, first used for diabetes and weight, are now common in joint clinics where obesity and diabetes are frequent. Real-world data in this setting were limited.

The study followed one hundred nineteen outpatients over a year of treatment. Weight fell steadily, reaching an average loss near eight percent at twelve months, and blood sugar control improved. Cholesterol measures also got better. One inflammation marker fell clearly at twelve months, while another fell without reaching significance. Side effects were mainly stomach-related.
pmc-13536720:
Emanuela Mari and co-authors review the normal prion protein and its fragments in brain disease in a 2026 synthesis. The protein sits on nerve cell surfaces and helps with signaling and protection, yet its altered form drives prion illness. The review covers how the protein is cut into smaller pieces, what those pieces do, and how the protein interacts with harmful clumps seen in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Some fragments calm inflammation and limit harm from toxic protein clumps, while others may aid damage. New ultra-sensitive tests that detect tiny seeding activity have changed prion diagnosis and raise the chance that protein fragments in body fluids could track disease. The authors outline future options ranging from fragment-based treatments to fluid markers of onset and progression.
pmc-13536820:
Grace LeBleu and Fawaz Haj published this review in 2026 on diabetic kidney disease. About a third of people with diabetes develop the condition, and it remains a leading cause of kidney failure in the United States. The review centers on a family of enzymes called classical protein tyrosine phosphatases. These enzymes remove phosphate tags from proteins, counterbalancing the kinases that add them. Faulty tagging is a hallmark of the disease.

Of the hundred-plus phosphatase genes in humans, 38 are classical, and several are tied to damage in the kidney's filtering cells, vessels, tubules, and immune cells. The review sums up what each does in insulin signaling, cell structure, inflammation, and scarring. It then surveys drug strategies, from active-site blockers to allosteric agents and antibodies. The authors argue that aiming drugs at specific phosphatases could complement today's standard kidney care.
pmc-13538320:
Weiying Qin and Sufang Zhou review light-related polymers for sound-based tumor therapy, in work from 2026. Sound therapy uses ultrasound to wake agents inside tumors. The agents then make reactive oxygen that harms tumor cells.

Ultrasound reaches deep tissue and can be aimed with care, but real use faces hurdles. Low delivery to the tumor, low oxygen, and weak immune response all limit gains. The reviewed polymers absorb in a deep light band and can carry drugs and imaging in one system. The authors cover how they work, how they are checked, and recent study gains. They also list what must be standardized before wide clinical use.
pmc-13538520:
Özlem Saraç Atagün and colleagues assess teeth grinding awareness before implant therapy in a 2026 survey of 150 healthy adults aged 18 to 65 years seeking implants. Grinding can overload implants and crowns, so spotting it early matters. Clinical exams hunted grinding signs, while questionnaires covered self-reported grinding, jaw symptoms, stress, and personal awareness before surgery. Device-based measures were not used.

About three in ten patients met clinical signs for grinding, while about one quarter reported grinding in sleep, waking hours, or both. Age alone linked clearly to grinding status among tested traits. Awareness stayed limited overall, with schooling showing little sway except for one tooth loss belief link. Stress scores tied to neither diagnosis nor type. The authors recommend routine screening plus awareness raising before implant work.
pmc-13539020:
Lane Moore and six co-authors compare outcomes after rotator cuff repair among tobacco users, non tobacco nicotine users, and nonusers. Tobacco harms healing after shoulder repair, yet effects of vaping and other non tobacco nicotine products were unclear. A large database study matches groups one to one on background traits, with at least two years of follow up.

Non tobacco users show only one mildly raised complication, a procedure to free adhesions, versus nonusers. Tobacco users show higher rates of kidney injury, pneumonia, infection, emergency visits, readmission, and revision surgery. Against tobacco users, non tobacco users carry lower risks of pneumonia, emergency visits, and readmission. The gradient suggests combustion products, not nicotine alone, drive much of the harm.
pmc-13539220:
Antoine Plumacker and co-authors test cheap drone photos in a 2026 study of rainforest crowns. To watch a forest at land scale, teams must bridge ground counts and space reads. Drone photos can fill that gap, but each crown-cut tool gives its own tale of the same trees.

The team ran three such tools on fine photos over a vast span of forest. One is a taught tree finder, one a broad cut tool, and one a blend of the two. Crown marks were set side by side for their match. Forest teams gain a check on which crown facts stay true no matter the tool.
pmc-13539620:
Małgorzata Rak and co-authors use the glow of a berry pigment to track spoilage in dried chokeberry fruit. Published in 2026, the study starts from a known marker: when anthocyanins oxidize, a new band appears in their fluorescence spectrum. Chokeberries are rich in these pigments and are often dried or freeze dried for storage.

Extracts from fruit dried slowly at sixty degrees showed the oxidation band rising in step with drying time. Stored freeze dried samples at room and warm temperatures showed the same steady rise. Whole or ground fruit did not behave as regularly, so the extract route is the reliable one. The authors offer the measure as a quick first check of freshness in dried fruit products.
pmc-13539820:
Zuojun Liu and six colleagues report a 2026 engineering study of a probiotic bacterium, Limosilactobacillus reuteri, reworked to make a useful antimicrobial compound called 3-HPA from cheap glucose. Three tangled problems held output back: a missing vitamin, an unbalanced cell chemistry, and a brake on sugar use.

Comparing sugars with multi-omics tools, the team found that galactose switches on the needed genes and reroutes carbon flow, even though cells grow poorly on it. Copying that program into a glucose-fed strain, plus feeding four supplements, lifted output many times over the starting level. The authors claim the highest yield yet reported for this bacterial group in flask culture.
pmc-13539920:
Yung-Shu Lee and five colleagues examine, in a 2026 genetic study, whether inherited variants in a gene called NUCB2 relate to how prostate cancer behaves. The gene makes a precursor of nesfatin-1, a protein first found in brain cells that also circulates as a hormone-like signal.

Four variants were compared between patients and healthy men, alongside tumor stage and spread details. Carrying a G letter at one variant site went with lower odds of advanced stage and of cancer invading along nerves. Public tissue data showed that variant also tied to lower NUCB2 levels. The authors read the variant as possibly protective against progression, while noting lifestyle links remain untested.
pmc-13540620:
Hui Zhang and ten co-authors test what sales scores miss in AI teach hands for med school. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Eight AI hands taught a gland class span in four play roles. Twenty-two fourth-year students made one hundred sixty-seven talks, each scored by the sales side and by a plain eight-part rubric, with an expert re-check on a slice.

Sales and rubric ranks split for most hands: one sales star sat last on true grade, and a sales mid hand sat first. Hands split most on grasp span and least on play worth. Weak aim set was shared. AI grades tied with the expert in whole.
pmc-13540720:
A forty year old man came to hospital with worsening pain in the middle of his back after a feverish illness. Joshua Estin and co-authors report the case. Scans showed a calcified mass in the epidural space of his spine, squeezing the spinal cord, and the picture looked like an abscess. Surgeons removed the bone over the area to relieve the pressure. Instead of pus, they found a white mass stuck firmly to the tissues.

Under the microscope the mass was a calcified growth with cartilage like tissue, matching a rare tumor type called calcified chondroid mesenchymal neoplasm. That tumor usually appears in hands, feet, or the jaw joint, never in the spine. A year later his scans showed no remaining narrowing, and at eighteen months he had no symptoms. The authors warn that this rare tumor belongs on the list when a spinal lesion mimics infection.
pmc-13540820:
Five authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on a yam virus found in Brazil. Yam virus X is a flexible rod-shaped RNA virus first reported from Guadeloupe in the Caribbean. Only one full genome of it existed in public databases, so its spread and variety were unknown.

The team sequenced pooled yam samples from Bahia state with high-throughput methods. The virus appeared only around one region, and follow-up tests pinned it to one yam species. Three infected plants were sequenced individually, yielding three complete genomes. Those genomes let the authors compare the Brazilian isolates with the known one.
pmc-13540920:
Han Ma and colleagues present a computer framework in a 2026 paper. The framework infers how cells talk to each other. It works on spatial transcriptomics data. Such data map gene activity across a tissue slice. Older graph models freeze their view of cell relations too early.

Their system is called CAGNet. It works in two stages. First, an attention-based graph network learns a rich profile for each spot. Then the system alternates two steps. It refines cell clusters, then rebuilds the spatial graph. Each step improves the other. Across three public datasets, CAGNet beat six rival methods. It won on every accuracy measure used.
pmc-13542220:
Ramezani and colleagues fix a measurement problem in a promising kidney monitor. Urine oxygen tension, read from a bladder catheter, could warn of kidney oxygen starvation hours before blood tests react. The reading at the catheter's far end, though, is corrupted: urine dawdles in transit and oxygen leaks through the catheter wall. The distortion is worst when urine flow is low and the patient sickest. Their 2026 physics-based algorithm models both distortions and works backwards to reconstruct the true bladder value.

On a bench rig the correction cut average error from nearly eleven units of pressure to under one. It tightened the agreement band dramatically, while correlation with truth jumped from mediocre to strong in the reported figures. In eight pigs driven through haemorrhagic shock and resuscitation, nearly sixty-nine thousand paired samples showed the same pattern. Bias and absolute error roughly halved, with the largest gains at low flow.
pmc-13542620:

pmc-13548520:
