The survey covered 269 fathers in Turkey with babies up to two years old. Fathers had to read Turkish and agree to take part. Questions probed attitudes, hands-on participation, and sway over feeding choices. Links between those three areas were the core analysis. The authors frame the findings for family-centered support programs. Better father engagement is the practical aim.
pmc-13556420:
Fernández, Dios, and Justo report early results in a 2026 conference abstract. They study adult ADHD care by telemedicine over time and across cultures. Adult ADHD is often missed. It is often tied to anxiety, depression, and unstable moods. Real world outcome data across cultures are scarce. Their private clinic group spans Portugal, Brazil, Spain, France, Colombia, Venezuela, and Russia.

Staff used a structured interview scale to diagnose patients. They have followed them by teleconsultation since 2022. Care centers on stimulant medicines. The team tracks response, tolerability, and behavior over time. That work covers risky behaviors and the effects of late diagnosis. The authors present the study as a rare window on how standard ADHD drugs perform in very unlike cultural settings. Results so far are preliminary, and follow-up goes on.
pmc-13556520:
A Mitrea, D Lambert, and M Kosel present a 2026 case report on catatonia. Their patient had autism and a schizoaffective disorder. The episode was a severe hyperactive form of the syndrome.

Catatonia is a grave movement and behavior syndrome that can be missed. In an autistic patient, normal repetitive acts and speech limits can hide new signs. The report shows how drug response helped the team reach the right diagnosis. It also looks at the role of cutting back baseline mood drugs. Readers learn why a careful drug history matters when catatonia and autism appear in the same person.
pmc-13556620:
Stress feeds schizophrenia risk, but the brain path between them differs from person to person. Feng, Ma, Pu, and Luo sort that path into patterns in a 2026 report. Their data cover 975 nineteen-year-olds with brain scans and gene scores.

A sorting method found four groups with unlike relay patterns. One group's relay ran through three core networks. That group also carried higher gene risk scores. Only that pattern reappeared in relatives and young patients. Immune and stress pathways enriched its gene set. Sorting first, they argue, beats one average path.
pmc-13556720:
H J Robson, J F du Hoffmann, and J W Dalley build a new attention task for rodents in 2026. Real-world attention must split across senses at once. Most rodent tasks test one sense at a time.

Past cross-modal tasks needed very long training, which limited their use. The new task aims to be faster to learn and still demanding. The team blocked NMDA receptors to test the task sensitivity. Performance fell under the blockade, as hoped. Readers see a practical tool for studying divided attention, a skill that fails in many brain disorders.
pmc-13556820:
B Richardson and co-authors test a fast-acting drug in mice in 2026. The drug is 5-MeO-DMT, which has shown rapid mood effects in human trials. The team asked which of two serotonin receptors the drug needs to work.

Mice received the drug at three doses, with or without blockers for each receptor. The team watched movement, head twitch behavior, and signs linked to mood. Blocking either receptor changed the drug effects, which points to both being needed. Female and male mice were both included in the work. Readers learn how careful blocking tests can reveal how a drug acts in the brain.
pmc-13556920:
Yang Li and co-authors build a model to forecast the long term outcome for patients with a moderate to severe brain injury from trauma, using many kinds of brain monitoring at once. Such injury is a top cause of lasting disability and death, and the monitors give a live view of the brain.

The study covered 143 adults watched for at least two days with probes for pressure, blood flow, oxygen, and chemistry in the brain. Data from the first five days fed the model. Six months on, about six in ten had a good outcome. The model was checked on how well it split good from bad outcomes.
pmc-13557920:
Jiao and Zhao pool the trial evidence on immune therapy for advanced lung cancer. Checkpoint inhibitors free the immune system to attack non-small cell lung cancer, and the review gathers seventeen randomized trials covering the drugs alone and combined with chemotherapy. Survival and time without the cancer growing are the measures.

The drugs alone extend both, with a survival hazard ratio of 0.73. Adding chemotherapy does better still, at 0.68 for survival and 0.55 for progression. Smaller trials and pembrolizumab-based regimens look especially strong, though results vary between trials and some carry bias concerns. The authors conclude that immune-based treatment clearly beats the old standard, while calling for larger trials to pick the best form.
pmc-13558320:
Cecília Peruch and five co-authors test hearing harm from chemotherapy drugs beyond the platinum family, in a study from 2026. Platinum drugs are well known for harming hearing, but other cancer drugs may do so too. The team used a sensitive ear test before and after treatment.

They followed 174 adults treated between 2022 and 2023 and tested six tones in each ear. About four in five patients lost response at one or more tones after treatment. Rates were about the same with and without platinum drugs. Harm grew at higher tones in both groups, with the top tone hit most often. The authors urge hearing checks for all regimens.
pmc-13558420:
Nihal Babiker and nine colleagues pooled in 2026 the trial evidence for luspatercept, a drug that helps red blood cells mature in people with beta-thalassaemia. The inherited disorder leaves patients anaemic and dependent on lifelong transfusions. Their systematic review searched five databases to May 2025 for randomised trials in adults and assessed bias with a standard Cochrane tool.

Three trials and one single-arm study, 608 patients in all, qualified. About six in ten treated patients cut their transfusion burden by at least a third, four in ten halved it, and over a third stopped transfusions entirely for a period. Headache, bone pain, and joint pain were the common side effects, and serious events touched about a fifth of patients. The authors judge the drug effective while urging longer safety follow-up.
pmc-13558720:
Yitao Wu and eight colleagues rebuilt in 2026 a compact object detection network to perform fine-grained lung cancer reading on scans, sorting seven classes at once. Existing aids mostly answer cancer or not, leaving subtype and stage as separate chores. Their unified model must find each lesion. It names the tissue class among normal lung and the three main non-small cell subtypes. It also places anatomical location with staging detail. Tumours vary wildly in size and look nearly alike, which makes the task hard.

Three upgrades carry the design. A dilated block widens the view without slowing inference. A positional gating attention spotlights telling textures and mutes background. A dynamic upsampler preserves lesion borders during fusion. On a set of 1,886 images the model posted precision near ninety-eight percent with very strong detection scores, all at a small parameter count suited to clinical hardware.
pmc-13559020:
Bladder control after spinal cord injury recovers unevenly, and doctors cannot tell early who will fare well. Behnaz Afrashteh and co-authors tracked bladder function around the clock in female rats for four weeks after injury.

Ten injured rats sorted into three recovery types: good, moderate, and poor voiding. No single early measurement separated the groups. But models combining early measures, especially how voided volume interacts with efficiency, predicted the final type with high accuracy. The findings suggest the prognosis hides in how measures combine, not in any one reading. That insight could open a window for tailored early treatment after injury.
pmc-13559220:
Shao and colleagues review in 2026 advances in Fourier ptychographic microscopy, a label-free imaging method that watches living cells without dyes or fluorescent tags. Tags bleach and poison cells over time, which limits how long biologists can observe them.

The technique stitches together many low-resolution images taken under angled LED lighting to reconstruct one sharp, wide picture. It reaches resolution near 150 nanometers while keeping a broad field of view. Since its introduction in 2013 it has spread quickly, but speed remains its weakness, because hundreds of LEDs must fire in sequence. The review gathers the field's collective fixes: two-dimensional super-resolution schemes that beat the diffraction limit by iterative reconstruction, faster illumination patterns, and smarter algorithms. The authors chart how these advances turned a slow novelty into a practical tool for dynamic live-cell imaging.
pmc-13559520:
Three authors describe new fungi found on the roots of a medicinal plant in Anhui Province, China. Meng-Lan Chen, Nilita Mukjang, and Xia Luo surveyed root-linked fungi on Lindera aggregata, a plant used in traditional medicine. Their 2026 work sorts the finds by shape and form, and by family trees built from several genes.

Two of the fungi are new to science. One joins the group Hawksworthiomyces, and the other joins Melnikomyces, and the text gives each a formal name and account. A third fungus, already known, turns up on this host for the first time. Fine shape details help set the new finds apart. The study adds to the map of fungi that live with this plant.
pmc-13559620:
Xuran Zhang and Runfang Gao mine single-cell and bulk gene data to characterize an exhausted-looking T cell state in breast cancer and turn its genes into a survival predictor. Their 2026 study centers on CD8 T cells carrying both TIM3 and CD101 markers. Single-cell data came from a public repository, while bulk data came from cancer atlas and GEO cohorts.

Clustering resolved seventeen cell groups across seven types, and T cells split further into four subtypes. Trajectory analysis hinted that one TIM3-positive state can transition into the CD101-positive state. From 121 genes differing around this population, the team built an eleven-gene prognostic model using penalized regression. The signature predicted survival strongly across the cohorts tested. The authors frame the work as a map of breast tumor immune diversity, with the gene model offered for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13559820:
Salma Abouchiba and co-authors report in 2026 a brain tumor case that looked like a white matter disease. The tumor spread widely through both sides of the brain in a strikingly even pattern. Such even, mirror-image damage usually points to inherited or metabolic disease, not cancer, so the pattern can badly delay diagnosis.

A 46-year-old woman had months of fading thinking, slurred speech, and stiff legs. Scans showed even bright patches across the white matter and the bridge between brain halves, with no dye uptake. Special scans hinted at tumor chemistry at the edges. A biopsy confirmed a high-grade tumor lacking a common gene change. The authors stress that even symmetry does not rule out cancer.
pmc-13559920:
Sekar and colleagues studied in 2026 twenty years of hospital admissions in England for miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy, a pregnancy growing outside the womb. Using national NHS admissions data from 2004 to 2024, the team tracked yearly counts by age group and by deprivation level. That level measures the poverty of a patient's home area. Trend software then found turning points in the curves.

Sekar found miscarriage admissions fell clearly between 2018 and 2021, then rose slightly afterward. Ectopic pregnancy admissions rose until 2012, dipped as gentler treatment guidelines spread, and rose again after 2021. A steady deprivation gap ran through the whole period: the poorest tenth of areas had about twice the admissions of the richest. The share of admissions among women aged 25 to 34 also grew, reaching roughly half. The authors urge fairer access and targeted prevention.
pmc-13560020:
Fereshteh Rajaeiramsheh and co-authors test in this 2026 paper a Persian version of a scale that measures problem gaming thoughts in teens. Habits of mind, such as overrating game rewards, are thought to keep gaming problems alive. The scale existed in other languages but had no checked Persian form. The team translated it with forward and back steps, then surveyed 1,191 Iranian adolescents online.

The four-part structure of the scale held up well, and total reliability was excellent. Scores rose with gaming addiction and fell with self-esteem, as theory predicts. Since the four parts overlap heavily, the authors advise using the total score as the main readout and treating part scores with care.
pmc-13560320:
Xin Guo and colleagues review a proposed outside-in pathway for aortic dissection, in which fat wrapped around the aorta turns from protector to aggressor. Their 2026 article focuses on perivascular adipose tissue, sometimes called the vessel wall's fourth layer. Under inflammation or metabolic stress, this fat releases mediators, most notably TGF-β1, that cross into the wall's middle layer.

Sustained TGF-β1 stimulation may push smooth muscle cells into a cooperative gene-control network built around the transcription factors RUNX1 and NF-κB. That network would silence the cells' contractile program while switching on inflammation and matrix breakdown, destabilizing the wall. The authors evaluate the findings for this fat-to-muscle axis and mark its limitations honestly. They suggest future drugs against the axis will need local delivery, since systemic blockade risks bleeding and immune suppression.
pmc-13560420:
Rui Xu and co-authors present the first full mitochondrial genome for a fungus of medical and industrial use, in a 2026 paper. The fungus belongs to a group valued for chemistry and medicine. No member of its genus had a complete, annotated copy of that genome. The team sequenced and mapped the whole molecule.

The genome is a circle of about 41,500 letters. It holds fourteen core protein genes, two ribosomal genes, and twenty-four transfer genes. Six extra reading frames sit outside the core set. Comparisons with kin species showed shifting introns and repeats. Family analysis placed the fungus beside a known relative. A reference genome of this kind anchors future work on the group's history.
pmc-13560720:
Adrian S. Turner and colleagues assemble the genome of Yamadazyma mexicana, an industrial yeast, to near-chromosome completeness. Their 2026 genome announcement covers strain NCYC 1483, the species' type strain, first isolated from rot pockets of organ-pipe cacti during surveys in the 1970s. Long-read Nanopore sequencing generated nearly ten million reads at very deep coverage.

The final assembly holds eight contigs, seven of them chromosome-sized, improving on an earlier short-read version scattered across fifty-five pieces totaling 11.8 million bases. The yeast earns its keep several ways: it suppresses post-harvest anthracnose in avocados, lives across cacti, soil, and insect debris, and has lately appeared as a rare cause of human eye infection. A complete reference genome for the type strain supports all those research threads, from biocontrol breeding to clinical identification.
pmc-13561420:
Typhoid and paratyphoid fevers are hard to count where labs are scarce. Meiwen Zhang and co-authors estimate them from antibodies instead. A household survey in rural western Cambodia collected 529 samples from people aged 5 to 25. Antibody patterns against a Salmonella protein, read through decay models, gave an incidence rate. Overall seroincidence came to about 162 per 1,000 person-years. Rates in children aged 5 to 15 ranged higher in some districts.

Households with unimproved water or sanitation showed more infection. Districts with worse water and sanitation did too. The authors say the numbers support bringing in the typhoid conjugate vaccine. They note the split between typhoid and paratyphoid still needs pinning down.
pmc-13561520:
Zhengcan Xie and co-authors grade patient-facing tools built on the REDCap research platform with a four-step maturity ladder, in this 2026 review. REDCap began as a data capture system, and clinics now stretch it toward patients. The ladder climbs from plain data collection, through system integration and personalized insights, to a visionary intelligence hub that acts ahead of need. Fourteen studies from a decade were sorted onto the rungs.

Most tools still sit on the bottom two rungs; only a few reach personalized insights, and none reach the hub. Publications surged after 2021, and most work is American pilot testing. The authors say the gap between today's tools and the smart hub is the field's real agenda. They urge long, rigorous trials and deeper integration.
pmc-13561820:
Qingyang Song and Yong-Gwan Song review in 2026 psychological traits tied to resilience in long-distance and ultra-endurance runners. Past reviews treated mental health, motivation, and personality apart. This review joins traits linked to both mental adaptation and continued performance in one synthesis.

Searches of three databases yielded 469 records, and fifty-three studies were included. Most were observational, with some qualitative and mixed work. Poor pain coping was most consistently tied to worse pain adaptation and lower race completion. Emotional skill tied mainly to mood and stress outcomes. The review maps where evidence clusters and where gaps remain.
pmc-13562420:
Yea-Ji Kim and co-authors add defatted insect protein to plant based meat analogues and test the fiber build. Their paper from 2026 uses high moisture extrusion on a soy and gluten base. Three insect kinds, mealworm, a beetle larva, and a cricket, were added at four and eight percent.

Insect choice changed spread, density, and color, with darker and redder results at the higher dose. The mealworm form gained most: better key amino acids, a top essential amino index, and stronger links between molecules, which steadied the structure. Microscope views showed tighter, better lined fibers. Texture was most balanced at the middle dose. Species choice, not just dose, drove the gains.
pmc-13562620:
Chuandong Wu and eight colleagues test whether a giant linked renewable base could untangle the Yellow River Basin's clash of energy, water, and ecology. The basin mines over half of China's coal yet holds little of its fresh water. Their 2026 proposal combines hydropower, solar, wind, and pumped storage into one coordinated system, leaning on basin-wide cooperation and grid expansion. Modelling asked what a full build-out would replace, and what it would cost or save the environment.

Each year the base could displace 23.8 percent of coal-fired generation, some 249.4 terawatt-hours. Energy emissions would fall by 28.0 percent, electricity-sector water use by 31.5 percent, and ecosystem carbon storage would recover by 9.0 percent. All the parts rely on established technology rather than breakthroughs. The authors offer the scheme as a worked example of how one region can chase several sustainability goals at once instead of trading them off.
pmc-13562720:
Tatiana Iakovleva and two colleagues stress-test a shortcut for measuring how much information a quantum system holds about a quantity worth estimating. Quantum Fisher information sets the ultimate precision limit for quantum sensors, but real systems leak into their surroundings, which makes it hard to compute. A reformulation in Liouville space, where states become vectors, promised an easier dissipative version. Their 2026 paper derives exact relations between the two quantities for a qubit, for qudit systems, and for a harmonic oscillator.

For a qubit, the true value can be recovered from the dissipative one by a mapping that depends on purity. In higher dimensions the conversion tangles beyond any compact form. The dissipative quantity sometimes sits above and sometimes below the true one, so it bounds nothing reliably. The authors conclude its numbers cannot be read at face value, and map where the Liouville approach helps or misleads.
pmc-13563720:
Janina Österman-Udd and co-authors subject a wood-decay fungus to oxidative stress in a 2026 study. White rot fungi digest deadwood and must endure swings in oxygen and chemistry. Peroxide shock mimics one harsh stress they meet in that habitat.

Gene activity was read eighteen hours after the shock, under normal and low oxygen. Over seven hundred genes changed strongly, but the pattern split by atmosphere. Low oxygen cultures mostly switched genes off, many of unknown role. Normal air cultures switched more genes on, led by small secreted proteins and redox enzymes. Sugar pathways, including pentose use and alcohol making, shut down under both. Prior metabolic state likely explains the split.
pmc-13563820:
Zhirong Li and five colleagues ask what biology might connect sugary drinks to later depression. The link has appeared in population data, but the middle steps are guesswork. Their 2026 study followed 192,045 UK Biobank participants, relating sweetened drink intake to new depression diagnoses over time. Three datasets, from American surveys and a Chinese school health study, checked the direction of the result. Blood proteins, metabolites, inflammation markers, and brain scan features were screened as statistical go-betweens.

Heavy drinkers faced an 18 percent higher risk of developing depression than non-drinkers, and the datasets leaned the same way. A signature of 229 blood proteins tied both to the drinks and to the risk. Mediation screening nominated 72 proteins, 36 metabolites, and 5 inflammatory markers, with an interleukin-related protein showing the strongest share at 9.6 percent. The authors label all of it exploratory: candidate pathways for experiments, not proof that soda works through them.
pmc-13564620:
Stefania Briganti and three co-authors survey the lab models used to study sebaceous glands, the small oil glands of the skin, in a review published in two thousand twenty-six. These glands keep skin in balance through oil output, immune work, and ties with skin microbes. When they fail, acne and other skin diseases can follow. Models range from animals and human skin samples to grown sebocyte cells.

New three-dimensional models are the high point: cell balls, organoids grown from stem cells, and skin-like builds that include the glands. They copy real gland form and work far better than flat cell sheets. Still, most models lack full cell maturity and miss immune and blood vessel parts. The authors chart what each model does well and where the field must go next.
pmc-13565220:
Jiani Li and five co-authors published an ecotoxicology study in twenty twenty-six on how a common insecticide stresses midge larvae over time. Chironomid larvae tolerate many pollutants, yet the molecular effects of chlorantraniliprole were unclear. The team exposed Propsilocerus akamusi larvae to low and high doses and sampled at two time points.

Biochemical tests, metabolomics, and gene expression profiling were combined into one picture. The pesticide raised antioxidant enzymes and protein damage, worst at the high dose. Early responses defended against oxidation, while later ones shifted toward protein repair or, at the high dose, energy collapse. Silencing a heat-shock gene confirmed its protective role. The timeline shows dose deciding between adaptation and breakdown.
pmc-13566220:
Ji Yun, Jin Suh, Yun Lee, and Jun Choi study infection and toenail surgery outcomes. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with the Winograd procedure. The surgery is a common fix for ingrown great toenails.

Past data on outcomes with active infection were scarce. Hundreds of great toes treated over a decade were reviewed. One group had severe local infection before surgery. Signs were abscess, excess tissue growth, or foul odor. The other larger group had no such infection signs. Post surgery infection, drug length, and recurrence were compared. Follow up ran at least six months for all.
pmc-13566420:
Elahe Zare Borzeshi and colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic analysis, whether body chemistry measured in blood or urine can predict who will respond to blood pressure drugs. From more than two thousand papers between 2013 and 2023, only five studies qualified, covering water pills, beta-blockers, and two other common drug families.

Forty-six chemical markers linked to drug response, touching fat processing, energy cycles, and amino acid pathways. A few markers stood out across studies, yet the base is tiny and narrow. The authors call for testing in larger, more varied groups and in combined drug treatment before chemical profiling can guide prescribing.
pmc-13567220:
Csongor Szepesi and co-authors track students' eyes over food photos to spot eating risk signs in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Eating disorders may act like processing disorders, with attention skewed toward food cues. Whether such skew shows before illness was unclear.

Eighty-nine university students took an eating attitudes test and viewed paired rich and lean food images. Overall risk scores tracked a bias index of gaze direction. One subscale, oral control, went with more looks at lean foods. Bulimia-leaning scores went with long gazes at rich foods and few at lean ones. The authors say eye tracking could flag hidden risk patterns without treatment seeking.
pmc-13568120:
Jieli Chen, Kah Phooi Seng, Chee Shen Lim, and co-authors present a vision model that both classifies satellite images and explains itself in this 2026 paper. Hyperspectral images record many wavelengths per pixel, which separates materials finely. Land regions have ragged shapes, though, and fixed square patches fit them badly.

Their model runs two branches. One groups pixels into adaptive superpixels and treats them as a graph of tokens for a transformer. The other keeps fine local detail with windowed attention. The two views are fused for the final call on each pixel. From its own gradients the model draws maps of which regions and which wavelengths drove each class. Benchmark tests showed better accuracy than patch-based rivals, with clearer explanations. The authors aim the tool at land mapping where users need reasons, not just labels.
pmc-13568420:
Andrea Bernardi and co-authors rework shredded cellulose so it can reinforce tyre rubber, in a 2026 paper. Tyre makers want out of fossil carbon black, the standard filler, by mid-century pledges. Microfibrillated cellulose, spun from plant waste, is light, renewable, and eager to react, but its water-loving surface clashes with oily rubber. The team's modification aims to flip that surface chemistry.

Their approach treats the fibres so they bond into the rubber network instead of clumping. The host material here is epoxidized natural rubber. Success would cut a tyre's fossil content while using farm waste. The paper presents the chemistry and the compound tests behind the claim.
pmc-13569420:
Jessica Schiele and a large team shared a study in twenty twenty-six. It is about a kind of inheritance that no gene carries. Stress resilience passed from mother mice to their sons through microbes. Female mice got a heat-killed soil bacterium by stomach tube. The bacterium was Mycobacterium vaccae. They got it before they bred. Their male offspring never got the microbe at all.

Yet as adults under chronic stress, the sons were safe from many harms. Their unexposed counterparts were not. The sons' gut microbiomes were more diverse too. Statistical analyses tie the protection to that altered microbial community. The study stretches the old friends hypothesis across a generation. A mother's microbial exposures can pre-arm her children's stress defenses. The hunt for the mechanism now turns to which microbes carry the message.
pmc-13569520:
Li-Chao-Yue Sun and colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric analysis, global research on monitoring antifungal drug levels in patients. Such monitoring matters because these drugs vary widely between people and have narrow safe ranges. Publications from 2014 to late 2024 in a major citation database totaled 569 from thirty-four countries.

The United States, China, and Germany published most, output rose steadily, and two journals led the field. Hot topics included monitoring one widely used drug, drug interactions, a newer agent, severe fungal lung infection, life-support circuits, and immune-weakened children. Machine learning for dose prediction emerged most recently. Clinicians and funders can see where the field is heading.
pmc-13570620:
When a pandemic overwhelms hospitals, doctors must decide who gets scarce care first, and that is an ethical minefield. Faris Tbayshat, Omar Khabour, Karem Alzoubi, and Wael Al-Delaimy survey three hundred physicians who worked in Jordanian hospitals through COVID-19. They ask how aware the doctors were of the ethical dilemmas and how confident they felt deciding.

Doctors who had COVID-specific training were more aware of the dilemmas than those without it. Experience mattered for confidence: physicians past ten years of practice felt surer than mid-career colleagues. Generalists and specialists reported more awareness than subspecialists and non-clinical staff. Heavy workload looked linked to confidence at first, but the link faded under adjustment. The authors push for built-in ethics training before the next emergency.
pmc-13570720:
Mohamed Hag Elagib and seven co-authors systematically review heart and metabolic outcomes in subclinical hypothyroidism and the effects of levothyroxine treatment. In this common disorder, stimulating hormone is high while free thyroxine stays normal. Whether it harms the heart and metabolism, and whether hormone therapy helps, remains unsettled.

Searches to August 2026 gather 50 reports from 48 study populations with at least 46,746 participants. Study designs range from randomized trials to observational cohorts. Wide differences in populations, definitions, comparators, and outcomes block a meaningful pooled analysis, so findings are synthesized as a narrative. The review maps where evidence is firm and where trials still disagree on treatment benefit.
pmc-13570820:
Serap Savci and Ebru Kocadag Kocazorbaz turned waste loquat seeds into silver nanoparticles with a green, plant-based method. Standard ways of making these tiny particles use harsh chemicals and much energy, while seed extracts can both form silver particles and keep them stable. Their 2026 study checked the particles with light, X-ray, and microscope tests, finding mostly round particles averaging about 13.5 nanometres.

Compared with the raw seed extract, the nanoparticles blocked two diabetes-linked enzymes more strongly. They also fought glycation, a damaging sugar-protein reaction, far more strongly. The dose that halved glycation was far lower for the particles than for the extract, about 11 versus 165 on the same scale. The authors stress that all results so far come from lab-bench tests, not patients.
pmc-13571420:
Victoria Clower, Andrew Hansen, Jeff Jones, and Asli Aslan test whether a home water report moves rural well owners toward cancer screening. Private wells can hide cancer risks, and rural screening rates lag. Their 2026 study ran 14 weeks in southeast Georgia with 100 well owners. Half received water testing plus health education, and half testing alone.

At least one contaminant turned up in 68 percent of wells, and radon ran high in 56 percent. Intent to get screened rose by about a third in both groups. Grasping one's own results was the strongest spur, at nearly five times the odds of planning a check. Finding any contaminant also lifted intent. The team frames a home report as a cheap cue bridging environmental health and cancer care.
pmc-13571720:
Zouina Sarfraz, Rupesh Kotecha, Arun Maharaj, and Manmeet Ahluwalia review new treatment options for cancer that has spread to the brain in a 2026 paper. Brain metastases shape care across many cancers. Disease inside the skull often behaves differently from disease outside it. Drugs cross into the brain unevenly, and the local immune setting differs too.

The review covers how metastases diverge from their parent tumors and how prognosis models have evolved. It then surveys which drug therapies now work inside the brain. The biggest gains are in lung cancer, breast cancer, melanoma, and kidney cancer. It also weighs pairing drugs with focused radiation, and newer ideas like ultrasound opening of the blood-brain barrier. The authors call for brain-specific trial endpoints.
pmc-13571920:
Hiroaki Okada and colleagues reported a vessel repair case in 2026. A rare abnormal channel joined two artery systems in the chest. One system serves the body, and the other serves the lungs. Such channels can burst and cause life-threatening coughing of blood. Their patient was a woman in her forties. The channel was found by chance on imaging. It grew from a winding branch off the main chest artery. It joined a lung artery in the right lower lobe.

The feeding vessel was too twisted for one-sided work. Blocking from the body side alone risked backflow from the lung side. The team placed coils from both sides instead. The channel closed fully, with no complications. A scan three months later showed no remaining flow. The authors present the two-sided route as a safe fix. It suits cases where vessel shape defeats a single approach.
pmc-13572320:
Antonis Armoundas wrote a comment piece in 2026 on deep questions behind the use of smart computer tools in tailored medicine. Care is shifting from average-patient rules toward plans fitted to each person. Yet core terms such as disease, risk, and proof are less settled than daily practice suggests. Cut points that turn a measure into a diagnosis rest on time, cost, and harm, not on the number alone.

Armoundas focuses on three linked issues: how diseases are sorted, what a disease is, and what counts as proof. The piece argues that smart tools can expose these hidden choices rather than hide them. It urges care built around choices, where a diagnosis stays open to revision and the grounds for action stay clear.
pmc-13572420:
Ekaterina Timonova and co-authors show that a wheat growth-gene pair can unlock gene editing in stubborn barley varieties, in a 2026 study. Editing barley is bottlenecked by transformation: many elite varieties refuse to regrow after DNA delivery. A fused pair of regulators, GRF4 and GIF1, boosts regrowth in wheat. The team shot the pair, with editing machinery, into three commercial barley cultivars using a gene gun.

With the pair aboard, all three varieties yielded stable transformed plants, at two and a half to five percent efficiency. Without it, the control construct produced none at all. Among the first-generation plantlets, editing succeeded in nearly two-thirds, mostly in both gene copies, and the edits passed to the next generation. Some edited plants carried no leftover plasmid DNA. The authors offer the system as a practical route to precision breeding in barley.
pmc-13572820:
Hassan and co-authors survey Nigerian women's knowledge and habits around breast cancer checks in a 2026 study. Late finding of the disease drives poor outcomes in the country. An online survey drew 711 women from all six regions in early 2024. The team is clear that web recruits skew educated and cannot stand in for the nation.

Nearly all women knew the disease and backed screening. Yet only about a third knew early screening options, and fewer than half knew how to do a self-exam. pmc-13573320:
Maria Zulema Cabail and co-authors write a 2026 commentary on student ratings of teaching. New faculty learn fast that these ratings shape progress through the ranks. The ratings can also help a teacher refine a course over time, if they are read with care.

pmc-13573420:
Wenzhe Chen, with 13 colleagues, presents a 2026 design for hybrid nano bubbles that treat sudden kidney injury. pmc-13573620:
Yuri Tanuma and co-authors study a newly made ring molecule of twelve carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom, in this 2026 paper. pmc-13574520:

pmc-13574720:

pmc-13575020:

pmc-13575220:

pmc-13575920:
Dandan Liang, Qinghua Liu, Min Liu, and Yi Li pool past studies in a 2026 paper on lung cancer care. pmc-13576320:
Fundagül Bilgiç Zortuk, Eyüp Burak Küçük, and Çağrı Yeşildağ compare root shortening across three ways of fixing a Class II bite problem in a 2026 study. pmc-13576420:
Benelli and co-authors map the brain network changes tied to cognitive problems after breast cancer, in this 2026 study. Many survivors live with foggy attention, memory, and processing speed for years. The biology behind that impairment is still being traced.

Strong overlaps appeared in networks for attention, self-directed thought, and high-level control. Statistical tests confirmed these links were not chance patterns. pmc-13577520:
Marika D'Avanzo and co-authors build an early warning method for new virus forms in a 2026 study of the virus that caused COVID-19. Health teams need weeks of lead time when a new form starts to spread. The team tracked how far each new form's spike gene sat from past forms.

pmc-13577620:

pmc-13578320:

pmc-13578420:
Allison Perko and co-authors test a body-made rinse that may cut infections after implant breast rebuilds. Their 2026 study reviews cases at one center from 2021 to 2024. pmc-13578720:
Xiaonian Chen and colleagues simulate how concrete crushes under load when its stones are jagged polygons, in a 2026 study. pmc-13578920:

pmc-13579420:

pmc-13579720:

pmc-13579920:

pmc-13581220:

pmc-13583720:

pmc-13588120:

Form checks named the species by its fin free back and blunt head. Gene reads of its full small code were compared with kin. Most gene order and make up was shared and stable. Code use and change rates are set out in detail. The mix of form, gene, and habitat work aids saving plans.
pmc-13588920:
Marco Raffaelli and co-authors test a single-port robotic route for thyroid removal through the armpit. Their 2026 study reports the first European series of the method, run over two summer months. One hidden armpit cut gives the view of a two-side approach, with the gland reached from the midline.

Sixteen patients had half-gland removal with no switch to open surgery. Mean total time sat near one hundred minutes. Three patients also had central neck nodes cleared. One brief voice dip healed in a week, and no other snag arose. Pain and drug needs stayed low, and most rated looks as excellent. Larger, longer studies must follow.
pmc-13589220:
Vorapot Siramangkhalanon, Harirak Artamnuayvipas, and Kran Sophonpatima set out a zone-based plan for improving skin quality with injections, in this 2026 article. Beauty medicine has shifted focus from adding volume to the quality of the skin itself. Texture and glow shape how old a face looks. Fluids based on hyaluronic acid, which holds water in skin, are widely used to hydrate and smooth, but their use has been guided more by habit than by a shared plan.

The authors divide the face into target treatment zones, each with its own anatomy and needs. Their framework matches each zone to the right depth for a soft, non-setting form of the acid mixed with glycerol. The aim is better texture without changing the face's shape. Worked examples show the plan in use, and the authors argue a shared map makes results steadier between doctors.
pmc-13589320:
Ehrsam and co-authors review mediastinal tracheostomy, a rare salvage airway operation, in this 2026 systematic review. The procedure routes the lower windpipe into the upper chest when the upper windpipe is too damaged for standard reconstruction. It is technically demanding and uncommon.

The review found 70 publications covering 437 operations across 85 years. Nearly all were the permanent front-of-chest type. Most surgeons removed the full breastbone top, though a half-removal variant has grown popular lately. A windpipe stump of at least 5 centimeters is advised, yet 12.6 percent of cases used shorter stumps. The authors also summarize complications and quality of life evidence for this last-resort operation.
pmc-13590320:
Silviu-Ionuț Borş and four co-authors test a culture supplement for cattle embryos in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lab-made bovine embryos rely on fetal bovine serum, which varies by batch and can distort embryo structure. The team tried platelet lysate from a heifer in estrus instead.

Oocytes from slaughterhouse ovaries were pooled and split at random between the lysate medium and a control. Across five sessions, over five hundred egg complexes were recovered. By day eight, the lysate group had far more hatched blastocysts, about forty percent versus seventeen. Total blastocyst yield also trended higher, though not significantly. Early cleavage and other stages matched the control. The authors see the supplement as a promising serum alternative.
pmc-13590920:
Jean Baptiste Deloges and colleagues developed a method to measure knee joint space in 3D from CT scans over time. X-rays and MRI dominate knee osteoarthritis imaging, but CT offers high-resolution 3D views of bone that could add value if joint space could be quantified. Their 2026 study applied semi-automatic segmentation, manually correctable, to CT scans of 54 patients with medial knee osteoarthritis taken 36 months apart, and trained a nnU-Net algorithm to automate it.

Mean joint-space thickness proved highly reproducible, varying about 2.7 percent, and changed significantly in the medial compartment over three years, with 22 percent of patients losing over 0.5 millimetres there. Automatic and semi-automatic measurements agreed closely. The authors present automatic segmentation as a potential replacement for manual work in osteoarthritis follow-up.
pmc-13591020: Yi-Yun Sun and co-authors report surgery for a deadly gut complication of pesticide poisoning in a 2026 case paper. Organophosphate poisoning can raise pressure inside the abdomen and starve the small intestine of blood, even without a blocked vessel. Dead bowel then bleeds and rots, and death rates run high. Their patient gets early open surgery to remove the necrotic bowel segment, plus broad supportive care, and survives. The authors argue that fast surgery, resection of dead tissue, and full therapy together can improve survival in this rare emergency.
pmc-13591320:
Mariagrazia Piscione and six co-authors review how cholesterol handling links cancer and heart disease. Tumors gorge on cholesterol to build membranes and feed growth signals, and they twist the body's fat balance in the process. Studies tying blood cholesterol to cancer risk disagree, partly because tumors differ and because illness itself lowers cholesterol, muddying cause and effect. The review walks through the cell biology, from uptake and synthesis to effects on inflammation, blood vessel growth, and immune escape.

Cancer treatments then disturb fat levels further, speeding artery disease in survivors. Cholesterol-lowering drugs, above all statins, already protect the heart in this setting and may also slow tumors by choking a key production pathway. Newer agents add options and may pair well with immune therapy. The authors map the two-way traffic for cardio-oncology care.
pmc-13591820:
Soheila Majidi and Amin Rouhi study, in 2026, whether obsessive compulsive symptoms dent the job performance of front line health workers in Hamadan, Iran. Such symptoms mix unwanted thoughts with repeated acts, and health staff face heavy mental strain at work. Their survey drew 403 workers from 50 urban health centers and posts, using standard scales for symptoms and performance.

About half the workers showed symptoms below the clinical line, while nearly all rated their job performance as good. Total symptom scores showed no firm link to performance. Symptoms ran higher in women and in staff with less schooling. Sex and contract type, not symptoms, predicted performance scores. Majidi and Rouhi advise mental health support and training for staff.
pmc-13592020:
Brandon Foley and co-authors present a 2026 study on predicting how vapors dissolve in plastics. Such data matter for films, coatings, and storage, but lab tests for every pair are slow. The team used machine learning with a low-rank factor model. In that model, each vapor and each polymer gets a short list of hidden traits, and their match gives the solubility.

A model with just two hidden traits worked best, without the instability of larger ones. It predicted values within a factor of 1.5 in 95 percent of cases, across 43 vapors and nine polymers. The two traits seem to map to plain stickiness and to polar bonding. New polymers can be added with tests on as few as four vapors.
pmc-13592320:
Lawson and colleagues published a 2026 study on forcing a dye molecule to twist one way. Perylene diimide dyes can form helices that bend light in useful ways. Most twisted versions flip between hands and lose their special glow. The team used a rotaxane, a ring threaded on an axle, as the guide.

Their rotaxane's built-in twist is stable and cannot flip over time. It pushed the dye into a single-handed helix that stayed put. The dye then showed steady light-bending and glowing effects in tests. The flat dye face also let rotaxanes stack together, a rare trick. Control reached from single molecules up to grouped assemblies alike. Lasting single-handed glow suits sensing, imaging, and catalyst design work.
pmc-13592420:
Xue Zhao and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study of retbindin, the retina's vitamin B2 handler, shifting location with diet and daily rhythm. The retina burns energy fiercely and depends on flavin cofactors. A retina-only binding protein keeps those cofactors stocked, but its regulation was unclear.

Protein levels rose as outer segments matured, peaked in early adulthood, and declined with age alongside flavin stores. Fasting moved the protein toward cone-associated zones without changing its total amount. Refeeding and daylight restored its usual position. Retbindin actively redistributes to defend flavin balance under changing demand.
pmc-13592620:
Jian Zhang and four colleagues ask what drives strong learning when professional training and entrepreneurship teaching merge. Their framework runs from resource input through mental construction to active engagement, drawing on three theories. A survey of 584 university students measured teaching content, teacher skill, student engagement, campus company resources, and policy support against combined learning outcomes. Statistical paths traced how each factor connected, directly or through teaching practice quality.

Content, teacher skill, engagement, and company resources each linked positively to outcomes, mostly by lifting how well teaching worked in practice. Policy support showed no direct link, only an indirect one through the same practice channel. Zhang and the team advise course redesign, stronger practice based teaching, and deeper campus company collaboration.
pmc-13592720:
The authors present a counting-based method to infer how neurons in a network drive each other, without one giant global fit. Their 2026 method answers a known weakness of standard tools: in tightly balanced networks, strong opposing links become hard to estimate at once. The new framework maps spike trains onto flows between network states.

Each state change gets its own rate, read directly from the data. The method beat two standard tools in strongly coupled networks and matched them in calm ones. Paired with a minimal dynamics builder, it captured spike timing patterns better than entropy-based models. It shrugged off hidden, unrecorded units. Tests on salamander retina recordings close the case for real-world use.
pmc-13593620:
Frederik Viktor Bang Jespersen and co-authors study heart valve infection caused by mouth microbes in a 2026 paper. Such infections are severe and can return, and germs from the mouth are a common cause. Yet little was known about how often blood infection with the same germs follows after treatment ends.

The team reviewed patients at one large hospital in Copenhagen and split them by whether mouth germs caused the first infection. A quarter of cases fell in the mouth-germ group, and those patients were younger and had fewer other diseases. Return of blood infection was rare in both groups over three years, and no relapse at all was seen in the mouth-germ group. The authors say the long-term outlook after such infections looks better than feared.
pmc-13593920:
Guang-Liang Chen and colleagues report lasting brain response to a targeted drug in a rare salivary cancer. Their case report from twenty twenty-six concerns salivary duct carcinoma. This aggressive cancer often follows hormone and HER2 signals. Options shrink when HER2 is absent and other treatments fail.

The patient tumour carried high levels of the TROP2 marker. Brain-area metastases grew despite surgery, radiation, and several drug regimens. An antibody-drug aimed at TROP2 was used off-label next. Dosing ran every two weeks without steroids or local brain treatment. The dominant brain lesion had grown large before this switch. Response inside the skull lasted, per the report title and case course. Rare cancers may benefit from marker-guided borrowing of drugs.
pmc-13594520:
Gizemnaz Kara and Aylin Yaba reviewed in 2026 how a cell control path called the Hippo pathway may drive endometriosis. In this chronic condition, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, causing pain and trouble conceiving. The path in question governs cell growth, survival, and how cells sense force.

When the path falters, its growth switch YAP1 stays on, feeding cell spread, invasion, and resistance to cell death. The review ties the path to scarring, hormone resistance, and cross-talk with other disease paths. Blocking parts of the path looks promising in lab work, yet no such drug is proven in patients. The switch also keeps healthy tissue in repair, so care is needed. The authors call for finer studies by disease subtype.
pmc-13594620:
Zhang and seven co-authors study biological aging and pancreas disease, in work from twenty twenty-six. Biological age can run ahead of calendar age as body function declines. Whether that speedup links to pancreas problems was unclear.

More than three hundred thousand adults from the UK Biobank, recruited over four years, were followed. Two established methods scored age acceleration, split into four bands and used as a continuous scale. Outcomes held overall pancreas disease, acute and chronic pancreatitis, cysts, cancer, and pancreas linked death. Risk models and mediation tests checked dose response and possible pathways.
pmc-13595220:
Antibiotics cannot kill viruses, yet they are often given for viral chest infections. Siti Mardhiah Muhamad Fauzii and co-authors studied 241 hospital admissions with confirmed influenza, RSV, or COVID-19. The setting was a tertiary center during the 2025/26 winter. Antibiotics were started in 86 percent of cases, for a median of seven days. Extra cultures found bacteria in only 22 percent of those tested.

Needing oxygen made doctors about 4.6 times more likely to start antibiotics. A higher inflammation marker also pushed toward treatment. Staying on oxygen lengthened the course. The authors question the reflex to treat confirmed viral illness with antibiotics.
pmc-13595520:
Romain Hollard and co-authors surveyed 118 pig vets across 25 countries about how they treat mycoplasma infections in pigs, then set practice against published rules and guidance. Mycoplasmas are hard to diagnose and treat, antibiotics are often the only option, and resistance is a growing worry in their 2026 report.

Practice matched the guidance on the main choices: macrolides dominated prescriptions, followed by tetracyclines and pleuromutilins, and nearly all vets used lab tests at least sometimes. Testing for drug response lagged, with only about a third requesting it in most cases. A small minority at times prescribed antibiotics that cannot work against mycoplasmas or that are key for human health, and doses sometimes drifted from the label. The authors urge wider drug-response testing and wider sharing of treatment guidelines.
pmc-13595720:
Jiayin Du and colleagues used a long-running Chinese aging cohort to untangle how childhood adversity, uric acid, and digestive disease in later life connect. Their 2026 longitudinal study followed 3,666 middle-aged and older adults, of whom 617 developed digestive disorders, modeling risks with survival analysis and testing uric acid as a go-between.

Growing up around household mental illness, or in an unsafe neighborhood, each predicted later digestive disease, and uric acid levels were themselves tied to digestive disorders. The mediation result was subtle: the unsafe neighborhood effect ran partly through uric acid in a negative direction, complicating any simple story that more uric acid means more harm. The pattern held across demographic subgroups. The authors call for work on mechanisms and on preventing childhood adversity whose health shadow reaches into old age.
pmc-13595820:
Blood parts are scarce, and a third of requests at one Indian hospital failed set rules for sound use. Vidhi Jain, Devanshi Gosai, and Dipali Shukla audit those requests in a 2026 study. They review 8,752 requests over six months, from July to December 2025, at the blood bank of a large hospital. Each request was checked against set rules drawn from blood guidance groups.

Sound requests made up seventy point nine percent of the total. Plasma requests broke rules most often, at thirty-five point two percent. Red cell requests followed at twenty-eight point seven percent. Cancer and intensive care wards scored highest on sound use, at eighty-two point two and eighty-one point one percent. Birth wards sat near the bottom at sixty-four point one percent. Cross-matched red cells outran transfused ones by two point one to one.
pmc-13596720:
Yuqing Hu and colleagues traced how pressure overload in the right side of a child's heart stalls the maturation of heart muscle cells. In samples from children with tetralogy of Fallot and in newborn rats with a banded lung artery, the tiny tunnels called T-tubules, which synchronize each heartbeat's contraction, failed to develop normally.

Gene activity scans showed tubule-related genes switched down, with Bin1, a builder of those tunnels, among the most suppressed. Restoring Bin1 in the banded rats rescued tubule maturation. The chain ran through chromatin. Pressure closed access to the Bin1 gene. A transcription factor, Mef2d, proved to be the brake. Silencing it freed Bin1, and mutating its binding sites erased its effect. The authors present the pathway as a therapeutic direction for children's heart diseases driven by right-sided pressure.
pmc-13596920:
Noriyasu Magari, Tomoko Kagenishi, and Ken Yokawa study how a numbing drug slows the flow inside plant cells, in a paper from 2026. The drug is best known for blocking nerve signals in animals, yet it also slows the steady stream that moves parts inside the cells of the pond plant Egeria densa. The team asks what chain of changes links the drug to the slowdown.

Leaf cells slowed in a way that reversed after the drug was washed off. Close views showed the drug broke up the fine actin strands that drive the flow. Tests also found a rise in harsh oxygen based chemicals near the cell wall, tied to calcium entry. When the team added agents that mop up those chemicals, the flow slowed far less.
pmc-13597120:
Omar Darawsheh and Matthew Bashton present EnzymeSifter, a software tool that hunts for useful industrial enzymes in metagenomes. These vast DNA collections from environmental samples hold countless sequences, and picking candidates by hand is hopeless. Industry needs enzymes judged on several traits at once, such as solubility, heat tolerance, and the acidity they work in. Single-trait predictors exist, but their separate scores are hard to combine.

EnzymeSifter predicts the traits together and merges them into one composite score. It then builds a family tree of the candidates and keeps the best scorer from each branch. That rule preserves diversity and samples the sequence space evenly, leaving a short, non-redundant list for lab testing. The tool acts as a sieve driven by user settings. It is released freely under an MIT licence, with code in a public repository.
pmc-13597220:
Tube feeding in brain-injured patients fails often through stomach trouble, and a checklist built around the whole feeding course may steady it. Ying Wang, Hong Fu, Yue Xuan, Deqi Xia, Jiajia Huo, Hui Li, and Yueqin Zhou test that checklist in a 2026 study. Forty-one intensive care patients split into earlier standard care and later checklist care. Five tolerance troubles, from diarrhea to aspiration, were counted for each group.

Diarrhea and retained stomach contents fell clearly under the checklist. Aspiration dropped to zero in the checklist group, though the gap missed firm proof. Feed interruptions and discharge outcomes were also tracked. The study ran in one neuro intensive care unit over two and a half years.
pmc-13597520:
Graciela Sotelo and ten co-authors wrote a 2026 study on how fossil record biases distort what we infer about mammal evolution. Fossils are the key to past biodiversity, but the record is patchy. Preservation depends on sediment, species range, body size, and sampling effort. How badly those filters skew evolutionary conclusions was poorly measured.

The team simulated a future fossil record from today's land mammals. They filtered species by sediment cover, range, body size, and sampling biases at three preservation rates, then pruned them from the mammal family tree. Analyses of body mass and diet evolution followed. Biological and taxonomic filters strongly skewed the results. Spatial filters, surprisingly, did not. The work gives first estimates of how incompleteness bends readings of deep-time change.
pmc-13597820:
Yuhang Zhang and Gyuil Lee published a combined analysis in two thousand twenty-six on exercise and aggression in the young. Aggressive behaviour in childhood predicts poor schooling, social trouble, and mental health problems. Exercise is a drug-free candidate remedy, but which kind works best was unclear.

Trials up to December two thousand twenty-five were pooled across four databases. Programmes were classed as open-skill, closed-skill, or multicomponent training. Outcomes covered overall aggression plus anger, hostility, and physical and verbal aggression. Network methods ranked the exercise types against each other. Consistency and sensitivity checks probed the findings' robustness. The authors aim to guide schools and clinics choosing activity programmes.
pmc-13598120:
Yang and co-authors identify in 2026 a nucleolar protein as an essential helper in fixing the worst kind of DNA damage, snapped double strands. The protein, GNL3, must carry a small SUMO tag to do the job. With the tag, it joins a helicase crew that chews back broken ends so repair can start.

A mutant lacking the tag site could not rescue damaged cells. Two enzymes add and remove the tag, balancing the system. Breast cancer variants that break the tag or its docking site fail the same way. Removing the protein left cancer cells open to two standard drugs.
pmc-13598320:
Toshiki Otoda and four co-authors introduce a set of studies on how chemical stress and inflammation damage organs in type 2 diabetes, in this 2026 editorial. Diabetes is no longer seen as a simple problem of blood sugar. Inside the body, excess sugar drives harmful chemistry, stirs immune activity, starves tissues of oxygen, and strains the cell's power stations. Over years, that mix injures the heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves.

The ten articles in the set range from cell mechanisms to diet and drug effects. One pooled forty trials with over 6,000 participants and found that a class of diabetes drugs lowered major inflammation markers beyond their effect on sugar. Others examine blood markers that might warn of damage early. The editors draw the threads together into one picture: many pathways, one steady march toward organ harm, and several points where treatment might interrupt it.
pmc-13598420:
Guojun Li and co-authors described a surgical technique for a tumor-driven dislocation at the top of the spine in 2026. Such atlantoaxial dislocation is rare but can threaten the junction of skull and cord when a tumor destroys the axis bone. Standard reduction tricks lean on the atlas and axis as anchors, which fails when those bones are ruined.

In the single reported case, neither bone could anchor the repair. The team used a plate on the back of the skull as the pulling handle and the lower neck as the firm base. A pre-bent rod was locked below; the plate was then drawn to the skull and screwed fast. Letting go of the squeeze let the skull settle into the rod's alignment.
pmc-13598520:
Behçet's disease inflames blood vessels throughout the body, and one of its rarest dangers is a clot inside the heart itself. Houssam Ait Boutargante and co-authors report in 2026 a 37-year-old man who arrived with a pulmonary embolism. Scans revealed extensive clots in his central veins and a giant clot in the right atrium of his heart.

The pattern pointed to Behçet's, confirmed against the 2014 international criteria. Heart ultrasound and contrast CT mapped the atrial clot and a blocked superior vena cava. The team treated him medically rather than surgically, and he recovered well. The authors stress the lesson: in a young patient with unusual venous clots, a heart clot should raise suspicion of Behçet's early, because immune-suppressing treatment, started promptly, drives the good outcomes.
pmc-13598620:
Judging how stiff the relaxing heart has become is central to spotting a common form of heart failure, yet standard ultrasound rules often leave the answer unclear. Cian Murray and six co-authors review whether artificial intelligence can firm up that judgment in this 2026 systematic review. They gather studies where learning models read heart ultrasound to grade the relaxing phase or estimate filling pressures.

Fourteen studies met their rules, checked against either direct pressure measurements inside the heart or standard guideline grading. Reported accuracy scores against the direct standard ranged from fair to good, with wide spread between studies. Test groups ranged from small held-out sets to large outside data sets, and the team graded each study for bias. They conclude the tools look promising but uneven, and need more shared standards before clinic use.
pmc-13599720:
Yara Alhenaki and co-authors review why eyes can drift outward again after surgery. Their 2026 paper covers two forms of that drift, one that comes and goes and one tied to poor vision in an eye. Knowing what raises the risk can improve surgical plans. The team searched four databases for studies from 2010 to 2025.

They found 53 studies with about 7,470 patients. Success rates ranged widely, from about 38% to about 92%. Big drift before surgery, poor control, lazy eye, and weak depth vision raised the risk of drift returning. Early alignment after surgery was a strong sign of long-term success. No clear gap showed between surgical techniques. Risk drivers differed between the two forms.
pmc-13599820:
May Ee Png and co-authors publish a protocol for a scoping review on how economic evaluations done alongside clinical trials get validated. Their 2026 paper notes that such evaluations guide health spending decisions. Model-based evaluations have agreed validation frameworks, but trial-based ones do not: validation there is loosely defined and often buried in routine analysis.

The planned review will search major medical databases and health technology agency sources, plus grey literature and dissertations. It aims to map how validation is described and actually done in published work. The map feeds a wider program building a validation tool for trial-based economic evaluation, the authors explain. Reference lists of included sources will also be screened.
pmc-13600020:
Karthik Chetlapalli and eleven co-authors track fatty liver in folks who got donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. Their case set appeared in twenty twenty-six. Fat and flare states can shape the graft niche and immune watch, so their role here counts. Eighteen such patients found on scans at one hub from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty were tracked for at least five years.

Most had sound liver blood marks before the graft, yet most skewed in the first year with no last harm. No vein-block liver ill came. Comeback hit near half and drove most deaths, with germs next. The team says fatty liver is no bar to graft, with more work due.
pmc-13600620:
Jiaqi Hu and co-authors ask whether genetic risk for cancer is shared across cancer types, in a 2026 study. Shared risk at the whole-genome level is known but modest. Whether that sharing gathers in set regions or pathways was unclear. The team combined two approaches to find out.

They estimated local genetic links across sixteen cancers and one combined cancer trait. Regions where several cancers' effects aligned were then annotated with other trait data. In parallel, they tested risk scores built for one cancer against the others. Scores for chosen pairs were split into shared and pathway parts. Structured sharing, if real, could reshape how risk models borrow strength across diseases.
pmc-13600720:
Anu Elsa Swaroop and co-authors characterized a drug-loaded nanosponge meant to regrow tooth pulp in a 2026 paper. Regenerative endodontics aims to revive a dead tooth's inner tissue instead of just filling it. Success needs a delivery system that kills germs and feeds regeneration at once.

Their sponge, built from a ring-shaped sugar polymer, carries freeze-dried platelet concentrate from blood and a modified triple antibiotic paste. The paper measures the sponge's physical and chemical traits: size, loading, and release behavior. Those numbers decide whether the system can work inside a narrow root canal. The work is a materials step toward fillings that help teeth heal themselves.
pmc-13601220:
Leptin, a fat cell signal, runs far high in women than in men, and a top heart drug may shift it as it works. Zornitsa Shomanova and co-authors watch that shift in a 2026 study of seventy four adults with weak heart squeeze. Each adult starts the drug, a pair in one pill, and gives blood at start and at a later check.

Women's leptin ran near four times men's at the start, at much the same body mass. On the drug, leptin rose in both sexes. The size of the rise did not split by sex. Heart squeeze rose in both groups too. The team says sex sets the base level of leptin, but not the reply to the drug.
pmc-13602120:
Huang and co-authors reviewed the CCL2-CCR2 signaling axis, a chemical call-and-receptor pair that draws immune cells into lung tumors. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and spread, drug resistance, and a suppressive tumor environment drive that toll. This pathway recruits monocytes and other cells that help tumors grow blood vessels, invade, spread, and shrug off chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy.

The review maps how the signal links into major cancer pathways and notes rare settings where it seems to fight tumors instead. It then surveys treatments aimed at the axis, including receptor blockers and signal-neutralizing agents, plus combinations with immune checkpoint drugs. The authors judge the case for targeting the pathway strong but early: well-designed clinical trials are still needed before doctors can know whether blocking it helps patients.
pmc-13602420:
Hazem Elewa and four co-authors evaluate a pharmacist-led program that fine-tunes medications for Medicare patients in an accountable care group. Drug problems drive much avoidable spending on seniors. The program mixed genetic testing, a nine-factor risk score, full pharmacist review, and written advice to prescribers. Using matched comparisons on claims from 2022 to 2025, the study tracked 1,003 treated members against 14,031 similar controls.

Total medical costs fell 19.4 percent for treated members, about two hundred forty-six dollars per member per month. The saving deepened with time in the program, reaching 31.9 percent after nine months. Hospital admissions dropped forty-three percent, emergency visits forty-one percent, and outpatient visits twenty-eight percent. Checks on pre-trends and the steady dose-response support a real effect. The authors warn that short studies will badly underrate such programs.
pmc-13602820:
Ireneusz Sobolewski and four colleagues present an integrated lab system for engineering a heat-loving bacteriophage. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria, and TP-84 attacks Geobacillus stearothermophilus, a bacterium that thrives at high temperatures. Delivering a full phage genome into wall-stripped host cells, called protoplasts, had worked for plasmids but never for rebooting a whole phage. The team tuned cell density, enzyme levels, polymer type, and DNA dose until uptake became reliable.

With the tuned method, natural and fully synthetic TP-84 genomes entered protoplasts and restarted, producing infectious phage. A simplified single-layer agar step then yielded high-titer stocks and enough DNA for sequencing from one Petri dish. Recombinant variants also proved more stable grown this solid way than in liquid culture. The authors offer the combined workflow as a platform for rapidly building and testing engineered thermophilic phages.
pmc-13602920:
Daniel Conde-Torres, Rebeca García-Fandiño, and Ángel Piñeiro present a design model for helical peptides in this 2026 paper. Peptides at cell surfaces often work by fitting a chemical setting, a membrane or water, rather than by locking onto one target molecule. That taste for an environment can be programmed, if the rules are known.

The authors build a physics-based energy score for alpha-helical peptides. It blends helix-forming tendency, local sequence context, residue contacts, solvent exposure, and how membrane charges couple and screen. Scores are scaled against a random reference, so peptides of any length or setting compare fairly. In tests, the model sorts water-loving helices from membrane-spanning ones. It also flags known antimicrobial peptides as favored at charged membrane surfaces over plain water or neutral ones.
pmc-13603420:
Ottavia Avola and co-authors review child cases of a parasite disease in southern Italy in a 2026 study. Visceral leishmaniasis is spread by sand flies and attacks inner organs. Children in the Mediterranean region face high risk. An older drug class long counted as first-line care has grown scarce and raised safety worries, so a fat-wrapped drug, liposomal amphotericin B, has taken its place in practice.

Three referral centers in Catania shared records from 2016 to 2025. Nineteen children, with an average age near four, were treated. Long fever, low blood counts, and swollen liver and spleen were the main signs. All got the fat-wrapped drug, most on a two-day high-dose plan. Three children relapsed, and more of the same drug cured them, giving a full cure rate. No child got the older drugs at all.
pmc-13604420:
Ching-Chieh Lin and co-authors present a 2026 review on how the daily body clock and the hormone melatonin shape bone renewal. Bone is rebuilt in a rhythm, and melatonin has been cast as a messenger in that rhythm. The authors warn that many lab findings use doses far above what the body makes at night, so care is needed before drawing health claims.

Four databases were searched for work on melatonin, clock genes, and bone. In bone-forming cells, the hormone supports growth through one of its receptors and known signaling paths. Direct effects that block bone-eating cells, though, appear mostly at doses thousands of times above night levels. The review sorts which claims rest on receptors and which do not.
pmc-13604920:
Zaid Khoury and seven co-authors compared AI tools that write patient handouts in a 2026 study. Their test topic was children's mouth and jaw diseases, including rare tumors, where parents often find no readable material. The team pitted a new autonomous AI agent against leading chatbots.

Five systems, among them ChatGPT and Claude, produced information sheets on common childhood conditions and rare head and neck tumors. Three experts, not told which system wrote which sheet, scored them for quality, soundness, and how easy they were to understand and act on. Reading level was also graded. The authors say such head-to-head tests are needed before clinics trust AI-written handouts for worried families.
pmc-13605320:
Xuesong Liu and co-authors test an ultrasound method for stiff skin in a 2026 study. Systemic sclerosis is an immune disease that scars and hardens skin. Doctors grade skin involvement by touch, a rough scale. The team asked whether shear wave elastography, which measures stiffness with sound, could grade skin more exactly and tell patients from healthy people.

pmc-13627320:

pmc-13628220:

pmc-13631520:

pmc-13661820:
Taha Taka and co-authors count spine fractures after hormone-blocking therapy for prostate cancer. The treatment starves tumors but also bone, thinning vertebrae until they crumple. Matching treated men one-to-one with untreated patients, 122,511 per side, the team tracked compression fractures and the cement procedures that repair them over five years.

Fractures ran 1.95 percent in treated men against 1.29 percent in controls, a hazard ratio of 1.49, roughly one extra fracture per 143 men treated. Among those who fractured, cement augmentation was also half again as common after hormone therapy, while bigger fusion surgery and dependency rates matched. The authors press for bone screening and protection from day one of therapy.
pmc-13662220:
Yi-Heng Zhu and six colleagues present a 2026 bioinformatics paper on sorting raw DNA reads into species bins without assembling them first. Binning long reads directly would speed the recovery of microbial genomes from mixed samples, but methods struggle to guess the right number of bins and to learn good read representations. Their tool, DecBin, tackles both.

A variational autoencoder compresses each read, deep clustering groups them, and Bayesian optimization picks the bin count by a global quality score rather than guesswork. Clustering feedback also reshapes the learned representations as training proceeds. On simulated and mock communities, DecBin beat current tools at binning and genome recovery, and even resolved strains in a simple natural microbiome.
pmc-13669220:
Shih-Ching Huang and co-authors build copper sites that rebuild themselves to turn nitrate into ammonia in a 2026 study. The electric route promises a double win: clean nitrate-polluted water and make ammonia, a key fertilizer and fuel, without the usual fossil-heavy process. How the copper site's local wiring steers that rebuild across acidic and alkaline baths was not understood.

The team made two clean starting points, single copper atoms held by three nitrogen neighbors or by four. Live X-ray watching showed the four-nitrogen sites rebuilt fast in every bath, dropping to leaner shapes that favor the reaction. The three-nitrogen sites followed a different path. Linking the starting wiring to the rebuilt, working form gives catalyst designers a rule: pick the cage and you pick the worker it becomes.
pmc-13669320:
Elisabeth Piault and five co-authors present a framework for building remote monitoring tools into clinical trials, so patients can be watched from home instead of traveling to sites. Their blueprint starts from three directions at once: what patients need, what care teams need, and what regulators demand. They illustrate it with recent deployments that tracked skin toxicity and mouth sores in trial patients.

Remote monitoring promises richer data and lighter patient burden, but adoption stalls on practical problems: device burden, data overload, and trust in measurements made outside the clinic. The article walks through strategies for those obstacles, from choosing only measures that change decisions to easing patients into the tools. The authors write for trial designers weighing digital transformation, arguing that monitoring succeeds when the framework, not the gadget, leads. Their examples show the approach working in real oncology trial settings.
pmc-13671720:
A blood clot in the lungs is a medical emergency, and doctors need fast ways to judge how dangerous each case is. Ramazan Amanvermez and Fatih Çalışkan write to the editor in 2026 about one proposed shortcut: the EASIX index, built from routine lab values and meant to reflect damage to blood vessel linings.

The letter credits a recent study that linked high EASIX values to severe clots and deaths in hospital. It then presses points the study left thin: how the index connects to platelet and hemoglobin drops and to clotting test changes, and how emergency doctors would use it at the door. The writers ask for a clearer account of the vessel damage picture and of the index's place in first assessment.
pmc-13674320:
Sara Ho and co-authors test finger-prick style blood collection for Alzheimer's markers against vein blood and spinal fluid, in a 2026 study. Blood markers aid diagnosis, but vein draws need on-site processing. Two small skin devices that gather capillary blood could allow remote collection.

Patients at a Johns Hopkins centre gave all three sample types on the same visit. Both devices succeeded in most attempts and hurt far less than vein draws. Three markers from skin blood tracked vein values strongly. One tau marker tracked weakly, and skin values did not match spinal fluid for two markers. Age and one marker predicted match quality. The authors see promise for wider testing, with caveats.
pmc-13675320:
Surgery for laryngeal cancer can save a life while taking the voice and easy swallowing with it. Jing Liu, Gaiping Fan, and Wenjuan Li followed 120 patients for two years. Half got systematic voice training plus swallowing exercises, and half got routine care. The team compared voice handicap, swallowing scores, quality of life, and complications at 6, 12, and 24 months.

By one year the rehabilitation group was clearly ahead. Voice handicap scores were far lower, and swallowing problems hit 10 percent against 30. Quality-of-life scores were higher, complications less than half as frequent, and satisfaction well up. Adjusted analysis kept the training as an independent protective factor across voice, swallowing, and complications. The authors conclude that combined, structured rehabilitation should be standard after this surgery rather than an afterthought.
pmc-13675520:
Leandro Brito and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, whether the body's internal clock guides heart control as day turns to night. Melatonin rise in dim light marks the start of biological night. The team asked whether heart and blood pressure control shifts at that same moment.

Ten healthy adults, with an average age near 25, sat through a tightly controlled routine in very dim light.
