MINURSO, the UN team there, gained a year, to 30 April 2011. Both sides had to honor the truce pacts in full. Small, loose talks would pave a fifth round. Real will to deal was called for, on a base of give and take. Family visits, by land as well as air, won warm words. States were asked to fund such steps. The text is firm that the old standstill could not last for good.

How to cage the atom was the young UN's gravest task. Its Atomic Energy Commission sent a first report on the last day of 1946. The plan sketched world checks on the new force. Resolution 20 passed with no dissent on 10 March 1947. The Council had read the report with care.

No part of the plan bound a state on its own. Each vote of yes was a first step, not a last word. The full plan had to be taken as one whole. The record of the talks went back to the team. It was urged to press on with all speed. A draft treaty on world control was the goal. A second report was due before the Assembly next sat. Hope still ran high that the bomb could be ruled by law.

Cyprus still needed its United Nations peacekeeping force in the spring of 1966. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still required to keep the peace on the island. The government of Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 26 March 1966. The island's basic problem, though, remained unsolved. Resolution 220 was adopted unanimously on 16 March 1966.

The Council reaffirmed all its Cyprus resolutions, back to Resolution 186 of 1964. It urged everyone involved to show the utmost restraint. The force was extended for three more months, ending on 26 June 1966. The Council stated its firm hope that real progress toward a settlement would come within that period. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place while the search for a settlement went on.

Sanctions against Southern Rhodesia were being broken openly by 1972. Several states still traded with the illegal regime despite the mandatory embargo. The United States had reported that it authorized imports of Rhodesian chrome ore and other minerals. Resolution 320 was adopted on 29 September 1972.

The Council reaffirmed that the sanctions would stay fully in force. They would last until the goals of Resolution 253 of 1968 were met. All states were called on to apply the sanctions in full. The United States was urged to cooperate with the United Nations on enforcement. South Africa and Portugal were condemned for refusing to cooperate. The Council's sanctions committee was told to study stronger action as a matter of urgency.

The Golan Heights observer force received six more months on 30 November 1977, under Resolution 420. The force watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council noted the efforts made toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East. It also noted the urgent need to press on with those efforts. Tension in the area still prevailed.

The parties were called on to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text had demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another period of six months, until 31 May 1978. At the end of that time, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to carry out Resolution 338.

Lebanon's president-elect was murdered in September 1982, during Israel's invasion of the country. Bashir Gemayel, named in the text, had been elected to lead Lebanon. Days after his death, Israeli forces moved into Beirut in breach of the cease-fire. Resolution 520 was adopted on 17 September 1982.

The Council condemned the murder of the president-elect. It also condemned every effort to block, by violence, the return of a strong and stable government in Lebanon. Its resolutions on Lebanon from earlier in 1982 were reaffirmed in full. The Israeli incursions into Beirut were condemned. Israel was told to return its forces at once to the positions held before 15 September. The Council also backed the United Nations observers stationed around Beirut. Lebanon's sovereignty was to be respected, under the authority of its own army.

Resolution 620, adopted on 26 August 1988, returns to chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq war with harder evidence. Three missions sent by the Secretary-General that summer had confirmed continued poison gas use, and gas attacks on Iranians had grown fiercer and more often. The Council said it was deeply dismayed and worried about future use.

The Council condemned resolutely the use of chemical weapons in defiance of the 1925 Geneva Protocol and of its own demand that spring. It encouraged the Secretary-General to investigate new allegations from any member state quickly, with expert help. It also backed the Geneva disarmament talks then negotiating a total ban on developing, producing, and stockpiling chemical weapons, work that produced the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention.

Choosing a Secretary-General is among the Council's gravest tasks. In 1991 the members met behind closed doors to pick a successor to Javier Pérez de Cuéllar. Resolution 720 was adopted unanimously at that closed meeting on 21 November 1991. The question was the recommendation for the UN's top job.

The Council put forward Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt. His proposed term ran from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996. The General Assembly accepted the choice. Boutros-Ghali became the first African and first Arab to lead the UN. His tenure covered Somalia, Rwanda, and Bosnia. This one-line recommendation set all of that in motion.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s18-20:
Section 18.20 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers naming of subjects in agency regulations. The rule sits in a part on preparation and transmittal of documents generally. It is issued for the Federal Register system under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six.

Each agency that submits a document for the Rules or Proposed Rules sections of the Federal Register must act, the rule states. It must include a list of index terms for the document. Those terms name the subjects the rule touches, so readers can find it. Indexing is thus made part of the filing duty, not an afterthought by the publisher.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-20: Section 21.20 of Title 1 of the federal rules sets rules for change documents. It sits in the part on documents bound for the rule book. Each document that changes a rule must name the unit it changes. It must do so in clear and full terms in the text. It must also state how far the changes it makes run. The number and head of each section changed must be set out. They must be set out in full on a line of their own.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-20:
Section 304.20 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations is a general clause on a set of privacy rules. It sits in Part 304, on the release of records, for the Administrative Conference of the United States. The subpart holds the rules that the agency keeps under the Privacy Act of 1974. Those rules deal with the guard of records about men and women. They also deal with the right of a man to the use of such records.

The rules are to be read with the Privacy Act, and they are ruled by that act. The act gives more facts about records kept on men and women. The rules in the subpart apply to all records in the Privacy Act sets of the agency.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-20:
Section 601.20 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations orders the National Capital Planning Commission to keep impact statements lean. It sits in Part 601, the part that carries out the National Environmental Policy Act. As lead agency the Commission must use all means at hand to cut the length of such a statement.

Named means include writing in clear, brief language and keeping the work focused on study, not bulk. Stress on background facts is to be cut down. The scoping process is to lift up weighty issues and play down slight ones. Facts may be brought in by reference rather than reprinted. A broad program statement with tiering can spare repeat work in later statements. The set format rules of a sister section are also to be followed.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1820:
Section 1820 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers buying real property for the Capitol Police. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on the Architect of the Capitol. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. The Architect, not the police force itself, holds the buying power.

Subject to approval by two named bodies, the Architect may acquire property for the Capitol Police. Those bodies are a House commission and a Senate committee. The purchase may be by purchase, lease, or transfer from another holder. That approval gate keeps a major land step under direct congressional oversight.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6320:
Section 6320 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers purchase of office equipment by senators who leave office. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the rules for Senate members, expenses, and allowances. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It lets a departing senator buy gear from his or her own office.

Despite any other provision of law, a senator may purchase office equipment or furnishings upon leaving office. The same right applies when a person otherwise stops being a senator, except by expulsion. Conditions on such purchases are set in the section. The rule gives a lawful path for keepsakes and work gear, rather than informal taking.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6620:
Section 6620 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the grant of services and gear by the Sergeant at Arms. It sits in Chapter 65, on Senate officers. With the grant of the Committee on Rules and Administration, that officer may give services and gear to men and bodies not paid for by Senate funds. The services and gear in view are those paid for by funds free for the Senate.

A second clause sets a bar on such grants. The grant of services and gear is to be on a base of pay-back. A third clause deals with the sums so won back. For services or gear bought with funds free for that officer, a rule is set for those sums. That rule is cut off in the text shown here.
vinogradoff-outlines-historical-jurispru:
Vinogradoff began his Outlines of Historical Jurisprudence with a first volume in 1920. The Oxford jurist, born in Russia and formed by several legal traditions, planned a survey of law's whole history. The Outlines were to be his synthesis, the fruit of a lifetime spent comparing legal systems.

Volume 1 begins with the ancient world: law born of custom, kingship, and the needs of early states. He moves from the Near East through Greece to the Rome of the emperors, tracing how legal ideas travel and change. Vinogradoff writes as a comparatist, always asking what one system's solution teaches about another's. The wide-ranging survey opens his grand design with characteristic calm. Few scholars of any age could have attempted the whole history of law in two volumes and carried it off.
wallas-human-nature-politics-1920:
Graham Wallas founded political psychology with Human Nature in Politics, first issued in 1908. The text here is the third edition of 1920, from Project Gutenberg. Older political thought pictured voters as reasoning machines, weighing each claim. Wallas, a Fabian socialist and teacher, found that picture false to life.

Impulse, habit, party symbols, and crowd feeling move real politics, he argues. Statesmen work with human nature as it is, not as theory wishes. His chapters urge honest study of how opinions actually form. The book opened a field that now studies campaigns and media. Its calm tone hides its radical break. Politicians ignore it at their cost.
wegener-entstehung-kontinente-1920:
Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, argued that continents slowly drift across the globe. His book The Origin of Continents and Oceans, shown here in German, first appeared in 1915 and grew in later editions. The 1920 text states his case in full.

Wegener points to matching coastlines, matching fossils, and matching rock layers on lands now split by oceans. South America and Africa, he says, were once joined. Most geologists mocked him, since he could not name the force that moves continents. Plate tectonics later proved the drift itself was real. Later finds on the ocean floor at last gave drift its engine.
wharton-age-of-innocence-1920:
Edith Wharton published The Age of Innocence in 1920, her novel of 1870s New York and its rigid codes. The tale tells Newland Archer's doomed love for the Countess Olenska inside that shuttered, tribal world. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, the first awarded to a woman for a novel in America.

Archer, engaged to May Welland, is shaken by her cousin Ellen, returned from a scandalous marriage in Europe alone. Ellen's freedom exposes the cruelty and fear beneath his tribe's polished manners, dinners, and opera boxes in old New York. Archer chooses duty, weds May, and lives a respectable life haunted by the road not taken with Ellen. Decades later, in Paris, he sits below her window and sends his son up alone at dusk. Wharton's archaeology of her parents' world is tender, ironic, and quietly devastating in its close.
whitbourne-discovery-newfoundland-1620:
Richard Whitbourne, a Devon sea captain, wrote A Discovery of New-found-land in 1620 to promote English settlement there. He knew the island from years of fishing voyages. His tract praises the colony's wealth in cod, timber, and safe harbors for ships.

Whitbourne also reports a famous sight. He describes a mermaid that swam up to his boat and looked at the crew. That account became the classic English colonial mermaid story. The wonder sits atop a practical sales pitch for Newfoundland. Whitbourne hoped marvels and profit together would draw settlers and backers across the Atlantic.
whitehead-concept-nature-1920:
Alfred North Whitehead published The Concept of Nature in 1920, based on his Tarner Lectures at Cambridge. Whitehead asks what we mean by nature in modern science. He argues that nature is a process of events, not a set of static objects. Sense awareness, he says, shows passage and relation first of all.

He rejects the split between nature as sensed and nature as cause of sense. Points, moments, and objects are abstractions from the flow of events. The book laid groundwork for his later process philosophy. It also influenced modern philosophy of science. Readers meet Whitehead's key ideas here in compact form.
williams-kora-in-hell-1920:
Kora in Hell, published in 1920, is Williams's book of improvisations: short prose pieces written fast, day by day, during the war years. Kora is Persephone, the maiden carried to the underworld, and hell here is the modern world at war.

Each improvisation leaps from image to image, a doctor's day, a patient's face, spring fought out of winter, with commentaries that explain and argue with the text. Williams was testing how far spontaneity could carry meaning. The result is uneven, electric, and very personal. It is the first sounding of the American grain he would explore for decades.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol20:
With Volume XX in 1880, the Journal of Discourses entered its fourth decade of printed sermons. Liverpool still printed the set, and shorthand reporters still caught the words as they were spoken in Utah. Speakers include senior apostles and other elders, preaching to a church now led from the Twelve after Young's death.

Two decades of volumes behind it give this one a settled, archival feel for any reader. The talks instruct, correct, and encourage in the familiar pulpit voice of the movement at work. Volume XX adds a round number to the running doctrinal record of nineteenth-century Mormonism, with six volumes yet to come.
